datasets.name: 7th_graders
datasets.description:
A small multiplex network of social relations among the 29 students of a seventh-grade class in a school in Victoria, Australia, collected by M. Vickers. Students were asked to nominate their classmates on several relations, of which three form the layers of this network: who they get on with in the class (`get_on_with`), who their best friends in the class are (`best_friends`), and who they would prefer to work with (`work_with`). A directed edge $i \to j$ in a given layer means that student $i$ nominated student $j$ for that relation. The data were made available as a multiplex network by M. De Domenico.

Nodes are numbered from 0 to 28 (corresponding to students 1 to 29 in the original data); students 1 to 12 are boys, and 13 to 29 are girls.

The network has the following properties:

- (Edge) `layer`: the relation (1: get on with, 2: best friends, 3: work with; the names are stored in the graph property `layer_key`).
- (Edge) `weight`: which is always 1 (the upstream data are unweighted).
citations: M. Vickers and S. Chan, "Representing Classroom Social Structure." Melbourne: Victoria Institute of Secondary Education, (1981).

datasets.name: a_blue_start
datasets.description:
The starter packs of the social network Bluesky, from the dataset "A Blue Start" of Hasegawa Smith, Amburg, Kumar, Foucault Welles and Landry: all starter packs available on Bluesky in late October 2025 (retrieved until November 16, 2025). A starter pack is a list of 6 to 150 users (and feeds) curated by any user, which other users can follow with a single click. The network is bipartite: its nodes are users and starter packs, and an edge connects each starter pack with each user listed in it. The users and starter packs are identified by anonymized ids (non-reversible hashes of their identifiers, DIDs).

The dataset of the authors also contains the follow network of the users (26.7 million users), which is available only from SOMAR/ICPSR with a data use agreement, and is not part of this entry; the starter packs were published openly on Zenodo, in the HIF format for higher-order networks (users as nodes, starter packs as sets).

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `is_starter_pack`: whether the node is a starter pack (otherwise a user).
- (Node) `user_id`: the anonymized id of the user (-1 for starter packs).
- (Node) `pack_id`: the anonymized id of the starter pack (-1 for users).
- (Node) `created`: the date of creation of the user account or of the starter pack (Unix time).
- (Node) `active` (users): whether the account is active.
- (Node) `status` (users): the status of the account (e.g. `normal`, `deactivated`, `takendown`).
- (Node) `creator_id` (starter packs): the id of the user who created it (-1 if unknown).
- (Edge) `time`: the date on which the user was added to the starter pack (Unix time; -1 if unknown).
citations: A. Hasegawa Smith, I. Amburg, S. Kumar, B. Foucault Welles, N. W. Landry, "A Blue Start: A large-scale pairwise and higher-order social network dataset." Scientific Data 13, 585 (2026)

datasets.name: academia_edu
datasets.description:
A snapshot of the follower network among users of Academia.edu, a platform where academics share their papers and follow the research of other academics. Nodes are users, and a directed edge $i \to j$ means that user $i$ follows user $j$. The data were collected (around 2011) and anonymized by M. Fire and collaborators at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, and used as one of the social networks in their study of link prediction.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the anonymized user identifier.
citations: M. Fire et al. "Computationally Efficient Link Prediction in a Variety of Social Networks." ACM Transactions on Intelligent Systems and Technology 5(1), Article 10 (2013)

datasets.name: accounting_firm
datasets.description:
Work and social ties among the 24 members of a small accounting firm, collected by C. M. Webster in 1991 and 1992 to compare observed and reported relational data: six were partners in the firm, three were managers, nine were staff accountants and six were support staff. Social interactions were observed by ad libitum sampling in a wide range of settings, and work assignment sheets were used to determine who had worked with whom. Then each individual was asked to report with whom he or she had socialized and worked. The data were distributed by L. C. Freeman on his network data page at the University of California, Irvine (no longer online), from which this version was obtained via the Internet Archive.

Nodes are the members of the firm. The four relations are given as separate networks, in which an edge connects two members who were observed to interact socially or to work together (undirected), or a directed edge (i, j) indicates that member i reported socializing or working with member j:

- `observed_social`: observed social interactions, undirected.
- `observed_work`: observed work together, from the work assignment sheets, undirected.
- `reported_social`: socializing reported by i about j, directed.
- `reported_work`: work reported by i with j, directed.

The values of the matrices are not documented. The observed relations have nonzero diagonal values, which are represented as self-loops.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `sex` (1: male, 2: female).
- (Node) `job` (1: partner, 2: manager, 3: accountant, 4: staff member).
- (Edge) `weight`: the value of the relation (integers).
citations: C. M. Webster, "Detecting context-based constraints in social perception." Journal of Quantitative Anthropology 5, 285-303 (1995)
C. M. Webster, "Task-related and context-based constraints in observed and reported relational data." Doctoral dissertation, University of California, Irvine (1993)

datasets.name: acl_anthology
datasets.description:
Citations and authorships of the papers of the ACL Anthology, the digital archive of the publications in computational linguistics and natural language processing (the journals, conferences and workshops of the Association for Computational Linguistics and related organizations), from the ACL OCL corpus of S. Rohatgi et al. The corpus covers the 73,285 papers of the Anthology up to September 2022, with their metadata from the Anthology, and their references from Semantic Scholar, which identifies the papers (cited or citing) with its corpus identifiers.

- `acl`: the citation network among the papers of the Anthology: a directed edge goes from a paper to a paper of the Anthology that it cites.
- `full`: the citations to and from the papers of the Anthology, including those of papers outside the Anthology (citing papers of the Anthology, or cited by them), known only by their Semantic Scholar identifier. Citations between two papers outside the Anthology are not included.

The citation networks include only the papers with at least one citation in these tables (64,185 papers of the Anthology in `acl`, 68,241 in `full`).
- `authorship`: the undirected bipartite network of the authors and all the papers of the Anthology (including a few hundred without authors in the data), where an edge links a paper to each of its authors. Authors are identified by their names as written in the BibTeX records of the Anthology (as "Last, First", with the LaTeX markup of accented letters), which the Anthology partly normalizes; different persons with the same name are merged, and the same person under different spellings is split.

In the upstream citation tables, every citation between two papers of the Anthology appears twice (as identical rows); it is included once here. A few hundred citations appear twice with different identifiers (as different references of the citing paper) and give parallel edges. The abstracts and full texts of the papers (extracted with GROBID), and the topic labels of the corpus (given only for a part of the papers, in Python pickle files), are left out.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `s2_id` (citation networks): the Semantic Scholar corpus identifier of the paper (its page is `https://api.semanticscholar.org/CorpusID:<s2_id>`).
- (Node) `is_acl` (`full`): whether the paper belongs to the ACL Anthology (the following properties are empty, or -1, for those that do not).
- (Node) `is_paper` (`authorship`): whether the node is a paper (otherwise it is an author).
- (Node) `name`: the title of the paper (with the LaTeX markup of the BibTeX record), or the name of the author.
- (Node) `acl_id`: the identifier of the paper in the Anthology (its page is `https://aclanthology.org/<acl_id>`).
- (Node) `year`: the year of publication.
- (Node) `month`: the month of publication, as given (e.g. `August`).
- (Node) `venue`: the proceedings (book title) or the journal in which the paper appeared.
- (Node) `entry_type`: the BibTeX entry type (e.g. `inproceedings`, `article`).
- (Node) `publisher`, `doi`, `url`: the publisher, the DOI, and the URL of the paper (e.g. its PDF).
- (Node) `num_cited_by`: the number of citations of the paper according to Semantic Scholar (in September 2022), counting all citing papers.
- (Edge) `id` (citation networks): the Semantic Scholar identifier of the citation.
citations: S. Rohatgi, Y. Qin, B. Aw, N. Unnithan, M.-Y. Kan, "The ACL OCL Corpus: Advancing Open Science in Computational Linguistics." Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, 10348-10361 (2023)

datasets.name: actor_movie
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of movies and the actors who appeared in them, extracted from the Internet Movie Database (IMDb) and distributed by the network research group of A.-L. Barabási (then at the University of Notre Dame). Nodes are movies and actors, and an edge connects an actor to a movie in which the actor appeared. These are the data used by A.-L. Barabási and R. Albert to construct the movie actor collaboration network (two actors are connected if they were cast together in the same movie), one of the networks for which they reported a power-law degree distribution. The source file lists the actors of each movie, with actors identified by numbers. It contains 127,823 movies and 383,640 actors, connected by 1,470,404 appearances; 14 actors listed twice for the same movie are included only once, so there are no multiple edges. Nodes are anonymous (no names are given).

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `is_actor`: whether the node is an actor (otherwise it is a movie).
- (Node) `id`: the number of the actor in the source file, or the line number of the movie (starting at 0).
citations: A.-L. Barabási and R. Albert, "Emergence of scaling in random networks." Science 286(5439), 509-512 (1999).

datasets.name: add_health
datasets.description:
Directed friendship networks among students in 84 communities in the United States, from the in-school questionnaire of the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent Health (Add Health), administered in 1994–95 to 90,118 students in grades 7 to 12. Each community consists of one high school, and in some cases also of a "sister" school (typically a feeder junior high school); each community is a separate network (`comm1` to `comm84`). The networks were prepared by J. Moody.

Each student was given a paper-and-pencil questionnaire and a roster of all students in the school (and in the sister school, if any), and was asked to list up to five closest male friends and up to five closest female friends, in order of closeness. For each nominated friend, the student indicated in which of five activities they had participated together: visiting the friend's house in the last seven days; meeting after school to hang out in the last seven days; spending time together last weekend; talking about a problem in the last seven days; and talking on the telephone in the last seven days. A directed edge $i \to j$ means that student $i$ nominated student $j$ as a friend. Since nominations across schools were allowed, the networks are given at the community level.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `sex` (1: male, 2: female, 0: unreported).
- (Node) `race` (1: white, 2: black, 3: hispanic, 4: asian, 5: mixed/other, 0: unreported).
- (Node) `grade`: the school grade (7 to 12, 0: unreported).
- (Node) `school`: the school (0 or 1) within the community, only for communities with two schools. Node attributes are missing for community 48.
- (Edge) `activities`: the tie value, equal to one plus the number of the five activities the student reported doing with the friend (from 1, a nomination with no reported activities, to 6, all five activities).
citations: J. Moody. "Peer influence groups: Identifying dense clusters in large networks." Social Networks 23(4), 261-283 (2001)

datasets.name: adjnoun
datasets.description:
A network of adjacencies between common adjectives and nouns in the novel "David Copperfield" by Charles Dickens, compiled by M. E. J. Newman. Nodes are the 112 most commonly occurring adjectives and nouns in the book, and an undirected edge connects two words if they occur in adjacent positions anywhere in the text. Since in English adjectives typically precede nouns, the network is approximately bipartite, and it has been used as a test case for community detection and for detecting disassortative structure.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `label`: the word.
- (Node) `value`: the word class (0 for adjectives, 1 for nouns).
citations: M.E.J. Newman, "Finding community structure in networks using the eigenvectors of matrices." Phys. Rev. E 74, 036104 (2006).

datasets.name: advogato
datasets.description:
A network of trust relationships among users of Advogato, an online community platform for free software developers launched in 1999. On Advogato, users certify each other at one of the levels Apprentice, Journeyer and Master, and these certifications are used by the site's trust metric to compute the users' own levels; a certification at the level Observer is equivalent to no trust. Advogato published the whole certification graph at www.advogato.org/person/graph.dot, and the Trustlet project (P. Massa and collaborators) downloaded a daily snapshot of it between 2007 and 2014 (together with older snapshots from 2000 onwards). This network is the last such snapshot, taken on 7 July 2014.

Nodes are all users listed in the file, including those who neither give nor receive any certification (almost half of them), and a directed edge from $i$ to $j$ means that user $i$ certified user $j$. Users can certify themselves, so the network has self-loops, and the source file lists 15 certifications twice.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the Advogato user name.
- (Edge) `level`: the certification level (Observer, Apprentice, Journeyer or Master).
- (Edge) `weight`: the numerical trust value 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 or 1.0 of these levels, following the mapping suggested by Trustlet for the last three.
citations: P. Massa, M. Salvetti, and D. Tomasoni. "Bowling alone and trust decline in social network sites." Dependable, Autonomic and Secure Computing, 2009. DASC'09. Eighth IEEE International Conference on. (2009).

datasets.name: aids_blogs
datasets.description:
The pattern of links among 146 blogs related to AIDS, patients, and their support networks, collected by S. Gopal over a randomly selected three-day period in August 2005. This version was distributed with the R package `sand`, accompanying the book "Statistical Analysis of Network Data with R" by E. D. Kolaczyk and G. Csárdi, where it is used as an example.

A directed edge (i, j) indicates that blog i links to blog j in its "blogroll" (list of recommended blogs). Blog names are not included.
citations: S. Gopal, "The evolving social geography of blogs." In H. J. Miller (ed.), Societies and Cities in the Age of Instant Access, 275-293, Springer (2007)
E. D. Kolaczyk, G. Csárdi, "Statistical Analysis of Network Data with R", 2nd edition, Springer (2020)

datasets.name: air500
datasets.description:
Directed network of scheduled flight connections among the 500 airports of the world with the largest total passenger volume, from J. Marcelino and M. Kaiser, who used it in a metapopulation model of the spreading of influenza A (H1N1) over the airline network. The connections were extracted from the scheduled flight data of OAG Aviation Solutions for one year (flights operating from July 1, 2007 to June 30, 2008; 1,341,615 records, estimated by OAG to cover 99% of commercial flights), after removing short-distance links corresponding to rail, boat, bus or limousine connections. Nodes are airports, identified by their IATA codes, and an edge connects two airports if at least one scheduled flight connected them in the period. The source adjacency matrix is not symmetric (about 9% of the connections are listed in only one direction); following the usual convention, the entry $(i, j)$ is taken as an edge from airport $i$ to airport $j$ (the convention is not stated explicitly with the data). Only the network among the top 500 airports is distributed, since the complete OAG data set, with all airports and traffic volumes, is proprietary.

The nodes have the property `name`, the IATA code of the airport (e.g. "FRA", "JFK").
citations: J. Marcelino, M. Kaiser, "Critical paths in a metapopulation model of H1N1: Efficiently delaying influenza spreading through flight cancellation." PLoS Currents 4, e4f8c9a2e1fca8 (2012)

datasets.name: airports_struc2vec
datasets.description:
Three networks of airports connected by commercial flights in 2016, collected by Ribeiro et al. to evaluate the struc2vec node embedding method, as distributed in their repository:

- `brazil`: airports of Brazil, from the data of the National Civil Aviation Agency (ANAC), from January to December 2016;
- `europe`: airports of Europe, from the data of Eurostat, from January to November 2016;
- `usa`: airports of the USA, from the data of the Bureau of Transportation Statistics, from January to October 2016.

An undirected edge connects two airports if there were commercial flights between them during the period. Each airport is labeled with its level of activity, by the quartiles of its distribution in each network (so that the four classes have the same size): the number of landings plus takeoffs (Brazil and Europe), or the number of passengers who arrived or departed (USA). The edges are as in the files: `brazil` has 71 self-loops, and `europe` 2; the numbers of edges thus differ slightly from those stated in the paper (1,038 for Brazil). The data do not identify the airports, except presumably for `usa`, whose node identifiers look like the airport identifiers of the Bureau of Transportation Statistics.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `id`: the identifier of the airport in the source data.
- (Node) `activity`: the activity class of the airport, from 0 (the 25% most active airports) to 3 (the 25% least active ones); the order is not stated by the source, but is evident from the degrees of the airports in each class.
citations: L. F. R. Ribeiro, P. H. P. Saverese, D. R. Figueiredo, "struc2vec: Learning Node Representations from Structural Identity." Proceedings of the 23rd ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining, 385-394 (2017)

datasets.name: alaska_subsistence
datasets.description:
Multiplex, directed and weighted networks of the flows of subsistence-related goods and services among households in three remote Alaska Native communities exposed to climate change and industrial development: Kaktovik (`kaktovik`; the upstream file is named "Kaktovi"), Venetie (`venetie`) and Wainwright (`wainwright`). The data was collected in in-person socio-economic surveys of the heads of household in 2009 and 2010, which covered 70 of the 85 households of Kaktovik, 84 of 89 in Venetie and 146 of 156 in Wainwright.

Nodes are households or crews, and also other sources of resources, such as organizations; they are identified only by anonymous numbers. Each layer corresponds to a pair of a resource (7 to 10 core resources in each community, such as caribou, bowhead whale, beluga, moose, seal, ducks, geese or berries) and a social relation through which it flows (7 to 10 kinds, such as sharing or trading), giving 37 layers in Kaktovik, 43 in Venetie and 36 in Wainwright. A directed edge from one node to another in a layer represents the flow of the resource through the social relation, in the direction given in the source file (from the first to the second node), weighted by the value of the flow; according to the paper, the wild food data was converted to edible pounds, but how the other flows were converted is not stated. The layers are numbered only: the names of the layers (resource-relation pairs) are not included in the upstream data, and the mapping of the numbers to the resource and relation codes of the paper is not available.

The source files also contain interlayer edges, which connect every node to itself in every pair (in both directions) of the layers in which it has edges, all with the same weight in each community (163.8675568 in `kaktovik`, 58.2647048 in `venetie`, 252.8067854 in `wainwright`). They carry no information beyond the layers in which each node is active, and are not included here; their weight is stored as the graph property `interlayer_weight`. A few node pairs are listed twice in the same layer and direction (38 in `kaktovik`, 14 in `venetie`, 29 in `wainwright`), sometimes with different weights; both edges are kept. The nodes are numbered from 1 to 164, 206 and 218, respectively, as in the source; in each community one of these numbers does not appear in any edge, and the corresponding node is isolated.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `node_id`: the anonymous number of the node in the source.
- (Edge) `layer`: the number of the layer (resource-relation pair), from 1 to the number of layers.
- (Edge) `weight`: the value of the flow.
- (Graph) `interlayer_weight`: the weight of the interlayer edges of the source, which are not included.
citations: J. A. Baggio, S. B. BurnSilver, A. Arenas, J. S. Magdanz, G. P. Kofinas, M. De Domenico, "Multiplex social ecological network analysis reveals how social changes affect community robustness more than resource depletion." Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 113(48), 13708-13713 (2016)

datasets.name: allset_3d_objects
datasets.description:
Bipartite networks of 3D object models and their nearest-neighbor groups in a feature space, as compiled by Chien et al. as benchmarks for node classification, following the construction of Feng et al. (2019). The objects come from two collections of 3D shapes: ModelNet40, a set of computer-aided design (CAD) models of common objects (such as airplanes, chairs and cars) collected from the web by Wu et al. and classified into 40 categories, and the NTU 3D model dataset of Chen et al. (in the version known as NTU2012, with 67 categories). According to Chien et al., the objects are described by visual features extracted from rendered views of the models with the Multi-View Convolutional Neural Network (MVCNN) and the Group-View Convolutional Neural Network (GVCNN). For each object, a group was formed consisting of the object and its four nearest neighbors in feature space (the source does not state exactly which features were used for this), so that every group has exactly five objects and every object is the center of exactly one group. Nodes are objects and groups, and an edge connects each group to each of its five member objects (including its center). Groups centered on different objects can have the same members; they are kept as separate nodes. The groups cannot be reproduced from the 100-dimensional features included in the data, which were presumably derived differently (how they were obtained is not documented).

- `modelnet40`: 12,311 objects from ModelNet40, in 40 categories, and their 12,311 groups (of which 10,630 have distinct sets of members).
- `ntu2012`: 2,012 objects from the NTU dataset, in 67 categories, and their 2,012 groups (of which 1,635 have distinct sets of members).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `is_neighborhood`: whether the node is a group (otherwise it is an object). Objects are the nodes 0 to n-1, in the order of the source data, and groups the nodes n to 2n-1.
- (Node) `label` (objects): the category of the object, as an integer index (1 to 40 for `modelnet40` and 0 to 66 for `ntu2012`, as in the source); the category names are not included in the source data.
- (Node) `features` (objects): the 100-dimensional feature vector of the object, as given in the source data.
- (Node) `center` (groups): the index of the object node on which the group is centered. This is inferred from the order of the groups in the source data: the i-th group always contains the i-th object, which is consistent with groups being listed in the order of their centers.
- (Node) Object nodes have `center` set to -1, and group nodes have `label` set to -1 and empty `features`.
citations: E. Chien, C. Pan, J. Peng, O. Milenkovic, "You are AllSet: A Multiset Function Framework for Hypergraph Neural Networks." International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR) (2022)
Y. Feng, H. You, Z. Zhang, R. Ji, Y. Gao, "Hypergraph Neural Networks." Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence 33(01), 3558-3565 (2019)

Z. Wu, S. Song, A. Khosla, F. Yu, L. Zhang, X. Tang, J. Xiao, "3D ShapeNets: A deep representation for volumetric shapes." 2015 IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), 1912-1920 (2015)
D.-Y. Chen, X.-P. Tian, Y.-T. Shen, M. Ouhyoung, "On Visual Similarity Based 3D Model Retrieval." Computer Graphics Forum 22(3), 223-232 (2003)

datasets.name: amazon_book_similarity
datasets.description: A directed network of similarities among books sold by the Amazon store, collected in 2008 and distributed by the Laboratory for Web Algorithmics (LAW). The data were obtained with SimilarityLookup queries to the Amazon E-Commerce Service API, which return, for a given product, a list of products that Amazon considers similar to it. Nodes are books, and a directed edge from one book to another indicates that the second is listed among the books similar to the first. The network has 735,323 books and 5,158,388 edges. Nodes are anonymous (no book identifiers are distributed), and edges are unweighted (no similarity scores are given).
citations: P. Boldi and S. Vigna, "The WebGraph framework I: compression techniques." Proceedings of the 13th International Conference on World Wide Web (WWW 2004), 595-602 (2004).

P. Boldi, M. Rosa, M. Santini, and S. Vigna, "Layered label propagation: a multiresolution coordinate-free ordering for compressing social networks." Proceedings of the 20th International Conference on World Wide Web (WWW 2011), 587-596 (2011).

datasets.name: amazon_coauthor_shchur
datasets.description:
Four networks introduced by Shchur et al. as benchmarks for node classification, as distributed in their repository:

- `amazon_computers` and `amazon_photo`: products of the categories "Computers" and "Camera & Photo" of Amazon, from the Amazon product data of McAuley et al. (2015). A directed edge from product A to product B means that B is listed among the products frequently bought together with A (the relation is not symmetric in the data: about a third of the pairs are listed in both directions, and there is one self-loop in `amazon_photo`). Each product is labeled with its subcategory (e.g. "Laptops" or "Lenses").
- `coauthor_cs` and `coauthor_physics`: authors of papers in computer science and in physics, from the Microsoft Academic Graph of the KDD Cup 2016 challenge. Two authors are connected by an undirected edge if they co-authored a paper. Each author is described by the keywords of their papers, and labeled with their most active field of study (for `coauthor_physics`, the journal of the Physical Review in which they publish most).

The benchmarks use only the largest connected component of each network (treating the edges as undirected), but the files include all the nodes, which are kept here. The node features of the Amazon networks (bag-of-words encodings of the product reviews, without the words) are left out, as are the product identifiers, which are not given.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `category` (Amazon networks): the subcategory of the product.
- (Node) `mag_id` (co-authorship networks): the identifier of the author in the Microsoft Academic Graph (in hexadecimal, as given).
- (Node) `field` (co-authorship networks): the most active field of study of the author (for `coauthor_physics`, a journal, e.g. `phys rev b`).
- (Node) `keywords` (co-authorship networks): the keywords of the author's papers.
- (Node) `keyword_counts` (co-authorship networks): the count given for each keyword in `keywords` (presumably the number of the author's papers with that keyword).
citations: O. Shchur, M. Mumme, A. Bojchevski, S. Günnemann, "Pitfalls of Graph Neural Network Evaluation." Relational Representation Learning Workshop (R2L 2018), NeurIPS 2018 (2018)

J. McAuley, C. Targett, Q. Shi, A. van den Hengel, "Image-based recommendations on styles and substitutes." Proceedings of the 38th International ACM SIGIR Conference on Research and Development in Information Retrieval, 43-52 (2015)

datasets.name: amazon_copurchases
citations: J. Leskovec, L. Adamic and B. Huberman. "The Dynamics of Viral Marketing." ACM Transactions on the Web (ACM TWEB), 1 (2007)

datasets.name: amazon_ratings
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of users and products on Amazon.com. Each user connects to all products they have rated. Edge weight denotes the rating score, and edges are timestamped.[^icon]
[^icon]: Description obtained from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.
citations: E. Lim, et al. "Detecting product review spammers using rating behaviors." Proc. of 19th ACM Internat. Conf. on Info. and Know. Management (CIKM 2010).

datasets.name: amazon_reviews
datasets.description:
Bipartite networks of reviewers and products derived from the Amazon review data collected by J. Ni, J. Li and J. McAuley ([source](https://nijianmo.github.io/amazon/index.html)), which contains product reviews (with ratings, text and product metadata) from the Amazon online store, spanning May 1996 to October 2018. The networks were assembled by A. R. Benson and collaborators. Reviewers and products are anonymized and given only as integer indices.

- `reviews`: products and the users who reviewed them, built from the "5-core" subsets of the data, in which, for each of the 29 product categories, only the users and products with at least five reviews in that category were kept. Each user is connected to every product they reviewed. The 33 products listed in the source data without any reviewer were removed.
- `music_blues`: reviewers of music products tagged "regional blues" (a subset of vinyl records), grouped by time and sub-genre. The reviews were split into calendar months, and for each month and each sub-genre (e.g. "Chicago Blues") there is a group node connected to all users who reviewed a product of that sub-genre during that month. The same sub-genre can therefore give rise to many groups, and identical sets of users can appear in several groups. The reviews span the years 1998 to 2018, but the month of each group is not given in the source data. Users who belong to no group were removed.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `is_user` (`reviews`): whether the node is a user (otherwise a product).
- (Node) `category` (`reviews`): the product category (e.g. "Appliances", "Video_Games"; empty for users).
- (Node) `is_group` (`music_blues`): whether the node is a group of users who reviewed products of a given sub-genre in a given month (otherwise a user).
- (Node) `genre` (`music_blues`): the blues sub-genre of the group (empty for users).
citations: J. Ni, J. Li, J. McAuley, "Justifying Recommendations using Distantly-Labeled Reviews and Fine-Grained Aspects." Proceedings of the 2019 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing and the 9th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing (EMNLP-IJCNLP), 188-197 (2019)

N. Veldt, A. R. Benson, J. Kleinberg, "Minimizing Localized Ratio Cut Objectives in Hypergraphs." Proceedings of the 26th ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery & Data Mining, 1708-1718 (2020)
I. Amburg, N. Veldt, A. R. Benson, "Diverse and Experienced Group Discovery via Hypergraph Clustering." Proceedings of the 2022 SIAM International Conference on Data Mining (SDM), 145-153 (2022)

datasets.name: amazon_webbase
datasets.description:
A small web graph of pages of the amazon.com domain (and of related domains, such as images-amazon.com), obtained by Šubelj and Bajec from the Stanford WebBase project, a repository of web crawls. Nodes are web pages (and other web resources, such as style sheets), and an undirected edge represents a hyperlink between two pages (the direction of the hyperlinks was discarded); repeated edges and self-loops are present, as in the source data. How the pages were sampled from the crawl is not documented. A large group of the pages are product pages of musical instruments of different brands.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `url`: the URL of the page (without the protocol prefix).
citations: L. Šubelj, M. Bajec, "Ubiquitousness of link-density and link-pattern communities in real-world networks." The European Physical Journal B 85, 32 (2012)

datasets.name: ambassador
datasets.description:
Networks of relations among 16 individuals directly or indirectly involved in the bombing of the residence of the Philippine ambassador in Jakarta, Indonesia, on 1 August 2000. The data are part of the John Jay & ARTIS Transnational Terrorism Database (JJATT), assembled by S. Atran and collaborators from open sources such as court documents and news reports, and were distributed in the UCINET covert networks collection.

Nodes are individuals, and an undirected edge connects two individuals who had a relation (in a given time period, or of a given kind); there are several such networks on the same set of nodes:

- `1985_1989`, `1990_1994`, `1995_1999` and `2000` to `2007`: the relations existing during each time period. The edge `weight` takes values 1 to 3 and encodes the strength of the tie; the exact coding is not documented in the source files (in other JJATT networks, 1 denotes acquaintances or distant family, 2 friends or moderately close family, and 3 close friends, family or tight-knit operational cliques). The source also contains a file for 2001, which is identical to the one for 2000 (including the weights), and is therefore omitted; the network `2000` thus also describes the relations in 2001.
- `KINSHIP`: kinship relations, with the `weight` encoding the kind of kinship tie (values 1 to 3; coding undocumented).
- `ties`: all the relations among the individuals (the same 69 ties as in the network `2000`), with three coded attributes, given in the source as three separate matrices with the same nonzero entries: the edge properties `tie_year` and `tie_extinguish` are codes for the year in which the relation was formed and in which it ended, respectively (the meaning of these codes is not documented in the source files), and `operation_id` is the identifier of the operation (attack) in which both individuals were involved (36 for all ties).

In all networks, the node property `name` is the numeric JJATT identifier of the person.
citations: S. Atran et al., "Philippines Ambassador Residence Bombing 2000, Jakarta." John Jay & ARTIS Transnational Terrorism Database (2009)

datasets.name: aminer_citation
datasets.description:
Citation networks of scientific publications, mostly in computer science, extracted from DBLP, ACM and other sources by the AMiner (formerly ArnetMiner) academic search system of Tsinghua University, and released in several versions between 2010 and 2016 as the "AMiner Citation Network Dataset". Nodes are papers, and a directed edge $i \to j$ indicates that paper $i$ cites paper $j$ (i.e. $j$ is in the reference list of $i$).

| Network | Release | Source |
|---|---|---|
| `v1` | Citation-network V1, 2010-05-15 | DBLP, ACM and others |
| `v2` | Citation-network V2, 2010-09-13 | DBLP, ACM and others |
| `v3` | DBLP-Citation-network V3, 2010-10-22 | DBLP |
| `v4` | DBLP-Citation-network V4, 2011-01-08 | DBLP (with ACM citations) |
| `v5` | DBLP-Citation-network V5, 2011-02-21 | DBLP |
| `v6` | DBLP-Citation-network V6, 2013-09-29 | DBLP |
| `v7` | DBLP-Citation-network V7, 2014-05-25 | DBLP |
| `v8` | DBLP-Citation-network V8, 2016 | DBLP |
| `acm_v8` | ACM-Citation-network V8, 2016 | ACM |

Only references to papers contained in the same data set are included as edges, and the numbers of papers and citations can differ from those stated by AMiner (e.g. the `v7` file contains 2,146,341 papers instead of the stated 2,244,021; many papers have no citations within the data set). Papers with identical identifiers in different versions are not necessarily the same paper.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `index`: the identifier of the paper in the data set (a number, or a 24-digit hexadecimal string in `v8` and `acm_v8`).
- (Node) `title`: the title of the paper.
- (Node) `authors`: the list of authors.
- (Node) `year`: the year of publication (-1 if missing).
- (Node) `venue`: the publication venue (conference or journal).
- (Node) `citations` (`v5`, `v6` only): the number of citations of the paper, according to AMiner (-1 or 0 if none).
- (Node) `arnetid` (`v5`, `v6` only): the identifier of the paper in the AMiner database.

The abstracts included in some versions are not stored. According to the source, the data are designed for research purposes only.
citations: J. Tang, J. Zhang, L. Yao, J. Li, L. Zhang, Z. Su, "ArnetMiner: extraction and mining of academic social networks." Proceedings of the 14th ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining, 990-998 (2008)

datasets.name: aminer_cross_domain
datasets.description:
Bipartite networks of papers and their authors in five subfields of computer science, extracted from AMiner (ArnetMiner) by J. Tang, S. Wu, J. Sun and H. Su to study cross-domain collaboration recommendation. The data cover papers published from 1990 to 2005 in the main venues of each subfield:

- `data_mining`: KDD, SDM, ICDM, WSDM and PKDD.
- `medical_informatics`: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association, Journal of Biomedical Informatics, Artificial Intelligence in Medicine, IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging and IEEE Transactions on Information Technology in Biomedicine.
- `theory`: STOC, FOCS and SODA.
- `visualization`: CVPR, ICCV, VAST, TVCG, IEEE Visualization and Information Visualization.
- `database`: SIGMOD, VLDB and ICDE.

Nodes are papers and authors (identified by their names), and an undirected edge connects a paper to each of its authors.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `is_paper`: whether the node is a paper (otherwise it is an author).
- (Node) `name`: the title of the paper or the name of the author.
- (Node) `venue` (papers): the publication venue (empty for authors).
- (Node) `year` (papers): the year of publication (-1 for authors).

The abstracts of the papers (replaced by the titles when missing) are not included.
citations: J. Tang, S. Wu, J. Sun, H. Su, "Cross-domain collaboration recommendation." Proceedings of the 18th ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining, 1285-1293 (2012)

datasets.name: aminer_social_influence
datasets.description:
Networks released by J. Tang and colleagues (Tsinghua University) with their study of topic-based social influence analysis, extracted from the AMiner (ArnetMiner) academic search system and from Wikipedia. The academic networks cover research topics found by an author-conference-topic model of AMiner: 16 (Data Mining / Association Rules), 24 (Database Systems / XML Data), 75 (Information Retrieval), 107 (Web Services), 131 (Bayesian Networks / Belief Function), 144 (Web Mining / Information Fusion), 145 (Semantic Web / Description Logics), 162 (Machine Learning), 182 (Pattern Recognition / Image Analysis) and 199 (Natural Language Systems / Statistical Machine Translation).

- `coauthors_T<topic>_sub<k>`: coauthorship networks of the authors of a topic (topics 16, 24, 75, 107, 131, 144, 145 and 162; for some topics there are several separate networks, numbered by `k`). Nodes are authors, and an undirected edge connects two authors who coauthored papers, with `weight` equal to the number of coauthored papers.
- `citations_T<topic>`: citation networks of the papers of a topic (all ten topics). Nodes are papers, and a directed edge connects two papers with a citation relationship. The direction is not documented for these files; in `citations_all`, where publication years are available, the source paper is the later one for most edges, so that an edge presumably goes from the citing to the cited paper.
- `citations_all`: a citation network of 2,555 papers of the ten topics (6,101 citations) with paper metadata. A directed edge goes from the source to the target paper of a citation relationship (see above).
- `movies`: a network of the English-language films on Wikipedia and their actors ("starring"), directors and writers. Nodes are films and persons, and an undirected edge connects two nodes whose names appear on the same Wikipedia page. Some pairs are listed several times (kept as parallel edges), and some edges are self-loops.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name` (coauthors, movies): the name of the author, film or person.
- (Node) `papers` (coauthors): the number of papers of the author.
- (Edge) `weight` (coauthors): the number of coauthored papers.
- (Node) `title` (citations): the title of the paper.
- (Node) `cited` (`citations_T<topic>`): the number of citations of the paper.
- (Node) `year`, `venue`, `authors` (`citations_all`): the year of publication, publication venue and authors of the paper.
- (Node) `type` (movies): the kind of node: "movie", "starring" (actor), "director" or "writer".
- (Node) `words` (movies): the number of words introducing the node on Wikipedia.
- (Node) `categories` (movies): the Wikipedia categories of the page of the node.

According to the source, the data are for research purposes only.
citations: J. Tang, J. Sun, C. Wang, Z. Yang, "Social influence analysis in large-scale networks." Proceedings of the 15th ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining, 807-816 (2009)

J. Tang, J. Zhang, L. Yao, J. Li, L. Zhang, Z. Su, "ArnetMiner: extraction and mining of academic social networks." Proceedings of the 14th ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining, 990-998 (2008)

datasets.name: ancient_metabolism
datasets.description:
Bipartite networks of metabolic reactions and metabolites from the KEGG database, assembled by J. E. Goldford, H. Hartman, T. F. Smith and D. Segrè as a model of the metabolism of the whole biosphere, and used to find a core metabolic network that could have functioned without phosphate in an early, prebiotic environment. Nodes represent reactions and metabolites, and an undirected edge connects a reaction to each metabolite that it consumes or produces, with the stoichiometric coefficient as edge property.

The reactions of KEGG were filtered to keep only those whose compounds all have a known structure (SMILES string) and no polymer subunits of undefined size, and which are elementally balanced (for every element except hydrogen; generic "R" groups are allowed if balanced). There are three networks:

- `kegg`: the elementally balanced KEGG network (the "full KEGG network" of the paper), with 6,880 reactions and the 5,944 metabolites listed in the source data (146 of which take part in none of the reactions, and are isolated nodes).
- `anaerobic`: the anaerobic (oxygen-independent) network, obtained by removing all reactions that involve molecular oxygen, and keeping only the largest connected component of the remaining bipartite graph, with 5,651 reactions and 5,252 metabolites.
- `core`: the phosphate-free core network, with 315 reactions and 260 metabolites, obtained by "network expansion" from a seed set of eight simple compounds thought to be available in prebiotic environments (lacking phosphate), i.e. by iteratively adding all reactions of the KEGG network whose substrates are available (reactions considered reversible, except the ones that would produce oxygen), together with their products, until no new reactions can be added.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `is_reaction`: whether the node is a reaction (otherwise it is a metabolite).
- (Node) `kegg_id`: the KEGG identifier (e.g. R00004 for reactions and C00001 for compounds).
- (Node) `name`: the name of the reaction or compound (empty for some reactions).
- (Node) `formula`: for reactions, the reaction equation with KEGG compound identifiers (reactions involving oxygen are written with "=>", the others with "<=>"), and for metabolites, the chemical formula.
- (Node) `smiles`: the SMILES string of metabolites.
- (Node) `delta_g`: the standard molar free energy of reactions in kJ/mol (at pH 7 and ionic strength 0.1 M; NaN if unavailable).
- (Node) `anaerobic`: whether the node belongs to the anaerobic network.
- (Node) `core`: whether the node belongs to the phosphate-free core network.
- (Edge) `stoichiometry`: the stoichiometric coefficient of the metabolite in the reaction, negative for metabolites on the left-hand side of the reaction equation (substrates in the direction written) and positive for those on the right-hand side (products).[^icon].

[^icon]: Description obtained in part from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.
citations: J. E. Goldford, H. Hartman, T. F. Smith, D. Segrè, "Remnants of an Ancient Metabolism without Phosphate." Cell 168(6), 1126-1134.e9 (2017)

datasets.name: ant_dominance
datasets.description:
Ritual dominance displays among female ants of the species Leptothorax allardycei, in two laboratory colonies observed by B. J. Cole, who studied dominance hierarchies among workers in relation to egg-laying. The data were distributed by L. C. Freeman on his network data page at the University of California, Irvine (no longer online), from which this version was obtained via the Internet Archive.

- `colony1`: 16 ants of a colony with a queen, observed over 18.2 hours.
- `colony2`: 13 ants of a queenless colony, observed over 14.8 hours.

A directed edge (i, j) indicates that ant i performed dominance displays towards ant j.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the label of the ant.
- (Edge) `weight`: the number of dominance displays observed.
citations: B. J. Cole, "Dominance hierarchies in Leptothorax ants." Science 212(4490), 83-84 (1981)

datasets.name: anybeat
datasets.description:
A snapshot of the social network among users of Anybeat, an online community described as a public gathering place where people can interact with others from their neighborhood or across the world. Nodes are users, and a directed edge $i \to j$ means that user $i$ follows user $j$. The data were collected and anonymized by M. Fire and collaborators at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, and released in 2012 as part of their study of link prediction. The service has since been shut down.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the anonymized user identifier.
citations: M. Fire, R. Puzis, & Y. Elovici. "Link prediction in highly fractional data sets." In Handbook of Computational Approaches to Counterterrorism. Springer, pp. 283-300 (2013)

datasets.name: ao3
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of the works of fan fiction published on the Archive of Our Own (AO3), the fan works repository of the Organization for Transformative Works (OTW), and the tags attached to them, from the one-time data dump released by the OTW on 26 February 2021 "for fan statisticians". It covers all the works on AO3 at the time, from 2008 to February 2021, except those hidden by the site (e.g. drafts and works hidden by its administrators).

An edge connects a work to each of its tags. AO3 tags describe the works along several dimensions, each a tag type: the rating (e.g. `General Audiences`, `Explicit`), the archive warnings, the categories of relationships (e.g. `F/M`, `M/M`, `Gen`), the fandoms (the source works, e.g. `Harry Potter - J. K. Rowling`), the characters, the relationships between characters (e.g. `Draco Malfoy/Harry Potter`), and free-form tags (e.g. `Fluff`, `Alternate Universe`). Tags are written freely by the authors, and the volunteer "tag wranglers" of AO3 mark one tag of each set of synonyms as canonical, and the others as synonyms of it (merged into it); the works are linked to the tags as written by their authors, and the canonical tag of a tag is given by the property `merger_id`.

To protect the privacy of the authors, the names of the tags used fewer than five times were redacted by the OTW (their name is `Redacted`, about 12.8 million of the 14.5 million tags). The works carry no identifiers, titles or authors, and are numbered in the order of the dump (roughly by decreasing creation date). Only the tags used by some work are nodes of the network (tags that are only canonical versions of other tags, without works of their own, are left out; they are still identified by `merger_id`). 8,139 tags used by works are missing from the tag file of the dump; their name and type are empty, `canonical` is false, and `cached_count` and `merger_id` are -1. Three empty items in the tag lists of the works are left out.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `is_work`: whether the node is a work (otherwise it is a tag).
- (Node) `time` (works): the creation date of the work, as Unix time.
- (Node) `language` (works): the language of the work, as a code (e.g. `en`, `zh`).
- (Node) `restricted` (works): whether the work is visible only to registered users.
- (Node) `complete` (works): whether the work is complete.
- (Node) `word_count` (works): the number of words of the work (-1 if not given).
- (Node) `tag_id` (tags): the identifier of the tag on AO3 (-1 for works).
- (Node) `name` (tags): the name of the tag (`Redacted` if it was used fewer than five times).
- (Node) `type` (tags): the type of the tag: `Rating`, `ArchiveWarning`, `Category`, `Fandom`, `Character`, `Relationship`, `Freeform`, `Media` or `UnsortedTag` (tags not yet sorted by the wranglers).
- (Node) `canonical` (tags): whether the tag is canonical.
- (Node) `cached_count` (tags): the approximate number of uses of the tag, as given by AO3.
- (Node) `merger_id` (tags): the identifier of the canonical tag of which the tag is a synonym (-1 if none).
citations: Organization for Transformative Works, "Selective data dump for fan statisticians." Archive of Our Own (2021)

datasets.name: arabidopsis_interactome
datasets.description:
A network of protein-protein interactions of the plant *Arabidopsis thaliana*, from the Arabidopsis Interactome Mapping Consortium (Dreze et al., 2011), as distributed by the Center for Cancer Systems Biology (CCSB, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute). It combines Arabidopsis Interactome version 1 (AI-1), a binary interaction map obtained with a high-throughput yeast two-hybrid (Y2H) screen of the pairwise combinations of a set of about 8,000 cloned protein-coding genes ("space 1"), with interactions curated from the literature (LCI). Nodes are proteins, identified by their Arabidopsis Genome Initiative (AGI) gene locus, and an undirected edge connects two proteins that interact according to at least one of the sources, which are indicated by edge properties. The network has 11,374 interactions among 4,866 proteins; the 5,664 interactions of the main Y2H screen involve 2,661 proteins. Self-loops are proteins interacting with themselves.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the AGI locus of the protein (e.g. "AT1G05410").
- (Edge) `main_screen` (edges): whether the interaction was found in the main AI-1 Y2H screen (AI1_M).
- (Edge) `repeat_screen` (edges): whether the interaction was found in the repeat of the Y2H screen (AI1_R).
- (Edge) `lci` (edges): whether the interaction is reported in the literature, from the curated interaction databases.
- (Edge) `lci_binary` (edges): whether the literature-curated interaction is binary (direct).
- (Edge) `lci_core` (edges): whether the binary literature-curated interaction is supported by at least two publications or two experimental methods.
citations: Arabidopsis Interactome Mapping Consortium, "Evidence for network evolution in an Arabidopsis interactome map." Science 333(6042), 601-607 (2011)

datasets.name: arxiv_authors
citations: J. Leskovec, J. Kleinberg and C. Faloutsos. "Graph Evolution: Densification and Shrinking Diameters." ACM Transactions on Knowledge Discovery from Data 1(1), article 2 (2007).

datasets.name: arxiv_citation
datasets.description:
Citation networks among papers posted on the arXiv e-print repository in two categories of high energy physics, phenomenology (`HepPh`) and theory (`HepTh`). The data cover papers posted from January 1993 to April 2003 (124 months), beginning a few months after the inception of arXiv, and were originally released as part of the 2003 KDD Cup (with data provided by P. Ginsparg and arXiv). A directed edge $i \to j$ means that paper $i$ cites paper $j$. Only citations among papers in the data set are included: citations to or from papers outside of it are not recorded.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the arXiv identifier of the paper within its category, as an integer, i.e. without the leading zeros (e.g. `9301253` is hep-ph/9301253, and `1001` is hep-th/0001001).
- (Node) `date`: the date the paper was first submitted to arXiv (YYYY-MM-DD). In `HepPh`, the dates are those published by SNAP, and are empty for the 3,988 papers without a date there; in `HepTh`, they are SLAC's submission dates from the original KDD Cup 2003 data, available for all papers (SNAP's file of `HepTh` dates is a copy of the `HepPh` one).
citations: J. Gehrke, P. Ginsparg, J. M. Kleinberg. "Overview of the 2003 KDD Cup." SIGKDD Explorations 5(2), 149-151 (2003)

datasets.name: arxiv_collab
datasets.description:
Weighted co-authorship networks of scientists who posted preprints on the arXiv e-print repository, compiled by M. E. J. Newman. Nodes are authors, identified by their surname and initials, and an undirected edge connects two authors if they co-authored at least one preprint. There is one network for each of three arXiv archives over the period 1995–1999 (`astro-ph-1999`: astrophysics; `cond-mat-1999`: condensed matter physics; `hep-th-1999`: high energy physics, theory), and two updated versions of the condensed matter network, covering preprints posted between January 1, 1995 and June 30, 2003 (`cond-mat-2003`) and between January 1, 1995 and March 31, 2005 (`cond-mat-2005`).

Edge weights account for the fact that authors of papers with many co-authors know each other less well on average: each paper $k$ with $n_k$ authors contributes $1/(n_k-1)$ to the weight of the edge between each pair of its authors, so that $w_{ij} = \sum_k \delta_i^k\delta_j^k/(n_k-1)$, where $\delta_i^k=1$ if $i$ is an author of paper $k$ and $0$ otherwise. Papers with a single author do not contribute. Since authors are identified by surname and initials, different people with the same surname and initials may be merged into a single node, and the same person may appear under different names.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `label`: the author's name ("SURNAME, INITIALS").
- (Edge) `value`: the collaboration weight $w_{ij}$ described above.
citations: M. E. J. Newman, "The structure of scientific collaboration networks." Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA 98(2), 404-409 (2001). arxiv:cond-mat/0007214

datasets.name: as_skitter
datasets.description: An Internet topology graph obtained from traceroute measurements carried out daily during 2005 by CAIDA's skitter infrastructure, in which monitors at several scattered locations probed paths to about a million destinations. Nodes correspond to hosts or routers identified along the measured paths, and an undirected edge connects two nodes that were observed as adjacent hops. The aggregate graph was compiled by J. Leskovec and collaborators (SNAP); nodes are identified only by anonymous numeric identifiers, and the network has no node or edge properties.
citations: "The CAIDA UCSD Macroscopic Skitter Topology Dataset"

datasets.name: as_topology_sources
datasets.description:
Networks of the Internet at the level of Autonomous Systems (ASes), constructed by Mahadevan et al. at CAIDA from the three kinds of data most frequently used to study the AS-level topology: traceroute measurements, BGP routing data, and the WHOIS database. In all networks, nodes are ASes, and an undirected edge connects two ASes that are found to be directly connected (peering or exchanging traffic) according to the data source.

- `skitter`: traceroute measurements of CAIDA's skitter monitors. The daily AS-level graphs of the 31 days of March 2004 were merged, after filtering AS-sets, multi-origin ASes and private ASes, and discarding indirect links.
- `bgp_tables`: snapshots of the BGP routing tables collected by RouteViews (University of Oregon), for the 31 days of March 2004, where two ASes are connected if they are adjacent in some AS path; AS-sets and private ASes were filtered and the daily graphs merged.
- `bgp_updates`: as `bgp_tables`, but from the BGP update messages (updates and withdrawals) collected by RouteViews in March 2004.
- `whois`: the RIPE WHOIS database dump of April 7, 2004, which covers primarily European networks. An AS $x$ declared in an "aut-num" record is connected to the ASes $y$ in its "import: from AS$y$" and "export: to AS$y$" policy lines. ASes that do not appear in the "aut-num" lines and private ASes were excluded. The source file includes 24 self-loops.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the AS number.
citations: P. Mahadevan, D. Krioukov, M. Fomenkov, X. Dimitropoulos, k. c. claffy, A. Vahdat, "The Internet AS-level topology: three data sources and one definitive metric." ACM SIGCOMM Computer Communication Review 36(1), 17-26 (2006)

datasets.name: asu_social_networks
datasets.description:
Friendship networks of several online social websites, crawled in 2010 by students of H. Liu's group at Arizona State University and distributed by the Social Computing Data Repository (originally at Arizona State University, now at Syracuse University). Nodes are users (anonymized), and a directed edge $i \to j$ indicates that user $j$ is listed as a friend of user $i$ (the source data state that "user $i$ is friend with user $j$"; the meaning of the direction depends on the site, e.g. on Twitter a "friend" is presumably an account followed by the user). The crawls collected the friend lists of a set of users (marked by the property `crawled`); their friends that were not crawled are also included as nodes.

| Network | Website | Crawled | Crawled users | Nodes | Edges |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `digg` | Digg (social news) | December 2010 (M. Nagendra) | 116,893 | 771,231 | 7,261,524 |
| `foursquare` | Foursquare (location-based social network) | December 2010 (F. Morstatter) | 106,218 | 639,014 | 3,473,834 |
| `friendster` | Friendster (social networking) | November 2010 (S. Booher) | 100,199 | 5,689,498 | 14,067,887 |
| `lastfm` | Last.fm (music) | December 2010 (M. Kearl) | 108,493 | 1,193,699 | 5,115,300 |
| `buzznet` | Buzznet (photo, journal and video sharing) | November 2010 | 101,168 | 101,168 | 4,284,534 |
| `delicious` | Delicious (social bookmarking) | December 2010 (A. Anand) | 103,144 | 537,387 | 1,385,843 |
| `twitter` | Twitter (microblogging) | (not documented) | 11,316,811 | 11,316,811 | 85,331,845 |

For `twitter`, all users are marked as crawled, and the file contains one edge less than the 85,331,846 stated in the source documentation. Some edges are self-loops; in `buzznet`, 166,989 friend listings are repeated, and are kept as parallel edges. The source documentation of `delicious` states 1,419,519 edges, more than are contained in the file. The Douban, Flixster, Hyves and Livemocha networks of the same repository are in the separate entries `douban`, `flixster`, `hyves` and `livemocha`, and the LiveJournal network is in `livejournal_asu`.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `user_id`: the identifier of the user in the source data.
- (Node) `crawled`: whether the friend list of the user was crawled (i.e. the user is listed in the node file of the source data).
citations: R. Zafarani, H. Liu, "Social Computing Data Repository at ASU." Arizona State University, School of Computing, Informatics and Decision Systems Engineering (2009)

datasets.name: at_migrations
datasets.description: A network of migrations between municipalities in Austria, from 2002 to 2021. Nodes are municipalities (with their boundaries as of 2022), and a directed edge from municipality $i$ to municipality $j$ represents the migrations (changes of residence) from $i$ to $j$ in a given year by people of a given nationality (Austrian or foreign) and sex, so that a pair of municipalities can be connected by several parallel edges; migrations within the same municipality appear as self-loops. Edges are annotated with the number of migrations (`count`), nationality, sex, and year.
citations: "Internal migration within Austria acc.to communes since 2002 (status of 2022)", Statistik Austria

datasets.name: australian_bank
datasets.description:
Relations among the 11 employees of a branch of a large Australian bank, from a study by G. Robins of the structure of several branches, analyzed by P. Pattison, S. Wasserman, G. Robins and A. M. Kanfer (2000). The data were distributed by L. C. Freeman on his network data page at the University of California, Irvine (no longer online), from which this version was obtained via the Internet Archive.

The network has four directed layers (relations), in which an edge (i, j) indicates that employee i named employee j in response to the questions:

- `advice-seeking`: "With whom might you check out a course of action if an issue arises in your work?"
- `satisfying`: "With whom do you feel that your work interactions are particularly satisfying?"
- `confiding`: "In whom do you feel you would be able to confide if a problem arose that you did not want everyone to know about?"
- `close friend`: "Whom do you consider to be a particularly close friend?"

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `position`: the job of the employee (the first is the branch manager, the second the deputy manager, the third, fourth and fifth are service advisers, a middle-ranking position, and the others are tellers).
- (Edge) `layer`: the relation.
citations: P. Pattison, S. Wasserman, G. Robins, A. M. Kanfer, "Statistical evaluation of algebraic constraints for social networks." Journal of Mathematical Psychology 44(4), 536-568 (2000)

datasets.name: australian_embassy_bombing
datasets.description:
Time series of networks of relationships among 27 individuals, from the John Jay & ARTIS Transnational Terrorism Database (JJATT). The JJATT data treat specific attacks as endpoints, and depict the evolution of the relations among the individuals directly or indirectly associated with them; here, the bombing of the Australian embassy in Jakarta, Indonesia, on 9 September 2004 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Australian_Embassy_bombing_in_Jakarta)). The data were coded from open sources (e.g. court documents, news reports and books), and were made available in matrix form by the UCINET datasets collection (University of Manchester).

Nodes are individuals (labeled by their JJATT identifier in `name`), and each time-period network contains the relationships present in that period (networks named `YYYY_1` and `YYYY_2` refer to the first and second halves of year YYYY). The edge property `weight` gives the strength of the tie: 1 = acquaintances or distant family ties (interaction limited to radical organization activities), 2 = friends or moderately close family ties (including co-workers and roommates), operational or organizational leadership, or operational ties (e.g. having worked closely together on a bombing), 3 = close friends or family, tight-knit operational cliques. The `kinship` network contains kinship ties, with the edge property `kinship` coding the type: 1 = in-laws, 2 = cousins, 3 = siblings, 4 = parent/child, 5 = married, 6 = grandparent/grandchild, 7 = significant other (cells coded 99 in the source matrix, whose meaning is not documented, are omitted). The source matrices are meant to be symmetric; in the few cases where the two directions differ, the tie with the larger value is used. The JJATT tie-start, tie-end and operation matrices, which use undocumented codes, are not included.[^ucinet]

[^ucinet]: Description obtained in part from the [UCINET datasets page](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/datasets/covert-networks/australian-embassy-bombing-indonesia-2004).
citations: S. Atran, M. Sageman, et al., "John Jay & ARTIS Transnational Terrorism Database (JJATT)." John Jay College of Criminal Justice (2009)

datasets.name: austria_comorbidity
datasets.description:
Networks of comorbidity between diagnoses, from the hospital claims data of the whole Austrian population: all hospital stays between 1997 and 2014 (44.6 million stays of 9 million patients), from the database of the Austrian Ministry of Health, aggregated by Dervić, Ledebur, Thurner and Klimek. Each stay has a primary diagnosis and possibly secondary ones, coded with the ICD-10 classification. The study is limited to the stays between 2003 and 2014 of the patients who had no hospital stay between 1997 and 2002 (3,378,906 patients), and to the 1,080 three-digit ICD-10 codes between A00 and N99 (leaving out pregnancy, injuries, poisoning and other external causes).

Nodes are diagnoses, at three levels of resolution: the three-digit ICD-10 codes (1,080 nodes; networks starting with `icd`), the blocks of the ICD-10 classification (131 nodes; `blocks`), and 46 chronic conditions (`chronic`). Patients are stratified by sex (`female`, `male`), by ten-year age group (from 0-9 to 70-79 years), and by two-year period (from 2003-2004 to 2013-2014). An undirected edge connects two diagnoses for which a two-by-two contingency table of the patients of a stratum was computed, counting the patients with both diagnoses, with only one of them, or with neither.

There are two kinds of networks:

- The comorbidity networks of the authors (e.g. `icd_female_age_30-39` or `icd_female_2003-2004`), for each sex and age group (pooling the periods) or each sex and period (pooling the age groups): an edge connects two diagnoses whose odds ratio, estimated with the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel method over the strata (periods, or age groups), is larger than 1.5, with a $p$-value smaller than 0.05 and at least 100 patients with both diagnoses. The networks of chronic conditions of the age group 0-9 have no edges and are left out.
- The unthresholded contingency tables, for every pair of diagnoses with at least one patient with both, in each stratum (e.g. `raw_icd_female_30-39_2003-2004`) and in all strata together (e.g. `raw_icd_female`, with the values of the strata as vectors).

All networks of a level of resolution have all its diagnoses as nodes, including those without edges. The attributes of the nodes are taken from the GEXF file of the network `*_male_2003-2004` of each level (in the files of the three-digit codes of the female age groups, the codes and descriptions of 164 nodes are shifted with respect to their labels, e.g. the node H43 has those of F15). The positions, sizes and colors of the nodes in the GEXF files of the authors (the colors are the chapters of the ICD-10 classification) are left out, and so is the prevalence of each diagnosis per sex, age group and year, which the source also gives.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the ICD-10 code (`icd`), the range of codes of the block (`blocks`), or the name of the chronic condition (`chronic`), as given.
- (Node) `icd_code` (`icd`, `chronic`): the ICD-10 code, or the range of codes of the chronic condition.
- (Node) `description` (`icd`): the description of the ICD-10 code, in German.
- (Node) `short_description`, `long_description` (`icd`): the short and long descriptions of the ICD-10 code, in English.
- (Node) `patients` (`raw_*`): the number of patients with the diagnosis, as given in the contingency tables (in the networks of all strata, a vector with the value of each stratum).
- (Edge) `weight` (comorbidity networks): the odds ratio of the two diagnoses.
- (Edge) `a` (`raw_*`): the number of patients with both diagnoses.
- (Edge) `b` (`raw_*`): the number of patients with the diagnosis of the target node but not that of the source node.
- (Edge) `c` (`raw_*`): the number of patients with the diagnosis of the source node but not that of the target node.
- (Edge) `d` (`raw_*`): the number of patients with neither diagnosis.
- (Graph) `strata` (networks of all strata): the strata (age group and period) of the entries of the vector properties, in order.
citations: E. Dervić, K. Ledebur, S. Thurner, P. Klimek, "Comorbidity Networks From Population-Wide Health Data: Aggregated Data of 8.9M Hospital Patients (1997–2014)." Scientific Data 12, 215 (2025)

datasets.name: baad_terrorist_orgs
datasets.description:
Networks of 394 terrorist organizations from the Big Allied and Dangerous (BAAD) dataset, version 1, which contains a snapshot of terrorist organizations that perpetrated at least one attack between 1998 and 2005, built from the Terrorism Knowledge Base of the Memorial Institute for the Prevention of Terrorism (MIPT), with independent verification and coding (Asal and Rethemeyer, 2008).

- `locations`: bipartite network of organizations and 65 countries or territories, described by the source as the locations of their attacks (each organization is connected to exactly one location); the vertex property `is_country` marks the locations.
- `co_location`: one-mode projection connecting organizations based in the same location.

The organizations have the following vertex properties, with the variable names of the BAAD codebook: `fatalities19982005` (number of fatalities caused, 1998-2005), `statespond` (state sponsorship), `masterccode` (Correlates of War code of the home country), `orgage` (age of the organization), `containrelig`, `containethno`, `leftnoreligethno`, `purerelig`, `pureethno`, `religethno`, `containrelig2`, `containethno2` and `islam` (indicators of religious, ethno-nationalist and leftist ideologies, and their combinations), `ordsize` (ordinal size), `degree` (number of connections to other organizations, as given by the source) and `terrstrong` (control of territory). These properties are set only for the organizations (in the bipartite network, they are zero for the locations). Data distributed by the UCINET datasets collection (University of Manchester).[^ucinet]

[^ucinet]: Description obtained in part from the [UCINET datasets page](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/datasets/covert-networks/big-allied-and-dangerous-baad).
citations: V. Asal and R. K. Rethemeyer, "The nature of the beast: Organizational structures and the lethality of terrorist attacks." The Journal of Politics 70(2), 437-449 (2008)

datasets.name: bacillus_megaterium_metabolism
datasets.description:
Metabolic network of the bacterium *Bacillus megaterium* strain DSM319, from the manually curated genome-scale metabolic model iJA1121 of Aminian-Dehkordi et al. The model was reconstructed from a draft network obtained by aligning the genome of DSM319 with those of other *B. megaterium* strains and comparing with the existing models of the strain WSH002 and of *B. subtilis*, followed by manual curation and gap filling, and was validated against growth phenotypes on different carbon and nitrogen sources. The model contains 1,709 reactions, 1,349 metabolites in two compartments (cytosol and extracellular space), and 1,121 genes, and it is distributed in the SBML format for flux balance analysis.

The network is bipartite and directed, with reactions on one side, and metabolites and genes on the other. Each reactant (substrate) of a reaction points to the reaction, and each reaction points to its products, as written in the model (reversible reactions can also proceed in the reverse direction). Each gene associated with a reaction (as a catalysing enzyme, or a subunit of an enzyme complex) points to the reaction. The same compound in different compartments corresponds to different metabolite nodes. Exchange reactions, which model the uptake and secretion of extracellular metabolites, have a single metabolite. The 46 genes of the model that are not associated with any reaction (some of which have malformed identifiers in the model, such as "orBMD_0557") are isolated nodes.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the metabolite or reaction, or the locus tag of the gene.
- (Node) `id`: the identifier in the SBML model.
- (Node) `kind`: either "metabolite", "reaction", or "gene".
- (Node) `is_reaction`: whether the node is a reaction.
- (Node) `compartment` (metabolites): "c" for cytosol, "e" for extracellular.
- (Node) `formula` (metabolites): the chemical formula.
- (Node) `charge` (metabolites): the charge.
- (Node) `kegg` (metabolites): the KEGG compound identifier, if available.
- (Node) `subsystem` (reactions): the metabolic subsystem (e.g. "Amino acid metabolism", "Transporting system").
- (Node) `ec` (reactions): the EC number(s) of the enzyme, if available.
- (Node) `reversible` (reactions): whether the reaction is reversible.
- (Node) `lower_bound` and `upper_bound` (reactions): the flux bounds in the model (in mmol per gram dry weight per hour).
- (Node) `gene_rule` (reactions): the gene-reaction rule, as a boolean expression of the genes required by the reaction ("and" for enzyme complexes and "or" for isozymes).
- (Edge) `role`: either "reactant", "product", or "gene".
- (Edge) `stoichiometry`: the stoichiometric coefficient of the metabolite in the reaction (1 for genes).
citations: J. Aminian-Dehkordi, S. M. Mousavi, A. Jafari, I. Mijakovic, S.-A. Marashi, "Manually curated genome-scale reconstruction of the metabolic network of Bacillus megaterium DSM319." Scientific Reports 9, 18762 (2019)

datasets.name: bag_of_words
datasets.description:
Five text collections in the form of bags-of-words, i.e. a bipartite document–word network. Nodes are documents and words, and an edge connects a document to each word that occurs in it, with the edge property `count` giving the number of occurrences of the word in the document. 

After tokenization and removal of stopwords, the vocabulary of unique words was truncated by only keeping words that occurred more than ten times. Individual document names (i.e. a identifier for each docID) are not provided for copyright reasons.
citations: David Newman, "Bag of Words Data Set"
Dua, D. and Graff, C. (2019). UCI Machine Learning Repository. Irvine, CA: University of California, School of Information and Computer Science.

datasets.name: baidu
datasets.description: Network of hyperlinks between articles of the Chinese online encyclopedia Baidu (百度百科, http://baike.baidu.com/), from the Zhishi.me project, as distributed by KONECT ("internal links" network). Nodes are articles, and a directed edge from article $i$ to article $j$ indicates that article $i$ hyperlinks to article $j$.
citations: X. Niu et al., "Zhishi.me -- weaving Chinese linking open data." Proc. Internat. Semantic Web Conf. (2011).

datasets.name: bali_bombing_2005
datasets.description:
Time series of networks of relationships among 27 individuals, from the John Jay & ARTIS Transnational Terrorism Database (JJATT). The JJATT data treat specific attacks as endpoints, and depict the evolution of the relations among the individuals directly or indirectly associated with them; here, the bombings in Bali, Indonesia, on 1 October 2005, by Jemaah Islamiyah ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_Bali_bombings)). The data were coded from open sources (e.g. court documents, news reports and books), and were made available in matrix form by the UCINET datasets collection (University of Manchester).

Nodes are individuals (labeled by their JJATT identifier in `name`), and each time-period network contains the relationships present in that period (networks named `YYYY_1` and `YYYY_2` refer to the first and second halves of year YYYY). The edge property `weight` gives the strength of the tie: 1 = acquaintances or distant family ties (interaction limited to radical organization activities), 2 = friends or moderately close family ties (including co-workers and roommates), operational or organizational leadership, or operational ties (e.g. having worked closely together on a bombing), 3 = close friends or family, tight-knit operational cliques. The periods 1985_1989, 2006_2 have no ties in the source, and are not included. The source matrices are meant to be symmetric; in the few cases where the two directions differ, the tie with the larger value is used. The JJATT tie-start, tie-end and operation matrices, which use undocumented codes, are not included.[^ucinet]

[^ucinet]: Description obtained in part from the [UCINET datasets page](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/datasets/covert-networks/bali-bombing-2005).
citations: S. Atran, M. Sageman, et al., "John Jay & ARTIS Transnational Terrorism Database (JJATT)." John Jay College of Criminal Justice (2009)

datasets.name: bank_wiring_room
datasets.description:
Observed interactions among 14 employees of the bank wiring room of the Western Electric Company (Hawthorne plant, Chicago), from the Hawthorne studies, first presented by F. J. Roethlisberger and W. J. Dickson (1939). The data became better known through the analysis of G. Homans (1950), and the blockmodel (CONCOR) analysis of R. Breiger, S. Boorman and P. Arabie (1975). The employees worked in a single room, and include two inspectors (I1 and I3), three solderers (S1, S2 and S3), and nine wiremen or assemblers (W1 to W9). The data were distributed by L. C. Freeman on his network data page at the University of California, Irvine (no longer online), from which this version was obtained via the Internet Archive.

Nodes are employees, and in each network an edge connects two employees who were observed engaging in the corresponding relation with each other. The six relations are given as separate networks:

- `RDGAM`: participation in horseplay (games), undirected.
- `RDCON`: participation in arguments about open windows (controversy), undirected.
- `RDPOS`: friendship (positive relations), undirected.
- `RDNEG`: antagonistic (negative) behavior, undirected.
- `RDHLP`: helping others with work, directed; an edge (i, j) indicates that i helped j.
