- `RDJOB`: trading of job assignments, directed (the meaning of the edge direction is not documented).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the label of the employee (I: inspector, S: solderer, W: wireman).
- (Edge) `weight` (`RDJOB`): the number of times the workers traded job assignments.
citations: F. J. Roethlisberger, W. J. Dickson, "Management and the Worker." Harvard University Press (1939)

R. L. Breiger, S. A. Boorman, P. Arabie, "An algorithm for clustering relational data with applications to social network analysis and comparison with multidimensional scaling." Journal of Mathematical Psychology 12(3), 328-383 (1975)

datasets.name: baseball
datasets.description:
Networks of steroid use among Major League Baseball players, compiled by V. Krebs from the Mitchell Report (2007), the independent investigation into the use of steroids and other illegal performance-enhancing substances in Major League Baseball. There are two undirected networks:

- `user-provider`: a bipartite network of 72 players and the 12 providers (individuals, clinics and pharmacies) that the report identified as their suppliers of steroids and other illegal performance-enhancing substances. An edge connects a player to each of his providers.
- `player-player`: the one-mode projection of the bipartite network onto the players, in which two players are connected if they share at least one provider. The edge `weight` is the number of shared providers. Each player also has a self-loop whose `weight` is his number of providers.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the player or provider.
- (Node) `is_provider` (only in `user-provider`): whether the node is a provider (otherwise a player).
- (Edge) `weight` (only in `player-player`): as described above.
citations: V. Krebs, "The Spread of Steroids in Baseball."

datasets.name: berkstan_web
datasets.description: The web graph of Berkeley and Stanford Universities (berkeley.edu and stanford.edu), as collected in 2002. Nodes represent pages and directed edges represent hyperlinks between them.
citations: J. Leskovec, K. Lang, A. Dasgupta, M. Mahoney. Community Structure in Large Networks: Natural Cluster Sizes and the Absence of Large Well-Defined Clusters. Internet Mathematics 6(1) 29--123, 2009

datasets.name: bible_nouns
datasets.description:
Co-occurrences of proper nouns (people and places) in the verses of the King James Version of the Bible. C. Römhild recorded 1773 proper nouns, and tallied 63,779 occasions in which pairs of them appeared in the same verse; together with C. Harrison, he used the data to produce visualizations of the Bible. The data were distributed by L. C. Freeman on his network data page at the University of California, Irvine (no longer online), from which this version was obtained via the Internet Archive.

An undirected edge (i, j) indicates that the nouns i and j appear together in at least one verse.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the proper noun (in lower case).
- (Edge) `weight`: the number of verses in which the two nouns appear together.

datasets.name: bibsonomy
datasets.description: The bipartite tag–item network of the BibSonomy social bookmark and publication management system, as distributed by KONECT, from the official BibSonomy dump. Nodes are 204,673 tags and 767,447 items (vertex property `is_item`), the latter being 487,304 publications and 280,143 bookmarks, and each edge is a tag assignment, connecting a tag to an item it was assigned to; since an item can be tagged several times with the same tag, the network contains multiple edges. The vertex property `name` gives the tag, or the item identifier in the dump (of the form "bibtex:ID" or "bookmark:ID"). The edges are annotated with the time of the tag assignment; almost all of them are between 2005 and the end of 2009, with a few earlier ones (from 1989 on). The exact date of this snapshot is uncertain.
citations: D. Benz et al., "The social bookmark and publication management system BibSonomy." The VLDB Journal 19(6),849-875 (2010)

datasets.name: bindingdb
datasets.description:
Bipartite networks of small molecules (ligands) and the protein targets they bind, from BindingDB, the public database of measured binding affinities, mostly of drug-like molecules and drug targets. The measurements are curated by BindingDB from articles and US and WO patents, or imported from ChEMBL, PubChem BioAssay, the PDSP Ki database, and other sources (D3R, CSAR, the Taylor group at UCSD).

Nodes are ligands (BindingDB monomers) and targets (proteins, or complexes of several protein chains), and an edge connects a ligand to a target for each measurement of their binding (an inhibition constant $K_i$, a half-maximal inhibitory or effective concentration $IC_{50}$ or $EC_{50}$, a dissociation constant $K_d$, or association and dissociation rates), so that a ligand and a target can be connected by many edges (e.g. measurements in different articles or assays). Since the data do not give identifiers of the targets, targets are identified by the amino-acid sequences of their chains (the name of a target varies, e.g. with the range of residues of the construct, and the first one is given); the few targets without sequences are identified by their name and organism. The authors, institutions and publication dates of the measurements, the InChI strings and the links to other databases of the ligands, and the other properties of the target chains (PDB identifiers, names) are left out.

There is one network for each year from 2023 to 2026, from the quarterly archives of BindingDB in the UC San Diego Library Digital Collections (which start in October 2023), from the archives of October: 2023-10-01, 2024-10-01, 2025-10-01 and 2026-10-01.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `is_ligand`: whether the node is a ligand (otherwise it is a target).
- (Node) `name`: the name of the ligand (often several synonyms separated by `::`), or of the target.
- (Node) `monomer_id`: the BindingDB identifier of the ligand (`-1` for targets).
- (Node) `smiles`, `inchi_key`: the SMILES string and the InChIKey of the ligand.
- (Node) `pubchem_cid`, `chebi_id`, `chembl_id`, `drugbank_id`: the identifiers of the ligand in other databases.
- (Node) `organism`: the organism of the target, as given by the curator or the data source.
- (Node) `num_chains`: the number of protein chains of the target (more than one for complexes).
- (Node) `uniprot_ids`: the UniProt (Swiss-Prot or, failing that, TrEMBL) accessions of the chains of the target.
- (Node) `chain_sequences`: the amino-acid sequences of the chains of the target.
- (Edge) `reactant_set_id`: the BindingDB identifier of the measurement.
- (Edge) `ki`, `ic50`, `kd`, `ec50` (nM), `kon` (1/(M s)), `koff` (1/s): the measured values (NaN when not given).
- (Edge) `qualifiers`: the qualifiers of the measured values, when given as bounds (e.g. `ic50 >`, for $IC_{50} > 10000$ nM).
- (Edge) `ph`, `temp`: the pH and the temperature (°C) of the measurement (NaN if not given).
- (Edge) `source`: the source of the measurement (e.g. `ChEMBL`, `US Patent`, `Curated from the literature by BindingDB`).
- (Edge) `article_doi`, `pmid`, `pubchem_aid`, `patent_number`: the article, PubChem assay or patent of the measurement.
- (Edge) `date` (2025, 2026): the date at which the measurement was added to BindingDB (as Unix time; `-1` if not given).
citations: T. Liu, L. Hwang, S. K. Burley, C. I. Nitsche, C. Southan, W. P. Walters, M. K. Gilson, "BindingDB in 2024: a FAIR knowledgebase of protein-small molecule binding data." Nucleic Acids Research 53, D1633-D1644 (2025)

datasets.name: biogrid
datasets.description:
Networks of the physical (protein-protein) and genetic interactions between the genes (or their protein products) of ten model organisms, from release 5.0.262 (September 2026) of BioGRID, the Biological General Repository for Interaction Datasets. BioGRID is a database of interactions curated by hand from the biomedical literature, both from focused studies and from high-throughput experiments.

There is one network for each organism (species or strain) of BioGRID. The ten most common model organisms have short names: `human` (*Homo sapiens*), `yeast` (the budding yeast *Saccharomyces cerevisiae*, strain S288c), `fission_yeast` (*Schizosaccharomyces pombe*, strain 972h-), `mouse` (*Mus musculus*), `fly` (*Drosophila melanogaster*), `worm` (*Caenorhabditis elegans*), `arabidopsis` (*Arabidopsis thaliana*, Columbia), `ecoli` (*Escherichia coli*, strain K-12 W3110), `rat` (*Rattus norvegicus*) and `zebrafish` (*Danio rerio*). The networks of the other organisms are named after the organism files of BioGRID, in lower case, e.g. `candida_albicans_sc5314`, `plasmodium_falciparum_3d7`, `xenopus_laevis`, `escherichia_coli_k12_mg1655` (another strain of *E. coli*) or `severe_acute_respiratory_syndrome_coronavirus_2`. Organisms without any interaction among their own genes have no network, and many networks of the less studied organisms have only a handful of edges.

The viruses are an exception: since their interactions are mostly with the proteins of their hosts (mostly human), the network of a virus contains all the interactions in which at least one of the interactors belongs to the virus, so that it also contains host proteins, and the nodes have the properties `taxid`, `organism` and `is_virus` (see below). The viruses are the organisms of BioGRID whose names contain "virus" (e.g. `human_immunodeficiency_virus_1`, `human_papillomavirus_16`, `severe_acute_respiratory_syndrome_coronavirus_2`, `tobacco_mosaic_virus`); the taxonomy identifier of each of them, which BioGRID gives for each interactor, belongs to the superkingdom Viruses in the NCBI taxonomy, and appears in every interaction of its file. The networks of the other organisms contain only the interactions between their own genes.

These are the networks of the current release, 5.0.262 (September 2026, 88 organisms, 42 of them viruses). The entry also contains the networks of the last release of each earlier major version of BioGRID, named `<organism>_v<release>`, e.g. `human_v4.4.249`: release 4.4.249 (August 2025, 88 organisms), release 3.5.188 (July 2020, 67 organisms) and release 2.0.63 (March 2010, 15 organisms; its budding yeast, fission yeast and *Arabidopsis* are not identified by strain, and have the same short names as in the later releases). The other releases (about 240) are not included.

Nodes are genes, and each edge is one interaction record of BioGRID: an interaction between two genes found by a given experimental system (e.g. two-hybrid, affinity capture followed by mass spectrometry, synthetic lethality) in a given publication, so that two genes can be connected by several edges. Edges are directed from interactor A to interactor B of the record: BioGRID records interactions with a bait-hit directionality (e.g. the bait and the prey of an affinity capture or two-hybrid experiment, or the protein exerting a biochemical activity and its substrate), which for some experimental systems is arbitrary or up to the curator. Self-loops (e.g. proteins forming homodimers) are kept. The edges are divided in two layers, physical and genetic interactions. Except for the viruses, only interactions where both genes belong to the organism of the network are included; interactions with genes of other organisms (e.g. host-pathogen interactions, 113,903 records in the human data) are left out. Other attributes of the records (e.g. their qualifications, tags, ontology terms, and the protein accessions of the genes) are also left out.

The files of release 2.0.63 are in an older format, with fewer attributes: they identify genes by an identifier of their own (e.g. `ETG324243` for the Entrez Gene 324243, or the systematic name, e.g. `YDR001C`), and give neither the BioGRID identifiers of genes and interactions, nor the type of interaction (physical or genetic), which is set here from the experimental system, as in the later releases (all the experimental systems of 2.0.63 exist in the later releases, each with a single type).

See also the `yeast_biogrid_2007` entry (yeast protein interactions from the 2007 version of BioGRID) and the `genetic_multiplex` entry (multiplex networks of several organisms from the 2014 version of BioGRID, where the layers are the interaction types).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the official symbol of the gene.
- (Node) `systematic_name`: the systematic name of the gene, if any (e.g. the ORF name of yeast genes); not in release 2.0.63.
- (Node) `biogrid_id`: the identifier of the gene in BioGRID; not in release 2.0.63.
- (Node) `entrez_id`: the identifier of the gene in Entrez Gene (-1 if absent); not in release 2.0.63.
- (Node) `taxid` (viruses only): the NCBI taxonomy identifier of the organism of the gene (e.g. 9606 for human genes).
- (Node) `organism` (viruses only, not in release 2.0.63): the name of the organism of the gene, as given by BioGRID (e.g. `Homo sapiens`).
- (Node) `is_virus` (viruses only): whether the gene belongs to the virus of the network (otherwise to another organism, typically its host).
- (Node) `id` (release 2.0.63 only): the identifier of the gene in that release (`ETG` followed by the Entrez Gene identifier, or another identifier, e.g. the systematic name).
- (Edge) `layer`: the type of the interaction, `physical` or `genetic`.
- (Edge) `experimental_system`: the experimental system that detected the interaction (e.g. `Two-hybrid`, `Affinity Capture-MS`, `Synthetic Lethality`, `Negative Genetic`); see the [BioGRID wiki](https://wiki.thebiogrid.org/doku.php/experimental_systems) for their definitions.
- (Edge) `pubmed_id`: the PubMed identifier of the publication reporting the interaction (-1 if the publication is identified by its DOI instead).
- (Edge) `author`: the first author and year of the publication, e.g. `Xu Z (2008)`.

The following edge properties are not given in release 2.0.63:

- (Edge) `doi`: the DOI of the publication, for publications without a PubMed identifier (empty otherwise).
- (Edge) `throughput`: whether the interaction comes from a `High Throughput` or `Low Throughput` experiment (or both, `High Throughput|Low Throughput`).
- (Edge) `score`: the quantitative score of the interaction reported by high-throughput studies (NaN if absent).
- (Edge) `modification`: the post-translational modification of the substrate, for interactions of the experimental system `Biochemical Activity` (empty otherwise).
- (Edge) `interaction_id`: the identifier of the interaction record in BioGRID.
citations: R. Oughtred, J. Rust, C. Chang, B.-J. Breitkreutz, C. Stark, A. Willems, L. Boucher, G. Leung, N. Kolas, F. Zhang, S. Dolma, J. Coulombe-Huntington, A. Chatr-aryamontri, K. Dolinski, M. Tyers, "The BioGRID database: A comprehensive biomedical resource of curated protein, genetic, and chemical interactions." Protein Science 30(1), 187-200 (2021)
C. Stark, B.-J. Breitkreutz, T. Reguly, L. Boucher, A. Breitkreutz, M. Tyers, "BioGRID: a general repository for interaction datasets." Nucleic Acids Research 34(suppl 1), D535-D539 (2006)

datasets.name: bioplex
datasets.description:
Networks of protein interactions in human cell lines from the BioPlex project of the Gygi and Harper labs (Harvard Medical School). BioPlex maps the human interactome by affinity purification and mass spectrometry (AP-MS): each of thousands of human proteins (the *baits*, expressed from the ORFeome collection with an epitope tag) is purified from the cells together with the proteins bound to it (the *preys*), which are identified by mass spectrometry. The candidate bait-prey pairs are scored with the CompPASS-Plus classifier, which estimates for each pair the probabilities of a wrong protein identification, of a nonspecific (background) association, and of a genuine interaction; the published networks keep the pairs classified as interactions. Since the proteins in a purification may be bound indirectly, through other members of the same complex, the interactions are co-complex associations rather than necessarily direct (binary) contacts. Nodes are proteins, identified by the Entrez (NCBI) Gene IDs of the genes that encode them.

The entry contains every network offered for download on the BioPlex site:

- `1.0_293T`, `2.0_293T`, `3.0_293T`, `3.0_HCT116`: the official undirected networks of BioPlex 1.0 (2,594 baits in HEK293T cells, Huttlin et al. 2015), BioPlex 2.0 (5,891 baits in HEK293T cells, Huttlin et al. 2017), and BioPlex 3.0 (10,128 baits in HEK293T cells and 5,522 baits in HCT116 cells, Huttlin et al. 2021). An undirected edge joins two proteins found to interact, whichever was the bait.
- `1.0_293T_directed`, `2.0_293T_directed`, `3.0_293T_directed`, `3.0_HCT116_directed`: the same networks as directed bait-prey interactions, with a directed edge from the bait to each of its interacting preys (as distributed separately by the BioPlex site; a pair of proteins that found each other as baits is joined by two opposite edges, so that the numbers of edges differ slightly from the undirected networks).
- `2.0_293T_unfiltered`, `3.0_293T_unfiltered`, `3.0_HCT116_unfiltered`: all the candidate bait-prey pairs of BioPlex 2.0 and of BioPlex 3.0 (HEK293T and HCT116 cells) before filtering, i.e. every protein detected in the purification of every bait, with the CompPASS scores and classifier probabilities (the BioPlex site warns that these lists contain background and nonspecific interactors). A directed edge goes from the bait to each protein detected with it, so that the bait's own detection is a self-loop. Each edge is one identified protein (database entry), so that several isoforms or entries of the same gene give multiple edges between the same pair of nodes.
- `293T_2015-12`, `293T_2016-05`, `293T_2016-08`, `293T_2016-12`, `293T_2017-04`, `293T_2017-10`: the quarterly releases of interactions of new baits in HEK293T cells (U41 grant), released before their publication in BioPlex 3.0.
- `HCT116_2018-11`, `HCT116_2019-03`, `HCT116_2019-05`, `HCT116_2019-08`, `HCT116_2019-11`, `HCT116_2020-02`, `HCT116_2020-05`, `HCT116_2021-02`, `HCT116_2021-05`, `HCT116_2021-08`, `HCT116_2021-11`: the quarterly releases of interactions of new baits in HCT116 cells (U24 grant); the releases of August and November 2020 were not made because of the COVID-19 shutdown.
- `U2OS_0.1`, `RPE1_0.1`: preliminary networks (version 0.1) of 2,279 baits in U2OS cells (released in August 2021) and of 1,925 baits in RPE-1 cells (released in February 2022).

In the quarterly releases and the preliminary networks, a directed edge goes from the bait to each interacting prey (as classified by CompPASS-Plus), including the bait itself as a self-loop when it was detected, and, in the quarterly releases, each edge is one identified protein, so that several isoforms or entries of the same gene give multiple edges. The BioPlex site describes the quarterly releases and the preliminary networks as unpublished data, and asks users not to publish large-scale analyses of them before they are published by the authors. In the unfiltered lists and the quarterly releases, the few detected proteins without a Gene ID are identified by their UniProt entry instead (e.g. `sp|P01891|1A68_HUMAN`). Baits that were not found to interact with anything do not appear in the networks. The descriptions of the proteins in the unfiltered lists (taken from UniProt) and the proteome comparison of HEK293T and HCT116 cells (also available on the site) are not included.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the Entrez Gene ID of the protein (or the UniProt entry of a detected protein without a Gene ID).
- (Node) `symbol`: the gene symbol.
- (Node) `is_bait`: whether the protein was used as a bait (from the lists of baits of the official networks, and otherwise whether the node is the source of edges).
- (Node) `uniprot` (official undirected networks): the UniProt accession of the protein (or isoform) identified.
- (Edge) `p_wrong_id`, `p_no_interaction`, `p_interaction` (official undirected networks, unfiltered lists, quarterly releases and preliminary networks): the CompPASS-Plus probabilities that the pair is a wrong identification, a nonspecific (background) association, or a genuine interaction.
- (Edge) `protein_id` (unfiltered lists and quarterly releases): the UniProt entry of the identified protein (e.g. `sp|P05387|RLA2_HUMAN`).
- (Edge) `ave_apsm`, `nwd_score`, `z_score`, `plate_z_score`, `entropy`, `unique_peptides`, `ratio`, `total_psms`, `ratio_total_psms`, `unique_to_total_ratio` (unfiltered lists): the CompPASS scores of the pair (Sowa et al. 2009, Huttlin et al. 2015), named `ave_apsm`, `nwdscore`, `zscore`, `plate_zscore`, `entropy`, `uPeps`, `ratio`, `total_psms`, `ratioTotalPSMs` and `UtoTratio` upstream; `ave_apsm` is the average number of assembled peptide spectral matches of the prey, and `nwd_score` the normalized weighted D score.
- (Node) `compass_id` (unfiltered lists): the CompPASS id of the bait's purification (-1 for proteins that were not baits).
- (Edge) `plate`, `well` (quarterly releases and preliminary networks): the plate and well of the purification.
citations: E. L. Huttlin, L. Ting, R. J. Bruckner, F. Gebreab, M. P. Gygi, J. Szpyt, et al., "The BioPlex Network: A Systematic Exploration of the Human Interactome." Cell 162, 425-440 (2015)

E. L. Huttlin, R. J. Bruckner, J. A. Paulo, J. R. Cannon, L. Ting, K. Baltier, et al., "Architecture of the human interactome defines protein communities and disease networks." Nature 545, 505-509 (2017)

E. L. Huttlin, R. J. Bruckner, J. Navarrete-Perea, J. R. Cannon, K. Baltier, F. Gebreab, et al., "Dual proteome-scale networks reveal cell-specific remodeling of the human interactome." Cell 184, 3022-3040 (2021)

datasets.name: bitcoin
datasets.description:
A network of payment transactions between Bitcoin addresses, spanning January 2009 to April 2013. The data were derived from the public Bitcoin blockchain in the Bitcoin Transaction Network Dataset published in 2013 by I. Brugere, and comprise over 37 million transactions between public-key "addresses". They were aggregated into a network by M. Fire and C. Guestrin for their study of the evolution of network stars. Nodes are addresses (identified only by numeric identifiers), and a directed edge points from one address to another if at least one payment was made from the first to the second; multiple transactions between the same pair of addresses are aggregated into a single edge.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `id`: the numeric identifier of the address in the source data.
- (Node) `first_transaction`: the date and time of the first transaction of the address (format YYYYMMDDTHHMMSS).
- (Edge) `count`: the number of transactions between the two addresses.
- (Edge) `min_date` and `max_date`: the date and time of the first and last of these transactions (format YYYYMMDDTHHMMSS).
citations: M. Fire and C. Guestrin, "The Rise and Fall of Network Stars." Preprint, arXiv:1706.06690 (2017)

datasets.name: bitcoin_alpha
datasets.description:
A who-trusts-whom network of users of Bitcoin Alpha, an online platform for trading with Bitcoin. Since Bitcoin users are anonymous, the platform let members rate each other to build a record of reputation that helps prevent transactions with fraudulent or risky users. A directed edge $i \to j$ means that user $i$ rated user $j$, on a scale from -10 (total distrust) to +10 (total trust) in steps of 1 (a rating of 0 is not possible). The data, covering ratings made from November 2010 to January 2016, were collected and released by S. Kumar and collaborators as the first explicit weighted signed directed network available for research.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the anonymized user identifier.
- (Edge) `rating`: the rating (an integer from -10 to +10, excluding 0).
- (Edge) `time`: the time of the rating, in seconds since the Unix epoch (with a resolution of one day).
citations: S. Kumar, F. Spezzano, V.S. Subrahmanian, and C. Faloutsos, "Edge weight prediction in weighted signed networks." IEEE 16th International Conference on Data Mining (ICDM), 221-230 (2016)

datasets.name: bitcoin_transactions
datasets.description:
Directed bipartite networks of Bitcoin addresses and the transactions in which they send or receive bitcoins, for three samples of the Bitcoin blockchain: the first 1.5 million transactions recorded in November 2014, June 2015 and January 2016. A Bitcoin transaction spends outputs of earlier transactions (its inputs), each controlled by an address, and creates new outputs, each paid to an address; the newly mined bitcoins enter through the first transaction of each block (the coinbase transaction), which has no inputs. The data are extracted from the public Bitcoin dataset of Google BigQuery (`bigquery-public-data.crypto_bitcoin.transactions`), which is produced from the blockchain with the open-source bitcoin-etl software.

- `2014_11`: blocks 327,939 to 330,624 (2014-11-01 00:03 to 2014-11-18 21:12 UTC), 1,501,123 transactions.
- `2015_06`: blocks 358,881 to 360,815 (2015-06-01 00:02 to 2015-06-13 23:14 UTC), 1,500,742 transactions.
- `2016_01`: blocks 391,182 to 392,551 (2016-01-01 00:03 to 2016-01-09 23:15 UTC), 1,500,831 transactions.

Each sample consists of the complete blocks from the first block of the month (by block timestamp, in UTC) to the block that contains the 1,500,000th transaction of the month.

A node is either an address or a transaction. An edge from an address to a transaction is an input of the transaction, spending an output previously paid to the address; an edge from a transaction to an address is an output of the transaction, paying bitcoins to the address. Addresses are included only as they occur in the inputs and outputs of the sampled transactions. An address that occurs in several inputs (or outputs) of the same transaction is connected to it by parallel edges. An output whose script involves several public keys (bare multisignature outputs) is connected to each of them, with the full value of the output on each edge. Outputs whose script does not encode an address (e.g. data-carrying OP_RETURN outputs or nonstandard scripts) are assigned by bitcoin-etl a pseudo-address `nonstandard<hash of the script>`, and have script type "nonstandard".

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `is_transaction`: whether the node is a transaction (otherwise an address).
- (Node) `name`: the address or the transaction hash.
- (Node) `block_number` (transactions): the height of the block containing the transaction (-1 for addresses).
- (Node) `time` (transactions): the block timestamp (Unix time, in seconds; -1 for addresses).
- (Node) `is_coinbase` (transactions): whether the transaction is a coinbase transaction (false for addresses).
- (Node) `fee` (transactions): the transaction fee in satoshi (10^-8 bitcoin), i.e. the total value of the inputs minus that of the outputs (-1 for addresses).
- (Node) `size` (transactions): the size of the transaction in bytes (-1 for addresses).
- (Edge) `index`: the position of the input or output in the transaction.
- (Edge) `value`: the value of the input or output in satoshi.
- (Edge) `script_type`: the type of the script as classified by bitcoin-etl (pubkeyhash, scripthash, multisig, pubkey or nonstandard).

**Relation to the hypergraphx datasets.** These samples correspond to the datasets bitcoin-2014, bitcoin-2015 and bitcoin-2016 of Kim et al. (2023), which contain the first 1,500,000 transactions of each month as collected by Wu et al. (2022), and to the datasets crypto-bitcoin-201411, crypto-bitcoin-201506 and crypto-bitcoin-201601 of the hypergraphx-data repository, derived from them. Hypergraphx represents each transaction by the set of distinct addresses of its inputs (here: its in-neighbors) and the set of distinct addresses of its outputs (here: its out-neighbors), annotated with the total input value and the block time. Compared with the networks here, the hypergraphx datasets (i) contain no coinbase transactions, and only about 91% (2014), 94% (2015) and 98% (2016) of the other transactions, with no evident selection rule (the omitted transactions are presumably missing from the data of Wu et al.); (ii) end exactly at the 1,500,000th transaction, inside the last block, while here the last block is complete (at most about 1,100 extra transactions); and (iii) give the block times shifted by the offset of Central European time (one hour earlier in the 2014 and 2016 samples, two hours in the 2015 one).
citations: J. Wu, J. Liu, W. Chen, H. Huang, Z. Zheng, Y. Zhang, "Detecting Mixing Services via Mining Bitcoin Transaction Network With Hybrid Motifs." IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics: Systems 52(4), 2237-2249 (2022)
S. Kim, M. Choe, J. Yoo, K. Shin, "Reciprocity in directed hypergraphs: measures, findings, and generators." Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery 37, 2330-2388 (2023)

datasets.name: bitcoin_trust
datasets.description:
A who-trusts-whom network of users of Bitcoin OTC, an online over-the-counter marketplace for trading with Bitcoin. Since Bitcoin users are anonymous, the platform let members rate each other to build a record of reputation that helps prevent transactions with fraudulent or risky users. Nodes are users, and a directed edge $i \to j$ means that user $i$ rated user $j$, on a scale from -10 (total distrust) to +10 (total trust) in steps of 1 (a rating of 0 is not possible). The data, covering ratings made from November 2010 to January 2016, were collected and released by S. Kumar and collaborators.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the anonymized user identifier.
- (Edge) `rating`: the rating (an integer from -10 to +10, excluding 0).
- (Edge) `time`: the time of the rating, in seconds since the Unix epoch (a floating-point number, with sub-second resolution).
citations: S. Kumar, F. Spezzano, V.S. Subrahmanian, and C. Faloutsos, "Edge weight prediction in weighted signed networks." IEEE 16th International Conference on Data Mining (ICDM), 221-230 (2016)

datasets.name: bks_interactions
datasets.description:
Social interactions in bounded groups, collected by H. R. Bernard, P. D. Killworth and L. Sailer in their studies of the accuracy of informants' recall of their interactions. For each group, they obtained a behavioral measure of the interactions among all actors, and rankings based on the subjects' memory of those interactions (cognitive data). The data were distributed in UCINET format (from the UCINET data collection of S. P. Borgatti, M. G. Everett and L. C. Freeman) on the Pajek datasets page of V. Batagelj and A. Mrvar, from which this version was obtained.

- `frat_behavioral`, `frat_cognitive`: a fraternity at a West Virginia college (58 students who had lived in the fraternity from three months to three years); the behavioral data are the number of times a pair of students were seen in conversation by an unobtrusive observer, who walked through the public areas of the building every fifteen minutes, 21 hours a day, for five days.
- `ham_behavioral`, `ham_cognitive`: 44 amateur (HAM) radio operators; the behavioral data are the radio calls made over a one-month period, as monitored by a voice-activated recording device.
- `off_behavioral`, `off_cognitive`: 40 employees of a small business office; the behavioral data are the observed frequencies of interactions, recorded by an unobtrusive observer who patrolled a fixed route through the office every fifteen minutes during two four-day periods.
- `tec_behavioral`, `tec_cognitive`: 34 members of a technical research group at a West Virginia university; the behavioral data are the interactions recorded by an observer every half-hour during one five-day work week.

In the behavioral networks (undirected), two actors are connected if they were observed interacting, and the edge is weighted by the number of observed interactions. In the cognitive networks (directed), an edge points from the subject to another actor, and is weighted by the subject's ranking of how frequently they interacted in the observation period (the scale of the rankings differs between groups).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Edge) `weight`: the number of observed interactions (behavioral networks) or the ranking given by the subject (cognitive networks).
citations: P. D. Killworth, H. R. Bernard, "Informant Accuracy in Social Network Data." Human Organization 35(3), 269-286 (1976)

H. R. Bernard, P. D. Killworth, L. Sailer, "Informant accuracy in social network data IV: a comparison of clique-level structure in behavioral and cognitive network data." Social Networks 2(3), 191-218 (1979)
S. P. Borgatti, M. G. Everett, L. C. Freeman, "UCINET for Windows: Software for Social Network Analysis." Analytic Technologies, Harvard, MA (2002)

datasets.name: blogcatalog_asu
datasets.description:
Networks of friendships among the bloggers of BlogCatalog, a social blog directory website, from two crawls distributed by the Social Computing Data Repository (originally at Arizona State University, now at Syracuse University; the versions used here, in XML format, are those of 2010, obtained from the Internet Archive, which include the metadata of the blogs). In BlogCatalog, users register their blogs under a hierarchy of predefined categories, tag them, and declare friendships with other users. In both networks, nodes are bloggers.

- `july_2009`: crawled in July 2009 by N. Agarwal, X. Wang and H. Liu. An undirected edge connects two bloggers who are friends (the source lists each friendship under both users; 2,093,195 friendships among 88,784 bloggers). For the 80,950 bloggers whose blogs were also crawled, the nodes are annotated with the categories, languages and tags of their blogs.
- `june_2010`: crawled in June 2010 by R. Zafarani and H. Liu. The friend lists of 10,152 bloggers were crawled; a directed edge $i \to j$ indicates that blogger $j$ is listed as a friend of blogger $i$ (97,884 bloggers and 2,043,701 friend listings, of which 634,683 are reciprocated within the data; 55 are self-loops).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `user_id`: the identifier of the blogger in the source data (the identifiers of the two crawls are not necessarily related).
- (Node) `name`: the user name of the blogger.
- (Node) `blogs` (`july_2009`): the number of blogs of the blogger in the data (0 if none were crawled).
- (Node) `categories` (`july_2009`): the categories of the blogger's blogs (out of 344), e.g. "Personal" or "Green".
- (Node) `languages` (`july_2009`): the languages of the blogger's blogs.
- (Node) `tags` (`july_2009`): the tags of the blogger's blogs.
citations: R. Zafarani, H. Liu, "Connecting corresponding identities across communities." Proceedings of the International AAAI Conference on Weblogs and Social Media 3(1), 354-357 (2009)

N. Agarwal, H. Liu, S. Murthy, A. Sen, X. Wang, "A social identity approach to identify familiar strangers in a social network." Proceedings of the International AAAI Conference on Weblogs and Social Media 3(1), 2-9 (2009)
R. Zafarani, H. Liu, "Social Computing Data Repository at ASU." Arizona State University, School of Computing, Informatics and Decision Systems Engineering (2009)

datasets.name: blumenau_drug
datasets.description:
A network of known drug–drug interactions (DDI) co-administered to patients in the city of Blumenau, in Southern Brazil, constructed by R. Brattig Correia and collaborators from 18 months (January 2014 to June 2015) of drug dispensation records of the city's public health information system. Medications were matched to their DrugBank identifiers, and a pair of drugs is considered a known interaction if it is listed in DrugBank (2011 version). Nodes are the 75 drugs involved in at least one co-administration of a known DDI, and an undirected edge connects two drugs if they form a known DDI and were co-administered (dispensed with overlapping administration periods) to at least one patient.

The strength of association of a drug pair is measured by $\tau_{ij}$: for each patient $u$, the overlap of the administration of drugs $i$ and $j$ is $\tau^u_{ij} = \lambda^u_{ij}/(\lambda^u_i + \lambda^u_j - \lambda^u_{ij})$, where $\lambda^u_i$ is the length of administration of drug $i$ and $\lambda^u_{ij}$ the length of co-administration, and $\tau_{ij}$ is the average of $\tau^u_{ij}$ over all patients co-administered the pair. The gender bias of an interaction is measured by the relative risk of interaction for women, $RRI^F_{ij}$, the ratio between the fraction of female and of male patients who were co-administered the pair, with $RRI^M_{ij} = 1/RRI^F_{ij}$.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the DrugBank identifier.
- (Node) `label`: the drug name.
- (Node) `class`: the primary action class of the drug (from Drugs.com).
- (Node) `hormone`: whether the drug is a hormone ("True" or "False").
- (Node) `p_node`: the probability of interaction of the drug, i.e. the fraction of its co-administrations that are known DDIs.
- (Node) `len_i`: a numerical value whose meaning is not documented in the source data.
- (Node) `color`: the color used for the drug class in the visualization of the original publication.
- (Edge) `tau`: the association strength $\tau_{ij}$ (rounded to two decimals).
- (Edge) `tau_norm` and `weight`: $\tau_{ij}$ rescaled to the range 1 to 10 (for visualization).
- (Edge) `patients`: the number of patients who were co-administered the pair.
- (Edge) `patients_norm`: the same rescaled to the range 1 to 15.
- (Edge) `RRI^F` and `RRI^M`: the relative risks of interaction for women and men.
- (Edge) `gender`: the gender with the higher relative risk.
- (Edge) `severity`: the severity of the interaction according to Drugs.com ("Major", "Moderate", "Minor", "None", or "\*", the latter undocumented).
- (Edge) `color`: the edge color used in the original publication.
citations: R. Brattig Correia et al. "City-wide electronic health records reveal gender and age biases in administration of known drug–drug interactions." npj Digital Medicine 2, 74 (2019)

datasets.name: bnlearn
datasets.description:
Directed acyclic graphs of reference (discrete) Bayesian networks commonly used as benchmarks for Bayesian network learning and inference, as collected in the Bayesian Network Repository of the bnlearn R package by M. Scutari. Most of these networks were constructed by domain experts as probabilistic expert systems, and many were previously distributed by the Bayesian Network Repository of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. Nodes are random variables, and a directed edge from A to B means that A is a parent of B, i.e. that the probability distribution of B is specified conditionally on A. The networks in bnlearn have been checked and fixed where needed (e.g. so that the conditional probability tables sum to one, and without dummy single-state nodes or dependencies on nonexistent nodes), so their sizes may differ from other versions of the same networks.

The networks are:

- `asia`: a small fictitious model relating lung diseases, visits to Asia, smoking, X-ray results and dyspnoea (Lauritzen and Spiegelhalter, 1988).
- `cancer` and `earthquake`: small textbook examples from Korb and Nicholson, "Bayesian Artificial Intelligence" (2010).
- `sachs`: a causal protein-signaling network in human immune system cells, inferred from flow cytometry data (Sachs et al., 2005).
- `survey`: a textbook example on the usage of different means of transport, from Scutari and Denis, "Bayesian Networks: with Examples in R" (2021).
- `alarm`: the ALARM (A Logical Alarm Reduction Mechanism) system for patient monitoring in intensive care (Beinlich et al., 1989).
- `barley`: a preliminary model for a decision support system for growing malting barley without pesticides (Kristensen and Rasmussen, 2002).
- `child`: a diagnostic system for congenital heart disease in newborn babies ("blue babies") (Spiegelhalter and Cowell, 1992).
- `insurance`: a network for estimating the expected claim costs of car insurance policyholders (Binder et al., 1997).
- `mildew`: a model for the management of mildew in winter wheat (Jensen and Jensen, 1996).
- `water`: an expert system for the control of waste water treatment (Jensen et al., 1989).
- `hailfinder`: a system for forecasting severe weather in northeastern Colorado (Abramson et al., 1996).
- `hepar2`: a system for diagnosis of liver disorders (Onisko, 2003).
- `win95pts`: a system for troubleshooting printing problems in Microsoft Windows 95.
- `andes`: a model of a student's knowledge in the ANDES intelligent tutoring system for Newtonian physics (Conati et al., 1997).
- `diabetes`: a model of carbohydrate metabolism used for insulin dose adjustment (Andreassen et al., 1991).
- `link`: a model for linkage analysis in genetics, over a large pedigree (Jensen and Kong, 1999).
- `munin`, `munin1`, `munin2`, `munin3`, `munin4`: the MUNIN expert system for electromyography (Andreassen et al., 1989), as the full network and four subnetworks.
- `pathfinder`: the PATHFINDER expert system for the diagnosis of lymph-node diseases (Heckerman et al., 1992).
- `pigs`: a pedigree model for the breeding of pigs.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the variable.
- (Node) `n_states`: the number of values (states) the discrete variable can take.
- (Node) `states`: the names of the states.
citations: M. Scutari, "Learning Bayesian Networks with the bnlearn R Package." Journal of Statistical Software 35(3), 1-22 (2010)

S. Lauritzen, D. Spiegelhalter, "Local Computations with Probabilities on Graphical Structures and Their Application to Expert Systems." Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B 50(2), 157-194 (1988)
K. Sachs, O. Perez, D. Pe'er, D. A. Lauffenburger, G. P. Nolan, "Causal Protein-Signaling Networks Derived from Multiparameter Single-Cell Data." Science 308, 523-529 (2005)

I. A. Beinlich, H. J. Suermondt, R. M. Chavez, G. F. Cooper, "The ALARM Monitoring System: A Case Study with two Probabilistic Inference Techniques for Belief Networks." AIME 89, Lecture Notes in Medical Informatics 38, 247-256 (1989)

K. Kristensen, I. A. Rasmussen, "The use of a Bayesian network in the design of a decision support system for growing malting barley without use of pesticides." Computers and Electronics in Agriculture 33(3), 197-217 (2002)
D. J. Spiegelhalter, R. G. Cowell, "Learning in probabilistic expert systems." In Bayesian Statistics 4, 447-466, Clarendon Press (1992)
J. Binder, D. Koller, S. Russell, K. Kanazawa, "Adaptive Probabilistic Networks with Hidden Variables." Machine Learning 29, 213-244 (1997)
