datasets.name: board_directors
datasets.description:
Monthly snapshots of the boards of directors of Norwegian public limited companies (allmennaksjeselskap, ASA), from May 2002 to August 2011, compiled by C. Seierstad and T. Opsahl from the Norwegian Business Register. The period covers the introduction of the Norwegian law requiring at least 40% of the board members of public limited companies to be women. For each month there are two undirected networks (112 months, 224 networks in total), named by the date of the snapshot:

- `net2m_YYYY-MM-01`: a bipartite network of companies and directors, in which an edge connects a director to each company on whose board they sit.
- `net1m_YYYY-MM-01`: the one-mode projection onto the directors, in which two directors are connected if they sit on at least one common board (unweighted).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `vid`: the identifier of the director (or company) in the source data, consistent across snapshots.
- (Node) `name`: the name of the director or company.
- (Node) `gender`: the gender of the director (1: male, 2: female; 0 for companies).
- (Node) `is_company` (`net2m` only): whether the node is a company (otherwise a director).
- (Node) `organization` (companies, `net2m` only): the company's registration number in the Norwegian Business Register.
- (Node) `location` (companies, `net2m` only): the postal code and city of the company.
citations: C. Seierstad and T. Opsahl, "For the few not the many? The effects of affirmative action on presence, prominence, and social capital of women directors in Norway." Scand. J. Manag. 27(1), 44-54 (2011).

datasets.name: bookcrossing
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of users of the BookCrossing community (a website for exchanging books) and the books they rated, collected by C.-N. Ziegler in a 4-week crawl in August and September 2004, with the permission of the site's operators. Nodes are users and books, and an edge connects a user to a book the user rated, with the rating as edge weight. Ratings are either explicit, on a scale from 1 to 10 (higher values denoting higher appreciation), or implicit (a recorded interaction with the book without a rating), which are given the value 0. User ids are anonymized, and books are identified by their ISBN; according to the source, invalid ISBNs were removed from the book table, but the rating table contains some ISBNs that are malformed or not in the book table. Book information was obtained from Amazon Web Services. The network includes only the users and books that appear in some rating (the source also lists 173,575 users without ratings).

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `is_book`: whether the node is a book (otherwise it is a user).
- (Node) `user_id` (users): the anonymized user id.
- (Node) `location` (users): the user's location as given ("city, region, country").
- (Node) `age` (users): the user's age as given (-1 if unknown; some values are implausible).
- (Node) `isbn` (books): the ISBN of the book.
- (Node) `title`, `author`, `year`, `publisher` (books): the title, the author (only the first, if several), the year of publication (0 if unknown) and the publisher, for the 270,170 rated books listed in the book table (empty otherwise).
- (Edge) `rating`: the rating, from 1 to 10, or 0 for an implicit rating.
citations: C.-N. Ziegler, S. M. McNee, J. A. Konstan, G. Lausen, "Improving recommendation lists through topic diversification." Proceedings of the 14th International Conference on World Wide Web (WWW 2005), 22-32 (2005)

datasets.name: brain_coactivation
datasets.description:
Weighted networks of 638 regions of the human brain (the gray matter excluding the cerebellum, parcellated into regions of similar size that respect anatomical landmarks), from Crossley et al., as distributed with the Brain Connectivity Toolbox. Nodes are brain regions, and an undirected edge connects two regions with strong functional coactivation or connectivity, as defined below.

- `coactivation`: the functional coactivation network, from a meta-analysis of the BrainMap database comprising 6,884 task-related contrasts from 1,641 functional MRI and PET studies of healthy adults published between 1985 and 2010. Each reported activation was modeled as a 1 cm³ sphere around its coordinates, and a region was considered activated by a contrast if at least 20% of a sphere overlapped it. Two regions are connected if their coactivation, measured by the Jaccard index (the number of contrasts activating both regions divided by the number of contrasts activating either), is significantly larger than expected by chance (P < 0.01, false-discovery-rate corrected).
- `rsfmri`: the resting-state functional connectivity network of the same regions, from 3T functional MRI scans of 27 healthy volunteers (5 min, eyes closed). The Pearson correlations between the band-pass filtered (0.01-0.1 Hz) regional time series were Fisher-transformed and averaged over the volunteers, and two regions are connected if their correlation is among the strongest, keeping as many edges as in the coactivation network. Two regions have no connections in this network.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `coord`: the (x, y, z) coordinates of the region in standard stereotactic space, in millimeters (the regions have no names in the source data).
- (Edge) `weight`: the Jaccard index of coactivation (`coactivation`), or the group-average Fisher-transformed correlation (`rsfmri`).
citations: N. A. Crossley, A. Mechelli, P. E. Vértes, T. T. Winton-Brown, A. X. Patel, C. E. Ginestet, P. McGuire, E. T. Bullmore, "Cognitive relevance of the community structure of the human brain functional coactivation network." Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 110(28), 11583-11588 (2013)
M. Rubinov, O. Sporns, "Complex network measures of brain connectivity: Uses and interpretations." NeuroImage 52(3), 1059-1069 (2010)

datasets.name: budapest_connectome
datasets.description:
Consensus human structural brain networks (connectomes) from the Budapest Reference Connectome Server v3.0, built by B. Szalkai, C. Kerepesi, B. Varga and V. Grolmusz from the diffusion MRI data of 477 healthy adult subjects of the Human Connectome Project. For each subject, a connectome was computed by tractography (with the Connectome Mapper Toolkit), in which nodes are 1,015 anatomical regions of the brain (1,000 cortical and 15 subcortical) and edges connect regions linked by tracked fibers (streamlines). The individual connectomes were then combined into a consensus graph, where an edge is present if it occurs in at least one of the subjects.

There are nine networks, depending on the subject population (`all` subjects, `female` or `male` only) and on the total number of fibers tracked per subject (`20k`, `200k` or `1m`), named `<population>_<fibers>`.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `dn_name`: the name of the region, prefixed by the hemisphere (e.g. `rh.lateralorbitofrontal_9`).
- (Node) `dn_fsname`: the region name without the hemisphere prefix.
- (Node) `dn_hemisphere`: the hemisphere (`left` or `right`).
- (Node) `dn_region`: whether the region is `cortical` or `subcortical`.
- (Edge) `occurences`: the number of subjects in whose connectome the edge is present.
- (Edge) `fiber_count_mean` and `fiber_count_median`: the mean and median number of fibers connecting the two regions.
- (Edge) `fiber_length_mean` and `fiber_length_median`: the mean and median average length of those fibers.
- (Edge) `fractional_anisotropy_mean` and `fractional_anisotropy_median`: the mean and median average fractional anisotropy along the fibers.
- (Edge) `electrical_connectivity_mean` and `electrical_connectivity_median`: the mean and median "electrical connectivity", i.e. the number of fibers divided by their average length. Means and medians are taken over the subjects in which the edge is present.
citations: B. Szalkai, C. Kerepesi, B. Varga and V. Grolmusz, "Parameterizable consensus connectomes from the Human Connectome Project: the Budapest Reference Connectome Server v3.0." Cognitive Neurodynamics 11, 113-116 (2017)
B. Szalkai et al., "The Budapest Reference Connectome Server v2.0." Neuroscience Letters 595, 60-62 (2015)

datasets.name: caida_as
datasets.description:
A sequence of 122 snapshots of the network of relationships between Autonomous Systems (AS) of the Internet, from January 2004 to November 2007, from the CAIDA AS Relationships Dataset as compiled by J. Leskovec and collaborators. An autonomous system is a network or group of networks under a single administrative policy (such as an Internet service provider, university or company), and the AS graph describes which of them exchange traffic. Each snapshot is derived from a set of RouteViews BGP routing table snapshots, and the business relationship of each pair of connected ASes (customer–provider, peer–peer, or sibling, i.e. belonging to the same organization) was inferred by CAIDA with the Serial-1 method and a set of heuristics. Snapshots are approximately weekly in 2006 and later, and monthly before, and are named by their date (YYYYMMDD).

Nodes are ASes, and an undirected edge connects two ASes that have a business relationship (i.e. exchange traffic), with one edge for each pair of connected ASes (the source lists each relationship in both directions).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `as_id`: the AS number.
- (Edge) `relationship`: the type of relationship, as seen from the source node of the edge: $-1$ (the source is a customer of the target), $0$ (peers) or $2$ (siblings). Customer–provider edges are always stored with the customer as the source node.

datasets.name: caida_as_relationships
datasets.description:
Monthly snapshots, from January 1998 to October 2026, of the network of business relationships between the Autonomous Systems (AS) of the Internet, from the CAIDA AS Relationships Dataset. An autonomous system is a network or group of networks under a single administrative policy (such as an Internet service provider, a university or a company), identified by its AS number. CAIDA infers the relationships between the ASes that are seen connected in the AS paths of public BGP routing tables (from the RouteViews and RIPE RIS collectors, over the first days of each month), with the method of Luckie et al. (IMC 2013) and its later revisions (e.g. the use of the IANA AS number assignments since 2015, and a fixed set of the largest providers, the "clique", since 2016, inferred automatically again at times between 2017 and 2019; earlier snapshots were not inferred again after these changes). Two kinds of relationships are distinguished: customer–provider (the customer pays the provider for transit to the rest of the Internet) and peer–peer (two ASes exchange the traffic of their own customers, usually without payment).

The data set has three series, all of which are included, with every snapshot available in the source (the snapshots of some months are missing, e.g. those of January, November and December 1999 in `serial-1`, and those of February and March 2020 in `serial-2`, withdrawn by CAIDA because of errors):

- `serial1_<date>` (e.g. `serial1_20260101`): the relationships inferred from the BGP data of IPv4 routes (`serial-1`; 343 snapshots, from January 1998).
- `serial1_v6_<date>`: the relationships inferred from the BGP data of IPv6 routes (the "v6-stable" files of `serial-1`; 142 snapshots, from January 2015).
- `serial2_<date>`: the `serial-1` relationships (IPv4) combined with relationships inferred from traceroutes of CAIDA's Archipelago (Ark) infrastructure (until August 2018) and from multilateral peering at Internet exchange points, from looking glass servers (missing from January to November 2023) (`serial-2`; 129 snapshots, from December 2015).

The snapshots are named by their date (YYYYMMDD, the first day of the month). Nodes are ASes, and directed edges are relationships: a customer–provider relationship is an edge from the customer to the provider, and a peer–peer relationship is a single edge in an arbitrary direction (from the smaller to the larger AS number).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `asn`: the AS number.
- (Node) `clique`: whether the AS belongs to the clique of the largest providers (inferred by the method, or given to it).
- (Node) `ixp`: whether the AS is an Internet exchange point (these are excluded from the inference).
- (Edge) `relationship`: $-1$ for customer–provider (the source node is the customer) and $0$ for peer–peer.
- (Edge) `step`: the step of the inference algorithm that inferred the relationship (given in the `serial1_<date>` snapshots of April 2012, of December 2018 to June 2020 and since December 2022, and $0$ in the others, including all the `serial1_v6_<date>` and `serial2_<date>` snapshots): $1$ (peering in the clique), $2$ (initial provider assignment), $3$ (providers for stub ASes), $4$ (provider to larger customer), $5$ (provider-less networks), $6$ (customer–provider for stub–clique relationships), $7$ (folding of peering links), $8$ (everything else is peering).
- (Edge) `source` (`serial2_<date>` only): the source of the inference: `bgp`, `mlp` (multilateral peering), `ark` (traceroutes), or several of these separated by commas.
citations: M. Luckie, B. Huffaker, A. Dhamdhere, V. Giotsas, k. claffy, "AS relationships, customer cones, and validation." Proceedings of the 2013 Internet Measurement Conference (IMC 2013), 243-256 (2013)
V. Giotsas, S. Zhou, M. Luckie, k. claffy, "Inferring multilateral peering." Proceedings of the 9th ACM Conference on Emerging Networking Experiments and Technologies (CoNEXT 2013), 247-258 (2013)
CAIDA, "The CAIDA UCSD AS Relationships Dataset (serial-1 and serial-2)." (1998-2026)

datasets.name: california_estuaries
datasets.description:
Food webs of three estuaries of the Pacific coast of California and Baja California, including parasites (infectious agents), life stages, body sizes and biomasses, compiled by R. F. Hechinger and colleagues: Carpinteria Salt Marsh, California, USA (CSM, 61 ha, data from 2003 to 2008), Estero de Punta Banda, Baja California, Mexico (EPB, 707 ha, 1992 to 2005), and Bahía Falsa in Bahía San Quintín, Baja California, Mexico (BSQ, 144 ha, 1994 to 2005). Most nodes and their body sizes and biomasses come from a stratified random sampling of the intertidal zone of each estuary (including birds, fishes and plankton), which quantified the plants and animals larger than about 1 mm and many infectious agents (mostly metazoan parasites, such as trematodes, cestodes, nematodes and acanthocephalans, but also some microbes); this was complemented with published sources and additional sampling of unrepresented groups. Nodes are species, or life stages of species with complex life cycles (e.g. the parthenitae, cercariae, metacercariae and adults of trematodes, or the larvae and adults of polychaetes and bivalves, each of which is a separate node), as well as some aggregated assemblages (e.g. phytoplankton, benthic diatoms, meiofauna) and non-living resources (detritus, carrion). A directed edge goes from a consumer to its resource (prey or host). The links include 21 possible types of interaction (13 of which occur in the data), covering four general kinds of interaction: predators consuming prey, parasites consuming hosts, predators consuming parasites, and parasites consuming parasites. Note that some link types do not represent resource dependencies (e.g. "concurrent predation on symbionts", i.e. a predator consuming the parasites of its prey, "trophic transmission", "commensalism"), and may need to be excluded from some analyses. Free-living links were constructed by extending the earlier Carpinteria Salt Marsh web of Lafferty et al. (2006), which this one supplants (the earlier web is the network `food_web_lafferty` of the entry `iwdb`, and is also included in `gateway_foodwebs`): links were assumed to occur in the other estuaries when the nodes co-occur, and links of new nodes were modeled after similar nodes of the earlier web, and then modified based on the literature and observations; most parasite links were directly observed. Some groups are missing or under-represented, such as plant parasites, bird and fish ectoparasites, flying insects, protists, viruses, fungi and bacteria.

The entry contains four networks:

- `metaweb`: the "metaweb" compiled from the nodes of all three estuaries (500 nodes, belonging to 314 species), with all 11,270 links projected to occur given the co-occurrence of the nodes. Of these, 9,247 are present in at least one of the estuaries, and the remaining 2,023 are hypothetical links between nodes that do not co-occur in any of the estuaries.
- `carpinteria`: the web of Carpinteria Salt Marsh.
- `punta_banda`: the web of Estero de Punta Banda.
- `bahia_falsa`: the web of Bahía Falsa in Bahía San Quintín.

The estuary webs are the subsets of the metaweb present in each estuary. Versions of the three estuary webs aggregated by species (with the life stages of each parasite merged into a single node, and fewer node attributes) are in the entry `coastal_parasite_webs`. The node "roots" (belowground biomass of the terrestrial plants) has no links, but is included because of its biomass. There are two self-loops (cannibalism) in the metaweb.

Node properties (all networks):

- `node_id`: the node identifier in the source, consistent across all four networks.
- `species_id`: the species identifier, shared by the nodes corresponding to different life stages of the same species; `stage_id`: the life stage within the species, where 1 is the adult, and higher numbers are younger stages (with a meaning that depends on the group, e.g. for trematodes 2 = parthenitae); `stage`: the name of the life stage ("adult", "larva", "pupa", "cercaria", "metacercaria", "parthenitae", "procercoid", "plerocercoid", or empty for non-living nodes).
- `name`: the working name of the node (common name, scientific name or descriptive name).
- `organismal_group`: a broad group of organisms (e.g. "trematode", "bird", "fish", "snail", "plant", "detritus").
- `node_type`: what the node represents ("taxon", "life stage" or "detritus").
- `resolution`: the lowest taxonomic level that the node represents (e.g. "Species", "Genus", "Family", "assemblage"); `resolution_notes`: notes on the resolution.
- `feeding`: whether the node is "feeding", "nonfeeding" (e.g. detritus and non-feeding life stages, such as cercariae) or an "autotroph".
- `lifestyle_stage` and `lifestyle_species`: whether the life stage, or the species as a whole, is "free-living", "infectious", "commensal" or "non-living".
- `consumer_strategy`: the consumer strategy of the life stage ("predator", "micropredator", "macroparasite", "parasitic castrator", "pathogen", "parasitoid", "trophically transmitted parasite", "detritivore", "autotroph", "nonfeeding", or empty for non-living nodes).
- `mobility`: the short-term mobility of the free-living nodes ("low", "intermediate" or "high"; empty if not given).
- `kingdom`, `phylum`, `subphylum`, `class`, `subclass`, `order`, `suborder`, `family`, `genus`, `specific_epithet`: the taxonomy of the node (empty if not given).
- `notes`: notes on the node.

Node properties (`metaweb` only):

- `in_csm`, `in_epb`, `in_bsq`: whether the node is present in the respective estuary.

Node properties (estuary webs only, specific to the estuary; numeric values are NaN when not given):

- `residency`: the long-term residency of the free-living nodes ("resident" or "migrant"; empty if not given).
- `body_size`: the mean body mass of an individual, in grams of wet weight (including hard parts, such as shells); `body_size_sd`: its standard deviation; `body_size_n`: the number of individuals measured; `body_size_estimation`: the method used to estimate the body size ("population": from the individuals sampled in the estuary; "species": from the literature, voucher specimens or volumetric estimates; "approximation": approximated from the body size of other nodes); `body_size_notes`: notes on the estimate.
- `abundance`: the mean density of individuals (number per hectare); `abundance_cl`: its 95% confidence limit, as given in the source; `abundance_df`: the degrees of freedom of the confidence limit (fractional, due to the stratified sampling).
- `biomass`: the mean biomass density, in kg (wet weight) per hectare; `biomass_cl`: its 95% confidence limit; `biomass_df`: the degrees of freedom of the confidence limit; `biomass_estimation`: the method used to estimate the biomass (e.g. "quantification, estuary-wide sampling", "quantified apportionment", "approximation, ratio", "field experience"; see Table 2B of the metadata of the source); `biomass_notes`: notes on the estimate.

Edge properties (all networks):

- `link_type`: the type of interaction, one of "predation", "micropredation", "parasitic castration", "pathogen infection", "macroparasitism", "parasitoid infection", "commensalism", "trophically transmitted parasitism", "concurrent predation on symbionts", "trophic transmission", "predation on free-living non-feeding stage", "detritivory" and "parasite intraguild antagonism" (see Table 3C of the metadata of the source for definitions); `link_type_id`: the corresponding numeric code of the source.
- `present_csm`, `present_epb`, `present_bsq`: whether the link is present in the respective estuary (in the estuary webs, these indicate whether the link is also present in the other estuaries).

Edge properties (`metaweb` only):

- `present_any`: whether the link is present in at least one of the estuaries.

Edge properties (estuary webs only):

- `evidence`: the evidence for the link ("observed": directly observed in the field, in gut contents or in parasitological examinations; "inferred": observed at other localities or in experiments, or based on expert opinion; "modeled": modeled after the interactions of similar species; "speculated": inferred from general knowledge of the taxon; empty if not given); `evidence_notes`: notes on the evidence.

According to the source, the data are freely available for non-commercial scientific use, given the appropriate citation.
citations: R. F. Hechinger, K. D. Lafferty, J. P. McLaughlin, B. L. Fredensborg, T. C. Huspeni, J. Lorda, P. K. Sandhu, J. C. Shaw, M. E. Torchin, K. L. Whitney, A. M. Kuris, "Food webs including parasites, biomass, body sizes, and life stages for three California/Baja California estuaries." Ecology 92(3), 791 (2011)

datasets.name: cambrian_food_webs
datasets.description:
Food webs of two Cambrian fossil assemblages, compiled by J. A. Dunne and collaborators: the Early Cambrian Chengjiang Shale (China, about 520 million years ago) and the Middle Cambrian Burgess Shale (Canada, about 505 million years ago), both known for their exceptional preservation of soft-bodied organisms. Nodes are taxa (mostly species), and a directed edge from a resource to a consumer means that the consumer is inferred to feed on the resource. In addition to the taxa found in the fossil record, five taxa commonly used in modern marine food webs were assumed to be present in both ecosystems: phytoplankton, bacterioplankton, suspended organic matter, benthic detritus, and zooplankton. The feeding links were assigned from the inferred ecology of the taxa (trophic role, position in the habitat), based on evidence such as preserved gut contents (in a few cases) and the morphology of the gut, appendages and mouthparts, and each link was given a certainty level. The networks are the "original-species webs" of the paper:

- `chengjiang`: 85 taxa and 559 links.
- `burgess`: 142 taxa and 771 links.

(The paper also analyses versions of these webs in which taxa with identical consumers and resources are aggregated into "trophic species".)

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the taxon, as in the source (an asterisk marks species with possible synonymous identifications).
- (Node) `taxon_id`: its number in the master taxa list of the paper (Tables S1 and S2).
- (Edge) `certainty`: the certainty of the feeding link: 1 (possible), 2 (probable) or 3 (certain).[^icon].

[^icon]: Description obtained in part from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.
citations: J. A. Dunne, R. J. Williams, N. D. Martinez, R. A. Wood, D. H. Erwin, "Compilation and network analyses of Cambrian food webs." PLoS Biology 6(4), e102 (2008)

datasets.name: cat_cortex
datasets.description:
Directed network of anatomical connections between regions of the cat cerebral cortex, as collated by Scannell et al. from tract-tracing studies in the published literature, and analyzed by de Reus and van den Heuvel. Nodes are cortical areas (65 in total, covering the visual, auditory, somatosensory-motor and frontolimbic systems), and a directed edge indicates a reported axonal projection from one area to another (1139 connections). The connection strengths reported in the original collation are not included, and the source file does not contain the names of the areas.

The data were obtained from the graph collection of the Open Connectome Project (now NeuroData), whose servers are offline, via the Internet Archive.
citations: M. A. de Reus, M. P. van den Heuvel, "Rich Club Organization and Intermodule Communication in the Cat Connectome." Journal of Neuroscience 33(32), 12929-12939 (2013)
J. W. Scannell, C. Blakemore, M. P. Young, "Analysis of connectivity in the cat cerebral cortex." Journal of Neuroscience 15(2), 1463-1483 (1995)

datasets.name: cat_corticothalamic
datasets.description:
Directed and weighted networks of the extrinsic anatomical connections among the cortical areas and thalamic nuclei of the cat cerebral hemisphere, from the collation of Scannell et al., as distributed with the Brain Connectivity Toolbox (contributed by O. Sporns). Scannell et al. compiled the connections reported in the published tract-tracing literature into a database of the cortico-cortical, cortico-thalamic, thalamo-cortical and thalamo-thalamic connections of the cat. Nodes are brain regions (cortical areas or thalamic nuclei), and a directed edge $i\to j$ indicates a reported axonal projection from region $i$ to region $j$ (an entry $a_{ij}>0$ of the source matrix, following the Brain Connectivity Toolbox convention), weighted by its reported strength (1 to 3).

- `all`: all 95 regions, cortical areas and thalamic nuclei (2126 connections).
- `cortex`: only the 52 cortical areas (818 connections; the toolbox documentation states 820). This is the same as the subnetwork of `all` induced by the cortical areas.

Note that this differs from the 65-area cortico-cortical version of the cat connectome in the `cat_cortex` entry.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the cortical area (e.g. "17", "AES", "PFCL"). The source data contain names only for the cortical areas; the thalamic nuclei in `all` are unnamed (empty string).
- (Node) `cortical` (`all` only): whether the region is a cortical area (the first 52 regions), otherwise it is a thalamic nucleus.
- (Edge) `weight`: the strength of the connection as classified in the collation, from 1 (weak or sparse) to 3 (strong or dense).
citations: J. W. Scannell, G. A. P. C. Burns, C. C. Hilgetag, M. A. O'Neil, M. P. Young, "The connectional organization of the cortico-thalamic system of the cat." Cerebral Cortex 9(3), 277-299 (1999)
M. Rubinov, O. Sporns, "Complex network measures of brain connectivity: Uses and interpretations." NeuroImage 52(3), 1059-1069 (2010)

datasets.name: caviar
datasets.description:
Directed networks of communication among participants in a drug importation network (hashish and cocaine) operating out of Montreal, Canada, targeted by Project Caviar, a joint investigation by the Montreal Police, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and law-enforcement agencies of several other countries between 1994 and 1996. Instead of arresting participants, the investigation used a "seize and wait" strategy: 11 drug consignments were seized over two years, and arrests took place only at the end, making it possible to study the evolution of the network under disruption (Morselli and Petit, 2007).

The data come from evidence submitted during the trials of 22 participants, comprising 4279 paragraphs of transcripts of intercepted telephone conversations. Of the 318 individuals named in them, the 110 who took part in the trafficking operations are included. Nodes are participants (numbered in `name`, as in the source), and a directed edge indicates communication from one participant to another, with the edge property `weight` giving the level of communication activity. The networks `phase1` to `phase11` correspond to the 11 two-month phases of the investigation, and `full` aggregates all of them. Data reconstructed from the appendix of Morselli's book "Inside Criminal Networks" (2009) by the UCINET datasets collection (University of Manchester).[^ucinet]

[^ucinet]: Description obtained in part from the [UCINET datasets page](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/datasets/covert-networks/caviar).
citations: C. Morselli and K. Petit, "Law-enforcement disruption of a drug importation network." Global Crime 8(2), 109-130 (2007)
C. Morselli, "Inside Criminal Networks." Springer, New York (2009)

datasets.name: cbdb
datasets.description:
Networks of the kinship relations and social associations of persons of Chinese history, mainly from the 7th to the 19th century, from the China Biographical Database (CBDB), the relational database of biographical information compiled by Harvard University, Academia Sinica and Peking University from biographies, local gazetteers, official records, collected works and other sources (about 660,000 persons in 2026).

There are two networks for each release of the database, all the 50 releases of the database's archive, from April 2019 to 24 October 2026 (weekly in 2026), named after the date of the release (e.g. `kinship_20261024`; `kinship_20220727_build20220831` is a rebuild of the release of 2022-07-27; the dates are given as graph properties):

- `kinship_<release>`: nodes are persons, and a directed edge from person $i$ to person $j$ means that $j$ is a kin of $i$ of the given type, as recorded (e.g. "F" for father, "S" for son, "W" for wife, "B-" for younger brother, and more distant relations, e.g. "FBS" for the son of the father's brother). Most relations are recorded in both directions (e.g. father and son).
- `association_<release>`: nodes are persons, and a directed edge from person $i$ to person $j$ is a social association of $i$ with $j$ of the given type (e.g. teacher and student, friendship, exchange of letters or poems, recommendation, writing an epitaph or a preface for someone, political alliances). Some associations are recorded through kin of the persons (e.g. writing the epitaph of someone's father), with the kin relations as edge properties.

Only the persons that take part in some relation of the network are included; the few relations with the placeholder person 0 ("unknown"; e.g. 42 kinship and 297 association records in 2019) are left out. The offices, entries into government service, addresses, texts, institutions and the other data of the database are not included.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`, `name_chn`: the name of the person, in transliteration (Pinyin) and in Chinese characters.
- (Node) `person_id`: the identifier of the person in CBDB (`c_personid`; e.g. `https://cbdb.fas.harvard.edu/cbdbapi/person.php?id=<person_id>`).
- (Node) `female`: whether the person is a woman.
- (Node) `birth_year`, `death_year`: the years of birth and death (0 if unknown).
- (Node) `index_year`: the index year of the person (an estimate of the year in which the person was 60, used to order persons in time; 0 if unknown).
- (Node) `dynasty`: the dynasty of the person, or empty.
- (Edge) `code`: the code of the kinship relation (`KINSHIP_CODES`) or of the association (`ASSOC_CODES`).
- (Edge) `relation`, `relation_chn`: the relation, in English and Chinese.
- (Edge) `source`: the identifier of the text that is the source of the record (in the `TEXT_CODES` of CBDB; 0 if not given).
- (Edge) `first_year`, `last_year` (associations): the first and last years of the association (0 if unknown; older releases (e.g. 2019), which record a single year, give it as both).
- (Edge) `count` (associations): the number of instances of the association (e.g. letters; 0 if not given).
- (Edge) `kin_id`, `kin_relation` (associations): the kin of the first person through which the association is recorded and its kinship relation (0 and empty if none), and `assoc_kin_id`, `assoc_kin_relation`, the same for the second person.
- (Graph) `release`: the date of the release (YYYY-MM-DD).
citations: Harvard University, Academia Sinica and Peking University, "China Biographical Database (CBDB)." (2019-2026)

datasets.name: celegans_2019
datasets.description:
Whole-animal connectomes of both sexes of the nematode *Caenorhabditis elegans*, the adult hermaphrodite and the adult male, reconstructed by S. J. Cook and collaborators from serial-section electron microscopy (EM) series, including both new reconstructions and a re-analysis of the original EM material of J. G. White and others. Nodes are cells: neurons, as well as the muscles and other end organs that they innervate. Edges are either chemical synapses (directed, from the pre-synaptic to the post-synaptic cell) or gap junctions (electrical synapses, undirected). To cover the entire nervous system, the connectomes were assembled from several animals, and connections were added by extrapolation in regions where no EM data were available.

There are twelve networks, named `<sex>_<type>[_<version>]`, for each sex (`hermaphrodite`, `male`) and connection type (`chemical`, `gap_junction`):

- no suffix: the connectome adjacency matrices, where the edge property `connectivity` is the total number of EM serial sections in which the connection is observed, which accounts for both the number and the size of the synapses.
- `_corrected`: corrected versions of the connectome matrices, released by the authors in July 2020.
- `_synapse`: the synapse adjacency matrices, where the edge property `synapses` is the number of synapses scored between each pair of cells. These do not take into account the size of the synapses, include only connections scored on electron micrographs, and do not include connections inserted by extrapolation; hence some cells that are connected in the other networks are not connected here.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the cell.
- (Node) `node_type`: the cell category (e.g. sensory neurons, interneurons, motor neurons, pharynx, bodywall muscles, other end organs, sex-specific cells).
- (Node) `node_subtype`: a sub-category for some cells (e.g. head, sublateral or body motor neurons; empty otherwise). `node_type` and `node_subtype` are not available in `male_chemical_synapse` and `male_gap_junction_synapse`.
- (Edge) `connectivity` or `synapses`: as described above.
citations: Cook et al., "Whole-animal connectomes of both Caenorhabditis elegans sexes." Nature 571, 63-71 (2019)

datasets.name: celegans_contactome
datasets.description:
Membrane contact networks ("contactomes") of the nerve ring, the main neuropil of the brain of the nematode *Caenorhabditis elegans*, reconstructed by Brittin et al. from the serial-section electron microscopy (EM) images of two animals, an L4 larva (series JSH) and an adult hermaphrodite (series N2U), originally imaged by White et al. (1986). The neurites of the cells were segmented in each EM section, and the membrane contacts between them were measured. Nodes are cells (neurons, identified by their standard names, e.g. `AVAL`), and an edge indicates that the membranes of two cells are adjacent.

There are two kinds of networks:

- `l4`, `adult`: the membrane contacts of each animal, aggregated over the EM sections (410 sections for the L4 animal, 302 for the adult). These are undirected.
- `reference_*`: the authors' graphs of the connections classified by their reproducibility across the four available nerve ring sides (left and right of the two animals, with left and right cells mapped onto each other): `*_delta1` to `*_delta4` contain the connections found in exactly $\delta$ = 1 to 4 of the four sides:
  - `reference_contact_delta*`: membrane contacts, after removing the contacts below the 35th percentile of contact area (`reference_contact_delta4_classes`: the same for $\delta=4$, with the left and right cells of each class merged into a single node);
  - `reference_chemical_delta*`: chemical synapses (directed), computed by the authors on the membrane contacts with $\delta=4$; `reference_chemical_delta*_pruned` leaves out the C1 polyadic synapses (see the paper);
  - `reference_gap_delta*`: gap junctions (undirected), likewise.

The reference graphs include the nodes `PVR`, `PVNL`, `HSNL`, `PVR.`, `HSNR`, `SABD`, `VB02`, `PLNL`, `PLNR` and `PVNR`, which the authors remove for their "restricted" data set (they are kept here, as in the upstream files). The membrane contacts of individual animals with their synapses are also available upstream as SQL databases, which are not included here (the synapses of both animals are in the `celegans_2019` entry).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the cell (or of the cell class, in `reference_contact_delta4_classes`).
- (Edge) `weight` (edges): in `l4` and `adult`, the total membrane contact area in μm² (the number of adjacent pixels, scaled by $4.5\times 10^{-4}$); in the reference graphs, the average over the $\delta$ sides where the connection is found of the membrane contact in pixels (contacts) or of the number of EM sections with synapses (chemical synapses and gap junctions), as given by the authors (whose documentation describes it as the total).
- (Edge) `pixels` (edges, `l4` and `adult` only): the total membrane contact in pixels.
- (Edge) `sections` (edges, `l4` and `adult` only): the number of EM sections in which the two cells are in contact.
citations: C. A. Brittin, S. J. Cook, D. H. Hall, S. W. Emmons, N. Cohen, "A multi-scale brain map derived from whole-brain volumetric reconstructions." Nature 591, 105-110 (2021)

datasets.name: celegans_development
datasets.description:
Connectomes of the brain (the nerve ring and ventral ganglion) of eight isogenic hermaphrodite nematodes *Caenorhabditis elegans* of different ages, from birth to adulthood, reconstructed by D. Witvliet and collaborators from serial-section electron microscopy images. Nodes are cells: neurons, as well as the body wall muscles and glia that they contact in the volume. Edges are either chemical synapses (directed, from the presynaptic to the postsynaptic cell) or gap junctions (electrical synapses, undirected).

There are sixteen networks, named `<stage>_<connection type>`, one for each animal and connection type (`chemical`, `gap_junction`). The animals are, by developmental stage and approximate age (hours after birth, at 25°C, estimated from the cell division pattern):

- `L1_1`, `L1_2`, `L1_3`, `L1_4`: first larval stage, at 0, 5, 8 and 16 hours.
- `L2`: second larval stage, at 23 hours.
- `L3`: third larval stage, at 27 hours.
- `adult_1`, `adult_2`: young adults, at about 45 to 50 hours (their exact ages are uncertain).

The nodes of both networks of an animal are all the cells that make any connection in that animal, so that cells without connections of a given type are isolated nodes. Self-loops are synapses of a cell onto itself, as recorded in the data.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the cell (e.g. `AVAL`, `BWM-DL01` for body wall muscles).
- (Edge) `synapses` (edges): the number of synapses between the two cells.
citations: D. Witvliet et al., "Connectomes across development reveal principles of brain maturation." Nature 596, 257-261 (2021)

datasets.name: celegans_extrasynaptic
datasets.description:
Directed networks of extrasynaptic ("wireless") signaling between the neurons of the nematode *Caenorhabditis elegans* (adult hermaphrodite), mediated by monoamines and neuropeptides, from Bentley et al. These networks complement the synaptic and gap-junction connectome, forming a multilayer connectome of the worm.

The networks were inferred from gene expression data, curated from new experiments (GFP reporters for the dopamine receptors *dop-5*, *dop-6* and *lgc-53*) and from the literature (assisted by the WormBase and WormWeb expression databases). A directed edge goes from a neuron that releases a transmitter (i.e. expresses the transmitter, its biosynthetic enzymes, or transporters) to a neuron that expresses a receptor for it. Edges are not restricted by the physical distance between the neurons.

- `monoamine`: the draft monoamine network, comprising dopamine, serotonin, tyramine and octopamine signaling.
- `monoamine_dop5_dop6`: the same, but including also the putative dopamine receptors *dop-5* and *dop-6* (a "provisional" dopamine network analyzed in the supplementary material of the paper).
- `neuropeptide`: the partial neuropeptide network, including only the peptide-receptor systems with sufficient expression and ligand-receptor interaction data, with interactions limited to biologically plausible peptide-receptor EC50 values (15 neuropeptides matched to 12 receptors).
- `monoamine_classes`, `monoamine_classes_dop5_dop6`, `neuropeptide_classes`: the same networks, between neuron classes instead of individual neurons (e.g. the left/right pairs AIAL and AIAR form the class AIA).

Each edge corresponds to one combination of transmitter and receptor, so that a pair of neurons can be connected by several parallel edges (one per receptor expressed by the receiving neuron); self-loops correspond to neurons that express both a transmitter and one of its receptors. In the analyses of the paper, the parallel edges of each monoamine are collapsed into a single edge, and the neuropeptide network is divided into layers by receptor.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the neuron (or neuron class).
- (Edge) `transmitter`: the monoamine (dopamine, serotonin, tyramine, or octopamine) or neuropeptide (e.g. flp-1, pdf-1) released by the source neuron.
- (Edge) `receptor`: the receptor gene expressed by the target neuron.
citations: B. Bentley, R. Branicky, C. L. Barnes, Y. L. Chew, E. Yemini, E. T. Bullmore, P. E. Vértes, W. R. Schafer, "The multilayer connectome of Caenorhabditis elegans." PLOS Computational Biology 12(12), e1005283 (2016)

datasets.name: celegans_genetic_byrne
datasets.description:
Weighted network of similarity among genes of the nematode *Caenorhabditis elegans*, derived from the systematic genetic interaction analysis (SGI) of A. B. Byrne and collaborators. In that study, 11 "query" strains carrying mutations in conserved signal transduction pathways were each combined with the RNA interference (RNAi) knockdown of hundreds of "target" genes, and a genetic interaction was inferred when a mutant-RNAi combination grew more slowly than expected. The data were compiled by M. Cantor and collaborators for a study of nestedness across levels of biological organization, and are distributed in the repository of that study (file `mol_genes_celegans.txt`). Using the interactions as given in the BioGRID database, they projected the query-target interactions onto the 454 target genes: nodes are target genes, and an undirected edge connects two target genes that interact with at least one common query gene, weighted by the Simpson index of their sets of interacting query genes (the number of shared query genes divided by the smaller of the two numbers of query genes each target interacts with), which ranges from 0 to 1. The genes are not identified in the source data.

The edges have the property `weight`, the Simpson index.
citations: A. B. Byrne, M. T. Weirauch, V. Wong, M. Koeva, S. J. Dixon, J. M. Stuart, P. J. Roy, "A global analysis of genetic interactions in Caenorhabditis elegans." Journal of Biology 6, 8 (2007)
C. Stark, B.-J. Breitkreutz, T. Reguly, L. Boucher, A. Breitkreutz, M. Tyers, "BioGRID: a general repository for interaction datasets." Nucleic Acids Research 34, D535-D539 (2006)

M. Cantor, M. M. Pires, F. M. D. Marquitti, R. L. G. Raimundo, E. Sebastián-González, P. P. Coltri, S. I. Perez, D. R. Barneche, D. Y. C. Brandt, K. Nunes, F. G. Daura-Jorge, S. R. Floeter, P. R. Guimarães Jr., "Nestedness across biological scales." PLoS ONE 12(2), e0171691 (2017)

datasets.name: celegans_interactomes
citations: N. Simonis et al., "Empirically controlled mapping of the Caenorhabditis elegans protein-protein interactome network." Nature Methods 6(1), 47-54 (2009)

datasets.name: celegans_kaiser
datasets.description:
Directed network of the neurons of the nematode *Caenorhabditis elegans*, with the two-dimensional positions of their cell bodies, from M. Kaiser and C. C. Hilgetag. Nodes are 277 neurons, and a directed edge connects two neurons linked by a chemical synapse or by an electrical synapse (gap junction), without distinction between them. The connectivity was taken from the compilation of T. B. Achacoso and W. S. Yamamoto (1992), which is largely based on the electron microscope reconstructions of J. G. White and collaborators (1986); the neurons of the pharyngeal ring, for which there was no internal connection information, were removed, leaving 280 neurons, and three neurons (AIBL, AIYL and SMDVL) were removed because their positions were not available. The positions of the somata, in the lateral plane (anterior-posterior and dorsal-ventral axes), in millimeters, were provided by Y. Choe (temporally augmented *C. elegans* web, Choe et al. 2004). Following the usual convention, the entry $(i, j)$ of the source adjacency matrix is taken as an edge from neuron $i$ to neuron $j$ (the convention is not stated explicitly with the data).

The source also provides, as a separate data set, the "local" network of the 131 neurons in the rostral ganglia (anterior, dorsal, lateral and ring ganglia), with 764 connections; it is exactly the subgraph of the network here induced by these neurons (with the same positions), which are marked by the node property `rostral_ganglia`.

The nodes have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the neuron (e.g. "ADAL", "AVAR").
- (Node) `position`: the $(x, y)$ position of the soma, in millimeters ($x$ along the anterior-posterior axis, increasing towards the head).
- (Node) `rostral_ganglia`: whether the neuron belongs to the local network of the 131 neurons of the rostral ganglia.
citations: M. Kaiser, C. C. Hilgetag, "Nonoptimal component placement, but short processing paths, due to long-distance projections in neural systems." PLoS Computational Biology 2(7), e95 (2006)
Y. Choe, B. H. McCormick, W. Koh, "Network connectivity analysis on the temporally augmented C. elegans web: A pilot study." Society for Neuroscience Abstracts 30, 921.9 (2004)
T. B. Achacoso, W. S. Yamamoto, "AY's Neuroanatomy of C. elegans for Computation." CRC Press, Boca Raton (1992)

J. G. White, E. Southgate, J. N. Thomson, S. Brenner, "The structure of the nervous system of the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans." Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London B 314, 1-340 (1986)

datasets.name: celegans_male
datasets.description:
Directed network of the posterior nervous system of the adult male nematode *Caenorhabditis elegans*, reconstructed by Jarrell et al. from serial-section electron micrographs. This part of the nervous system controls the male's mating behaviour. Nodes are the neurons of the posterior (tail) region, together with the muscles and other end organs they connect to (e.g. body wall muscles "dBWM"/"vBWM", diagonal muscles, spicule muscles, gonad, hypodermis, intestine); names in square brackets follow the notation of the source. An edge points from the presynaptic to the postsynaptic cell, and carries the strengths of both chemical and electrical (gap junction) connections, as given in the source; in the publication, connection strength is an anatomical measure derived from the extent of the synaptic contacts in the electron micrographs.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the cell name.
- (Edge) `chemical_weight` and `electrical_weight`: the strength of the chemical and of the electrical connection (0 if there is none of that type).

The data were obtained from the graph collection of the Open Connectome Project (now NeuroData), whose servers are offline, via the Internet Archive.
citations: T. A. Jarrell et al., "The Connectome of a Decision-Making Neural Network." Science 337(6093), 437-444 (2012)

datasets.name: celegans_metabolic
datasets.description:
The metabolic network of the nematode *Caenorhabditis elegans*, as used by J. Duch and A. Arenas to test their community detection method based on extremal optimization. Nodes are metabolites (substrates), and an undirected edge connects two metabolites that participate in the same metabolic reaction. The data are derived from the metabolic network reconstructions of H. Jeong et al., *Nature* 407, 651 (2000), which are based on the WIT database. Nodes are identified only by anonymous labels (`v1` to `v453`), so the identities of the metabolites are not available. The network contains parallel edges (pairs of metabolites connected by more than one edge) and a few self-loops, as present in the source file.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name` and `id`: the node label (`v1` to `v453`).
- (Node) `x`, `y` and `z`: the node coordinates in the Pajek source file (without meaning).
- (Edge) `weight`: which is always 1.
citations: J. Duch and A. Arenas, "Community identification using Extremal Optimization." Physical Review E 72, 027104 (2005).

datasets.name: celegans_multiplex
datasets.description:
A multiplex network of the neurons of the hermaphrodite nematode *Caenorhabditis elegans*, distributed by M. De Domenico and based on the wiring diagram compiled by Chen, Hall and Chklovskii (2006) from the serial-section electron micrographs of White et al. (1986). Nodes are the 279 neurons, identified by their names, and an undirected edge in a layer connects two neurons joined by a synapse of the corresponding type. There are three layers:

- `ElectrJ` (517 edges): electrical junctions (gap junctions);
- `MonoSyn` (888 edges): monadic chemical synapses, with a single postsynaptic partner;
- `PolySyn` (1,703 edges): polyadic chemical synapses, with several postsynaptic partners.

The README of the data set describes the network as undirected and unweighted. Although it says that only one direction of each edge is specified, most pairs of neurons are listed in both orientations within a layer (all of them in `ElectrJ`, and about 90% in the two chemical layers), so the direction does not distinguish pre- from postsynaptic neurons; such pairs are included here only once, which reduces the 5,863 listed connections to 3,108 edges. The `ElectrJ` layer contains three self-loops (`RIBL`, `RIBR` and `VA08`). Neither the number of synapses nor their direction is available.

The same neurons, with the direction and the number of synapses of each connection, are in the entry `celegans_varshney`, which is based on the updated and revised reconstruction of Varshney et al. (2011), in which chemical synapses are not separated into monadic and polyadic ones.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name` and `nodeLabel`: the neuron name (e.g. `ADAL`).
- (Edge) `layer`: the synapse type (1: electrical junction, 2: monadic chemical synapse, 3: polyadic chemical synapse; the names are stored in the graph property `layer_key`).
- (Edge) `weight`: which is always 1.
citations: B. L. Chen, D. H. Hall, D. B. Chklovskii, "Wiring optimization can relate neuronal structure and function." Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 103(12), 4723-4728 (2006)
M. De Domenico, M. A. Porter, A. Arenas, "MuxViz: a tool for multilayer analysis and visualization of networks." Journal of Complex Networks 3(2), 159-176 (2015)

datasets.name: celegans_varshney
datasets.description:
Directed network of the somatic nervous system of the adult hermaphrodite nematode *Caenorhabditis elegans*, as compiled by Varshney et al. from the serial-section electron micrographs of White et al. (1986), with revisions and additions from new reconstructions. It comprises the 279 non-pharyngeal neurons that make synapses (the 20 pharyngeal neurons, and CANL/R and VC06, which make no synapses, are excluded). There is one edge for each pair of neurons and type of connection: chemical synapses, directed from the presynaptic to the postsynaptic neuron, and gap junctions (electrical synapses), which are symmetric. Edges are weighted by the number of synapses.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the neuron name.
- (Node) `cell_class`: the neuron class (e.g. "VA" for VA01 to VA12).
- (Node) `role`: "S" for sensory, "M" for motor, or "NA" (interneurons and others).
- (Node) `neurotransmitters`: the known neurotransmitters ("Ach", "GABA", "DA", "5-HT", or "NA" if unknown).
- (Node) `soma_pos`: the position of the cell body along the anterior-posterior body axis (0 at the head, 1 at the tail).
- (Edge) `synapse_type`: "C" for chemical synapse and "E" for gap junction.
- (Edge) `weight`: the number of synapses.

The OpenConnectome file is labeled as the "pharynx" network, but contains the somatic (non-pharyngeal) network described above. The data were obtained from the graph collection of the Open Connectome Project (now NeuroData), whose servers are offline, via the Internet Archive.
citations: L. R. Varshney, B. L. Chen, E. Paniagua, D. H. Hall, D. B. Chklovskii, "Structural Properties of the Caenorhabditis elegans Neuronal Network." PLoS Computational Biology 7(2), e1001066 (2011)

datasets.name: celegansneural
datasets.description:
The neural network of the nematode *Caenorhabditis elegans*, compiled by D. J. Watts and S. H. Strogatz from the original reconstruction of its nervous system from serial-section electron micrographs by J. G. White, E. Southgate, J. N. Thomson and S. Brenner (1986), and used in their study of small-world networks. Nodes are 297 neurons, and a directed edge represents a synaptic connection or gap junction between two neurons; the meaning of the edge direction is not documented in the source. The data were obtained from the website of D. J. Watts and redistributed by M. E. J. Newman, who renumbered the nodes consecutively.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `label`: the node number in Watts' original data file (the neuron names are not included).
- (Edge) `value`: the edge weight given by Watts (an integer from 1 to 70), which reflects the number of connections between the two neurons; its precise definition is not documented in the source.
citations: J. G. White, E. Southgate, J. N. Thomson, and S. Brenner, "The structure of the nervous system of the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans", Phil. Trans. R. Soc. London 314, 1-340 (1986)
D.J. Watts and S.H. Strogatz, "Collective dynamics of 'small-world' networks." Nature 393, 440-442 (1998).

datasets.name: centrality_literature
datasets.description:
Citations among 129 publications on network centrality between 1948 and 1979, from the study of N. P. Hummon, P. Doreian and L. C. Freeman of the centrality-productivity literature that preceded (and includes) Freeman's 1979 paper on centrality. Edges represent citations and point from the cited to the citing paper. Papers citing one another (e.g. papers by the same author appearing at about the same time) were shrunk into a single node, so the network is acyclic. The data were distributed on the Pajek datasets page of the book *Exploratory Social Network Analysis with Pajek* (de Nooy, Mrvar and Batagelj), from which this version was obtained.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the label of the publication (author and the last two digits of the publication year).
- (Node) `year`: the year of publication.
- (Edge) `weight`: 1 for a regular citation, or 2 for a double citation (when the citing or the cited paper is a node combining two papers that cite each other).
citations: N. P. Hummon, P. Doreian, L. C. Freeman, "Analyzing the Structure of the Centrality-Productivity Literature Created Between 1948 and 1979." Knowledge 11(4), 459-480 (1990)
W. de Nooy, A. Mrvar, V. Batagelj, "Exploratory Social Network Analysis with Pajek." Cambridge University Press (2005)

datasets.name: ceo_club
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of the memberships of 26 chief executive officers (CEOs) of corporations in the Minneapolis–St. Paul metropolitan area in 15 organizations (labeled as clubs in the data), collected by Galaskiewicz (1985) for his study of corporate philanthropy, and published by Wasserman and Faust (1994) as a subset of a larger data set that is not publicly available. The data are from Cory Brunson's bitriad R package (data set `minneapolis1970s`, built from the `CEOclubsAM` matrix of the Bioconductor SNAData package). The CEOs and organizations are anonymous.

Nodes are CEOs and organizations, and an edge connects a CEO to an organization of which they are a member.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the anonymous label of the CEO (CEO1 to CEO26) or the organization (Club1 to Club15).
- (Node) `is_organization`: whether the node is an organization.
citations: J. Galaskiewicz, "Social Organization of an Urban Grants Economy: A Study of Business Philanthropy and Nonprofit Organizations." Academic Press (1985)
S. Wasserman, K. Faust, "Social Network Analysis: Methods and Applications." Cambridge University Press (1994)
K. Faust, "Centrality in affiliation networks." Social Networks 19(2), 157-191 (1997)

datasets.name: chad_dogs
datasets.description:
Contact networks of free-ranging domestic dogs (*Canis familiaris*) in two rural settlements along the Chari River, in the Guelendeng district of Chad, recorded between 24 June and 12 July 2016 by J. K. Wilson-Aggarwal and colleagues to study the transmission of infections such as rabies. Each settlement comprises two neighboring villages: Kakale (Kakale-Mberi and Awine) and Magrao (Magrao and Sawata). All dogs were owned and associated with a household; with the consent of the owners, all dogs except puppies (younger than 6 months) were fitted with collars carrying a GPS unit and a wearable proximity sensor (of the OpenBeacon/SocioPatterns design), which exchanges low-power radio packets and detects close-range contacts (within about 1 to 1.5 m). Data from the first and last day of deployment in each village, as well as corrupted sensors and anomalous signals, were discarded.

Nodes are dogs, and an undirected edge connects two dogs that were in contact at least once. Since the dogs were collared for different numbers of days, the edge weight is the average duration of contact per day: the total duration of the contacts between the two dogs (in seconds), divided by the shorter of the two monitoring periods (in days), and then $\log_{10}$-transformed.

The entry contains two networks:

- `kakale`: the dogs of the Kakale settlement (48 dogs, 160 edges).
- `magrao`: the dogs of the Magrao settlement (60 dogs, 191 edges).

Node properties:

- `name`: the dog identifier (the village code, the household number and a letter for the dog, e.g. "AW_02B").
- `village`: the village ("Awine", "Kakale Mberi", "Magrao" or "Saouata").
- `household`: the household that owns the dog; `household_dogs`: the number of dogs owned by the household, as reported by the owner.
- `sex`: "Male" or "Female".
- `age_class`: the age class, from the age reported by the owner ("Juvenile": up to 12 months, "Subadult": 13 to 24 months, "Adult": older than 24 months, "NA": unknown).
- `body_condition`: the body condition score, categorized as "Poor" (score at most 2) or "Moderate" (score at least 3), or "NA" if unknown.
- `core_range`: the area of the core range (60% kernel density estimate of the GPS locations), in km$^2$ (NaN if unknown).
- `total_range`: the area of the total range (99% minimum convex polygon of the GPS locations), in km$^2$ (NaN if unknown).

Edge properties:

- `weight`: $\log_{10}$ of the average contact duration per day, in seconds (as given in the source).
- `duration`: the average contact duration per day, in seconds ($10^{\text{weight}}$).

The source also provides the distances between the households of each settlement, which are not included.

McDonald, "High-resolution contact networks of free-ranging domestic dogs Canis familiaris and implications for transmission of infection." PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases 13(7), e0007565 (2019)

datasets.name: charnet
datasets.description:
Networks of encounters among the characters of twelve books of different genres (fiction, legendary texts, biographies), from the CharNet project of A. J. Holanda and collaborators. Nodes are characters (sometimes a group of people acting as a character, such as "the Thessalians"), and an undirected edge connects two characters who meet in the book, i.e., who take part together in at least one encounter; edges are weighted by the number of encounters in which both take part. The encounters were annotated manually, chapter by chapter, as groups of characters who interact in a part of the book, following the format of the character data of D. E. Knuth's Stanford GraphBase, from which the data for two of the books are taken. Characters listed in a book's data file but without any encounter appear as isolated nodes. The networks are:

- `acts`: the Acts of the Apostles (Bible).
- `luke`: the Gospel of Luke (Bible).
- `apollonius`: "The Life of Apollonius of Tyana", by Flavius Philostratus (English translation by F. C. Conybeare).
- `pythagoras`: "The Life of Pythagoras", by Iamblichus.
- `arthur`: "The Winter King" (first volume of "The Warlord Chronicles"), by Bernard Cornwell.
- `hobbit`: "The Hobbit", by J. R. R. Tolkien.
- `tolkien`: "J. R. R. Tolkien", a biography by Michael White.
- `newton`: "Isaac Newton", a biography by James Gleick.
- `hawking`: a biography of Stephen Hawking ("The Theory of Everything").
- `dick`: "A vida de Philip K. Dick" (a biography of Philip K. Dick), by Anthony Peake.
- `david`: "David Copperfield", by Charles Dickens (from the Stanford GraphBase).
- `huck`: "Huckleberry Finn", by Mark Twain (from the Stanford GraphBase).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `code`: the two-letter label of the character in the source files.
- (Node) `name`: its name or description (e.g. "Gandalf", "Aunt Polly, aunt who raises TS").
- (Edge) `weight`: the number of encounters in which both characters take part.[^icon].

[^icon]: Description obtained in part from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.

D. E. Knuth, "The Stanford GraphBase: A Platform for Combinatorial Computing." Addison-Wesley, Reading, MA (1993)

datasets.name: chembl_bioactivity
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of the compounds and the biological targets of ChEMBL, the manually curated database of bioactive molecules with drug-like properties of the European Bioinformatics Institute (EMBL-EBI), release 37 (May 2026). An edge is a bioactivity measurement of a compound in an assay on a target, e.g. an inhibition constant ($K_i$) or a half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50), so that a compound and a target are connected by as many edges as there are measurements. The measurements are mostly extracted from the scientific literature (medicinal chemistry journals), and also come from deposited datasets (e.g. PubChem BioAssays, patents via BindingDB and SureChEMBL, screening campaigns against malaria and other neglected diseases).

The targets are mostly single proteins, but also protein complexes and families, nucleic acids, cell lines, tissues and whole organisms, as given by the node property `target_type`; the compounds are mostly small molecules, but also e.g. antibodies and other proteins. All the 24.5 million activities of the release are included, also those with a comment about their validity (e.g. a possible transcription error, or units that are outside the typical range for that activity type) and those flagged as possible duplicates, as well as activities without a numerical value (e.g. those only reported as active or inactive). The assays and documents of the activities (other than the year of publication), their original (unstandardized) values, and the structures of the compounds are not included.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `is_compound`: whether the node is a compound (otherwise it is a target).
- (Node) `chembl_id`: the ChEMBL identifier of the compound or target (e.g. `CHEMBL25`, aspirin; `CHEMBL203`, the epidermal growth factor receptor), whose page is `https://www.ebi.ac.uk/chembl/explore/compound/<chembl_id>` or `https://www.ebi.ac.uk/chembl/explore/target/<chembl_id>`.
- (Node) `name`: the preferred name of the compound or target (empty for most compounds, which have no name).
- (Node) `molecule_type` (compounds): the type of the compound, e.g. `Small molecule`, `Protein`, `Antibody` (empty for targets).
- (Node) `max_phase` (compounds): the maximum clinical phase reached by the compound: 4 (approved drug), 3, 2, 1, 0.5 (early phase 1), or -1 (preclinical or unknown, also for targets).
- (Node) `target_type` (targets): the type of the target, e.g. `SINGLE PROTEIN`, `PROTEIN COMPLEX`, `CELL-LINE`, `ORGANISM` (empty for compounds).
- (Node) `organism` (targets): the organism of the target (empty if none, and for compounds).
- (Node) `tax_id` (targets): the NCBI taxonomy identifier of the organism (-1 if none, and for compounds).
- (Edge) `standard_type`: the type of the measurement, standardized, e.g. `IC50`, `Ki`, `Potency`, `Inhibition`.
- (Edge) `standard_relation`: the relation of the measured value: `=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`, `~` (empty if there is no value).
- (Edge) `standard_value`: the measured value, standardized (NaN if there is none).
- (Edge) `standard_units`: the units of the value, e.g. `nM`, `%` (empty if none).
- (Edge) `pchembl_value`: the negative logarithm (base 10) of the molar concentration (e.g. IC50, Ki, EC50), for comparable measures of potency (NaN if not applicable).
- (Edge) `assay_type`: the type of the assay: `B` (binding), `F` (functional), `A` (absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion), `T` (toxicity), `P` (physicochemical) or `U` (unclassified).
- (Edge) `year`: the year of publication of the document the measurement comes from (-1 if not known, e.g. for deposited datasets).
- (Edge) `data_validity_comment`: a comment on the validity of the measurement, e.g. `Outside typical range`, `Potential transcription error` (empty if none).
- (Edge) `potential_duplicate`: whether the measurement is a possible duplicate of one reported in another document.
citations: B. Zdrazil et al., "The ChEMBL Database in 2023: a drug discovery platform spanning multiple bioactivity data types and time periods." Nucleic Acids Research 52, D1180-D1192 (2024)
D. Mendez et al., "ChEMBL: towards direct deposition of bioassay data." Nucleic Acids Research 47, D930-D940 (2019)

datasets.name: chess
datasets.description:
A network among chess players (nodes) giving the chess match outcomes (edges), for game-by-game results among the world’s top chess players. The direction of edge (i,j) denotes white player (i) and black player (j). Each edge is timestamped (approximate). Edge sign is +1 for a win by white, 0 for draw, and -1 for a win by black.[^icon]
[^icon]: Description obtained from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.
citations: Kaggle, "Chess ratings - Elo versus the Rest of the World."

datasets.name: chicago_police_complaints
datasets.description:
Networks of the officers of the Chicago Police Department (CPD) and the complaints of misconduct against them, the reports of their use of force, and their awards, from the Citizens Police Data Project (CPDP) of the Invisible Institute, which obtained the records through Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) requests and litigation, and matched the officers across the files of several FOIA responses to unique ids. The entry contains three bipartite networks, each with all 37,545 officers of the matched profiles (also those without complaints, reports or awards):

- `complaints`: the nodes are officers and complaints (complaint register, CR, numbers), and an edge connects a complaint with each officer accused in it. Complaints are filed by civilians or by CPD employees, and investigated by the CPD's Bureau of Internal Affairs (BIA) or civilian review agencies (OPS, IPRA, COPA). Officers accused together in complaints form the co-accusal networks used in studies of police misconduct. The network contains all 234,971 complaints (also the 89,776 complaints whose accused officers are unknown), with 263,315 accusations, from 1967 to 2023 (most complaints from 2000 onward). Four accused officers are missing from the profiles; they are included as nodes without attributes (`has_record` false).
- `use_of_force`: the nodes are officers and incidents in which they used force, from the Tactical Response Reports (TRR) of 2004 to 2023 that officers file after using force. An edge connects an officer with an incident for each report of the officer on it (one per subject: an officer and an incident can be connected by several edges). The incidents are the CPD event numbers of the reports; the 15,252 reports without event number are incidents of their own. There are 65,816 incidents and 98,055 reports; the 809 reports without officer are left out (557 incidents have no reports with officers, and are included without edges).
- `awards`: the nodes are officers and awards (e.g. honorable mentions, commendations, attendance and crime reduction awards), and an edge connects an award with each officer who received it (or for whom it was requested): 113,775 awards and 807,173 officer awards, from 1967 to 2020.

Left out are the investigators and the police witnesses of the complaints (not matched to officer ids), the complainants, victims and civilian witnesses; of the use of force, the reports that are only in the secondary files of the TRR (without officer), the subject records, the details of the weapon discharges, and the chain of review of the reports (by other officers, not matched to officer ids); and the salaries and unit histories. The officers are named, as in the public records.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `is_complaint`, `is_incident` or `is_award`: whether the node is a complaint, incident or award (otherwise an officer).
- (Node) `uid` (officers): the officer's id in the data of the Invisible Institute (-1 for the other nodes).
- (Node) `has_record` (officers): whether the officer is in the file of profiles.
- (Node) `officer_id` (officers): the id of the officer on the CPDP site (`https://cpdp.co/officer/<officer_id>`; -1 if unknown).
- (Node) `first_name`, `last_name`, `middle_initial`, `middle_initial2` and `suffix_name` (officers): the name of the officer.
- (Node) `appointed_date`, `resignation_date`, `org_hire_date` and `start_date` (officers): the dates of appointment, resignation, hire (by any police organization) and start in the CPD, as given (`M/D/YY`, with two-digit years).
- (Node) `birth_year` (officers): the year of birth (-1 if unknown).
- (Node) `gender`, `race` (officers): the gender and race of the officer.
- (Node) `current_star` (officers): the last star (badge) number.
- (Node) `cleaned_rank` (officers): the standardized rank.
- (Node) `current_rank` and `current_unit` (officers): the last rank and unit.
- (Node) `active` (officers): whether the officer is active (1, or 0).
- (Node) `profile_count` (officers): the number of datasets in which the officer appears.
- (Node) The properties of the officers are the most common values over the files, as determined by the Invisible Institute.
- (Node) `cr_id` (complaints, in `complaints`): the complaint register number (-1 for officers).
- (Node) `complaint_date`, `closed_date` and `incident_date` (complaints): the dates of filing, closure and incident (Unix time; -1 if unknown).
- (Node) `incident_time` (complaints): the time of the incident (as given).
- (Node) `days_to_closure` (complaints): the number of days to closure.
- (Node) `address` (complaints): the block address of the incident (number and street).
- (Node) `beat` (complaints): the police beat.
- (Node) `city` (complaints): the city.
- (Node) `location_code` (complaints): the type of location.
- (Node) `old_complaint_address` (complaints): the address in the older format.
- (Node) `latitude` and `longitude` (complaints): the geocoded block address (NaN if unknown).
- (Node) `current_status` (complaints): the current status of the complaint.
- (Node) `investigating_agency` (complaints): the last agency investigating the complaint.
- (Node) `investigating_agencies` (complaints): all agencies investigating the complaint.
- (Node) `complainant_type` (complaints): `CIVILIAN` or `CPD EMPLOYEE`.
- (Node) `filename` (complaints): the last FOIA response with the complaint.
- (Edge) `complaint_category` and `complaint_code` (`complaints`): the category of the allegation against the officer (e.g. `Excessive Force`).
- (Edge) `complaint_categories` and `complaint_codes` (`complaints`): all categories and codes listed for the complaint in all files.
- (Edge) `disciplined` (`complaints`): whether the complaint resulted in discipline.
- (Edge) `final_finding` (`complaints`): the final finding (e.g. `SU` sustained, `NS` not sustained, `UN` unfounded, `EX` exonerated, `NAF` no affidavit, `AC` administratively closed).
- (Edge) `final_outcome` and `final_outcome_desc` (`complaints`): the final outcome (e.g. `Reprimand`, `5 Day Suspension`) and its description.
- (Edge) `recc_finding` and `recc_outcome` (`complaints`): the recommended finding and outcome.
- (Edge) `days` (`complaints`): the recommended days of suspension (NaN if none).
- (Edge) `cv` (`complaints`): the version of the complaint files from which the row comes.
- (Node) `event_no` (incidents, in `use_of_force`): the event number (-1 if none).
- (Node) `incident_date` and `incident_time` (incidents): the date (Unix time of the day) and time (as given) of the incident.
- (Node) `block`, `direction` and `street` (incidents): the block address.
- (Node) `beat` (incidents): the police beat.
- (Node) `latitude` and `longitude` (incidents): the geocoded block address (NaN if unknown).
- (Node) `indoor_or_outdoor`, `lighting_condition`, `weather_condition`, `location` and `location_recode` (incidents): the type of location.
- (Node) The properties of the incidents are the values of the first report on the incident; the reports of different officers sometimes differ, and their own values are edge properties.
- (Edge) `trr_id` (`use_of_force`, the reports): the id of the report.
- (Edge) `date` and `time` (`use_of_force`): the date (Unix time of the day) and time.
- (Edge) `block`, `direction`, `street`, `beat`, `latitude`, `longitude`, `indoor_or_outdoor`, `lighting_condition`, `weather_condition`, `location`, `location_recode` (`use_of_force`): the place, as for the incidents.
- (Edge) `trr_status` (`use_of_force`): the status of the report.
- (Edge) `firearm_used` and `taser` (`use_of_force`): whether the officer used a firearm or a taser (1 or 0).
- (Edge) `notify_DET_division`, `notify_OEMC`, `notify_OP_command` and `notify_district_sergeant` (`use_of_force`): whether the detective division, the emergency management office, the OP command or the district sergeant were notified (as given; empty if not).
- (Edge) `number_of_officers_using_firearm`, `number_of_weapons_discharged` and `total_number_of_shots` (`use_of_force`): the numbers of officers using a firearm, of weapons discharged and of shots (-1 if not given).
- (Edge) `party_fired_first` (`use_of_force`): the party that fired first.
- (Edge) `officer_assigned_beat`, `officer_on_duty`, `officer_in_uniform`, `officer_injured`, `officer_rank`, `officer_unit_id` and `officer_unit_detail_id` (`use_of_force`): the officer at the time of the incident (-1 if unknown).
- (Edge) `subject_armed`, `subject_injured`, `subject_alleged_injury`, `subject_age`, `subject_birth_year`, `subject_gender` and `subject_race` (`use_of_force`): the subject of the force.
- (Edge) `member_actions` and `subject_actions` (`use_of_force`): the actions of the officer (e.g. `VERBAL COMMANDS`, `TAKE DOWN/EMERGENCY HANDCUFFING`, `TASER`) and of the subject (e.g. `PULLED AWAY`), each listed once.
- (Edge) `max_action_category` (`use_of_force`): the highest level of the officer's actions, from 0 (member presence) to 6 (firearm; NaN if not given, as in the older files).
- (Edge) `subject_weapons` (`use_of_force`): the types of weapons of the subject (e.g. `HANDS/FISTS`).
- (Edge) `cv` (`use_of_force`): the version of the files from which the report comes.
- (Node) `award_id` (awards, in `awards`): the id of the award.
- (Node) `award_type`, `award_start_date` and `award_end_date` (awards): the type of the award and its start and end dates (Unix time; -1 if unknown), the values of the first record of the award.
- (Edge) `current_award_status` (`awards`): the status of the award (`FINAL`, `DELETED`, `DENIED`, `PENDING APPROVAL` or `PRELIMINARY`), as recorded for the officer.
- (Edge) `award_type` (`awards`): the type of the award, as recorded for the officer.
- (Edge) `award_request_date` and `ceremony_date` (`awards`): the dates of the request and of the ceremony (Unix time; -1 if unknown), as recorded for the officer.
- (Edge) `requester_full_name` (`awards`): the name of the officer who requested the award (`REDACTED` for some), as recorded for the officer.
citations: Invisible Institute, "Citizens Police Data Project: Chicago police data." GitHub repository (2025)
L. Zhao, A. V. Papachristos, "Network Position and Police Who Shoot." The Annals of the American Academy of Political and Social Science 687, 89-112 (2020)

datasets.name: chicago_road
datasets.description:
The road network of the Chicago region, USA, as a detailed representation prepared by the Chicago Area Transportation Study (CATS) for traffic assignment (the year of the underlying data is not documented), from the Transportation Networks for Research repository maintained by B. Stabler, H. Bar-Gera and E. Sall, which continues H. Bar-Gera's earlier "Transportation Network Test Problems" (TNTP) collection. Nodes are intersections or other points of the road network, or zone centroids (artificial nodes representing the 1,790 traffic analysis zones, where trips start and end), and directed edges are road links, including the artificial "centroid connector" links that join the zones to the road network. Some ramps that are one-way in reality are coded as bidirectional links, and three nodes (numbers 9365, 12976 and 12977) have no links. The origin-destination demand table that accompanies the network in the repository is not included. (This network is also part of the `tntp` entry, as `chicago_regional`.)

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `is_zone`: whether the node is a zone (zones are numbered first, and only the nodes from number `first_thru_node`, a graph property, on can be traversed by through traffic).
