- (Node) `pos`: the position of the node, in planar coordinates of unspecified units.
- (Edge) `capacity`: the link capacity.
- (Edge) `length`: in miles.
- (Edge) `free_flow_time`: the travel time at zero flow, in minutes.
- (Edge) `b` and `power`: the parameters of the link travel time function, travel time = free_flow_time * (1 + b * (flow / capacity)^power).
- (Edge) `speed`: the speed limit (inconsistent with the free flow time on some links, according to the repository).
- (Edge) `toll`: in cents.
- (Edge) `link_type`: a link classification (undocumented).
- (Edge) `flow` and `flow_cost`: the best known user-equilibrium link flow and the corresponding link travel cost, provided with the network.
citations: Transportation Networks for Research Core Team, "Transportation Networks for Research."

datasets.name: chilean_power_grid
datasets.description:
Networks of the Central Chilean power grid (the Sistema Interconectado Central, SIC), with the hourly power generation and consumption of its nodes, compiled by H. Kim, D. Olave-Rojas, E. Álvarez-Miranda and S.-W. Son. The data were assembled from three sources published by the grid operator (CDEC-SIC, now the Coordinador Eléctrico Nacional): the geographical coordinates of the facilities, the single line diagram of the grid, and the operation records. The sources were harmonized and cleaned (with manual corrections of mismatched or missing coordinates and duplicate names), keeping only the facilities present in all sources, and adding edges between the neighbors of removed facilities to keep the grid connected.

A node is a power plant, a substation, a junction (a branching point of transmission lines), or a tap node (where a facility connects to the middle of a transmission line through a short extension line), and an edge is a transmission line. Three versions of the network are provided:

- `with_tap`: the most detailed version, keeping the tap connections, with 124 plants, 94 substations, 85 junctions and 44 tap nodes.
- `without_tap`: the tap nodes are removed (except where they are branching points, in which case they are kept as junctions), with 124 plants, 94 substations and 100 junctions.
- `reduced`: only the 124 plants and 94 substations, with the junctions removed via star-mesh transformations, which connect all the neighbors of each removed node, preserving the electrical relations between the remaining nodes.

The activity of a node is its net power generation (MWh, per hour) during one year, from 16 September 2015 to 15 September 2016 (8,784 hours), which is non-negative for plants and non-positive for substations. Facilities without activity records (e.g. due to maintenance) have zero activity, as do junctions and tap nodes. In the original data, the total generation (47,005 GWh) exceeds the total consumption (43,829 GWh) by the reserve capacity. In the Kirchhoff-adjusted version, the generation of the plants is scaled so that the net activity of all nodes is zero.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the facility.
- (Node) `owner`: the company that owns it.
- (Node) `role`: the kind of node (`Plant`, `Substation`, `Tap node`, or `Switch` and `Tap-ed`, which are both junctions).
- (Node) `latitude` and `longitude`: the geographical position.
- (Node) `ref` (`with_tap` and `without_tap` only): an undocumented flag of the source files (`original`, `converted` or `corrected`; mostly `converted` for junctions and tap nodes).
- (Node) `activity`: the hourly series of original activity (MWh) (`with_tap` and `reduced` only).
- (Node) `activity_kirchhoff`: the hourly series of Kirchhoff-adjusted activity (MWh) (`with_tap` and `without_tap` only).
- (Edge) `distance`: the length of the transmission line (km).
- (Edge) `voltage`: the voltage of the line (kV).
- (Edge) `lines`: a column of the source files not described in the documentation, presumably the number of circuits.
citations: H. Kim, D. Olave-Rojas, E. Álvarez-Miranda, S.-W. Son, "In-depth data on the network structure and hourly activity of the Central Chilean power grid." Scientific Data 5, 180209 (2018)
H. Kim, D. Olave-Rojas, E. Álvarez-Miranda, S.-W. Son, "An in-depth network structural data and hourly activity on the Central Chilean power grid." figshare, collection (2018)

datasets.name: christmas_eve_bombings
datasets.description:
Time series of networks of relationships among 45 individuals, from the John Jay & ARTIS Transnational Terrorism Database (JJATT). The JJATT data treat specific attacks as endpoints, and depict the evolution of the relations among the individuals directly or indirectly associated with them; here, the coordinated bombings of churches in Indonesia on Christmas Eve 2000 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Christmas_Eve_Indonesia_bombings)). The data were coded from open sources (e.g. court documents, news reports and books), and were made available in matrix form by the UCINET datasets collection (University of Manchester).

Nodes are individuals (labeled by their JJATT identifier in `name`), and each time-period network contains the relationships present in that period (networks named `YYYY_1` and `YYYY_2` refer to the first and second halves of year YYYY). The edge property `weight` gives the strength of the tie: 1 = acquaintances or distant family ties (interaction limited to radical organization activities), 2 = friends or moderately close family ties (including co-workers and roommates), operational or organizational leadership, or operational ties (e.g. having worked closely together on a bombing), 3 = close friends or family, tight-knit operational cliques. The `kinship` network contains the kinship ties present in the data, with the edge property `kinship` coding the type (1 = in-laws, 3 = siblings; no other types occur). The source's matrix of pairs coded as having no kinship (code 0) is not included. The source matrices are meant to be symmetric; in the few cases where the two directions differ, the tie with the larger value is used. The JJATT tie-start, tie-end and operation matrices, which use undocumented codes, are not included.[^ucinet]

[^ucinet]: Description obtained in part from the [UCINET datasets page](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/datasets/covert-networks/christmas-eve-bombings-indonesia-2000).
citations: S. Atran, M. Sageman, et al., "John Jay & ARTIS Transnational Terrorism Database (JJATT)." John Jay College of Criminal Justice (2009)

datasets.name: ciel
datasets.description:
Directed network of communication among the 25 participants in a small drug-importation network bringing liquid hashish from Jamaica to Montreal, Canada, targeted by Project Ciel, an investigation by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the Montreal Police from May 1996 to June 1997. The investigation produced three seizures (two at Mirabel airport near Montreal and one at Sangster airport in Jamaica); of the 75 people in the surveillance net, the 25 who were active in the importation operations are included. Nodes are participants (labelled N1 to N25 in `name`), and a directed edge indicates communication from one participant to another, from police wiretapping, with the edge property `weight` giving the level of communication activity. Data reconstructed from the appendix of Morselli's book "Inside Criminal Networks" (2009) by the UCINET datasets collection (University of Manchester).[^ucinet]

[^ucinet]: Description obtained in part from the [UCINET datasets page](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/datasets/covert-networks/cielnet).
citations: C. Morselli, "Inside Criminal Networks." Springer, New York (2009)

datasets.name: cintestinalis
datasets.description: Entire connectivity matrix for the complete brain of a larva of Ciona intestinalis. Each directed edge represents a synaptic connection from pre-synaptic cell i to post-synaptic cell j (may not be a neuron). Edge weights represent the cumulative depth of presynaptic contacts in µm.
citations: K. Ryan, Z. Lu, & I. A. Meinertzhagen, "The CNS connectome of a tadpole larva of Ciona intestinalis (L.) highlights sidedness in the brain of a chordate sibling." eLife 5, e16962 (2016)

datasets.name: cisco_hosts
datasets.description:
Networks of communications among computing hosts running distributed applications in various enterprises, provided by the Cisco Secure Workload group (O. Madani, S. A. Averineni and S. Gandham) and distributed by SNAP, for research on the clustering of hosts by their function. Software sensors on the hosts recorded, in samples of one hour, the connections between hosts with the (service) port and protocol used and the number of packets exchanged. Nodes are hosts (IP addresses), and an edge points from the client (consumer) of a connection to its server (provider). The hosts and ports are anonymized as integers (separately for each network); the protocols are given by their numbers (6 for TCP, 17 for UDP). There are 27 networks:

- `g1` to `g20`: 20 disjoint networks of different applications (from 86 to 278,739 hosts), recorded in 27 hourly samples on four days, one in January and three in March 2019 (6 or 7 samples per day).
- `g21`: a small network (317 hosts), recorded in 96 hourly samples from 10 to 13 February 2022. For 59 of the hosts, which had a sensor and a host name, the data give a ground-truth grouping of the hosts by function (based on their host names, which are not given).
- `g21_4days`, `g21_2days`, `g21_12hrs`: the connections of `g21` among the hosts with a ground-truth group, aggregated over 4 days, 2 days and 12 hours from 10 February 2022 (without the numbers of packets).
- `g21_few_sensors_6days`, `g21_few_sensors_1day`: the same application observed with fewer than 10 sensors (instead of about 50), aggregated over 6 days and 1 day until 9 February 2022 (without the numbers of packets), so that only part of the network is observed.
- `e1` (also called `g22`): a network of machines doing software builds and regression tests (33,241 hosts), recorded in 99 hourly samples between January 2021 and October 2022, with a candidate ground-truth grouping of 486 hosts (based on their host names).

In the networks recorded in hourly samples (`g1` to `g21` and `e1`), each edge is a connection observed in one sample, so that repeated connections between the same hosts in different samples are separate edges (a multigraph). In the aggregated networks, each pair of hosts appears once. The dates and hours of the samples are not given exactly: the samples are identified by the names of their files (see `snapshots` below).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `host_id`: the anonymized identifier of the host.
- (Node) `g21` networks and `e1`: `group`, the index of the host's ground-truth group (starting from 1; -1 if none); `prefix_code`, the prefix code of the host name, which encodes the position of the host name in the prefix tree of all host names (e.g. "b1l8c2_b1l1c1": first branch, prefix of length 8, 2 hosts below, and so on; empty if none). `g21` networks: `group_prefix5`, the index of the host's group according to the grouping of the host names with a common prefix of at least 5 characters (-1 if none).
- (Edge) `ports`: the ports and protocols of the connection, with the numbers of packets, as given, e.g. "1p6-22,1p17-4" (port 1 on protocol 6 with 22 packets, and port 1 on protocol 17 with 4 packets); for the aggregated networks, the numbers of packets are omitted.
- (Edge) `packets` (sampled networks): the total number of packets of the connection.
- (Edge) `snapshot` (sampled networks): the index (starting from 0) of the hourly sample in the graph property `snapshots`, which lists the names of the sample files (e.g. "out1_4" for the 4th sample of day 1, "202202130300" for 13 February 2022 at 03:00, "out2022_7_5" for the 5th sample of July 2022).
citations: O. Madani, S. A. Averineni, and S. Gandham, "A Dataset of Networks of Computing Hosts." Proceedings of the 2022 ACM International Workshop on Security and Privacy Analytics (IWSPA), 100-104 (2022).

datasets.name: citeseer
datasets.description:
Citations among papers indexed by the CiteSeer digital library. If a paper i cites a paper j also in this data set, then a directed edge connects i to j. (Papers not in the data set are excluded.) Self-loops may be present.[^icon]
[^icon]: Description obtained from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.
citations: K. Bollacker, S. Lawrence, & C. L, Giles, "CiteSeer: An autonomous Web agent for automatic retrieval and identification of interesting publications." In Proc. Int. Conf. on Autonomous Agents, 116-123 (1998)

datasets.name: citeseer_linqs
datasets.description:
A directed citation network of computer science papers, from the version of the CiteSeer dataset distributed by the LINQS group (Lu & Getoor; Sen et al.) as a benchmark for collective classification, also used (as one of the "Planetoid" datasets) in many works on graph neural networks. CiteSeer was a digital library and search engine for scientific papers, built by Giles, Bollacker and Lawrence by automatically crawling the web for papers and extracting their references. This dataset is a selection of 3,312 papers, each classified into one of six topics, chosen such that every paper cites or is cited by at least one other paper of the selection. Each paper is described by the presence or absence of 3,703 words of a vocabulary obtained after stemming and removing stopwords, and discarding words that appear in fewer than 10 papers. The words themselves are not included in the data. This is different data from the one in the `citeseer` entry; see also the `cora_linqs` and `pubmed_linqs` entries.

An edge from paper A to paper B means that A cites B. The citation list refers to 15 papers that are not in the list of papers (17 citations); they are included as nodes without topic and words. The data contain 124 self-loops (papers citing themselves), which are kept.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `id`: the identifier of the paper in the source data.
- (Node) `subject`: the topic of the paper, one of `Agents`, `AI` (artificial intelligence), `DB` (databases), `HCI` (human-computer interaction), `IR` (information retrieval) and `ML` (machine learning), or empty for the papers missing from the list of papers.
- (Node) `words`: a vector of 3,703 binary values, where the i-th value is 1 if the i-th word of the vocabulary appears in the paper, and 0 otherwise (empty for the papers missing from the list of papers).
citations: C. L. Giles, K. D. Bollacker, S. Lawrence, "CiteSeer: An Automatic Citation Indexing System." Proceedings of the Third ACM Conference on Digital Libraries, 89-98 (1998)
Q. Lu, L. Getoor, "Link-based Classification." Proceedings of the Twentieth International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), 496-503 (2003)
P. Sen, G. Namata, M. Bilgic, L. Getoor, B. Gallagher, T. Eliassi-Rad, "Collective Classification in Network Data." AI Magazine 29(3), 93-106 (2008)

datasets.name: citeulike
datasets.description: The bipartite tag–publication network of CiteULike, a social bookmarking service for scholarly publications, as distributed by KONECT. Nodes are 153,277 tags and 731,769 publications (vertex property `is_publication`; neither tags nor publications are named), and each edge is a tag assignment, connecting a tag to a publication it was assigned to; since the same tag can be assigned to a publication by several users, the network contains multiple edges. The edges are annotated with the creation time of the tag assignment, which ranges from 2004 to 2008. The exact date of this snapshot is uncertain.
citations: K. Emamy and R. Cameron. "CiteULike: A researcher's social bookmarking service." Ariadne 51 (2007)

datasets.name: citibike
datasets.description:
Monthly networks of the trips made with Citi Bike, the bicycle sharing system of New York City (operated by Lyft), from the trip data published by the operator: one network for each month from June 2013, when the system opened, to September 2026, named `nyc_<year>_<month>` (e.g. `nyc_2013_06`, 160 networks), and one for each month of its extension to Jersey City and Hoboken (New Jersey), from September 2015 to September 2026, named `jc_<year>_<month>` (133 networks), whose trips are published separately.

Each node is a station, and each directed edge goes from the station where a bicycle was taken out to the station where it was returned, weighted by the number of such trips in the month (trips that return to the same station are self-loops). The networks contain 328,053,007 trips in New York City and 6,995,957 in New Jersey. Left out are the 769,188 trips without a start or an end station (e.g. electric bicycles left away from a station), and the details of individual trips (times, durations, bicycles, and the birth year and gender of the riders, given in the older files).

The station ids are numbers in the older files (for New York City until 2019, and for New Jersey until January 2021) and codes such as `5329.03` or `JC105` in the newer ones (the trips of 2020 in New York City were republished in the newer format), so the stations of different months can be matched by `station_id` only within each period. The coordinates of a station are the most common ones given for the trips that start or end there (in the newer files, those of electric bicycles are recorded by GPS). The yearly archives of the older files contain some months twice (the whole month, and the same trips split into several files); each trip is counted once.

The station-to-station networks are not planar spatial networks (trips may connect any two stations), so they are laid out as other networks, with the coordinates as vertex properties.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `station_id`: the id of the station.
- (Node) `name`: its name (the most common one in the month).
- (Node) `lat` and `lon`: its geographic coordinates (NaN if unknown).
- (Edge) `weight`: the number of trips.
- (Edge) `member_trips`: the number of trips by members, i.e. subscribers with an annual membership (the others are by casual users, with single rides or day passes).
citations: Lyft Bikes and Scooters, "Citi Bike System Data." (2026)

datasets.name: cjeu_citations
datasets.description:
A directed network of citations between the decisions (judgments and orders) of the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU), compiled by K. Moodley and P. Hernandez-Serrano (Institute of Data Science, Maastricht University) from the decisions published on EUR-Lex, the portal of EU law, until December 2018, for a study of the similarity and relevance of court decisions.

Each node is a decision, identified by its CELEX number (e.g. `61997CJ0147`), and a directed edge from A to B means that decision A cites decision B (as recorded by EUR-Lex). The nodes are the 13,780 decisions with metadata in the dataset, and the 543 cited decisions without metadata (which have empty attributes). A few decisions (82) cite themselves (self-loops).

The data were released in two versions on Zenodo, with the same citations: the first (used here) also contains the metadata and the subject topics of the decisions, which the second leaves out. The full texts of the decisions (also in the dataset) are not included, and neither are the columns of the metadata derived from the others (year and month of the dates, duration of the case, number of countries, country and chamber combined, and the number of main subjects).

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `celex`: the CELEX number of the decision (the document identifier of EUR-Lex).
- (Node) `has_metadata`: whether the decision has metadata in the dataset.
- (Node) `case_label`: the case number (e.g. `Case C-32/95 P`, `Joined cases C-147/97 and C-148/97`).
- (Node) `ecli`: the European Case Law Identifier (e.g. `EU:C:2000:74`).
- (Node) `case_type`: `Judgement` or `Order` (empty if not specified).
- (Node) `judge`: the judge-rapporteur; `advocate`: the advocate general.
- (Node) `country`: the country of origin of the case (e.g. of the court that asked for a preliminary ruling).
- (Node) `chamber`: the formation of the Court (e.g. `Sixth Chamber`; empty if not specified).
- (Node) `lodge_date`, `document_date`: the dates on which the case was lodged and the decision was issued (`YYYY-MM-DD`).
- (Node) `joined_cases`: the number of joined cases decided.
- (Node) `ruling_title`, `ruling_name`, `ruling_type`, `ruling_content`: the title of the decision, the names of the parties, the type of proceedings (e.g. reference for a preliminary ruling by a given court), and the keywords of its subject matter.
- (Node) `topics`: the subject matters of the decision in EUR-Lex (e.g. `Free movement of goods`, `Competition`).
citations: K. Moodley, P. V. Hernandez Serrano, G. van Dijck, M. Dumontier, "Similarity and Relevance of Court Decisions: A Computational Study on CJEU Cases." Legal Knowledge and Information Systems (JURIX 2019), Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence and Applications (2019)
K. Moodley, P. Hernandez-Serrano, "Court of Justice of the EU case citations and full texts." Zenodo (2020)

datasets.name: clinical_trials
datasets.description:
The clinical studies registered in ClinicalTrials.gov, the registry of clinical research studies of the U.S. National Library of Medicine, which covers studies in the U.S. and in more than 200 other countries (about 610,000 studies in October 2026), with the conditions they study, the interventions they test, their sponsors and collaborators, the sites (facilities) where they take place, and their investigators. Each network is an undirected bipartite network of the studies and one kind of related entity:

- `conditions`: studies and the conditions (diseases) they study, as the Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) descriptors assigned to the conditions by ClinicalTrials.gov.
- `interventions`: studies and their interventions (drugs, devices, procedures, ...), as the MeSH descriptors assigned to the interventions by ClinicalTrials.gov.
- `sponsors`: studies and the organizations that sponsor them (the lead sponsor and the collaborators), identified by their names as given.
- `sites`: studies and their sites (facilities, e.g. hospitals), identified by their name, city, state and country as given.
- `investigators`: studies and their investigators, i.e. the persons responsible for the scientific conduct of the study as given by the registry ("overall officials": principal investigators, study directors and study chairs), identified by their name and affiliation exactly as given (not disambiguated: the same person with differently written names or affiliations appears as several nodes, and different persons of the same name and affiliation are merged).

The registry is updated daily, and its downloads are not versioned: the networks are of the download date (the data were checked on 31 October 2026). The contact persons of the studies (central and site contacts) and the investigators of the individual sites are left out, as are the free-text descriptions, the outcomes and the results of the studies. Studies whose conditions or interventions were not mapped to MeSH descriptors have no edges in those networks (their conditions and interventions as given are in the properties `conditions` and `intervention_names`).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `is_study`: whether the node is a study.
- (Node) `name`: the NCT number of the study (its page is `https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/<name>`), the MeSH descriptor (e.g. `Lung Neoplasms`), the name of the organization, the name of the facility, or the name of the investigator (as given, often with degrees, e.g. `Jane Doe, MD`).
- (Node) `title` (studies): the brief title.
- (Node) `study_type` (studies): `INTERVENTIONAL`, `OBSERVATIONAL`, `EXPANDED_ACCESS`.
- (Node) `phases` (studies): the phases (e.g. `PHASE2|PHASE3`).
- (Node) `status` (studies): the overall recruitment status, e.g. `COMPLETED`, `RECRUITING`.
- (Node) `start_date`, `completion_date` and `first_posted` (studies): the dates of start, completion and first posting (Unix time, -1 if unknown; dates given as a month are taken as its first day).
- (Node) `enrollment` (studies): the number of participants, actual or anticipated; -1 if unknown.
- (Node) `has_results` (studies): whether the study has results.
- (Node) `sponsor_class` (studies): the class of the lead sponsor: `INDUSTRY`, `NIH`, `FED`, `OTHER_GOV`, `NETWORK`, `OTHER`, ...
- (Node) `conditions` (studies): the conditions as given, separated by `|`.
- (Node) `intervention_names` (studies): the interventions as given, as `<type>: <name>`, separated by `|`.
- (Node) `mesh_id` (MeSH descriptors, `conditions`, `interventions`): the MeSH identifier (e.g. `D008175`).
- (Node) `org_class` (organizations, `sponsors`): the class of the organization, as above.
- (Edge) `role` (`sponsors`): `lead_sponsor` or `collaborator`.
- (Node) `city`, `state`, `zip`, `country` (sites, `sites`): the address of the site.
- (Node) `latitude`, `longitude` (sites, `sites`): the coordinates of the site (`NaN` if unknown).
- (Edge) `site_status` (`sites`): the recruitment status of the site, if given.
- (Node) `affiliation` (investigators, `investigators`): the affiliation, as given.
- (Edge) `role` (`investigators`): the role of the investigator: `PRINCIPAL_INVESTIGATOR`, `STUDY_DIRECTOR`, `STUDY_CHAIR` (or empty if not given).
citations: A. Tasneem, L. Aberle, H. Ananth, S. Chakraborty, K. Chiswell, B. J. McCourt, R. Pietrobon, "The Database for Aggregate Analysis of ClinicalTrials.gov (AACT) and Subsequent Regrouping by Clinical Specialty." PLoS ONE 7(3), e33677 (2012)

datasets.name: coastal_parasite_webs
datasets.description:
Seven coastal marine or estuarine food webs that include metazoan parasites, in the species-level (aggregated) versions compiled by J. A. Dunne and colleagues for a comparative analysis of how parasites affect food web structure. Three webs are from the North American Pacific coast, compiled by R. F. Hechinger and colleagues: Carpinteria Salt Marsh (California, USA), Estero de Punta Banda and Bahía Falsa in Bahía San Quintín (both in Baja California, Mexico). Three are from Europe and New Zealand, compiled by a second research group: Flensburg Fjord (Baltic Sea, between Germany and Denmark), Sylt Tidal Basin (North Sea, between Germany and Denmark) and Otago Harbour (Dunedin, New Zealand). The seventh is the Ythan Estuary web (North Sea, near Aberdeen, Scotland) of M. Huxham, S. Beaney and D. Raffaelli (1996). The parasite data were mostly obtained by dissecting individuals of the free-living species sampled in each habitat, supplemented with the literature for the same or nearby sites and with inferences from host and parasite biology; some groups (e.g. protozoans and bacteriophages) are not, or only poorly, identified.

The original webs represent the life stages of parasites with complex life cycles (e.g. the cercariae, metacercariae and adults of trematodes) as separate nodes. In these versions, the life stages of each parasite species, and their links, were aggregated into a single node. Nodes are therefore species (or coarser taxa, functional groups and non-living resources, such as detritus and carrion), and a directed edge points from a consumer to its resource (prey or host). Self-loops represent cannibalism.

Each network contains the most complete version of the web (with parasites and concomitant links), and the edge property `link_type` identifies the nested subsets that correspond to the three versions of each web analyzed in the source:

- `"free-living"`: links among free-living taxa only (the free-living web).
- `"parasitic"`: the additional links of the web with parasites but without concomitant links, i.e. parasites consuming their hosts, free-living taxa consuming parasites (targeted predation, e.g. on free-living parasite stages), and parasite–parasite links. The Ythan Estuary web only has parasite–host links here.
- `"concomitant"`: concomitant predation links, i.e. predators consuming the parasites of their prey, inferred by assuming that a predator eats all the parasites of infected prey. In the Ythan Estuary web, this set also contains all the links of free-living taxa to parasites and the parasite–parasite links, and in the three Californian webs it also contains a few (8 to 11) links among free-living taxa.

The networks are:

| Network | Location | Nodes (parasites) | free-living | parasitic | concomitant |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `bahia_falsa` | Bahía Falsa, Baja California | 171 (52) | 1,077 | 1,157 | 1,486 |
| `carpinteria` | Carpinteria Salt Marsh, California | 165 (58) | 970 | 1,217 | 1,521 |
| `punta_banda` | Estero de Punta Banda, Baja California | 214 (76) | 1,657 | 1,677 | 2,319 |
| `flensburg` | Flensburg Fjord, Germany/Denmark | 123 (46) | 579 | 389 | 438 |
| `otago` | Otago Harbour, New Zealand | 142 (19) | 1,206 | 281 | 357 |
| `sylt` | Sylt Tidal Basin, Germany/Denmark | 161 (35) | 1,052 | 898 | 1,055 |
| `ythan` | Ythan Estuary, Scotland | 133 (42) | 420 | 177 | 794 |

The `bahia_falsa`, `carpinteria` and `punta_banda` networks are derived from the life-stage resolved webs in the entry `california_estuaries`, and `flensburg` from the one in the entry `flensburg_fjord`; the ones here differ by the aggregation of parasite life stages into species, and contain fewer node attributes. An earlier version of the Carpinteria Salt Marsh web (Lafferty et al. 2006) is the network `food_web_lafferty` of the entry `iwdb`, and is also included in `gateway_foodwebs`. In the Ythan Estuary web, the species 100 of the original data, an animal without resources, was removed together with its only link; the remaining nodes were not renumbered.

Node properties:

- `node_id`: the identifier of the node in the source (in the Ythan web, 100 is missing).
- `name`: the name of the taxon or resource.
- `is_parasite`: whether the node is a parasite taxon (type 2 in the source) or a free-living taxon or non-living resource (type 1).

Edge properties:

- `link_type`: the version of the web in which the link first appears (`"free-living"`, `"parasitic"` or `"concomitant"`, see above).
citations: J. A. Dunne, K. D. Lafferty, A. P. Dobson, R. F. Hechinger, A. M. Kuris, N. D. Martinez, J. P. McLaughlin, K. N. Mouritsen, R. Poulin, K. Reise, D. B. Stouffer, D. W. Thieltges, R. J. Williams, C. D. Zander, "Parasites affect food web structure primarily through increased diversity and complexity." PLoS Biology 11(6), e1001579 (2013)

J. A. Dunne, K. D. Lafferty, A. P. Dobson, R. F. Hechinger, A. M. Kuris, N. D. Martinez, J. P. McLaughlin, K. N. Mouritsen, R. Poulin, K. Reise, D. B. Stouffer, D. W. Thieltges, R. J. Williams, C. D. Zander, "Data from: Parasites affect food web structure primarily through increased diversity and complexity." Dryad (2013)

datasets.name: cocaine_dealing_nyc
datasets.description:
Directed network of communication among 28 members of a large cocaine trafficking organization in New York City, reconstructed by Natarajan (2000) from the transcripts of 151 telephone conversations intercepted by police wiretaps. Nodes are individuals (vertex property `name`, with the nicknames used in the source), and a directed edge indicates communication (flow of information) from one person to the other, with the edge property `weight` giving the number of conversations. Data distributed by the UCINET datasets collection (University of Manchester).[^ucinet]

[^ucinet]: Description obtained in part from the [UCINET datasets page](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/datasets/covert-networks/cocaine-dealing-natarajan).
citations: M. Natarajan, "Understanding the structure of a drug trafficking organization: a conversational analysis." Crime Prevention Studies 11, 273-298 (2000)

datasets.name: codex_kg
datasets.description:
Knowledge graphs extracted from Wikidata by Safavi and Koutra as benchmarks for knowledge graph completion (link prediction and triple classification), the CoDEx datasets. Each node is an entity of Wikidata (e.g. a person, a country, an organization, a language or a disease), and a directed edge from entity A to entity B is a triple (A, relation, B), e.g. that a person has the country of citizenship B. Pairs of entities may be connected by several edges with different relations.

The authors first defined a seed set of entity types and relations of 13 domains (e.g. business, geography, medicine, music, politics, science, sports), and queried Wikidata for the statements whose subject has a seed type and whose relation is a seed relation, which gives the raw dump (`raw`: 380,038 entities, 75 relations, 1,156,222 triples). From it, they extracted three benchmarks of increasing size, as k-cores of the raw graph, from which they removed the relations that largely overlap with the inverse of another one:

- `codex_s` (k = 15): 2,034 entities and 42 relations;
- `codex_m` (k = 10): 17,050 entities and 51 relations;
- `codex_l` (k = 5): 77,951 entities and 69 relations.

The triples of the benchmarks are divided into training, validation and test sets; all of them are included, and the set is given as an edge property. The "hard negatives" of `codex_s` and `codex_m`, triples verified to be false that are used for triple classification, are left out, as are the Wikipedia page extracts of the entities and the labels in other languages than English.

The labels, descriptions, URLs and types are given by the data only for the entities of `codex_l`, so they are empty for the other entities of `raw` (302,087 of them).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `wikidata_id`: the Wikidata identifier of the entity, e.g. `Q7604`.
- (Node) `label`: the English label of the entity (empty if absent).
- (Node) `description`: the English description of the entity in Wikidata (empty if absent).
- (Node) `wikipedia_url`: the URL of the English Wikipedia article of the entity (empty if absent).
- (Node) `types`: the English labels of the types of the entity in Wikidata (e.g. `human`).
- (Edge) `relation_id`: the Wikidata property of the relation, e.g. `P27`.
- (Edge) `relation`: the English label of the relation, e.g. `country of citizenship` (empty for the relations of `raw` that are not described in the data).
- (Edge) `split` (not for `raw`): the set of the benchmark the triple belongs to: `train`, `valid` or `test`.
citations: T. Safavi, D. Koutra, "CoDEx: A Comprehensive Knowledge Graph Completion Benchmark." Proceedings of the 2020 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP), 8328-8350 (2020)

datasets.name: cofe
datasets.description:
Network of authors and commenters of papers in financial economics, obtained from the acknowledgment sections of over 5,000 published research papers.

Nodes are persons (authors or commenters, identified by name), and a directed edge from a commenter to an author exists if the commenter is acknowledged for comments in a paper by the author. Each paper contributes one edge from each of its commenters to each of its authors, so that pairs appearing in several papers are connected by parallel edges.
citations: Rose, Michael E. and Georg, Co-Pierre, “What 5,000 Acknowledgements Tell Us About Informal Collaboration in Financial Economics”, Research Policy 50(6) (2021)

datasets.name: collectri
datasets.description:
The human gene regulatory network of CollecTRI ("Collection of Transcriptional Regulatory Interactions"), compiled by Müller-Dott et al. from twelve resources of transcription factor (TF) to target gene interactions: the text-mining resource ExTRI, the curated databases HTRI, TRRUST, TFactS, GOA, IntAct, SIGNOR, CytReg and GEREDB, the curations of NTNU and of Pavlidis et al. (2021), and the highest-confidence interactions of DoRothEA. Nodes are genes (identified by their gene symbols), and a directed edge $(i, j)$ indicates that the transcription factor $i$ regulates the expression of gene $j$.

There are two networks:

- `regulons`: the authors' signed regulons (43,175 interactions), in which each interaction is an activation or a repression. The sign was taken from the resources when available, otherwise from the TF's known role as activator or repressor, and otherwise set to activation by default. Two sources (`AP1` and `NFKB`) are protein complexes rather than single TFs.
- `source`: all TF-target pairs of the integrated resources (48,681 pairs), from the authors' source table, before the filtering and the assignment of signs.

Self-loops are autoregulation. The regulons for mouse and rat distributed with the tools of the authors are translated from the human ones by orthology, and are not included here.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the gene symbol of the gene (e.g. `MYC`).
- (Edge) `sign` (edges, `regulons` only): the mode of regulation, +1 for activation and -1 for repression.
- (Edge) `sign_decision` (edges, `regulons` only): how the sign was decided (`PMID`: from the literature evidence in the resources; `regulon`: from the role of the TF; `default activation`).
- (Edge) `resources` (edges): the resources in which the interaction is found, separated by `;`.
- (Edge) `references` (edges, `regulons` only): the PubMed identifiers of the publications supporting the interaction, separated by `;`.
- (Edge) `extri_confidence` (edges, `source` only): the confidence of the text-mined interaction in ExTRI (`High` or `Low`); empty if not in ExTRI.
citations: S. Müller-Dott, E. Tsirvouli, M. Vazquez, R. O. Ramirez Flores, P. Badia-i-Mompel, R. Fallegger, D. Türei, A. Lægreid, J. Saez-Rodriguez, "Expanding the coverage of regulons from high-confidence prior knowledge for accurate estimation of transcription factor activities." Nucleic Acids Research 51, 10934-10949 (2023)

datasets.name: college_freshmen
datasets.description:
Relationships among 32 university freshmen in the Netherlands, collected by G. G. van de Bunt in 1994–1995, and analyzed with an actor-oriented model of network dynamics by van de Bunt, van Duijn and Snijders (1999). Except for a few existing relationships (acquaintances from a former school), the students did not know each other at the first measurement. The data were collected at seven time points (waves 0 to 6); the first four are three weeks apart, and the last three are six weeks apart. The original group consisted of 49 students, but after removing university drop-outs and those who did not fill in the questionnaire four or more times, a group of 32 students with almost complete data was obtained. At each wave, the students rated their relationship with each of the others as: 1, best friendship (persons whom they would call their "real" friends); 2, friendship (a good relationship, but not (yet) a "real" friend); 3, friendly relationship (regular pleasant contact during classes, which could grow into a friendship); 4, neutral relationship (not much in common; the chance of a friendship is not large); 5, troubled relationship (a person with whom they cannot get on very well, with a certain risk of conflict); or 0, unknown person. The students followed three different education programs, which overlapped largely during the first months, but diverged afterwards. Smoking was only allowed in special areas, so smokers had to separate themselves from non-smokers when they wished to smoke. The data were distributed by L. C. Freeman on his network data page at the University of California, Irvine (no longer online), from which this version was obtained via the Internet Archive.

A directed edge $i \to j$ indicates that student $i$ rated their relationship with student $j$ with a code from 1 to 5 in a given wave; there is one edge per wave in which a rating was given. Ratings coded as 0 (unknown person), 6 (item non-response) or 9 (actor non-response) are not represented as edges.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `male`: whether the student is male.
- (Node) `program`: the length of the education program (2, 3 or 4 years).
- (Node) `smoker`: whether the student smokes.
- (Node) `nonresponse`: the waves in which all the ratings of the student are coded as actor non-response.
- (Edge) `wave`: the wave of the rating (0 to 6).
- (Edge) `rating`: the relationship code (1: best friendship, 2: friendship, 3: friendly relationship, 4: neutral relationship, 5: troubled relationship).
citations: G. Van de Bunt, M. Van Duijn, & T. Snijders, "Friendship networks through time: An actor-oriented dynamic statistical network model." Comp. & Math. Org. Theory 5(2), 167-192 (1999)
G. G. van de Bunt, "Friends by Choice: An Actor-Oriented Statistical Network Model for Friendship Networks Through Time." Thesis Publishers, Amsterdam (1999)

datasets.name: collins_philosophers
datasets.description:
Networks of personal relationships among philosophers and other intellectuals throughout world history, as coded by W. de Nooy from the diagrams of R. Collins's book "The Sociology of Philosophies: A Global Theory of Intellectual Change" (1998). The book traces intellectual networks in China, India, Japan, the Islamic world, Jewish thought, Greece and Europe, from antiquity to the twentieth century. Nodes are philosophers (and some non-philosophers, such as politicians or patrons, who appear in the diagrams), and there are two networks with the same nodes:

- `acquaintance`: an undirected edge connects two persons who knew each other (acquaintanceship ties).
- `master_pupil`: a directed edge from $i$ to $j$ means that $i$ was a master (teacher) of $j$.

Ties are signed: the edge property `value` is 2 for a positive tie, 1 for a probable tie, and -2 for a negative tie (a conflictual relationship), as coded in the source (see the book's diagrams for the meaning of the codes). Three master-pupil ties that refer to persons missing from the list of philosophers are omitted.

The nodes have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the label of the person, as coded (e.g. "CONFUCIUS", "1 Teng Hsi").
- (Node) `info`: a short description of the person (e.g. "Confucian", "lawyer/debater").
- (Node) `date`: the date of the person's generation, as a year (negative for BCE; NaN if not coded).
- (Node) `stature`: the stature of the person (1: major philosopher, 2: secondary philosopher, 3: minor philosopher, 4: non-philosopher, 5: major non-philosopher; -1 if not coded).
- (Node) `school`: the school or group of the person (e.g. "Confucian school", "Mohists"), empty if none is coded.

The data are distributed as a relational database; de Nooy notes that in case of doubt about the codes, one should consult the diagrams in the book.[^icon]

[^icon]: Description obtained in part from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.
citations: R. Collins, "The Sociology of Philosophies: A Global Theory of Intellectual Change." Belknap Press of Harvard University Press, Cambridge, MA (1998)

datasets.name: collins_yeast
datasets.description:
A network of physical protein–protein interactions in the budding yeast *Saccharomyces cerevisiae*, from the study of S. R. Collins and collaborators. The authors re-analyzed the two large-scale data sets of protein complexes identified by tandem affinity purification followed by mass spectrometry (AP/MS) of Gavin et al. (2006) and Krogan et al. (2006), and combined them with a purification enrichment (PE) scoring system calibrated against a reference set of known protein complexes. Nodes are proteins, and an undirected edge connects two proteins that were found to be co-complex associated (i.e. members of the same complex) in the high-confidence set of interactions. The node property `name` holds the systematic (ORF) name of the protein (e.g. `YAL001C`); the network has no edge properties.

This network comes from the yeast download page of the CCSB Interactome Database (Center for Cancer Systems Biology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute), whose other data sets are in the entries `yeast_interactome_ccsb` (the yeast binary Y2H maps CCSB-YI1, Ito core and Uetz screen, and literature-curated and gold-standard reference sets), `interactome_vidal` (the first human binary map CCSB-HI1/HI-I-05), `human_interactome_2014` (the human maps HI-II-14 and Lit-BM-13) and `celegans_interactomes` (the *C. elegans* interactome networks).
citations: S.R. Collins et al., "Toward a comprehensive atlas of the physical interactome of Saccharomyces cerevisiae." Mol. Cell. Proteomics 6(3), 439-450 (2007)

datasets.name: colobus_monkeys
datasets.description:
Affiliative behavior among the ten members of a captive colony of black-and-white colobus monkeys (Colobus guereza), observed by N. Kutsukake, N. Suetsugu and T. Hasegawa (according to ICON, in 2003). Greeting was defined as non-sexual mounting, and was described by the authors as functioning as a tension-reducing mechanism in nonagonistic situations. The data were distributed by L. C. Freeman on his network data page at the University of California, Irvine (no longer online), from which this version was obtained via the Internet Archive.

The network has two directed layers, in which an edge (i, j) indicates that monkey i directed the behavior at monkey j:

- `greeting`
- `grooming`

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the label of the monkey.
- (Node) `sex` (1: male, 2: female).
- (Node) `age_grade` (1: juvenile, 2: sub-adult, 3: adult).
- (Edge) `layer`: the behavior.
- (Edge) `weight`: the number of times the behavior was observed.
citations: N. Kutsukake, N. Suetsugu, T. Hasegawa, "Pattern, distribution, and function of greeting behavior among black-and-white colobus." International Journal of Primatology 27(5), 1271-1291 (2006)

datasets.name: colombia_calls_mobility
datasets.description:
Two networks among the 863 municipalities of Colombia, derived from the anonymized metadata of mobile phone calls of the operators of Colombia, from Coscia and Hausmann. For each call, the data record the (anonymized) caller and callee, the time of the call, and the phone tower to which the caller was connected. Only phones that made and received at least six calls during the observation period were kept, to remove foreign phones and special numbers (e.g. call centers). The towers were aggregated by municipality. The paper does not state the observation period precisely (its example call is from December 2013); ICON dates the data to 2014.

- `calls`: each phone is assigned to the municipality of the tower it connected to most frequently, and each call is counted as a directed edge from the municipality of the caller to the municipality of the callee.
- `mobility`: a directed edge from municipality A to municipality B is counted whenever a phone made two consecutive calls, the first in A and the second in B.

These are the complete aggregated networks distributed with the paper. In the paper, the most significant edges were then selected, keeping the maximum spanning tree and the edges that are statistically significant according to the disparity filter of Serrano et al. (this filtering is not applied here).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `code`: the code of the municipality (DANE code prefixed with "M").
- (Node) `name`: the name of the municipality.
- (Edge) `weight`: the number of calls (`calls`) or observed movements (`mobility`) from the source to the target municipality.
citations: M. Coscia, R. Hausmann, "Evidence That Calls-Based and Mobility Networks Are Isomorphic." PLOS ONE 10(12), e0145091 (2015)

datasets.name: colombia_urban_mobility
datasets.description:
Networks of trips between the transportation zones of two Colombian cities, from household origin-destination surveys (ODS), as distributed by Lotero et al. In these surveys, each member (older than 5 years) of the sampled households reported the trips performed on the working day before the interview (Medellín), or the trips usually made on working days (Manizales), including their origin and destination zones, departure and arrival times and, in Medellín, the trip purpose. The surveys were carried out by the Universidad Nacional de Colombia for the Área Metropolitana del Valle de Aburrá (Medellín, 2005-2006, 413 zones, 56,513 people interviewed) and the Alcaldía de Manizales (2005, 57 zones, 4,089 people interviewed). Each node is a zone, and each directed edge is a trip from its origin to its destination zone (trips within a zone are self-loops), so that the networks are multigraphs. The trips are annotated with the socio-economic stratum of the household of the traveler, which allows the network to be split into six layers, as analyzed in the paper.

- `medellin`: trips in the metropolitan area of Medellín (Valle de Aburrá).
- `manizales`: trips in the municipality of Manizales.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `zone`: the identifier of the zone (from 1 to 413 or 57).
- (Edge) `stratum`: the socio-economic stratum ("estrato") of the household of the traveler, from 1 (lowest income) to 6 (highest income); in Colombia, households are officially classified into these strata according to the characteristics of their housing, to set the rates of public utilities.
- (Edge) `departure` and `arrival`: the departure and arrival times of the trip, in decimal hours.
- (Edge) `mid_time`: the mean of the departure and arrival times.
- (Edge) `weight`: the expansion factor of the trip, i.e. the number of trips in the population that it represents, which depends on the zone and stratum.
- (Edge) `purpose` (`medellin`): the purpose of the trip (1: work, 2: study, 3: shopping, 4: health, 5: recreation, 6: return home, 7: others).
citations: L. Lotero, R. G. Hurtado, L. M. Floría, J. Gómez-Gardeñes, "Rich do not rise early: spatio-temporal patterns in the mobility networks of different socio-economic classes." Royal Society Open Science 3(10), 150654 (2016)

L. Lotero, R. G. Hurtado, L. M. Floría, J. Gómez-Gardeñes, "Data from: Rich do not rise early: spatio-temporal patterns in the mobility networks of different socio-economic classes." Dryad, dataset (2016)

datasets.name: community_notes
datasets.description:
The ratings of the Community Notes of X (formerly Twitter; the program was called Birdwatch until 2022), the crowd-sourced fact-checking system in which enrolled contributors write notes that add context to posts, and rate the notes of others as helpful or not; a note is shown to all users when its ratings come from contributors with diverse perspectives, as determined by a matrix-factorization ("bridging") algorithm. X publishes all notes, ratings, note statuses and contributor enrollments every day, with pseudonymous contributor ids.

The entry contains two bipartite networks of contributors and notes, which have the same nodes (all contributors and notes of the data):

- `ratings`: an edge connects a contributor to each note they rated, with the rating (helpful, somewhat helpful, or not helpful) and the reasons given.
- `authorship`: an edge connects each note to its author.

The data are published as cumulative snapshots, which are kept online for only a few days (deleted notes and ratings disappear from them); the networks are built from the most recent snapshot at the time of the download, whose date is stored as the network property `snapshot_date` (the snapshot of 2026-10-30 had five files of notes and nine files of ratings, the first of 5.6 GB uncompressed). Left out are the ids of the posts on which ratings were made (for notes matching several posts), the source buckets of the ratings and the suggestions of the raters. Notes and contributors that are referenced but missing from the files of notes and of enrollments (e.g. deleted notes) are included without attributes (`has_record` false).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `is_note`: whether the node is a note (otherwise a contributor).
- (Node) `has_record`: whether the note (or contributor) is in the file of notes (or of enrollments).
- (Node) `participant_id` (contributors): the pseudonymous id of the contributor (empty for notes).
- (Node) `enrollment_state` (contributors): the enrollment state (e.g. `newUser`, `earnedIn`, `atRisk`, `earnedOutNoAcknowledge`).
- (Node) `successful_rating_needed_to_earn_in` (contributors): the number of successful ratings needed to earn in.
- (Node) `time_last_state_change` and `time_last_earn_out` (contributors): the times of the last state change and of the last earn-out (Unix time; small values such as 1 or 0, as in the data, mean never; -1 if unknown).
- (Node) `modeling_population` (contributors): the modeling population (e.g. `CORE`, `EXPANSION`).
- (Node) `modeling_group` (contributors): the modeling group (NaN if none).
- (Node) `number_of_times_earned_out` (contributors): the number of times the contributor earned out.
- (Node) `note_id` (notes): the id of the note (-1 for contributors).
- (Node) `author_id` (notes): the participant id of its author.
- (Node) `created` (notes): its time of creation (Unix time).
- (Node) `tweet_id` (notes): the id of the post it is about.
- (Node) `classification` (notes): `MISINFORMED_OR_POTENTIALLY_MISLEADING` or `NOT_MISLEADING`.
- (Node) `believable`, `harmful` and `validation_difficulty` (notes): answers of the author in the first version of the form.
- (Node) `summary` (notes): the text of the note, as in the data (line breaks replaced by spaces, some characters HTML-escaped, e.g. `&`).
- (Node) `misleading_other`, `misleading_factual_error`, `misleading_manipulated_media`, `misleading_outdated_information`, `misleading_missing_important_context`, `misleading_unverified_claim_as_fact`, `misleading_satire`, `not_misleading_other`, `not_misleading_factually_correct`, `not_misleading_outdated_but_not_when_written`, `not_misleading_clearly_satire` and `not_misleading_personal_opinion` (notes): the reasons checked by the author, one property each (1 if checked, 0 if not, -1 if unknown).
- (Node) `trustworthy_sources` (notes): whether the author considers the sources trustworthy.
- (Node) `is_media_note` and `is_collaborative_note` (notes): whether the note is a media note, and whether it is a collaborative note.
- (Node) `current_status` and `time_current_status` (notes, from the status history): the current status (`CURRENTLY_RATED_HELPFUL`, `CURRENTLY_RATED_NOT_HELPFUL` or `NEEDS_MORE_RATINGS`) and its time (Unix time, -1 if none).
- (Node) `first_non_nmr_status` and `time_first_non_nmr_status` (notes, from the status history): the first status other than "needs more ratings", and its time (Unix time, -1 if none).
- (Node) `locked_status` and `time_status_lock` (notes, from the status history): the locked status and the time of the lock (Unix time, -1 if none).
- (Node) `current_decided_by` (notes, from the status history): the scoring model that decided the status.
- (Edge) `time` (`ratings`): the time of the rating (Unix time).
- (Edge) `version` (`ratings`): the version of the rating form (1 or 2).
- (Edge) `helpfulness` (`ratings`): the rating, 2 (helpful), 1 (somewhat helpful) or 0 (not helpful), from the `helpful` and `notHelpful` answers in version 1.
- (Edge) `reasons` (`ratings`): the reasons given, as a bit mask (bits 0 to 23: `agree`, `disagree`, `helpfulOther`, `helpfulInformative`, `helpfulClear`, `helpfulEmpathetic`, `helpfulGoodSources`, `helpfulUniqueContext`, `helpfulAddressesClaim`, `helpfulImportantContext`, `helpfulUnbiasedLanguage`, `notHelpfulOther`, `notHelpfulIncorrect`, `notHelpfulSourcesMissingOrUnreliable`, `notHelpfulOpinionSpeculationOrBias`, `notHelpfulMissingKeyPoints`, `notHelpfulOutdated`, `notHelpfulHardToUnderstand`, `notHelpfulArgumentativeOrBiased`, `notHelpfulOffTopic`, `notHelpfulSpamHarassmentOrAbuse`, `notHelpfulIrrelevantSources`, `notHelpfulOpinionSpeculation`, `notHelpfulNoteNotNeeded`).
- (Edge) `time` (`authorship`): the time of creation of the note (Unix time).
citations: S. Wojcik, S. Hilgard, N. Judd, D. Mocanu, S. Ragain, M. B. F. Hunzaker, K. Coleman, J. Baxter, "Birdwatch: Crowd Wisdom and Bridging Algorithms can Inform Understanding and Reduce the Spread of Misinformation." arXiv:2210.15723 (2022)

datasets.name: compgeom_collab
datasets.description:
Collaborations among authors in computational geometry, from the Computational Geometry Database *geombib* (version of February 2002), a BibTeX bibliography started in 1986 by merging lists of references compiled by H. Edelsbrunner and J. van Leeuwen, and by L. Guibas and J. Stolfi, and maintained by B. Jones. Two authors are connected if they wrote a common work (paper, book, etc.), and the edge is weighted by the number of their common works. The network was produced by V. Batagelj and M. Zaveršnik, who manually unified the different spellings of the names of the same author (e.g. "R.L. Drysdale" and "Robert L. Scot Drysdale"), reducing the network from 9072 to 7343 authors. No provision is made to discern different persons with the same name. Authors without coauthored works appear as isolated nodes. The data were distributed in Pajek format on the Pajek datasets page of V. Batagelj and A. Mrvar, from which this version was obtained.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the author.
- (Edge) `weight`: the number of common works.

datasets.name: congress_bills
datasets.description:
Bipartite networks of members of the US Congress and the legislation they sponsored or cosponsored, from the 93rd to the 108th Congress (1973-2004). The data were compiled by James Fowler (with later contributions by Andrew Scott Waugh and Yunkyu Sohn) by retrieving the records of legislation (bills, resolutions and amendments) from the Library of Congress THOMAS legislative database, and matching its sponsor and cosponsors to legislators. Each piece of legislation is connected to its sponsor and all of its cosponsors. The data are known to contain some errors from the original database and from the matching procedure.

- `congress`: legislation from both chambers, with the date when it was introduced. A few dates fall before 1973 (from 1971-04-29), likely errors in the source data. Legislators are identified by name only, and older members appear by surname only.
- `house`: legislation from the House of Representatives, with the party of each legislator.
- `senate`: legislation from the Senate, with the party of each legislator.

The `house` and `senate` networks are subsets of the same data, prepared separately from the `congress` network (so their legislator nodes do not correspond one-to-one to those of `congress`, and they carry no dates). All legislation in them has at least one cosponsor; the selection criteria are otherwise not documented in the source. Different pieces of legislation can have exactly the same sponsor and cosponsors; they are kept as separate nodes.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `is_bill`: whether the node is a piece of legislation, otherwise a legislator.
- (Node) `name` (legislators): the name of the legislator, as it appears in the source: either a surname only (mostly for older records), or "Last, First [State-District]" (state only for senators).
- (Node) `time` (`congress`, legislation only): the date when the legislation was introduced, in days since 1970-01-01.
- (Node) `party` (`house` and `senate`, legislators only): the political party of the legislator, "Democrat" or "Republican" (the source data only distinguish these two parties).
citations: J. H. Fowler, "Connecting the Congress: A Study of Cosponsorship Networks." Political Analysis 14(4), 456-487 (2006)
J. H. Fowler, "Legislative cosponsorship networks in the US House and Senate." Social Networks 28(4), 454-465 (2006)
A. R. Benson, R. Abebe, M. T. Schaub, A. Jadbabaie, J. Kleinberg, "Simplicial closure and higher-order link prediction." Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 115(48), E11221-E11230 (2018)
P. S. Chodrow, N. Veldt, A. R. Benson, "Generative hypergraph clustering: From blockmodels to modularity." Science Advances 7(28), eabh1303 (2021)

datasets.name: congress_committees
datasets.description:
Bipartite networks of members of the US Congress and the congressional committees they were assigned to, from the 103rd Congress (1993) to 2017. The data derive from the committee assignment records compiled by Charles Stewart III and Jonathan Woon, which record the membership of all committees of each chamber in each Congress, with dates of assignment and termination. Each committee node corresponds to the membership of one committee during one Congress (so the same committee appears once per Congress), and is connected to the legislators assigned to it during that Congress. A legislator listed more than once for the same committee in the source data is connected to it only once. Committee names and Congress numbers are not included.

- `house`: committees of the House of Representatives and their members.
- `senate`: committees of the Senate and their members.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `is_committee`: whether the node is a committee (in a given Congress), otherwise a legislator.
- (Node) `name` (legislators): the name of the legislator.
- (Node) `party` (legislators): the political party of the legislator, "Democrat" or "Republican" (the source data only distinguish these two parties).
citations: C. Stewart III, J. Woon, "Congressional Committee Assignments, 103rd to 114th Congresses, 1993-2017: House" and "...: Senate" (2017)
P. S. Chodrow, N. Veldt, A. R. Benson, "Generative hypergraph clustering: From blockmodels to modularity." Science Advances 7(28), eabh1303 (2021)

datasets.name: congress_twitter
datasets.description:
A directed network of influence on Twitter among the members of the 117th United States Congress (House of Representatives and Senate), collected by C. G. Fink, G. Sprint and collaborators from the Twitter API. It is based on the tweets of the members between February 9 and June 9, 2022. Nodes are members of Congress, identified by their Twitter user names. An edge points from member A to member B if B retweeted, quote tweeted, replied to or mentioned A at least once (a mention is not counted again if it is also a reply, retweet or quote of the same member). The weight of the edge is the number of such interactions divided by the number of tweets of A in the period, an empirical estimate of the probability that a tweet of A is passed on by B.

The authors left out the members with fewer than 100 tweets in the period, and self-interactions. Only the normalized weights are given, not the numbers of interactions or tweets, and the tweets themselves can only be retrieved (rehydrated) through the Twitter API, so the network cannot be recomputed without that threshold.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the Twitter user name of the member.
- (Edge) `weight`: the fraction of the tweets of the source member that the target member retweeted, quote tweeted, replied to or mentioned.
citations: C. G. Fink, N. Omodt, S. Zinnecker, and G. Sprint, "A Congressional Twitter network dataset quantifying pairwise probability of influence." Data in Brief 50, 109521 (2023).
C. G. Fink, K. Fullin, G. Gutierrez, N. Omodt, S. Zinnecker, G. Sprint, and S. McCulloch, "A centrality measure for quantifying spread on weighted, directed networks." Physica A 626, 129083 (2023).

datasets.name: contact
datasets.description:
A network of the contacts between Bluetooth devices carried by attendees of the IEEE Infocom 2005 conference in Miami, recorded by the Haggle project (University of Cambridge and Intel Research Cambridge). Small Bluetooth devices (iMotes) were distributed to about 50 students attending a workshop of the conference on 7 March 2005, between lunch time and 5 pm, and collected on 10 March 2005 in the afternoon; each iMote scanned periodically for the other Bluetooth devices in its range, i.e. the other iMotes and any other device with Bluetooth (phones, laptops, ...), and recorded these sightings. Of the 54 iMotes distributed, 41 yielded useful data: two were lost, and the others did not record data because of failures with the batteries and packaging, or accidental resets; the contacts with these were removed from the traces of the other iMotes. The first six hours, when the participants were attending the same workshop, were also discarded. This is the experiment 3 of the Haggle traces (`imote-trace3`), as sent by the authors and distributed in a GitHub repository.

Each node is a device: nodes 1 to 41 are the iMotes, and nodes 42 to 274 are the other devices they recorded (each identified by its Bluetooth address, which is not given). A directed edge from device A to device B is a contact, i.e. an interval of time during which the iMote A recorded the device B in successive scans, so that pairs of devices are connected by several edges, one per contact (a multigraph). Only iMotes record contacts, and the contacts between two iMotes need not be mutual, since the scans of the iMotes were not synchronized and the sightings need not be symmetric. The times are given in seconds from the beginning of the trace, whose exact date and time is not given.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `is_imote`: whether the device is one of the iMotes (otherwise an external device).
- (Edge) `time`: the first time at which the iMote recorded the device in the contact, in seconds from the beginning of the trace.
- (Edge) `end_time`: the last time at which it recorded it (equal to `time` for contacts seen in a single scan).
- (Edge) `duration`: the difference of these two times, in seconds.
- (Edge) `contact_number`: the number of the contact among those of the same pair of devices (1, 2, ...).
- (Edge) `gap`: the time between the beginning of the contact and the end of the previous contact of the same pair, in seconds (0 for the first contact of a pair).
citations: A. Chaintreau, P. Hui, J. Crowcroft, C. Diot, R. Gass, J. Scott, "Impact of Human Mobility on Opportunistic Forwarding Algorithms." IEEE Transactions on Mobile Computing 6(6), 606-620 (2007)

P. Hui, J. Crowcroft, E. Yoneki, "BUBBLE Rap: Social-based Forwarding in Delay Tolerant Networks." Proceedings of the 9th ACM International Symposium on Mobile Ad Hoc Networking and Computing (MobiHoc), 241-250 (2008)
J. Scott, R. Gass, J. Crowcroft, P. Hui, C. Diot, A. Chaintreau, "CRAWDAD dataset cambridge/haggle (v. 2009-05-29)." CRAWDAD (2009)

datasets.name: contiguous_usa
datasets.description:
A network of the 48 contiguous states of the USA and the District of Columbia, in which each node is a state (or the District of Columbia), and an edge connects two states that share a land border. The data were compiled by D. E. Knuth and distributed with the Stanford GraphBase as the "contiguous USA" graph used in *The Art of Computer Programming*. The two states not connected by land with the others (Alaska and Hawaii) are not included. The source does not document how borders meeting at a single point (e.g. the Four Corners of Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah) are treated; in the data, such diagonal pairs are not adjacent.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the two-letter postal code of the state (DC for the District of Columbia).
citations: D. E. Knuth, "The Stanford GraphBase: A Platform for Combinatorial Computing." ACM Press, New York (1993)

datasets.name: convote_mentions
datasets.description:
A directed signed network of the by-name references between the speakers of floor debates of the US House of Representatives in 2005, from the ConVote corpus of Thomas, Pang and Lee (2006). The authors downloaded the 2005 record of the House from govtrack.us, associated each page with the bill it discussed most, kept the bills that came to a vote, split the pages into speech segments, and labeled each segment by the vote (yes or no) of its speaker on the bill; speakers who abstained were discarded, and only the debates (the speeches on a bill) with at least 20% of speeches of each label were kept, 53 debates in total. In the speeches, the references by name to other members of the House who spoke in the same debate were identified, and a classifier (a support vector machine) was trained on those of the training set (39 debates) to tell whether a reference expresses agreement or disagreement with the referenced member.

The network contains the references of the 14 debates of the development and test sets (the references of the training set are not distributed), with the scores of the classifier. Each node is a speaker (a member of the House), and a directed edge from speaker A to speaker B is a reference to B in a speech of A in a debate. Pairs of speakers may be connected by several edges, and speakers may refer to themselves. The sign of an edge is the true label of the reference: agreement if both speakers voted the same way on the bill, and disagreement otherwise. Only the speakers making or receiving some reference are included (219 of the 302 speakers of these debates). The texts of the speeches, the scores of the individual speeches by the classifier of support or opposition (and the strengths of the corresponding links of the authors' graphs), and the indicators of whether a speech mentions the bill directly are not included.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `speaker_id`: the index of the speaker in the corpus.
- (Node) `party`: the party of the speaker ("D" for Democratic, "R" for Republican, "I" for independent).
- (Edge) `sign`: +1 for a reference between speakers who voted the same way on the bill (agreement), -1 otherwise (disagreement).
- (Edge) `debate`: the index of the bill under discussion (identifying the debate).
- (Edge) `source_vote` and `target_vote`: the votes ("yes" or "no") of the referring and the referenced speaker on the bill.
- (Edge) `raw_score`: the score of the agreement classifier (positive for references classified as agreements).
- (Edge) `normalized_score`: the score divided by the standard deviation of the scores of the references of the debate.
- (Edge) `strength`: the strength of the link between the speakers in the authors' graph, 2500 times the normalized score (0 for negative normalized scores).
- (Edge) `normalized_score_high_precision` and `strength_high_precision`: the same, but with the score minus the average score of the debate, which keeps only the references with above-average scores in the graph.
citations: M. Thomas, B. Pang, L. Lee, "Get out the vote: Determining support or opposition from congressional floor-debate transcripts." Proceedings of the 2006 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, 327-335 (2006)

datasets.name: coop_purchases
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of the customers of the Italian retail company Coop and the products they bought, released by D. Pennacchioli, M. Coscia, S. Rinzivillo, D. Pedreschi and F. Giannotti as the companion data set of their study of the "product range effect". The data cover the purchases recorded between January 2007 and December 2011 by 60,365 anonymized customers (holders of a loyalty card) in five shops of the company, and 4,567 products. Nodes are customers and products, and an edge connects a customer to a product they bought in a given shop, with `quantity` equal to the total number of items of the product bought by the customer in that shop over the whole period. A customer and a product are thus connected by up to five parallel edges, one for each shop.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `is_customer`: whether the node is a customer (otherwise it is a product).
- (Node) `id`: the identifier of the customer or of the product in the source data.
- (Node) `price` (products): the unit price of the product in euros, averaged over the time span of the data set.
- (Node) `shop_distance` (customers): the distances, in meters, from the customer's home to each of the five shops (shop identifiers 1 to 5, in this order), measured as straight lines, not along the road network.
- (Edge) `shop` (edges): the identifier of the shop (1 to 5) where the purchases were made.
- (Edge) `quantity` (edges): the number of items bought.

The customer with identifier 44,617 (in the range from 1 to 60,366) has no purchases in the data, and is included as an isolated node.
citations: D. Pennacchioli, M. Coscia, S. Rinzivillo, D. Pedreschi, F. Giannotti, "Explaining the product range effect in purchase data." 2013 IEEE International Conference on Big Data, 648-656 (2013)

datasets.name: copenhagen
datasets.description:
Networks of interactions among about 700 university students at the Technical University of Denmark, from the Copenhagen Networks Study. Participants were given smartphones that recorded physical proximity to other participants (via Bluetooth), phone calls and text messages; their Facebook friendships were also collected. The data released by P. Sapiezynski and collaborators cover a period of four weeks, during which Bluetooth scans were performed every five minutes. There are four networks, all on participants of the study:

- `sms`: an edge from the sender to the recipient of each text message, with its `timestamp`.
- `calls`: an edge from the caller to the recipient of each phone call, with its `timestamp` and `duration` in seconds (-1 for a missed call).
- `bt`: an undirected edge for each Bluetooth scan in which two participants' phones detected each other, with its `timestamp` and `rssi`, the received signal strength indicator (in dBm, a proxy for physical proximity). Scans that detected no participant, or only devices outside the study, are not included.
- `fb_friends`: an undirected edge for each Facebook friendship between participants that existed throughout the observation period.

Timestamps are in seconds since the beginning of the observation period.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `id`: the participant's identifier in the original data, shared across the four networks.
- (Node) `female`: the participant's gender: 1 for female, 0 otherwise, and -1 where unknown.
- (Edge) `timestamp`, `duration` and `rssi`: as described above.
citations: P. Sapiezynski, et al., "Interaction data from the Copenhagen Networks Study." Scientific Data 6, 315 (2019)

datasets.name: cora
datasets.description:
Citations among computer science research papers from the Cora collection, assembled by A. McCallum and collaborators in the late 1990s for the Cora research paper search engine. Cora gathered research papers from the web, automatically extracted their references, and classified the papers into a hierarchy of computer science topics. The network was extracted from the Cora data by L. Šubelj and M. Bajec, and contains only papers that were assigned a topic. Nodes are papers and a directed edge $(i,j)$ indicates that paper $i$ cites paper $j$. Citations to papers outside the data set are excluded. The dates of the papers are not included.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `cora_id`: the paper ID in the original Cora data set.
- (Node) `topic`: the topic of the paper in the Cora topic hierarchy, given as a path, e.g. `/Artificial_Intelligence/Machine_Learning/Neural_Networks/` (70 topics in total).
citations: A. McCallum, K. Nigam, J. Rennie, K. Seymore, "Automating the Construction of Internet Portals with Machine Learning." Information Retrieval 3(2), 127-163 (2000)
L. Šubelj, M. Bajec, "Model of complex networks based on citation dynamics." Proceedings of the 22nd International Conference on World Wide Web (LSNA '13), 527-530 (2013)

datasets.name: cora_arxiv_dblp
datasets.description:
Paper citation, author citation and co-authorship networks constructed by Šubelj, Bajec, Mileva Boshkoska, Kastrin and Levnajić from three bibliographic databases, to study the consistency among scientific databases. From each database, the following networks were constructed:

- Paper citation (`*_cit`, directed): nodes are papers, and a directed edge means that one paper cites another.
- Author citation (`*_act`, directed): nodes are authors, and a directed edge means that an author cites another author in at least one of their papers.
- Co-authorship (`*_acl`, undirected): nodes are authors, and an edge means that two authors co-authored at least one paper.

The databases are:

- `cora_*`: the Cora computer science research paper search engine, which collected publication records from the websites of computer science departments at major universities in August 1998 (195,950 papers, 24,911 authors and 623,287 citations).
- `arxiv_*`: the arXiv High Energy Physics Theory category, between 1992 and 2003 (27,770 papers and 12,820 authors), as distributed by SNAP. The corresponding paper citation network is available separately (see the `arxiv_citation` entry, `HepTh` network).
- `dblp_act`: the DBLP Computer Science Bibliography, as of September 2014 (1,424,895 authors). Only the author citation network is available. Citation information in DBLP is scarce, so that only about 15 thousand of the authors are connected by citations; the remaining authors are isolated nodes.

According to the authors, papers and authors neither citing nor cited were discarded, together with authors not collaborating, and self-citations of papers that occur due to errors were discarded; however, the distributed author networks include all authors of each database, which leaves some isolated nodes. The `cora_cit` network contains repeated edges.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the author name (in the normalized form used by the source), or the paper identifier (Cora identifier or arXiv identifier).
citations: L. Šubelj, M. Bajec, B. Mileva Boshkoska, A. Kastrin, Z. Levnajić, "Quantifying the Consistency of Scientific Databases." PLOS ONE 10(5), e0127390 (2015)

datasets.name: cora_linqs
datasets.description:
A directed citation network of machine learning papers, from the version of the Cora dataset distributed by the LINQS group (Sen et al.) as a benchmark for collective classification. Cora was a search engine for computer science research papers, built by McCallum et al. by automatically crawling the web for papers and extracting their references, which were classified into a hierarchy of topics. This dataset is a selection of the papers in the machine learning topic, each assigned to one of seven subtopics, chosen such that every paper cites or is cited by at least one other paper of the selection. Each paper is described by the presence or absence of 1,433 words of a vocabulary obtained after stemming and removing stopwords, and discarding words that appear in fewer than 10 papers. The words themselves are not included in the data. This is a different version of the Cora data from the one in the `cora` entry.

An edge from paper A to paper B means that A cites B. The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `id`: the identifier of the paper in the source data.
- (Node) `subject`: the machine learning subtopic of the paper, one of `Case_Based`, `Genetic_Algorithms`, `Neural_Networks`, `Probabilistic_Methods`, `Reinforcement_Learning`, `Rule_Learning` and `Theory`.
- (Node) `words`: a vector of 1,433 binary values, where the i-th value is 1 if the i-th word of the vocabulary appears in the paper, and 0 otherwise.
citations: A. K. McCallum, K. Nigam, J. Rennie, K. Seymore, "Automating the Construction of Internet Portals with Machine Learning." Information Retrieval 3(2), 127-163 (2000)
P. Sen, G. Namata, M. Bilgic, L. Getoor, B. Gallagher, T. Eliassi-Rad, "Collective Classification in Network Data." AI Magazine 29(3), 93-106 (2008)
