datasets.name: cordis_projects
datasets.description:
Participations of organizations in the research projects funded by the European Union under its Framework Programmes for research and innovation, from FP1 (1984-1987) to Horizon Europe (2021-2027), from the project data of CORDIS (Community Research and Development Information Service) of the European Commission. Each network is the undirected bipartite network of the organizations (universities, research centers, companies, public bodies, ...) and the projects of one Framework Programme, where an edge links an organization to a project in which it takes part, as coordinator, participant, partner, associated partner or third party.

The networks are the programs:

- `fp1` (1984-1987), `fp2` (1987-1991), `fp3` (1990-1994), `fp4` (1994-1998), `fp5` (1998-2002), `fp6` (2002-2006), `fp7` (2007-2013): the closed earlier Framework Programmes;
- `h2020`: Horizon 2020 (2014-2020);
- `horizon_europe`: Horizon Europe (2021-2027), still ongoing;
- `combined`: all the programs together, in one network.

Organizations are identified by the participant identification code (PIC) of the European Commission where the data give one (in FP7, Horizon 2020 and Horizon Europe, and for a few organizations of FP4-FP6); otherwise (almost all organizations of FP1-FP6) they are identified by their exact name and country as given in the data, so that an organization whose name is spelled differently in different projects appears as several nodes. In the network `combined`, the organizations of all programs are merged in the same way: by their PIC where they have one, otherwise by their exact name and country. Since the PICs are missing before FP7, an organization that took part in earlier programs is thus usually split into several nodes (one with its PIC, from FP7 on, and one or more without, from the earlier programs, one per spelling of its name), and different organizations of the same name and country before FP7 are merged into one node. The attributes of an organization in `combined` are those of the last program in which it appears; the projects are those of all programs, with their program as a property (the project ids of different programs are kept apart). An organization that takes part in a project in several roles (e.g. as participant and as third party) has several edges to it, one per participation. Every project of the program is a node, including the few without any listed participant.

The data of CORDIS are updated in place (in particular those of Horizon 2020 and Horizon Europe, which change as projects are signed and closed); the networks are of the files of October 2026 (the earlier programs were last updated in October 2024 and January 2025). The descriptions of the projects ("objective"), their reports, publications and deliverables, and the street addresses and contact forms of the organizations are left out.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `is_project`: whether the node is a project (otherwise it is an organization).
- (Node) `name`: the name of the organization, or the title of the project.
- (Node) `id`: the identifier of the organization (its PIC; empty if there is none) or of the project (its grant agreement number or reference).
- (Node) `acronym`: the acronym of the project, or the short name of the organization.
- (Node) `program` (network `combined` only): the program of the project (`fp1`, ..., `h2020`, `horizon_europe`; empty for organizations).
- (Node) `sme` (organizations): whether it is a small or medium-sized enterprise: `true`, `false` or empty if unknown.
- (Node) `activity_type` (organizations): `HES`: higher or secondary education, `REC`: research organization, `PRC`: private company, `PUB`: public body, `OTH`: other, and in FP6 also `IND`: industry and `GOV`: government; empty if unknown, as for almost all organizations before FP7.
- (Node) `city`, `post_code` (organizations): the city and post code of the organization.
- (Node) `country` (organizations): two-letter code, e.g. `UK` for the United Kingdom and `EL` for Greece.
- (Node) `nuts_code` (organizations): the NUTS region code.
- (Node) `latitude` and `longitude` (organizations): the coordinates of the organization (`NaN` if unknown).
- (Node) `url` (organizations): its web site.
- (Node) `status` (projects): `CLOSED`, `SIGNED`, `TERMINATED`; mostly empty before FP7.
- (Node) `start_date` and `end_date` (projects): the start and end dates of the project (Unix time, -1 if unknown).
- (Node) `ec_signature_date` (projects): Unix time of the signature of the grant, -1 if unknown.
- (Node) `total_cost` and `ec_max_contribution` (projects): the total cost and the maximum contribution of the EU (in euros, `NaN` if unknown).
- (Node) `legal_basis` (projects): the specific program, e.g. `FP1-BRITE`, `H2020-EU.1.1.`.
- (Node) `topics`, `master_call`, `sub_call` (projects): the topics, master call and sub call of the project.
- (Node) `funding_scheme` (projects): the funding scheme (e.g. `ERC-STG`, `RIA`).
- (Node) `grant_doi` (projects): the DOI of the grant.
- (Node) `keywords` (projects): the keywords (from Horizon 2020).
- (Node) `euroscivoc` (projects): the fields of science of the European Science Vocabulary assigned to the project, as paths such as `natural sciences/physical sciences/nuclear physics/nuclear fusion`, separated by `|`.
- (Edge) `role`: the role of the organization in the project: `coordinator`, `participant`, `partner`, `associatedPartner`, `internationalPartner` or `thirdParty` (a few rows with misplaced fields in the data have other values).
- (Edge) `order`: the position of the organization in the list of participants of the project.
- (Edge) `ec_contribution` and `net_ec_contribution`: the (net) contribution of the EU to the organization for the project, in euros (`NaN` if unknown, as before FP7).
- (Edge) `total_cost`: the total cost of the participation of the organization, in euros (`NaN` if unknown).
- (Edge) `end_of_participation`: whether the participation ended early (`true`, `false`, or empty if unknown).
citations: Publications Office of the European Union, "CORDIS - EU funded projects under FP1 (1984-1987)." data.europa.eu (2026)
Publications Office of the European Union, "CORDIS - EU funded projects under FP2 (1987-1991)." data.europa.eu (2026)
Publications Office of the European Union, "CORDIS - EU funded projects under FP3 (1990-1994)." data.europa.eu (2026)
Publications Office of the European Union, "CORDIS - EU research projects under FP4 (1994-1998)." data.europa.eu (2026)
Publications Office of the European Union, "CORDIS - EU research projects under FP5 (1998-2002)." data.europa.eu (2026)
Publications Office of the European Union, "CORDIS - EU research projects under FP6 (2002-2006)." data.europa.eu (2026)
Publications Office of the European Union, "CORDIS - EU research projects under FP7 (2007-2013)." data.europa.eu (2026)
Publications Office of the European Union, "CORDIS - EU research projects under Horizon 2020 (2014-2020)." data.europa.eu (2026)
Publications Office of the European Union, "CORDIS - EU research projects under HORIZON EUROPE (2021-2027)." data.europa.eu (2026)

datasets.name: corporate_directors
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of company directors and the boards on which they sit, for about 36,000 companies traded on stock exchanges in 54 countries worldwide, compiled by A. Evtushenko and M. T. Gastner to study the representation of women in a global network of directors. The data were collected (c. September 2016) from the website of the Financial Times, which obtains its information from Thomson Reuters. For each company, the name, sector, industry, country and number of employees were recorded, and for each director the name, gender and age, when available. Directors appearing in different companies were identified as the same person if their name, gender and age all matched. No distinction is made between executive and non-executive directors. An undirected edge connects a director to each company on whose board they sit.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `is_company`: whether the node is a company (otherwise it is a director).
- (Node) `age` (directors): the age in years.
- (Node) `gender` (directors): `Male` or `Female`.
- (Node) `country`, `sector` (companies): the country and sector of the company.
- (Node) `industry` (companies): the industry (a subsector).
- (Node) `employeesnum` (companies): the number of employees.

Where the information is unavailable or not applicable (e.g. company properties of directors), the text properties have the value `NA` and the numerical properties (`age` and `employeesnum`) the value NaN. Names are not included.
citations: A. Evtushenko and M. T. Gastner, "Beyond Fortune 500: Women in a Global Network of Directors." In H. Cherifi et al. (Eds.), Complex Networks and Their Applications VIII, Volume 1, pp. 586-598 (2020)

datasets.name: corporate_interlocks_nl_de
datasets.description:
Interlocking directorates among the major business companies of the Netherlands and West Germany, from a six-year research project on corporate power in nine European countries and the United States, concluded in 1976, and published by F. Stokman, R. Ziegler and J. Scott (1985). The data were distributed by L. C. Freeman on his network data page at the University of California, Irvine (no longer online), from which this version was obtained via the Internet Archive.

- `netherlands`: 16 Dutch companies.
- `germany`: 15 West German companies.

An undirected edge connects two companies with interlocking directorates (shared board members).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the abbreviated name of the company.
- (Edge) `weight`: the value given in the data (integers from 1 to 6, not documented, presumably the number of interlocks between the two companies).
citations: F. N. Stokman, R. Ziegler, J. Scott (eds.), "Networks of Corporate Power: A Comparative Analysis of Ten Countries." Polity Press (1985)

datasets.name: correspsearch_letters
datasets.description:
Networks of historical letters from the knowledge graphs of the LetterSampo project (Semantic Computing Research Group, Aalto University and University of Helsinki), which harmonized the metadata of letters (sender, recipient, date and places) from several sources:

- `correspsearch_v2` and `correspsearch_v1`: the letters of correspSearch, the service of the Berlin-Brandenburg Academy of Sciences that aggregates the metadata of letters (in the CMIF format) from hundreds of printed and digital scholarly editions of correspondence, mostly of German-speaking persons from the 16th to the 20th century, as converted to RDF by LetterSampo, in the two versions of the data publication (`v2` of June 2022, with 132,138 letters, and `v1` of February 2022). correspSearch has grown since; only these conversions are available as a bulk download.
- `finland`: LetterSampo Finland (version 1.0.0, May 2025), the letters of 19th-century (and later) Finnish archives and editions (the Finnish Literature Society, the National Archives and National Library of Finland, the Swedish Literature Society in Finland, Åbo Akademi University Library, the editions of the letters of Topelius, Snellman, Lönnrot, Edelfelt, ...), with about 1.3 million letters.

Each node is a correspondent (a person or a group, e.g. a society, a firm or an office), as identified by the sources and harmonized by LetterSampo, and a directed edge from $i$ to $j$ is a letter sent by $i$ to $j$; letters with several senders or recipients give an edge for each pair. Pairs of correspondents exchanged many letters (multigraphs). Letters without a known sender or recipient are left out. In `finland`, the correspondents of the sources ("proxies") are merged into the harmonized actors of LetterSampo, as in its portal; proxies without a harmonized actor are kept as they are.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the correspondent.
- (Node) `uri`: the URI of the correspondent in the knowledge graph.
- (Node) `type`: `Person` or `Group` (`correspsearch_*`: both, for a few actors typed as both).
- (Node) `gender`: `Female`, `Male`, or empty if not known.
- (Node) `birth`, `death`: the dates of birth and death (or of the beginning and end of groups), as in the data (YYYY-MM-DD, or a year), or empty.
- (Node) `gnd`, `viaf`, `wikidata` (`correspsearch_*`): the identifiers of the correspondent in the GND (German National Library), VIAF and Wikidata, or empty.
- (Node) `sent_letters`, `received_letters` (`finland`): the numbers of letters sent and received by the actor in LetterSampo Finland.
- (Edge) `date_from`, `date_to`: the range of possible dates of the letter (YYYY-MM-DD, or as given in `finland`, e.g. `1899-1909`), or empty if unknown.
- (Edge) `label`: the label of the letter in the knowledge graph (e.g. "1520 Jul 22: Melanchthon, Philipp (Wittenberg) to Spalatin, Georg (Lochau)").
- (Edge) `place_from`, `place_to` (`correspsearch_*`): the places from which the letter was sent and to which it was sent, or empty.
- (Edge) `latitude_from`, `longitude_from`, `latitude_to`, `longitude_to` (`correspsearch_*`): the coordinates of these places (NaN if not known).
- (Edge) `source`: the edition (`correspsearch_*`) or the source organization (`finland`) of the letter's metadata.
- (Edge) `fonds` (`finland`): the archival fonds (collection) of the letter.
citations: E. Hyvönen, P. Leskinen and J. Tuominen, "LetterSampo correspSearch data publication." Zenodo (2022)
A. Ahola, M. Björklund, S. Drobac, et al., "LetterSampo Finland." Zenodo (2025)
S. Dumont, "correspSearch - Connecting Scholarly Editions of Letters." Journal of the Text Encoding Initiative 10 (2016)

datasets.name: costa_rica_visits
datasets.description:
Visiting relations among families in two rural neighborhoods (Attiro and San Juan Sur) of the Turrialba region in Costa Rica, from a large field study performed in 1948 by C. P. Loomis and collaborators on the impact of formal and informal social systems on social change. Nodes are families, and a directed edge represents frequent visits from one family to another (the number of visits was not recorded), classified as ordinary visits, visits among kin, or visits among ritual kin (between godparent and godchild). For San Juan Sur, there is also a network of the answers of the (heads of) families to the question "In case of a death in the family, whom would you notify first?". The investigators classified the families into family-friendship groupings on substantive (ethnographic) criteria. The data were distributed on the Pajek datasets page of the book *Exploratory Social Network Analysis with Pajek* (de Nooy, Mrvar and Batagelj), from which this version was obtained.[^icon]

- `attiro`: visiting ties among 60 families in Attiro.
- `san_juan_sur`: visiting ties among 75 families in San Juan Sur.
- `san_juan_sur_death`: the families notified first in case of a death, among the same 75 families in San Juan Sur (one edge appears twice in the source); an edge presumably points from a family to a family it named in reply to the question (the direction is not documented in the source files).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the identifier of the family.
- (Node) `grouping`: the ethnographic family-friendship grouping (San Juan Sur: nine groupings, numbered 1 to 9; Attiro: the documentation describes six groupings numbered 1 to 6, but the values in the source file are 0, 1, 4, 5, 7 and 10).
- (Node) `status` (San Juan Sur only): the social status group of the family, from 1 to 14, indicating the average importance of its members (higher values represent higher status).
- (Node) `leader` (San Juan Sur only): whether the family contains a prestige leader, i.e. a person who received more than 10 nominations within the community to the question "Which persons would you pick to represent you and the people of this place on a commission?".
- (Edge) `kind` (visiting networks only): the kind of visit (1: ordinary, 2: among kin, 3: among ritual kin).

[^icon]: Description obtained in part from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.
citations: C. P. Loomis, J. O. Morales, R. A. Clifford, O. E. Leonard, "Turrialba: Social Systems and the Introduction of Change." The Free Press, Glencoe, Illinois (1953)
W. de Nooy, A. Mrvar, V. Batagelj, "Exploratory Social Network Analysis with Pajek." Cambridge University Press (2005)

datasets.name: cow_signed_relations
datasets.description:
A temporal signed network of relations between countries after the Second World War, constructed by P. Doreian and A. Mrvar from the Correlates of War data to study structural balance in international relations. The data are split in 51 overlapping four-year time windows, from 1946–1949 to 1996–1999, shifted by one year. The networks were distributed by A. Mrvar on the Pajek website, and collected by S. Aref in a collection of signed networks used to compute the frustration index (Aref and Wilson, 2019).

Nodes are countries, and an undirected edge between two countries has sign $+1$ for a positive relation (joint membership in alliances, unions of states, or inter-governmental agreements) and $-1$ for a negative relation (being at war, being in conflict without military involvement, or having border disputes or sharp disagreements on ideology or policy) during the time window. Each network contains only the countries with at least one relation in its window, from 64 countries and 362 relations in 1946–1949 to 151 countries and 1,247 relations in 1996–1999. The networks are named after their window (e.g. `1946-1949`).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name` (vertices): the Correlates of War three-letter abbreviation of the country (e.g. `USA`, `RUS`).
- (Edge) `sign` (edges): $+1$ for a positive and $-1$ for a negative relation.

The source also contains a separate copy of the first window (`N46.net`), the signed triads that Doreian and Mrvar use as balance "fragments", and an undocumented 21-node directed signed network (`haddate1.net`); these are not included.
citations: P. Doreian and A. Mrvar, "Structural balance and signed international relations." Journal of Social Structure 16(1), 1–49 (2015)
S. Aref and M. C. Wilson, "Balance and frustration in signed networks." J. Complex Networks 7(2), 163–189 (2019)
J. Pevehouse, T. Nordstrom and K. Warnke, "The Correlates of War 2 international governmental organizations data version 2.0." Conflict Management and Peace Science 21(2), 101–119 (2004)
S. Aref, "Signed networks from sociology and political science, systems biology, international relations, finance, and computational chemistry." Figshare (2017)

datasets.name: cpan
datasets.description:
Networks of the Comprehensive Perl Archive Network (CPAN), the repository of software packages ("distributions") of the Perl programming language, from the CPAN-Explorer visualization project of RTGI/Linkfluence and the Gephi team. The networks were built from the data of CPANTS (the CPAN Testing Service), and were distributed as Gephi example data sets, as a snapshot from July 2009.

- `authors`: nodes are CPAN authors (developers), and a directed edge $i \to j$ indicates that author $i$ uses a module written by author $j$, with `weight` equal to the number of such uses (the "cardinal" of the edge in the source file). 110 edges are self-loops (authors using their own modules).
- `distributions`: nodes are CPAN distributions, and a directed edge $i \to j$ indicates that distribution $i$ depends on distribution $j$. Some dependencies are listed more than once in the source file, and are kept as parallel edges.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the author or distribution.
- (Node) `pauseid` (`authors`): the author's identifier in PAUSE, the Perl authors upload server.
- (Node) `totalmodules` (`authors`): the total number of modules of the author.
- (Node) `avg_kwalitee`, `avg_total_kwalitee` (`authors`): the average "kwalitee" of the author's distributions, the quality score computed by CPANTS from a set of automated checks (the exact definitions of the two variants are not documented in the source).
- (Node) `rank` (`authors`): a rank of the author given in the source data, whose definition is not documented.
- (Edge) `weight` (`authors`): the number of uses.
citations: S. Heymann, "CPAN-Explorer, an interactive exploration of the Perl ecosystem." Gephi blog (2009)

datasets.name: cptond_china_transit
datasets.description:
Bus networks of 350 cities and metro networks of 46 cities in mainland China, Hong Kong and Macao (and one metro network of Taiwan, `taiwan_metro`, around Taipei), from the China Public Transport Operation Network Dataset (CPTOND-2025) compiled by L. Wang, H. Wei, Y. Guan and collaborators. The routes and stops were collected in June 2025 by systematically enumerating the routes listed by the public transport information platform 8684 (8684.cn) and retrieving their courses, stops and operational attributes from the Amap (Gaode) map API; the coordinates were converted from the Chinese GCJ-02 system to WGS 84. The English names of stops and cities in the data are automatic translations of the Chinese names, and some are mistranslations (e.g. the city of Jixi, 鸡西, appears as "Chicken West", and Dezhou, 德州, as "Texas").

There is one network for each city and mode, named after the city, in pinyin without tones, and the mode (e.g. `beijing_bus`, `beijing_metro`, `jixi_bus`, `xianggang_metro`), since the English names of the data are automatic translations, some of them wrong (e.g. "Chicken West" for 鸡西, Jixi); the five pairs of cities with the same name in pinyin are told apart by their province (e.g. `fuzhou_fujian_bus` for 福州 and `fuzhou_jiangxi_bus` for 抚州); the network properties `city_cn` and `city_en` give the city's name. A node is a stop (bus stop or metro station, deduplicated over the routes of the city), and a directed edge from stop $i$ to stop $j$ means that some route serves $j$ immediately after $i$; the edges are the segments between consecutive stops provided by the authors, aggregated over the routes and directions, with the number of routes passing through them. Some segments join a stop to itself (9,853 self-loops over all networks), presumably where consecutive stops of a route share the same stop id. The courses of the segments and routes (as polylines) are not included, and neither are the routes themselves with their operational attributes (operating hours, fares, companies). The dataset has two versions on figshare (July and September 2025); the second, used here, separates the bus networks of five pairs of cities with the same name in pinyin (Fuzhou, Suzhou, Taizhou, Yichun and Yulin), which are merged in the first.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the stop (Chinese).
- (Node) `name_en`: its (automatic) English translation.
- (Node) `stop_id`: its id in the data.
- (Node) `num_routes`: the number of routes serving it (counting the two directions of a route separately).
- (Node) `latitude` and `longitude`: its position.
- (Edge) `num_routes`: the number of routes passing through the segment.
- (Edge) `distance`: its length along the route (km).
- (Graph) `city_cn` and `city_en`, the name of the city in Chinese and (automatically translated) in English; `mode`, `bus` or `metro`.
citations: L. Wang, H. Wei, Y. Guan, L. Ouyang, D. Xu, X. Han, M. Zhang, M. Chen, D. Sun, D. Gong, Z. Zhang, X. Zhang, X. Zhang, "China Public Transport Operation Network Dataset (CPTOND-2025): National-Scale Bus-Metro Vector Dataset." Scientific Data 13, 188 (2026)
L. Wang, H. Wei, Y. Guan, L. Ouyang, D. Xu, X. Han, M. Zhang, M. Chen, D. Sun, D. Gong, Z. Zhang, X. Zhang, X. Zhang, "CPTOND-2025." figshare, dataset, version 2 (2025)

datasets.name: cricsheet
datasets.description:
Networks of cricket matches from Cricsheet, the open collection of ball-by-ball data of cricket matches compiled by S. Rushe: international matches (Tests, one-day internationals, T20 internationals and other international matches) and the main domestic and franchise T20 leagues and competitions (e.g. the Indian Premier League, the Big Bash League, the County Championship), of men and women, from 2001 to October 2026. Following its policy, Cricsheet withholds the matches of the Afghanistan men's team and of the Afghanistan Premier League, which are therefore not included. The archives of Cricsheet are updated in place as matches are added; the data are those of the download of 31 October 2026 (with the matches added up to 25 October 2026).

The players and officials are identified by the identifiers of the Cricsheet register (`people.csv`), which also give their names and their identifiers in other databases. There are three networks:

- `deliveries`: the bowler-batter network. A directed edge from player $i$ to player $j$ means that $i$ bowled to $j$ in an innings of a match, with the numbers of deliveries, runs and dismissals; there is one edge per pair of players, match and innings (a multigraph). Super overs are included as innings of their own.
- `matches`: the team network. Nodes are teams (men's and women's teams of the same name are different nodes), and an edge connects the two teams of a match, with the match's metadata (one edge per match, a multigraph).
- `player_matches`: the bipartite network of players and matches: an edge connects each player of a match's teams (as listed in the match data, usually the playing eleven) to the match. The property `is_player` tells the two kinds of nodes apart.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the player in the register (or, for teams, the name of the team; for matches, the names of the teams, "A vs B").
- (Node) `unique_name` (players): the unique name of the player in the register.
- (Node) `identifier` (players): the identifier of the player in the register (e.g. `ba607b88`).
- (Node) `key_cricinfo` (players): the identifier of the player in ESPNcricinfo, or empty.
- (Node) `gender`: the gender of the matches of the player (or team, or match): `male` or `female`.
- (Node) `is_player` (`player_matches`): whether the node is a player (otherwise a match).
- (Node) `team_type` (teams): `international` or `club`.
- (Edge) `match_id` (`deliveries`, `matches`): the Cricsheet identifier of the match, as in `https://cricsheet.org/matches/` and the file names.
- (Edge) `time` (`deliveries`, `matches`): the date of the first day of the match, in Unix time.
- (Edge) `date` (`deliveries`, `matches`): the date of the match (YYYY-MM-DD).
- (Edge) `match_type` (`deliveries`, `matches`): `Test`, `ODI`, `T20`, `IT20`, `ODM`, `MDM`.
- (Edge) `team_type` (`deliveries`, `matches`): `international` or `club`.
- (Edge) `event` (`deliveries`, `matches`): the name of the competition or tour, or empty.
- (Edge) `season`, `venue`, `city` (`deliveries`, `matches`): the season, venue and city of the match.
- (Edge) `winner` (`deliveries`, `matches`): the winning team, or empty.
- (Edge) `result` (`deliveries`, `matches`): `win`, or `draw`, `tie`, `no result`.
- (Edge) `toss_winner` (`matches`): the winner of the toss.
- (Node) `match_id`, `time`, `date`, `match_type`, `team_type`, `event`, `season`, `venue`, `city`, `winner`, `result` (matches, `player_matches`): the match properties, as for the edges of `deliveries` and `matches`.
- (Edge) `innings` (`deliveries`): the number of the innings in the match (from 1).
- (Edge) `deliveries` (`deliveries`): the number of deliveries bowled by the bowler to the batter in the innings (including wides and no-balls).
- (Edge) `runs` (`deliveries`): the runs scored by the batter off these deliveries.
- (Edge) `extras` (`deliveries`): the extras of these deliveries (wides, no-balls, byes, leg byes, penalties).
- (Edge) `dismissals` (`deliveries`): 1 if the batter was dismissed by the bowler (bowled, caught, caught and bowled, lbw, stumped, hit wicket) in the innings, otherwise 0.
- (Edge) `dismissal` (`deliveries`): the kind of the batter's dismissal on a delivery of this bowler (also run outs and others not credited to the bowler), or empty.
- (Edge) `team` (`player_matches`): the team of the player in the match.
citations: S. Rushe, "Cricsheet: Freely-available structured data for cricket." (2026)

datasets.name: crime
datasets.description:
Involvement of individuals in crime events in St. Louis (Missouri, USA), collected from police records by R. Rosenfeld and N. White in the 1990s. Starting from five homicides, they recorded the names of all the individuals involved as victims, suspects or witnesses, then searched the files for all the other crimes in which the same individuals appeared, and continued this snowball process until they had data on 557 crime events, with 870 participants: 569 appearances as victims, 682 as suspects, 195 as witnesses, and 41 as both victim and suspect in the same crime. The sex of each individual was also recorded. The data were distributed by L. C. Freeman on his network data page at the University of California, Irvine (no longer online), from which this version was obtained via the Internet Archive.

The network is bipartite: an undirected edge connects an individual to a crime event in which they were involved. One cell of the source matrix is coded as missing ("?"), and is not represented as an edge. The file contains 40 individuals and 4 crime events without any involvement, which are isolated nodes.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `is_crime`: whether the node is a crime event (otherwise, it is an individual).
- (Node) `name`: the name of the individual (with the family name first, without a space), or the identifier of the crime event (two identifiers, 930011 and 930019, are each used for two different crime events).
- (Node) `sex`: the sex of the individual ("F" or "M"; empty for crime events). The coding of sex is not documented in the source (it is given as 0 or 1); it is inferred here from the first names.
- (Edge) `role`: the role of the individual in the crime event ("victim", "suspect", "witness", or "victim and suspect").
citations: S. Decker, C. W. Kohfeld, R. Rosenfeld, & J. Sprague, "St. Louis Homicide Project: Local Responses to a National Problem." University of Missouri-St. Louis (1991)

datasets.name: cross_parker
datasets.description:
Advice and knowledge networks among the employees of two organizations, collected by surveys and used by R. Cross and A. Parker in their book on informal networks in organizations. The data were distributed by T. Opsahl.

- `consulting`: 46 employees of a consulting company, with two relations (layers):
  - `advice`: frequency of information or advice requests ("Please indicate how often you have turned to this person for information or advice on work-related topics in the past three months"), from 1 to 5 (1: never, 2: seldom, 3: sometimes, 4: often, 5: very often).
  - `value`: the value placed on the information or advice received ("For each person in the list below, please show how strongly you agree or disagree with the following statement: In general, this person has expertise in areas that are important in the kind of work I do"), from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).
- `manufacturing`: 77 employees of the research team of a manufacturing company, with two relations (layers):
  - `advice`: extent to which the person provides information used to accomplish one's work ("Please indicate the extent to which the people listed below provide you with information you use to accomplish your work"), from 1 (very infrequently) to 6 (very frequently).
  - `awareness`: awareness of the person's knowledge and skills ("I understand this person's knowledge and skills. This does not necessarily mean that I have these skills or am knowledgeable in these domains but that I understand what skills this person has and domains they are knowledgeable in"), from 1 (strongly disagree) to 6 (strongly agree).

In all cases, the value 0 ("I do not know this person" / "I have never met this person") corresponds to the absence of an edge. A directed edge (i, j) corresponds to the answer of employee i about employee j. A few self-loops are present in the source data.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `orglevel` (`consulting`): the organizational level (1: research assistant, 2: junior consultant, 3: senior consultant, 4: managing consultant, 5: partner).
- (Node) `gender` (`consulting`): 1: male, 2: female.
- (Node) `region` (`consulting`): 1: Europe, 2: USA.
- (Node) `location` (`consulting`): 1: Boston, 2: London, 3: Paris, 4: Rome, 5: Madrid, 6: Oslo, 7: Copenhagen.
- (Node) `location` (`manufacturing`): 1: Paris, 2: Frankfurt, 3: Warsaw, 4: Geneva.
- (Node) `tenure` (`manufacturing`): 1: 1-12 months, 2: 13-36 months, 3: 37-60 months, 4: 61+ months.
- (Node) `orglevel` (`manufacturing`): the organizational level (1: global department manager, 2: local department manager, 3: project leader, 4: researcher).
- (Edge) `layer`: the relation (see above).
- (Edge) `weight`: the answer in the scale of the relation.
citations: R. Cross, A. Parker, "The Hidden Power of Social Networks: Understanding How Work Really Gets Done in Organizations." Harvard Business School Press (2004)

datasets.name: cs_department
datasets.description:
A multiplex network of five kinds of relationships among 61 employees of the Department of Computer Science at Aarhus University, Denmark, collected by M. Magnani, B. Micenková and L. Rossi. The relationships, one per layer, are: having lunch together regularly (`lunch`), being friends on Facebook (`facebook`), having co-authored a publication (`coauthor`), doing leisure activities together (`leisure`), and working together (`work`). Nodes are employees, and an undirected edge in a layer connects two employees that have the corresponding relationship (a pair of employees can thus be connected by one edge per layer). The data were made available as a multiplex network by M. De Domenico.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name` and `nodeLabel`: the anonymized identifier of the employee (e.g. `U102`).
- (Edge) `layer`: the relationship (1: lunch, 2: Facebook, 3: co-authorship, 4: leisure, 5: work; the names are stored in the graph property `layer_key`).
- (Edge) `weight`: which is always 1.
citations: Matteo Magnani, Barbora Micenkova, and Luca Rossi, "Combinatorial Analysis of Multiple Networks." arXiv:1303.4986 (2013)

datasets.name: cs_phd
datasets.description:
Advisor-student relations among 1025 theoretical computer scientists, from the SIGACT Theoretical Computer Science Genealogy started by D. S. Johnson (1984) and maintained by I. Parberry (version of July 22, 1996). Each directed edge points from a PhD advisor to the student. The network is acyclic. A few nodes, labeled "---" or "?" in the source, represent persons whose names are unknown. The data were distributed on the Pajek datasets page of the book *Exploratory Social Network Analysis with Pajek* (de Nooy, Mrvar and Batagelj), from which this version was obtained.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the computer scientist, followed by the year of the PhD when known.
- (Node) `year`: the (known or estimated) year in which the PhD was obtained.
citations: D. S. Johnson, "The genealogy of theoretical computer science." ACM SIGACT News 16(2), 36-49 (1984)
W. de Nooy, A. Mrvar, V. Batagelj, "Exploratory Social Network Analysis with Pajek." Cambridge University Press (2005)

datasets.name: ctd_associations
datasets.description:
Bipartite networks of chemicals, genes and diseases from the Comparative Toxicogenomics Database (CTD), which curates from the scientific literature how environmental chemicals and drugs interact with genes and proteins, and how chemicals and genes are related to diseases, in many species. The data are those of the release of September 2026.

- `chemical_disease`: chemicals and diseases. An edge is either a curated association from the literature, with its direct evidence (`marker/mechanism`: the chemical correlates with the disease or may play a role in its etiology; `therapeutic`: the chemical has a known or potential therapeutic role in the disease), or an association inferred by CTD through a gene that has curated interactions with the chemical and a curated association with the disease, with the inference gene and an inference score (higher for better connected networks of chemicals, genes and diseases). A chemical and a disease are connected by one edge per inference gene, and by an edge per kind of direct evidence.
- `chemical_gene`: chemicals and genes. An edge is a curated interaction between a chemical and a gene product (or the gene itself) in an organism, e.g. "Aspirin results in decreased expression of PTGS2 mRNA", with the interaction actions (e.g. `decreases^expression`); the genes are identified by their NCBI Gene identifier, irrespective of the organism of the interaction (CTD maps the genes of all organisms to the identifiers of the genes it lists, mostly of vertebrates).
- `gene_disease`: genes and diseases, with an edge for each curated association (marker/mechanism or therapeutic) of a gene with a disease.
- `gene_disease_inferred`: genes and diseases, with an edge for each association inferred by CTD through chemicals that have curated interactions with the gene and curated associations with the disease, with the inference chemicals and the inference score of the gene-disease pair. CTD lists the association once per inference chemical (130 million rows in the release of September 2026); these are merged into one edge per gene-disease pair (about 36 million).

The diseases are terms of the "merged disease vocabulary" (MEDIC) of CTD, which combines the MeSH disease terms and OMIM; the chemicals are MeSH terms. The chemical-pathway, gene-pathway, disease-pathway, chemical-phenotype and exposure data of CTD are not included.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `ctd_id`: the identifier of the node: the MeSH identifier of the chemical (e.g. `D001241`, aspirin), the NCBI Gene identifier of the gene (e.g. `5743`), or the MeSH or OMIM identifier of the disease (e.g. `MESH:D003920`, `OMIM:125853`).
- (Node) `name`: the name of the chemical, the symbol of the gene, or the name of the disease.
- (Node) `cas_rn`: the CAS Registry Number of the chemical (empty if none, and for other nodes).
- (Node) `is_chemical` (`chemical_disease`, `chemical_gene`): whether the node is a chemical.
- (Node) `is_gene` (`gene_disease`, `gene_disease_inferred`): whether the node is a gene (otherwise it is a disease).
- (Edge) `direct_evidence` (`chemical_disease`, `gene_disease`): the kind of curated evidence, `marker/mechanism` or `therapeutic` (empty for inferred associations).
- (Edge) `inference_gene` (`chemical_disease`): the symbol of the gene through which the association is inferred (empty for curated associations).
- (Edge) `inference_score` (`chemical_disease`, `gene_disease_inferred`): the inference score of the association (NaN for curated associations).
- (Edge) `inference_chemicals` (`gene_disease_inferred`): the names of the chemicals through which the association is inferred, separated by `|`; `num_chemicals`, their number.
- (Edge) `omim_ids` (`chemical_disease`, `gene_disease`): the OMIM identifiers of the evidence, separated by `|` (empty if none).
- (Edge) `pubmed_ids`: the PubMed identifiers of the articles that support the association or interaction, separated by `|` (in `gene_disease_inferred`, those of all its inference chemicals).
- (Edge) `organism`, `organism_id` (`chemical_gene`): the name and NCBI taxonomy identifier of the organism of the interaction (empty and -1 if not given).
- (Edge) `gene_forms` (`chemical_gene`): the forms of the gene product involved, e.g. `protein`, `mRNA`, separated by `|`.
- (Edge) `interaction` (`chemical_gene`): the description of the interaction.
- (Edge) `interaction_actions` (`chemical_gene`): the actions of the interaction, e.g. `increases^expression`, separated by `|`.
- (Node) `inferred_associations` (graph, `gene_disease`): the number of inferred gene-disease associations, which are in `gene_disease_inferred`.
citations: A. P. Davis, T. C. Wiegers, D. Sciaky, F. Barkalow, M. Strong, B. Wyatt, J. Wiegers, R. McMorran, S. Abrar, C. J. Mattingly, "Comparative Toxicogenomics Database's 20th anniversary: update 2025." Nucleic Acids Research 53, D1328-D1334 (2025)

datasets.name: currency_trading
datasets.description:
Directed networks of the international circulation of 45 currencies in 1890, 1900 and 1910, compiled by M. Flandreau and C. Jobst. Nodes are countries (each with its own currency), and a directed edge from country $i$ to country $j$ means that the currency of country $j$ was actively traded (i.e., regularly quoted with changing prices, revealing an underlying flow of transactions) in a foreign exchange market of country $i$ in that year. The data were collected from local stock exchange bulletins, newspapers and cambists' handbooks of the main financial centers of each country, and include virtually all currencies of the world at the time; a currency counts as traded in a country if there is evidence of active trading in at least one of its financial centers. There is one network for each year (`1890`, `1900` and `1910`).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the three-letter code of the country (e.g. "GBR", "DEU", "AUH" for Austria-Hungary, "OTT" for the Ottoman Empire).
- (Node) `gold`, `debtburden`, `rlong`, `rshort1900`, `rshort1890`, `rgdp`, `rgdpcap`, `poldemo`, `coverage`: explanatory variables used by Flandreau and Jobst (2009), which refer to 1900 unless stated otherwise (NaN if missing), as follows.
- (Node) `gold`: whether the currency was convertible in gold.
- (Node) `debtburden`: the ratio of government debt over government revenues.
- (Node) `rlong`: the secondary market yield of gold-denominated government debt.
- (Node) `rshort1900` and `rshort1890`: the market rate for three-month lending in 1900 and 1890.
- (Node) `rgdp` and `rgdpcap`: the logarithm of the real GDP and of the real GDP per capita.
- (Node) `poldemo`: Vanhanen's index of democracy.
- (Node) `coverage`: the logarithm of the number of currencies traded in the country.
- (Edge) `colony`: whether country $i$ was a colony of country $j$.
- (Edge) `dist`: the logarithm of the distance between the financial centers of the two countries (the shortest one, if there are several).
- (Edge) `bitrade`: the total trade between the two countries in 1900, in thousand US dollars (zero if not reported).[^icon].

[^icon]: Description obtained in part from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.
citations: M. Flandreau, C. Jobst, "The ties that divide: a network analysis of the international monetary system, 1890-1910." The Journal of Economic History 65(4), 977-1007 (2005)
M. Flandreau, C. Jobst, "The empirics of international currencies: network externalities, history and persistence." The Economic Journal 119(537), 643-664 (2009)

datasets.name: czech_corruption
datasets.description:
Network of co-appearances in the press of 16 actors in a political corruption and espionage scandal in the Czech Republic (the 2013 affair that led to the resignation of prime minister Petr Nečas). The data were collected by Tomáš Diviák from the Czech media database Newton Media Search, covering all major Czech newspapers from 4 June 2013 to 4 June 2014. The actors are the former prime minister and the head of his office (Jana Nagyová), deputies of the governing conservative party (ODS), high government officials and intelligence agents, and influential businessmen ("godfathers"); vertex property `name`.

An edge connects two actors mentioned in the same article. The edge property `weight` is an integer on a scale of 0 to 10, where 10 is the strongest tie (Nagyová - Nečas): the number of co-appearances of each pair was divided by that of the strongest tie, and the resulting fraction was assigned the integer corresponding to the tenth into which it falls (so that ties with less than 10% of the maximum have weight 0, and are not included). Data distributed by the UCINET datasets collection (University of Manchester).[^ucinet]

[^ucinet]: Description obtained in part from the [UCINET datasets page](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/datasets/covert-networks/czech-corruption).
citations: T. Diviák, "Czech Corruption." UCINET datasets, University of Manchester (2016)

datasets.name: darkweb
datasets.description:
The hyperlink network among the websites of the "darkweb" (Tor onion services), collected by V. Griffith, Y. Xu and C. Ratti. The darkweb was crawled through the tor2web proxy onion.link using the commercial service scrapinghub.com, starting from two popular lists of darkweb sites and following all links in breadth-first order; pages requiring a login were not crawled. According to ICON[^icon], the crawl took place between November 2016 and February 2017. Pages were aggregated by second-level (onion) domain, ignoring links within a domain. The data were distributed by A. Clauset.

A directed edge (i, j) indicates that some page on domain i links to some page on domain j.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the onion domain name (without the .onion suffix).
- (Edge) `weight`: the number of pages on domain i linking to pages on domain j.

[^icon]: Information obtained from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.
citations: V. Griffith, Y. Xu, C. Ratti, "Graph theoretic properties of the darkweb." arXiv:1704.07525 (2017)

datasets.name: davis_southern_women
datasets.description:
The participation of 18 women in 14 informal social events in Natchez, Mississippi, in the 1930s, observed by A. Davis, B. B. Gardner and M. R. Gardner as part of their study of social class in a city of the US Deep South. This is one of the classic examples of a two-mode (affiliation) network, analyzed in many studies, e.g. Breiger (1974), Freeman (2003), and Wasserman and Faust (1994). This version was distributed by T. Opsahl.

A bipartite edge connects a woman to an event she attended.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `is_woman`: whether the node is a woman (otherwise it is an event).
- (Node) `name`: the first name of the woman (empty for the events, which are numbered in the order of the source data).
citations: A. Davis, B. B. Gardner, M. R. Gardner, "Deep South: A Social Anthropological Study of Caste and Class." University of Chicago Press (1941)

datasets.name: dawn
datasets.description:
Bipartite networks of drugs and the hospital emergency department visits in which they were reported, from the Drug Abuse Warning Network (DAWN). DAWN was a public health surveillance system of the U.S. Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) that collected, from a national sample of hospitals, records of emergency department visits related to drug use. For each visit, the data list the drugs the patient reported having used, which include illicit substances, prescription and over-the-counter medication, and dietary supplements. The data were assembled by A. R. Benson and collaborators from the public DAWN files, and cover the years 2004 to 2011.

- `visits`: each visit is a node connected to the drugs reported in it. Visits are dated at the resolution of quarter-years. Distinct visits with the same drugs are kept as separate nodes.
- `dispositions`: each distinct combination of drugs reported in some visit is a node connected to its drugs, and annotated with the most common patient disposition (where the patient went after the visit, e.g. sent home, surgery, or released to detox) among the visits with that combination.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name` (drugs): the name of the drug.
- (Node) `code` (drugs, `visits` only): the DAWN drug code.
- (Node) `is_visit` (`visits`): whether the node is a visit (otherwise it is a drug).
- (Node) `year` and `quarter` (`visits`): the year and quarter (1 to 4) of the visit.
- (Node) `is_combination` (`dispositions`): whether the node is a drug combination (otherwise it is a drug).
- (Node) `disposition` (`dispositions`): the disposition category, numbered 1 to 10. The names of the categories are not included in the source data (its file of category names lists drug names instead), and the 375 combinations with a category number larger than 10 have `disposition` set to -1.
citations: A. R. Benson, R. Abebe, M. T. Schaub, A. Jadbabaie, J. Kleinberg, "Simplicial closure and higher-order link prediction." Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 115(48), E11221-E11230 (2018)

datasets.name: dblp_author_paper
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of authors and the publications they wrote, from the dblp computer science bibliography. The data are from the XML dump of dblp, the computer science bibliography maintained by the University of Trier and Schloss Dagstuhl, which lists publications from journals, conference proceedings, books, theses and the arXiv Computing Research Repository (CoRR). The collection contains one network for each of two monthly releases of the dump: `2017`, from the release of 2 May 2017, and `2026-10`, from the release of 3 October 2026. Each record of the dump is a publication of one of the types `article` (journal articles and CoRR preprints), `inproceedings` (conference papers), `proceedings` (edited proceedings volumes), `book`, `incollection` (book chapters), `phdthesis` or `mastersthesis`, and, in the release of 2026, also `data` (research data and artifacts); the person records (homepages) of the dump are not used. Authors are identified by their dblp name, which dblp disambiguates by hand where it can (homonymous authors are distinguished by a numeric suffix, e.g. "Wei Wang 0001"), but some of which may still refer to several persons. Nodes are authors and publications, and each edge connects a publication to one of its authors; editors of proceedings volumes are not included, and neither are publications without authors.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the author, or the dblp key of the publication.
- (Node) `is_publication`: whether the node is a publication (otherwise it is an author).
- (Node) `title`: the title of the publication.
- (Node) `year`: the year of publication (-1 if missing).
- (Node) `type`: the record type of the publication (see above).
- (Node) `venue`: the journal (for articles) or the proceedings or book title (for papers in proceedings and book chapters); empty for other types. (Empty, or -1, for authors.)
- (Edge) `position` (edge): the position of the author in the author list of the publication, starting from 1.

datasets.name: dblp_coauthor
datasets.description:
Scientific collaborations among authors of publications in the dblp computer science bibliography. The data are from the XML dump of dblp, the computer science bibliography maintained by the University of Trier and Schloss Dagstuhl, which lists publications from journals, conference proceedings, books, theses and the arXiv Computing Research Repository (CoRR). The collection contains one network for each of two monthly releases of the dump: `2017`, from the release of 2 May 2017, and `2026-10`, from the release of 3 October 2026. Each record of the dump is a publication of one of the types `article` (journal articles and CoRR preprints), `inproceedings` (conference papers), `proceedings` (edited proceedings volumes), `book`, `incollection` (book chapters), `phdthesis` or `mastersthesis`, and, in the release of 2026, also `data` (research data and artifacts); the person records (homepages) of the dump are not used. Authors are identified by their dblp name, which dblp disambiguates by hand where it can (homonymous authors are distinguished by a numeric suffix, e.g. "Wei Wang 0001"), but some of which may still refer to several persons. Nodes are authors, and an undirected edge between two authors means that they co-authored a publication; each publication with $k$ authors contributes $k(k-1)/2$ undirected edges, one between each pair of its authors, so that the network is a multigraph, with as many edges between two authors as their joint publications (i.e. it is a projection of the bipartite network of authors and publications). Editors of proceedings volumes are not included, and neither are authors without co-authors.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the author.
- (Edge) `year` (edge): the year of the joint publication (-1 if missing).
- (Edge) `n_authors` (edge): the number of authors of the joint publication.

datasets.name: dblp_simplices
datasets.description:
A temporal bipartite network of co-authorship among computer scientists, constructed by A. R. Benson and collaborators from the DBLP computer science bibliography, as of 3 September 2017. Each publication is a simplex formed by the set of its authors, and is timestamped with the year of publication. The networks are named `<dataset>-<representation>`, where the dataset is either `full`, with all publications, or `max-25`, restricted to publications with at most 25 authors, and the representation is one of:

- `bip`: a bipartite network of publications and authors, in which each publication is connected to each of its authors. Publication nodes come first, followed by the author nodes.
- `proj`: the one-mode projection onto the authors, where each publication adds an edge between every pair of its authors, so that pairs of authors who wrote several papers together are connected by multiple parallel edges, one for each paper. Publications with a single author do not contribute edges.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `label`: the name of the author (empty for publication nodes).
- (Node) `is_simplex` (`bip` only): whether the node is a publication (otherwise an author).
- (Edge) `time`: the year of the publication.
citations: A. R. Benson et al., "Simplicial Closure and Higher-order Link Prediction." Preprint, arXiv:1802.06916 (2018)

datasets.name: dbpedia_all
datasets.description:
A directed network of the relations between the entities of DBpedia, a project that extracts structured information from Wikipedia. The data are from version 3.9 of DBpedia, which was extracted from the English Wikipedia dumps of late March / early April 2013 and published in September 2013. It contains every triple of the "Mapping-based Properties (Cleaned)" dataset of the release whose object is a resource rather than a literal value; this dataset holds the information of the Wikipedia infoboxes mapped onto the DBpedia ontology, from which the statements identified as incorrect by heuristic inference were removed. Nodes are resources (mostly entities with a Wikipedia article, such as people, places, organizations or works), and a directed edge $(i,j)$ is a triple stating that resource $i$ has a relation to resource $j$, e.g. that a person ($i$) was born in a place ($j$); repeated edges correspond to different relations between the same resources, and self-loops (7,665 triples) are kept. The relations are almost all properties of the DBpedia ontology (e.g. `dbo:birthPlace`, `dbo:team`, `dbo:genre`), but also include `rdf:type` statements pointing to the class `gml:_Feature` (for places with coordinates), `skos:subject`, and FOAF properties whose objects are web pages and images (e.g. `foaf:homepage`, `foaf:depiction`), which are nodes as well.

Objects do not necessarily have an infobox, or even a Wikipedia article, of their own (e.g. when the infobox links to a missing article). Besides proper Wikipedia articles, some resources are intermediate nodes created by DBpedia for parts of an infobox, named after the article with a suffix `__<n>`.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: for DBpedia resources, the name of the resource, i.e. the title of the corresponding English Wikipedia article (with underscores instead of spaces), with the percent-encoding of the URI decoded; for other nodes, the full URI.
- (Node) `type`: the most specific class of the resource in the DBpedia ontology, from the "Mapping-based Types" dataset of the same release (empty if the resource has no type, e.g. because it has no infobox mapped to the ontology).
- (Edge) `relation`: the predicate of the triple, abbreviated with the prefixes `dbo:` (DBpedia ontology), `rdf:`, `skos:` and `foaf:`.
citations: S. Auer, C. Bizer, G. Kobilarov, J. Lehmann, R. Cyganiak, Z. Ives, "DBpedia: A nucleus for a web of open data." In The Semantic Web (ISWC 2007 + ASWC 2007), Lecture Notes in Computer Science 4825, 722-735 (2007)
J. Lehmann et al., "DBpedia - A large-scale, multilingual knowledge base extracted from Wikipedia." Semantic Web 6(2), 167-195 (2015)

datasets.name: dbpedia_country

Objects of the relation do not necessarily have an infobox, or even a Wikipedia article, of their own (e.g. when the infobox links to a missing article). Besides proper Wikipedia articles, some resources are intermediate nodes created by DBpedia for parts of an infobox, named after the article with a suffix `__<n>`.

- (Node) `is_country`: whether the node is a country (otherwise it is an entity).

datasets.name: dbpedia_link
datasets.description:
The network of hyperlinks among the articles of the English Wikipedia, as extracted by DBpedia, a project that extracts structured information from Wikipedia. The data are the "Wikipedia Pagelinks" dataset of version 3.9 of DBpedia, which was extracted from the English Wikipedia dumps of late March / early April 2013 and published in September 2013; it contains the internal links (wikilinks) found in the text of the articles. Nodes are Wikipedia pages, and a directed edge $(i,j)$ means that page $i$ contains at least one link to page $j$, weighted by the number of links from $i$ to $j$ in the dataset (the dataset has one triple per link occurrence, i.e. 172,308,906 triples for about 136.6 million distinct pairs of pages). Links of pages to themselves are kept as self-loops.

The pages include redirect pages, pages that do not exist (links to missing articles), and pages in other namespaces: in particular, the category memberships of the articles appear as links to the category pages (`Category:...`, about 16.6 million triples), and embedded images as links to file pages (`File:...` or `Image:...`, about 2.7 million triples). The network `en` of the entry `wikipedia_links_2013` was extracted from a slightly earlier dump (February 2013) with different processing: redirects are resolved to their targets, and redirect pages, pages in other namespaces and missing pages are excluded.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the DBpedia resource, i.e. the title of the corresponding English Wikipedia page (with underscores instead of spaces), with the percent-encoding of the URI decoded.
- (Node) `type`: the most specific class of the resource in the DBpedia ontology, from the "Mapping-based Types" dataset of the same release (empty if the resource has no type, e.g. because it has no infobox mapped to the ontology).
- (Edge) `count`: the number of links from the source page to the target page.
