citations: S. Auer, C. Bizer, G. Kobilarov, J. Lehmann, R. Cyganiak, Z. Ives, "DBpedia: A nucleus for a web of open data." In The Semantic Web (ISWC 2007 + ASWC 2007), Lecture Notes in Computer Science 4825, 722-735 (2007)
J. Lehmann et al., "DBpedia - A large-scale, multilingual knowledge base extracted from Wikipedia." Semantic Web 6(2), 167-195 (2015)

datasets.name: dbpedia_team
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of athletes and the sports teams they played for. The data are from version 3.9 of DBpedia, which extracts structured information from the infoboxes of Wikipedia articles and maps it onto the DBpedia ontology; this release was extracted from the English Wikipedia dumps of late March / early April 2013, and was published in September 2013. Each edge is one triple of the [`dbo:team`](http://dbpedia.org/ontology/team) relation in the "Mapping-based Properties (Cleaned)" dataset of the release, from which the statements identified as incorrect by heuristic inference were removed. Nodes are athletes (and other subjects of the relation) on one side and teams on the other, and each edge connects an athlete (or a sports season, manager or other entity) to a team listed in its infobox. Most subject nodes are intermediate nodes: stations of a player's career (e.g. `Ned_Zelić__1`, of type `CareerStation`), members of a team's squad list (e.g. `K.A.A._Gent__Wallace__1`, of type `SportsTeamMember`), and other time periods (type `TimePeriod`); the athletes themselves are linked to these nodes by other relations, which are not part of this network. The teams are mostly football clubs, but also universities, basketball, hockey and rugby teams, and national teams.

A resource that appears on both sides of the relation is represented by two distinct nodes, one on each side, and repeated triples are included only once. Objects of the relation do not necessarily have an infobox, or even a Wikipedia article, of their own (e.g. when the infobox links to a missing article). Besides proper Wikipedia articles, some resources are intermediate nodes created by DBpedia for parts of an infobox, named after the article with a suffix `__<n>`.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the DBpedia resource, i.e. the title of the corresponding English Wikipedia article (with underscores instead of spaces), with the percent-encoding of the URI decoded.
- (Node) `type`: the most specific class of the resource in the DBpedia ontology, from the "Mapping-based Types" dataset of the same release (empty if the resource has no type, e.g. because it has no infobox mapped to the ontology).
- (Node) `is_team`: whether the node is a team (otherwise it is an athlete or another subject of the relation).
citations: S. Auer, C. Bizer, G. Kobilarov, J. Lehmann, R. Cyganiak, Z. Ives, "DBpedia: A nucleus for a web of open data." In The Semantic Web (ISWC 2007 + ASWC 2007), Lecture Notes in Computer Science 4825, 722-735 (2007)
J. Lehmann et al., "DBpedia - A large-scale, multilingual knowledge base extracted from Wikipedia." Semantic Web 6(2), 167-195 (2015)

datasets.name: dbpedia_writer
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of writers and the works they wrote. The data are from version 3.9 of DBpedia, which extracts structured information from the infoboxes of Wikipedia articles and maps it onto the DBpedia ontology; this release was extracted from the English Wikipedia dumps of late March / early April 2013, and was published in September 2013. Each edge is one triple of the [`dbo:writer`](http://dbpedia.org/ontology/writer) relation in the "Mapping-based Properties (Cleaned)" dataset of the release, from which the statements identified as incorrect by heuristic inference were removed. Nodes are works and writers, and each edge connects a work to a writer listed in its infobox. Most works are films, singles, television episodes, songs, comics and anime, and the writers are mostly persons (screenwriters, songwriters, comics writers) and bands.

A resource that appears on both sides of the relation is represented by two distinct nodes, one on each side, and repeated triples are included only once. Objects of the relation do not necessarily have an infobox, or even a Wikipedia article, of their own (e.g. when the infobox links to a missing article). Besides proper Wikipedia articles, some resources are intermediate nodes created by DBpedia for parts of an infobox, named after the article with a suffix `__<n>`.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the DBpedia resource, i.e. the title of the corresponding English Wikipedia article (with underscores instead of spaces), with the percent-encoding of the URI decoded.
- (Node) `type`: the most specific class of the resource in the DBpedia ontology, from the "Mapping-based Types" dataset of the same release (empty if the resource has no type, e.g. because it has no infobox mapped to the ontology).
- (Node) `is_work`: whether the node is a work (otherwise it is a writer).
citations: S. Auer, C. Bizer, G. Kobilarov, J. Lehmann, R. Cyganiak, Z. Ives, "DBpedia: A nucleus for a web of open data." In The Semantic Web (ISWC 2007 + ASWC 2007), Lecture Notes in Computer Science 4825, 722-735 (2007)
J. Lehmann et al., "DBpedia - A large-scale, multilingual knowledge base extracted from Wikipedia." Semantic Web 6(2), 167-195 (2015)

datasets.name: dbtropes_feature
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of artistic works (films, series, novels, games, etc.) and the tropes (writing devices and conventions) they use, from the TV Tropes wiki (tvtropes.org), as converted into RDF by the DBTropes project of M. Kiesel (DFKI). DBTropes parsed the pages of TV Tropes, and each example of a trope listed on the page of a work (or each work listed on the page of a trope) became a "feature instance" linking the work to the trope. Nodes are works and tropes, and an edge connects a work to a trope exemplified in it, with one edge per feature instance, so a pair can be connected by several edges when the example appears more than once (e.g. on both pages). This is the monthly DBTropes snapshot of 1 July 2016 (with pages fetched from TV Tropes at various earlier dates). The "item name" pseudo-features that DBTropes attaches to every work are not included.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `is_trope`: whether the node is a trope (otherwise it is a work).
- (Node) `name`: the page title (for works, prefixed by the TV Tropes namespace, e.g. "Film: The Matrix"; empty for the 3,053 pages without a title in the dump).
- (Node) `page`: the TV Tropes page ("Namespace/PageName").
- (Edge) `applicability`: a value given by DBTropes to each example: 1 for most examples, -1 for some examples (at least those marked as averted on TV Tropes), or -0.3 (whose meaning is not documented).
citations: M. Kiesel, G. A. Grimnes, "DBTropes - a linked data wrapper approach incorporating community feedback." EKAW 2010 Demo & Poster Abstracts, International Conference on Knowledge Engineering and Knowledge Management (2010)

datasets.name: debian_dependencies
datasets.description:
Networks of the dependencies between the binary packages of the Debian GNU/Linux distribution, one for each stable release, from Debian 0.93R6 (1995) and 1.1 "buzz" (1996) to 13 "trixie" (2025), built from the package indices (the `Packages` files) of the Debian archive, for the i386 architecture (the only one present in all releases), with all the components of each release (`main`, and `contrib`, `non-free` and `non-free-firmware`, when present).

Nodes are packages, and a directed edge from package $i$ to package $j$ is a relationship declared by $i$ in its control fields: a dependency (`Depends`, `Pre-Depends`), a weaker dependency (`Recommends`, `Suggests`, `Enhances`), a conflict (`Conflicts`, `Breaks`), a replacement (`Replaces`), or the provision of a virtual package (`Provides`). Dependencies of the form "a | b" (any of several alternatives) give an edge to each alternative, with the number of alternatives as an edge property. The packages named in relationships that are not in the index of the release (other architectures, removed packages, ...) are also nodes, as are the virtual packages (names provided by other packages, e.g. `mail-transport-agent`), with a property that tells them apart; architecture qualifiers (e.g. `:any`) and restrictions to architectures or build profiles are left out. Packages listed several times in an index, with several versions (a few in most releases, 223 in jessie), are taken once, with their first entry.

The archived releases are those of the final point release (e.g. 11.11 for bullseye), as kept on archive.debian.org; the releases bookworm (12) and trixie (13), still updated in place, are taken from the snapshot of 30 October 2026 of snapshot.debian.org. The networks are named after the codename of the release (`0.93r6` for Debian 0.93R6, which has no codename).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the package.
- (Node) `kind`: `package` for the packages of the index, `virtual` for names provided by some package but without a package of their own, and `missing` for names that only appear in relationships.
- (Node) `version`: the version of the package (with the revision, for 0.93R6).
- (Node) `component`: the component of the archive (`main`, `contrib`, `non-free`, `non-free-firmware`; empty for 0.93R6, whose index has no components).
- (Node) `section`, `priority`: the section (e.g. `admin`, `libs`, `net`) and priority (`required`, `important`, `standard`, `optional`, `extra`) of the package.
- (Node) `essential`: whether the package is marked essential.
- (Node) `architecture`: `i386` or `all` (architecture-independent packages; empty when not given).
- (Node) `source`: the source package, if it differs from the package's name (and it is given).
- (Node) `maintainer`: the maintainer of the package, as given in the index.
- (Node) `installed_size`: the installed size in kilobytes (-1 if not given), and `size`, the size of the package file in bytes (-1 if not given).
- (Node) `description`: the short (one-line) description of the package.
- (Edge) `type`: the field of the relationship (`Depends`, `Pre-Depends`, `Recommends`, `Suggests`, `Enhances`, `Conflicts`, `Breaks`, `Replaces`, `Provides`).
- (Edge) `constraint`: the version constraint of the relationship (e.g. `>= 2.3`), or empty.
- (Edge) `alternatives`: the number of alternatives of the dependency (1 if there are none).
- (Graph) `release` (the version number), `codename` and `release_date` (of the first release of the version, YYYY-MM-DD; only the month for 0.93R6).
citations: M. A. Fortuna, J. A. Bonachela and S. A. Levin, "Evolution of a modular software network." Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA 108(50), 19985-19989 (2011)

datasets.name: deezer_friends
datasets.description:
Social networks of users of the music streaming service Deezer, collected from its public API by B. Rozemberczki and collaborators for benchmarks of node embedding and classification methods. Nodes are users, and an undirected edge connects two users who are friends (follow each other). The users were reindexed for anonymity. There are two data sets:

- GEMSEC (collected in November 2017): three networks of users from Croatia (`HR`), Hungary (`HU`) and Romania (`RO`). Each user has the list of music genres they like, compiled by the authors from the songs the user liked (84 distinct genres).
- `deezer_europe` (FEATHER, collected in March 2020): a network of 28,281 users from European countries. Each user has a list of binary features, extracted from the artists liked by the user (only the indices of the features are given, not their meaning; 6,159 users have none), and a binary gender label, which the authors derived from the user's name; which value stands for which gender is not documented.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `genres` (GEMSEC networks): the list of music genres liked by the user (e.g. "Pop", "Rap/Hip Hop").
- (Node) `gender` (`deezer_europe`): the binary gender label (stored as a Boolean: false and true for the labels 0 and 1 of the data).
- (Node) `features` (`deezer_europe`): the indices of the user's binary features.
citations: B. Rozemberczki, R. Davies, R. Sarkar, and C. Sutton, "GEMSEC: Graph Embedding with Self Clustering." Proceedings of the 2019 IEEE/ACM International Conference on Advances in Social Networks Analysis and Mining (ASONAM), 65-72 (2019).

B. Rozemberczki and R. Sarkar, "Characteristic Functions on Graphs: Birds of a Feather, from Statistical Descriptors to Parametric Models." Proceedings of the 29th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM), 1325-1334 (2020).

datasets.name: delicious
datasets.description: Three bipartite networks that make up the del.icio.us folksonomy, representing the tag-URL, user-URL, and user-tag networks, as distributed by KONECT. In `ti`, nodes are tags and URLs, and an edge indicates that a URL was tagged with a tag; in `ui`, nodes are users and URLs, and an edge indicates that a user tagged a URL; in `ut`, nodes are users and tags, and an edge indicates that a user tagged a URL with a tag. Each edge corresponds to a tagging event, so that the networks contain multiple edges, and the edges are timestamped. The date of this snapshot is uncertain.

datasets.name: dgidb
datasets.description:
Bipartite networks of drugs and genes from the Drug-Gene Interaction Database (DGIdb), which collects drug-gene interactions (e.g. a drug that inhibits the product of a gene) from about 40 sources (e.g. ChEMBL, DrugBank, the Guide to Pharmacology, TTD, CIViC, the FDA, clinical trial and cancer knowledge bases, the literature), and normalizes the drugs and genes they name to common concepts. Each edge is an interaction claim of a source, so that a drug and a gene are often connected by several edges, one per source (and the networks are multigraphs).

There is one network for each data release of DGIdb that is available for download, named by its date: `2021-05` and `2022-02` (DGIdb 4), `2023-12`, `2024-06`, `2024-12`, `2026-06`, `2026-06b` (a corrected release of the same month) and `2026-10` (DGIdb 5); the release `2026-09` is identical to `2026-10`, and is left out. The drugs and genes of the claims that DGIdb could not normalize (about a tenth of the claims) are kept as nodes identified by the name given by the source (with an empty `concept_id`), so that the same drug or gene may appear in several of these nodes.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `is_drug`: whether the node is a drug (otherwise it is a gene).
- (Node) `concept_id`: the identifier of the normalized concept of the drug (e.g. `rxcui:12574`, `chembl:CHEMBL296468`, `ncit:C70982`) or of the gene (in DGIdb 5 its HGNC identifier, e.g. `hgnc:5466`; in DGIdb 4 its NCBI Gene identifier, written here as `ncbigene:1022`); empty for the drugs and genes that were not normalized.
- (Node) `name`: the name of the normalized drug or the gene symbol, or the name given by the source if it was not normalized.
- (Node) `approved`, `immunotherapy`, `antineoplastic` (from `2023-12`): whether the drug is approved, an immunotherapy, and an antineoplastic drug (false if not given).
- (Edge) `source`: the source of the claim, and `source_version` its version (from `2023-12`).
- (Edge) `gene_claim`, `drug_claim`: the names of the gene and the drug as given by the source.
- (Edge) `interaction_types`: the types of the interaction, e.g. `inhibitor`, `agonist`, separated by `|` in DGIdb 5 and by `,` in DGIdb 4 (empty if not given).
- (Edge) `interaction_score`: the interaction score of DGIdb, which grows with the number of sources and publications supporting the interaction, and with the specificity of the drug and the gene (NaN if not given).
- (Edge) `drug_specificity_score`, `gene_specificity_score`, `evidence_score` (from `2024-12`): the parts of the interaction score (NaN or -1 if not given).
- (Edge) `pmids` (`2021-05`, `2022-02`): the PubMed identifiers of the articles supporting the claim, separated by `,`.
citations: M. Cannon, J. Stevenson, K. Stahl, R. Basu, A. Coffman, S. Kiwala, J. F. McMichael, K. Kuzma, D. Morrissey, K. Cotto, E. R. Mardis, O. L. Griffith, M. Griffith, A. H. Wagner, "DGIdb 5.0: rebuilding the drug-gene interaction database for precision medicine and drug discovery platforms." Nucleic Acids Research 52, D1227-D1235 (2024)

S. L. Freshour, S. Kiwala, K. C. Cotto, A. C. Coffman, J. F. McMichael, J. J. Song, M. Griffith, O. L. Griffith, A. H. Wagner, "Integration of the Drug-Gene Interaction Database (DGIdb 4.0) with open crowdsource efforts." Nucleic Acids Research 49, D1144-D1151 (2021)

datasets.name: digg_reply
datasets.description:
A network of replies among users of the social news site Digg, collected by M. De Choudhury and collaborators with crawlers based on the Digg API. The data comprise stories on 56 topics, their comments, and the replies to these comments, written between late October and mid-November 2008. Each node is a Digg user, and a directed edge from $i$ to $j$ means that user $i$ replied to a comment by user $j$, with one edge per reply. Only replies to top-level comments included in the data are present (1,313 replies whose parent comment is not included are left out), and users replying to their own comments give self-loops.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the Digg user name.
- (Edge) `time`: the time of the reply (Unix time, from the date given in the data, whose time zone is not documented and is assumed to be UTC).
- (Edge) `story`: the Digg id of the story on which the comment was made.
- (Edge) `comment`: the Digg id of the comment that was replied to.
citations: M. De Choudhury et al., "Social synchrony: Predicting mimicry of user actions in online social media." In Proc. Int. Conf. on Computational Science and Engineering (CSE '09), 151-158, (2009)

datasets.name: digg_votes
datasets.description:
Votes on stories and friendship links among users of the social news site Digg, collected by K. Lerman and R. Ghosh. The data cover 3,553 stories promoted to Digg's front page over a period of a month in 2009. For each story, all votes ("diggs") made up to the time of data collection were retrieved, together with their time (the votes span 31 May to 5 July 2009); the earliest vote on each story is that of its submitter. The friendship links of the voters were also retrieved. Users and stories are anonymized, but user ids are consistent across the two data sets, so that a user with a given id in one network is the same user in the other. The collection comprises two networks:

- `votes`: a bipartite network of 139,409 users and the stories they voted for. Nodes are users and stories, and an edge connects a user to a story the user voted for, with one edge per vote. A few users voted more than once on the same story, so the network has some multiple edges.
- `friends`: the friendship links of the 71,367 voters who had specified friends at the time of data collection (voters who do not appear had none). Nodes are users, and a directed edge $(i,j)$ means that user $i$ added $j$ as a friend, i.e. that $i$ watches the activities of (is a fan of) $j$. Only the friend lists of voters were retrieved, so the users who appear only as friends have no out-going edges, and the reverse of a mutual friendship is present only if both users are voters. Five users list themselves as friends (self-loops). The links were created between November 2005 and July 2009.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `is_user` (`votes`): whether the node is a user (otherwise it is a story).
- (Node) `id` (`votes`): the anonymized id of the user or story in the source data.
- (Edge) `time` (`votes`): the time of the vote (Unix time).
- (Node) `id` (`friends`): the anonymized id of the user in the source data (the same as in the `votes` network).
- (Edge) `time` (`friends`): the time when the friendship link was created (Unix time; 0 if unknown, for 1,670 links).
- (Edge) `mutual` (`friends`): whether the friendship is mutual, i.e. whether $j$ also added $i$ as a friend.
citations: K. Lerman, R. Ghosh, "Information contagion: An empirical study of the spread of news on Digg and Twitter social networks." Proceedings of the International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media 4(1), 90-97 (2010)
T. Hogg, and K. Lerman. "Social dynamics of digg." EPJ Data Science 1, 5 (2012)

datasets.name: dining_table
datasets.description:
Choices of dining-table partners among 26 girls living in one cottage (dormitory) of the New York State Training School for Girls in Hudson, New York, from the sociometric studies of J. L. Moreno and H. H. Jennings. Each girl was asked to choose the girls she would like to sit with at the dining table, and her first and second choices are recorded as directed edges from the choosing girl to the chosen one. The network was coded by W. de Nooy from a sociogram published in Moreno's *The Sociometry Reader* (1960). The data were distributed on the Pajek datasets page of the book *Exploratory Social Network Analysis with Pajek* (de Nooy, Mrvar and Batagelj), from which this version was obtained.[^icon]

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the (first) name of the girl.
- (Edge) `choice`: the rank of the choice (1: first choice, 2: second choice).

[^icon]: Description obtained in part from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.
citations: J. L. Moreno, "The Sociometry Reader." The Free Press, Glencoe, Illinois (1960), p. 35
W. de Nooy, A. Mrvar, V. Batagelj, "Exploratory Social Network Analysis with Pajek." Cambridge University Press (2005)

datasets.name: discogs_affiliation
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of musical artists and the record labels of their releases, from the Discogs database. Discogs (discogs.com) is a user-built online database of music recordings, whose contributors catalogue releases (albums, singles, compilations, etc.) together with their credits; its content is published as monthly XML dumps. This network is built from the releases dump of 1 October 2015, which contains the 6,379,659 releases accepted in the database at that time (drafts and the few rejected or deleted releases of the dump are excluded). Nodes are artists and labels, and an edge connects an artist to a label for each release of that label in which the artist is credited; repeated edges correspond to different releases. An artist is credited in a release either as one of its main artists or with a release-wide credit (e.g. producer, mixer, or performer on all tracks, the "extra artists"); credits limited to individual tracks are not included. When a release has several labels (co-releases, sublabels, distributors listed as labels), the artist is connected to each of them.

Artists are identified by their Discogs id, and their names are the Discogs names, which include a numeric suffix (e.g. "John Smith (2)") to distinguish artists with the same name. The dump of 2015 does not contain label ids, and labels are therefore identified by their names, which are unique in Discogs. Discogs uses placeholder artists such as "Various" (for compilations) and "Unknown Artist", and placeholder labels such as "Not On Label" (with variants for self-released records), which are kept as nodes.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `is_artist`: whether the node is an artist (otherwise it is a label).
- (Node) `name`: the name of the artist or label.
- (Node) `discogs_id`: the Discogs id of the artist (-1 for labels).
- (Edge) `release`: the Discogs id of the release.
- (Edge) `year`: the release year as entered in Discogs (-1 if unknown; a few values are evidently mistyped, e.g. 198 or 4198).
- (Edge) `extra`: whether the artist is credited only as an extra artist of the release (otherwise it is one of its main artists).

datasets.name: discogs_genre
datasets.description:
Two bipartite networks of musical artists and the genres or styles of their releases, from the Discogs database. Discogs (discogs.com) is a user-built online database of music recordings, whose contributors catalog releases (albums, singles, compilations, etc.) together with their credits, and classify each release into one or more of 15 broad genres (e.g. Rock, Electronic, Jazz) and, optionally, into finer styles (e.g. Deep House, Free Jazz, Punk); its content is published as monthly XML dumps. These networks are built from the releases dump of 1 October 2015, which contains the 6,379,659 releases accepted in the database at that time (drafts and the few rejected or deleted releases of the dump are excluded). Nodes are artists and genres (`genre`) or styles (`style`), and an undirected edge connects an artist to a genre or style if the artist is credited in at least one release of that genre or style, weighted by the number of such releases. An artist is credited in a release either as one of its main artists or with a release-wide credit (e.g. producer, mixer, or performer on all tracks); credits limited to individual tracks are not included.

- `genre`: artists and genres.
- `style`: artists and styles.

Artists are identified by their Discogs id, and their names are the Discogs names, which include a numeric suffix (e.g. "John Smith (2)") to distinguish artists with the same name. Discogs uses placeholder artists such as "Various" (for compilations) and "Unknown Artist", which are kept as nodes. Artists without any release with a genre (or style) are not included in the corresponding network.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `is_artist`: whether the node is an artist (otherwise it is a genre or style).
- (Node) `name`: the name of the artist, genre or style.
- (Node) `discogs_id`: the Discogs id of the artist (-1 for genres and styles).
- (Edge) `count`: the number of releases of that genre or style in which the artist is credited.
- (Edge) `first_year` and `last_year`: the earliest and latest release years among them (-1 if none of them has a known year; the years are as entered in Discogs, and a few are evidently mistyped).

datasets.name: discogs_label
datasets.description:
Two bipartite networks of record labels and the genres or styles of their releases, from the Discogs database. Discogs (discogs.com) is a user-built online database of music recordings, whose contributors catalog releases (albums, singles, compilations, etc.) with their labels, and classify each release into one or more of 15 broad genres (e.g. Rock, Electronic, Jazz) and, optionally, into finer styles (e.g. Deep House, Free Jazz, Punk); its content is published as monthly XML dumps. These networks are built from the releases dump of 1 October 2015, which contains the 6,379,659 releases accepted in the database at that time (drafts and the few rejected or deleted releases of the dump are excluded). Nodes are labels and genres (`genre`) or styles (`style`), and an undirected edge connects a label to a genre or style if the label has at least one release of that genre or style, weighted by the number of such releases. When a release has several labels (co-releases, sublabels, distributors listed as labels), each of them is connected to the genres and styles of the release.

- `genre`: labels and genres.
- `style`: labels and styles.

The dump of 2015 does not contain label ids, and labels are therefore identified by their names, which are unique in Discogs. Discogs uses placeholder labels such as "Not On Label" (with variants for self-released records), which are kept as nodes. Labels without any release with a genre (or style) are not included in the corresponding network.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `is_label`: whether the node is a label (otherwise it is a genre or style).
- (Node) `name`: the name of the label, genre or style.
- (Edge) `count`: the number of releases of that label with that genre or style.
- (Edge) `first_year` and `last_year`: the earliest and latest release years among them (-1 if none of them has a known year; the years are as entered in Discogs, and a few are evidently mistyped).

datasets.name: diseasome
datasets.description:
Bipartite network of human genetic disorders and disease genes, from the "diseasome" of K.-I. Goh and collaborators, as distributed by the Gephi project. Nodes are disorders and genes, and an undirected edge connects a disorder to a gene whose mutations are associated with it. The disorder-gene associations were obtained from the Morbid Map of the Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man (OMIM) database (December 2005 version), in which the authors merged the subtypes of the same disorder into a single disorder and manually assigned each disorder to one of 22 classes according to the physiological system affected. This version contains the 516 disorders of the giant component of the human disease network (the projection in which two disorders are connected if they share a gene), and 903 disease genes connected to them.

The source file also contains the edges of this projection (two disorders connected if they share at least one gene, each listed twice); they are not included here, since they can be obtained from the bipartite network.

The nodes have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the disorder (e.g. "Alzheimer disease"), or the symbol of the gene.
- (Node) `is_disorder`: whether the node is a disorder (otherwise it is a gene).
- (Node) `disorder_class`: the class of the disorder (e.g. "Cancer", "Neurological", "Multiple"), as given in the source (with its spelling, e.g. "Ophthamological"); empty for genes.[^icon]

[^icon]: Description obtained in part from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.
citations: K.-I. Goh, M. E. Cusick, D. Valle, B. Childs, M. Vidal, A.-L. Barabási, "The human disease network." Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 104(21), 8685-8690 (2007)

datasets.name: divvy
datasets.description:
Monthly networks of the trips made with Divvy, the bicycle sharing system of Chicago (operated by Lyft), from the trip data published by the operator: one network for each month from June 2013, when the system opened, to September 2026, named `<year>_<month>` (e.g. `2013_06`), 160 networks in all.

Each node is a station, and each directed edge goes from the station where a bicycle was taken out to the station where it was returned, weighted by the number of such trips in the month (trips that return to the same station are self-loops); trips are assigned to the month in which they started. The networks contain 49,171,160 trips in total. Left out are the 9,035,807 trips (all since 2020) without a start or an end station, mostly of electric bicycles taken out or left away from a station, and the details of individual trips (times, durations, bicycles, and the age and gender of the riders, given until 2019). The trip data until 2019 were published per quarter or half year and are split here by month.

The station ids changed in December 2020 (from the numbers used until then to new codes), so the stations of different months can be matched by `station_id` only within each period. Until March 2020, the coordinates of the stations are those of the station tables published with the trip data (for 2014, the table of the second half of the year; for 2018 and 2019, for which none was published, the table of the second half of 2017, and for the stations missing from it, the coordinates in the trips of early 2020); since then they are the most common coordinates of the trips that start or end at the station (those of electric bicycles are recorded by GPS). The coordinates of a few stations are unknown.

The station-to-station networks are not planar spatial networks (trips may connect any two stations), so they are laid out as other networks, with the coordinates as vertex properties.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `station_id`: the id of the station.
- (Node) `name`: its name (the most common one in the month).
- (Node) `lat` and `lon`: its geographic coordinates (NaN if unknown).
- (Edge) `weight`: the number of trips.
- (Edge) `member_trips`: the number of trips by members, i.e. subscribers with an annual membership (the others are by casual users, with single rides or day passes).
citations: Lyft Bikes and Scooters, "Divvy System Data." (2026)

datasets.name: dnc
datasets.description: A network representing the exchange of emails among members of the Democratic National Committee, in the email data leak released by WikiLeaks in 2016, as distributed by KONECT (co-recipient network). Nodes are 906 persons, and an undirected edge connects two persons who were both on the recipient list of the same email, with the edge `weight` giving the number of such emails. For 1,656 pairs of persons, the KONECT file lists the pair twice, in both orientations and mostly with different weights, so that these pairs are connected by two parallel edges.
citations: J. Kunegis, "DNC emails co-recipients." KONECT, the Koblenz Network Collection (2016)

datasets.name: dolphins
datasets.description:
An undirected social network of frequent associations among 62 bottlenose dolphins (*Tursiops* sp.) of a community living in Doubtful Sound, a fjord in New Zealand, compiled by D. Lusseau and collaborators from boat-based observations made between 1994 and 2001. Individual dolphins were identified from photographs of natural markings on their dorsal fins. During surveys, groups of dolphins were followed and photographed, and two dolphins were considered associated when they were observed in the same group. An edge connects two dolphins whose association, measured by the half-weight index, was significantly stronger than expected by chance, i.e. pairs that were observed together more often than random association would predict (preferred companionships).

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `label`: the name given to the dolphin by the researchers.
citations: D. Lusseau et al., "The bottlenose dolphin community of Doubtful Sound features a large proportion of long-lasting associations." Behavioral Ecology and Sociobiology 54(4), 396-405 (2003).

datasets.name: dolphins_caravelas
datasets.description:
Weighted social network of a population of Guiana dolphins (*Sotalia guianensis*) in the Caravelas River estuary, Bahia, Brazil, from the study of M. Cantor and collaborators on the temporal structure of this dolphin society. The data were compiled by M. Cantor and collaborators for a study of nestedness across levels of biological organization, and are distributed in the repository of that study (file `pop_sotalia.txt`). Individuals were identified by photo-identification of natural markings on the dorsal fin, and two individuals were considered associated when observed in the same group. Nodes are individuals, and an undirected edge connects two individuals that were observed together at least once, weighted by their association index, the half-weight index (HWI), an estimate of the proportion of time the two individuals spend together (from 0, never seen together, to 1, always together). Only the 33 individuals that were seen in the study area more than three times during the study period are included. The individuals are not identified in the source data.

The edges have the property `weight`, the half-weight association index.
citations: M. Cantor, L. L. Wedekin, P. R. Guimarães Jr., F. G. Daura-Jorge, M. R. Rossi-Santos, P. C. Simões-Lopes, "Disentangling social networks from spatiotemporal dynamics: the temporal structure of a dolphin society." Animal Behaviour 84, 641-651 (2012)

M. Cantor, M. M. Pires, F. M. D. Marquitti, R. L. G. Raimundo, E. Sebastián-González, P. P. Coltri, S. I. Perez, D. R. Barneche, D. Y. C. Brandt, K. Nunes, F. G. Daura-Jorge, S. R. Floeter, P. R. Guimarães Jr., "Nestedness across biological scales." PLoS ONE 12(2), e0171691 (2017)

datasets.name: dolphins_laguna
datasets.description:
Weighted social network of the resident bottlenose dolphins (*Tursiops truncatus*) of Laguna, southern Brazil, a population in which a subset of the dolphins forages in cooperation with local, beach-casting artisanal fishermen, from the study of F. G. Daura-Jorge and collaborators. The data were compiled by M. Cantor and collaborators for a study of nestedness across levels of biological organization, and are distributed in the repository of that study (file `pop_tursiops.txt`). Individuals were identified by photo-identification of natural markings on the dorsal fin, and two individuals were considered associated when observed in the same group. Nodes are individuals, and an undirected edge connects two individuals that were observed together at least once, weighted by their association index, the half-weight index (HWI), an estimate of the proportion of time the two individuals spend together (from 0, never seen together, to 1, always together). Only the 35 individuals that were seen in the study area more than three times during the study period are included. The individuals are not identified in the source data.

The edges have the property `weight`, the half-weight association index.
citations: F. G. Daura-Jorge, M. Cantor, S. N. Ingram, D. Lusseau, P. C. Simões-Lopes, "The structure of a bottlenose dolphin society is coupled to a unique foraging cooperation with artisanal fishermen." Biology Letters 8, 702-705 (2012)

M. Cantor, M. M. Pires, F. M. D. Marquitti, R. L. G. Raimundo, E. Sebastián-González, P. P. Coltri, S. I. Perez, D. R. Barneche, D. Y. C. Brandt, K. Nunes, F. G. Daura-Jorge, S. R. Floeter, P. R. Guimarães Jr., "Nestedness across biological scales." PLoS ONE 12(2), e0171691 (2017)

datasets.name: dom
datasets.description:
Animal dominance interaction data published over a century of research. The archive contains 436 agonistic interaction datasets (418 interaction matrices and 18 sequences of interactions) from 190 studies of 367 groups of 135 species, totaling about 243,000 interactions. (The README of the DomArchive repository gives an outdated count of 434 datasets and over 241,000 interactions; the data file and the accompanying paper have 436 datasets.) Each dataset is a separate network, named after its source study (with the study's metadata, such as the species and study site, as graph properties). Nodes are individual animals of the observed group, identified by the names or codes used in the source study (vertex property `name`), and a directed edge (i,j) corresponds to an agonistic interaction between i (winner) and j (loser). For datasets given as interaction matrices, all individuals of the matrix are included (even those without any interaction), there is one edge per pair, and the `weight` edge property counts the number of such interactions (or is 1 for binary data); for datasets given as lists of interactions, each interaction is a separate edge, with its position in the sequence of interactions (`sequence`) and, when available, its date or time as given in the source (`time`, whose meaning is given by the graph property `edgelist_time_meaning`).

Some of the datasets were also distributed by L. C. Freeman on his network data page at the University of California, Irvine (no longer online), in UCINET format:

- `Lott_1979`: dominance encounters among 26 mature male American bison on the National Bison Range in Moiese, Montana, observed by D. F. Lott for 12 hours per day from 25 July to 14 August 1972 (fighting, nod-threats, broadside threats, head-on threats, rush threats and supplanting). Freeman's version has the same matrix, with the animals numbered 1 to 26 instead of `a01` to `a26`, and in addition the breeding success of each bull, which is included here as the vertex property `breeding` (the number of breeding successes, available only for this network; it is obtained from Freeman's page via the Internet Archive).
- `ScheinFohrman_1955`: contests (most of which were mere threats) among 28 cows of a herd of dairy cattle at the Iberia Livestock Experiment Station in Jeanerette, Louisiana, observed by M. W. Schein and M. H. Fohrman. Freeman's version has the same matrix, with the names without the `X` prefix.
- `VanHooffWensing_1987`: "low posture" displays among the 16 members of a captive wolf pack in a large wooded enclosure in Arnhem (the Netherlands), observed in 1978 by J. A. R. A. M. van Hooff and J. A. B. Wensing. Freeman's version (file `wolf.dat`) is transposed (the row wolf is the one that displays low posture, i.e. the loser) and has only 148 of the 161 nonzero entries of the matrix (4,458 of the 10,405 displays). Freeman's page also gives the age and sex of each wolf (with the same names as here), which are included as the vertex properties `age` (the age in years) and `male` (true for males), available only for this network and obtained from Freeman's page via the Internet Archive.
citations: Strauss Eli D., DeCasien Alex R., Galindo Gabriela, Hobson Elizabeth A., Shizuka Daizaburo and Curley James P., "DomArchive: a century of published dominance data", Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B377: 20200436 (2022)
D. F. Lott, "Dominance relations and breeding rate in mature male American bison." Zeitschrift für Tierpsychologie 49(4), 418-432 (1979)
M. W. Schein and M. H. Fohrman. "Social dominance relationships in a herd of dairy cattle." The British J. of Animal Behaviour 3(2), 45-55 (1955)

J. A. R. A. M. van Hooff, J. A. B. Wensing, "Dominance and its behavioral measures in a captive wolf pack." In H. Frank (ed.), Man and Wolf: Advances, Issues, and Problems in Captive Wolf Research, 219-252, Dr W. Junk Publishers (1987)

datasets.name: domestic_terror_web
datasets.description:
Directed network of hyperlinks among the websites of domestic extremist and terrorist groups in the United States, collected c. 2005 as part of a study of the web presence of these groups (Zhou et al., 2005). Nodes are websites, labeled by their domain names (vertex property `name`), and a directed edge indicates that one site links to the other. Data distributed by the UCINET datasets collection (University of Manchester). One self-link in the source matrix is not included.[^ucinet]

[^ucinet]: Description obtained in part from the [UCINET datasets page](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/datasets/covert-networks/domestic-terrorist-web-links).
citations: Y. Zhou, E. Reid, J. Qin, H. Chen, and G. Lai, "US domestic extremist groups on the Web: link and content analysis." IEEE Intelligent Systems 20(5), 44-51 (2005)

datasets.name: douban
datasets.description:
A friendship network among users of Douban.com, a Chinese website (launched in 2005) for reviews and recommendations of movies, books and music, crawled in December 2010 by Long Qiu at Arizona State University and distributed by the Social Computing Data Repository (originally at Arizona State University, now at Syracuse University). Nodes are users (anonymized), and an undirected edge connects two users who are friends.

The source data list the friendships as lines stating that "user $i$ is friend with user $j$", almost all of them in both directions: of the 654,188 lines, 654,052 are mirrored by the line of the opposite direction (327,026 pairs), and 136 are not. Each pair of users listed in either direction is one edge (327,162 edges in all); the direction of the 136 unmirrored lines is not kept. The node list of the source data contains 154,907 users; one more user (with identifier 154908) occurs only in the edges.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `user_id`: the identifier of the user in the source data.
- (Node) `in_node_list`: whether the user is listed in the node list of the source data.
citations: R. Zafarani, H. Liu, "Social Computing Data Repository at ASU." Arizona State University, School of Computing, Informatics and Decision Systems Engineering (2009)

datasets.name: drkg
datasets.description:
A biomedical knowledge graph of genes, compounds, diseases and other biological entities, the Drug Repurposing Knowledge Graph (DRKG) assembled by Amazon and collaborators for drug repurposing, notably for COVID-19. It integrates DrugBank, Hetionet, GNBR (relations mined from the literature), STRING, IntAct, DGIdb and data from publications related to COVID-19 (the "bibliography"). The nodes are entities of 13 types (`Gene`, `Compound`, `Disease`, `Anatomy`, `Atc`, `Biological Process`, `Cellular Component`, `Molecular Function`, `Pathway`, `Pharmacologic Class`, `Side Effect`, `Symptom`, `Tax`), and each directed edge is a triple (head, relation, tail) with one of 107 relation types, from the head entity to the tail entity. Two entities can be joined by several edges with different relations (e.g. from different sources), so that the network is a multigraph. The data are those of the release of June 2020.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `entity`: the identifier of the entity in DRKG, made of its type and its identifier in the source (e.g. `Gene::2157`, an NCBI Gene identifier, `Compound::DB00001`, a DrugBank identifier, `Disease::MESH:D015673`).
- (Node) `kind`: the type of the entity, e.g. `Gene`.
- (Edge) `relation`: the relation, made of its source, its name and the types of the entities it joins (e.g. `DRUGBANK::ddi-interactor-in::Compound:Compound`, `GNBR::E+::Compound:Gene`).
- (Edge) `source`: the source of the relation (`DRUGBANK`, `Hetionet`, `GNBR`, `STRING`, `INTACT`, `DGIDB`, `bioarx`).
- (Edge) `interaction_type`: the type of interaction of the relation, from the glossary of DRKG (e.g. `activation`; empty if not given).
- (Graph) `relation_glossary`: the glossary of the relations of DRKG, in JSON: for each relation, its data source, the types of entities it joins, its interaction type, its description and the reference of the description.
citations: V. N. Ioannidis, X. Song, S. Manchanda, M. Li, X. Pan, D. Zheng, X. Ning, X. Zeng, G. Karypis, "DRKG - Drug Repurposing Knowledge Graph for Covid-19." GitHub repository (2020)

datasets.name: drosophila_flybi
datasets.description: Binary protein-protein interactions (PPIs) for Drosophila melanogaster, containing 8723 PPIs among 2939 proteins. The interactions were identified using a yeast two-hybrid (Y2H) analysis. Nodes are proteins, and an undirected edge connects two proteins that were found to interact.
citations: Tang, HW., Spirohn, K., Hu, Y. et al. Next-generation large-scale binary protein interaction network for Drosophila melanogaster. Nat Commun 14, 2162 (2023)

datasets.name: drugnet
datasets.description:
Directed network of acquaintanceship among 293 drug users in Hartford, Connecticut, United States, from a study of the social networks of drug users in high-risk sites, based on two years of ethnographic observation (Weeks et al., 2002). Nodes are drug users (numbered in `name`), and a directed edge indicates that one person named the other as an acquaintance. Vertex properties: `ethnicity` (1, 5, 6, 7 = white or other, 2 = African American, 3 = Puerto Rican or Latino), `gender` (1 = male, 2 = female, 0 = unknown), and `hastie` (whether the person has any tie). Data distributed by the UCINET datasets collection (University of Manchester).[^ucinet]

[^ucinet]: Description obtained in part from the [UCINET datasets page](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/datasets/covert-networks/drugnet).
citations: M. R. Weeks, S. Clair, S. P. Borgatti, K. Radda, and J. J. Schensul, "Social networks of drug users in high-risk sites: Finding the connections." AIDS and Behavior 6(2), 193-206 (2002)

datasets.name: dutch_classrooms
datasets.description:
Emotional support networks among the pupils of 19 school year groups in Dutch secondary schools, from the Dutch Social Behavior study of C. Baerveldt and collaborators, a two-wave survey on petty crime and social networks of adolescents. The pupils followed the MAVO track (the lower middle level of the Dutch secondary school system) in urban high schools, and filled in a questionnaire during a lesson in their third year (1994/1995, first wave) and fourth year (second wave, about one year later). All pupils of the same year of MAVO in a school form one network, and only pupils who responded in both waves are included (990 pupils in total). The data were distributed by T. Snijders with the SIENA software.

A directed edge (i, j) indicates that pupil i reported receiving emotional support from, or giving emotional support to, pupil j ("Which pupils help you when you are depressed, for example, after the end of a love affair or when you have a conflict with other people?", and "Which pupils do you help when they are depressed...?"). Up to twelve pupils could be named in each question. The network `schoolH_wW` corresponds to the school number H (as numbered in the source data) and wave W. A few diagonal entries of the source matrices are nonzero, and are ignored.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `gender` (1: girl, 2: boy).
- (Node) `delinquency`: the number of minor offenses (from a list of 23, such as shoplifting, petty theft, vandalism and unarmed fights) which the pupil reports to have committed in the last twelve months, at the first wave, transformed as ln(1+x).
- (Node) `delinquency_rounded`: the same measure at the wave of the network, rounded to integer values.
- (Node) `school_friends`: the importance of school friends, from 1 to 4 (the documentation describes this scale inconsistently, as either from 1: very important to 4: unimportant, or from 1: friends outside school are more important to 4: no friends outside school).
citations: B. Houtzager, C. Baerveldt, "Just like normal: A social network study of the relation between petty crime and the intimacy of adolescent friendships." Social Behavior and Personality 27(2), 177-192 (1999)
T. A. B. Snijders, C. Baerveldt, "A multilevel network study of the effects of delinquent behavior on friendship evolution." Journal of Mathematical Sociology 27(2-3), 123-151 (2003)

datasets.name: dutch_criticism
datasets.description:
A network of literary criticism among 35 Dutch literary authors and critics in 1976, compiled by W. de Nooy for his study of balance theory in literary criticism, and used as an example in the book "Exploratory Social Network Analysis with Pajek" by W. de Nooy, A. Mrvar and V. Batagelj. Nodes are persons (authors and critics), and a directed edge $i \to j$ means that $i$ passed judgment on the work of $j$ in an interview or a review published in 1976.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name` and `id`: the name of the person ("Surname, First name").
- (Node) `x`, `y` and `z`: the node coordinates in the Pajek source file (their meaning is not documented).
- (Edge) `weight`: which is always 1.
citations: W. De Nooy, "A literary playground: Literary criticism and balance theory." Poetics 26 (5-6), 385-404 (1999).

datasets.name: dutch_elite
datasets.description:
Memberships of persons in the administrative bodies (boards, councils, committees, etc.) of the administrative elite in the Netherlands in April 2006, collected and analyzed by the newspaper de Volkskrant and W. de Nooy for a series of articles on the 200 most influential people in the country, later collected in the book *De elite* by W. Dekker and B. van Raaij. The networks are bipartite, connecting persons to the administrative bodies of which they are members, with the role of the person in the body. The data were converted into Pajek format by W. de Nooy (2006) and improved by V. Batagelj (2007). The data were distributed in Pajek format on the Pajek datasets page of V. Batagelj and A. Mrvar, from which this version was obtained.

- `full`: the 3810 persons and 937 administrative bodies.
- `top200`: the subnetwork of the 200 most influential persons and the 395 bodies of which they are members.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the person or administrative body.
- (Node) `is_person`: whether the node is a person (otherwise an administrative body).
- (Node) `weight` (`full` only; bodies only, 0 for persons): the importance class of the body (1: a point of reference whose chairman belongs to the absolute top of the ranking, 2: other bodies that function as a point of reference to the government, 3: remaining bodies).
- (Node) `organisation` and `mother_organisation` (bodies only, 0 for persons): the identifiers of the organization to which the body belongs, and of the mother organization of that organization.
- (Node) `domain` (bodies only, 0 for persons): the social sector in which the organization is primarily active, categorized by Ministry (1: General Affairs, 2: Foreign Affairs, 3: Defence, 4: Economic Affairs, 5: Finance, 6: Justice, 7: Agriculture and Nature, 8: Education and Science, 9: Culture, 10: Social Affairs, 11: Transport, 12: Health and Welfare, 13: Sports, 14: Spatial Planning and Environment, 15: Interior, 18: Media).
- (Node) `task` (bodies only, 0 for persons): the primary task of the body (1: advice, 2: administration, 3: management, 4: unknown, 5: other, 6: inspection, 7: representation of the people, 8: arbitration/administration of justice).
- (Node) `sex` (persons only): the sex of the person ("F" or "M"; empty if unknown, and for bodies).
- (Node) `birth_year` (persons only, 0 for bodies): the year of birth of the person (-1 if unknown).
- (Node) `rank`: the position of the person in the Top 200 of the most influential people published by de Volkskrant in 2006 (0 for persons outside the Top 200 and for bodies).
- (Edge) `relation`: the code of the role of the person in the body, and `role`, its name (in Dutch and English; e.g. "Voorzitter/Chairman", "Lid/member", "Directeur/Director"). The codes 52 and 37 are considered equivalent to 29 ("Vennoot/partner") and 34 ("Hoofddirecteur/general manager"), respectively, and are labeled as such.
citations: W. Dekker, B. van Raaij, "De elite: De Volkskrant Top 200 van invloedrijkste Nederlanders." Meulenhoff, Amsterdam (2006)
W. de Nooy, "Ringen om de macht." In W. Dekker, B. van Raaij, De elite, Meulenhoff, Amsterdam (2006), pp. 85-94

datasets.name: dutch_school
datasets.description:
Friendship networks among the 26 pupils of a school class (class "12b") in the first year of secondary school in the Netherlands, collected by A. Knecht in 2003–2004 for her PhD research on friendship dynamics in early adolescence, and used by T. A. B. Snijders, G. G. van de Bunt and C. E. G. Steglich to illustrate stochastic actor-oriented models. Friendship nominations were surveyed four times (waves 1 to 4), at intervals of three months. Nodes are pupils, and a directed edge $i \to j$ means that pupil $i$ nominated pupil $j$ as a friend. The same pupils are present in all networks, in the same order.

The networks are:

- `klas12b-net-1` to `klas12b-net-4`: friendships in each of the four waves;
- `klas12b-net-3m` and `klas12b-net-4m`: variants of waves 3 and 4 in which all missing values are coded as 9 (their purpose is not documented in the source);
- `klas12b-primary`: friendships in primary school, as reported in the first wave.

In the source data, missing values are coded with 9 (incidentally missing nominator) or 10 (structurally missing nominator or nominee, e.g. a pupil who left the class); these entries are not represented as edges.

The networks have the following node properties (in the attributes, 0 denotes a missing value):

- `missing`: whether the nominations of the pupil are missing in the network.
- `sex` (1: female, 2: male), `age` (in years, at wave 1), `ethnicity` (1: Dutch, 2: other) and `religion` (of the father; 1: Christian, 2: non-religious, 3: other religion).
- `advice`: the school advice at the end of primary school (from 4, low, to 8, high).
- `delinquency`: a scale of minor delinquency in waves 1 to 4 (1: never, 2: once, 3: 2–4 times, 4: 5–10 times, 5: more than 10 times).
- `alcohol`: alcohol consumption in waves 2 to 4 (same scale as `delinquency`).
- `present`: the first and last waves in which the pupil was present in the class.
citations: T. Snijders, G. van de Bunt, and C. Steglich, "Introduction to stochastic actor-based models for network dynamics." Social Networks 32(1), 44-60 (2010)

datasets.name: ecoli_transcription
datasets.description:
The transcriptional regulation network of the bacterium *Escherichia coli*, compiled by S. S. Shen-Orr, R. Milo, S. Mangan and U. Alon to study network motifs. Nodes are operons (groups of genes transcribed together), and a directed edge connects a transcription factor to an operon whose transcription it regulates (a transcription factor is itself encoded by an operon, so it is represented by the corresponding node; self-loops represent autoregulation). The interactions were assembled from the RegulonDB database (version 3.2, excluding interactions of unknown type and interactions supported only by ChIP experiments), complemented by a literature search.

There are two versions of the data:

- `v1.0`: the original data set used in the publication;
- `v1.1`: an updated version with 578 interactions, in which three errors were corrected (the misspelled operon moaABDE renamed to maoABDE; hycA merged into the autoregulated operon hycABCDE; and a missing interaction of ArcA added).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the operon (e.g. `crp`).
- (Edge) `regulation_type`: the kind of regulation (1: activation, 2: repression, 3: dual, i.e. both activation and repression depending on conditions).
citations: Shen-Orr et. al, "Network motifs in the transcriptional regulation network of Escherichia coli." Nature Genetics 31, 64-68 (2002).

datasets.name: edit_wikibooks
datasets.description:
Bipartite networks of users and the pages they edited, one for each of the 122 language editions of Wikibooks, the collaboratively edited collection of open textbooks, named by their language code (e.g. `en`, `fr`). They were extracted from the Wikimedia "stub-meta-history" dumps of 1 October 2026, which list, for every page existing at the time of the dump, all its revisions (edits) that have not been deleted, with their time, author and size, but without their text. Nodes are users and pages, and an edge connects a user to a page for each edit of that page made by the user, so that a user who edited the same page several times is connected to it by multiple edges. Pages of all namespaces are included (content pages, talk pages, user pages, templates, categories, etc.). Edits by unregistered users are attributed to their IP addresses (or, since 2025, to their automatically created temporary accounts, whose names start with "~"); edits whose author has been hidden are omitted, as are the edits of deleted pages. Edit summaries are not included. Pages imported from other wikis keep their edit history, so that some edits predate the creation of the wiki.

These networks replace an earlier version extracted from the dumps of July 2017, which contained only registered users and no node names. The language edition `als` (a deleted wiki) of the earlier version no longer exists.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the page title (including its namespace prefix), or the user name or IP address.
- (Node) `is_page`: whether the node is a page (otherwise it is a user).
- (Node) `namespace`: the MediaWiki namespace number of the page (0 for content pages, 1 for their talk pages, 2 for user pages, 3 for user talk pages, 4 for project pages, 10 for templates, 14 for categories, etc.), and $-1$ for users.
- (Node) `is_redirect`: whether the page was a redirect at the time of the dump (false for users).
- (Node) `anonymous`: whether the user is unregistered and identified only by an IP address (false for pages).
- (Edge) `time`: the time of the edit (Unix time, in seconds).
- (Edge) `minor`: whether the edit was marked as minor by its author.
- (Edge) `size`: the size of the page text in bytes after the edit ($-1$ if unknown).

datasets.name: edit_wikinews
datasets.description:
Bipartite networks of users and the pages they edited, one for each of the 36 language editions of Wikinews, the collaboratively written news site (all its language editions are marked as closed, i.e. read-only, in the dumps of this date), named by their language code (e.g. `en`, `fr`). They were extracted from the Wikimedia "stub-meta-history" dumps of 1 October 2026, which list, for every page existing at the time of the dump, all its revisions (edits) that have not been deleted, with their time, author and size, but without their text. Nodes are users and pages, and an edge connects a user to a page for each edit of that page made by the user, so that a user who edited the same page several times is connected to it by multiple edges. Pages of all namespaces are included (content pages, talk pages, user pages, templates, categories, etc.). Edits by unregistered users are attributed to their IP addresses (or, since 2025, to their automatically created temporary accounts, whose names start with "~"); edits whose author has been hidden are omitted, as are the edits of deleted pages. Edit summaries are not included. Pages imported from other wikis keep their edit history, so that some edits predate the creation of the wiki.

These networks replace an earlier version extracted from the dumps of July 2017, which contained only registered users and no node names.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the page title (including its namespace prefix), or the user name or IP address.
- (Node) `is_page`: whether the node is a page (otherwise it is a user).
- (Node) `namespace`: the MediaWiki namespace number of the page (0 for content pages, 1 for their talk pages, 2 for user pages, 3 for user talk pages, 4 for project pages, 10 for templates, 14 for categories, etc.), and $-1$ for users.
- (Node) `is_redirect`: whether the page was a redirect at the time of the dump (false for users).
- (Node) `anonymous`: whether the user is unregistered and identified only by an IP address (false for pages).
- (Edge) `time`: the time of the edit (Unix time, in seconds).
- (Edge) `minor`: whether the edit was marked as minor by its author.
- (Edge) `size`: the size of the page text in bytes after the edit ($-1$ if unknown).
