citations: N. Blagus, L. Šubelj, M. Bajec, "Self-similar scaling of density in complex real-world networks." Physica A 391(8), 2794-2802 (2012)

datasets.name: facebook_wall
datasets.description:
Wall posts and friendship links among users of the New Orleans regional network of Facebook, collected by B. Viswanath, A. Mislove, M. Cha and K. P. Gummadi. The authors joined the regional network with several accounts, crawled its friendship graph in a breadth-first fashion between 29 December 2008 and 3 January 2009, starting from a single user, and then downloaded, between 20 and 22 January 2009, the entire wall history of the users found, as far as their profiles were visible to the members of the regional network (the default privacy setting). On Facebook, a user's friends can post messages on the user's wall, which are visible to the visitors of the user's profile. Only users in the giant connected component of the regional network could be crawled. The user IDs were anonymized, but are the same in both networks of the collection:

- `wall`: the wall posts. Nodes are users and a directed edge $(i,j)$ indicates that user $i$ posted on the wall of user $j$. Each wall post is a separate edge, so a pair of users can be connected by multiple edges, and posts by users on their own walls appear as self-loops. The posts span from September 2004 to January 2009.
- `friends`: the friendship links. Nodes are users and a directed edge $(i,j)$ indicates that user $j$ appeared in the friend list of user $i$. Friendships are symmetric on Facebook, but the links are given as directed in the source data, with their own times of establishment; for most (94%) of the links, the reverse link is also present. The times, determined by the authors when possible, span from September 2006 to January 2009, and are unknown for 41% of the links.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `user_id`: the anonymized user ID in the source data.
- (Edge) `time` (edge): for `wall`, the time of the wall post; for `friends`, the time of the establishment of the link (-1 if unknown). In Unix time.
citations: B. Viswanath, A. Mislove, M. Cha, K. P. Gummadi, "On the evolution of user interaction in Facebook." Proceedings of the 2nd ACM Workshop on Online Social Networks (WOSN '09), 37-42 (2009)

datasets.name: faculty_hiring
datasets.description:
Three networks of faculty hiring among PhD-granting departments in the United States (and, for computer science, Canada), in Computer Science (`computer_science`), Business (`business`) and History (`history`). Each node is an institution, and each directed edge $(u, v)$ is a tenure-track or tenured faculty member who received their doctorate at $u$ and was employed as faculty at $v$ at the time of collection, so that multiple edges and self-loops (faculty hired by their own doctoral institution) are present. The data were collected and validated by hand by A. Clauset, S. Arbesman and D. B. Larremore from primary sources (mainly departmental web pages and faculty homepages), covering 205 computer science departments (May 2011 to March 2012), 112 business schools (March to December 2012) and 144 history departments (January to August 2013). Faculty who received their doctorate outside the sampled institutions (mainly from foreign universities) are assigned to an additional source node named "All others".

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `institution`: name of the institution.
- (Node) `pi`: the institution's prestige rank, inferred from the hiring network with a minimum violation ranking (lower values mean higher prestige).
- (Node) `USN2010` (computer science), `USN2012` (business), `USN2009` (history): the institution's U.S. News & World Report rank closest to the collection period.
- (Node) `NRC95` (computer science), `NRC2010` (history): the institution's National Research Council rank.
- (Node) `NRC--` (business): empty, since no such rank exists.
- (Node) `Region`: geographic region of the institution: a US Census region (`Northeast`, `Midwest`, `South`, `West`), `Canada`, or `Earth` for the "All others" node.
- (Node) Missing values are denoted by a period ".".
- (Edge) `rank`: the faculty member's rank at $v$: assistant (`Asst`), associate (`Assoc`) or full (`Full`) professor.
- (Edge) `gender`: the faculty member's gender, `M` or `F`.
citations: A. Clauset, S. Arbesman, and D. B. Larremore, "Systematic inequality and hierarchy in faculty hiring networks." Science Advances 1(1), e1400005 (2015).

datasets.name: faculty_hiring_us
datasets.description:
Networks of faculty hiring for all PhD-granting US universities over the decade 2011–2020. A directed edge (i,j) indicates that people who received their doctorate from institution i were tenure-track faculty at institution j during the time of collection (2011–2020). Faculty with doctorates from anywhere are included, so the doctoral institutions (sources) also include non-US institutions and institutions outside the ranking, which appear only as sources; the US PhD-granting institutions that the authors analyze are marked by the `ranked` node property. This dataset is divided into separate networks for all 107 fields, as well as aggregate networks for 8 domains, and an overall network for all of academia.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `id` and `name`: the id and name of the institution.
- (Node) `ranked`: whether the institution is one of the US PhD-granting institutions ranked by the authors in this network (restricting to these nodes gives the network analyzed in the paper).
- (Node) `non_attrition` and `attrition`: the number of faculty-years (2011–2019) in which faculty trained at the institution and employed in this network did not leave, or left, the sample (-1 where not available, i.e. for institutions that are not ranked).
- (Edge) `total`: the number of faculty at institution j with a doctorate from institution i.
- (Edge) `men` and `women`: the same count by gender (faculty whose gender could not be determined are counted only in `total`).
citations: Wapman, K.H., Zhang, S., Clauset, A., Larremore, D. B., "Quantifying hierarchy and dynamics in US faculty hiring and retention." Nature (2022).

datasets.name: fao_trade
datasets.description:
A multiplex network of the worldwide trade of food and agricultural products among countries in 2010, assembled by M. De Domenico and collaborators from data of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO). Nodes are countries (214), and each of the 364 layers corresponds to a specific product (e.g. "Cheese, whole cow milk", "Cigarettes", "Cotton lint"); a directed, weighted edge in layer $\ell$ represents an import/export relationship of that product between two countries. The direction convention (exporter to importer or the reverse) and the units of the weights are not documented by the source. The analysis in the cited paper used a subset of these layers.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name` and `nodeLabel`: name of the country.
- (Edge) `layer` (edges): the product (layer), numbered 1 to 364; the graph property `layer_key` maps these numbers to product names.
- (Edge) `weight` (edges): weight of the trade relationship, an integer (units not documented).
citations: M. De Domenico, V. Nicosia, A. Arenas and V. Latora, "Structural reducibility of multilayer networks". Nature Communications 6, 6864 (2015)

datasets.name: fediverse
datasets.description: An early snapshot of the federation network among web publishers using the ActivityPub protocol. Nodes are instances, and a directed edge exists if an instance follows another instance.

datasets.name: fics_games
datasets.description:
A network of the games of chess played on the Free Internet Chess Server (FICS) from January 1999 to the end of 2015, as extracted by M. Fire and C. Guestrin from the FICS Games Database for their study of the evolution of network stars. Each node is a player (an account of the server), and an edge connects two players for each game they played (a multigraph), with the time of the game. The data give each game twice, once in each direction, without the colors of the players; each game is included once, and the network is undirected (games of a player against itself, if any, are left out). The results, the ratings, the time controls and the moves of the games are not part of the data.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the account name of the player.
- (Node) `first_game`, `last_game`: the times of the first and last games of the player, in Unix time.
- (Edge) `time`: the time of the game, in Unix time (as given in the data, at the precision of minutes).
citations: M. Fire and C. Guestrin, "The rise and fall of network stars: Analyzing 2.5 million graphs to reveal how high-degree vertices emerge over time." Information Processing & Management 57(2), 102041 (2020)

datasets.name: fifa_committees
datasets.description:
Networks of co-membership in the standing committees of FIFA, the international governing body of association football, in 2006 and in 2015, reconstructed by Gemma Edwards (University of Manchester) from FIFA activity reports, as examples of "overt networks with covert elements". Nodes are committee members (vertex property `name`), and an edge connects two members who sat on the same standing committee, with the edge property `weight` giving the number of committees they shared. The networks are one-mode projections of person-committee memberships. Data distributed by the UCINET datasets collection (University of Manchester).[^ucinet]

[^ucinet]: Description obtained in part from the [UCINET datasets page](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/datasets/covert-networks/fifa).
citations: G. Edwards, "FIFA networks." UCINET datasets, University of Manchester (2015)

datasets.name: flavor_network
datasets.description:
Bipartite networks of food ingredients, the flavor compounds they contain, and the recipes that use them, compiled by Ahn et al. to study the "food pairing" hypothesis, i.e. whether ingredients sharing flavor compounds are more likely to be combined in recipes.

- `compounds`: each food ingredient is connected to the flavor compounds it contains, as listed in Fenaroli's Handbook of Flavor Ingredients (5th edition). Five ingredients of the source list have no compounds and are not included. Note that, as stated in the upstream documentation, "farnesol" appears both as an ingredient and as a compound (as two distinct nodes).
- `recipes`: each recipe is connected to its ingredients. The recipes were collected from the websites allrecipes.com and epicurious.com (in English) and menupan.com (in Korean), and the ingredient names were mapped onto the ingredient list of the `compounds` network; each recipe is labeled by the cuisine given by the website, and by the broader geographic region it was assigned to (the paper's analysis uses the 56,498 recipes with an assigned region).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name` (ingredients): the ingredient name.
- (Node) `category` (ingredients): the ingredient category (e.g. "fruit", "plant derivative", "dairy").
- (Node) `is_compound` (`compounds`): whether the node is a flavor compound (otherwise an ingredient).
- (Node) `ingredient_id` (ingredients, `compounds`): the ingredient id in the source.
- (Node) `name` (compounds, `compounds`): the compound name.
- (Node) `cas` (compounds, `compounds`): its CAS registry number.
- (Node) `compound_id` (compounds, `compounds`): the compound id in the source.
- (Node) `is_recipe` (`recipes`): whether the node is a recipe (otherwise an ingredient).
- (Node) `source` (recipes, `recipes`): the website the recipe was collected from ("allrecipes", "epicurious" or "menupan").
- (Node) `cuisine` (recipes, `recipes`): the cuisine label of the recipe as given in the source (e.g. "Italian", "Korea", "Southern_SoulFood").
- (Node) `region` (recipes, `recipes`): the regional cuisine it was mapped to (one of NorthAmerican, LatinAmerican, SouthernEuropean, WesternEuropean, EasternEuropean, NorthernEuropean, MiddleEastern, African, SouthAsian, SoutheastAsian, EastAsian; empty for the 1,193 recipes labeled generically as "Asian", which were not assigned a region).
- (Node) `index` (recipes, `recipes`): the position of the recipe in its source file (starting from 0).
citations: Y.-Y. Ahn, S. E. Ahnert, J. P. Bagrow, A.-L. Barabási, "Flavor network and the principles of food pairing." Scientific Reports 1, 196 (2011)

datasets.name: flensburg_fjord
datasets.description:
A food web of the Flensburg Fjord, a brackish, shallow water inlet of the Baltic Sea between Germany and Denmark, which includes metazoan parasites and other infectious agents. The data on the free-living assemblages and on parasitism were gathered in field sampling, and supplemented with published sources and local expert knowledge. Nodes are the life cycle stages of species (or of coarser taxonomic or functional groups, such as phytoplankton, macroalgae, meiofauna, or some groups of birds, which are lumped into single nodes); each life cycle stage of a parasite with a complex life cycle (e.g. the cercariae, metacercariae, parthenitae and adults of trematodes) is a separate node. There are 180 nodes, corresponding to 123 species or assemblages. A directed edge goes from a consumer to a resource (prey or host). Besides predation, edges include parasitic interactions (macroparasitism, parasitic castration, pathogen infection, trophically transmitted parasitism), the consumption of the parasites of a prey by its predator (concomitant predation on symbionts), the trophic transmission of parasites to their next hosts, and predation among parasites within the same host. Each pair of nodes has at most one link type, and there are two self-loops. The data follow the format of R. F. Hechinger and colleagues for food webs with parasites; columns that are not filled in the source (e.g. body sizes, biomasses) are omitted. A version of this web aggregated by species (with the life stages of each parasite merged into a single node) is the network `flensburg` of the entry `coastal_parasite_webs`. The authors list some missing or under-represented groups: bird and fish ectoparasites, bacteria, free-living protists, parasitic protists, fungi and viruses were not, or only partially, sampled.

Node properties:
- `name`: working name of the node (common or scientific name, or a descriptive name).
- `species_id`: species identifier, shared by the nodes corresponding to the different life cycle stages of the same species.
- `stage_id`: life cycle stage within the species, where 1 is the adult, and higher numbers are younger stages (the meaning of the numbers depends on the group).
- `stage`: name of the life cycle stage (e.g. "Adult", "Cercariae", "Metacercariae", "Parthinitae", "Larvae").
- `organismal_group`: broad group of organisms (e.g. "Trematode", "Fish", "Bird", "Amphipod").
- `node_type`: the level at which the node is built ("Taxon", "Lifecycle Stage", "Common Name Group", "Detritus/Stock").
- `resolution`: the lowest taxonomic level that the node represents (e.g. "Species", "Family", "Assemblage"); `resolution_notes`: notes on the resolution.
- `feeding`: whether the node is "Feeding", "Non-Feeding" or "Autotroph".
- `lifestyle_stage` and `lifestyle_species`: whether the life cycle stage, or the species as a whole, is "Freeliving" or "Infectious".
- `consumer_strategy`: consumer strategy of the life cycle stage (e.g. "predator", "macroparasite", "trophically transmitted parasite", "parasitic castrator", "pathogen", "detritivore", "autotroph", "non-feeding").
- `mobility`: short-term mobility ("Low", "Intermediate" or "High", empty if not given); `residency`: long-term residency of free-living nodes ("resident" or "migrant", empty if not given).
- `kingdom`, `phylum`, `class`, `order`, `family`, `genus`, `specific_epithet`: taxonomy (empty if not given).
- `notes`: notes on the node.

Edge properties:
- `link_type`: type of the interaction, one of "Predation", "Concomitant Predation on Symbionts", "Macroparasitism", "Trophic Transmission", "Trophically Transmitted Parasitism", "Predation on free-living non-feeding stages", "Detritivory", "Parasite intraguild trophic interaction", "Parasitic Castration", "Pathogen Infection" and "Micropredation" (see the metadata of the source for definitions).
- `link_type_id`: the corresponding numeric code used by the source.
citations: C. D. Zander, N. Josten, K. C. Detloff, R. Poulin, J. P. McLaughlin, D. W. Thieltges, "Food web including metazoan parasites for a brackish shallow water ecosystem in Germany and Denmark." Ecology 92(10), 2007 (2011)

datasets.name: flickr_aminer
datasets.description:
A snapshot of the social network of Flickr, a photo-sharing website where users can follow (add as contacts) other users. The network is part of a collection of several online social networks distributed by AMiner (Tsinghua University) for research on social network integration, i.e. on identifying the accounts of the same person across different services (Y. Zhang and J. Tang); judging from the references given with the data, parts of it originate from earlier studies on linking user accounts across services (D. Perito et al., 2011; T. Chen et al., 2012). The crawling procedure is not documented. According to the ICON index, the data were collected in early 2014. Nodes are users, identified by integer IDs, and include all users listed in the source data, 869 of which have no connections. In the source data each connected pair of users is listed only once, always with the smaller ID first, and the source does not document whether the relationship is directed; the edges are therefore stored as undirected. An edge connects two users that are linked as contacts.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the user ID in the source data.
- (Node) `username`: the user name.
citations: T. Chen, M. A. Kaafar, A. Friedman, and R. Boreli. "Is more always merrier?: a deep dive into online social footprints." In 2012 ACM workshop on Workshop on online social networks, pages 67–72, 2012.
D. Perito, C. Castelluccia, M. A. Kaafar, and P. Manils. "How unique and traceable are usernames? In Privacy Enhancing Technologies", pages 1–17. Springer, 2011

H. Kwak, C. Lee, H. Park, and S. Moon. "What is Twitter, a social network or a news media?" In WWW ’10: Proceedings of the 19th international conference on World wide web, pages 591–600, New York, NY, USA, 2010. ACM.
Yutao Zhang, Jie Tang, "Social Network Integration: Towards Constructing the Social Graph", arxiv:1311.2670

datasets.name: flickr_growth
datasets.description:
Growth of the network of contacts among users of the photo sharing site Flickr, collected by A. Mislove and collaborators. Flickr users can add other users as contacts, which does not require the consent of the latter. The authors crawled the network once per day with automated scripts, using the Flickr API and following forward links from the users already discovered, between 2 November and 3 December 2006 and between 3 February and 18 May 2007 (104 days in total), and recorded the day on which each link was first observed. Since Flickr does not provide the creation times of the links, the times have a resolution of one day, and links that existed when the crawl started have the date of the first crawl (2 November 2006). New users could only be discovered once they became connected to an already crawled user.

Nodes are users and a directed edge $(i,j)$ indicates that user $i$ added user $j$ as a contact. The network contains a single self-loop. The user IDs were anonymized.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `user_id`: the anonymized user ID in the source data.
- (Edge) `time`: the day on which the link was first observed, as the Unix time of 00:00 UTC of that day.
citations: A. Mislove, H. S. Koppula, K. P. Gummadi, P. Druschel, B. Bhattacharjee, "Growth of the Flickr social network." Proceedings of the 1st Workshop on Online Social Networks (WOSN '08), 25-30 (2008)

datasets.name: flickr_images
datasets.description:
A network of images on the photo-sharing website Flickr, constructed by McAuley and Leskovec to study image classification using social-network metadata. The images are those of four image-classification benchmarks whose images originate from Flickr (PASCAL VOC, ImageCLEF, MIR Flickr and NUS-WIDE), and two images are connected by an undirected edge if they share some metadata on Flickr: if they were taken at the same location, submitted to the same gallery, group or set, share common tags, or were taken by friends, among others. The type of shared metadata is not included (the source provides it separately, together with image features, as large additional files).

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `photo_id`: the Flickr identifier of the image.
citations: J. McAuley, J. Leskovec, "Image Labeling on a Network: Using Social-Network Metadata for Image Classification." Computer Vision - ECCV 2012, Lecture Notes in Computer Science 7575, 828-841 (2012)

datasets.name: flixster
datasets.description:
A friendship network among users of Flixster, a social movie website where users share movie ratings, discover new movies and meet others with similar movie taste, crawled in December 2010 by Javier Parra at Arizona State University and distributed by the Social Computing Data Repository (originally at Arizona State University, now at Syracuse University). Nodes are users (anonymized), and a directed edge $i \to j$ is a line of the source data stating that "user $i$ is friend with user $j$".

Some friendships are listed in both directions: of the 9,197,337 edges, 2,557,072 are reciprocated (1,278,536 mutual pairs) and 6,640,265 are listed in one direction only (7,918,801 distinct pairs of users in all). The edges are kept as they are listed. (The source documentation states 9,197,338 edges, counting a blank first line of the file.) The users' identifiers range up to 2,523,388, but only the 2,523,386 users of the node list occur in the data.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `user_id`: the identifier of the user in the source data.
citations: R. Zafarani, H. Liu, "Social Computing Data Repository at ASU." Arizona State University, School of Computing, Informatics and Decision Systems Engineering (2009)

datasets.name: florentine_families
datasets.description:
A multiplex network of marriage and business ties among 16 elite families of Renaissance Florence, from the historical data on the rise of the Medici (c. 1400-1434) compiled by J. F. Padgett and collaborators from archival sources. This is the widely used subset of 16 families selected by R. Breiger and P. Pattison from Padgett's larger data set; the version here is the one distributed by M. De Domenico. Nodes are families, and an undirected edge in the marriage layer connects two families linked by a marriage, while an edge in the business layer connects families with recorded financial ties, such as loans, credits and joint partnerships. The marriage layer has 20 edges and the business layer 15; the Pucci family has no ties in either layer.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name` and `nodeLabel`: the family name (abbreviated to at most nine letters, e.g. `ACCIAIUOL`, `TORNABUON`).
- (Edge) `layer` (edges): 1 for marriage alliances, 2 for business ties; the graph property `layer_key` maps these numbers to layer names.
- (Edge) `weight` (edges): always 1.
citations: JF Padgett and CK Ansell, "Robust Action and the Rise of the Medici, 1400-1434". American journal of sociology, 1259-1319 (1993).

datasets.name: fly_banc
datasets.description:
The connectome of the entire central nervous system of an adult female fruit fly *Drosophila melanogaster*, the brain together with the ventral nerve cord (VNC, the fly's analog of the spinal cord), from the "Brain And Nerve Cord" (BANC) data set. It was reconstructed by Bates, Phelps, Kim, Yang and collaborators from serial-section transmission electron microscopy images, with automated segmentation and synapse detection followed by extensive manual proofreading. Nodes are neurons, and a directed edge $(i, j)$ indicates chemical synapses from neuron $i$ (presynaptic) to neuron $j$ (postsynaptic). This is materialization v888 of the data set, as released by the authors with the published paper.

The connections were detected with two synapse detection models, both included here: the "v3" model (synapses of at least 10 voxels), which the authors recommend for new work, and the earlier "v2" model (synapses of at least 5 voxels), which the analyses of the paper use and which finds about 14% fewer connected pairs. Autapses (synapses of a neuron onto itself) were excluded by the authors from all tables except the v2 neuron-to-neuron table of the current release, which contains them (as self-loops, 140,032 in `v2_all`) although its documentation says otherwise; they are kept as given. Following the authors (and the convention of FlyWire Codex), pairs of neurons are considered connected if they have at least five synapses. The networks of the current release (Harvard Dataverse version 3.0, July 2026) are:

- `v3_min5`, `v2_min5`: only the pairs of neurons with at least five synapses: these are 1,861,418 of the 12,923,260 connected pairs (23.1 million of 40.7 million synapses) with the v3 model, and 1,562,742 of the 11,176,571 connected pairs (19.3 million of 34.4 million synapses) with the v2 model.
- `v3_all`, `v2_all`: all connections, without threshold on the number of synapses.
- `v3_split`, `v2_split`: all connections, split according to the compartments of the two neurons where the synapses are located (the axon, the dendrite, the primary dendrite, the primary neurite, or unknown, from the authors' split of each neuron by flow centrality), so that the same pair of neurons may be connected by several parallel edges, one per pair of compartments. For neurons truncated at the boundary of the volume, the authors set the compartment on the side facing the nervous system (axon for afferent neurons, dendrite for efferent ones).

All these networks have the same nodes: the 150,802 segments marked as proofread, leaving out those classified as glia, trachea or not a neuron (neurons without connections are isolated nodes).

The earlier versions of the Dataverse dataset, all of the same materialization v888, are included as the networks with the prefixes `dv2_` (versions 2.0 and 2.1, June 2026, which share their files) and `dv1_` (version 1.0, May 2026), with the same six networks each. Their neuron annotations differ from those of the current release (e.g. 74 neurons were not yet marked as proofread, so that they have 150,728 nodes, and versions 2.0 and 2.1 lack the side of most neurons); their connection tables are the same as those of the current release, except for version 1.0, whose v2 tables were later replaced: its `dv1_v2_all` has no autapses, and its compartment table `dv1_v2_split` contains only 15.9 million synapses, about half of those of the other v2 tables.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `banc_id`: the neuron's identifier (root ID) in materialization v888 of the BANC data set.
- (Node) `side`: the side of the body of the neuron (`left`, `right`).
- (Node) `region`: the part of the nervous system where the neuron is (`central_brain`, `optic_lobe`, `ventral_nerve_cord`); empty if not assigned.
- (Node) `flow`: whether the neuron is `intrinsic`, `afferent` or `efferent`; empty if not assigned.
- (Node) `super_class`, `cell_class`, `cell_sub_class`, `cell_type`: the four levels of the authors' cell type hierarchy (e.g. `central_brain_intrinsic`, `antennal_lobe_projection_neuron`, `multiglomerular_projection_neuron`, `M_lvPNm40`); empty if not assigned.
- (Node) `fafb_cell_type`: the matched cell type in the FlyWire (FAFB) brain connectome (see the `flywire` entry); empty if not assigned.
- (Node) `hemilineage`: the developmental hemilineage of the neuron; empty if not assigned.
- (Node) `nerve`: the nerve through which the neuron enters or exits the nervous system; empty if not assigned.
- (Node) `neuromere`: the developmental neuromere (segment) of the neuron, for neurons of the ventral nerve cord; empty if not assigned.
- (Node) `neurotransmitter`: the neurotransmitter predicted for the neuron from its synapses; empty if not assigned.
- (Node) `neurotransmitter_score`: the confidence of the prediction (NaN if not assigned).
- (Node) `sexually_dimorphic`: whether the neuron's type is `isomorphic`, `dimorphic` or `female-specific`, from comparison with male connectomes; empty if not assigned.
- (Edge) `weight`: the number of synapses from $i$ to $j$ (in the given compartments, in the `*_split` networks).
- (Edge) `pre_compartment`, `post_compartment` (only in the `*_split` networks): the compartments of neurons $i$ and $j$ where the synapses are located (`axon`, `dendrite`, `primary.dendrite`, `primary.neurite`, `unknown`).
- (Edge) `neurotransmitter`, `neurotransmitter_score` (only in the `*_split` networks): the neurotransmitter predicted for the presynaptic neuron $i$ in the compartment table, and the confidence of the prediction.
citations: A. S. Bates, J. S. Phelps, M. Kim, H. H. Yang et al., "Distributed control circuits across a brain-and-cord connectome." Nature 656, 957-970 (2026)

datasets.name: fly_hemibrain
datasets.description:
The connectome of a large part of the central brain (the "hemibrain") of an adult female fruit fly *Drosophila melanogaster*, reconstructed by the FlyEM project at the Janelia Research Campus from focused ion beam scanning electron microscopy (FIB-SEM) images, with automated segmentation followed by extensive manual proofreading. Nodes are neurons, and a directed edge $(i, j)$ indicates chemical synapses from neuron $i$ (presynaptic) to neuron $j$ (postsynaptic) within a given brain region. This is version v1.2 of the data set, as exported from neuPrint, and includes only the "traced" neurons that are not cropped by the boundaries of the imaged volume.

Connections between a pair of neurons are split according to the primary region of interest (ROI, i.e. brain region) where the synapses reside, so that the same pair of neurons may be connected by several parallel edges, one per ROI. Synapses that lie outside any primary ROI are not included.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `bodyId`: the neuron's identifier in the hemibrain data set (neuPrint body ID).
- (Node) `type`: the cell type of the neuron (e.g. `CL141`, `FS4C`); empty if not assigned.
- (Node) `instance`: the neuron's instance name, typically the cell type followed by additional qualifiers and the brain side (e.g. `FS4C(FQ12)_C4_R`).
- (Edge) `roi` (edges): the primary brain region in which the synapses of the connection are located (e.g. `SLP(R)`).
- (Edge) `weight` (edges): the number of synapses from $i$ to $j$ in that region.
citations: L. K. Scheffer et al., "A connectome and analysis of the adult Drosophila central brain." eLife 9, e57443 (2020)

datasets.name: fly_larva
datasets.description: A complete synaptic map of the brain connectome of the larva of the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster. Nodes are neurons, and edges are synaptic connections, traced individually from brain image sections using three-dimensional electron microscopy–based reconstruction. A directed edge points from the presynaptic to the postsynaptic neuron (from the rows to the columns of the published connectivity matrices), with a separate edge for each type of connection between the pair, according to the presynaptic and postsynaptic compartments (`'ad'`: axo-dendritic, `'aa'`: axo-axonic, `'dd'`: dendro-dendritic, `'da'`: dendro-axonic), so that a pair of neurons can be connected by several parallel edges; each edge is weighted by its number of synapses. Node metadata include the neuron hemisphere, hemispherical homologue, cell type, annotations, and inferred cluster. Edge metadata include the type of interaction (`'aa'`, `'ad'`, `'da'`, `'dd'`), and synapse count.
citations: M. Winding et al., "The connectome of an insect brain", Science 379 eadd9330 (2023)

datasets.name: fly_manc
datasets.description:
The connectome of the ventral nerve cord (VNC, the fly's analog of the spinal cord) of an adult male fruit fly *Drosophila melanogaster*, the "Male Adult Nerve Cord" (MANC) data set, reconstructed by the FlyEM project at the Janelia Research Campus and collaborators from focused ion beam scanning electron microscopy (FIB-SEM) images, with automated segmentation and synapse detection followed by extensive manual proofreading, and annotated systematically by the Cambridge Drosophila Connectomics Group. Nodes are neurons, and a directed edge $(i, j)$ indicates chemical synapses from neuron $i$ (presynaptic) to neuron $j$ (postsynaptic). This is release v1.0 (June 2023) of the data set, as exported by the authors from neuPrint: the 23,188 neurons with status "Traced" (the proofread neurons) and the connections between them.

There are three networks of v1.0:

- `traced_min5`: only the pairs of neurons with at least five synapses are considered connected, since weak connections are unreliable, and for consistency with the `flywire`, `fly_banc` and `fly_male_cns` entries. These are 1,360,021 of the 5,243,574 connected pairs, carrying 24.0 million of their 30.7 million synapses.
- `traced_all`: all connections, without threshold on the number of synapses.
- `traced_roi`: all connections, split according to the primary region of interest (ROI, i.e. neuropil or nerve) where the synapses reside, so that the same pair of neurons may be connected by several parallel edges, one per ROI; synapses outside the primary ROIs have the ROI `NotPrimary`.

All networks of v1.0 have the same nodes, so that neurons without connections (with at least five synapses, in `traced_min5`) are isolated nodes. Self-loops are synapses of a neuron onto itself (autapses).

The entry also contains two networks of the later release v1.2 of the data set, which is not available as a connection table, but as a table of the individual synaptic connections ("synapse partners": 87 million pairs of a presynaptic T-bar and a postsynaptic density) with the confidence of the automated detection of each side (a value between 0 and 1). They are aggregated here into one weighted edge per pair of neurons:

- `v1.2_minconf0`: all the synaptic connections of the table. Despite its name ("minconf-0.0"), the table only contains presynaptic T-bars with a confidence of at least 0.75 and postsynaptic densities with a confidence of at least 0.2; this corresponds to the "high recall" weights (`weightHR`) of neuPrint.
- `v1.2`: only the synaptic connections whose postsynaptic density has a confidence of at least 0.4, the threshold that neuPrint uses for its default connection weights (`postHighAccuracyThreshold` in the metadata of the MANC database). The connection tables of v1.0 above have these default weights: for instance, the 136 synaptic connections of the table from neuron 10000 to neuron 14882 are 122 with this threshold, the weight of the pair in v1.0. (neuPrint also has "high precision" weights, `weightHP`, with confidences of at least 0.7 for both sides, which are not included.)

Their nodes are the 27,046 segments that have annotations in the neuroglancer segment properties of v1.2 published with the table (neurons, including sensory and motor neurons, and a few hundred glia; v1.2 has no export of the neuPrint neuron table with statuses as v1.0 has), and their edges are the synapses between them; the synaptic connections with the other segments (51 million of the 87 million) are left out. The v1.2 annotations are less detailed than those of v1.0, and are encoded as tags in neuroglancer (with underscores instead of spaces, e.g. `descending_neuron`). The later annotation releases v1.2.1 and v1.2.3 (in neuPrint) are not included.

The networks of v1.0 have the following properties:

- (Node) `body_id`: the neuron's identifier in the data set (neuPrint body ID).
- (Node) `type`, `systematic_type`: the cell type of the neuron (e.g. `DNp01`), and its systematic name (e.g. `DNlt002`); empty if not assigned.
- (Node) `instance`: the neuron's instance name, typically the cell type followed by the side or segment (e.g. `IN13B025_T2_L`).
- (Node) `class`, `subclass`: coarser classifications of the neuron (e.g. `descending neuron`, `intrinsic neuron`); empty if not assigned.
- (Node) `status_label`: the proofreading status of the neuron (e.g. `Roughly traced`).
- (Node) `soma_side`, `root_side`: the side of the neuron's soma, or for neurons without soma in the volume, of the place where they enter it (`LHS`, `RHS`, `Midline`, ...); empty if not assigned.
- (Node) `soma_neuromere`: the neuromere (segment) of the neuron's soma (e.g. `T1`, `A2`); empty if not assigned.
- (Node) `hemilineage`: the developmental hemilineage of the neuron; empty if not assigned.
- (Node) `birthtime`: the developmental birth time of the neuron (`primary`, `early secondary`, `secondary`); empty if not assigned.
- (Node) `entry_nerve`, `exit_nerve`: the nerve through which the neuron enters or exits the nerve cord; empty or `None` if none.
- (Node) `origin`, `target`: the region where the neuron's inputs come from and where its outputs go (e.g. `brain`, `LegNpT1_R`); empty if not assigned.
- (Node) `long_tract`: the longitudinal tract of the neuron; empty if not assigned.
- (Node) `serial_motif`: the type of the neuron's serial (segmentally repeated) homology; empty if not assigned.
- (Node) `modality`, `receptor_type`: the sensory modality and receptor type of sensory neurons; empty if not assigned.
- (Node) `transmission`: annotations of electrical or neurosecretory transmission; empty if none.
- (Node) `group`, `serial`: the identifiers of the neuron's group of left-right homologs and of its set of serial homologs (-1 if none).
- (Node) `predicted_nt`, `predicted_nt_prob`: the neurotransmitter predicted from the neuron's synapses, and its probability (empty and NaN if not available).
- (Node) `pre`, `post`: the numbers of presynaptic sites and of postsynaptic densities of the neuron.
- (Edge) `weight` (edges): the number of synapses from $i$ to $j$ (in the given ROI, in `traced_roi`).
- (Edge) `roi` (edges, `traced_roi` only): the primary ROI where the synapses are located.

The networks of v1.2 have the following properties:

- (Node) `body_id`: the neuron's identifier (segment ID of v1.2).
- (Node) `type`: the cell type of the neuron; empty if not assigned.
- (Node) `class`, `subclass`, `hemilineage`, `birthtime`, `soma_side`, `soma_neuromere`, `entry_nerve`, `exit_nerve`, `origin`, `target`, `long_tract`, `serial_motif`, `modality`: as above, from the tags of the segment properties; empty if not assigned.
- (Node) `pre`, `post`: the numbers of presynaptic sites and of postsynaptic densities of the neuron, as given by the segment properties (all those of the synapse table, including the ones with any partner, without the threshold of `v1.2`).
- (Edge) `weight` (edges): the number of synaptic connections from $i$ to $j$ (of the given confidence).
- (Edge) `mean_conf_pre`, `mean_conf_post` (edges): the mean detection confidence of their presynaptic T-bars and of their postsynaptic densities.
citations: S. Takemura et al., "A connectome of the male Drosophila ventral nerve cord." eLife 13, RP97769 (2024)
E. C. Marin et al., "Systematic annotation of a complete adult male Drosophila nerve cord connectome reveals principles of functional organisation." eLife 13, RP97766 (2024)

datasets.name: fly_medulla
datasets.description:
Directed network of synaptic connections between neurons in the optic medulla of the fruit fly *Drosophila melanogaster*, reconstructed by Takemura et al. from serial-section transmission electron microscopy of a volume spanning seven medulla columns. Neuron segments were traced semi-automatically and proofread by human annotators. Each edge is one synaptic contact, from the presynaptic to the postsynaptic body, so that a pair of bodies connected by several synapses is joined by parallel edges (33,641 synapses between 1,781 bodies). The bodies include identified neurons (named by cell type) and unidentified "orphan" fragments that could not be traced to a cell.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the cell-type label followed by the body identifier (e.g. "Mi1 ..."), or the body identifier alone for unnamed bodies.
- (Edge) `pre_x`, `pre_y`, `pre_z` and `post_x`, `post_y`, `post_z`: the voxel coordinates of the presynaptic and postsynaptic sites in the image volume.
- (Edge) `proofreading`: the proofreading status of the synapse (e.g. whether the partners reached named or "anchor" bodies, or are both orphans).

The data were obtained from the graph collection of the Open Connectome Project (now NeuroData), whose servers are offline, via the Internet Archive.
citations: S. Takemura et al., "A visual motion detection circuit suggested by Drosophila connectomics." Nature 500, 175-181 (2013)

datasets.name: fly_optic_lobe
datasets.description:
The connectome of the right optic lobe (the visual system) of an adult male fruit fly *Drosophila melanogaster*, together with the parts of the central brain that it connects to, reconstructed by the FlyEM project at the Janelia Research Campus and collaborators from focused ion beam scanning electron microscopy (FIB-SEM) images, with automated segmentation and synapse detection followed by extensive manual proofreading. The authors identified over 700 cell types among the roughly 53,000 neurons of the optic lobe. Nodes are neurons (segments of the reconstruction), and a directed edge $(i, j)$ indicates chemical synapses from neuron $i$ (presynaptic) to neuron $j$ (postsynaptic). The data come from the two releases of the data set that the authors exported as flat files, v1.1 (September 2024, with further proofreading and refined annotations) and v1.0.1 (August 2024).

Only synapses detected with a confidence of at least 0.5 are included, as in the authors' published data. There are six networks, named `<release>_<nodes>_<threshold>`:

- `*_primary_min5`, `*_primary_all`: the networks between the proofread bodies, from the authors' "primary-only" connection table. Its nodes are the bodies (53,735 in v1.1, 53,420 in v1.0.1) with the proofreading status "Roughly traced", "Prelim Roughly traced", "Leaves", "PRT Orphan" (together the "Traced" neurons of neuPrint) or "Primary Anchor" (large segments that were not fully traced); the upstream documentation does not describe this table, this is what it contains. In `*_min5` only the pairs of neurons with at least five synapses are considered connected, since weak connections are unreliable, and for consistency with the `flywire`, `fly_banc` and `fly_male_cns` entries; in `*_all` all connections are included. In `v1_1_primary_min5`, these are 1,555,385 of the 6,497,418 connected pairs, carrying 17.6 million of their 26.6 million synapses.
- `*_segments_all`: all 10.3 million segments of the reconstruction, most of them small fragments that could not be attached to a neuron, with all their connections (22.3 million connected pairs and 49.5 million synapses). The table also contains a few connections with the unsegmented background (body 0; 198 pairs with 207 synapses), which are left out. To keep these networks manageable, their nodes only have the properties `body_id`, `status_label`, `type`, `instance`, `class`, `pre` and `post`.

All networks of a release and node set have the same nodes, so that neurons without connections (with at least five synapses, in `*_min5`) are isolated nodes. Self-loops are synapses of a neuron onto itself (autapses). The annotations and neurotransmitter predictions are those of the corresponding release, from its neuPrint tables.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `body_id`: the neuron's identifier in the data set (neuPrint body ID).
- (Node) `status_label`: the proofreading status of the body (e.g. `Roughly traced`, `Primary Anchor`; empty for unproofread fragments).
- (Node) `type`: the cell type of the neuron (e.g. `Mi1`, `T4a`); empty if not assigned.
- (Node) `instance`: the neuron's instance name, typically the cell type followed by the side (e.g. `Mi1_R`).
- (Node) `class`: the coarse class of the neuron (e.g. `optic`, `visual_projection`, `visual_centrifugal`, `sensory`); empty if not assigned.
- (Node) `flywire_type`: the matched cell type in the female brain connectome FlyWire (see the `flywire` entry); empty if not assigned (always empty in v1.0.1, which has no such annotations).
- (Node) `hemilineage`: the developmental hemilineage of the neuron; empty if not assigned (always empty in v1.0.1).
- (Node) `neurotransmitter`: the consensus neurotransmitter of the neuron's cell type, from the predictions and the literature (`unclear` if ambiguous); empty if not available.
- (Node) `predicted_nt`, `predicted_nt_confidence`: the neurotransmitter predicted from the neuron's own synapses, and the confidence of that prediction (empty and NaN if not available).
- (Node) `hex1`, `hex2`: the coordinates of the column of the medulla's hexagonal grid (i.e. the point of the visual field) assigned to the neuron, for the columnar cell types (-1 if not assigned).
- (Node) `soma_x`, `soma_y`, `soma_z`: the position of the neuron's soma in the volume, in voxels of 8 nm (NaN if not known).
- (Node) `pre`, `post`: the numbers of presynaptic sites and of postsynaptic densities of the neuron.
- (Edge) `weight` (edges): the number of synapses from $i$ to $j$.
citations: A. Nern et al., "Connectome-driven neural inventory of a complete visual system." Nature 641, 1225-1237 (2025)

datasets.name: flying_teams
datasets.description:
Sociometric choices among 48 cadet pilots at a US Army Air Forces flying school in 1943, collected by L. D. Zeleny. The cadets were trained to fly a two-seated aircraft, taking turns in flying and aerial observing, and had been assigned at random to eight instruction groups of 5 to 7 members. Zeleny asked each cadet to name the members of his flight group with whom he would like to fly, as well as those with whom he would not like to fly, in order to improve the composition of the instruction groups. A directed edge points from the cadet making the choice to the chosen one, and is positive or negative. One edge appears twice in the source. The data were distributed on the Pajek datasets page of the book *Exploratory Social Network Analysis with Pajek* (de Nooy, Mrvar and Batagelj), from which this version was obtained.[^icon]

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the identifier of the cadet.
- (Node) `group`: the original (alphabetical) instruction group of the cadet (1 to 8).
- (Edge) `sign`: 1 if the chosen cadet qualifies as a flying partner, -1 otherwise.

[^icon]: Description obtained in part from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.
citations: L. D. Zeleny, "Adaptation of research findings in social leadership to college classroom procedures." In J. L. Moreno et al. (eds.), The Sociometry Reader, The Free Press, Glencoe, Illinois (1960), pp. 534-547
W. de Nooy, A. Mrvar, V. Batagelj, "Exploratory Social Network Analysis with Pajek." Cambridge University Press (2005)

datasets.name: flywire
datasets.description:
The connectome of the entire brain of an adult female fruit fly *Drosophila melanogaster*, reconstructed by the FlyWire Consortium from the serial-section transmission electron microscopy volume "Full Adult Fly Brain" (FAFB), with automated segmentation and synapse detection followed by extensive manual proofreading by a community of researchers and citizen scientists. This is the public release v783 of the data set. Nodes are the 139,255 proofread neurons, and a directed edge $(i, j)$ indicates chemical synapses from neuron $i$ (presynaptic) to neuron $j$ (postsynaptic) within a given brain region (neuropil).

Synapses were detected automatically, and only those with a cleft score of at least 50 are included, as in the authors' analyses. As in the `fly_hemibrain` entry, the connections between a pair of neurons are split according to the neuropil where the synapses reside, so that the same pair of neurons may be connected by several parallel edges, one per neuropil. There are three networks:

- `min5`: following the authors, who consider a pair of neurons to be connected if there are at least five synapses between them (which makes false-positive connections very unlikely), only the pairs of neurons with at least five synapses in total (summed over all neuropils) are included: these are 2,700,513 of the 15,091,983 connected pairs, carrying 34.2 million of the 54.5 million synapses between proofread neurons (the weight of an individual edge, in one neuropil, may be smaller than five).
- `all`: all connections, without threshold on the number of synapses.
- `synapses_all`: the same as `all`, but aggregated here from the table of all the individual synapses released with the data (130,054,535 synapses, with their positions, cleft scores and neurotransmitter predictions), instead of the table of connections between proofread neurons. This table is not unthresholded: the synapses with a cleft score below the threshold were not released (all the scores in the table are above 50), so that it contains the same synapses, and the network differs from `all` only in details. Of these synapses, the 54,492,970 between two proofread neurons are included, while the 75,561,565 that involve at least one segment that is not a proofread neuron (e.g. fragments that could not be attached to a neuron) are left out. The network has 16,848,018 edges, 21 more than `all` (in `ME_R`, with 48 synapses in total), which are missing from the table of connections. The synapses without a neuropil (marked `None` in the table) are assigned to `UNASGD`, as in the other networks. The neurotransmitter probabilities are the averages of the predictions for the individual synapses; they differ from those of the other networks for the outgoing connections of the Kenyon cells (whose predictions are mostly dopamine), for which the table of connections gives an acetylcholine probability of one. The predictions are missing for 5,347 synapses, which are left out of the averages (they are NaN for the 370 edges where they are missing for all the synapses). The edges also carry the averages of the cleft and connection scores of the synapses; the positions of the individual synapses are not included.

The neuron annotations are those published with the paper of Schlegel et al. (Supplementary Data 1), with cell types matched to the hemibrain and new ones; all networks have the same nodes, so that in `min5` the neurons that make no connection with at least five synapses are isolated nodes.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `root_id`: the neuron's identifier in the FlyWire data set (root ID of the v783 release).
- (Node) `flow`: whether the neuron is `intrinsic` to the brain, `afferent` or `efferent`.
- (Node) `super_class`: the coarsest neuron classification (e.g. `central`, `optic`, `sensory`, `visual_projection`, `ascending`, `descending`, `motor`, `endocrine`).
- (Node) `cell_class`, `cell_sub_class`: finer neuron classes (e.g. `Kenyon_Cell`, `ME>LO`); empty if not assigned.
- (Node) `cell_type`: the cell type of the neuron, either new or a refinement of a hemibrain type; empty if not assigned.
- (Node) `hemibrain_type`: the hemibrain cell type(s) matched to the neuron (see the `fly_hemibrain` entry); empty if not assigned.
- (Node) `hemilineage`: the developmental hemilineage of the neuron (Ito-Lee nomenclature); empty if not assigned.
- (Node) `side`: the side of the brain where the neuron's soma (or, for sensory neurons, its entry point) is located (`left`, `right`, `center`).
- (Node) `nerve`: the nerve through which the neuron enters or exits the brain, for afferent and efferent neurons; empty otherwise.
- (Node) `top_nt`: the neurotransmitter predicted for the neuron from its synapses (`acetylcholine`, `glutamate`, `gaba`, `dopamine`, `serotonin`, `octopamine`); empty if not assigned.
- (Node) `top_nt_conf`: the confidence of the neurotransmitter prediction (NaN if not assigned).
- (Edge) `neuropil` (edges): the neuropil in which the synapses of the connection are located (e.g. `ME_L` for the medulla of the left hemisphere; `UNASGD` if unassigned).
- (Edge) `weight` (edges): the number of synapses from $i$ to $j$ in that neuropil.
- (Edge) `gaba`, `ach`, `glut`, `oct`, `ser`, `da` (edges): the probabilities that the synapses of the connection release GABA, acetylcholine, glutamate, octopamine, serotonin or dopamine, predicted from the electron microscopy images and averaged over the synapses.
- (Edge) `cleft_score`, `connection_score` (edges, `synapses_all` only): the cleft score (from the synaptic cleft segmentation of Heinrich et al., used for the threshold) and the connection score (from the synaptic partner detection of Buhmann et al.) of the synapses, averaged over the synapses; higher is better.
citations: S. Dorkenwald et al., "Neuronal wiring diagram of an adult brain." Nature 634, 124-138 (2024)
P. Schlegel et al., "Whole-brain annotation and multi-connectome cell typing of Drosophila." Nature 634, 139-152 (2024)
J. Buhmann et al., "Automatic detection of synaptic partners in a whole-brain Drosophila electron microscopy data set." Nature Methods 18, 771-774 (2021)

L. Heinrich, J. Funke, C. Pape, J. Nunez-Iglesias, S. Saalfeld, "Synaptic cleft segmentation in non-isotropic volume electron microscopy of the complete Drosophila brain." Medical Image Computing and Computer Assisted Intervention (MICCAI 2018), 317-325 (2018)
N. Eckstein et al., "Neurotransmitter classification from electron microscopy images at synaptic sites in Drosophila melanogaster." Cell 187, 2574-2594 (2024)

datasets.name: foldoc
datasets.description:
A network of cross-references among the terms of the Free On-line Dictionary of Computing (FOLDOC), a searchable dictionary of acronyms, jargon, programming languages, tools, architecture, operating systems, networking, theory, standards, companies, products and history, and in fact anything to do with computing, edited by Denis Howe since 1985 with contributions from hundreds of people. The network was extracted from the dictionary and cleaned by Vladimir Batagelj and Andrej Mrvar in February/June 2002, and distributed in their Pajek data repository.

Nodes are dictionary terms, and a directed edge $(X, Y)$ exists if the term $Y$ is used in the dictionary to describe the meaning of the term $X$. The Pajek repository page describes a network with 13,380 nodes and 120,700 edges, while the distributed file contains 13,356 nodes and 120,238 edges.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the dictionary term.
- (Edge) `weight`: the multiplicity of the edge (as given in the source).
citations: V. Batagelj, A. Mrvar, M. Zaveršnik, "Network analysis of texts." Proceedings of the 5th International Multi-Conference Information Society - Language Technologies, 143-148, Ljubljana (2002)
D. Howe (Ed.), "FOLDOC: The Free On-line Dictionary of Computing" (2002)

datasets.name: foodweb_little_rock
datasets.description:
The food web of Little Rock Lake, Wisconsin (USA), a highly resolved food web first published by Martinez (1991), in which most taxa are resolved to the genus or species level. The data were obtained from the network collection of the Ma'ayan Laboratory (Mount Sinai School of Medicine), which distributed them in its SIG flat file format, with the taxa identified only by numbers (0 to 182). Taxon names and groups were assigned manually from the numbering of the taxa in the original publication.

Nodes are taxa (autotrophs, herbivores, carnivores and decomposers, as well as fine organic matter), and a directed edge points from a food source to its consumer. Taxon 0 has no counterpart in the publication's list of taxa: it has no incoming edges and points to all the algae and cyanobacteria, to fine organic matter, fish eggs and two insect taxa, so that it acts as a common source of the basal taxa; its meaning is not documented. Self-loops denote cannibalism.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `taxon`: the taxon number in the source file.
- (Node) `name`: the name of the taxon ("?" for taxon 0).
- (Node) `group`: the taxonomic or functional group of the taxon (its name, if it belongs to no group).
citations: N. D. Martinez, "Artifacts or attributes? Effects of resolution on the Little Rock Lake food web." Ecological Monographs 61(4), 367-392 (1991)

datasets.name: foodweb_ulanowicz
datasets.description:
Ecosystem networks of carbon flows (food webs) among the compartments of several aquatic and wetland ecosystems, selected from R. E. Ulanowicz's collection of ecosystem networks (Chesapeake Biological Laboratory, University of Maryland; version of July 22, 2002) and from the ATLSS project (Network Analysis of Trophic Dynamics in South Florida Ecosystems). The original data in SCOR format were converted into Pajek format by V. Batagelj (2003, 2004). Nodes are compartments: living compartments (taxa or groups of taxa), other non-living compartments (e.g. detritus and dissolved or particulate organic carbon), and three special nodes representing the inputs (imports and primary production sources), the outputs (exports) and respiration of the ecosystem. A directed edge points from a donor to a recipient compartment, and is weighted by the flow of carbon between them. The units are those of the original studies (typically milligrams or grams of carbon per square meter, per day or per year), and differ between networks. Some networks have self-loops (flows within a compartment, e.g. cannibalism). The data were distributed in Pajek format on the Pajek datasets page of V. Batagelj and A. Mrvar, from which this version was obtained. The general collection's "Florida" network is not included separately, since it is identical to the ATLSS Florida Bay wet season network (`baywet`).

- `chesapeake`: Chesapeake Bay mesohaline ecosystem, summer carbon flows (Baird and Ulanowicz, 1989).
- `ches_lower`: lower Chesapeake Bay in summer (Hagy, 2002).
- `ches_middle`: middle Chesapeake Bay in summer (Hagy, 2002).
- `ches_upper`: upper Chesapeake Bay in summer (Hagy, 2002).
- `crystal_control`: Crystal River Creek, Florida, control marsh (Homer and Kemp).
- `crystal_delta`: Crystal River Creek, Florida, marsh exposed to the thermal effluent of a power plant (Homer and Kemp).
- `everglades`: Everglades graminoid marshes (Ulanowicz et al., 2000), from the general collection.
- `maspalomas`: Charca de Maspalomas, a coastal lagoon in Gran Canaria (Almunia et al., 1999).
- `michigan`: Lake Michigan control network (Krause and Mason).
- `mondego`: Mondego Estuary, Zostera site, Portugal (Patrício).
- `narragansett`: Narragansett Bay model (Monaco and Ulanowicz, 1997).
- `rhode`: Rhode River watershed, water budget (Correll).
- `stmarks`: St. Marks River estuary, Florida (Baird, Luczkovich and Christian, 1998).
- `baydry`: Florida Bay, a shallow subtropical estuary in South Florida, dry season (Ulanowicz et al., 1998).
- `baywet`: Florida Bay, wet season (Ulanowicz et al., 1998).
- `cypdry`: cypress wetlands of South Florida, dry season (Ulanowicz et al., 1997).
- `cypwet`: cypress wetlands of South Florida, wet season (Ulanowicz et al., 1997).
- `gramdry`: Everglades graminoid marshes, dry season (Ulanowicz et al., 2000).
- `gramwet`: Everglades graminoid marshes, wet season (Ulanowicz et al., 2000).
- `mangdry`: mangrove estuary of South Florida, dry season (Ulanowicz et al., 1999).
- `mangwet`: mangrove estuary of South Florida, wet season (Ulanowicz et al., 1999).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the compartment.
- (Node) `type`: the type of compartment (1: living/producing compartment, 2: other compartment, 3: input, 4: output, 5: respiration).
- (Node) `biomass`: the biomass (standing stock) of the compartment (in the `maspalomas` and `rhode` networks, the source gives all biomasses as 1 or 0, i.e. they are not available).
- (Edge) `weight`: the flow of carbon from the donor to the recipient compartment.
citations: D. Baird, R. E. Ulanowicz, "The Seasonal Dynamics of The Chesapeake Bay Ecosystem." Ecological Monographs 59(4), 329-364 (1989)
J. D. Hagy, "Eutrophication, hypoxia and trophic transfer efficiency in Chesapeake Bay." PhD thesis, University of Maryland at College Park (2002)
J. Almunia, G. Basterretxea, J. Arístegui, R. E. Ulanowicz, "Benthic-Pelagic Switching in a Coastal Subtropical Lagoon." Estuarine, Coastal and Shelf Science 49(3), 363-384 (1999)
M. E. Monaco, R. E. Ulanowicz, "Comparative ecosystem trophic structure of three U.S. mid-Atlantic estuaries." Marine Ecology Progress Series 161, 239-254 (1997)

D. Baird, J. Luczkovich, R. R. Christian, "Assessment of Spatial and Temporal Variability in Ecosystem Attributes of the St Marks National Wildlife Refuge, Apalachee Bay, Florida." Estuarine, Coastal and Shelf Science 47(3), 329-349 (1998)

R. E. Ulanowicz, J. J. Heymans, M. S. Egnotovich, "Network Analysis of Trophic Dynamics in South Florida Ecosystems, FY 99: The Graminoid Ecosystem." Technical Report CBL 00-0176, Chesapeake Biological Laboratory (2000)

R. E. Ulanowicz, C. Bondavalli, M. S. Egnotovich, "Network Analysis of Trophic Dynamics in South Florida Ecosystem, FY 97: The Florida Bay Ecosystem." Technical Report CBL 98-123, Chesapeake Biological Laboratory (1998)

datasets.name: football
datasets.description:
A network of American football games between Division I-A colleges during the regular season of Fall 2000, compiled by M. Girvan and M. E. J. Newman. Nodes are college teams, and an undirected edge connects two teams that played each other in at least one game. Because teams play more often against teams in their own conference, the conferences form a well-known community structure, and the data are widely used as a benchmark for community detection. The original data contained duplicated edges (some pairs of teams met twice in the season, in the regular season and again in their conference final), which were removed both by T. S. Evans in his corrected version (three multiple edges) and later by the original authors (two edges, in 2014), so that both versions now have the same simple network.

As pointed out by T. S. Evans (J. Stat. Mech. P12037, 2010), the conference assignments of the original file correspond to the 2001 season rather than the 2000 season of the games, so that a few teams that changed conference between the two seasons are mislabeled (in 2000 there were 10 conferences and 8 independent teams, rather than the 11 conferences and 5 independents of 2001; e.g. the Big West conference existed for football until 2000, while the Sun Belt conference only started in 2001). Evans corrected the assignments for the 2000 season after checking the games against the College Football Data Warehouse; they differ from the original ones for 22 of the 115 teams. Both assignments are given as vertex properties.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `label`: the name of the team.
- (Node) `conference`: the original conference assignment of Girvan and Newman: 0 = Atlantic Coast, 1 = Big East, 2 = Big Ten, 3 = Big Twelve, 4 = Conference USA, 5 = Independents, 6 = Mid-American, 7 = Mountain West, 8 = Pacific Ten, 9 = Southeastern, 10 = Sun Belt, 11 = Western Athletic.
- (Node) `conference_evans`: the conference assignment corrected by T. S. Evans for the 2000 season: 0 = Atlantic Coast, 1 = Big East, 2 = Big Ten, 3 = Big Twelve, 4 = Conference USA, 5 = Big West, 6 = Mid-American, 7 = Mountain West, 8 = Pacific Ten, 9 = Southeastern, 10 = Western Athletic, and 11-18 for the independent teams Notre Dame, Navy, Connecticut, Central Florida, Middle Tennessee State, Louisiana Tech, Louisiana Monroe and Louisiana Lafayette, respectively (instead of grouping the independent teams, which belong to no conference, under a single label, each independent team has its own label).
citations: M. Girvan and M. E. J. Newman, "Community structure in social and biological networks." Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA 99(12), 7821-7826 (2002).
T.S. Evans, "Clique Graphs and Overlapping Communities", J. Stat. Mech. (2010) P12037

datasets.name: football_league_results
datasets.description:
Results of the games of the regular seasons of four national football (soccer) leagues, one network per season, from the results tables of the Wikipedia articles on the seasons:

- `be1_2016`: Belgian First Division A, season 2016/2017 (regular season, before the play-offs);
- `de1_2016`: German Bundesliga, season 2016/2017;
- `fr1_2016`: French Ligue 1, season 2016/2017;
- `uk1_2013`: English Premier League, season 2013/2014.

Each node is a team, and a directed edge from team A to team B is the game that A played at home against B, so that every team played every other team once at home and once away. The edges carry the scores, and are signed by the goal difference (positive if the home team won, negative if it lost, zero for a draw).

Two games have an annotation in the source, which is kept in the edge property `note`: in `be1_2016`, the game Charleroi–Standard Liège was stopped after 68 minutes because of crowd trouble, with Standard leading 3–1; the score was kept, but no points were awarded to either team. In `fr1_2016`, the game Bastia–Lyon was abandoned at half-time, with no score, when Bastia fans attacked the Lyon players, and was awarded 3–0 to Lyon, the score recorded here (as 0–3 for the home team).

The data are taken from pinned revisions of the Wikipedia articles "2016–17 Belgian First Division A", "2016–17 Bundesliga", "2016–17 Ligue 1" and "2013–14 Premier League". The `uk1_2013` season was analyzed by Fanuel and Suykens.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the team.
- (Node) `code`: the three-letter code of the team in the Wikipedia table.
- (Edge) `home_goals`, `away_goals`: the goals scored by the home and the away team.
- (Edge) `goal_difference`: the goals of the home team minus the goals of the away team.
- (Edge) `note`: an annotation of the game in the source (empty for most games).
citations: M. Fanuel, J. A. K. Suykens, "Deformed Laplacians and spectral ranking in directed networks." Applied and Computational Harmonic Analysis 47(2), 397-422 (2019)

datasets.name: foursquare
datasets.description:
Two bipartite networks of users and restaurant venues in New York City on the location-based social network Foursquare, collected by D. Yang and collaborators. Nodes are users and venues, and user and venue identifiers are anonymized but consistent across the two networks.

- `NYC_restaurant_checkin`: each edge is a check-in of a user at a restaurant, between 24 October 2011 and 20 February 2012; repeated check-ins of the same user at the same venue appear as parallel edges.
- `NYC_restaurant_tips`: each edge is a tip (a short text comment) left by a user on a restaurant. Tips were collected without time limit, so a user may have left a tip on a venue without checking in there during the check-in collection period.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `is_user`: whether the node is a user (True) or a venue (False).
- (Node) `name`: the anonymized user or venue ID.
- (Node) `tags`: for venues, the list of tags that users added to the venue (e.g. "cupcake", "trendy"); empty for users and for venues without tags.
- (Edge) `tip_text` (edges, `NYC_restaurant_tips` only): the text of the tip.
citations: D. Yang, et al. "Fine-grained preference-aware location search leveraging crowdsourced digital footprints from LBSNs." Proceedings of the 2013 ACM international joint conference on Pervasive and ubiquitous computing. ACM. (2013).

datasets.name: foursquare_global
datasets.description:
A global data set of check-ins and social ties of users of the location-based social network Foursquare, collected by D. Yang and collaborators. Since Foursquare check-ins are not publicly accessible, they were obtained from Foursquare-tagged tweets in Twitter's public stream between April 2012 and January 2014, keeping only active users (with at least one check-in per month). Since Foursquare friendships are not publicly available either, the social ties were obtained from Twitter: for each user, their Twitter followers and followees were crawled, and two users are connected if they follow each other. Users without social ties were removed, and only users appearing in both friendship snapshots were kept. The entry contains the following networks:

- `checkins`: a bipartite network of users and venues (points of interest), where each edge is a check-in of a user at a venue, worldwide. The network contains 22,809,624 check-ins by 114,324 users at 3,820,891 venues; repeated check-ins of a user at the same venue appear as parallel edges.
- `friendship_old`: an undirected social network among the users, from a snapshot taken before the check-in collection period (March 2012), with 363,704 friendships.
- `friendship_new`: the same, from a snapshot taken after the check-in collection period (May 2014), with 607,333 friendships.

The two friendship networks have the same node set. The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the anonymized user ID (an integer, the same in all three networks) or, in `checkins`, the Foursquare venue ID (a hexadecimal string).
- (Node) `is_user` (`checkins` only): whether the node is a user (True) or a venue (False).
- (Node) `latitude` and `longitude` (`checkins` only): coordinates of the venue, in degrees.
- (Node) `venue_cat` (`checkins` only): the Foursquare category of the venue (e.g. "Train Station").
- (Node) `country` (`checkins` only): the ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code of the country of the venue.
- (Edge) `timestamp` (edges, `checkins` only): the time of the check-in (UTC).
- (Edge) `timezone_offset` (edges, `checkins` only): the offset in minutes between the local time of the check-in and UTC (UTC time plus the offset gives the local time).
citations: D. Yang, B. Qu, J. Yang, and P. Cudré-Mauroux, "Revisiting User Mobility and Social Relationships in LBSNs: A Hypergraph Embedding Approach." The World Wide Web Conference (WWW '19), 2147-2157 (2019)

datasets.name: foursquare_nyc_tokyo
datasets.description:
Two bipartite networks of users and venues of the location-based social network Foursquare, from check-ins in New York City (`NYC`) and Tokyo (`TKY`) collected by D. Yang and collaborators between 12 April 2012 and 16 February 2013 (about ten months). Nodes are users and venues, and an undirected edge is a check-in of a user at a venue, annotated with its time and GPS coordinates; repeated check-ins of the same user at the same venue appear as parallel edges. The `NYC` network contains 227,428 check-ins and the `TKY` network 573,703 check-ins. The data were originally used to study the spatio-temporal regularity of user activities.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `is_user`: whether the node is a user (otherwise it is a venue).
- (Node) `name`: the anonymized user ID or the Foursquare venue ID.
- (Node) `category`, `category_id`: the name and Foursquare ID of the fine-grained venue category (e.g. "Bridge", "Home (private)"; empty for users). A few hundred venues have check-ins with different categories; for these, the category of their first check-in in the file is used.
- (Edge) `time`: the time of the check-in (Unix time, UTC).
- (Edge) `tz_offset`: the offset of the local time with respect to UTC, in minutes.
- (Edge) `latitude` and `longitude`: the GPS coordinates of the check-in (which may vary slightly between check-ins at the same venue).[^icon].

[^icon]: Description obtained in part from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.
citations: D. Yang, D. Zhang, V. W. Zheng, Z. Yu, "Modeling user activity preference by leveraging user spatial temporal characteristics in LBSNs." IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics: Systems 45(1), 129-142 (2015)

datasets.name: freebase_fb15k
datasets.description:
Two subsets of the Freebase knowledge base, widely used as benchmarks for knowledge graph completion (link prediction):

- `fb15k`: the FB15k dataset of Bordes et al. (2013), with the 14,951 entities of Freebase that are also present in the Wikilinks database and have at least 100 mentions in Freebase, and the 1,345 relations between them that have at least 100 instances (592,213 triples); relations that merely reverse another one (e.g. the reverse of `/people/person/nationality`) were removed.
- `fb15k_237`: the FB15k-237 dataset of Toutanova and Chen (2015), a subset of FB15k from which near-duplicate and inverse relations were removed (as well as the triples of the validation and test sets that link entities directly linked in the training set), keeping 237 relations and 14,541 entities (310,116 triples). The textual mentions of pairs of entities in the ClueWeb12 corpus, distributed with this dataset, are left out.

Each node is an entity (e.g. a person, a place, a film or a profession), identified by its Freebase machine identifier (mid); the data do not include the names of the entities. A directed edge from entity A to entity B is a triple (A, relation, B), e.g. that a person has a given profession. Some relations of Freebase are two-hop relations, in which an intermediate entity (a "compound value type") was collapsed out (e.g. `/film/film/release_date_s./film/film_regional_release_date/film_release_region`). Pairs of entities may be connected by several edges with different relations.

The triples are divided into training, validation and test sets by the benchmarks; all of them are included, and the set is given as an edge property.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `mid`: the Freebase identifier of the entity, e.g. `/m/027rn`.
- (Edge) `relation`: the Freebase relation, e.g. `/people/person/profession`.
- (Edge) `split`: the set of the benchmark the triple belongs to: `train`, `valid` or `test`.
citations: A. Bordes, N. Usunier, A. Garcia-Durán, J. Weston, O. Yakhnenko, "Translating Embeddings for Modeling Multi-relational Data." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 26, 2787-2795 (2013)

K. Toutanova, D. Chen, "Observed versus latent features for knowledge base and text inference." Proceedings of the 3rd Workshop on Continuous Vector Space Models and their Compositionality, 57-66 (2015)

K. Toutanova, D. Chen, P. Pantel, H. Poon, P. Choudhury, M. Gamon, "Representing Text for Joint Embedding of Text and Knowledge Bases." Proceedings of the 2015 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, 1499-1509 (2015)

datasets.name: freeman_eies
datasets.description:
Networks among researchers working on social network analysis, who took part in the Electronic Information Exchange System (EIES) study of S. C. Freeman and L. C. Freeman in 1978, which examined the impact of a computer-based communication system on the relationships among its users. These data are also used as examples in Wasserman and Faust (1994). This version was distributed by T. Opsahl.

- `time1` and `time2`: the personal relationships among 48 researchers at the beginning and at the end of the study, respectively. A directed edge (i, j) indicates how researcher i regards researcher j. Only 34 of the 48 researchers appear in the edge lists; the others are isolated nodes.
- `messages`: the number of messages sent among 32 of the researchers who used the electronic communication system. A directed edge (i, j) indicates messages sent from i to j. The source data contain self-loops, whose meaning is not documented.

The node numbering of the `messages` network does not necessarily correspond to the one of the other two networks.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Edge) `weight` (`time1` and `time2`): from 1 to 4 (1: has heard of the person, but not met; 2: has met the person; 3: friend; 4: close personal friend).
- (Node) `name` (`messages`): the name of the researcher.
- (Node) `discipline` (`messages`): the main disciplinary affiliation (1: sociology, 2: anthropology, 3: mathematics or statistics, 4: others).
- (Node) `citations` (`messages`): the number of citations of the researcher in the Social Science Citation Index in 1978.
- (Edge) `weight` (`messages`): the number of messages.
citations: S. C. Freeman, L. C. Freeman, "The networkers network: A study of the impact of a new communications medium on sociometric structure." Social Science Research Reports 46, University of California, Irvine (1979)
S. Wasserman, K. Faust, "Social Network Analysis: Methods and Applications." Cambridge University Press (1994)

datasets.name: french_financial_elite
datasets.description:
Relationships among 28 members of the French financial elite, collected by C. Kadushin in 1990. Kadushin collected data from 127 members of the elite, used several criteria to determine the top 28, and recorded their answers to questions about who was influential, who belonged to the elite, and who were their friends, together with information on their backgrounds and characteristics. The data were distributed by L. C. Freeman on his network data page at the University of California, Irvine (no longer online), from which this version was obtained via the Internet Archive.

The network has three directed layers (relations), in which an edge (i, j) indicates that person i named person j in response to the questions:

- `WHO INFLUENCES YOU`
- `WHO IS IN THE ELITE`
- `WHO ARE YOUR FRIENDS` (this relation is symmetric in the data, and appears as reciprocal edges)

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the label of the person.
- (Node) `birthdate`, `birthplace`, `sciencepoly`, `polytech`, `polyyear`, `university`, `normal-sch`, `ena`, `enayear`, `inspec-gen`, `igyear`, `cabinet`, `finance-min`, `party`, `religion`, `masons`, `zipcode`, `socialreg`, `elitevote`, `eliteprom`, `prestige`, `fathers-lev`, `clubs`, `topboards`: the 24 attributes recorded by Kadushin, as integer codes (-1 if missing). The codes are not documented with the data; they refer to e.g. the year of birth, attendance of elite schools (Sciences Po, École polytechnique, École normale supérieure, ENA) and the year of graduation, membership in the Inspection générale des finances, ministerial cabinets and the finance ministry, political party, religion, freemasonry, postal code of residence, listing in the social register, number of votes and prominence as elite, club memberships, and board memberships, as described by Kadushin (1995).
- (Edge) `layer`: the relation.
citations: C. Kadushin, "Friendship among the French financial elite." American Sociological Review 60(2), 202-221 (1995)

datasets.name: freshmen
datasets.description:
Friendship ratings among the 34 freshmen majoring in Sociology at the University of Groningen (Netherlands) in the academic year 1998-1999, collected by E. Zeggelink in collaboration with G. van de Bunt with questionnaires. Except for a few prior acquaintances, the students did not know each other at the start. Each student rated their relationship with every other student on a scale from best friendship to troubled relationship.
