The data were collected at seven time points, of which five are available: `t0`, at the start of the year (during an introduction period), and `t2`, `t3`, `t5` and `t6`, about 6, 9, 21 and 27 weeks later. There is increasing nonresponse at the later time points.

Each network is a complete directed graph with self-loops, in which the edge $(i, j)$ stores the rating given by student $i$ to student $j$; therefore, edges should be selected according to their `weight` values.

The networks have the following properties (the vertex attributes were collected at `t0`):

- (Node) `id`: the student's ID.
- (Node) `gender`: 1 = male, 2 = female.
- (Node) `age`: age in years (99 = missing).
- (Node) `program`: 1 = regular four-year program, 2 = two-year program (for students who previously completed higher vocational training; these are typically older).
- (Node) `smoking`: 1 = no, 2 = yes, at parties, 3 = 1-3 cigarettes per day, 4 = 4-10 per day, 5 = more than 10 per day, 99 = missing.
- (Edge) `weight` (edges): the rating of $j$ by $i$: 1 = best friendship, 2 = friendship, 3 = friendly relationship, 4 = neutral relationship, 5 = troubled relationship, 6 = item non-response (according to the data providers, also often used to express "unknown person", for which the code 0 is otherwise reserved), 8 = diagonal (after `t0`), 9 = actor non-response.
citations: G. Van de Bunt, M. Van Duijn, and T. Snijders. "Friendship networks through time: An actor-oriented dynamic statistical network model." Computational & Mathematical Organization Theory 5.2. 167-192. (1999).

datasets.name: frozen
datasets.description:
Weighted network of the dialogue between the characters of the Disney animated film "Frozen" (2013), compiled by P. Holme for an article with M. A. Porter and H. Sayama on network centrality for young readers. Nodes are characters (including groups such as "Crowd" or "Trolls"), and an undirected edge connects two characters if one speaks to the other, weighted by the number of lines they say to each other. The network was built from a transcript of the film listing who speaks each line, by watching the film and noting to whom each line is said (and correcting the transcript where necessary). The figure in the article shows a subnetwork without the edges of weight one.

The edges have the property `weight`, the number of lines said between the two characters.[^icon]

[^icon]: Description obtained in part from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.
citations: P. Holme, M. A. Porter, H. Sayama, "Who is the most important character in Frozen? What networks can tell us about the world." Frontiers for Young Minds 7, 99 (2019)

datasets.name: fullerene_structures
datasets.description:
Fifteen molecular graphs of fullerenes, closed-cage molecules made only of carbon atoms, with sizes from 60 atoms (C60, buckminsterfullerene) to 6000 atoms. Nodes are carbon atoms and undirected edges are the chemical bonds between them; as in every fullerene graph, each atom is bonded to exactly three others, and the bonds form 12 pentagonal and otherwise hexagonal rings. The graphs were assembled by S. Aref and M. C. Wilson from published three-dimensional atomic coordinates (the Yoshida fullerene library and a collection of icosahedral fullerenes), and published in a collection of networks used in their study of balance and frustration in signed networks (Aref and Wilson, 2019), where they were used to compute the bipartite edge frustration and other bipartivity measures, which have been proposed as indicators of the chemical stability of fullerenes. Each network is named after the molecular formula of the fullerene (e.g. `C240`). The other networks of the same collection are in the entries `lazy_portfolios`, `cow_signed_relations`, `signed_biological` and `signed_social_relations`; the atomic coordinates from which the graphs were built are also part of the collection but are not included.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `label`: the index of the atom in the source file.
- (Edge) `weight` (edges): always 1.
citations: S. Aref and M. C. Wilson, "Balance and frustration in signed networks." J. Complex Networks 7(2), 163–189 (2019)

datasets.name: funcoup_cancer
datasets.description:
A global network of functional couplings between human genes, used by S. K. Merid, D. Goranskaya and A. Alexeyenko for the network enrichment analysis of somatic mutations in glioblastoma and ovarian cancer genomes (named `merged6_and_wir1_HC2` by the authors). Nodes represent genes (or their protein products), and an undirected edge between two genes means that they are predicted or known to be functionally coupled, e.g. by physical interaction, membership in the same pathway or protein complex, or regulation. The network was built by merging a higher-confidence version (FClim_HC2) of the FunCoup network, which integrates diverse high-throughput evidence (e.g. protein interactions, co-expression, sub-cellular co-localization) from human and other eukaryotes via orthologs, with curated functional links from CORUM (protein complex membership), PhosphoSite (kinase-substrate pairs), KEGG (pathways and protein complexes) and MSigDB (pairs of genes regulated by the same transcription factor), and with a network of regulatory links reverse-engineered by the authors from cancer data (wir1). Among the networks benchmarked by the authors, this one best recovered known members of cancer-related gene sets. The types, origins and confidence of the links are not included in the distributed file. The network contains self-loops (genes coupled to themselves, as given in the source data).

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the gene symbol, in lower case (as in the source data; the symbol of SEPT11 appears in the date-converted form "11-sep").[^icon].

[^icon]: Description obtained in part from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.
citations: S. K. Merid, D. Goranskaya, A. Alexeyenko, "Distinguishing between driver and passenger mutations in individual cancer genomes by network enrichment analysis." BMC Bioinformatics 15, 308 (2014)

datasets.name: fungal_networks
datasets.description:
Spatial networks formed by the mycelia of saprotrophic woodland fungi and by the slime mould *Physarum polycephalum*, grown in the laboratory under different conditions, from S. H. Lee, M. D. Fricker and M. A. Porter, as distributed by A. R. Benson. The networks were extracted from images of the growing organisms: nodes are located at hyphal tips, branch points and fusions (anastomoses) of the mycelium, and an undirected edge represents a cord (a bundle of hyphae, or a tube for *Physarum*) connecting two of them. Edges are weighted by the conductance of the cord, $G = r^2/L$, where $r$ is the cord's radius and $L$ its length (the release does not state which of the weightings of the paper it contains; its weights are inversely proportional to the Euclidean edge length, as expected for the conductance-based "structural" networks, rather than the "path score" weights). There are 270 networks, each named after its experimental conditions in the form `<species>_<?>_<resources>_<grazing>_<interaction>_<age>_<replicate>`, where:

- species: `Pp`, *Physarum polycephalum* (an acellular slime mold, taxonomically distinct from fungi); `Pv`, *Phanerochaete velutina*; `Ag`, *Agrocybe gibberosa*; `Pi`, *Phallus impudicus*; `Rb`, *Resinicium bicolor*; `Sc`, *Stropharia caerulea*.
- the second field (`M` or `L`) is not explained in the paper; it probably refers to the size of the microcosm (some *P. velutina* networks were grown in large, 57 cm × 57 cm, microcosms).
- resources: `I`, initial colonized wood block (inoculum) only; `I+R`, inoculum plus one additional wood block; `I+4R` and `I+4xR`, inoculum plus four additional wood blocks (placed either as a cross or together); `5xI`, five inocula in a pentagonal arrangement; `Tokyo` and `UK`, (for *Physarum*) oat flakes placed to match the major cities around Tokyo or in the UK.
- grazing: `U`, ungrazed; `Fc`, `Fc-L`, `Fc-M`, `Fc-H`, grazed by the collembolan *Folsomia candida* (a small soil arthropod), at low (10 per microcosm), medium (20) or high (40) density.
- interaction: `N`, grown alone; `Hf`, grown in competition with the fungus *Hypholoma fasciculare*.
- age: the age of the network, in days (`d`) or hours (`h`); and the replicate number.

The growth substrates were agar (*Physarum*), black sand, or compressed soil, depending on the experiment.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `coordinates`: the horizontal and vertical position of the node in the image (in the units of the source data).
- (Edge) `weight`: the conductance of the cord (in arbitrary units).
citations: S. H. Lee, M. D. Fricker, M. A. Porter, "Mesoscale analyses of fungal networks as an approach for quantifying phenotypic traits." Journal of Complex Networks (2016)

datasets.name: gab_followers
datasets.description:
Networks of the users of Gab, a microblogging platform popular with the alt-right, from the dataset of Zannettou et al., who crawled Gab through its API with a snowball method: starting from the most popular users, they collected iteratively the followers and followings of all users found (lists of February 1, 2018), and then all posts of the 336,752 users found (22 million posts, from August 2016 to January 2018).

The entry contains four networks:

- `follows`: a directed edge from user u to user v means that u follows v, from the lists of followers and of followings (the union of both; users are identified by their usernames).
- `reposts`: a directed edge from a user to the author of a post they reposted, for each repost.
- `replies`: a directed edge from the author of a reply to the author of the post replied to, for each reply.
- `quotes`: a directed edge from the author of a quote to the author of the quoted post, for each quote.

The posts file lists the posts of each user's timeline, including the user's reposts, so that posts appear several times: in `replies` and `quotes`, each post is counted once (by its id), and in `reposts`, each pair of reposting user and post once. Replies and quotes whose parent post is not given are left out. Repeated interactions between the same users appear as multiple edges, and self-interactions as self-loops. The `follows` network and the others use different identifiers (usernames, and numeric ids with the usernames at the time of the post), and their nodes are not matched. Left out are the texts of the posts, their topics, attachments and the users' profile pictures.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `username`: the user's name.
- (Node) `user_id` (`reposts`, `replies` and `quotes`): the user's id on Gab.
- (Node) `verified`, `is_pro`, `is_donor`, `is_investor`, `is_private` (`reposts`, `replies` and `quotes`): the flags of the account (as in the last post seen).
- (Edge) `in_followers`, `in_followings` (`follows`): whether the relation is in the list of followers of v, and in the list of followings of u.
- (Edge) `time`: in `follows`, the time when the relation was first collected (Unix time, from the MongoDB object id); in `reposts`, `replies` and `quotes`, the time of the repost or of the post (Unix time).
- (Edge) `post_id` (`reposts`, `replies` and `quotes`): the id of the reposted post, or of the reply or quote.
- (Edge) `parent_id` (`replies` and `quotes`): the id of the parent post.
citations: S. Zannettou, B. Bradlyn, E. De Cristofaro, H. Kwak, M. Sirivianos, G. Stringhini, J. Blackburn, "What is Gab: A Bastion of Free Speech or an Alt-Right Echo Chamber." Companion Proceedings of The Web Conference 2018, 1007-1014 (2018)

datasets.name: gab_users_fair
datasets.description:
The follower network of the users of Gab, a microblogging platform popular with the alt-right, from the database of Fair and Wesslen, who scraped the profiles of the users of Gab, with their lists of followers and followings, from January to February 2019 (the profiles of the users created from August 2016 to December 2018). A directed edge from user u to user v means that u follows v; the edges are the union of the lists of followers and followings of the 757,363 scraped users (each relation once). For some users, the lists were not scraped completely (`followers_complete` or `following_complete` false); the follower lists of 135,630 users and the following lists of 121,331 users are incomplete. The users that appear only in the lists of others are included, with the profile attributes given in the lists (including their display names and biographies). The data contain no phone numbers or e-mail addresses.

The posts described by Fair and Wesslen (35.9 million) are not in the published data. Left out are the profile pictures and cover images of the users, and the separate list of usernames. Another crawl of Gab, of 2018, with posts, is the entry `gab_followers`.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `user_id`: the id of the user on Gab.
- (Node) `username`.
- (Node) `display_name`: the name shown on the profile.
- (Node) `bio`: the biography of the profile (empty if none).
- (Node) `has_record`: whether the user's profile was scraped (otherwise the user only appears in the lists of others).
- (Node) `created`: the month of creation of the account (Unix time of its first day; -1 if unknown).
- (Node) `follower_count`, `following_count` and `post_count`: as shown on the profile (-1 if unknown).
- (Node) `score` (-1 if unknown).
- (Node) `verified`, `is_pro`, `is_donor`, `is_investor`, `is_premium`, `is_tippable`, `is_private` and `is_accessible`: the flags of the account (1 or 0; -1 if unknown).
- (Node) `collected`: the time when the profile was scraped (Unix time; -1 for users not scraped).
- (Node) `followers_complete` and `following_complete`: whether the lists of followers and followings of the user were scraped completely (1 or 0; -1 if unknown).
- (Edge) `in_followers` and `in_following`: whether the relation is in the list of followers of v, and in the list of followings of u.
citations: G. Fair, R. Wesslen, "Shouting into the Void: A Database of the Alternative Social Media Platform Gab." Proceedings of the International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media 13, 608-610 (2019)

datasets.name: galesburg_physicians
datasets.description:
Friendship and discussion ties among 31 physicians in Galesburg (Illinois, USA), from the Columbia University drug study of J. S. Coleman, E. Katz and H. Menzel on the diffusion of a new drug (gammanym, a pseudonym for tetracycline) in the mid-1950s. The researchers recorded the date at which each physician first prescribed the drug, and asked the physicians to name three doctors whom they considered personal friends, and three doctors with whom they would choose to discuss medical matters. The data were taken from Knoke and Burt (1983), who used the archives of the original authors. Each edge points from the physician making the nomination to the nominated one. The data were distributed on the Pajek datasets page of the book *Exploratory Social Network Analysis with Pajek* (de Nooy, Mrvar and Batagelj), from which this version was obtained. The Pajek site also distributes a combined undirected network of the 17 physicians who adopted the drug, which is not included here. The data of all four towns of the same study, in the preparation of R. S. Burt (with 35 physicians and 86 friendship ties in Galesburg, and also the advice relation), are in the entry `physician_trust`.

- `friendship`: the friendship nominations.
- `discussion`: the discussion nominations.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the identifier of the physician.
- (Node) `adoption_time`: the number of months between the introduction of the drug and its first prescription by the physician (-1 for the 14 physicians who did not adopt it).
citations: J. S. Coleman, E. Katz, H. Menzel, "Medical Innovation: A Diffusion Study." Bobbs-Merrill, Indianapolis (1966)
D. Knoke, R. S. Burt, "Prominence." In R. S. Burt, M. J. Minor (eds.), Applied Network Analysis: A Methodological Introduction, Sage, Beverly Hills (1983), pp. 195-222
W. de Nooy, A. Mrvar, V. Batagelj, "Exploratory Social Network Analysis with Pajek." Cambridge University Press (2005)

datasets.name: game_thrones
datasets.description:
Networks of interactions between the characters of George R. R. Martin's fantasy series "A Song of Ice and Fire" and of its TV adaptation, HBO's "Game of Thrones", compiled by A. Beveridge and collaborators. Nodes are characters, and edges are undirected and weighted by the number of interactions between the two characters.

In the networks of the books, two characters are connected whenever their names (or nicknames) appear within 15 words of each other in the text. The first network, `stormofswords`, is the original network of the third book, "A Storm of Swords", of Beveridge and Shan (2016), with 107 characters and only the pairs that co-occur at least 4 times. The other book networks are the later versions in the author's GitHub repository `mathbeveridge/asoiaf`, which contain only the pairs that co-occur at least 3 times: one network per book, `book1` ("A Game of Thrones"), `book2` ("A Clash of Kings"), `book3` ("A Storm of Swords"), `book4` ("A Feast for Crows") and `book5` ("A Dance with Dragons"), a network `book45` of books 4 and 5 together (which tell simultaneous events), and a network `all_books` of all five books.

In the networks of the TV series (from the repository `mathbeveridge/gameofthrones`), one per season, `season1`, ..., `season8`, the interactions were extracted from fan-made scripts of the episodes (from genius.com): two characters A and B interact whenever A speaks directly after B, A speaks about B, a third character speaks about both A and B, A and B are mentioned in the same stage direction, or A and B appear in a scene together. Only the pairs with at least 2 interactions in a season are included in the data. The data of seasons 5 and 6 contain one pair twice each (Mace and Meryn Trant in season 5, Bowen Marsh and Othell Yarwyck in season 6), with different weights; both are kept, as parallel edges.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the character's name (in the networks of the TV series, often only the first name).
- (Node) `id`: the identifier of the character in the data (not present in `stormofswords`).
- (Edge) `weight` (edges): the number of interactions of the two characters.
citations: A. Beveridge and J. Shan, "Network of Thrones." Math Horizons 23(4), 18-22 (2016)

A. Beveridge and M. Chemers, "The Game of Game of Thrones: Networked Concordances and Fractal Dramaturgy." In: P. Brembilla and I. A. De Pascalis (eds.), Reading Contemporary Serial Television Universes: A Narrative Ecosystem Framework, Routledge, 201-225 (2018)

datasets.name: garfield_citations
datasets.description:
Citation networks from E. Garfield's collection of datasets produced with the HistCite software for algorithmic historiography, each obtained from a search in the Web of Science (used with the permission of ISI), and converted into Pajek format by V. Batagelj and A. Mrvar. Nodes are publications, and each directed edge points from a cited publication to the citing one. The data were distributed in Pajek format on the Pajek datasets page of V. Batagelj and A. Mrvar, from which this version was obtained.

- `smallworld`: papers citing S. Milgram's 1967 *Psychology Today* paper on the small world problem, or with "small world" in the title (1967-2002).
- `small_griffith`: citations to H. Small and B. Griffith's 1974 papers on co-citation clustering, and their descendants (1973-2001).
- `scientometrics`: articles from or citing the journal *Scientometrics* (1978-2000).
- `kohonen`: articles with the topic "self-organizing maps" or with references to T. Kohonen (1963-2002).
- `zewail`: articles by or citing A. H. Zewail (1970-2002).
- `lederberg`: articles by or citing J. Lederberg (1946-2002).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the first author of the publication.
- (Node) `year`: the year of publication.
- (Node) `gcs`: the global citation score of the publication (its number of citations in the whole Web of Science, at the time of the search).
- (Node) `reference` (`small_griffith` and `zewail` only): a short reference to the publication (author, year, volume and page).
citations: E. Garfield, "From Computational Linguistics to Algorithmic Historiography." Symposium in Honor of Casimir Borkowski, University of Pittsburgh (2001)
E. Garfield, "Historiographic Mapping of Knowledge Domains Literature." Journal of Information Science 30(2), 119-145 (2004)

datasets.name: gateway_foodwebs
datasets.description:
The GlobAL daTabasE of traits and food Web Architecture (GATEWAy, version 1.0), compiled by Brose et al., which contains 290 food webs from freshwater (lakes and streams), marine and terrestrial (aboveground and belowground) ecosystems on all continents, with 222,151 feeding interactions between consumers and resources, annotated with their body masses, metabolic and movement types. The food webs were assembled from published studies (23 sources) and were established by various methods (published accounts, expert knowledge, direct field observation, gut content analysis, extrapolation from similar taxa, etc.). Here, all food webs are combined into a single network, in which each node is a taxon at a given life stage in a given food web, so that the food webs are disjoint components (a taxon that appears in more than one food web corresponds to more than one node). A directed edge goes from a consumer to its resource. A few interactions (432) are listed more than once within a food web, and are kept as parallel edges. Some of the food webs are also available separately: the Carpinteria Salt Marsh web of Lafferty et al. (2006) is the network `food_web_lafferty` of the entry `iwdb` (later versions, resolved by life stage or aggregated by species, are in `california_estuaries` and `coastal_parasite_webs`), and the ten New Zealand stream webs of Townsend et al. (1998) match the corresponding `food_web_thompson_*` networks of `iwdb` (which have no taxon names), with the same or nearly the same number of links.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the taxon, at the highest available taxonomic resolution.
- (Node) `taxonomy_level`: the taxonomic level of the name (e.g. "species", "genus", "family").
- (Node) `common_name`: its common name.
- (Node) `lifestage`: the life stage (e.g. "adults", "juveniles", "larvae").
- (Node) `metabolic_type` ("invertebrate", "ectotherm vertebrate", "endotherm vertebrate", "primary producer", "heterotrophic bacteria", "heterotrophic fungi").
- (Node) `movement_type` ("walking", "swimming", "flying", "sessile", "other").
- (Node) `mass_mean`, `mass_min` and `mass_max`: the mean, minimum and maximum body mass in grams of the population involved in the interactions.
- (Node) `length_mean`, `length_min` and `length_max`: the corresponding body lengths in cm (missing values are NaN; for a few nodes, the values differ between interactions, and the first is used).
- (Node) `foodweb`: the name of the food web.
- (Node) `ecosystem_type` ("marine", "lakes", "streams", "terrestrial aboveground", "terrestrial belowground").
- (Node) `location`: the geographic location of the food web.
- (Node) `latitude` and `longitude`: its coordinates. Missing string values (given as "NA" in the source) are empty.
- (Edge) `interaction_type`: the type of interaction ("predacious", "herbivorous", "detritivorous", "fungivorous", "parasitoid", "parasitic", "bacterivorous", "pathogen").
- (Edge) `dimensionality`: whether the search space of the consumer is two- or three-dimensional ("2D" or "3D").
- (Edge) `classification`: whether the interaction is individual-based ("ibi") or non-individual-based ("nibi") intake and attack.
- (Edge) `methodology`: how the link was established.
- (Edge) `citation`: the source of the link.
citations: U. Brose et al., "Predator traits determine food-web architecture across ecosystems." Nature Ecology & Evolution 3(6), 919-927 (2019)
U. Brose, "GlobAL daTabasE of traits and food Web Architecture (GATEWAy) version 1.0." iDiv Data Repository, dataset (2018)

datasets.name: gb_public_transport
datasets.description:
Public transport networks of Great Britain in 2011, constructed by de Regt, von Ferber, Holovatch and Lebovka from the timetables of the National Public Transport Data Repository (NPTDR) of the UK Department for Transport, which contains a snapshot of all public transport services for a sample week (usually in early October) of each year. The networks are in the so-called L-space representation: nodes are stations (stops), and an undirected edge connects two stations if they are visited consecutively by a vehicle on some route. Only outgoing routes were considered, and multiple edges were reduced to single ones.

- `bristol`, `london`, `manchester`, `west_midlands`: the bus networks of Bristol, Greater London, Greater Manchester and the West Midlands.
- `coach`: the national coach network.
- `rail`: the national rail network.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `station_id`: the unique station identifier of the NPTDR (the NaPTAN ATCO code).
- (Node) `pos`: the position of the station as Easting and Northing (British National Grid), in meters. The positions are missing (empty) for 31 stations of `london` and one of `bristol`. The `west_midlands` network contains 12 self-loops, as in the source data.
citations: R. de Regt, C. von Ferber, Yu. Holovatch, M. Lebovka, "Public transportation in Great Britain viewed as a complex network." Transportmetrica A: Transport Science 15(2), 722-748 (2019)

datasets.name: gd2006_java
datasets.description:
Directed network of compile-time dependencies among the classes of the core `java.*` packages of the Java Development Kit (JDK) 1.4.2, distributed as a data set for the graph drawing contest of the 14th International Symposium on Graph Drawing (GD 2006, Karlsruhe). Nodes are Java classes, and a directed edge $A \to B$ means that class $A$ depends on class $B$ at compile time, i.e., that $A$ explicitly uses $B$, so that $B$ must be compiled for $A$ to be compiled. Only dependencies among classes in the `java.*` packages are included (the `javax.*` packages and any other classes are excluded), and classes without any dependency within this set were removed.

The nodes have the property `name`, the fully qualified name of the class (e.g. `java.util.Calendar`).[^icon]

[^icon]: Description obtained in part from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.
citations: "Graph Drawing Contest", 14th International Symposium on Graph Drawing (GD 2006), Karlsruhe, Germany (2006)

datasets.name: gd2006_world_cup
datasets.description:
Directed temporal network of the matches played in the final tournaments of the FIFA World Cup (football/soccer) from the first edition in 1930 to 2006, distributed as a data set for the graph drawing contest of the 14th International Symposium on Graph Drawing (GD 2006, Karlsruhe), in the category "History of the World Cup". Nodes are national teams, and a directed edge represents a match between two teams in a given year, pointing from the winner to the loser (for a draw, the direction is the order in which the teams are listed in the source, and carries no meaning). Two teams that met several times are connected by parallel edges. Qualification matches are not included. Teams are named as in the source, which keeps the political changes of the participating countries as distinct nodes (e.g. "Germany", "W. Germany" and "E. Germany"; "USSR"; "Czechoslovakia" and "Czech Republic"; "Yugoslavia" and "Serbia and Montenegro").

Scores include the goals of penalty shoot-outs: for a match decided by penalties, the score is the sum of the goals in regular (and extra) time and in the shoot-out, and the score at the end of play is given separately. In 1938, Austria withdrew and Sweden advanced without a match; the source records it with a score of 0:-1. Some matches were replayed, because the first match was a draw, or as a decision match after the group stage; both the original and the decision match are included.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the team as in the source (e.g. "Brazil", "W. Germany", "So. Korea").
- (Edge) `year`: the year of the tournament.
- (Edge) `goals_source` and `goals_target`: the goals scored by the source and target teams (including penalty shoot-out goals).
- (Edge) `draw`: whether the match was a draw at the end of play (true for all matches decided by penalties).
- (Edge) `penalties`: whether the match was decided by a penalty shoot-out.
- (Edge) `goals_source_play` and `goals_target_play`: the score at the end of play before the shoot-out (equal to `goals_source` and `goals_target` for matches without a shoot-out).
- (Edge) `note`: the annotation of the source: "withdrawal" (the loser withdrew), "replayed" (a match that was repeated as a decision match), "decision" (a decision match), "penalties" (decided by penalty shoot-out), or empty.
citations: "Graph Drawing Contest", 14th International Symposium on Graph Drawing (GD 2006), Karlsruhe, Germany (2006)

datasets.name: gdelt_outlinks
datasets.description:
The hyperlink network of the world's online news outlets, from the Global Knowledge Graph (GKG) of the GDELT Project, which records the hyperlinks in the body text of every news article that it monitors (links in headers, footers, insets and ads are excluded). From April 22, 2016 to January 28, 2019, GDELT recorded 1.78 billion links in 304 million articles, which it aggregated to a network of web domains: a directed edge from domain u to domain v means that articles of the news outlet u linked to pages of v (a registered domain, collapsed with BigQuery's `NET.REG_DOMAIN()`; the outlet is GDELT's `SourceCommonName`), weighted by the number of days with at least one such link, and by the total number of links. Links of an outlet to its own domain are left out. The network has 4,407,927 domains, of which 99,270 are news outlets with outgoing links. Domain names are as recorded, and are case-sensitive: domains that appear with different capitalizations are different nodes (138,884 of the nodes differ from others only in capitalization).

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `domain`: the web domain.
- (Edge) `num_days`: the number of days on which articles of the source linked to the target.
- (Edge) `num_links`: the total number of links (including repeated ones).
citations: The GDELT Project, "Who Links To Whom? The 30M Edge GKG Outlink Domain Graph April 2016 To Jan 2019." GDELT Blog (2019)
K. Leetaru, P. A. Schrodt, "GDELT: Global data on events, location, and tone, 1979-2012." International Studies Association Annual Convention (2013)

datasets.name: gelada_baboons
datasets.description:
Grooming relations in a colony of gelada baboons (unit H22), from the field study of R. Dunbar and P. Dunbar in Ethiopia, as analyzed by K. Stephenson and M. Zelen. The network was observed at two time points: at the first there were 12 baboons (seven females and five males), and before the second two more baboons (a female and a male) were introduced to the group and accepted. Nodes are baboons, and an undirected edge connects two baboons that were observed grooming each other, weighted by the frequency of grooming. The data were distributed on the Pajek datasets page of the book *Generalized Blockmodeling* (Doreian, Batagelj and Ferligoj), from which this version was obtained. The binarized versions of the networks also distributed there are not included.

- `t1`: the 12 baboons at the first time point (H22A).
- `t2`: the 14 baboons at the second time point (H22B).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: a label encoding the sex (F: female, M: male), age class ("adult", or the age in years) and role (D: dominant, L: leader, F: follower, N: newcomer) of the baboon.
- (Node) `code`: a short identifier (f1 to f8 for females, m1 to m6 for males) used in the book *Generalized Blockmodeling*.
- (Node) `female`: whether the baboon is female.
- (Edge) `weight`: the frequency of grooming.
citations: R. Dunbar, P. Dunbar, "Social Dynamics of Gelada Baboons." Contributions to Primatology 6, 1-157 (1975)
K. Stephenson, M. Zelen, "Rethinking centrality: Methods and examples." Social Networks 11(1), 1-37 (1989)
P. Doreian, V. Batagelj, A. Ferligoj, "Generalized Blockmodeling." Cambridge University Press (2004)

datasets.name: gene_fusion
datasets.description: A network of gene fusions observed in human cancers, from Höglund et al. (2006), as distributed by KONECT (from P. Holme's collection). Each node is a gene, and an undirected edge connects two genes that were observed to fuse (through chromosomal rearrangements) in neoplasia, according to the Mitelman Database of Chromosome Aberrations in Cancer. The data identify the genes only by indices (their names are not included).
citations: M. Höglund, A. Frigyesi, F. Mitelman, "A gene fusion network in human neoplasia." Oncogene 25(18), 2674-2678 (2006)
J. Kunegis, "KONECT -- The Koblenz Network Collection." Proceedings of the 22nd International Conference on World Wide Web Companion, 1343-1350 (2013)

datasets.name: genetic_multiplex
datasets.description:
Multiplex networks of genetic and protein interactions in several organisms, assembled by M. De Domenico and collaborators. Nodes are genes (or their protein products), identified by their gene symbols, and each layer corresponds to a different type of interaction.

Most networks were extracted from BioGRID (Biological General Repository for Interaction Datasets, version 3.2.108 of 1 January 2014), a curated database of genetic and protein interactions from high-throughput data sets and focused studies in the literature. These are directed multiplex networks with up to seven layers, named according to BioGRID's interaction types: direct interaction, physical association, association, colocalization, and additive, suppressive and synthetic genetic interactions defined by inequality. An edge connects two genes that have an interaction of the type of its layer; the direction of the edges follows the order of the two genes in the source files, and its meaning is not documented. Not every organism has every layer, and the numbering of the layers differs between organisms (see the graph property `layer_key`). The organisms are: *Arabidopsis thaliana* (`Arabidopsis`), *Bos taurus* (`Bos_Multiplex_Genetic`), *Candida albicans* (`Candida`), *Caenorhabditis elegans* (`Celegans`), *Danio rerio* (`DanioRerio`), *Drosophila melanogaster* (`Drosophila`), *Gallus gallus* (`Gallus`), Hepatitis C virus (`HepatitusCVirus`), *Homo sapiens* (`Homo`), human herpesvirus 4 (`HumanHerpes4`), HIV-1 (`HumanHIV1`), *Mus musculus* (`Mus`), *Oryctolagus cuniculus* (`Oryctolagus`), *Plasmodium falciparum* (`Plasmodium`), *Rattus norvegicus* (`Rattus`), *Saccharomyces cerevisiae* (`Sacchcere`), *Schizosaccharomyces pombe* (`Sacchpomb`) and *Xenopus laevis* (`Xenopus`).

The network `YeastLandscape` is different: it is based on the genetic interaction map of *Saccharomyces cerevisiae* of Costanzo et al. (Science 327, 425-431, 2010), obtained with synthetic genetic array experiments. It has four layers: positive and negative genetic interactions, and positive and negative correlations between the genetic interaction profiles of genes. Unlike the other networks, it is undirected. It contains all pairs present in the original data set (pairs listed twice, in both orientations with the same value, are included only once), without any threshold applied, so the edges should be filtered by their `weight` value before use.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name` and `nodeLabel`: the gene symbol.
- (Edge) `layer` (edges): the interaction type (layer); the graph property `layer_key` maps the layer numbers to their names.
- (Edge) `weight` (edges): always 1, except in `YeastLandscape`, where it is the genetic interaction score (interaction layers) or the Pearson correlation coefficient between interaction profiles (correlation layers).
citations: M. De Domenico, M. A. Porter, & A. Arenas. "MuxViz: a tool for multilayer analysis and visualization of networks". Journal of Complex Networks, cnu038. (2014).

datasets.name: genius_expertise
datasets.description:
Users, songs and artists of the lyrics annotation website Genius (genius.com), crawled between September 2019 and January 2020 by D. Lim and A. R. Benson to study the expertise and dynamics of crowdsourced knowledge curation. On Genius, users write annotations explaining passages of song lyrics; annotations are edited collaboratively and reviewed by moderators, and verified annotations are written by the artists themselves. Users can follow each other. There are three networks:

- `follows`: a directed network of users, where an edge $i \to j$ means that user $i$ follows user $j$ (users who appear only in the user information file are included as isolated nodes; 1,219 users follow themselves, as given).
- `annotations`: a bipartite multigraph of users and songs, where each edge is an edit of an annotation of the song's lyrics by the user. Reviewed annotations come with their edit histories, where each edit is an edge; unreviewed annotations have only their author, and verified annotations only the artist account that wrote them, each of which is a single edge with the time of the annotation.
- `artist_songs`: a bipartite network of artists (as given by their Genius artist pages) and the songs they contributed to (e.g. as performers, writers or producers).

User names and the names of songs and artists are the identifiers of their pages on the site (e.g. `https://genius.com/<name>`); artist and user accounts are distinct, so that artists in `artist_songs` are not identified with users. The user information file lists 2,513 users more than once, and the artist information file 2,543 artists, in part with different values; the first entry is used (for the artists, with the songs of all their entries). The times are given without time zone, and are interpreted as UTC. Left out are the texts of the annotations and their edits, the lyrics of the songs, the contribution shares of the users to each reviewed annotation computed by Genius, and the users who accepted the annotations.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the user, song or artist page.
- (Node) `is_song` (`annotations`, `artist_songs`): whether the node is a song.
- (Node) `iq` (users, in `follows` and `annotations`): the user's IQ (Genius reputation points); -1 for users without information.
- (Node) `roles` (users, in `follows` and `annotations`): the roles of the user (e.g. "Editor", "Contributor").
- (Node) `annotations_num`, `suggestions_num`, `transcriptions_num`, `questions_num`, `answers_num`, `pyongs_num` (users, in `follows` and `annotations`): the numbers of annotations, suggestions, transcriptions, questions, answers and pyongs (shares) of the user; -1 for users without information.
- (Node) `followers_num`, `following_num` (users, in `follows` and `annotations`): the numbers of followers and of followed users; -1 for users without information.
- (Node) `title`, `primary_artist`, `release_date`, `views`, `pyongs` (songs, in `annotations` and `artist_songs`): the title, primary artist, release date (as given, e.g. "July 31, 2012"), views and pyongs of the song; empty or -1 for songs without information.
- (Node) `contributors` (songs, in `annotations` and `artist_songs`): the number of contributors; -1 for songs without information.
- (Node) `has_bio` (songs, in `annotations` and `artist_songs`): whether the song has a description.
- (Node) `tags` (songs, in `annotations` and `artist_songs`): genre tags; empty for songs without information.
- (Node) `iq`, `followers`, `roles` (artists, in `artist_songs`): the IQ, followers and roles of the artist.
- (Edge) `time` (`annotations`): the time of the edit (or of the annotation), in Unix time.
- (Edge) `annotation` (`annotations`): the numeric identifier of the annotation.
- (Edge) `type` (`annotations`): the type of the annotation ("reviewed", "unreviewed" or "verified").
- (Edge) `votes` (`annotations`): the votes of the annotation.
citations: D. Lim and A. R. Benson, "Expertise and Dynamics within Crowdsourced Musical Knowledge Curation: A Case Study of the Genius Platform." Proceedings of the International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media (ICWSM) 15, 373-384 (2021).

datasets.name: german_autobahn
datasets.description:
Network of the German highway (Autobahn) system, from M. Kaiser and C. C. Hilgetag. Nodes are 1,168 locations along the highways (named after towns or places, e.g. at exits and junctions), and an undirected edge connects two locations that are directly connected by a highway, without other locations in between. The network was derived from the Autobahn-Informations-System (AIS) of the German Federal Highway Research Institute (BASt) in 2002, and was used to compare the spatial growth of transportation and neural networks.

The nodes have the property `name`, the name of the location, as given in the source (characters outside ASCII, such as umlauts, appear as "?").[^icon]

[^icon]: Description obtained in part from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.
citations: M. Kaiser, C. C. Hilgetag, "Spatial growth of real-world networks." Physical Review E 69, 036103 (2004)

datasets.name: german_polisci
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of political scientists in Germany and their publications, from Leifeld et al. The authors compiled a list of 85 university departments and research institutes hosting political scientists in Germany, and of their researchers holding a doctorate (postdocs and professors), with their affiliation, gender and seniority status. For each researcher, all publications from 2009 to 2013 listed in their CV or homepage (journal articles, book chapters, monographs, edited volumes, and other items such as working papers and book reviews; newspaper articles were excluded) were recorded, including their co-authors. The data collection took place mostly between the fall of 2013 and mid-2014, and was completed at the beginning of 2015. Of the 1,583 researchers covered, 1,339 had a publication list with publications in that period, and are the researchers included in the network. Each publication is connected to the researchers that co-authored it (co-authors that are not among the 1,339 researchers are not included). Although the analysis of the paper is restricted to the years 2009 to 2013 (22,080 publications), the distributed network contains also 2,704 publications from 2014 and 2015, which are kept here, with their year as a node property. In 77 cases the source matrix has a value of 2 instead of 1 for an authorship; these are kept as single edges.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `is_publication`: whether the node is a publication (otherwise a researcher).
- (Node) `name` (researchers): the name of the researcher.
- (Node) `affiliations` (researchers): the list of research organizations of the researcher (some researchers have more than one).
- (Node) `chairs` (researchers): the title of the chair or research group of the researcher at each of these affiliations (as listed on their homepage or CV).
- (Node) `status` (researchers): "Postdoc" or "Professor".
- (Node) `gender` (researchers): "male" or "female".
- (Node) `birth_year`, `phd_year` (researchers): the year of birth and of the PhD (-1 if missing, which is common).
- (Node) `pub_id` (publications): the identifier of the publication.
- (Node) `type` (publications): the type of publication ("article", "book chapter", "monograph", "edited volume" or "other").
- (Node) `year` (publications): the year of publication.
- (Node) `language` (publications): the language code of the publication (e.g. "de", "en").
- (Node) `reporting_author` (publications): the researcher on whose homepage or CV the publication was found.
citations: P. Leifeld, S. Wankmüller, V. T. Z. Berger, K. Ingold, C. Steiner, "Collaboration patterns in the German political science co-authorship network." PLOS ONE 12(4), e0174671 (2017)
P. Leifeld, "German Political Science Co-Authorship Network." Harvard Dataverse, dataset (2017)

datasets.name: german_power_grid
datasets.description:
Networks of the German 380 kV electrical transmission grid, compiled by M. Mureddu for the analysis of the impact of renewable energy sources (RES). The topology and parameters of the grid were extracted from a validated power flow model of the continental European transmission network (the former UCTE), keeping all German 380 kV buses and the lines among them, together with the foreign border nodes with the largest exchanges (with Denmark, the Netherlands, Luxembourg, France, Switzerland, Austria, the Czech Republic and Poland), which are modeled as constant loads (positive for outflows, negative for inflows). The installed photovoltaic and wind generation in Germany at the end of 2014 (from the EnergyMap census of RES generators) was assigned to the geographically nearest bus (via a Voronoi tessellation), and scaled to scenarios in which RES supply 20%, 30%, 40%, 50% or 60% of the total load, using the 2014 load. For each scenario, the dispatch of the 82 conventional generators was obtained with a DC optimal power flow.

A node is a transmission substation (bus), and an edge is a transmission line between two buses. The five networks share the same topology, and differ in the RES generation and conventional dispatch: `res20`, `res30`, `res40`, `res50` and `res60` correspond to the RES shares of 20% to 60%. There are two pairs of parallel lines.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the bus code (with a prefix indicating the country, e.g. `D` or `E` for German buses, `PL` for Poland).
- (Node) `latitude` and `longitude`: the geographical position (the source files label these columns the other way around).
- (Node) `load`: the load of the bus (MW).
- (Node) `pv` and `wind`: the estimated photovoltaic and wind power production at the bus in the scenario (MW).
- (Node) `gen_power`, `gen_capacity` and `num_generators`: the total dispatched power (MW), the total maximum power (MW) and the number of the conventional generators attached to the bus.
- (Node) `inertia`: the estimated rotating inertia of the bus (kg m²), estimated from the nominal power of its generators, or of its load (the source files label this column as `Id`, and the bus index as `Inertia`).
- (Edge) `x`: the reactance of the line (per unit, with a base power of 400 MVA).
- (Edge) `capacity`: the estimated capacity of the line (MW).
citations: M. Mureddu, "Representation of the German transmission grid for Renewable Energy Sources impact analysis." arXiv:1612.05532 (2016)
M. Mureddu, "Representation of the German transmission grid for Renewable Energy Sources impact analysis." figshare, dataset (2016)

datasets.name: gerstein_regulatory
datasets.description:
Directed regulatory networks of several organisms, used by the Gerstein lab to study the organization of regulatory networks into hierarchies. Nodes are genes (or proteins), and a directed edge points from a regulator to one of its targets.

From Yu and Gerstein (2006), transcriptional regulatory networks, where the regulators are transcription factors:

- `yeast_2006`: the yeast *Saccharomyces cerevisiae* (genes identified by systematic ORF names).
- `ecoli_2006`: the bacterium *Escherichia coli* (genes identified by Blattner b-numbers).

From Bhardwaj, Yan and Gerstein (2010) (also used by Bhardwaj, Kim and Gerstein, 2010):

- `yeast`: transcriptional regulatory network of *S. cerevisiae*, from genetic and biochemical experiments of several previous studies.
- `ecoli`: transcriptional regulatory network of *E. coli*, from RegulonDB (version 6.2, July 2009).
- `mouse`, `rat`, `human`: transcriptional regulatory networks from the Transcriptional Regulatory Element Database (TRED, as of June 2008).
- `mtuberculosis`: transcriptional regulatory network of *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*, from published microarray data.
- `human_modification`: protein modification network of human, where the regulators modify their target proteins post-translationally, from the Human Protein Reference Database (HPRD).
- `yeast_phosphorylation`: phosphorylation network of *S. cerevisiae*, where the regulators are kinases that phosphorylate their target proteins, from two large-scale experimental studies.

In the source files of the 2010 networks, regulators and targets are often spelled with different capitalization (e.g., the E. coli regulator `AcrR` and its gene `acrR`); here, names that differ only in capitalization are merged into a single node, named after its first occurrence. Self-loops (autoregulation) and, for `mtuberculosis` and `yeast_phosphorylation`, repeated edges are present, as in the source data.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the gene or protein name.
- (Node) `level` (2010 networks only): the level of regulators in the hierarchy of Bhardwaj, Yan and Gerstein (2010), "top" (regulators not regulated by other regulators), "middle" (regulators regulated by and regulating other regulators) or "bottom" (regulators regulated by other regulators but not regulating any), and empty for the non-regulator targets.
- (Node) `hierarchy_level` (`yeast` and `ecoli` only): the level of regulators in the hierarchy of Bhardwaj, Kim and Gerstein (2010), from 1 (bottom) to 4 (top), and 0 for the non-regulator targets. The levels are those given in the files of the source, which do not entirely match the networks: some regulators have no level, and some names in the level files do not correspond to nodes in the networks (these are ignored).
- (Edge) `regulation` (`ecoli` only): the type of regulation, `+` (activation), `-` (repression), `+-` (dual), or with a `?` when uncertain.
citations: H. Yu, M. Gerstein, "Genomic analysis of the hierarchical structure of regulatory networks." Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 103(40), 14724-14731 (2006)

N. Bhardwaj, K.-K. Yan, M. B. Gerstein, "Analysis of diverse regulatory networks in a hierarchical context shows consistent tendencies for collaboration in the middle levels." Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 107(15), 6841-6846 (2010)

N. Bhardwaj, P. M. Kim, M. B. Gerstein, "Rewiring of Transcriptional Regulatory Networks: Hierarchy, Rather Than Connectivity, Better Reflects the Importance of Regulators." Science Signaling 3(146), ra79 (2010)

datasets.name: giant_tissue_networks
datasets.description:
Functional gene networks of 144 human tissues and cell types, from GIANT (Genome-scale Integrated Analysis of gene Networks in Tissues), now part of HumanBase (Flatiron Institute). Nodes are human genes, and an edge between two genes is weighted by the probability that they are functionally related (e.g. take part in the same biological process) in the tissue. The networks were built by integrating about 38,000 genome-scale experiments (gene expression data sets, protein-protein interactions, transcription factor binding, chemical and genetic perturbations, microRNA targets) with a Bayesian approach: for each tissue, the gold standard of related genes was restricted to those expressed in the tissue (from tissue-specific expression data in the literature and the Human Protein Reference Database), so that the data sets informative of that tissue are weighted accordingly. The tissues and cell types are terms of the BRENDA Tissue Ontology (BTO), and include e.g. organs (`kidney`, `liver`, `heart`), brain regions (`hippocampus`, `substantia_nigra`), cell types (`neuron`, `t_lymphocyte`, `hepatocyte`) and fluids (`blood_plasma`); the network `global` is the tissue-naive network, built with the gold standard of all genes.

The complete networks give a probability for every pair of about 25,000 genes (291 GB of files). The networks here are the "top edges" networks provided by HumanBase: they contain only the edges whose probability exceeds the prior probability of a functional relationship, 0.1, which leaves between about 30 and 280 million edges per network (e.g. 39 million for `global`, 62 million for `kidney`, 283 million for `cochlea`). Each network contains the genes with at least one such edge. The probabilities assume this prior (as the networks shown on the HumanBase website). The gold standards of the tissues (the positive and negative examples used for training) are not included.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `entrez_id`: the NCBI Entrez Gene identifier of the gene.
- (Node) `symbol`: the official symbol of the gene, e.g. `TP53`, from the current NCBI Gene database (empty if the identifier was discontinued since).
- (Node) `description`: the name of the gene, e.g. `tumor protein p53` (empty if the identifier was discontinued).
- (Edge) `weight`: the posterior probability of a functional relationship between the two genes in the tissue (between 0.1 and 1).
- (Node) `tissue` (graph): the name of the tissue or cell type in the BRENDA Tissue Ontology (`global` for the global network).
- (Node) `bto_id` (graph): the identifier of the tissue or cell type in the BRENDA Tissue Ontology, e.g. `BTO:0000671` (empty for the global network).
citations: C. S. Greene, A. Krishnan, A. K. Wong, E. Ricciotti, R. A. Zelaya, D. S. Himmelstein, R. Zhang, B. M. Hartmann, E. Zaslavsky, S. C. Sealfon, D. I. Chasman, G. A. FitzGerald, K. Dolinski, T. Grosser, O. G. Troyanskaya, "Understanding multicellular function and disease with human tissue-specific networks." Nature Genetics 47, 569-576 (2015)

datasets.name: giraffes
datasets.description:
Social relationships among a herd of six adult female giraffes (Giraffa camelopardalis) living in a large outdoor enclosure, observed for two years by M. J. Bashaw, M. A. Bloomsmith, T. L. Maple and F. B. Bercovitch (according to ICON, at the San Diego Zoo's Wild Animal Park, from April 2002 to April 2004). The authors studied whether giraffes associate randomly, or have social preferences, and found that affiliative interactions, proximity and nearest neighbors were all non-randomly distributed, and consistent across measures and time. The data were distributed by L. C. Freeman on his network data page at the University of California, Irvine (no longer online), from which this version was obtained via the Internet Archive.

The network has three layers (relations), all directed:

- `Affiliative Interaction`: affiliative interactions from giraffe i to giraffe j (integer values).
- `Nearest Neighbor`: nearest neighbor scores of giraffe j for giraffe i (non-integer values).
- `Proximity`: proximity scores between giraffe i and giraffe j (non-integer values, not symmetric).

The exact definitions of the scores (which appear to be counts and percentages of observations) are given in the original publication, and are not documented with the data.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the giraffe.
- (Edge) `layer`: the relation (see above).
- (Edge) `weight`: the value of the relation.
citations: M. J. Bashaw, M. A. Bloomsmith, T. L. Maple, F. B. Bercovitch, "The structure of social relationships among captive female giraffe (Giraffa camelopardalis)." Journal of Comparative Psychology 121(1), 46-53 (2007)

datasets.name: github
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of users of the software hosting site GitHub and the repositories they watch (i.e. subscribe to), released by GitHub (S. Chacon) for the 2009 GitHub Contest, in which participants had to recommend repositories to users based on the repositories they already watched. The data are an extract of the repository watches in GitHub's database in June 2009, from which a sample of the watches of 4,788 test users was withheld (and is not included). Nodes are users and repositories, and an edge connects a user to a repository that the user watches. Users and repositories are anonymized by numerical ids, but the repositories come with their names, creation dates, fork origin and language composition.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `is_user`: whether the node is a user (otherwise it is a repository).
- (Node) `id`: the numerical id of the user or repository in the source data.
- (Node) `name` (repositories): the repository name ("owner/repository").
- (Node) `created` (repositories): its creation date.
- (Node) `fork_of` (repositories): the name of the repository it was forked from (empty if none).
- (Node) `languages`, `lines` (repositories): the programming languages identified in the repository and the number of lines of code in each (empty for the 47,371 repositories without language data).
citations: S. Chacon, "The 2009 GitHub Contest." The GitHub Blog (2009)

datasets.name: github_developers
datasets.description:
A social network of developers on the software hosting platform GitHub, collected from its public API in June 2019 by B. Rozemberczki and collaborators (MUSAE study) for benchmarks of node embedding and classification methods. Nodes are developers who have starred at least 10 repositories, and an undirected edge connects two developers who follow each other (a mutual follower relationship). Each developer is labeled as a web or a machine learning developer, a label which the authors derived from the job title, and has a list of binary features extracted from the location, the starred repositories, the employer and the email address (only the indices of the features are given, not their meaning; 16 lists contain repeated indices, kept as given).

This network is unrelated to the `github` entry (users and the repositories they watched, from the GitHub contest of 2009).

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the GitHub user name.
- (Node) `is_ml`: whether the developer is a machine learning developer (otherwise a web developer).
- (Node) `features`: the indices of the developer's binary features.
citations: B. Rozemberczki, C. Allen, and R. Sarkar, "Multi-scale attributed node embedding." Journal of Complex Networks 9(2), cnab014 (2021).

datasets.name: gleif_ownership
datasets.description:
Networks of the corporate parent relationships, and of other relationships (fund management, subfunds, feeder funds, branches), among legal entities registered in the Global Legal Entity Identifier (LEI) System, from the Golden Copy of the Global Legal Entity Identifier Foundation (GLEIF) of 1 October 2026 (00:00 UTC). Every legal entity that takes part in financial transactions (companies, funds, branches, government bodies, etc.) can obtain an LEI, a 20-character identifier, and must report to the LEI issuing organization its direct accounting consolidating parent and its ultimate accounting consolidating parent (the parents that consolidate it in their financial statements), if these have an LEI themselves; the issuing organizations validate the data (to different degrees, see the GLEIF documentation), which the GLEIF publishes three times per day as the "Golden Copy".

The entry has two networks. In `parents`, nodes are the legal entities that appear in at least one parent relationship, and a directed edge $(i,j)$ means that entity $j$ is the direct or the ultimate consolidating parent of entity $i$ (from child to parent). The two kinds of relationship between the same pair of entities are merged into a single edge, whose properties `is_direct` and `is_ultimate` say which of them apply (a direct parent that is not itself consolidated by another entity is also the ultimate parent, and both relationships are then usually reported: this is the case of 89,676 of the 170,510 edges). The relationship records of other kinds in the Golden Copy, which are not parent relationships (fund management, subfunds, feeder funds and international branches, about 229,000 records), are left out of `parents`. The network `all` contains all the relationship records of the Golden Copy (489,614), as they are: nodes are the entities that appear in at least one of them, and each record is a directed edge $(i,j)$ from its start node to its end node (e.g. from a fund to its manager), with its type (property `type`); there can be several edges between two entities. The "reporting exceptions", in which entities state the reason why they do not report a parent (e.g. a parent without an LEI, or a natural person), are not included in either network. Relationship records whose registration has lapsed (i.e., has not been renewed) are included, as are the few marked as inactive (see the property `status`). Four entities are reported as their own parents, and appear with self-loops in `parents` (in `all`, 3,223 records have the same start and end node). Four LEIs that appear in relationships have no LEI record in the Golden Copy, and their entity properties are empty. The percentages of ownership are given only for some relationships, as reported (20,579 edges of `parents`, 32,815 of `all`), and a few of them are larger than 100.

The entity data (name, country, legal form, etc.) are those of the LEI records of the same Golden Copy.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the legal name of the entity.
- (Node) `lei`: the Legal Entity Identifier (LEI) of the entity.
- (Node) `country`: the country of the legal address of the entity (ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code).
- (Node) `hq_country`: the country of the headquarters address of the entity.
- (Node) `jurisdiction`: the legal jurisdiction of the entity (ISO 3166-1 country or subdivision code).
- (Node) `category`: the entity category (`GENERAL`, `FUND`, `BRANCH`, `SOLE_PROPRIETOR`, `RESIDENT_GOVERNMENT_ENTITY` or `INTERNATIONAL_ORGANIZATION`).
- (Node) `legal_form`: the legal form of the entity, as a code of the ISO 20275 Entity Legal Forms (ELF) code list, or `8888` if the legal form is not in the list (then given by `other_legal_form`).
- (Node) `other_legal_form`: the legal form of the entity, as text, if it has no ELF code.
- (Node) `entity_status`: `ACTIVE`, `INACTIVE` (e.g. dissolved or merged entities), or `NULL` if not known.
- (Node) `registration_status`: the status of the LEI registration (`ISSUED`, `LAPSED` if it has not been renewed, `RETIRED`, `DUPLICATE`, `ANNULLED`, `PENDING_TRANSFER` or `PENDING_ARCHIVAL`).
- (Edge) `type` (only in `all`): the type of the relationship: `IS_DIRECTLY_CONSOLIDATED_BY`, `IS_ULTIMATELY_CONSOLIDATED_BY`, `IS_FUND-MANAGED_BY`, `IS_SUBFUND_OF`, `IS_FEEDER_TO` or `IS_INTERNATIONAL_BRANCH_OF`.
- (Edge) `is_direct` (only in `parents`): whether $j$ is the direct consolidating parent of $i$.
- (Edge) `is_ultimate` (only in `parents`): whether $j$ is the ultimate consolidating parent of $i$.
- (Edge) `percentage`: the percentage of $i$ held by $j$, if reported (in `parents`, from the direct relationship if both are reported; NaN otherwise).
- (Edge) `status`: the status of the relationship (`ACTIVE`, `INACTIVE`, or `NULL` if not known; in `parents`, from the direct relationship if both are reported).
- (Edge) `registration_status`: the status of the registration of the relationship (`PUBLISHED`, `LAPSED` if it has not been renewed, and in a few records of `all`, `PENDING_TRANSFER` or `PENDING_ARCHIVAL`; in `parents`, from the direct relationship if both are reported).
citations: Global Legal Entity Identifier Foundation (GLEIF), "GLEIF Golden Copy and Delta Files." (2026)

datasets.name: global_language_network
datasets.description:
Networks of languages that are connected by multilingual speakers or by translations, from S. Ronen, B. Gonçalves, K. Z. Hu, A. Vespignani, S. Pinker and C. A. Hidalgo, built from three records of linguistic expression. Nodes are languages, and an edge connects two languages with a statistically significant number of shared users or translations, as follows:

- `books`: book translations. A directed edge from language $i$ to language $j$ means that a significant number of books were translated from $i$ into $j$, according to UNESCO's Index Translationum, which lists 2.2 million translations of printed books published between 1979 and 2011.
- `twitter`: an undirected edge connects two languages if users who tweet in one of them are significantly more likely to also tweet in the other, based on nearly 550 million tweets in 73 languages (language detected automatically) by more than 17 million users, collected from December 2011 to February 2012.
- `wikipedia`: an undirected edge connects two languages if editors who edit an article in the Wikipedia edition of one language are significantly more likely to also edit an article in the edition of the other, based on 382 million edits in 238 language editions by 2.5 million editors, until the end of 2011 (excluding edits by bots).

For each pair of languages, the strength of the connection is measured by the $\phi$ correlation between the occurrence of the two languages, computed from the number $M_{ij}$ of common users (or translations from $i$ to $j$), and its significance by the corresponding $t$ statistic. The networks contain only the connections that involve at least six common users or translations (ten for Twitter in this data) and that are significant at $P < 0.01$ ($t > 2.58$), as in the visualizations of the paper; languages without any such connection are not included. The data are those of the interactive visualization of the networks by the authors' group (MIT Media Lab, now Center for Collective Learning).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the ISO 639-3 code of the language.
- (Node) `language`: its name.
- (Node) `family` and `primary_family`: the language family at two levels (e.g. "Germanic" and "Indo-European").
- (Node) `speakers`: the number of native and non-native speakers, in millions (NaN if not given, for 74 languages of the `books` network).
- (Edge) `cooccurrences`: the number $M_{ij}$ of common users (Twitter, Wikipedia) or of translations from the source to the target language (books).
- (Edge) `phi`: the $\phi$ correlation.
- (Edge) `t_statistic`: the $t$ statistic.[^icon].

[^icon]: Description obtained in part from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.
citations: S. Ronen, B. Gonçalves, K. Z. Hu, A. Vespignani, S. Pinker, C. A. Hidalgo, "Links that speak: The global language network and its association with global fame." Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 111(52), E5616-E5622 (2014)

datasets.name: global_suicide_attacks
datasets.description:
Yearly networks of militant organizations (and other entities) that conducted suicide attacks between 1985 and 2006, from the study of the global suicide-attack network by Acosta and Childs (2013). Nodes are organizations (vertex property `name`, with abbreviations as in the source), and an edge indicates a known physical relationship between agents of the two organizations in that year. Only the years 1985, 1986, 1990 and 1993 to 2006 are present. Data distributed by the UCINET datasets collection (University of Manchester), with the diagonal entries of the matrices (which are not described) removed; where the two directions in the source matrix differ, the tie is included.[^ucinet]

[^ucinet]: Description obtained in part from the [UCINET datasets page](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/datasets/covert-networks/global-suicide-attacks).
citations: B. Acosta and S. J. Childs, "Illuminating the global suicide-attack network." Studies in Conflict & Terrorism 36(1), 49-76 (2013)

datasets.name: globi_interactions
datasets.description:
Species interactions compiled by Global Biotic Interactions (GloBI), an open infrastructure that indexes and integrates existing datasets of interactions between organisms: predator-prey (e.g. `eats`, `preysOn`), parasite-host (e.g. `parasiteOf`, `endoparasiteOf`, `hasHost`), pathogen-host, pollination and flower visits (`visitsFlowersOf`, `pollinates`), symbiosis, and many others, from hundreds of studies, museum collections, citizen-science observations (e.g. iNaturalist), and literature-mining efforts. The data are those of the "interpreted data products" release 0.11 of September 2026, in which the names of the organisms given in the datasets were linked to taxonomic name authorities (e.g. Catalogue of Life, NCBI Taxonomy, GBIF, WoRMS, ITIS, EOL, Wikidata).

Nodes are taxa (mostly species and genera), identified by their interpreted name; names that could not be linked to a taxonomic authority are kept as given in the dataset (their `taxon_id` is `no:match`). A directed edge from taxon A to taxon B is an interaction record, e.g. "A eats B" or "A is a parasite of B", in the direction of the source of the record; a pair of taxa is connected by as many edges as there are records of interactions between them, each with its type, the dataset it comes from, and, if given, the location and date of the observation.

- `interactions`: the interaction records.
- `refuted`: the refuted interaction records, i.e. records stating that an interaction does *not* happen (e.g. that a predator does not eat a prey), which GloBI publishes separately.

Left out are the occurrence-level details of the records (life stage, sex, body part, physiological state and basis of record of the organisms, the specimens' catalog numbers, and the locality names), the references (bibliographic citations of the studies, which are given by GloBI for each dataset), and the records whose source or target has no name at all (their number is given by the graph property `unnamed_records`). The names as given in the datasets ("verbatim" names, before their interpretation) are also not included.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the taxon.
- (Node) `taxon_id`: the identifier of the taxon in a name authority, e.g. `COL:...`, `NCBI:9606`, `GBIF:...` (`no:match` if the name could not be linked; that of the first record of the taxon, if several were used).
- (Node) `rank`: the taxonomic rank of the taxon, e.g. `species`, `genus` (empty if not known).
- (Node) `path`: the taxonomic hierarchy of the taxon, from the root down, separated by ` | ` (empty if not known).
- (Node) `kingdom`, `phylum`, `class`, `order`, `family`, `genus`: the names of the higher taxa of the taxon (empty if not known); they follow the name authority used, e.g. `Animalia` or `Metazoa` for the kingdom.
- (Edge) `interaction`: the type of the interaction, as named by GloBI (OBO Relation Ontology), e.g. `eats`, `parasiteOf`, `pollinates`, `interactsWith`.
- (Edge) `dataset`: the dataset (GitHub repository or other source indexed by GloBI) the record comes from, e.g. `globalbioticinteractions/inaturalist`.
- (Edge) `latitude`, `longitude`: the coordinates of the observation (NaN if not given).
- (Edge) `time`: the date of the observation, in Unix time (NaN if not given; some datasets give dates that are obviously wrong, e.g. in the year 5, which are kept as they are).
- (Node) `unnamed_records` (graph): the number of records left out, since their source or target has no name.
citations: J. H. Poelen, J. D. Simons, C. J. Mungall, "Global biotic interactions: An open infrastructure to share and analyze species-interaction datasets." Ecological Informatics 24, 148-159 (2014)

datasets.name: gnutella
datasets.description: Snapshots of the Gnutella peer-to-peer file sharing network, collected in August 2002 and distributed by the Stanford Network Analysis Project (SNAP). Nodes are hosts in the Gnutella overlay network, and a directed edge represents a connection between two hosts (the meaning of the edge direction is not documented by the source). Each network is named after the day of August 2002 on which the snapshot was taken (`04`, `05`, `06`, `08`, `09`, `24`, `25`, `30` and `31`). The vertex property `name` holds the node ID of the source data.
citations: M. Ripeanu, A. Iamnitchi, and I. Foster, "Mapping the Gnutella Network: Properties of Large-Scale Peer-to-Peer Systems and Implications for System Design." IEEE Internet Computing 6(1), 50-57 (2002).

datasets.name: google
datasets.description:
A directed network of the static webpages at www.google.com and the hyperlinks among them, assembled by G. Palla, I. J. Farkas, P. Pollner, I. Derényi and T. Vicsek, and distributed with the CFinder software for detecting overlapping communities. A directed edge from $i$ to $j$ means that page $i$ contains a hyperlink to page $j$. The source does not document when or how the pages were collected, other than through the file date (March 2007). The network contains self-loops (pages linking to themselves).

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the URL of the page.
citations: G. Palla et al., "Directed network modules." New Journal of Physics 9(6), 186 (2007)

datasets.name: google_plus
datasets.description:
A snapshot of the directed social network of Google+ users, collected in 2012 and anonymized by M. Fire and collaborators at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev, and used as one of the social networks in their study of link prediction. Nodes are users, and a directed edge $(i, j)$ means that user $i$ added user $j$ to one of their circles. The network is a partial crawl of Google+; the crawling procedure is not documented by the source.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the anonymized user identifier.
citations: M. Fire et al. "Computationally efficient link prediction in a variety of social networks." ACM Transactions on Intelligent Systems and Technology 5(1), Article 10 (2013)

datasets.name: google_web
datasets.description: A web graph released by Google in 2002 as part of the Google Programming Contest, as distributed by the Stanford Network Analysis Project (SNAP). Nodes are web pages and a directed edge $(i, j)$ is a hyperlink from page $i$ to page $j$. The URLs of the pages are not included. The vertex property `name` holds the node ID of the source data.
citations: J. Leskovec, K. Lang, A. Dasgupta, M. Mahoney. "Community Structure in Large Networks: Natural Cluster Sizes and the Absence of Large Well-Defined Clusters." Internet Mathematics 6(1) 29--123 (2009)

datasets.name: graph_glossary
datasets.description:
The network of the terms of Bill Cherowitzo's *Graph and Digraph Glossary* (version of February 3, 2001, prepared for a course on graph theory at the University of Colorado at Denver), converted to Pajek format by B. Zemljič. A directed edge points from a term X to a term Y if Y is used to describe the meaning of X in the glossary. The source file contains 114 such directed relations and 4 undirected ones (terms that describe each other), which are represented here as pairs of reciprocal edges. The data were distributed in Pajek format on the Pajek datasets page of V. Batagelj and A. Mrvar, from which this version was obtained.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the term.
citations: B. Cherowitzo, "Graph and Digraph Glossary." University of Colorado at Denver (2001)

datasets.name: grassland_web
datasets.description:
A food web of grassland species, consisting of grasses, the grass-feeding chalcid wasps (herbivores) that feed on them, and the parasitoids and hyper-parasitoids of these wasps, compiled by H. A. Dawah, B. A. Hawkins and M. F. Claridge (1995) from field collections in Britain (Wales and England, 1980-1992, according to the ICON index). This version was distributed by A. Clauset, who used it as an example of hierarchical network structure; according to ICON, it contains only the largest connected component of the sampled web. Species names are not included.

A directed edge $(i, j)$ indicates that species $i$ feeds on (or parasitizes) species $j$.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `id`: the node number in the source data (not contiguous).
- (Node) `group`: the trophic group of the species (1: plants, 2: herbivores, 3: parasitoids, 4: hyper-parasitoids, 5: hyper-hyper-parasitoids), as given by Clauset, Moore and Newman (2008).
citations: H. A. Dawah, B. A. Hawkins, M. F. Claridge, "Structure of the parasitoid communities of grass-feeding chalcid wasps." Journal of Animal Ecology 64(6), 708-720 (1995)
A. Clauset, C. Moore, M. E. J. Newman, "Hierarchical structure and the prediction of missing links in networks." Nature 453, 98-101 (2008)

datasets.name: gridkit
datasets.description:
Networks of the high-voltage electricity transmission grids of Europe and North America, extracted from OpenStreetMap (OSM) (`europe` and `north_america`) and from the interactive map of ENTSO-E (`entsoe`, see below) by B. Wiegmans with GridKit, a toolkit developed in the context of the SciGRID project that transforms the OSM power objects (lines, cables and stations) into a topologically connected network model by spatial analysis. The OSM extracts were made in March 2016, and contain the high-voltage part of the grids as selected by GridKit (according to its documentation, lines of 220 kV and above, at any frequency other than the 16.7 Hz of railway power; a part of the lines have no voltage in OSM, and some lines of lower voltage remain).

In the OSM extracts, a node is a station or a junction of lines, and an edge is a line or cable between two nodes. There is one network for each continent, `europe` and `north_america`. The networks are undirected; some pairs of nodes are joined by several lines (parallel edges), and the networks are not connected (they have 86 and 41 components, respectively). The geometries of the lines (their courses as polylines) are not included, and neither are the columns of the line parameters (resistance, reactance, capacitance, thermal limit, and the OSM relation), which are empty in the extracts. Most attributes are taken from the OSM tags, and can hold several values separated by semicolons (e.g. for lines with several circuits of different voltages).

The networks have the following properties:

The network `entsoe` comes from another dataset of B. Wiegmans: an unofficial extract (of May 11, 2016) of the interactive map of the European power system of ENTSO-E (the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Electricity), including to a limited extent North Africa and the Middle East, processed by GridKit to form a topologically connected network. It is neither approved nor endorsed by ENTSO-E, and, according to its documentation, its coordinates follow the map, which favors topological clarity over geographical accuracy, its voltages are the lower bounds of the ranges of the map (not available for all lines, especially DC lines), and its transformers and the connections of the generators are not in the map, but were inferred (transformers between buses of different voltages within the same station, and generators connected to the nearest station at its lowest voltage). Its nodes are buses (a station can have several buses, of different voltages, connected by transformers; junctions of lines are synthetic stations of type `joint`), and its edges are the lines and cables between them and the transformers within stations (edge property `kind`). It has parallel edges and is not connected (139 components). The generators are kept as node properties of the buses they are connected to, and the geometries of the lines are not included.

The networks `europe` and `north_america` have the following properties:

- (Node) `vid`: the GridKit id of the node.
