- (Node) `type`: the kind of node (`joint`, `merge`, `substation`, `sub_station`, `station`, `plant`, ...).
- (Node) `voltage`: the voltage(s) (V).
- (Node) `frequency`: the frequency(-ies) (Hz).
- (Node) `name`, `operator` and `ref`: the name, operator and reference of the station in OSM.
- (Node) `latitude` and `longitude`: the geographical position.
- (Edge) `lid`: the GridKit id of the line.
- (Edge) `voltage`: the voltage(s) (V).
- (Edge) `cables`: the number(s) of cables.
- (Edge) `wires`: the number(s) of wires per cable bundle.
- (Edge) `frequency`: the frequency(-ies) (Hz).
- (Edge) `name`, `operator` and `ref`: the name, operator and reference of the line in OSM.
- (Edge) `length`: the length of the line (m). Missing values are empty strings (or NaN).

The network `entsoe` has the following properties:

- (Node) `bus_id` and `station_id`: the ids of the bus and of its station.
- (Node) `type`: the type of station (e.g. `Substation`, `joint`, or a kind of power plant).
- (Node) `voltage`: the voltage (kV; empty if not available).
- (Node) `dc`: whether the bus is a HVDC terminal.
- (Node) `under_construction`: whether the station is under construction.
- (Node) `name` and `name_national`: the name of the station in English and in the national language.
- (Node) `country`: the country code.
- (Node) `tso`: the transmission system operator (where given).
- (Node) `tags`: all the attributes of the map (in hstore format).
- (Node) `latitude` and `longitude`: the position.
- (Node) `generator_types` and `generator_capacities`: the types and capacities (MW; -1 or NaN if unknown) of the generators connected to the bus.
- (Edge) `kind`, `line` (a line or cable): `transformer` or `ac/dc` (a converter).
- (Edge) `lid`: the id of the line or transformer.
- (Edge) `voltage`: the voltage of the line (kV), or the voltages of the two buses of a transformer separated by a semicolon.
- (Edge) `circuits`: the number of circuits of the line (0 for transformers).
- (Edge) `dc`: whether the line is a HVDC line, or the transformer a converter.
- (Edge) `underground`: whether the line is an underground cable.
- (Edge) `under_construction`: whether the line is under construction.
- (Edge) `length`: the length of the line (m; NaN for transformers).
- (Edge) `symbol`: the description of the line in the map (e.g. `380-400 kV Transmission Line, 1 Circuit`).
- (Edge) `tie_line`: whether the line is a tie line between countries.
- (Edge) `tags`: all the attributes of the line in the map (in hstore format).
citations: B. Wiegmans, "GridKit: European and North-American extracts." Zenodo, dataset (2016)
B. Wiegmans, "GridKit extract of ENTSO-E interactive map." Zenodo, dataset (2016)

datasets.name: groningen_freshmen
datasets.description:
Friendship ratings among the freshman cohort majoring in sociology at the University of Groningen (the Netherlands) in 1996-1997, collected by G. van de Bunt, M. van Duijn, F. Stokman and E. Zeggelink, and distributed by T. Snijders with the SIENA software. Except for a few acquaintances from a former school, the students did not know each other at the first measurement, which took place at the start of the academic year during an introduction period on the island of Schiermonnikoog. The networks were measured at five time points, 0, 3, 6, 13 and 35 weeks after the start (`t1` to `t5`); the number of responding students was 38, 25, 28, 18 and 18, respectively, part of the decrease being due to dropout. According to the authors, the data for the last time point are not fully reliable, since some of the questionnaires were handed in before and some after an unexpected event that had a great impact on the students. The data were collected in a similar way as the earlier van de Bunt data of 1994-1995.

A directed edge (i, j) indicates that student i rated their relationship with student j as one of the categories below (unknown persons, and missing answers, do not give rise to edges). Students who did not answer the questionnaire at a given time have no outgoing edges.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `responded`: whether the student answered the questionnaire at this time point.
- (Node) `gender` (1: male, 2: female).
- (Node) `program`: the study program (1: regular 4-year program, 2: 2-year program, followed by older students after higher vocational training).
- (Node) `smoking` (0: no, 2: yes, at parties, 3: 1-3 cigarettes per day, 4: 4-10 per day, 5: more than 10 per day, 9: missing).
- (Node) `soft_drugs`: use of soft drugs (1: no, 2: less than once a month, 3: 1-3 times per month, 4: 1-3 times per week, 5: more than 3 times per week). The node attributes were measured at the first time point.
- (Edge) `relation`: the rated relationship (1: best friendship, 2: friendship, 3: friendly relationship, 4: neutral relationship, 5: troubled relationship).
citations: M. A. J. van Duijn, E. P. H. Zeggelink, M. Huisman, F. N. Stokman, F. W. Wasseur, "Evolution of sociology freshmen into a friendship network." Journal of Mathematical Sociology 27(2-3), 153-191 (2003)

datasets.name: gwas_catalog
datasets.description:
Bipartite networks of genetic variants and the traits they are associated with, from the NHGRI-EBI Catalog of human genome-wide association studies (GWAS Catalog), which curates the associations reported in the published GWAS (with $p < 10^{-5}$) together with the details of the studies.

Nodes are variants (mostly single-nucleotide polymorphisms, identified by their dbSNP rsID, or by their position or another name when they have none) and traits (diseases, measurements and other phenotypes, as terms of the Experimental Factor Ontology, EFO, or of ontologies it imports, such as MONDO, HP, Orphanet or GO). There is an edge between a variant and a trait for each association reported in a study, so that a variant and a trait can be connected by several edges (e.g. associations found in several studies, or for several reported traits that are mapped to the same term). An association can involve several variants (haplotypes, written with `;`, and interactions between variants, written with ` x `) and several traits (a reported trait mapped to several terms): it then gives an edge between each of its variants and each of its traits. Associations that are not mapped to any trait term (up to 2% of the associations of a release) are kept: their trait is a node named by the trait as reported in the study (one node per distinct reported trait, without a term), marked by `is_mapped` false.

There is one network for each year from 2016 to 2026, from the last release of the year in the release archive of the catalog (which starts in March 2016): 2016-12-13, 2017-12-13, 2018-12-27, 2019-12-16, 2020-12-16, 2021-12-22, 2022-12-22, 2023-12-21, 2024-12-19, 2025-12-23 and 2026-10-22 (the latest one).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `is_variant`: whether the node is a variant (otherwise it is a trait).
- (Node) `is_mapped`: whether the node is a trait mapped to an ontology term (false for the traits of the associations that are not mapped to any term, which are named by the reported trait, and for variants).
- (Node) `name`: the identifier of the variant (e.g. `rs4950928`), or the name of the trait term (from the mappings of the reported traits of the same release; the name given in the associations if the term is not there), or the reported trait of the unmapped traits.
- (Node) `trait_uri`: the URI of the trait term (e.g. `http://www.ebi.ac.uk/efo/EFO_0000676`; empty for variants and unmapped traits).
- (Node) `parent_trait`: the category of the trait (e.g. `Cancer`, `Cardiovascular disease`, from the mappings of the reported traits; empty for variants).
- (Node) `chr_id`, `chr_pos`, `region`: the chromosome, the position on the chromosome (in the genome assembly of the release) and the cytogenetic region of the variant (empty for traits, and for variants found only in associations of several variants).
- (Node) `mapped_gene`: the genes mapped to the variant by the catalog (genes containing the variant, or the nearest upstream and downstream genes).
- (Node) `context`: the functional class of the variant (e.g. `intron_variant`).
- (Edge) `study`: the accession of the study (e.g. `GCST000177`).
- (Edge) `pubmed_id`: the PubMed identifier of the publication of the study.
- (Edge) `date_added`: the date at which the association was added to the catalog (as Unix time).
- (Edge) `reported_trait`: the trait as reported in the study.
- (Edge) `snps`: all the variants of the association, as given by the catalog.
- (Edge) `risk_allele`: the strongest variant and risk allele (e.g. `rs4950928-G`; `?` if the allele is unknown).
- (Edge) `risk_allele_frequency`: the frequency of the risk allele in the controls (NaN if not given).
- (Edge) `p_value`: the reported $p$-value of the association; `p_value_mlog`: $-\log_{10}$ of the $p$-value; `p_value_text`: additional information about the $p$-value (e.g. the subgroup).
- (Edge) `or_beta`: the reported odds ratio, or the beta coefficient (NaN if not given); `ci_text`: the 95% confidence interval, and the unit of the beta coefficient.
citations: M. Cerezo, E. Sollis, Y. Ji, E. Lewis, A. Abid, K. O. Bircan, P. Hall, J. Hayhurst, S. John, A. Mosaku, et al., "The NHGRI-EBI GWAS Catalog: standards for reusability, sustainability and diversity." Nucleic Acids Research 53, D998-D1005 (2025)

datasets.name: hacker_news
datasets.description:
Networks of the discussions on Hacker News, the news aggregation and discussion website of the startup accelerator Y Combinator, from its first item in October 2006 to the end of July 2026, from the complete archive of the items of the site (stories, comments, polls and jobs) published on Hugging Face by Open Index, a mirror of the official Hacker News API (via the ClickHouse public dataset). There are two networks:

- `replies`: each node is a user, and a directed edge from user $i$ to user $j$ is a comment of $i$ replying to an item (a story, a comment, a poll or a job posting) of $j$, with one edge per comment (a multigraph). Users replying to themselves give self-loops.
- `discussions`: a bipartite network of users and stories (including polls and job postings), where an edge connects a user to a story if the user commented somewhere in the discussion of the story (the tree of the comments below it), weighted by the number of comments. Only the users and stories with such comments are included.

Items deleted by their authors or by the moderators have no author in the data: the comments that are deleted, or that reply to a deleted item, are left out of `replies`, and the deleted comments are left out of `discussions` (the comments in a discussion below a deleted comment are kept). Comments killed by the moderators or flagged by users ("dead") are included and marked. Comments whose parent item is not in the archive are left out. The texts of the items, the URLs of the stories and the poll options are not included. The archive is updated continuously; the data are those of a pinned revision (of 23 August 2026), and the last, incomplete month (August 2026) is left out.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the user name, or, in `discussions`, the title of the story (for stories).
- (Node) `is_user` (`discussions` only): whether the node is a user (otherwise a story).
- (Node) `item` (`discussions` only): the item number of the story (-1 for users), as in its address `https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=<item>`.
- (Node) `author` (`discussions` only): the user name of the author of the story (empty for users).
- (Node) `kind` (`discussions` only): `story`, `poll` or `job` (empty for users).
- (Node) `score` (`discussions` only): the score (points) of the story (0 for users).
- (Node) `time` (`discussions` only): the submission time of the story, in Unix time (-1 for users).
- (Edge) `time`: in `replies`, the time of the comment; in `discussions`, the time of the first comment of the user in the discussion; in Unix time.
- (Edge) `comment` (`replies` only): the item number of the comment.
- (Edge) `parent` (`replies` only): the item number of the item replied to.
- (Edge) `story` (`replies` only): the item number of the story at the root of the discussion.
- (Edge) `dead` (`replies` only): whether the comment is dead (killed by the moderators or flagged).
- (Edge) `weight` (`discussions` only): the number of comments of the user in the discussion.
citations: Open Index, "Hacker News - Complete Archive." Hugging Face dataset (2026)

datasets.name: hamburg_cell
datasets.description:
Time series of networks of relationships among 34 individuals, from the John Jay & ARTIS Transnational Terrorism Database (JJATT). The JJATT data treat specific attacks as endpoints, and depict the evolution of the relations among the individuals directly or indirectly associated with them; here, the Hamburg cell of Al-Qaeda, which included several of the perpetrators of the 11 September 2001 attacks in the United States ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburg_cell)). The data were coded from open sources (e.g. court documents, news reports and books), and were made available in matrix form by the UCINET datasets collection (University of Manchester).

Nodes are individuals (labeled by their JJATT identifier in `name`), and each time-period network contains the relationships present in that period (networks named `YYYY_1` and `YYYY_2` refer to the first and second halves of year YYYY). The edge property `weight` gives the strength of the tie: 1 = acquaintances or distant family ties (interaction limited to radical organization activities), 2 = friends or moderately close family ties (including co-workers and roommates), operational or organizational leadership, or operational ties (e.g. having worked closely together on a bombing), 3 = close friends or family, tight-knit operational cliques. A few ties in the 1997-2006 networks have the value 4, which is not described in the source documentation. The source matrices are meant to be symmetric; in the few cases where the two directions differ, the tie with the larger value is used. The JJATT tie-start, tie-end and operation matrices, which use undocumented codes, are not included.[^ucinet]

[^ucinet]: Description obtained in part from the [UCINET datasets page](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/datasets/covert-networks/hamburg-cell-911-2001).
citations: S. Atran, M. Sageman, et al., "John Jay & ARTIS Transnational Terrorism Database (JJATT)." John Jay College of Criminal Justice (2009)

datasets.name: hamsterster
datasets.description:
Social networks of the users of hamsterster.com, a social website for hamster (and other small pet) owners, in which each user profile is a pet, as crawled and distributed by KONECT:

- `full`: friendships and family links between the users. Each node is a user, and an undirected edge connects two users who are friends, or whose profiles belong to the same household (the edge property `family` tells which). The users have the metadata of their profiles.
- `households`: the family links (links between profiles of the same household) only, from a separate KONECT dataset, whose user indices are not those of `full`, and without metadata. It has 4,032 links, while `full` has 4,097 family links.

KONECT also distributes the friendships alone (`petster-friendships-hamster` and `petster-hamster-friend`, identical up to the numbering of the users); they are not included as separate networks, since they are the edges of `full` that are not family links.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `full`: `name`, the name of the pet; `joined`, the date the profile was created; `species`, e.g. `Hamster (Syrian)`; `coloring`; `gender`; `birthday`; `age` (as given, e.g. `49 months` or `Gone to Hamster Heaven`); `hometown`; `favorite_toy` and `favorite_food` (all as given in the profile; empty for the 5 users without metadata). The data also have a field for the favorite activity, which is left out, since it is identical to the favorite toy for all users (an error of the data).
- (Edge) `family` (`full` only): whether the edge is a family link (otherwise a friendship).
citations: J. Kunegis, "Hamsterster full network dataset." KONECT, the Koblenz Network Collection (2017)
J. Kunegis, "KONECT -- The Koblenz Network Collection." Proceedings of the 22nd International Conference on World Wide Web Companion, 1343-1350 (2013)

datasets.name: harry_potter_support
datasets.description:
Peer support among 64 students of Hogwarts in the first six Harry Potter books by J. K. Rowling, coded by G. Bossaert and N. Meidert from the e-books, and distributed by T. Snijders with the SIENA software. Each book narrates one school year. A tie was coded when a student voluntarily gave another student one of four types of support: emotional support, instrumental help, information, or praise. Only interactions between two living students attending Hogwarts at the same time were coded. Of the 80 students mentioned in the series, 16 were excluded because the time they entered or left Hogwarts is not known. According to the authors, the networks are quite heterogeneous over time.

A directed edge (i, j) in network `bookN` indicates that student i supported student j in book N. The diagonal entries of the source matrices (some of which are nonzero) are ignored.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the character.
- (Node) `schoolyear`: the year the student entered Hogwarts.
- (Node) `gender` (1: male, 2: female).
- (Node) `house` (1: Gryffindor, 2: Hufflepuff, 3: Ravenclaw, 4: Slytherin).
- (Node) `present`: whether the student attended Hogwarts during the book, according to the composition change file of the data set.
citations: G. Bossaert, N. Meidert, "'We are only as strong as we are united, as weak as we are divided'. A dynamic analysis of the peer support networks in the Harry Potter books." Open Journal of Applied Sciences 3(2), 174-185 (2013)

datasets.name: haslemere
datasets.description:
Temporal network of physical proximity among residents of the town of Haslemere (Surrey, England), collected with the "BBC Pandemic" mobile phone app for the BBC Four documentary "Contagion! The BBC Four Pandemic" (2018). Volunteers installed the app, which recorded their GPS location about every five minutes during three days, from Thursday 12 to Saturday 14 October 2017. Kissler et al. kept the 469 users who logged a location in Haslemere in at least six different hours, aggregated each user's locations into five-minute time bins (filling the bins without data with the last recorded location, or with the user's home location at the start), and computed the distances between all pairs of users in each bin. To protect the users' privacy, only the bins between 07:00 and 22:55 (British Summer Time) of each day were released (576 bins), without the locations.

Nodes are users of the app, and each edge is an encounter, i.e. two users within 50 m of each other during one five-minute time bin, so that two users are connected by as many edges as the number of time bins in which they were close. The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `id`: the anonymous identifier of the user (from 1 to 469).
- (Edge) `time` (edges): the start of the five-minute time bin, in Unix time.
- (Edge) `distance` (edges): the distance between the two users in that time bin, rounded to the meter.
citations: S. M. Kissler, P. Klepac, M. Tang, A. J. K. Conlan, J. R. Gog, "Sparking 'The BBC Four Pandemic': Leveraging citizen science and mobile phones to model the spread of disease." bioRxiv 479154 (2018)
P. Klepac, S. Kissler, J. Gog, "Contagion! The BBC Four Pandemic - The model behind the documentary." Epidemics 24, 49-59 (2018)

datasets.name: hens
datasets.description:
The "peck order" of a flock of 32 White Leghorn hens studied by A. M. Guhl in 1946. According to the author, temporal changes are rare: once a hen dominates another, the pattern persists. The data were distributed by L. C. Freeman on his network data page at the University of California, Irvine (no longer online), from which this version was obtained via the Internet Archive.

A directed edge (i, j) indicates that hen i can peck hen j.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the label of the hen. The source file lists only 21 labels for the 32 hens; as prescribed by the file format, they are assigned to the first 21 hens, and the remaining 11 hens have empty labels.
citations: A. M. Guhl, "Social behavior of the domestic fowl." Technical Bulletin 73, Kansas State College, Agricultural Experiment Station, Manhattan, Kansas (1953)

datasets.name: heroin_dealing_nyc
datasets.description:
Directed network of communication among 38 members of a large heroin distribution organization in New York City in the 1990s, reconstructed by Natarajan (2006) from the transcripts of telephone conversations intercepted by police wiretaps. Nodes are individuals (vertex property `name`, anonymized), and a directed edge indicates communication (flow of information) from one person to the other. Data distributed by the UCINET datasets collection (University of Manchester).[^ucinet]

[^ucinet]: Description obtained in part from the [UCINET datasets page](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/datasets/covert-networks/heroin-dealing-natarajan).
citations: M. Natarajan, "Understanding the structure of a large heroin distribution network: A quantitative analysis of qualitative data." Journal of Quantitative Criminology 22(2), 171-192 (2006)

datasets.name: heterophilous_graphs
datasets.description:
Four of the networks assembled by Platonov et al. as benchmarks for node classification on graphs in which connected nodes tend to have different labels ("heterophily"), as distributed in their repository:

- `roman_empire`: the words of the English Wikipedia article "Roman Empire" (from the dump of 1 March 2022), one of the longest articles of Wikipedia. Each node is one occurrence of a word in the text, and two words are connected if they follow each other in the text, or if they are connected in the dependency tree of their sentence (as parsed by spaCy). The network is thus a chain with syntactic shortcuts. Each word is labeled with its syntactic role (as given by spaCy): the 17 most frequent roles are separate classes, and all the others form an 18th class.
- `amazon_ratings`: products of Amazon (books, music CDs, DVDs and VHS tapes), from the Amazon product co-purchasing metadata of SNAP (2006), connected if they are frequently bought together. The network is the largest connected component of the 5-core of the co-purchasing network. Each product is labeled with its average rating by reviewers, grouped into five classes.
- `questions`: users of the question-answering website Yandex Q who are interested in the topic "medicine", connected if one of them answered a question of the other between September 2021 and August 2022. Each user is labeled by whether they remained active (their account was neither deleted nor blocked) at the end of that period.
- `minesweeper`: a synthetic network, inspired by the game Minesweeper, and not derived from any real data: a regular 100 x 100 grid, in which each cell is connected to its (up to eight) neighbors, horizontally, vertically and diagonally. A random 20% of the cells are "mines", which is the label to predict. The node features of the benchmark give the number of mines among the neighbors of each cell, but only for a random half of the cells (for the other half it is marked as unknown), and they are kept as a property.

The edges are undirected. For the three real networks, the data do not include the words, products and users themselves (the text of the words, the product identifiers and the user names are not given), and the labels are given only as class indices: their meaning (e.g. which syntactic role, or which rating range, a class stands for) is not given. The node features of these benchmarks (averages of fastText embeddings of the words, or of the descriptions of products and users, with 300 dimensions) are left out, since they are derived data that would make the network files much larger; the only exception is the indicator of the users of `questions` without a description, kept as a property. The train, validation and test splits of the benchmarks are also left out. The fifth network of the benchmark, `tolokers`, is the entry `tolokers`.

The node indices are those of the source data. The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `label`: the class of the node, an index from 0 (the syntactic role for `roman_empire`, from 0 to 17, where 17 groups the less frequent roles; the rating class for `amazon_ratings`, from 0 to 4; for `questions`, 1 if the user was no longer active and 0 otherwise; for `minesweeper`, 1 if the cell is a mine and 0 otherwise).
- (Node) `has_description` (`questions` only): whether the user has a profile description.
- (Node) `row`, `column` (`minesweeper` only): the position of the cell in the grid, from 0 to 99.
- (Node) `neighbor_mines` (`minesweeper` only): the number of mines among the neighbors of the cell, as given by the node features (from 0 to 4, or 5 for five or more), or -1 if it is unknown.
citations: O. Platonov, D. Kuznedelev, M. Diskin, A. Babenko, L. Prokhorenkova, "A critical look at the evaluation of GNNs under heterophily: Are we really making progress?" International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR) (2023)

datasets.name: hetionet
datasets.description:
Hetionet is a heterogeneous network ("hetnet") of biomedical knowledge, built by Himmelstein et al. for Project Rephetio, which predicted new uses of existing drugs. It integrates data from 29 public resources (e.g. Entrez Gene, Gene Ontology, DrugBank, SIDER, Disease Ontology, Uberon, Reactome, WikiPathways, LINCS L1000, Bgee, MEDLINE topic co-occurrence), and contains nodes of 11 kinds: genes (20,945), biological processes (11,381), side effects (5,734), molecular functions (2,884), pathways (1,822), compounds (1,552, approved small-molecule drugs), cellular components (1,391), symptoms (438), anatomical structures (402), pharmacologic classes (345) and diseases (137). This is version 1.0 of the network.

The edges are of 24 kinds (metaedges), each a relation between nodes of two given kinds, e.g. a compound *treats* a disease, a gene *participates* in a pathway, an anatomical structure *expresses* a gene, or a gene *regulates* another gene. A directed edge from node $i$ to node $j$ means that $i$ has the relation to $j$ (the source and target nodes of the data); only the relation *regulates* (between genes) is directional, while the others are symmetric relations, stated in the order of the kinds of their nodes. Pairs of nodes may be connected by several edges of different kinds.

Some edges are "unbiased", i.e. come from systematic, genome-wide data (e.g. high-throughput experiments), rather than from the literature, which is biased towards well-studied genes. The original content of Hetionet is released into the public domain (CC0), but the integrated resources have their own licenses, recorded for each node and edge where known; some of them restrict the use of their data, e.g. to noncommercial purposes (CC BY-NC 4.0 for DrugBank, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 for SIDER), and for some resources without a license, the authors obtained permission to include their data.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `kind`: the kind of the node (`Gene`, `Compound`, `Disease`, ...).
- (Node) `identifier`: the identifier of the node in its source resource (e.g. the Entrez Gene id of a gene, the DrugBank id of a compound, the Disease Ontology id of a disease).
- (Node) `name`: the name of the node.
- (Node) `source`: the resource of the node.
- (Node) `license`: the license of the node's data.
- (Node) `url`: a web page of the node in its source resource (empty if absent).
- (Node) `description` and `chromosome`: the description of a gene, and the chromosome where it is located (empty for other nodes).
- (Node) `inchikey` and `inchi`: the InChIKey and InChI chemical identifiers of a compound (empty for other nodes).
- (Node) `mesh_id` and `bto_id`: the Medical Subject Headings and BRENDA Tissue Ontology identifiers of an anatomical structure (empty for other nodes or if absent).
- (Node) `class_type`: the type of a pharmacologic class (empty for other nodes).
- (Edge) `kind`: the relation (`treats`, `participates`, `regulates`, ...); together with the kinds of its nodes, it gives the kind of the edge (metaedge).
- (Edge) `sources`: the resources that the edge comes from.
- (Edge) `license`: the license of the edge's data (empty if not given).
- (Edge) `unbiased`: whether the edge comes from systematic, unbiased data.
- (Edge) `urls`: web pages of the evidence for the edge (empty if absent).
- (Edge) `pubmed_ids`: the PubMed identifiers of the publications supporting a compound-gene binding (empty if absent).
- (Edge) `actions`: the actions of a compound on the gene it binds (e.g. `inhibitor`, `agonist`; empty if absent).
- (Edge) `affinity_nm`: the binding affinity of a compound and a gene, in nanomolar (NaN if absent).
- (Edge) `similarity`: the chemical similarity (Dice coefficient of extended connectivity fingerprints) of two compounds that resemble each other (NaN for other edges).
- (Edge) `z_score`: the consensus z-score of the up- or downregulation of a gene by a compound in LINCS L1000 (NaN for other edges).
- (Edge) `log2_fold_change`: the log2 fold change of the up- or downregulation of a gene by a disease (NaN for other edges).
- (Edge) `method`: the LINCS L1000 method for the regulation of genes (`measured` or `imputed`; empty for other edges).
- (Edge) `subtypes`: the kinds of perturbation of a gene that regulate another (e.g. `knockdown downregulates`; empty for other edges).
citations: D. S. Himmelstein, A. Lizee, C. Hessler, L. Brueggeman, S. L. Chen, D. Hadley, A. Green, P. Khankhanian, S. E. Baranzini, "Systematic integration of biomedical knowledge prioritizes drugs for repurposing." eLife 6, e26726 (2017)

datasets.name: hf_model_tree
datasets.description:
The genealogy of the machine learning models on the Hugging Face Hub, as of March 11, 2025, from the "Model Atlas" of Horwitz, Kurer, Kahana, Amar and Hoshen. Each node is a model repository of the Hub (with weight files), and a directed edge from model u to model v means that v is a base model of u, i.e. that u was derived from v, e.g. by fine-tuning, as an adapter (e.g. LoRA), by quantization, or by merging several models. The network is a directed acyclic graph (mostly a forest of trees, since merged models have several base models).

The base models are those declared in the model cards (`base_model`), completed by the authors with base models extracted from the texts of the model cards with regular expressions, and with over 1,000 manual annotations; they removed loops and self-loops, and the models without weight files. Base models that were removed from the Hub but are still referenced by other models are included as "virtual" models (relation `virtual_recovered`, without attributes). The data derive from the `hub-stats` dataset of Hugging Face. Thirteen models appear twice in the file, with different (annotated) base models; their rows are merged.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `model_id`: the id of the model repository (`<author>/<name>`; its page is `https://huggingface.co/<model_id>`).
- (Node) `author`.
- (Node) `created`: the time of creation (Unix time; -1 if unknown).
- (Node) `last_modified`: the time of the last modification (Unix time; -1 if unknown).
- (Node) `downloads`: the number of downloads of the last 30 days, and `downloads_all_time` (-1 if unknown).
- (Node) `pipeline_tag`: the task of the model (e.g. `text-generation`).
- (Node) `license`.
- (Node) `architectures`: the model class (e.g. `LlamaForCausalLM`).
- (Node) `dataset`: a training dataset given in the tags (`unknown` if none).
- (Node) `tags`: the tags of the repository (as a Python list).
- (Node) `base_model_relation`: the relation of the model to its base models (`finetune`, `adapter`, `quantized`, `merge`, `finetune_adapter`, `finetune_quantized`; `source` for some original models; `unknown` if not declared; `unknown_readme_extracted` and `unknown_annotated` for base models extracted from the model card or annotated by the authors; `virtual_recovered` for virtual models; two values separated by a comma for the merged duplicates). Missing values are `unknown`, as in the data.
- (Edge) `relation`: the relation of the model to its base model (as `base_model_relation` of the model).
- (Edge) `base_index`: the position of the base model in the list of base models of the model (from 0).
citations: E. Horwitz, N. Kurer, J. Kahana, L. Amar, Y. Hoshen, "Charting and Navigating Hugging Face's Model Atlas." arXiv:2503.10633 (2025)

datasets.name: high_tech_company
datasets.description:
A multiplex network of relationships among the 21 managers of a small high-tech manufacturing company in the United States, collected by D. Krackhardt with questionnaires as part of his study of cognitive social structures. The version here, distributed by M. De Domenico, has three directed layers:

- advice (190 edges): $(i, j)$ means that manager $i$ reported going to manager $j$ for advice;
- friendship (102 edges): $(i, j)$ means that manager $i$ considers manager $j$ a friend;
- reports to (20 edges): $(i, j)$ means that manager $i$ reports to manager $j$ in the formal hierarchy of the company.

In the original study, each manager was also asked to describe the advice and friendship relations among all other managers; these perceptions are not included here.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `nodeAge`: age of the manager, in years.
- (Node) `nodeTenure`: length of service in the company, in years.
- (Node) `nodeLevel`: level in the corporate hierarchy: 1 = CEO, 2 = vice president, 3 = manager.
- (Node) `nodeDepartment`: department, coded 1 to 4 (0 for the CEO, who is not in a department).
- (Edge) `layer` (edges): 1 = advice, 2 = friendship, 3 = reports to; the graph property `layer_key` maps these numbers to layer names.
- (Edge) `weight` (edges): always 1.
citations: D. Krackhardt, "Cognitive social structures". Social Networks (1987), 9, 104-134.

datasets.name: highschool
datasets.description:
Friendships among the 73 boys of a small high school in Illinois, from the research reported by J. S. Coleman (1964). In the fall of 1957 and in the spring of 1958, the boys were asked: "What fellows here in school do you go around with most often?" The data were distributed by L. C. Freeman on his network data page at the University of California, Irvine (no longer online), from which this version was obtained via the Internet Archive.

A directed edge (i, j) indicates that boy i named boy j in at least one of the two surveys. Three boys neither named nor were named by anyone, and are isolated nodes.

The network has the following properties:

- (Edge) `weight`: the number of surveys in which i named j (1 or 2).
- (Edge) `fall_1957` and `spring_1958`: whether i named j in the survey of fall 1957 and spring 1958, respectively.
citations: J. S. Coleman, "Introduction to Mathematical Sociology." Free Press, New York (1964)

datasets.name: hint_interactomes
datasets.description:
Networks of high-quality protein-protein interactions of ten organisms, from HINT (High-quality INTeractomes), a database of the Yu lab (Cornell University) that compiles interactions from several public databases and filters them for quality. An interaction is included if it was found in a high-throughput (HT) study that validated its screen with orthogonal assays (studies are inspected manually), or if it was reported by at least two independent small-scale, literature-curated (LC) publications. Post-translational modifications are not considered interactions. This is the HINT release of July 2026.

For each organism there are two networks. In both, nodes are proteins (UniProt entries), and an undirected edge connects two proteins that interact:

- `<organism>_binary`: binary interactions, i.e. direct physical contacts between two proteins (e.g. from yeast two-hybrid assays).
- `<organism>_cocomplex`: co-complex associations, i.e. two proteins found in the same protein complex (e.g. by affinity purification followed by mass spectrometry), which need not be in direct contact. Not available for rice.

The organisms are: `human` (*Homo sapiens*), `mouse` (*Mus musculus*), `rat` (*Rattus norvegicus*), `fly` (*Drosophila melanogaster*), `worm` (*Caenorhabditis elegans*), `yeast` (*Saccharomyces cerevisiae*), `fission_yeast` (*Schizosaccharomyces pombe*), `arabidopsis` (*Arabidopsis thaliana*), `rice` (*Oryza sativa*) and `ecoli` (*Escherichia coli*). Self-loops are proteins that interact with themselves (homodimers).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the UniProt accession of the protein.
- (Node) `gene`: the gene name (empty if not available).
- (Edge) `evidence` (edges): the supporting evidence, a list separated by "|" of entries "PubMed ID:PSI-MI method code:HT or LC:binary or co-complex".
- (Edge) `in_pdb` (edges): whether the interaction is supported by a structure in the Protein Data Bank.
- (Edge) `pdb_ids` (edges): the PDB structures and chains supporting the interaction (empty if none).
citations: J. Das, H. Yu, "HINT: High-quality protein interactomes and their applications in understanding human disease." BMC Systems Biology 6, 92 (2012)

datasets.name: hiv_cluster_1984
datasets.description: A network of sexual contacts between 40 men with the acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS), from the cluster of early cases in the USA investigated by the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) by Auerbach et al. (1984), as distributed by KONECT (from P. Holme's collection). This network is the origin of the phrase "patient zero", for the patient who links several groups of cases (labeled "patient O", for "out of California", in the study). Each node is a patient, and an undirected edge connects two patients who reported a sexual contact. The data identify the patients only by indices (the labels and cities of the study are not included). Only the largest connected component is included.
citations: D. M. Auerbach, W. W. Darrow, H. W. Jaffe, J. W. Curran, "Cluster of cases of the acquired immune deficiency syndrome: Patients linked by sexual contact." The American Journal of Medicine 76(3), 487-492 (1984)
J. Kunegis, "KONECT -- The Koblenz Network Collection." Proceedings of the 22nd International Conference on World Wide Web Companion, 1343-1350 (2013)

datasets.name: hiv_transmission
datasets.description:
A network of sexual, drug-use, needle-sharing and social contacts among people at high risk of HIV and other sexually transmitted infections, from the "Network Metastudy Project" archive assembled by M. Morris and R. Rothenberg, which combines the data of eight network studies conducted in North America between 1988 and 2001 (with some interviews up to 2003): Colorado Springs Project 90, Bushwick (Brooklyn), Atlanta Urban, Flagstaff (rural Arizona), Atlanta Antiviral, Houston, Baltimore SHIELD, and Manitoba. The studies recruited participants with different designs (e.g. contact tracing from infected persons, chain-link referral from targeted seeds, egocentric and saturation sampling), and in each interview the respondent named their contacts in a recent time window (typically 6 months). Some studies were longitudinal, with repeated interviews of the same persons.

Nodes are persons (respondents and the contacts they named), and each directed edge is a record of a tie, pointing from the person who named it to the person named (the "egodyads" file of the archive; the file of ties among alters is not included). The same pair of persons can be connected by several edges, e.g. for different types of tie or different interviews. Since the person identifiers of the source data are only unique within each study, persons are identified here by their study and ID, and the nodes and edges of each study can be selected with the property `STUDYNUM`.

In all properties, the code -9 means "out of design" and -8 means "not asked", and missing dates are given as 01-Jan-1900. The properties are taken from the variables of the source data, as described in its codebook:

- Vertex properties: `name` (person ID within the study), `STUDYNUM` (study, with the codes given below), and the attributes of the person recorded in the dyad records: `testdat` (date of lab test), `SG` (sample generation, i.e. number of steps from a seed of the chain-referral sampling; 0 = seed), `NTYPE` (1 = respondent, 2 = eligible, 3 = alter), `FRSTTYP` (whether the person first appeared as respondent or alter), `IDKNOWN` (identity known), `LOCAL` (resided in the study jurisdiction), `RACE` (1 = American Indian, 2 = Black, 3 = Asian/Pacific Islander, 4 = White, 5 = other), `ETHN` (Hispanic), `SEX`, `ORIENT` and `BEHAV` (self-reported and behavioral sexual orientation), `OCCPRES` and `OCCCENS` (occupational prestige and census code), `OCC` and `OCCLOC` (occupation and its location), `AGE`, `YOB` (year of birth), `MARIT` (marital status), `EDUC` (educational attainment), indicators of being a sex worker (`PRO`), pimp (`PIMP`), client of sex workers (`JOHN`), drug dealer (`DEALER`), drug manufacturer (`DRUGMAN`), thief (`THIEF`), retired (`RETIRED`), housewife (`HWIFE`), on disability (`DISABLE`), unemployed (`UNEMP`) or homeless (`STREETS`), lab test results for gonorrhea, chlamydia, syphilis, HIV and hepatitis B (`GONO`, `GONOEV`, `CHLAM`, `CHLAMEV`, `SYPH`, `SYPHEV`, `HIV`, `HBV`), self-reported history of these infections (`GONOHX`, `CHLAMHX`, `SYPHHX`, `HIVHX`), `LINENUM` (order of elicitation), `FRSTYR` (study year of first appearance), `SOURCES` (number of persons that named this person) and `BACKFIL` (whether demographic information was backfilled from self-reports).
- Edge properties: `TIETYPE` (mode of connection: 0 = other, 1 = social, 2 = drug, 3 = sexual, 4 = needle), `DYADKEY` and `DYADTYPE` (0 = direct partner, otherwise suspect/associate), `RECENT` (1 = tie within the interview window, 0 = at any time in the past), `FREQ` (frequency of contact: 1 = once or twice, 2 = a few times, 3 = steady), `intdate`, `begdate`, `enddate` and `testdate` (dates of the interview, of the first and most recent contact, and of the respondent's lab test), `YEAR` (year of interview), `STDYYEAR` (years since the base interview), `ITER` (interview number), `WINDOW` (time window used to elicit contacts), `SAMPLE` (sampling scheme: 1 = saturation, 2 = contact tracing, 4 = chain-link tracing, 6 = egocentric, 7 = three-link chain and mixed), `CHAIN` and `NET_TYPE` (sampling chain identifiers), `RELTYPE` (relationship of the contact to the respondent, e.g. "FRIEND"), `STUDYNUM` (study: 1 = Colorado Springs Project 90, 2 = Bushwick, 3 = Atlanta Urban, 4 = Flagstaff, 5 = Atlanta Antiviral, 6 = Houston, 7 = Baltimore SHIELD, 8 = Manitoba), `RID` (ID of the interviewed respondent, which usually but not always coincides with the person who named the contact), and the attributes of that respondent at the time of the interview, with the same names and codes as the vertex properties above.
citations: M. Morris and R. Rothenberg. "HIV Transmission Network. Metastudy Project: An Archive of Data From Eight Network Studies, 1988–2001.” Inter-university Consortium for Political and Social Research (2011).

datasets.name: hollywood_actors
datasets.description:
Three snapshots, from 2009, 2011 and 2021, of the collaboration network of movie actors, built by the Laboratory for Web Algorithmics (LAW) from the Internet Movie Database (IMDb). Nodes are people whose participation in a movie (or other production listed in IMDb) is characterized as "actor", "actress" or "self", and an undirected edge connects two of them if they appeared together in at least one production. It is thus a one-mode projection of the bipartite actor-production network, and edges are unweighted (the number of joint appearances is not given).

LAW distributes the first two as `hollywood-2009` and `hollywood-2011`, and the third, built from the IMDb datasets (https://www.imdb.com/interfaces/), as `imdb-2021`: the series was renamed because the graphs contain people outside of Hollywood, and to make the data source clearer.

Sizes: `2009` has 1,139,905 actors and 113,891,327 arcs in the symmetric LAW graph (i.e. about 57 million undirected edges); `2011` has 2,180,759 actors and 228,985,632 arcs (about 114.5 million undirected edges); `2021` has 2,996,317 actors and 10,739,291 arcs (about 5.4 million undirected edges). LAW does not explain why the 2021 graph is so much sparser than the earlier ones.

Vertex property: `name`, the IMDb name of the person (`2009` and `2011`), or `imdb_id`, the IMDb identifier of the person (e.g. `nm0000001`; `2021`, for which LAW gives only identifiers).
citations: P. Boldi and S. Vigna, "The WebGraph framework I: compression techniques." Proceedings of the 13th International Conference on World Wide Web (WWW 2004), 595-602 (2004).

P. Boldi, M. Rosa, M. Santini, and S. Vigna, "Layered label propagation: a multiresolution coordinate-free ordering for compressing social networks." Proceedings of the 20th International Conference on World Wide Web (WWW 2011), 587-596 (2011).

datasets.name: hollywood_golden_age
datasets.description:
Collaborations among 55 actors representative of the Golden Age of Hollywood (1930-1959), compiled by A. Clauset from the full text of the Internet Movie Database (IMDb), downloaded in September 2011. The actors are those listed on the Wikipedia page "Classical Hollywood cinema" at that time (not a scientific selection). Each network is the directed actor-actor projection of the underlying actor-movie network, aggregated over decades from 1909 to 2009.

A directed edge from actor A to actor B exists if both appear in the billing of the same movie, and B has an equal or better (smaller) billing position than A; actors without a listed billing position are assumed to have the lowest rank. If only one of the 55 actors appears in a movie, a self-loop is added if the actor had the first billing position. Archive footage, unconfirmed and suspended entries, TV and video movies, and television series were excluded. Only movies released strictly within each decade are counted (the first period, 1909-1919, is eleven years long).

Two versions are provided:

- `s0`: edges follow the rule above exactly.
- `s2`: billing positions i and j are considered equal if |i-j| <= 2, as a heuristic to account for the fact that the billing order of women and men was not informative of their status during this period, and that small differences in billing may not be meaningful.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the actor name, as in IMDb.
- (Edge) `decade`: the first year of the decade (1909, 1920, ..., 2000).
- (Edge) `count`: the number of movies in that decade giving rise to the edge. Pairs of actors can be connected by several edges, one for each decade.
citations: D. Taylor, S. A. Myers, A. Clauset, M. A. Porter, P. J. Mucha, "Eigenvector-based centrality measures for temporal networks." Multiscale Modeling & Simulation 15(1), 537-574 (2017)

datasets.name: hollywood_music
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of the collaborations between composers of film scores and producers in Hollywood, compiled by R. R. Faulkner. It includes the 62 producers who produced at least five films in Hollywood between 1964 and 1976, and the 40 composers who created the soundtrack of their films. An edge connects a composer to a producer if the composer created the music for at least one film by the producer in that period, and is weighted by the number of such films. One of the composers (R. Lasalle) has no edges in the source data. The data were distributed on the Pajek datasets page of the book *Exploratory Social Network Analysis with Pajek* (de Nooy, Mrvar and Batagelj), from which this version was obtained.[^icon]

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the producer (or production company) or composer.
- (Node) `is_producer`: whether the node is a producer (otherwise a composer).
- (Node) `top_composer`: whether the composer is one of the five top composers, each of whom earned 1.5% or more of the total income of Hollywood film composers in the 1960s and 1970s.
- (Edge) `weight`: the number of films by the producer for which the composer created the music.

[^icon]: Description obtained in part from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.
citations: R. R. Faulkner, "Music on Demand: Composers and Careers in the Hollywood Film Industry." Transaction Books, New Brunswick (1983)
W. de Nooy, A. Mrvar, V. Batagelj, "Exploratory Social Network Analysis with Pajek." Cambridge University Press (2005)

datasets.name: host_pathogen_eid2
datasets.description:
Networks of interactions between species, where one (the "cargo") is likely to be a pathogen, parasite or other organism carried by the other (the "carrier", e.g. a host), and of the countries where species were found, from the ENHanCEd Infectious Diseases database (EID2) of Wardeh et al. The interactions were automatically extracted from the metadata of the NCBI Nucleotide sequence database (the organism of a sequence and its host) and from the PubMed literature database (publications mentioning both species, or a species and a location), based on evidence published between 1950 and 2012. Organism names were disambiguated with the NCBI Taxonomy database, and only organisms identified at the species or subspecies level are included; locations were disambiguated using GeoNames. The datasets were extracted from EID2 in 2015.

- `species`: directed network of species, where an edge goes from a cargo species to a carrier species. A species may appear both as a cargo and a carrier. A few cargo-carrier pairs appear more than once in the data, and are kept as parallel edges.
- `locations`: bipartite network of species and countries, where an edge connects a species to a country where it was found. Some records refer to a region (first-level administrative division) of the country, in which case it is stored as an edge property, so that a species and country can be connected by more than one edge.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: in `species`, the species name; in `locations`, the species or country name.
- (Node) `cargo_class`, `carrier_class` (`species`): the taxonomic classification of the species when it appears as a cargo (e.g. "Bacteria", "Virus", "Helminth") or as a carrier (e.g. "Human", "Domestic", "Mammal", "Higher Plants"), or empty if the species does not appear in that role. The carrier category "Domestic" comprises 46 species of domesticated mammals and birds in Europe, so that a few species have different cargo and carrier classifications.
- (Node) `is_country` (`locations`): whether the node is a country (otherwise a species).
- (Node) `classification` (`locations`): the taxonomic classification of the species (empty for countries).
- (Edge) `sequences`: the number of nucleotide sequences supporting the interaction.
- (Edge) `publications`: the number of PubMed publications supporting the interaction. The lists of sequence and publication identifiers in the source data are not included.
- (Edge) `region` (`locations`): the region of the country (empty if the record refers to the country as a whole).
citations: M. Wardeh, C. Risley, M. K. McIntyre, C. Setzkorn, M. Baylis, "Database of host-pathogen and related species interactions, and their global distribution." Scientific Data 2, 150049 (2015)

datasets.name: hosts_lepidoptera
datasets.description:
Bipartite network of butterflies and moths (Lepidoptera) and the plants their caterpillars feed on, from HOSTS, the database of the world's lepidopteran hostplants of the Natural History Museum, London, compiled by G. S. Robinson and collaborators from the published literature and from museum collections. The database is no longer updated; the data are those published on the NHM Data Portal in 2023.

Nodes are lepidopteran taxa (species or subspecies, or genera when the species is not given) and hostplant taxa (species, subspecies or varieties, or genera when the species of the plant is not given), and an edge connects a lepidopteran to a hostplant for each record of the database, i.e. each location (a country, or a biogeographic region) in which the caterpillar was recorded on the plant, so that a pair can be connected by several edges. Taxa are identified by their names as given in the database (genus, species and subspecies).

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `is_lepidoptera`: whether the node is a lepidopteran (otherwise it is a hostplant).
- (Node) `name`: the name of the taxon (genus, species and subspecies or variety).
- (Node) `family`, `genus`, `species`, `subspecies`: the family and the parts of the name of the taxon.
- (Node) `author` (lepidoptera): the author of the name of the lepidopteran taxon.
- (Edge) `hosts_id`: the identifier of the record.
- (Edge) `location`: the country or biogeographic region of the record.
- (Edge) `damage`: the parts of the plant fed upon by the caterpillar, and how (e.g. `on leaves`, `in fruits`, `in stems`; empty if not given).
- (Edge) `lab_rearing`: `Y` if the record comes from rearing in a laboratory (`?` if this is uncertain; empty otherwise).
citations: G. S. Robinson, P. R. Ackery, I. Kitching, G. W. Beccaloni, L. M. Hernández, "HOSTS - a Database of the World's Lepidopteran Hostplants." Natural History Museum (2023)

datasets.name: howler_monkeys
datasets.description:
Co-observations among 17 mantled howler monkeys (Alouatta palliata) on Barro Colorado Island (Panama). The monkeys were assigned to troops by J. W. Froehlich and R. W. Thorington Jr., and S. J. C. Gaulin recorded ad libitum co-observations of sets of individuals, analyzed by L. D. Sailer and S. J. C. Gaulin (1984) to study the definition of social groups from proximity data. The data were distributed by L. C. Freeman on his network data page at the University of California, Irvine (no longer online), from which this version was obtained via the Internet Archive.

An undirected edge connects two monkeys that were observed together.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the number of the monkey.
- (Node) `troop`: the troop (A, B, C or D) to which the monkey was assigned by Froehlich and Thorington.
- (Node) `male`: whether the monkey is male (monkeys 5, 9, 13, 16, 21, 25 and 27).
- (Node) `age`: the age class (monkeys 12 and 26 were juveniles, monkey 9 was an infant, and the others were adults).
- (Edge) `weight`: the number of co-observations.
citations: L. D. Sailer, S. J. C. Gaulin, "Proximity, sociality, and observation: The definition of social groups." American Anthropologist 86(1), 91-98 (1984)

J. W. Froehlich, R. W. Thorington Jr., "The genetic structure and socioecology of howler monkeys (Alouatta palliata) on Barro Colorado Island." In E. G. Leigh, A. S. Rand (eds.), Ecology of Barro Colorado Island: Seasonal Rhythms and Long Term Changes in a Tropical Forest, Smithsonian Press (1981)

datasets.name: hudong
datasets.description:
Directed networks of links between the articles of the Chinese online encyclopedia Hudong (互动百科, later Baike.com), from the Zhishi.me project of Chinese linked open data, as distributed by KONECT:

- `internal_links`: hyperlinks; an edge from article A to article B means that A links to B;
- `related_pages`: "related pages"; an edge from article A to article B means that A lists B as related.

The data identify the articles only by indices (their titles are not included). Some articles link to themselves. The hyperlinks of the encyclopedia Baidu Baike, from the same project, are the entry `baidu`.
citations: X. Niu, X. Sun, H. Wang, S. Rong, G. Qi, Y. Yu, "Zhishi.me - Weaving Chinese Linking Open Data." The Semantic Web - ISWC 2011, Lecture Notes in Computer Science 7032, 205-220 (2011)
J. Kunegis, "KONECT -- The Koblenz Network Collection." Proceedings of the 22nd International Conference on World Wide Web Companion, 1343-1350 (2013)

datasets.name: human_brains
datasets.description:
Structural brain networks (connectomes) of human subjects, estimated from diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) and structural MRI scans by tractography, as distributed by the NeuroData group at Johns Hopkins University. Edges are undirected and weighted by the number of reconstructed fiber tracts (streamlines) connecting two brain regions or voxels. The scans come from several publicly available data sets (some of them from the Consortium for Reliability and Reproducibility, CoRR), many of which include repeated scan sessions of the same subjects: `BNU1`, `BNU3`, `HNU1`, `Jung2015`, `KKI2009`, `MRN114`, `MRN1313`, `NKIENH` and `SWU4`.

There are two kinds of networks:

- Region-level networks, computed with version 0.0.11 of the `ndmg` pipeline (2016), named `<dataset>_<subject>_<session>_DTI_<atlas>`. Nodes are the regions of a brain parcellation (atlas), and the same scan is available for several atlases: anatomical parcellations such as `AAL` (116 regions), `desikan` (70 regions), `HarvardOxford`, `JHU`, `Talairach`, `CPAC200`, `slab907` and `slab1068`, and the `DSxxxxx` parcellations, which divide the brain into approximately xxxxx regions of similar size (from `DS00071` with about 70 regions to `DS72784` with about 72,800 regions).
- Voxel-level networks ("big graphs") computed with the earlier Magnetic Resonance One-Click Pipeline (MROCP), named with the suffix `-bg` or `_biggraphs`. Nodes are voxels of $1\,\mathrm{mm}^3$ in the MNI152 template brain, and edges connect voxels traversed by the same fiber tract. Only the largest connected component of these networks was retained. These networks are very large (millions of nodes and over $10^8$ edges).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Edge) `weight` (edges): the number of fiber tracts connecting the two nodes.
- (Node) `spatial_id` (voxel-level networks): the index of the voxel in the MNI152 1 mm template.
- (Node) `_graphml_vertex_id`: the node identifier in the source file (for region-level networks, the region label in the atlas).
citations: W. G. Roncal et al., "MIGRAINE: MRI Graph Reliability Analysis and Inference for Connectomics." Global Conference on Signal and Information Processing (GlobalSIP), 313-316 (2013).

datasets.name: human_connectomes_multiscale
datasets.description:
Structural connectomes of the human brain at five scales, for 84 healthy subjects from two data sets: 44 subjects of the test-retest data set of the Human Connectome Project (HCP), aged 22 to 35, and 40 healthy controls of the Lausanne psychosis cohort (UL), with a mean age of about 25. They were computed by Barjuan et al. from diffusion weighted magnetic resonance images with tractography. Nodes are gray matter regions of the multiscale Lausanne parcellation (Cammoun et al. 2012), without the brainstem, and an undirected edge indicates that white matter fibers connect the two regions, weighted by the fiber density.

There is one network per subject and scale, named `<data set>_<subject>_layer<scale>`, e.g. `hcp_05_layer0` or `ul_17_layer4`, where the subjects are numbered from `00` to `43` (HCP) and `00` to `39` (UL), and the scales (layers) are, from finest to coarsest, `layer0` (about 1014 regions), `layer1` (462), `layer2` (233), `layer3` (128) and `layer4` (82). The regions of finer scales subdivide those of coarser ones; their names consist of the name of the anatomical region of the coarsest scale followed by numbers. In three HCP networks of the finest scale (`hcp_11_layer0`, `hcp_20_layer0`, `hcp_32_layer0`) one region is missing. The UL networks contain self-loops (fibers within the same region), the HCP networks do not, as in the upstream files. The coordinates of the HCP and UL data sets are in different reference spaces.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the region (e.g. `rh_lateralorbitofrontal_9`, where `rh` and `lh` stand for the right and left hemisphere).
- (Node) `x`, `y`, `z`: the coordinates of the center of mass of the region.
- (Edge) `weight` (edges): the fiber density between the two regions.
- (Edge) `fiber_length` (edges): the mean length of the fibers between the two regions.
citations: L. Barjuan, J. Soriano, M. Á. Serrano, "Optimal navigability of weighted human brain connectomes in physical space." NeuroImage 297, 120703 (2024)
L. Barjuan, M. Zheng, M. Á. Serrano, "The multiscale self-similarity of the weighted human brain connectome." PLOS Computational Biology 21, e1012848 (2025)

datasets.name: human_cranium
datasets.description:
Weighted networks of correlations among cranial measurements of modern humans, from the craniometric data set of W. W. Howells. The data were compiled by M. Cantor and collaborators for a study of nestedness across levels of biological organization, and are distributed in the repository of that study (files `ind_craniam.txt`, `ind_craniaf.txt` and `ind_craniaeurope.txt`). Following the approach of S. I. Perez and collaborators for detecting modules in complex phenotypes, nodes are 44 anatomically defined cranial measurements (distances between craniometric landmarks), and an undirected edge connects every pair of measurements, weighted by the Pearson correlation coefficient between them, which can be negative (all networks are complete graphs with signed weights). The measurements are not identified in the source data, but are the same, and in the same order, in the three networks.

- `males`: correlations among the 44 measurements averaged per population, over 30 recent modern human populations distributed worldwide (1,367 male individuals).
- `females`: the same, for 1,823 female individuals.
- `europe_males`: correlations among the measurements of 164 individual males from three European samples (Norse, medieval Oslo; Zalavar, Hungary; and Berg, Carinthia, Austria).

The edges have the property `weight`, the Pearson correlation coefficient.
citations: W. W. Howells, "Cranial variation in man: A study by multivariate analysis of patterns of difference among recent human populations." Papers of the Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology 67, 1-259 (1973)
S. I. Perez, M. A. M. de Aguiar, P. R. Guimarães Jr., S. F. dos Reis, "Searching for Modular Structure in Complex Phenotypes: Inferences from Network Theory." Evolutionary Biology 36, 416-422 (2009)

M. Cantor, M. M. Pires, F. M. D. Marquitti, R. L. G. Raimundo, E. Sebastián-González, P. P. Coltri, S. I. Perez, D. R. Barneche, D. Y. C. Brandt, K. Nunes, F. G. Daura-Jorge, S. R. Floeter, P. R. Guimarães Jr., "Nestedness across biological scales." PLoS ONE 12(2), e0171691 (2017)

datasets.name: human_disease_comorbidity
datasets.description:
Networks of comorbidity between diseases, from the Human Disease Network (HuDiNe) project of Hidalgo, Blumm, Barabási and Christakis. The data were compiled from the Medicare inpatient claims (MedPAR records) of 1990 to 1993 of the elderly Americans (aged 65 or older) enrolled in Medicare and alive during the whole period: 32,341,347 hospital claims of 13,039,018 patients. Each claim lists a primary and up to nine secondary diagnoses, coded according to the ICD-9-CM classification. Nodes are diseases (ICD-9 codes), and an undirected edge connects two diseases that were diagnosed together in at least one patient, with properties giving the number of such patients and the strength of the comorbidity, measured by the relative risk and by the $\phi$-correlation (Pearson's correlation for binary variables).

Diseases are defined at two levels of resolution of the ICD-9 codes: 3 digits (the main disease categories; networks ending in `_3`), and up to 5 digits (the full codes, which add details to the category; networks ending in `_5`). For each resolution there are networks for all patients (`all`), and for patients of each sex (`female`, `male`), race (`white`, `black`), and their combinations (e.g. `black_female`). Of the 13,039,018 patients, 7,598,529 are female and 5,440,490 male, and 11,745,416 are white and 983,095 black.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the ICD-9-CM code of the disease (e.g. "250" or "250.00").
- (Node) `prevalence`: the number of patients diagnosed with the disease in the population of the network.
- (Edge) `cooccurrence` (edges): the number of patients diagnosed with both diseases.
- (Edge) `relative_risk` (edges): the relative risk $RR_{ij} = C_{ij} N / (P_i P_j)$, where $C_{ij}$ is the co-occurrence, $P_i$ and $P_j$ the prevalences and $N$ the number of patients, i.e. the ratio between the observed co-occurrence and the one expected if the diseases were independent.
- (Edge) `relative_risk_low`, `relative_risk_high` (edges): the lower and upper limits of the 99% confidence interval of the relative risk.
- (Edge) `phi` (edges): the $\phi$-correlation between the two diseases.
- (Edge) `t` (edges): the $t$-test value of the $\phi$-correlation.

The files are obtained from the Internet Archive, the only remaining copies. Two of them are truncated there, so that their networks lack the disease pairs whose first code is larger than the last one included: `white_5` ends after the pairs of code 585, and `black_5` after those of code 890.1 (the incomplete last line of each file is left out).

The data are free for academic use only (according to the source, for non-academic purposes C. A. Hidalgo should be contacted).
citations: C. A. Hidalgo, N. Blumm, A.-L. Barabási, N. A. Christakis, "A dynamic network approach for the study of human phenotypes." PLoS Computational Biology 5(4), e1000353 (2009)

datasets.name: human_gut_microbiome_compendium
datasets.description:
Bipartite networks of human gut microbiome samples and the bacterial and archaeal taxa found in them, from the Human Microbiome Compendium of Abdill et al., which gathers 168,464 publicly available 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing samples of the human gut (mostly stool) from 482 studies in the Sequence Read Archive, processed with a uniform pipeline (DADA2), and classified with the SILVA reference database.

Nodes are samples and taxa, and an edge connects a sample to each taxon observed in it, with the number of reads of the taxon in the sample as weight.

- `v1.0.0`, `v1.0.1`, `v1.1.2`: the taxonomic tables at the genus level of the releases of the compendium, where the amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) are classified with SILVA 138.0 (`v1.0.0`, also published as versions 0.1.0 and 0.2.0), with SILVA 138.0 and corrections of the names of 2,881 ASVs whose taxonomic levels were inferred incorrectly (`v1.0.1`), and with SILVA 138.2, with all the ASVs of the compendium classified together (`v1.1.2`, the table of the releases 1.1.0 to 1.1.2). Taxa are named by their lineage down to the genus (unclassified levels are `NA`).
- `asv` (release 1.1.2): the samples and the ASVs (exact sequence variants, shared across studies), from the per-study ASV tables, with the classification of each ASV with SILVA 138.2.
- `gg2` (release 1.1.2): the samples and the features of the classification with Greengenes2 (2022.10, closed-reference at 99% identity), with their Greengenes2 taxonomy (the 5,018 samples of the table without any classified reads are isolated nodes).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `is_sample`: whether the node is a sample (otherwise it is a taxon).
- (Node) `name`: the identifier of the sample (`<BioProject>_<SRA run>` in the genus tables, the SRA sample accession in `asv` and `gg2`), or the taxon (lineage in the genus tables, ASV identifier in `asv`, feature identifier in `gg2`).
- (Node) `taxonomy` (`asv`, `gg2`): the lineage of the ASV or feature (empty for samples).
- (Node) `srs`, `srr`, `project`: the SRA sample and run accessions and the BioProject of the sample.
- (Node) `pubdate`, `total_bases`, `instrument`: the publication date of the run in the SRA (as Unix time), the number of sequenced bases, and the sequencing instrument.
- (Node) `geo_loc_name`, `iso`, `region`: the location of the sample as given in BioSample, its country (ISO 3166-1 code, or `unknown`), and its world region.
- (Node) `amplicon`, `bead_beating`, `kit`, `sample_type`, `condition`, `subjects`, `publication`: the metadata of the study of the sample (annotated by the authors of the compendium): the amplified region of the 16S gene, whether the DNA extraction used mechanical lysis, the extraction kit, the material, the condition studied, the population, and the link to the publication.
- (Node) `tags`: the attributes of the sample in BioSample, as `tag=value` strings.
- (Edge) `count`: the number of reads of the taxon in the sample.
citations: R. J. Abdill, S. P. Graham, V. Rubinetti, M. Ahmadian, P. Hicks, A. Chetty, D. McDonald, P. Ferretti, E. Gibbons, M. Rossi, A. Krishnan, F. W. Albert, C. S. Greene, S. Davis, R. Blekhman, "Integration of 168,000 samples reveals global patterns of the human gut microbiome." Cell 188, 1100-1118.e17 (2025)

datasets.name: human_interactome_2014
datasets.description:
Networks of interactions between human proteins from the proteome-scale map of the human binary interactome of Rolland et al. (2014), from the Center for Cancer Systems Biology (CCSB) at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. In both networks, nodes are proteins (identified by the genes that encode them), and an undirected edge represents a binary (direct) protein-protein interaction. Self-loops are proteins that interact with themselves.

- `HI-II-14`: the binary interactions detected by a systematic high-throughput yeast two-hybrid (Y2H) screen of the pairwise combinations of the products of about 13,000 protein-coding genes ("Space II" of the human ORFeome), each screened twice and verified by pairwise retesting (13,944 interactions among 4,303 proteins).
- `Lit-BM-13`: binary interactions curated from the literature, supported by at least two pieces of evidence (multiple publications or methods), assembled by the authors for comparison with the systematic map (11,045 interactions among 5,545 proteins).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `entrez_id`: the Entrez Gene ID.
- (Node) `name`: the HGNC gene symbol.

Other data sets of the CCSB Interactome Database are in the entries `interactome_vidal` (the earlier human binary map CCSB-HI1/HI-I-05), `yeast_interactome_ccsb` (the yeast binary Y2H maps CCSB-YI1, Ito core and Uetz screen, and literature-curated and gold-standard reference sets), `collins_yeast` (the yeast co-complex associations of Collins et al.) and `celegans_interactomes` (the *C. elegans* interactome networks).
citations: T. Rolland, M. Taşan, B. Charloteaux, S. J. Pevzner, Q. Zhong, N. Sahni, et al., "A proteome-scale map of the human interactome network." Cell 159(5), 1212-1226 (2014)

datasets.name: human_interactomes_ndex
datasets.description:
Networks of human genes (or their protein products; a few networks are of other species) from many databases of molecular interactions, from the two collections of harmonized networks used to evaluate how well molecular networks recover disease genes and other biological knowledge, by Huang et al. (2018) and by Wright et al. ("State of the interactomes", 2025), both from the Ideker lab, and deposited on the Network Data Exchange (NDEx). In each network, the nodes are genes (the interactions of the sources were mapped to them), identified by their NCBI Gene identifiers in the networks of Wright et al. and by their HGNC symbols in those of Huang et al., and an edge is an interaction or functional association between two genes, with the attributes given by the source (e.g. scores, evidence, publications). The sources are of many kinds: curated protein-protein interactions (e.g. BioGRID, IntAct, HPRD, DIP, MINT), systematic screens (e.g. HuRI, BioPlex, Hein, Youn, Havugimana, Wan, ProteomeHD), integrated and predicted interactions (e.g. STRING, HumanNet, GeneMANIA, GIANT, FunCoup, ConsensusPathDB, HIPPIE, iRefIndex, IID, Mentha, APID, InBioMap, PrePPI, hu.MAP), pathways and signaling (e.g. Reactome, ReactomeFI, PathwayCommons, PID, SIGNOR, SignaLink, SPIKE, PhosphoSitePlus), and regulation (TFLink); and the Parsimonious Composite Networks (PCNet) built by the authors from the networks that perform best, keeping the interactions supported by at least two of them.

The networks are named by the collection and the source:

- `huang2018_<source>`: the 21 networks evaluated by Huang et al. (versions of 2017), with the composite networks `huang2018_full_composite` (the union of all of them) and `huang2018_pcnet` (PCNet 1.0), and two variants without text-mined interactions (`huang2018_humannet_no_textmining`, `huang2018_string_no_textmining`). These networks have no edge attributes.
- `pcnet_1.1`, `pcnet_1.2`, `pcnet_1.3`, `pcnet_1.4`: later versions of PCNet, with updated gene identifiers.
- `wright2025_<source>`: the 45 networks of the sources evaluated by Wright et al. (versions of 2016-2024), with the composite networks `wright2025_pcnet_2.0`, `wright2025_pcnet_2.1` and `wright2025_pcnet_2.2`, and the variants `wright2025_string_cocitation_free` and `wright2025_humannet_cocitation_free` without the interactions supported only by co-citation.
- `wright2025_interactome_dependencies`: the small directed network of the dependencies between the interactomes evaluated by Wright et al.: the nodes are the interactomes, and an edge goes from an interactome to each interactome whose data it incorporates (the edge attributes `source` and `target` give the full names of the incorporated and of the incorporating interactome, and `source_category` and `category` their kinds).

The same authors deposited networks of other species and of specific studies, which are also included:

- `pcnet_mouse`, `pcnet_rat`: PCNet (NDEx version 1.1) mapped to the genes of mouse and rat with the HCOP orthology database; `string_fly`: STRING of the fruit fly (with the combined score as edge `weight`); `string_11.5_rat_all`, `string_11.5_rat_mid`, `string_11.5_rat_high`: STRING v11.5 of the rat, with all links, and with those of combined score above 400 (medium confidence) and 700 (high confidence). The nodes of these networks are named by the gene symbols of the species.
- `wright2023_bmi_*`: the networks of the study of the body mass index (BMI) of Wright et al. (2023), subnetworks of PCNet 1.3 of the genes near the genes of the genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of BMI in humans and rats, found by network propagation (network colocalization, NetColoc): `wright2023_bmi_conserved` (genes near the GWAS genes of both species), `wright2023_bmi_human_specific`, `wright2023_bmi_rat_specific` (near those of one species but not the other) and `wright2023_bmi_expanded` (near those of either species); and the directed hierarchies of gene systems (communities found with HiDeF, named by enriched GO terms) of the conserved and the expanded network, `wright2023_bmi_conserved_systems_map` and `wright2023_bmi_expanded_systems_map`, whose nodes are the systems, with an edge from each system to its subsystems.
- `alzheimers_disease`, `autism_spectrum_disorder`, `bipolar_disorder` (NDEx user snwright, 2025): networks of the genes near the genes of common and of rare variants associated with Alzheimer's disease, autism spectrum disorder and bipolar disorder, found by network colocalization (unlisted networks on NDEx, linked from their systems maps); and their directed hierarchies of gene systems `alzheimers_disease_systems_map`, `autism_spectrum_disorder_systems_map`, `bipolar_disorder_systems_map`, whose nodes are the systems, with their member genes (`hcx_members`, NCBI Gene identifiers; `hgnc`, gene symbols), and with an edge from each system to the larger system that contains it (as stored in NDEx).

The direction of the interactions of directed sources (e.g. kinase to substrate in PhosphoSitePlus, transcription factor to target in TFLink) is kept as the order of the two ends of the edges, but the interaction networks are undirected; only the systems maps and `wright2025_interactome_dependencies` are directed. The attributes `name` (e.g. `A2M_APP`) and `Entrez_A`, `Entrez_B` of the edges, which repeat the genes of the edge, are left out.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the node in NDEx: the gene symbol (in `pcnet_1.4`, `alzheimers_disease`, `autism_spectrum_disorder` and `bipolar_disorder`, the NCBI Gene identifier; in the systems maps, the name or identifier of the system; in `wright2025_interactome_dependencies`, the short name of the interactome).
- (Node) `represents`: the identifier of the gene in NDEx, e.g. `ncbigene:2` or `hgnc.symbol:A2M` (empty if not given).
- (Node) `entrez_id`: the NCBI Gene identifier of the gene, from `represents`, or from `name` in the networks without `represents` (-1 if it is not an NCBI Gene identifier).
- (Node) Other attributes, as given in NDEx, e.g. `geneid` (the NCBI Gene identifier), `hgnc_symbol`; in the BMI networks, the network proximity scores `nps_h`, `nps_r`, `nps_hr` (to the human, rat and both GWAS genes) and `human_seed`, `rat_seed` (whether the gene is a GWAS gene); in the systems maps, the member genes and sizes of the systems (e.g. `community_genes`, `community_size`, `hcx_members`), their names, and the fractions of the kinds of genes they contain.
- (Edge) `interaction`: the kind of interaction, as given in NDEx (e.g. `interacts-with`).
- (Edge) Other attributes, as given by each source in NDEx, with their names in lower case and with underscores (e.g. `score`, `experimental_system`, `publication_source`, `supporting_databases`; columns named only by their number in the source file are named `column_<number>`); missing values are empty, -1 or NaN.
- (Graph) `ndex_uuid`: the identifier of the network in NDEx.
- (Graph) `ndex_<attribute>`: the attributes of the network in NDEx, e.g. `ndex_name`, `ndex_version`, `ndex_description`, `ndex_reference`, `ndex_prov_wasderivedfrom` (the source of the data).
citations: S. N. Wright, S. Colton, L. V. Schaffer, R. T. Pillich, C. Churas, D. Pratt, T. Ideker, "State of the interactomes: an evaluation of molecular networks for generating biological insights." Molecular Systems Biology 21, 1-29 (2025)
J. K. Huang, D. E. Carlin, M. K. Yu, W. Zhang, J. F. Kreisberg, P. Tamayo, T. Ideker, "Systematic Evaluation of Molecular Networks for Discovery of Disease Genes." Cell Systems 6, 484-495 (2018)

S. N. Wright, B. S. Leger, S. B. Rosenthal, S. N. Liu, T. Jia, A. S. Chitre, O. Polesskaya, K. Holl, J. Gao, R. Cheng, A. Garcia Martinez, A. George, A. F. Gileta, W. Han, A. H. Netzley, C. P. King, A. Lamparelli, C. Martin, C. L. St. Pierre, T. Wang, H. Bimschleger, J. Richards, K. Ishiwari, H. Chen, S. B. Flagel, P. Meyer, T. E. Robinson, L. C. Solberg Woods, J. F. Kreisberg, T. Ideker, A. A. Palmer, "Genome-wide association studies of human and rat BMI converge on synapse, epigenome, and hormone signaling networks." Cell Reports 42, 112873 (2023)
D. Pratt, J. Chen, R. Pillich, V. Rynkov, A. Gary, B. Demchak, T. Ideker, "NDEx 2.0: A Clearinghouse for Research on Cancer Pathways." Cancer Research 77, e58-e61 (2017)

datasets.name: human_microbiome
datasets.description:
