A multiplex network of microbial taxa across 18 sites of the human body, assembled by M. De Domenico and J. Biamonte from the data of Ding and Schloss (2014), who analyzed the 16S rRNA gene sequences of the bacterial communities sampled from healthy adults by the Human Microbiome Project, and found that the communities of each body site fall into a few distinct community types. Nodes are 305 operational taxonomic units (OTUs, groups of similar sequences that stand for bacterial taxa), and each layer corresponds to a body site. An undirected edge in a layer connects two taxa that are associated (interact) in the microbial communities of that body site; how the associations were inferred from the abundance data is not documented by the authors. There are 4,433 edges, at most one per pair of taxa and layer.

The layers are: `Anterior_nares` (55 edges), `Buccal_mucosa` (114), `Hard_palate` (241), `Keratinized_gingiva` (46), `L_Antecubital_fossa` (524), `L_Retroauricular_crease` (63), `Mid_vagina` (81), `Palatine_Tonsils` (483), `Posterior_fornix` (33), `R_Antecubital_fossa` (335), `R_Retroauricular_crease` (49), `Saliva` (324), `Stool` (244), `Subgingival_plaque` (590), `Supragingival_plaque` (359), `Throat` (442), `Tongue_dorsum` (324) and `Vaginal_introitus` (126).

The taxa are identified only by the last two levels of their taxonomic classification, so several nodes share the same label (e.g. 23 nodes are labeled `Clostridia(100);Clostridiales(100);`).

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name` and `nodeLabel`: the last two levels of the taxonomic classification of the OTU, each followed by the confidence of the classification in percent in parentheses (e.g. `Prevotellaceae(100);Prevotella(100);`).
- (Edge) `layer`: the body site (numbered from 1 to 18 in the order listed above; the names are stored in the graph property `layer_key`).
- (Edge) `weight`: which is always 1.
citations: T. Ding and P. D. Schloss, "Dynamics and associations of microbial community types across the human body." Nature 509, 357-360 (2014)
M. De Domenico and J. Biamonte, "Spectral Entropies as Information-Theoretic Tools for Complex Network Comparison." Physical Review X 6, 041062 (2016)

datasets.name: human_populations_microsat
datasets.description:
Weighted network of genetic differentiation among 62 human populations worldwide, from microsatellite genotypes: 43 populations of the HGDP-CEPH Human Genome Diversity Panel studied by N. A. Rosenberg and collaborators, and 19 Native American populations studied by S. Wang and collaborators, in both cases restricted to populations with more than 10 unrelated individuals. The data were compiled by M. Cantor and collaborators for a study of nestedness across levels of biological organization, and are distributed in the repository of that study (file `mep_human_Rst.txt`). Nodes are populations, and an undirected edge connects every pair of populations (the network is a complete graph), weighted by their pairwise genetic differentiation R<sub>ST</sub> (Slatkin, 1995), computed from the variance of microsatellite allele sizes (678 autosomal microsatellite loci). R<sub>ST</sub> is 0 for genetically identical populations and grows with differentiation; small negative values arise from sampling error. Note that the documentation of the source describes the weights as the genetic similarity 1 - R<sub>ST</sub>, but the file contains R<sub>ST</sub> itself (with zeros on the diagonal). The populations are not identified in the source data.

The edges have the property `weight`, the pairwise R<sub>ST</sub>.
citations: N. A. Rosenberg, J. K. Pritchard, J. L. Weber, H. M. Cann, K. K. Kidd, L. A. Zhivotovsky, M. W. Feldman, "Genetic Structure of Human Populations." Science 298, 2381-2385 (2002)

N. A. Rosenberg, S. Mahajan, S. Ramachandran, C. Zhao, J. K. Pritchard, M. W. Feldman, "Clines, Clusters, and the Effect of Study Design on the Inference of Human Population Structure." PLoS Genetics 1(6), e70 (2005)
S. Wang et al., "Genetic Variation and Population Structure in Native Americans." PLoS Genetics 3(11), e185 (2007)
M. Slatkin, "A measure of population subdivision based on microsatellite allele frequencies." Genetics 139(1), 457-462 (1995)

M. Cantor, M. M. Pires, F. M. D. Marquitti, R. L. G. Raimundo, E. Sebastián-González, P. P. Coltri, S. I. Perez, D. R. Barneche, D. Y. C. Brandt, K. Nunes, F. G. Daura-Jorge, S. R. Floeter, P. R. Guimarães Jr., "Nestedness across biological scales." PLoS ONE 12(2), e0171691 (2017)

datasets.name: human_symptoms_diseases
datasets.description:
Networks of human diseases and their symptoms, extracted from the biomedical literature by Zhou et al. The authors extracted the 7,109,429 records of the PubMed bibliographic database with at least one disease or symptom term (according to the Medical Subject Headings, MeSH) in their MeSH metadata field, yielding 4,442 disease terms and 322 symptom terms; 849,103 records contain at least one disease and one symptom term.

- `symptoms_diseases`: bipartite network of symptoms and diseases, where an edge connects a symptom and a disease that co-occur in the MeSH metadata of at least one PubMed record (322 symptoms and 4,219 diseases). The edges are weighted by the number of co-occurrences, and by their term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF), which discounts symptoms that occur with many diseases: w = W log(N / n), where W is the number of co-occurrences, N the number of diseases and n the number of diseases in which the symptom appears. From these weights, the authors computed the symptom similarity between diseases as the cosine similarity of their vectors of symptom weights, which defines the (dense) human symptoms disease network (HSDN).
- `disease_links`: network of the 133,106 links of the HSDN between 1,596 diseases that have both significant shared symptoms and shared genes or protein-protein interactions (as reported in Supplementary Data 4 of the paper), weighted by their symptom similarity.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the MeSH term.
- (Node) `pubmed_occurrence`: the number of PubMed records with the term in their MeSH metadata.
- (Node) `is_symptom` (`symptoms_diseases`): whether the node is a symptom (otherwise a disease). 248 terms are listed both as diseases and as symptoms in the source data, and correspond to two different nodes.
- (Edge) `occurrence` (`symptoms_diseases`): the number of PubMed records in which the symptom and disease co-occur.
- (Edge) `tfidf` (`symptoms_diseases`): the TF-IDF weight of the association.
- (Edge) `weight` (`disease_links`): the symptom similarity of the two diseases.
citations: X. Zhou, J. Menche, A.-L. Barabási, A. Sharma, "Human symptoms-disease network." Nature Communications 5, 4212 (2014)

datasets.name: humannet
datasets.description:
Networks of human genes from HumanNet (Network Biomedicine Lab, Yonsei University, and Marcotte Lab, University of Texas at Austin), in which an edge links two genes that are likely to work in the same biological process (co-functional links), weighted by a log-likelihood score (LLS) of their association. The scores are obtained from a Bayesian framework that measures how well each kind of evidence (protein interactions, co-expression, co-citation, pathway databases, protein domains, genetic interactions, gene neighborhood, phylogenetic profiles, interactions of orthologs in other organisms, ...) recovers known co-functional gene pairs (the gold standard). The component networks, each from one kind of evidence, are integrated into the networks HumanNet-FN (functional network) and the extended networks. The genes are identified by their NCBI Gene (Entrez) identifiers.

The networks of HumanNet v3 (2021) are `v3_xc` (HumanNet-XC, the functional network extended by co-citation), `v3_fn` (HumanNet-FN, integrating the components CX, DB, DP, GI, GN, PG and PI) and the component networks `v3_cc` (co-citation), `v3_cx` (co-expression), `v3_db` (pathway databases), `v3_dp` (protein domain profiles), `v3_gi` (genetic interactions), `v3_gn` (gene neighborhood), `v3_pg` (phylogenetic profiles) and `v3_pi` (protein-protein interactions); `v3_gsp` is the network of the gold standard positive gene pairs (unweighted).

The networks of HumanNet v2 (2018) are `v2_xn` (HumanNet-XN, the fully extended functional network), `v2_xc` (extended by co-citation), `v2_xi` (extended by interologs), `v2_fn` (functional network), `v2_cf` (co-functional network), `v2_pi` (protein-protein interaction network), the component networks `v2_cc` (co-citation), `v2_ce` (co-essentiality), `v2_cx` (co-expression), `v2_db` (pathway databases), `v2_dp` (protein domain profiles), `v2_gn` (gene neighborhood), `v2_ht` (high-throughput protein interactions), `v2_il` (protein interactions transferred from other organisms), `v2_lc` (literature-curated protein interactions), `v2_pg` (phylogenetic profiles), and the networks of human genes derived from the interactions of their orthologs in other organisms (interologs): `v2_ce_ht`, `v2_ce_lc` (high-throughput and literature-curated protein interactions in *C. elegans*), `v2_dm_ht`, `v2_dm_lc` (*D. melanogaster*), `v2_dr_lc` (*D. rerio*), `v2_mm_lc` (*M. musculus*), `v2_sc_gt` (genetic interactions in *S. cerevisiae*), `v2_sc_ht`, `v2_sc_lc` (protein interactions in *S. cerevisiae*), `v2_sc_ts` (3D-structure-based interactions in *S. cerevisiae*), `v2_clf_lc` (*C. lupus familiaris*), `v2_bt_lc` (*B. taurus*), `v2_rn_lc` (*R. norvegicus*) and `v2_gg_lc` (*G. gallus*).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `entrez_id`: the NCBI Gene identifier of the gene.
- (Node) `name`: the gene symbol, as given by HumanNet v3 (empty for the genes of v2 that are not in the v3 networks).
- (Edge) `lls` (all networks but `v3_gsp`): the log-likelihood score of the link.
- (Edge) `score2` (`v2_sc_ht`, `v2_sc_lc`, `v2_sc_ts`): a second score given in the files of these networks, without documentation (slightly lower than `lls`).
citations: C. Y. Kim, S. Baek, J. Cha, S. Yang, E. Kim, E. M. Marcotte, T. Hart, I. Lee, "HumanNet v3: an improved database of human gene networks for disease research." Nucleic Acids Research 50, D632-D639 (2022)
S. Hwang, C. Y. Kim, S. Yang, E. Kim, T. Hart, E. M. Marcotte, I. Lee, "HumanNet v2: human gene networks for disease research." Nucleic Acids Research 47, D573-D580 (2019)

datasets.name: humap_complexes
datasets.description:
Networks of human protein complexes and protein interactions from the three versions of hu.MAP, a map of human protein complexes obtained by integrating mass spectrometry proteomic experiments: hu.MAP 1.0 (2017; more than 9,000 experiments: co-fractionation, and affinity purification of tagged proteins of BioPlex and of Hein et al.), hu.MAP 2.0 (2020/2021; more than 15,000 experiments, adding proximity labeling (BioID), RNA pull-down and further affinity purification data) and hu.MAP 3.0 (2024; more than 25,000 experiments). In each version, a machine learning classifier, trained on known complexes (CORUM in 1.0 and 2.0, the Complex Portal in 3.0), gives the probability that two proteins interact (are in the same complex); the network of these interactions was then clustered, in two stages and with several parameters, to identify the complexes.

The networks are named by the version (`v1_`, `v2_`, `v3_`) and the kind of network:

- `v1_complexes`, `v2_complexes`, `v3_complexes`: bipartite network of proteins and the complexes in which they are members (a protein can be in several complexes): 4,659 complexes in 1.0, 6,965 in 2.0 and 15,326 in 3.0, with the confidence of each complex in 2.0 and 3.0.
- `v1_complex_pairs`, `v3_complex_pairs`: network of the pairs of proteins of the same complexes, weighted by the predicted probability that they interact. (hu.MAP 2.0 does not distribute this network as a file, only within its Cytoscape session; it is left out.)
- `v2_all_pairs`, `v3_all_pairs`: network of all the pairs of proteins for which the classifier gave a prediction (of August 2020 and May 2023), weighted by the predicted probability that they interact; most pairs have a low probability. (hu.MAP 1.0 does not distribute these predictions, only the feature matrix.)

The training and test sets of complexes and interactions, the feature matrices, the enrichment tables and the Cytoscape sessions are left out. The data of hu.MAP 2.0 are kept as given, with their repetitions, which come from proteins (gene identifiers) mapped to the same UniProt accession: 34 complexes of `v2_complexes` list a protein twice (parallel edges), and in `v2_all_pairs` 66,458 pairs of proteins appear twice, with different probabilities, and 21 pairs join a protein to itself (self-loops).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `uniprot`: the UniProt accession of the protein (empty for complexes, and for the proteins of hu.MAP 1.0 without one; in 2.0 and 3.0, the identifier given instead of an accession for a few proteins, e.g. an NCBI Gene identifier).
- (Node) `gene_id` (`v1_*`): the identifier of the protein in hu.MAP 1.0: its NCBI Gene identifier (an Ensembl gene identifier for 40 proteins).
- (Node) `name`: the gene name of the protein (several names separated by `; ` in 3.0; empty if not given, e.g. for the proteins of the `all_pairs` networks that are in no complex), or the identifier of the complex (e.g. `HuMAP2_00000`, `huMAP3_00000.1`; in 1.0, the number of the complex, from 0, in the order of the file).
- (Node) `is_protein` (`*_complexes`): whether the node is a protein (otherwise it is a complex).
- (Node) `confidence` (`v2_complexes`, `v3_complexes`): the confidence of the complex: the number of the most stringent of the clusterings in which it was found, from 1 (extremely high) to 5 (medium) in 2.0, and to 6 (medium) in 3.0 (0 for proteins).
- (Edge) `probability` (`*_pairs`): the probability that the two proteins interact, according to the classifier.
citations: K. Drew, C. Lee, R. L. Huizar, F. Tu, B. Borgeson, C. D. McWhite, Y. Ma, J. B. Wallingford, E. M. Marcotte, "Integration of over 9,000 mass spectrometry experiments builds a global map of human protein complexes." Molecular Systems Biology 13, 932 (2017)

K. Drew, J. B. Wallingford, E. M. Marcotte, "hu.MAP 2.0: integration of over 15,000 proteomic experiments builds a global compendium of human multiprotein assemblies." Molecular Systems Biology 17, e10016 (2021)

S. N. Fischer, E. R. Claussen, S. Kourtis, S. Sdelci, S. Orchard, H. Hermjakob, G. Kustatscher, K. Drew, "hu.MAP3.0: atlas of human protein complexes by integration of >25,000 proteomic experiments." Molecular Systems Biology 21 (2025)

datasets.name: huri
datasets.description:
Networks of binary interactions between human proteins from the Human Reference Interactome (HuRI) mapping project of the Center for Cancer Systems Biology (CCSB) at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, with the Roth, Tavernier and Bader labs (Luck et al. 2020). HuRI is a systematic map of the binary interactome: the products of about 17,500 protein-coding genes ("Space III" of the human ORFeome) were screened pairwise by yeast two-hybrid (Y2H) assays, with three versions of the assay, and the detected pairs were verified by pairwise retesting (with samples validated by orthogonal assays). In all networks, nodes are proteins, identified by the Ensembl gene IDs of the genes that encode them (gene names are not given in these files), and an undirected edge represents a binary (direct) protein-protein interaction; self-loops are proteins that interact with themselves. The files have not changed since 2020.

- `HuRI`: the HuRI map proper, the interactions detected in the screens of Space III (52,548 interactions among 8,272 proteins; the download page gives 52,569 interactions for this dataset).
- `HI-union`: the union of all the systematic binary maps of the CCSB: HuRI, the earlier maps H-I-05 (CCSB-HI1, Rual et al. 2005), Venkatesan-09, Yu-11, HI-II-14 (Rolland et al. 2014) and Yang-16, and the test-space screens of 2019 (all of which are also available separately on the HuRI site).
- `Lit-BM`: binary interactions curated from the literature and supported by at least two pieces of evidence (multiple publications or methods), as updated by Luck et al. for comparison with HuRI.
- `Test_space_screens-19`: the interactions found in the screens of a smaller test space of genes with the assay versions of HuRI, used by Luck et al. to benchmark the screening pipeline.
- `H-I-05`, `Venkatesan-09`, `Yu-11`, `HI-II-14`, `Yang-16`: the earlier systematic maps of the CCSB that make up `HI-union` besides HuRI, each on its own, with the proteins mapped to Ensembl gene IDs as in the other networks: H-I-05 (CCSB-HI1, Rual et al. 2005), the second-generation screens of Venkatesan et al. (2009) and Yu et al. (2011), HI-II-14 (Rolland et al. 2014) and the isoform screens of Yang et al. (2016).

H-I-05 (CCSB-HI1) is also in the entry `interactome_vidal`, and HI-II-14 and Lit-BM-13 in the entry `human_interactome_2014`, with the identifiers of the original publications. The PSI-MI files of the site (with protein isoforms, scores and the screens in which each interaction was found) are not included either.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the Ensembl gene ID.
citations: K. Luck, D.-K. Kim, L. Lambourne, K. Spirohn, B. E. Begg, W. Bian, et al., "A reference map of the human binary protein interactome." Nature 580, 402-408 (2020)

datasets.name: hyperbard
datasets.description:
Bipartite networks of the characters of the 37 plays of William Shakespeare and the groups of characters that are on stage together, one network per play, from the Hyperbard dataset of Coupette, Vreeken and Rieck, built from the TEI XML encoding of the Folger Shakespeare editions, as distributed by XGI-data (the "hg-group-mw" representation of Hyperbard). Each play is divided into consecutive parts during which the set of characters on stage does not change; each part is a node, connected to the characters on stage during it, and carries the act and scene it belongs to and the numbers of lines and tokens (words) spoken during it.

The character co-presence networks of the same plays (weighted by the number of scenes in common) are part of the entry `dracor`.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `is_group`: whether the node is an on-stage group (otherwise a character).
- (Node) `name` (characters): the identifier of the character in the Folger edition (e.g. `Hamlet` or `Ghost`; groups of unnamed characters, e.g. attendants, are identified as in the edition, e.g. `ATTENDANTS.CAESAR`).
- (Node) `index` (groups): the order of the group in the play (from 0).
- (Node) `act`, `scene` (groups): the act and scene of the group (acts 0 and 6 hold the parts before the first act and after the fifth one, e.g. prologues and epilogues).
- (Node) `n_lines`, `n_tokens` (groups): the numbers of lines and tokens spoken while the group is on stage.
- (Graph) `play_type`: the kind of play (`comedy`, `history` or `tragedy`).
citations: C. Coupette, J. Vreeken, B. Rieck, "All the world's a (hyper)graph: A data drama." Digital Scholarship in the Humanities 39(1), 74-96 (2024)
N. W. Landry, M. Lucas, I. Iacopini, G. Petri, A. Schwarze, A. Patania, L. Torres, "XGI: A Python package for higher-order interaction networks." Journal of Open Source Software 8(85), 5162 (2023)

datasets.name: hyves
datasets.description:
A friendship network among users of Hyves, at the time the most popular social networking site in the Netherlands (comparable to Facebook), crawled in December 2010 by Mahsa Mojtahedi at Arizona State University and distributed by the Social Computing Data Repository (originally at Arizona State University, now at Syracuse University). Nodes are users (anonymized), and an undirected edge connects two users who are friends.

The source data list the friendships as lines stating that "user $i$ is friend with user $j$", each friendship only once (no pair of users is listed twice, in either direction), so that each of the 2,777,419 lines is one edge. The node list of the source data contains 1,402,611 users, 19 of which occur in no edge (they are kept as isolated nodes); 81 further users occur only in the edges.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `user_id`: the identifier of the user in the source data.
- (Node) `in_node_list`: whether the user is listed in the node list of the source data.
citations: R. Zafarani, H. Liu, "Social Computing Data Repository at ASU." Arizona State University, School of Computing, Informatics and Decision Systems Engineering (2009)

datasets.name: iceland_sexual_contacts
datasets.description: A network of sexual contacts among homosexual men in Iceland, from a study of sexual networks in relation to the spread of HIV by Haraldsdottir et al. (1992), as distributed by KONECT (from P. Holme's collection). Each node is a person, and an undirected edge connects two persons who had sexual contact. The data identify the persons only by indices. Only the largest connected component is included.
citations: S. Haraldsdottir, S. Gupta, R. M. Anderson, "Preliminary studies of sexual networks in a male homosexual community in Iceland." Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes 5(4), 374-381 (1992)
J. Kunegis, "KONECT -- The Koblenz Network Collection." Proceedings of the 22nd International Conference on World Wide Web Companion, 1343-1350 (2013)

datasets.name: imdb_actors_2004
datasets.description: An undirected network of collaborations among movie actors, based on Internet Movie Database (IMDb) data from 2004. Nodes are actors, and two actors are connected if they appeared together in at least one movie; made-for-TV movies, direct-to-video releases and video game entries were removed. The network is thus a one-mode projection of the actor-movie network, and edges are unweighted (the number of joint movies is not given). The data were preprocessed by H. Jeong and distributed with the textbook "Network Science" by A.-L. Barabási. Nodes are anonymous (labelled consecutively from zero); there are 702,388 node labels and 29,397,908 edges.
citations: A.-L. Barabási, "Network Science." Cambridge University Press (2016).
A.-L. Barabási and R. Albert, "Emergence of scaling in random networks." Science 286(5439), 509-512 (1999).

datasets.name: imdb_movies_2005
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of actors and the movies they appeared in, based on the Internet Movie Database (IMDb), released as the data set of the evolving-graph drawing competition of the 13th International Symposium on Graph Drawing (GD 2005). Nodes are movies and actors, and an edge connects each movie to each of its actors. The network has 428,440 movies and 896,308 actors, connected by 3,792,390 edges; 124,823 movies have no actors in the data (isolated nodes), and 9,927 edges are repeated (an actor listed more than once in the same movie, e.g. in several roles).

Vertex properties: `is_movie`, which marks the movies (the remaining nodes are actors); `name`, the title of the movie or the name of the actor (titles are in the IMDb format, e.g. with leading articles moved to the end, as in "Matrix, The"); `year`, the release year of the movie (0 for actors, or if unknown; a few movies have invalid values, such as 1 or 9006); `genre`, the genre of the movie ("not available" for actors, or if unknown).
citations: Graph Drawing Contest 2005, "Evolving-graph drawing competition: IMDb movie-actor graph." 13th International Symposium on Graph Drawing (GD 2005).

datasets.name: imrich_bibliography
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of authors and works from the bibliography of the book *Product Graphs: Structure and Recognition* by W. Imrich and S. Klavžar. An edge connects an author to a work (paper or book) of which he or she is an author or coauthor. The data were distributed in Pajek format on the Pajek datasets page of V. Batagelj and A. Mrvar, from which this version was obtained.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the author, or the label of the work (as in the reference list of the book).
- (Node) `is_author`: whether the node is an author (otherwise a work).
citations: W. Imrich, S. Klavžar, "Product Graphs: Structure and Recognition." Wiley, New York (2000)

datasets.name: india_bus_routes
datasets.description:
Networks of the bus routes of six major Indian cities, compiled by A. Chatterjee, M. Manohar and G. Ramadurai from the route information published by the public bus operators: Ahmedabad Bus Rapid Transit System (`ahmedabad`), Metropolitan Transport Corporation, Chennai (`chennai`), Delhi Transport Corporation (`delhi`), Andhra Pradesh State Road Transport Corporation, Hyderabad (`hyderabad`), Calcutta State Transport Corporation, Kolkata (`kolkata`), and Brihanmumbai Electricity Supply and Transport, Mumbai (`mumbai`). Nodes are bus stops, and an undirected edge connects two stops that are consecutive on at least one bus route, with `weight` equal to the number of routes that overlap on that link (i.e. that serve the two stops in succession).

In the source files the links are listed as source/target pairs. For Ahmedabad, Delhi and Kolkata, some pairs of stops are listed twice, once in each order and usually with different weights (presumably the numbers of routes in each travel direction); these are kept as parallel edges. Some links are self-loops. The authors treat the networks as undirected, as buses run in both directions.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the bus stop (`ahmedabad`, `delhi`, `hyderabad`, `kolkata`), or its numeric code (`chennai`, `mumbai`), as given in the source files.
- (Edge) `weight`: the number of overlapping routes. One link of `delhi` has no weight in the source file, and has `weight` set to -1.
citations: A. Chatterjee, M. Manohar, G. Ramadurai, "Statistical analysis of bus networks in India." PLoS ONE 11(12), e0168478 (2016)

datasets.name: inploid
datasets.description: Inploid is a social question & answer website in Turkish. Users can follow others and see their questions and answers on the main page. Nodes are users, and a directed edge $(i, j)$ means that user $i$ follows user $j$ (according to the source, the followee exerts influence upon the follower). Each user is associated with a reputability score which is influenced by feedback of others about questions and answers of the user. Each user can also specify interest in topics. The data is crawled in June 2017 and consist of 39,749 nodes and 57,276 directed links between them. In addition, for each user, reputability scores and top five topics are included in the dataset. Usernames and topics are anonymized.
citations: F. Gursoy and D. Gunnec, "Influence maximization in social networks under deterministic linear threshold model", Knowledge-Based Systems (2018)

datasets.name: insee_commuting
datasets.description:
Networks of the commutes of workers between their communes of residence and of work in France, from the population census of the French national statistics institute (INSEE), as published in its "base flux de mobilité: mobilités professionnelles (déplacements domicile - lieu de travail)". The census of each year combines the surveys of five consecutive years (around that year), so that consecutive editions overlap; the flows are estimates (with decimals), based on samples of the households in the communes of 10,000 inhabitants or more, and INSEE warns that flows below 200 workers should be taken as orders of magnitude only. Because the data of a commune are collected over several years, the flows into and out of a commune may not refer to the same year.

There is one network for each edition, from 2006 to 2023, named after its year (e.g. `2023`); each uses the communes of the geography of its time (communes are frequently merged), so the nodes of different networks do not necessarily correspond. Nodes are the communes of metropolitan France and the overseas departments (with the municipal arrondissements instead of the communes of Paris, Lyon and Marseille), and the places of work abroad, which are given as foreign communes (or regions, mostly near the borders, e.g. `GENEVE` or `LUXEMBOURG`), or as a single node `ZZZZZ` for the workers whose place of work abroad was not given. A directed edge goes from the commune of residence to the place of work, weighted by the number of employed persons of 15 years or older that commute between them; workers who work in their commune of residence are counted by self-loops. Only the pairs of places with a nonzero flow are included, and only the places that take part in some flow. The edition of 2023 attributes to the commune of Maxey-sur-Vaise (55328), in the Meuse, many jobs that are actually in the quarter of Vaise in Lyon (an error noted by INSEE), and has 12 flows without a commune of residence, which start at a node with an empty code and name. Names that are encoded twice in UTF-8 in some editions (e.g. a few names of places abroad in the edition of 2017) were repaired. The coordinates of the communes are not given by the data, and are not included.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `code`: the code of the commune (the 5-character official geographic code of INSEE, e.g. `75056` or `2A004`; `75101` to `75120` for the arrondissements of Paris, etc.), or the code of the place abroad as given by INSEE (e.g. `SUC1L`, `LU320`, `ZZZZZ`).
- (Node) `name`: the name of the commune or place.
- (Node) `abroad`: whether the place is outside France (a place of work abroad).
- (Edge) `workers`: the estimated number of employed persons of 15 years or older that live in the source commune and work in the target place.
citations: INSEE, "Mobilités professionnelles: déplacements domicile - lieu de travail." Recensement de la population, base flux de mobilité, editions 2006-2023 (2009-2026)

datasets.name: insna_founders
datasets.description:
Teacher-student relationships among the 60 founding members of the International Network for Social Network Analysis (INSNA). When B. Wellman founded INSNA in 1977, he sent a questionnaire to all the founding members, which included questions on who taught each founder and who each founder taught. The data were analyzed by K. Reitz and D. R. White (1989). The data were distributed by L. C. Freeman on his network data page at the University of California, Irvine (no longer online), from which this version was obtained via the Internet Archive.

A directed edge (i, j) indicates that member i taught member j.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the member.
citations: K. Reitz, D. R. White, "Rethinking the role concept: Homomorphisms on social networks." In L. C. Freeman, D. R. White, A. K. Romney (eds.), Research Methods in Social Network Analysis, 429-488, George Mason University Press (1989)

datasets.name: inspire_hep
datasets.description:
Citations and authorships of the literature of high-energy physics (particle physics, and related fields of astrophysics, nuclear physics, gravitation and mathematical physics) from INSPIRE-HEP, the information system of the field, run by CERN, DESY, Fermilab, IHEP, IN2P3 and SLAC (the successor of SPIRES, started in 1974). INSPIRE covers about 1.9 million articles, preprints, conference papers, theses and books, whose references are matched to the INSPIRE records, and whose authors are disambiguated (partly by the authors themselves through their INSPIRE profiles).

The records are harvested from the INSPIRE REST API (by ranges of record numbers), so that the networks are of the date of the harvest; the API gives no versioned bulk dump.

- `citations`: the citation network: a directed edge goes from a record to each record of INSPIRE that it cites (references not matched to an INSPIRE record are left out).
- `authorships`: the undirected bipartite network of the records and their authors, where an edge links a record to each of its authors. Authors are identified by their INSPIRE author profile when the record links to one, and otherwise by their name as given (so that different persons with the same name are merged, and an author with several spellings is split).

The abstracts, keywords, e-mail addresses (whose download is not permitted by the terms of use of INSPIRE) and other metadata are left out.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `is_author` (`authorships`): whether the node is an author (otherwise it is a record).
- (Node) `name`: the record number (control number) of the literature record (its page is `https://inspirehep.net/literature/<name>`), or of the author profile (`https://inspirehep.net/authors/<name>`), or, for authors without a profile, empty.
- (Node) `title` (records): the title of the record.
- (Node) `date` (records): the earliest date of the record, as given, e.g. `1998-10-18` or `2020`.
- (Node) `document_type` (records): the type of document (e.g. `article`, `conference paper`, `thesis`; several separated by `|`).
- (Node) `arxiv_eprint` (records): the arXiv identifier.
- (Node) `arxiv_categories` (records): the arXiv categories, separated by `|`.
- (Node) `doi` (records): the DOI of the record.
- (Node) `collaborations` (records): the collaborations (e.g. `ATLAS`), separated by `|`.
- (Node) `citation_count` (records): the number of citations according to INSPIRE.
- (Node) `full_name` (authors, in `authorships`): the name of the author, as given in the first record of the author.
- (Edge) `affiliations` (`authorships`): the affiliations of the author given in the record, separated by `|`.
citations: R. Ivanov, L. Raae, "INSPIRE: A new scientific information system for HEP." Journal of Physics: Conference Series 219, 082010 (2010)

datasets.name: intact
datasets.description:
The molecular interactions curated by the IntAct database of the European Bioinformatics Institute (EBI), together with those of the other databases of the IMEx consortium that IntAct hosts (e.g. MINT, UniProt, MatrixDB). Curators extract the interactions from the literature and from direct submissions, with details of the experiments in which they were observed. Nodes are interacting molecules (mostly proteins, of any organism, but also nucleic acids, small molecules, complexes, etc.), and an undirected edge is an interaction between two of them. Interactions involving more than two molecules (e.g. complexes pulled down with a bait) are expanded by IntAct into binary interactions, typically between the bait and each of the other molecules ("spoke expansion"). This is the release of 17 October 2026, in the PSI-MITAB format.

There are four networks of the current release:

- `evidence`: one edge per binary interaction evidence (an interaction observed in one experiment), so that two molecules can be connected by many edges.
- `clustered`: the evidences clustered by IntAct into one edge per pair of molecules, with the MI score summarizing all the evidence for it.
- `evidence_negative`, `clustered_negative`: the same, for the negative interactions, i.e. pairs of molecules reported not to interact.

Interactions of a molecule with itself are self-loops.

The entry also contains the networks of earlier releases, named by their date: `evidence_<date>` and `clustered_<date>` (e.g. `evidence_2024-11-29`), built in the same way. IntAct made about 250 releases since 2006, and the last release of each year from 2008 to 2025 is included: 2008-12-12 (only `clustered`: the file of that release has one line per pair of molecules), 2009-11-27, 2010-12-15, 2011-11-18, 2012-12-14, 2013-11-20, 2014-12-18, 2015-11-26, 2016-12-12, 2017-12-12, 2018-11-30, 2019-12-16, 2020-12-16, 2021-10-13, 2022-07-11, 2023-10-06, 2024-11-29 and 2025-08-08. The releases of 2006 and 2007 are only available in PSI-MI XML (not in PSI-MITAB), and are not included, nor are the negative interactions of the earlier releases. The files of the earlier releases differ in a few ways: until 2011, they are in the earlier PSI-MITAB 2.5 format, where the short name of a molecule is taken from its first alias (e.g. `Lck` from `uniprotkb:Lck`), the expansion method is given as a word (e.g. `Spoke`), and there are no MI scores (`miscore` is NaN); the clustered files of 2008 to 2011 merge the evidences for each pair of molecules into one line, whose attributes are the lists of those of the evidences; and the clustered files of 2012 to 2023 (in the simpler 15-column PSI-MITAB 2.5 format) give neither the types of the molecules nor the expansion methods (`type` and `expansion` are empty). A few lines of the file of 2008 are broken by line breaks within annotations; they are joined.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `id`: the identifier of the molecule (e.g. `uniprotkb:P49418`, `chebi:"CHEBI:15422"`, `intact:EBI-...`).
- (Node) `name`: the short name of the molecule (e.g. the gene name `AMPH`); empty if not given.
- (Node) `taxid`: the NCBI taxonomy identifier of the molecule's organism (e.g. 9606 for human; negative values for special cases, e.g. -1 for in vitro, -2 for chemical synthesis; 0 if not given).
- (Node) `organism`: the name of the organism, as given; empty if not given.
- (Node) `type`: the type of molecule (e.g. `protein`, `small molecule`, `ribonucleic acid`); empty if not given.
- (Edge) `detection_method` (edges): the method(s) with which the interaction was detected (e.g. `two hybrid`, `anti bait coimmunoprecipitation`), separated by `|`.
- (Edge) `interaction_type` (edges): the type(s) of interaction (e.g. `physical association`, `direct interaction`, `phosphorylation reaction`), separated by `|`.
- (Edge) `publication` (edges): the identifiers of the publications (e.g. `pubmed:10542231`), separated by `|`.
- (Edge) `miscore` (edges): the IntAct MI score, a confidence score between 0 and 1 based on the evidence (in `evidence`, the score of the pair, rounded to two digits); NaN if not given (e.g. in the releases before 2012).
- (Edge) `interaction_id` (edges): the identifier(s) of the interaction evidence(s) in IntAct (e.g. `intact:EBI-7121552`), separated by `|`.
- (Edge) `expansion` (edges): the expansion method by which the binary interaction was derived (e.g. `spoke expansion`); empty if none.
citations: N. del Toro et al., "The IntAct database: efficient access to fine-grained molecular interaction data." Nucleic Acids Research 50, D648-D653 (2022)

datasets.name: interactome_figeys
datasets.description:
A network of interactions between human proteins, from the first large-scale study of protein–protein interactions in human cells using mass spectrometry, by Ewing et al. (2007). Flag-tagged versions of 338 bait proteins, selected for known or suspected disease and functional associations, were expressed in HEK293 cells and immunoprecipitated, and the co-purified proteins were identified by LC-ESI-MS/MS. Of the 24,540 potential interactions identified, false positives and redundant hits were removed using empirical criteria and a computed confidence score, giving 6,463 interactions between 2,235 proteins. The data were obtained from the network collection of the Ma'ayan Laboratory (Mount Sinai School of Medicine), which distributed them in its SIG flat file format, with proteins identified by gene symbols.

Nodes are proteins, and a directed edge points from a bait protein to a protein co-purified with it (the 338 nodes with outgoing edges are the baits). Twenty pairs of proteins are connected in both directions.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the gene symbol of the protein.
citations: R. M. Ewing et al., "Large-scale mapping of human protein–protein interactions by mass spectrometry." Molecular Systems Biology 3, 89 (2007)

datasets.name: interactome_pdz
datasets.description:
A network of protein–protein interactions mediated by PDZ domains, from PDZBase, a manually curated database of PDZ-domain-mediated interactions extracted from the literature (about 300 interactions from over 200 articles at the time of publication). The data were obtained from the network collection of the Ma'ayan Laboratory (Mount Sinai School of Medicine), which distributed a version of PDZBase in its SIG flat file format; PDZBase itself is no longer online. Nodes are proteins, identified by their gene symbols, and an edge represents a binding interaction between a PDZ-domain-containing protein and its partner. All interactions are of type "Binding" with neutral effect. Self-loops denote proteins that bind to themselves.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the gene symbol.
- (Node) `uniprot_human` and `uniprot_mouse`: the Swiss-Prot/UniProt accessions of the human and mouse proteins (empty if not available).
- (Node) `type`: the molecule types assigned to the protein (e.g. Adapter, Kinase, Receptor, Channel).
- (Node) `location`: its cellular localizations (Cytosol, Membrane, Extracellular, Vesicles). A few proteins are assigned different types or locations in different interactions, hence the last two are lists.
- (Edge) `pubmed`: the PubMed ID of the article reporting the interaction.
citations: T. Beuming, L. Skrabanek, M. Y. Niv, P. Mukherjee, H. Weinstein, "PDZBase: a protein–protein interaction database for PDZ-domains." Bioinformatics 21(6), 827-828 (2005)

datasets.name: interactome_stelzl
datasets.description:
A network of interactions between human proteins, from a systematic yeast two-hybrid (Y2H) screen by Stelzl et al. (2005), in which a matrix of 4,456 bait and 5,632 prey proteins was tested by automated interaction mating, identifying 3,186 mostly novel interactions among 1,705 proteins. The data were obtained from the network collection of the Ma'ayan Laboratory (Mount Sinai School of Medicine), which distributed them in its SIG flat file format, with proteins identified by gene symbols and, where available, UniProt accessions. All interactions are of type "Binding".

Nodes are proteins, and edges are directed, following the order of the two proteins in the source file; the meaning of the direction is not documented. Most interactions are listed in both directions (3,016 pairs of proteins are connected both ways), so that the 6,207 directed edges correspond to 3,191 unordered pairs. Self-loops denote proteins that interact with themselves.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the gene symbol of the protein.
- (Node) `uniprot_human` and `uniprot_mouse`: the UniProt accessions of the human protein and of its mouse orthologue (empty if not available).
citations: U. Stelzl et al., "A human protein-protein interaction network: a resource for annotating the proteome." Cell 122(6), 957-968 (2005)

datasets.name: interactome_vidal
datasets.description:
Networks of interactions between human proteins from the first version of a proteome-scale map of human binary protein–protein interactions by Rual et al. (2005), from the Center for Cancer Systems Biology (CCSB) at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute. In that study, pairwise interactions among the products of about 8,100 open reading frames (the "Space-I" of the human ORFeome) were tested with a stringent high-throughput yeast two-hybrid (Y2H) system, detecting 2,754 interactions among 1,549 proteins (the CCSB-HI1 data set, later called HI-I-05). The collection contains two versions of the data:

- `HI-I-05`: the CCSB-HI1 interactions, as released by the CCSB in its Interactome Database (file `HI-I-05.tsv`, with the gene identifiers of the original publication), with proteins identified by their Entrez Gene IDs.
- `maayan`: the network distributed by the network collection of the Ma'ayan Laboratory (Mount Sinai School of Medicine), in its SIG flat file format, as protein–protein interactions extracted from the paper, with proteins identified by gene symbols and, where available, UniProt accessions. This network is larger than CCSB-HI1: of its 6,726 interactions, only 2,509 match (by gene symbol) the 2,754 interactions of `HI-I-05`; the origin of the others is not documented.

In both networks, nodes are proteins (identified by the genes that encode them), and an undirected edge represents an interaction. Self-loops denote proteins that interact with themselves.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `entrez_id` (`HI-I-05`): the Entrez Gene ID.
- (Node) `name`: the HGNC gene symbol (`HI-I-05`), or the gene symbol of the protein (`maayan`).
- (Node) `uniprot_human`, `uniprot_mouse` (`maayan`): the UniProt accessions of the human protein and of its mouse orthologue (empty if not available).

Other data sets of the CCSB Interactome Database are in the entries `human_interactome_2014` (the later human maps HI-II-14 and Lit-BM-13), `yeast_interactome_ccsb` (the yeast binary Y2H maps CCSB-YI1, Ito core and Uetz screen, and literature-curated and gold-standard reference sets), `collins_yeast` (the yeast co-complex associations of Collins et al.) and `celegans_interactomes` (the *C. elegans* interactome networks).
citations: J.-F. Rual et al., "Towards a proteome-scale map of the human protein–protein interaction network." Nature 437(7062), 1173-1178 (2005)

datasets.name: interactome_yeast
datasets.description:
Protein-protein interactions in yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae), studied by H. Jeong, S. P. Mason, A.-L. Barabási and Z. N. Oltvai (2001), who found that highly connected proteins are more likely to be essential (lethal if removed) than proteins of lower degree; later studies (e.g. S. Coulomb et al., 2005) argued that this result could be an artifact of the incompleteness of the data. The interactions were distributed by the Barabási lab at the University of Notre Dame (no longer online), from which this version was obtained via the Internet Archive. The protein names and lethalities were distributed, together with the same interactions, by L. C. Freeman on his network data page at the University of California, Irvine (no longer online), also obtained via the Internet Archive.

An undirected edge (i, j) indicates an interaction between proteins i and j. The data contain self-loops. The protein list of L. C. Freeman contains 244 additional proteins without any interaction, which are not included.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `protein_id`: the number of the protein in the source files.
- (Node) `orf`: the systematic (ORF) name of the gene (missing for 35 proteins).
- (Node) `name`: the standard gene name.
- (Node) `lethality`: whether the deletion of the gene is lethal ("Lethal", "Non-Lethal" or "Unknown").
citations: H. Jeong, S. P. Mason, A.-L. Barabási, Z. N. Oltvai, "Lethality and centrality in protein networks." Nature 411, 41-42 (2001)
S. Coulomb et al. "Gene essentiality and the topology of protein interaction networks." Proc. Roy. Soc. London B: Biological Sciences 272(1573), 1721-1725 (2005).

datasets.name: internet_as
datasets.description:
A snapshot of the structure of the Internet at the level of autonomous systems (ASs), reconstructed by M. E. J. Newman from the BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) routing tables collected by the University of Oregon Route Views Project, for 22 July 2006. Nodes are autonomous systems, i.e. networks under a single administrative routing policy (such as Internet service providers, companies or universities), and an undirected edge connects two ASs that are adjacent in the observed BGP routes, indicating a direct peering or transit relationship. The network was symmetrized, i.e. edge directions were discarded.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `label`: the AS number.
citations: B. Karrer, M.E.J. Newman, and L. Zdeborova, "Percolation on sparse networks." Phys. Rev. Lett. 113, 208702 (2014).

datasets.name: internet_top_pop
datasets.description:
Network topologies of 261 backbone and regional computer networks from around the world, from the Internet Topology Zoo project of S. Knight and collaborators at the University of Adelaide. The topologies were transcribed manually from maps and descriptions published by the network operators (or, in a minority of cases, from secondary sources), and most correspond to the Point of Presence (PoP) level, i.e. nodes are the locations (typically cities) where the network has equipment, and edges are the links between them. Some networks are instead described at the physical (fiber) level. They include research and education networks (e.g. `Geant2012`, `Abilene`) and commercial networks (e.g. `Cogentco`, `Sprint`). Most snapshots are from 2006-2012, but historical networks are also included, such as several snapshots of ARPANET from 1969 to 1972 (e.g. `Arpanet196912` for December 1969); several networks are available at different dates, indicated by a suffix in the name (e.g. `Garr201201`). The networks are undirected and may contain parallel edges between the same pair of nodes.

The networks have the following properties (not all are present in every network):

- (Node) `label`: the name of the node, usually its city.
- (Node) `Latitude`, `Longitude` and `Country`: geographic location of the node, obtained by geocoding.
- (Node) `Internal`: 1 if the node is part of the network, 0 if it is an external node (e.g. a connection to another network).
- (Node) `type`: the node type as given in the source map (e.g. "PoP").
- (Node) `hyperedge`: 1 if the node represents a shared link connecting several nodes (a hyperedge), rather than a location.
- (Node) `geocode_id`, `geocode_country`, `geocode_append`, `doubted`, `x`, `y`: auxiliary node attributes present in a few networks (used for geocoding, or copied from the source).
- (Edge) `LinkLabel`, `LinkNote`, `LinkType` (edges): the label, note and type (e.g. "OC-192", "Fiber") of the link, as given in the source.
- (Edge) `LinkSpeed`, `LinkSpeedUnits` and `LinkSpeedRaw` (edges): the link capacity, its unit prefix (K, M or G) and its value in bits per second (0 if unknown).
- (Edge) `LinkStatus`, `description`, `label` (edges): additional link information present in a few networks.
- (Edge) `id`, `key`: internal identifiers of nodes and edges.
- (Graph) `Network`: the name of the network.
- (Graph) `NetworkDate`, `DateObtained`: the date of the network, and the date when it was obtained.
- (Graph) `DateType`: current, historic or dynamic.
- (Graph) `Source`: the URL of the source map.
- (Graph) `Provenance`: primary or secondary source.
- (Graph) `Type`: `REN` for research and education networks, `COM` for commercial.
- (Graph) `Layer`: e.g. IP or fiber.
- (Graph) `GeoLocation`, `GeoExtent`: the geographic coverage.
- (Graph) `Backbone`, `Customer`, `Transit`, `Access`, `Commercial`, `Testbed`, `IX`, `Developed`: flags (0/1) classifying the network.
- (Graph) `Note`: a note on the network.
citations: S. Knight, et al. "The Internet Topology Zoo." IEEE Journal on Selected Areas in Communications 29(9), 1765-1775 (2011)

datasets.name: iscas89_circuits
datasets.description:
Networks of the digital logic circuits of the ISCAS'89 benchmark set, a collection of sequential circuits (i.e. with memory elements) introduced by Brglez, Bryan and Kozminski at the 1989 International Symposium on Circuits and Systems and widely used to evaluate test generation, simulation and synthesis algorithms. The circuits are given in the ".bench" netlist format, as distributed by M. S. Hsiao (Virginia Tech). Each network (named after the circuit, e.g. `s27` or `s38584.1`) represents one circuit: nodes are signals, i.e. the primary inputs of the circuit and the outputs of its logic gates and D-type flip-flops, and a directed edge $u \to v$ indicates that signal $u$ is an input of the gate or flip-flop whose output is $v$. The circuits range from a few dozen to about 25,000 gates. The circuit s208.1, listed in the source, is not included as its file was not available.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the signal in the netlist (e.g. "G17").
- (Node) `type`: the kind of the node: "INPUT" for primary inputs, or the type of the element whose output it is ("AND", "NAND", "OR", "NOR", "NOT", "BUFF" (buffer), or "DFF" (D-type flip-flop)). A few signals are used in the netlists without being declared as inputs or driven by any element (e.g. the clock signal "Phi1H" of s400); their type is empty.
- (Node) `primary_output`: whether the signal is a primary output of the circuit.
citations: F. Brglez, D. Bryan, K. Kozminski, "Combinational profiles of sequential benchmark circuits." IEEE International Symposium on Circuits and Systems, 1929-1934 (1989)

datasets.name: islamic_state_allegiances
datasets.description:
Bipartite network of 47 militant groups (and a few individuals) that declared allegiance to, or support for, the Islamic State, and the 20 countries or regions in which they operate, compiled c. 2016. Each group is connected to the region where it operates. The vertex property `is_region` indicates whether a node is a country or region (True) or a group (False), and `name` gives their names (the Islamic Movement of Uzbekistan appears twice, for Pakistan and Afghanistan). Data distributed by the UCINET datasets collection (University of Manchester).[^ucinet]

[^ucinet]: Description obtained in part from the [UCINET datasets page](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/datasets/covert-networks/islamic-state-allegiances).
citations: UCINET datasets, "Islamic State Allegiances." University of Manchester (2016)

datasets.name: islamic_state_bbc
datasets.description:
Networks of relationships among 56 members of the Islamic State, reconstructed at the University of Manchester from the information published by the BBC in 2014 about the investigation of the group by a team of experts ("UK paying experts to build Islamic State war crimes case"). Nodes are individuals (vertex property `name`), and there are three types of relationship:

- `links`: links between members (relationship type not specified).
- `companions`: companions and friends (former companion, close friends, close coordination, most important companion, close relationship).
- `kinship`: kin (brothers, brothers working together, married to sister, son).

Data distributed by the UCINET datasets collection (University of Manchester).[^ucinet]

[^ucinet]: Description obtained in part from the [UCINET datasets page](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/datasets/covert-networks/islamic-state-group).
citations: BBC News, "UK paying experts to build Islamic State war crimes case." (2014)

datasets.name: islamic_state_europe
datasets.description:
Networks of the individuals involved in the terrorist attacks carried out in Europe by the Islamic State (IS) network that perpetrated the attacks of November 13, 2015 in Paris and of March 22, 2016 in Brussels (called IS in Europe, or IS-E, by the authors), compiled by Alexander Gutfraind and Michael Genkin. Besides the Paris and Brussels attacks, the network includes related operations such as the attack on the Jewish Museum of Belgium (May 2014), the interdicted plot in Verviers (January 2015), and the attack on the Brussels-Paris high-speed train (August 2015). The data were coded from large-circulation media sources (mostly French, Dutch and English-language newspapers, and the Lexis database), collected from November 17, 2015 to May 9, 2016, into a graph database of persons, attacks, covert or non-covert activities, sites (e.g. residences and safe houses), localities and countries, with relations such as a person involved in an attack or activity, linked to another person (kinship, affinity, operational work), or present in a site or locality. Persons were included if they were attackers, involved with an attacker in a terrorism-related task, or wanted or arrested in relation to the attacks. The social networks between persons were then inferred from the database. Nodes are persons, and undirected edges are inferred ties, obtained with three different rules for the sensitivity analysis of the authors:

- `network` (IS-E): two persons are tied if they took part in an attack on the same site, were involved in the same activity, had a pre-existing link and one of them is an attacker or a wanted or dead member, or shared a site (e.g. a residence or safe house) and are both suspects, or one is an attacker.
- `restricted` (IS-E restricted): as `network`, but without the ties based on shared sites.
- `extended` (IS-E extended): as `network`, plus ties between suspects present in the same locality (e.g. the Molenbeek district of Brussels).

All networks contain the same nodes: all persons in the data whose status is not "free" (i.e. arrested, dead or wanted), plus one person with status "free" who has ties, as in the GML files of the authors. Persons without ties under a given rule are isolated nodes. One self-loop of the source data in the `extended` network (a person tied to themself by a shared locality) is removed. This is the latest version of the data, as of August 2017 (the ICON record refers to an earlier version of November 2015, with 24 nodes and 35 edges).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the person (sometimes only partially known, or a placeholder description).
- (Node) `age`: the age of the person (-1 if unknown).
- (Node) `citizenship`: the citizenship of the person.
- (Node) `status`: "arrested", "dead", "wanted" or "free".
- (Node) `role`: the role of the person, if known (e.g. "logistics", "commander", "bomb maker").
- (Node) `ref`: the media source reporting on the person.
- (Node) `attacker`: whether the person was involved in an attack.
- (Node) `involved_in_activity`: whether the person was involved in an activity.
- (Node) `linked_to_attacker`: whether the person (a suspect) is linked to an attacker.
- (Edge) `common_attack`: a boolean flag for a ground of the tie (several can apply): involved in an attack on the same site.
- (Edge) `linked_to_attacker`: likewise, pre-existing link of a suspect with an attacker.
- (Edge) `linked_to_each_other`: likewise, any pre-existing link between the two persons (not used by itself as a ground for a tie).
- (Edge) `linked_to_wanted`: likewise, pre-existing link of a suspect with a wanted or dead person.
- (Edge) `common_involvement`: likewise, involved in the same activity.
- (Edge) `shared_site_with_attacker`: likewise, a suspect present in the same site as an attacker.
- (Edge) `shared_site_with_suspect`: likewise, two suspects related to the same site.
- (Edge) `shared_locality_with_suspect`: likewise, two suspects present in the same locality.
citations: A. Gutfraind, M. Genkin, "A graph database framework for covert network analysis: An application to the Islamic State network in Europe." Social Networks 51, 178-188 (2017)

datasets.name: isle_of_man_genealogy
datasets.description:
The combined genealogies of about 20 families from the Isle of Man (British Isles), from about 1600 to the end of the 20th century, including many descendants who emigrated (in particular to the USA). The genealogies were obtained from the GEDCOM files collected by the Isle of Man Family History Society, and combined into a single GEDCOM file by W. de Nooy (2001). Nodes are persons; directed edges point from parents to their children, and there is an edge from husband to wife for each marriage (family with both spouses known). The data were distributed on the Pajek datasets page of the book *Exploratory Social Network Analysis with Pajek* (de Nooy, Mrvar and Batagelj), from which this version was obtained.[^icon]

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the person.
- (Node) `sex`: "M", "F" or "U".
- (Node) `birth`, `birth_place`, `death`, `death_place`, etc.: for each of the events birth, death, christening, baptism, burial, cremation, confirmation, first_communion, census, will, emigration, immigration, naturalization, graduation, residence, a property with the date of the event (e.g. `birth`) and one with its place (e.g. `birth_place`), as given in the source (e.g. "26 Oct 1884", "ABT 1925", "BET 1868 AND 1870"; empty if not recorded; repeated events, such as several residences, are separated by "; ", in the same positions in the date and place properties).
- (Node) `occupation`, `title`, `religion`, `physical_description`, `note`: the values of these attributes in the source, followed by their date and place in parentheses when given (notes keep their line breaks).
- (Node) `reference_number`: a user reference number given for some persons.
- (Node) `events`: other events recorded in the source, as "type: value (date, place)" (e.g. "Military (from 23 Aug 1862 to 9 Aug 1865)"). Three events of type "SSN" (social security numbers) are not included.
- (Edge) `kind`: the kind of relation ("father" or "mother", for edges from a parent to a child, or "marriage", for edges from husband to wife).
- (Edge) `date`, `place` (marriage edges): the date and place of the marriage.
- (Edge) `note` (marriage edges): the notes on the family.
- (Edge) `divorce`, `engagement`, `marriage_license` (marriage edges): the date of these events ("Y" if their occurrence is recorded without a date; empty otherwise).

[^icon]: Description obtained in part from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.
citations: Isle of Man Family History Society, "Isle of Man genealogy GEDCOM files."
W. de Nooy, A. Mrvar, V. Batagelj, "Exploratory Social Network Analysis with Pajek." Cambridge University Press (2005)

datasets.name: italian_gangs
datasets.description:
Network of 67 members of gangs in Italy, connected if they are members of the same gang. Nodes are gang members (labeled N1 to N67 in `name`), and the vertex property `country` gives a numeric code for their country of origin (no codebook is available). No further contextual information is given by the source. Data distributed by the UCINET datasets collection (University of Manchester).[^ucinet]

[^ucinet]: Description obtained in part from the [UCINET datasets page](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/datasets/covert-networks/italian-gangs).
citations: UCINET datasets, "Italian Gangs." University of Manchester (2016)

datasets.name: itc99
datasets.description:
Gate-level netlists of the ITC'99 benchmark circuits developed by the CAD Group at Politecnico di Torino (the "I99T" set), a collection of synchronous digital circuits used as benchmarks for testing and verification (e.g. automatic test pattern generation) of integrated circuits. Each circuit was described at register-transfer level in VHDL and synthesized into gate-level netlists with the Synopsys Design Compiler; the netlists use only AND, NAND, OR, NOR and NOT gates and D-type flip-flops. The circuits implement, for example, finite-state machines that compare serial flows (b01) or recognize BCD numbers (b02), a resource arbiter (b03), a voting system (b10), and subsets of the Viper (b14) and Intel 80386 (b15) processors; the larger circuits combine several copies of these (b17: three copies of b15; b18 and b19: two copies of b14 and two of b17; b20 to b22: copies and modified versions of b14). Circuits b16 (parametric) and b30 have no gate-level netlist. The netlists are in the ISCAS'89 "bench" format of the second release of the benchmarks (2002). For each circuit, the collection contains up to four netlists: the network named after the circuit (e.g. `b01`) is the netlist synthesized with standard options, which may contain completely useless gates; the networks with the suffix `_opt` are the netlists synthesized with optimization options (which superseded the "stripped" netlists of the first release); and the networks with the suffixes `_C` and `_opt_C` are the combinational versions of these two, in which the flip-flops have been transformed into pairs of primary inputs and outputs (pseudo-inputs carrying the state, named after the flip-flop with the suffix `_SCAN_IN`, and pseudo-outputs carrying the next state), so that these networks have no directed cycles. Circuit b19 has no optimized netlists.

In each network, nodes represent the signals of the circuit, i.e. its primary inputs and the logic gates and flip-flops (each identified with its output signal), plus one terminal node for each primary output of the circuit; a directed edge from node $i$ to node $j$ means that the signal $i$ is an input of gate or flip-flop $j$ (or is the signal delivered at primary output terminal $j$). Since flip-flops feed back the state of the circuit, the networks of the sequential versions contain directed cycles. A gate may take the same signal more than once, resulting in parallel edges (e.g. 13 in b05), and in some circuits some gates drive no other gate or output (e.g. 22 and 44 in b18 and b19, respectively).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the signal in the netlist (e.g. `U34`, `STATO_REG_2_`), with the primary output terminals having the name of the output signal.
- (Node) `type`: the type of node: `INPUT` (primary input), `OUTPUT` (primary output terminal), `DFF` (D-type flip-flop, only in the sequential versions), or the logic gate (`AND`, `NAND`, `OR`, `NOR`, `NOT`).[^icon].

[^icon]: Description obtained in part from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.
citations: F. Corno, M. Sonza Reorda, G. Squillero, "RT-level ITC'99 benchmarks and first ATPG results." IEEE Design & Test of Computers 17(3), 44-53 (2000)

datasets.name: iui_collab
datasets.description:
A co-authorship network of the authors of papers published in the Slovenian computer science journals Informatica and Uporabna Informatika, up to 2013, constructed by Blagus and Bajec. Nodes are authors, and an undirected edge connects two authors for each paper they co-authored, so that repeated edges represent multiple co-authored papers. The network also contains 661 self-loops, apparently one for each single-authored paper.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the author (first initial and surname).
citations: N. Blagus, M. Bajec, "Mreža sodelovanj: Informatica in Uporabna informatika (The network of collaboration: Informatica and Uporabna Informatika)." Uporabna Informatika 23(1), 22-31 (2015)

datasets.name: iwdb
datasets.description:
A collection of ecological interaction networks from the Interaction Web Database (IWDB), a nonprofit, cooperative database of published data on species interaction networks, hosted for many years by the National Center for Ecological Analysis and Synthesis (NCEAS) at the University of California, Santa Barbara, USA, and since December 2020 by the Department of Ecology of the University of São Paulo, Brazil. The IWDB compiles data sets from the literature on several kinds of interactions: plant-pollinator, plant-ant, plant-herbivore, seed dispersal (plant-frugivore), anemone-fish, host-parasite and predator-prey. Each data set is documented on its own IWDB page (with the location, the type of data and the source), and is distributed as an interaction matrix, mostly as Excel spreadsheets with the species lists. The IWDB states that its data sets are freely available and reusable. This entry includes one or more networks for each of the IWDB data sets described below, from studies published between 1923 and 2011; since the IWDB server refuses automated requests, the files are obtained from snapshots of the Internet Archive.

The networks are named `<type>_<author>`, after the kind of interaction and the first author of the source, followed by `_<variant>` for data sets with several networks (sites, years, plots, etc.). Except for the two predator-prey data sets, the networks are bipartite and undirected, with the nodes of one kind marked by a boolean vertex property `is_<kind>` (e.g. `is_pollinator`). Unless stated otherwise, nodes have a `name` property, the taxon name (genus and species as given in the source, where "sp." denotes an unidentified species and "sp. 1" etc. a morphospecies), with `genus` and `species` the two parts of the name; for weighted networks, the edge property `count` is the number of observations given in the source (e.g. visits, or individuals caught). Unweighted networks record only the presence of an interaction.

**Plant-pollinator networks.** An edge connects a plant species to an animal species recorded visiting its flowers. Many studies caught the flower visitors on the flowers of each plant species, in which case `count` is the number of individuals caught, a rough estimate of the level of visitation.

- `pollination_arroyo_I`, `pollination_arroyo_II`, `pollination_arroyo_III` (Arroyo et al. 1982): plants and insect flower visitors in the high Andes of central Chile (Cordón del Cepo), from a community-level study of pollination mechanisms and how they change with altitude; one network for each of the three elevation levels of the study, each with its own set of species. Unweighted. Nodes: `name`, `genus`, `species` (with morphospecies labels such as "sp. 1" or "n.i." for unidentified taxa), `is_pollinator`.
- `pollination_barrett` (Barrett and Helenurm 1987): understory herbs and their insect flower visitors in the boreal forest of central New Brunswick, Canada, observed from May to September of 1978, 1979 and 1980, in a study of the breeding systems, pollination biology and phenology of boreal forest herbs. Nodes: `name`, `genus`, `species`, `is_pollinator`. Edges: `count`, the number of insect individuals caught on the flowers of the plant species.
- `pollination_bartomeus_<plot>` (Bartomeus et al. 2008): twelve quantitative networks of plants and insect flower visitors in Mediterranean shrublands of the Natural Park of Cap de Creus, Catalonia, Spain, from a study of how two invasive plants with large, showy flowers, *Carpobrotus* affine *acinaciformis* and *Opuntia stricta*, affect the structure of plant-pollinator networks. Plots of 50 x 50 m, at least 300 m apart, were either invaded or not by one of the invaders; they were sampled every two weeks during the flowering period of the invader (April to June for *Carpobrotus* and June to July for *Opuntia*), and each plant species was observed for 6 minutes per sampling round, with the flower visitors collected. Each network corresponds to one plot, named with the code of the source, made of a site abbreviation, a plot number, and the invasive species of the site (`CA` for *Carpobrotus*, `OP` for *Opuntia*); the source does not indicate which plots are invaded. (Two records with plot codes "SEL10P" and "SEL1P", evidently misspellings of "SEL1OP", are included in that plot.) Plant species without any visits are not included. Nodes: `name`, the taxon name (species, genus, or a morphospecies code, as given in the source, where "?" marks an identification that is not verified); `code`, the plant or insect identifier in the source (the same name may correspond to several insect morphospecies); `family`, the taxonomic family (as spelled in the source); `order`, the insect order (empty for plants); `is_pollinator`. Edges: `visits`, the total number of visits over all sampling rounds; `rounds`, the number of sampling rounds in which the interaction was recorded.
- `pollination_bezerra` (Bezerra et al. 2009): oil-flowers of the family Malpighiaceae and the oil-collecting bees visiting them in the caatinga (a semi-arid vegetation) of the Parque Nacional do Catimbau, Pernambuco State, Brazil. Bee visits were recorded on 138 individual plants in natural clumps of 13 Malpighiaceae species during the flowering peak of each species, over four consecutive days from 5:00 to 17:00, for a total of 1392 h of observation. Nodes: `name`, the species name; `is_pollinator` (bees). Edges: `count`, the number of visits.
- `pollination_clements` (Clements and Long 1923): plants and their insect flower visitors on Pikes Peak, Colorado, USA, from the observations of F. E. Clements and F. L. Long in the early 1920s, published in their book on experimental pollination, with the insect visitors of 96 plant species (94 native and two exotic). Unweighted. Nodes: `name`, `genus`, `species`; `code`, the short code of the flower visitor in the source (empty for plants); `is_pollinator`.
- `pollination_dupont` (Dupont et al. 2003): plants and all flower-visiting animals in the high-altitude sub-alpine desert of Las Cañadas, Tenerife, Canary Islands. Unweighted. Nodes: `name`, `genus`, `species`; `origin`, the biogeographic status of the species as coded in the source ("end" for endemic, "nat" for native, "int" for introduced); `is_pollinator`.
- `pollination_elberling` (Elberling and Olesen 1999): plants and their insect flower visitors in the subarctic alpine zone of Latnjajaure, northern Sweden, observed from 21 May to 23 August 1994, in a study of the structure of a high-latitude plant-flower visitor system and of the role of flies as flower visitors. All insects found on flowers were counted as flower visitors, whether they foraged for nectar or pollen or were sun-basking. Nodes: `name`, `genus`, `species`, `is_pollinator`. Edges: `count`, the number of visits.
- `pollination_hocking` (Hocking 1968): plants and their flower visitors (insects, and also spiders and mites) on Ellesmere Island, Northwest Territories (now Nunavut), Canada, from a study of the composition of the assemblage of flower visitors in the high Arctic and its relationship to nectar production. Unweighted. Nodes: `name`, `genus`, `species` (or a higher taxon such as a family when not identified further), `is_pollinator`.
- `pollination_inouye` (Inouye and Pyke 1988): alpine plants and their insect flower visitors in Kosciusko National Park, Snowy Mountains, New South Wales, Australia, observed from December 1983 to March 1984, in a community-level study of alpine pollination biology compared with montane Colorado, USA. The source lists 20 further plant species without any visitation data; they are not included. Nodes: `name`, `genus`, `species` (some insects are distinguished by sex); `order`, the insect order (Diptera, Hymenoptera or Lepidoptera; empty for plants); `is_pollinator`. Edges: `count`, the number of insect individuals caught on the flowers of the plant species.
- `pollination_kaiser_bunbury_control`, `pollination_kaiser_bunbury_restored` (Kaiser-Bunbury et al. 2009, 2010): quantitative networks of plants and their flower visitors (insects, birds and lizards) in the upland heathland of Mauritius, comparing an area heavily invaded by introduced plant species (`control`) with an area from which the non-native plants had been removed (`restored`). Interactions were recorded by static observations ("sit-and-observe") of flowers, with varying numbers of flowers and observation times; to account for these differences, visitation rates were computed as visits per flower per hour and averaged over the total observation time. For each edge, the visitation rate and the interaction strength (which in addition accounts for the floral abundance of the plant at the site) are given; a few interactions have a nonzero value in only one of the two matrices of the source. Plant species without any recorded visit appear as isolated nodes. Nodes: `name`, the species name (for animals with the authority, as given in the source); `family`, the taxonomic family; `origin`, the origin of the species as a numeric code (the codes are not explained in the data file); `flower_colour` and `flower_category`, numeric codes for the flower color and flower type of the plants (not explained in the data file; zero for animals); `floral_abundance`, the floral abundance of the plants at the site (zero for animals); `probed_flowers`, the number of flowers probed by the animal species (zero for plants); `is_pollinator`. Edges: `visitation_rate`, the visitation rate (visits per flower per hour); `interaction_strength`, the interaction strength.
- `pollination_kato` (Kato et al. 1990): plants and flower-visiting insect species (or morphospecies) in the primary beech forest of the Kyoto University Forest of Ashu, at the northeastern boundary of Kyoto Prefecture, Japan, studied by M. Kato, T. Makutani, T. Inoue and T. Itino between 1984 and 1987; the study recorded the flowering phenology of 91 plant species and collected the insects visiting their flowers. An edge connects an insect to a plant on whose flowers it was caught. Nodes: `is_pollinator`, whether the node is an insect (otherwise a plant); `idx`, the index of the species in the source matrix; `pol_ge_sp`, the name of the insect species, followed by abbreviations of its family and order in parentheses (as in "Actina jezoensis (Str. : Dip. )"; empty for plants); `plant_ge`, `plant_sp`, the genus and species of the plant (empty for insects). Edges: `count`, the number of individuals of the insect species collected on the plant species.
- `pollination_kevan` (Kevan 1970): plants and the arthropods visiting their flowers at Hazen Camp, near Lake Hazen on northern Ellesmere Island (81°49'N, 71°18'W), in the Canadian high Arctic, observed in 1967 for P. G. Kevan's PhD thesis on the importance of insect-flower relations for arctic plants and insects. For some interactions the source gives only a qualitative indication instead of a number ("few", "several", "many", "eggs", or "?"). The willow *Salix arctica* is split into three nodes, for its staminate, pistillate and undetermined catkins. Nodes: `name`, `genus`, `species` (or a higher taxon such as a family when not identified further), `is_pollinator`. Edges: `count`, the number of individuals caught (NaN if only a qualitative indication is given); `note`, the qualitative indication given instead of a number (empty otherwise).
- `pollination_mcmullen` (McMullen 1993): plants and their insect flower visitors in the Galápagos Islands, compiled by C. K. McMullen from records of plant-flower visitor interactions in the literature, together with a field study on Pinta Island of the flower visitors of six plant species (the IWDB spells the author's name "McCullen"). Unweighted. Nodes: `name`, `genus`, `species` (or a higher group such as "Beetles" when not identified further), `is_pollinator`.
- `pollination_medan_LD`, `pollination_medan_RB` (Medan et al. 2002): plants and their flower visitors at two sites at different altitudes in the Andes of Mendoza, Argentina: Laguna del Diamante (`LD`, xeric scrub) and Río Blanco (`RB`, woody riverine vegetation and xeric scrub), from a study comparing the structure of plant-pollinator networks between altitudes. Unweighted. Nodes: `name`, the scientific name of the taxon (for plants with the authority, for flower visitors a species or morphospecies name, as given in the source); `family`, the taxonomic family (given for all plants but only for some flower visitors); `order`, the order of the flower visitor, as a code (e.g. "D" for Diptera; given only for some flower visitors); `code`, the code of the species in the source (a number for plants, letters for flower visitors); `is_pollinator`.
- `pollination_memmott` (Memmott 1999): plants and their insect flower visitors in a 150 x 250 m meadow plot near Bristol, UK, observed in July 1997, in a study of the structure of a plant-pollinator web that took into account the abundances of the species and the frequency of their interactions. The insects are identified only by a number and their order in the source. Nodes: `name`, the common name of the plant, or, for insects, their order code and number (e.g. "DIP 31"); `code`, the number of the plant or insect in the source; `order`, the insect order as coded in the source ("COL" Coleoptera, "DIP" Diptera, "HY" Hymenoptera, "L" Lepidoptera; empty for plants); `is_pollinator`. Edges: `count`, the number of visits.
