- `pollination_mosquin` (Mosquin and Martin 1967): plants and their insect flower visitors on Melville Island, Northwest Territories (now Nunavut), Canada, observed from 19 to 31 July 1965, while the authors collected plants and made observations on flower-visiting insects and on the scent and other attractive features of the flowers. Nodes: `name`, `genus`, `species`, `is_pollinator`. Edges: `count`, the number of insect individuals caught on the flowers of the plant species.
- `pollination_motten` (Motten 1982, 1986): spring-flowering plants (herbs, shrubs and understory trees pollinated by insects) and their insect flower visitors in the deciduous forests of the piedmont of North Carolina, USA. Nodes: `name`, `genus`, `species` (for some bees the subgenus is given in parentheses); `code`, the abbreviation of the plant in the source (empty for insects); `is_pollinator`. Edges: `count`, the number of visits.
- `pollination_olesen_aigrettes`, `pollination_olesen_flores` (Olesen et al. 2002): plants and their flower visitors on two oceanic islands, Ile aux Aigrettes (`aigrettes`), a small island off Mauritius with coastal forest, and Flores in the Azores (`flores`), with rocky cliff and open herb vegetation, from a study of the invasion of island pollination networks by introduced species. The visitors are insects, and on Ile aux Aigrettes also a gecko. Nodes: `name`, `genus`, `species`; `origin`, the status of the species on the island as coded in the source ("end" for endemic, "nat" for native, "intr" for introduced); `is_pollinator`. Edges: `count`, the number of visits.
- `pollination_ollerton` (Ollerton et al. 2003): nine asclepiads (milkweeds, Apocynaceae: Asclepiadoideae) and their flower visitors at an upland grassland site in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, studied during three months of fieldwork, which documented, among others, pollination by fruit chafers and by pompilid wasps. Flower visitors were observed and/or caught on each plant species. (A note in the source states that bold cells mark insects found carrying pollinaria, but this formatting is not present in the distributed file.) Nodes: `name`, `genus`, `species` (or a morphospecies or higher group); `authority`, the taxonomic authority of the insect species (when given); `order`, the insect order (empty for plants); `is_pollinator`. Edges: `count`, the number of insect individuals observed or caught.
- `pollination_ramirez` (Ramirez and Brito 1992): plants and their flower visitors (insects and hummingbirds) in a "morichal", a palm swamp community dominated by *Mauritia flexuosa*, in the central plains of Guárico State, Venezuela, from field observations made in 1983, 1984 and 1989, in a study of the floral biology and pollination spectrum of the community. Five plant species (sedges and grasses) are listed without any recorded visitor, and appear as isolated nodes. Nodes: `name`, `genus`, `species`, `is_pollinator`. Edges: `pollen_load`, whether the visitors were found carrying a pollen load of the plant (value 1 in the source matrix, as opposed to 2; the interactions with a pollen load form what the source calls the pollination matrix).
- `pollination_robertson` (Robertson 1929): plants and their flower visitors, compiled by the naturalist C. Robertson, who recorded, over several decades around the turn of the 20th century, the animal species visiting the flowers of the plants that grew in a small area around Carlinville, in southwestern Illinois, USA (his methods are described by J. C. Marlin and W. E. LaBerge, Conserv. Ecol. 5, 2001). There are 456 plant species and 1,428 flower-visiting animal species (mostly bees and other insects, and a few birds). Unweighted; the source lists ten plant-visitor pairs twice, which appear as parallel edges. Nodes: `name`, the species name; `family`, the family of the species; `order`, the order of the animal (or "Aves" for birds; empty for plants); `is_pollinator`.
- `pollination_santos` (Santos et al. 2010): plants and the social bees and social wasps visiting them for nectar in the caatinga at Itatim, Bahia State, Brazil (12°42'S, 39°46'W). Samples were collected monthly from November 1996 to November 1997 along a transect 3 km long and 20 m wide, where two collectors inspected each flowering plant for 5 minutes and caught the flower-visiting bees and wasps with entomological nets; only legitimate visitors were considered. The plants are identified only by codes, which are listed in an appendix of the paper. Unweighted. Nodes: `name`, the species name of the bee or wasp, or the code of the plant; `group`, "wasp" or "bee" for the flower visitors (empty for plants); `is_pollinator`.
- `pollination_schemske` (Schemske et al. 1978): seven early-flowering, low-growing perennial woodland herbs and their insect flower visitors in Brownfield Woods, a 24 ha maple-oak woodland near Urbana, Illinois, USA. The sequence and variety of flowers visited by individual insects were recorded for the first foraging insect observed in randomly selected 1 m² quadrats within a 10 x 10 m grid. Nodes: `name`, `genus`, `species`, `is_pollinator`. Edges: `count`, the number of visits.
- `pollination_small` (Small 1976): the major insect-pollinated plants of the Mer Bleue peat bog near Ottawa, Canada, and their insect flower visitors, observed in 1973 in a preliminary evaluation of the pollination relationships in the bog. Nodes: `name`, `genus`, `species`, `is_pollinator`. Edges: `count`, the number of insect individuals caught on the flowers of the plant species.
- `pollination_vazquez_<site>` (Vázquez and Simberloff 2003): plants and their flower visitors from eight forest sites dominated by *Nothofagus dombeyi*, in and around Nahuel Huapi National Park, Río Negro, Argentina, studied from September 1999 to February 2000. Four of the sites were grazed by introduced cattle and four were not, and the study analyzed the effects of this disturbance on plants, pollinators and their interactions. There is one network for each site (`Llao_Llao`, `Cerro_Lopez`, `Safariland`, `Arroyo_Goye`, `Mascardi_nc`, `Mascardi_c`, `Quetrihue_nc`, `Quetrihue_c`, where "nc" and "c" are the parts of the site without and with cattle), plus `All_sites_pooled`, which aggregates all sites. All of them share the same set of nodes (all plant and visitor species of the study, including species that are isolated at a given site), and an edge connects a visitor species to a plant species whose flowers it visited, weighted by the interaction frequency; according to the IWDB, the weights are the number of visits, while the source spreadsheet labels the matrices as "effective visitation frequency (Matrix 1*Table A4.1)". Nodes: `is_pollinator`, whether the node is a flower visitor (otherwise a plant); `idx`, the species number in the source data; `Family`, the family of the species; `Plant species`, `Common name`, `Life form`, `Origin`: for plants, the species name, the local common name, the life form (e.g. herb, shrub, understory tree), and its origin ("Native" or "Exotic"); `Order`, `Species name`, `Catalog number`: for visitors, the order, the species name (or "—" if not identified to species), and the catalog number of the specimen. Edges: `count`, the interaction frequency.

**Plant-ant networks.**

- `ant_plant_bluthgen` (Blüthgen et al. 2004): ants and the plants whose nectaries they attend, in the rainforest at the Australian Canopy Crane site in Cape Tribulation, Far North Queensland, Australia (16°07'S, 145°27'E, 80 m a.s.l.), and in adjacent forests within 5 km of the crane, including patches of open secondary forest. Ant colonies attending extrafloral nectaries (EFN) and floral nectaries (FN) of plants were recorded, and an edge connects an ant species to a plant nectary type, weighted by the number of ant individuals of the species collected on the plant species. Plant species with both kinds of nectaries are represented by two nodes, one for each nectary type. The data also include independent abundance estimates of the ant species from sugar-bait experiments (Blüthgen and Fiedler 2004) and of the plants. Nodes: `name`, the species name; `family`, the plant family, or `subfamily`, the ant subfamily (each empty for the other kind of node); `nectaries`, the nectary type of the plant node ("EFN" extrafloral, "FN" floral; empty for ants); `life_form`, the life form of the plant ("cl" climber, "he" herb, "sh" shrub, "tr" tree, "pa" palm; empty for ants); `abundance`, for ants the abundance of colonies estimated from sugar-bait experiments (zero for ants not recorded at the baits), and for plants the number of plant individuals on whose nectaries any insect was recorded; `is_ant`. Edges: `count`, the number of ant individuals collected.
- `ant_plant_davidson` (Davidson et al. 1989): ants and eight myrmecophytes (plants housing ant colonies) in the tropical moist forests of western Amazonia, Peru, surveyed in September, October and November of 1985 and 1986, in a study of the variation in the ant associates of the myrmecophytes, of competition among ants for host plants and of the significance of plant trichomes. Species listed in the source without any recorded association appear as isolated nodes. Nodes: `name`, `genus`, `species`, `is_ant`. Edges: `count`, the number of recorded associations, as given in the source.
- `ant_plant_davidson_fisher` (Davidson and Fisher 1991): six *Cecropia* trees and the four ant species inhabiting them, from a study of the symbiosis of ants with *Cecropia* as a function of the light regime, in which the authors discuss how different kinds of asymmetry in specialization lead to different forms of coevolution. Nodes: `name`, `genus`, `species`, `is_ant`. Edges: `count`, the number of recorded associations, as given in the source.
- `ant_plant_fonseca` (Fonseca and Ganade 1996): ants and myrmecophytes in the Central Amazonian rainforest north of Manaus, Amazonas, Brazil, studied from June to August 1990, to describe the ant-myrmecophyte matrix quantitatively, search for patterns of compartmentalization, and compare the ant-plant system with other mutualistic systems. Ants not identified to species are labeled with letter codes. Nodes: `name`, `genus`, `species`, `is_ant`. Edges: `count`, the number of recorded associations, as given in the source.

**Plant-herbivore networks.**

- `herbivory_joern_altuda`, `herbivory_joern_marathon` (Joern 1979): grasshoppers (Orthoptera: Acrididae) and the plants they feed on, in two arid grassland communities of the Trans-Pecos region of Texas, USA, near Altuda (`altuda`) and Marathon (`marathon`), from a study of the feeding patterns and diet specialization of grasshoppers, carried out from May to November in 1974 and 1975. An edge connects a grasshopper species to a plant taxon it was found to feed on. Plants not identified to genus are labeled "Unknown Forb" with a letter. Unweighted. Nodes: `name`, `genus`, `species`, `is_herbivore`.
- `herbivory_leather_britain`, `herbivory_leather_finland` (Leather 1991): plum and cherry species (genus *Prunus*) and the macrolepidoptera (moths and butterflies) whose larvae feed on them, in Britain (`britain`) and Finland (`finland`), compiled at the scale of the whole country, from a study of the influence of host plant range and history on the diet breadth of the insects and on insect species richness. An edge connects a *Prunus* species to a lepidopteran species feeding on it. Unweighted. Nodes: `name`, `genus`, `species`, `is_herbivore` (lepidopterans).

**Seed dispersal (plant-frugivore) networks.** An edge connects a frugivore species to a plant species whose fruits it was seen eating.

- `seed_dispersal_beehler` (Beehler 1983): fruiting plants and frugivorous birds in a forest on the southwest slopes of Mount Missim, north-northeast of Wau, Morobe Province, Papua New Guinea, observed from July 1978 to November 1980 during a study of the behavior and ecology of four species of birds of paradise; the data cover the birds of paradise and other bird species sharing their fruit resources. The plants are identified by genus or species (some only to family), and the birds by their common names. Nodes: `name`, the common name of the bird, or the name of the plant taxon (as given in the source, with abbreviated genera such as "S. sogerensis"); `is_bird`. Edges: `count`, the number of feeding visits.
- `seed_dispersal_poulin_miconia`, `seed_dispersal_poulin_psychotria` (Poulin et al. 1999): bird-dispersed plants of the genera *Miconia* (`miconia`) and *Psychotria* (`psychotria`) and the birds eating their fruits, in the semideciduous tropical forest of Soberanía National Park, central Panama, from a study of the synchrony of fruiting phenologies of congeneric bird-dispersed plants (which also used phenological data from nearby Barro Colorado Island). The diet of the birds was determined from birds mist-netted in the national park. Nodes: `name`, `genus`, `species` (genus abbreviations of the source, such as "P. mentalis", are expanded using the full genus names given elsewhere in the file); `is_bird`. Edges: `count`, the number of fruits of the plant taken by the bird species.
- `seed_dispersal_schleuning` (Schleuning et al. 2011): fleshy-fruited plants and the frugivorous birds and mammals feeding on them in the northern Kakamega Forest, Kenya, a tropical montane rain forest. All plant species with fleshy fruits in an area of about 250 ha were studied from December 2007 to March 2008, covering species of different forest strata (canopy, midstory and understory) and forest types (primary and secondary forest). For each plant species, two to four individuals bearing many ripe fruits were each observed once from 7:00 to 14:00 by five ornithologists, standardizing the sampling effort to 28 hours per plant species, and all fruit-eating individuals (birds and monkeys) were recorded and identified to species. The source also provides the subnetworks of each forest stratum and forest type, which can be obtained from this network with the plant properties. Nodes: `name`, the scientific name of the species; `common_name`, the English name of the frugivores (empty for plants); `code`, the abbreviation of the plant species in the source (empty for frugivores); `forest_type`, the forest type of the plant ("Prim" primary or "Sec" secondary; empty for frugivores); `stratum`, the forest stratum of the plant ("C" canopy, "M" midstory, "U" understory; empty for frugivores); `height`, the plant height in meters (NaN for frugivores); `diet`, the diet specialization of the frugivore on fruits ("Ob" obligate, "Pt" partial, "Op" opportunistic; empty for plants); `forest_dependence`, the forest dependence of the frugivore ("F" forest species, "V" visitor species; empty for plants); `is_frugivore`. Edges: `count`, the interaction frequency, the number of fruit-eating individuals of the frugivore species recorded on the plant species (regardless of whether fruits were swallowed, pecked or dropped).
- `seed_dispersal_snow` (Snow and Snow 1988): fruiting plants and the birds eating their fruits in England, from the observations reported in the book "Birds and Berries". Species listed in the source without any recorded interaction appear as isolated nodes. Nodes: `name`, the common name of the species; `genus` and `species`, the scientific genus and species names (empty for some species without them in the source); `is_bird`. Edges: `count`, the number of feeding visits.
- `seed_dispersal_sorensen` (Sorensen 1981): fruiting plants and the birds eating their fruits in Wytham Woods, near Oxford, UK, from a study of the feeding preferences of frugivorous birds in relation to the seasonality, abundance, growth form and nutritive and energetic value of the fruits. Species listed in the source without any recorded interaction appear as isolated nodes. Nodes: `name`, the common name of the species (as spelled in the source); `is_bird`. Edges: `count`, the number of feeding visits.

**Anemone-fish networks.** An edge connects an anemonefish species (Pomacentridae: Amphiprioninae) to a sea anemone species in which it has been found living; the data record only the presence of the association.

- `anemone_fish_ollerton` (Ollerton et al. 2007): the anemonefishes (genera *Amphiprion* and *Premnas*) and the sea anemones that host them, across the whole distributional range of this mutualism, from coral reefs of the east coast of Africa and the Red Sea through the Indian Ocean to the western Pacific, and from southeastern Australia to the latitude of Tokyo. The data were taken from the monograph of Fautin and Allen (1997), supplemented by later observations by D. G. Fautin, and include the correction that the anemone *Macrodactyla doreensis* hosts *Amphiprion chrysopterus*, not *A. chrysogaster* as recorded in that monograph. All records are of natural occurrences (in captivity, anemonefishes can live with many more anemones). Nodes: `name`, the species name (as spelled in the source); `distribution`, the extent of the distributional range of the species ("widespread", "regional" or "local"); `is_fish`.
- `anemone_fish_ricciardi_<site>` (Ricciardi et al. 2010): anemonefishes and their host sea anemones (Stichodactylidae and Actiniidae) at 16 sites of the Manado region of Sulawesi, Indonesia, a marine biodiversity hotspot, from a study of the structure of the anemonefish-anemone mutualism at local and regional scales. The data are based on field records of 233 anemones and 772 anemonefish individuals observed during SCUBA dives of 45-60 min at depths between 1 and 40 m; the sites were chosen to cover a wide range of habitats (vertical slopes, patch reefs and sandy bottoms). There is one network per site (named as in the source, with spaces and dots replaced by underscores: `Bahowo`, `Bajo`, `Batu_Kapal`, `Bualo`, `Fukui`, `Jalan_m`, `Johnson`, `Kasegaran`, `Likuan_1`, `Mandolin`, `Mapia`, `Mike`, `Sachiko`, `T_Kopi`, `T_Pisok`, `Timur`), and `anemone_fish_ricciardi_regional` with the union of all sites. Nodes: `name`, the species name; `is_fish`. Edges (only in `regional`): `sites`, the number of sites where the association was recorded.

**Host-parasite networks.**

- `host_parasite_canada_<site>` (compiled by the IWDB): freshwater fish species and their metazoan parasites in Canadian lakes and rivers in which most fish species were surveyed for parasites, from six parasitological surveys: Aishihik Lake, Yukon (`aishihik`; Arthur et al. 1976); Cold Lake, Alberta (`cold`; Leong and Holmes 1981); Lake of the Woods, Ontario (`woods`; Dechtiar 1972); the headwaters of the McGregor (`mcgregor`) and Parsnip (`parsnip`) rivers, British Columbia (Arai and Mudry 1983); Lake Huron and Manitoulin Island, Ontario (`huron`; Bangham 1955); and the Smallwood Reservoir, Labrador (`smallwood`; Chinniah and Threlfall 1978). Only fish species with at least 5 individuals examined at a locality are included, since infection levels are inaccurate for smaller samples. All internal and external metazoan parasites are considered (nematodes, acanthocephalans, cestodes, trematodes, monogeneans, leeches, copepods and branchiurans); when a species of internal worm occurred both as larva and as adult, the two forms are treated as distinct parasite nodes, since they often have different modes of transmission and infect different hosts and organs. An edge connects a fish species to a parasite found in it, with the prevalence of infection (the percentage of examined host individuals harboring the parasite) and, for five of the localities, the mean intensity of infection (the average number of parasite individuals per host). Fish species without any recorded parasite appear as isolated nodes. Nodes: `name`, the species name (for parasites, "(L)" marks larval forms, as in the source); `genus` and `species`, the two parts of the parasite name (empty for hosts); `sample_size`, the number of host individuals examined (zero for parasites); `relative_abundance`, an independent estimate of the relative abundance of the host species, from Leong and Holmes (1981) (only in `cold`; NaN for parasites); `is_parasite`. Edges: `prevalence`, the prevalence of infection, in percent; `intensity`, the intensity of infection (NaN if not available; absent in `woods` and `huron`).

**Predator-prey networks.** These are directed food webs.

- `food_web_lafferty` (Lafferty et al. 2006): the food web of the Carpinteria Salt Marsh Reserve, Santa Barbara County, California, USA, including both free-living species and parasites, compiled by K. D. Lafferty and collaborators to study the effect of parasites on food-web topology. Nodes are taxa (species or groups of species, e.g. "Oligochaete"), basal resources such as detritus, carrion and primary producers, free-living animals, and parasites (larval and adult parasite stages, mostly trematodes and other helminths). The web consists of four subwebs: predator-prey, parasite-host, predator-parasite (predation on parasites, e.g. on free-living stages or on parasites inside eaten hosts) and parasite-parasite. The links come from a combination of published reports, direct observations, and logical but presumed interactions. A directed edge points from a resource (prey or host) to its consumer (predator or parasite), and is labeled by the type of trophic interaction, coded in the source as follows (a value N.1 marks a proposed or presumed link of type N): 1, first intermediate host (1.2: first and second intermediate host; 1.25: first and second intermediate host, with excystment outside the second intermediate host); 2, second intermediate host (2.5: second intermediate host, with an external, non-trophic cyst); 3, final host; 4, predator-prey (4.2: egg predator; 4.11 is the same as 4.1); 5, predation on free-living cercarial stage of a trematode; 6, micropredation (mosquito); 7, predation on a parasite in a host; 8, predation on a parasite in a host, with possible transmission to the predator; 9, parasite-parasite (mostly intraguild predation). This is an early version of the web, which was later updated and extended (Hechinger et al. 2011): the later version, resolved by life stage, is the network `carpinteria` of the entry `california_estuaries`, and a version of it aggregated by species is the network `carpinteria` of `coastal_parasite_webs`; this 2006 version is also included in `gateway_foodwebs`. Nodes: `name`, the name of the taxon or resource; `kind`, whether it is a basal resource ("Basal"), a free-living species ("Freeliving") or a parasite ("Parasite"); `group`, a one-letter taxonomic group code given in the source (not explained there, but apparently: "D" detritus, "K" carrion, "P" primary producers, "A" annelids, "B" birds, "C" crustaceans, "F" fishes, "G" gastropods, "I" insects, "V" bivalves, "R" mammals (raccoon), "L" leeches, "N" nematodes, "T" trematodes, "W" cestodes, "O" other parasites). Edges: `link_type`, the code of the type of interaction (see above).
- `food_web_thompson_<stream>` (Thompson and Townsend 2003, and related studies): 26 food webs of streams in New Zealand and in Maine and North Carolina (USA), compiled by R. M. Thompson, C. R. Townsend and collaborators in a series of studies on the effects of land use (e.g. native versus exotic forest), disturbance, resource supply, taxonomic resolution and season on stream food web structure. Nodes are taxa (algae, aquatic invertebrates, mostly insects, and fish), and a directed edge $(i, j)$ indicates that taxon $j$ feeds on taxon $i$. Each network is named after the stream; some streams were sampled in several seasons, indicated by the suffixes `Sp` (spring), `Su` (summer) and `Au` (autumn), and `AkatoreA` and `AkatoreB` are two webs from the Akatore stream. The IWDB distributes these data as binary interaction matrices without taxon names, so the networks carry no node metadata. Ten of the New Zealand webs (Blackrock, Broad, Canton, Dempsters, German, Healy, Kyeburn, LilKyeburn, Stony and Sutton) are also contained in `gateway_foodwebs` (as Townsend et al. 1998), with taxon names and the same or nearly the same number of links.

datasets.name: jakarta_bombing_2009
datasets.description:
Networks of relationships among 28 individuals associated with the bombings of the JW Marriott and Ritz-Carlton hotels in Jakarta, Indonesia, on 17 July 2009 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_Jakarta_bombings)), attributed to the network of Noordin Mohammad Top, from the John Jay & ARTIS Transnational Terrorism Database (JJATT). The data were coded from open sources, and were made available in matrix form by the UCINET datasets collection (University of Manchester).

Nodes are individuals (labeled by their JJATT identifier in `name`). The networks `pre_attack` and `post_attack` contain the relationships before and after the attack, with the edge property `weight` giving the strength of the tie: 1 = acquaintances or distant family ties (interaction limited to radical organization activities), 2 = friends or moderately close family ties (including co-workers and roommates), operational or organizational leadership, or operational ties (e.g. having worked closely together on a bombing), 3 = close friends or family, tight-knit operational cliques (a few ties have values 5 or 6, which are not described in the source documentation). The `kinship` network contains kinship ties, with the edge property `kinship` coding the type: 1 = in-laws, 2 = cousins, 3 = siblings, 4 = parent/child, 5 = married, 6 = grandparent/grandchild, 7 = significant other (cells coded 99 in the source matrix, whose meaning is not documented, are omitted). The source matrices are meant to be symmetric; where the two directions differ, the tie with the larger value is used. The JJATT operation matrix is not included.[^ucinet]

[^ucinet]: Description obtained in part from the [UCINET datasets page](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/datasets/covert-networks/jakarta-bombing-2009-noordin-top).
citations: S. Atran, M. Sageman, et al., "John Jay & ARTIS Transnational Terrorism Database (JJATT)." John Jay College of Criminal Justice (2009)

datasets.name: jazz_collab
datasets.description:
A collaboration network of jazz bands, compiled by P. Gleiser and L. Danon from The Red Hot Jazz Archive digital database. Nodes are the 198 bands in the database that performed between 1912 and 1940 (most of them in the 1920s), and an undirected edge connects two bands that have at least one musician in common. Since the database lists the musicians of each band without dates, the network has no temporal information; also, the same musician may appear under different names, and unknown musicians are all listed as "unknown". (The cited paper also studies the network among the 1,275 musicians, which is not included here.)

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the node number in the source data (band names are not included).
citations: P. Gleiser and L. Danon, "Community Structure in Jazz." Advances in Complex Systems 6(4), 565-573 (2003).

datasets.name: jester
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of users and the jokes they rated in Jester, an online joke recommender system developed by K. Goldberg and collaborators at the University of California, Berkeley. This is Jester's Dataset 1, with over 4.1 million ratings of 100 jokes by 73,421 anonymous users, collected between April 1999 and May 2003. Users rated jokes with a continuous slider, and each rating is a real value between -10 and +10. Each edge connects a user to a joke they rated. The data were released in three parts: two of users who rated 36 or more jokes (24,983 and 23,500 users), and one of users who rated between 15 and 35 jokes (24,938 users). Almost all users rated the ten jokes 5, 7, 8, 13, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19 and 20, which were used as the "gauge set" of the Eigentaste recommendation algorithm.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `is_joke`: whether the node is a joke (otherwise it is a user).
- (Node) `joke_id`: the number of the joke (1 to 100; -1 for users).
- (Node) `text`: the text of the joke (with the HTML markup removed).
- (Node) `part`: the part of the data set the user comes from (1, 2 or 3; -1 for jokes).
- (Edge) `weight`: the rating, between -10 and +10 (higher values for funnier jokes), with two decimal places.
citations: K. Goldberg, T. Roeder, D. Gupta, C. Perkins, "Eigentaste: A Constant Time Collaborative Filtering Algorithm." Information Retrieval 4(2), 133-151 (2001)

datasets.name: ji_koschade
datasets.description:
Network of interactions among the 17 members of the Jemaah Islamiyah cell responsible for the bombings in Bali, Indonesia, on 12 October 2002, as reconstructed by Koschade (2006) from the reports of the International Crisis Group (based on depositions of suspects, court documents and Indonesian press reports). The interactions were recorded from the meeting at the Hotel Harum in Denpasar on 6 October 2002, when the group went "operationally covert", until most of the group had left Bali before the attack. Nodes are individuals (vertex property `name`), and edges are exchanges of information (communications). The edge property `weight` gives the strength of the relationship, from 1 (weakest, e.g. a single text message or a financial transaction) to 5 (strongest, e.g. individuals who lived together, or who had numerous weak contacts during the period). Where the two directions in the source matrix differ, the larger value is used. Data distributed by the UCINET datasets collection (University of Manchester).[^ucinet]

[^ucinet]: Description obtained in part from the [UCINET datasets page](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/datasets/covert-networks/jemaah-islamiyah-koschade).
citations: S. Koschade, "A social network analysis of Jemaah Islamiyah: The applications to counterterrorism and intelligence." Studies in Conflict & Terrorism 29(6), 559-575 (2006)

datasets.name: jlaw_citegraph
datasets.description:
Directed networks of the citations between the national laws of Japan in force in September and October 2026, from JLaw-CiteGraph (versions 2.0 to 2.5), a dataset built by automatic extraction of the references in the texts of the laws of e-Gov 法令検索 (e-Gov Law Search, the official law database of the Japanese Digital Agency), from its bulk downloads. The laws are the national statutes in force (in the latest snapshot, of 20 October 2026, 8,981 laws: 法律 acts 2,100, 政令 cabinet orders 2,310, 府省令 ministerial ordinances 4,095, 規則 rules 409, 勅令 imperial ordinances 66, and the constitution), each at the version in force on the date of the snapshot; local ordinances, case law, administrative circulars, treaties, repealed laws and amending acts are not included as nodes, and the citations to them are left out. The references were extracted by rules (exact titles and law numbers of the cited laws, abbreviations, anaphoric references such as 同法 "the same act" and 前条 "the preceding article"), with resolution rates reported by the authors of 93 % for references within a law, 82 % between laws and 92 % for relative references.

There are two networks for each of the six snapshots of the e-Gov data in the history of the dataset (2026-09-27, 2026-09-28, 2026-10-01, 2026-10-03, 2026-10-19 and 2026-10-20; the dataset was rebuilt from each new e-Gov bulk download), named `laws_<date>` and `provisions_<date>` (e.g. `laws_2026-10-20`):

- `laws_<date>`: each node is a law (all of them, including those without citations), and a directed edge from law A to law B means that the text of A cites B (citations within the same law are not included), weighted by the number of citing provisions (70,774 edges in the latest snapshot).
- `provisions_<date>`: each node is a provision of a law (an article, a paragraph, an item, an article of the supplementary provisions, or an attached table, form or figure), or a law as a whole, and a directed edge from A to B is a reference from provision A to B, of one of four kinds: `CITES` (a citation of another provision, in the same law or another one), `DELEGATES_TO` (a delegation, such as "as provided by cabinet order", from a provision to the law that it delegates to, as a whole), `REFERS_TO_ATTACHMENT` (a reference to an attached table, form, etc.) and `AMENDS`. Only the provisions that take part in some reference are included. The network is a multigraph: a few pairs of provisions are joined by references of different kinds. The hierarchy of the provisions (law, chapter, article, paragraph, item) is not included as edges; it can be recovered from the identifiers of the nodes.

The nodes are identified by the e-Gov law ids (e.g. `129AC0000000089` for the Civil Code), followed for provisions by their position within the law (e.g. `129AC0000000089_a709` for article 709 of the Civil Code, `…_a10-2_p3_i12-2` for item 12-2 of paragraph 3 of article 10-2, `…_asup-sp1-2` for article 2 of the supplementary provisions, `…_at-style-1` for form 1). 

The `laws_<date>` networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `law_id`: the e-Gov law id; `name`: the title of the law (in Japanese); `type`: its type (`法律`, `政令`, `府省令`, `規則`, `勅令`, `憲法`); `url`: the page of the law on e-Gov.
- (Node) `enforcement_date`: the date on which the version of the law in the data came into force (`YYYYMMDD`); `next_enforcement_date`: the date of the next amendment that is already decided (empty if none); `pending_versions`: the number of amendments that are decided but not yet in force.
- (Edge) `count`: the number of citations (pairs of citing provision and cited provision of the two laws).

The `provisions_<date>` networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `node_id`: the identifier of the provision (see above).
- (Node) `level`: its kind: `law`, `article`, `paragraph`, `item`, `supplementary_article` or `attachment`.
- (Node) `law_id`, `law_name`, `law_type`: the id, the title and the type of the law that contains the provision.
- (Edge) `relation`: `CITES`, `DELEGATES_TO`, `REFERS_TO_ATTACHMENT` or `AMENDS`.
- (Edge) `raw`: the text of the reference (e.g. `前項`, `第一条`, `民法第七百九条`).
- (Edge) `extracted_from`: how the reference was resolved (e.g. `canonical`, `alias`, `same_as_last`, `INTERNAL_PAT`, `REFERENTIAL/前項`; see the data card).
- (Edge) `fallback_level`: how precisely the target was located (e.g. `exact`, or the enclosing provision when the cited one was not found; empty if not given).
- (Edge) `confidence`: the confidence of the resolution given by the authors (NaN if not given).
- (Edge) `pre_amendment`: whether the citation names the text of the law before an amendment (e.g. "the former act"), whereas only the current text is in the graph.
citations: yabooung, "JLaw-CiteGraph: a citation graph of Japanese statutory law." Hugging Face dataset, versions 2.0-2.5 (2026)

datasets.name: jodie_wikipedia
datasets.description:
Temporal bipartite networks of interactions between users and items, compiled by S. Kumar, X. Zhang and J. Leskovec as benchmarks for the JODIE method of dynamic embeddings. Each interaction is a timestamped edge between a user and an item; repeated interactions of the same user with the same item are separate edges. The times are given in seconds since the first interaction of each data set, without the absolute dates. User and item identifiers were anonymized (users and items are numbered separately). There are four networks:

- `wikipedia`: one month of public Wikipedia edit records, between the 1,000 most edited pages and the editors who made at least 5 edits to them. Each edit has a feature vector computed from its text, with the categories of the Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC) lexicon, and a label marking the last edit of the editors that were subsequently banned from Wikipedia (217 editors).
- `reddit`: one month of posts on Reddit, from the Pushshift data dump, between the 10,000 most active users and the 1,000 most active subreddits (the items; 984 of them appear in the data), 672,447 posts. Each post has a LIWC feature vector computed from its text, and a label marking the last post of the users that were subsequently banned from Reddit (366 users).
- `mooc`: the actions (e.g. viewing a video or submitting an answer) of 7,047 students on 97 items (videos, answers, etc.; 98 according to the authors) of a massive open online course (MOOC), from the data of the KDD Cup 2015, 411,749 actions. Each action has a 4-dimensional feature vector (whose meaning is not documented), and a label marking the actions after which the student dropped out of the course (4,066 drop-out events).
- `lastfm`: one month of songs listened to by 980 users of Last.fm (1,000 according to the authors), restricted to the 1,000 most listened songs, 1,293,103 listens, from the data of B. Hidasi and D. Tikk. There are no features or labels (the placeholder features of the data, all zero, are left out).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `id`: the identifier of the editor or page in the original data (`wikipedia`), or of the user or item in the data (`reddit`, `mooc`, `lastfm`).
- (Node) `is_page` (`wikipedia`): whether the node is a page (otherwise it is an editor).
- (Node) `is_item` (`reddit`, `mooc`, `lastfm`): whether the node is an item (a subreddit, course item or song; otherwise a user).
- (Edge) `time`: the time of the edit (`wikipedia`) or of the interaction (`reddit`, `mooc`, `lastfm`), in seconds since the first edit or interaction in the data.
- (Edge) `banned` (`wikipedia`): 1 if this is the last edit of an editor who was then banned, otherwise 0.
- (Edge) `label` (`reddit` and `mooc`): 1 if the user was banned after this post (`reddit`) or dropped out after this action (`mooc`), otherwise 0.
- (Edge) `features` (`wikipedia`, `reddit` and `mooc`): the feature vector of the edit text or of the interaction (172 LIWC categories for `wikipedia` and `reddit`, 4 values for `mooc`).
citations: S. Kumar, X. Zhang, J. Leskovec, "Predicting Dynamic Embedding Trajectory in Temporal Interaction Networks." Proceedings of the 25th ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery & Data Mining, 1269-1278 (2019)

datasets.name: kangaroo
datasets.description:
Frequencies of observed physical proximity among 17 free-ranging grey kangaroos (Macropus giganteus) in the Nadgee Nature Reserve in New South Wales (Australia), from the study of dominance and association by T. R. Grant (1973). The original report included 18 kangaroos, but one (M11) was never observed and is not included. The animals comprise five females (F1 to F5) and 12 males (M1 to M13); F4, F5 and M2 are juveniles. Two dominance rankings are also given: `SS` is the ratio of the number of "successes" of an animal to its number of "involvements"; `PS` assigns an animal two points for each other animal it bests in more than 50% of their contacts, and one point for a tie. Since there were no contests between the sexes, except for the juvenile male M2, males and females are ranked separately, with M2 ranked among the females. The data were distributed by L. C. Freeman on his network data page at the University of California, Irvine (no longer online), from which this version was obtained via the Internet Archive.

An undirected edge (i, j) indicates that kangaroos i and j were observed in proximity.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the label of the kangaroo (F: female, M: male).
- (Node) `ss_rank` and `ps_rank`: the two dominance ranks described above.
- (Node) `diagonal`: the diagonal entry of the proximity matrix (its meaning is not documented).
- (Edge) `weight`: the number of observed proximities.
citations: T. R. Grant. "Dominance and association among members of a captive and a free-ranging group of grey kangaroos (Macropus giganteus)." Animal Behaviour 21(3), 449-456, (1973)

datasets.name: kansas_sar
datasets.description:
Communication among the 20 organizations involved in a search and rescue (SAR) operation after a small tornado flipped a pleasure boat on Lake Pomona, in Kansas (USA), from the study of multiorganizational emergency responses of T. E. Drabek and collaborators. The organizations include law enforcement agencies, fire departments, underwater rescue teams, general emergency agencies, and county, state and federal agencies. The County Sheriff took control of the operation, and a command post was created in a Highway Patrol facility. A directed edge from one organization to another indicates communication between them, as in the rows and columns of the source matrix. The documentation describes the original data as valued (communication intensity from 1, about once a day, to 4, continuous), but the "valued" matrix distributed is identical to the binary one, so the network is unweighted. The data were distributed on the Pajek datasets page of the book *Generalized Blockmodeling* (Doreian, Batagelj and Ferligoj), from which this version was obtained.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the short name of the organization.
- (Node) `code`: its letter code (A to T) as used in the publications.
- (Node) `long_name`: its full name.
citations: T. E. Drabek, H. L. Tamminga, T. S. Kilijanek, C. R. Adams, "Managing Multiorganizational Emergency Responses: Emergent Search and Rescue Networks in Natural Disaster and Remote Area Settings." Institute of Behavioral Science, University of Colorado, Boulder (1981)
P. Doreian, V. Batagelj, A. Ferligoj, "Generalized Blockmodeling." Cambridge University Press (2004)

datasets.name: kapferer_mine
datasets.description:
Interactions among 15 men working on the surface of a mining operation in Zambia (then Northern Rhodesia), observed by B. Kapferer, who studied the development and resolution of a conflict among the workers. The conflict centered on two men, Abraham and Donald, and most workers ended up supporting Abraham. Kapferer recorded several types of interactions among the workers (conversation, joking, job assistance, cash assistance and personal assistance), but did not publish them; the available matrices only distinguish ties based on a single type of interaction from those based on several. These data were analyzed by P. Doreian (1974). The data were distributed by L. C. Freeman on his network data page at the University of California, Irvine (no longer online), from which this version was obtained via the Internet Archive.

- `uniplex`: undirected edges between workers joined by a tie based on only one type of interaction.
- `multiplex`: undirected edges between workers joined by ties based on several types of interaction.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the worker.
citations: B. Kapferer, "Norms and the manipulation of relationships in a work context." In J. C. Mitchell (ed.), Social Networks in Urban Situations, Manchester University Press (1969)
P. Doreian, "On the connectivity of social networks." Journal of Mathematical Sociology 3(2), 245-258 (1974)

datasets.name: kapferer_tailor
datasets.description:
Interactions among 39 workers of a tailor shop in a town of Zambia (then Northern Rhodesia), observed by the anthropologist B. Kapferer over a period of ten months, during extended negotiations for higher wages. Interactions were recorded at two times, seven months apart, each over a period of one month. An abortive strike occurred after the first set of observations, and a successful strike after the second. This extended version of the data was distributed by T. Snijders with the SIENA software.

Two types of interaction were recorded:

- `sociational_1` and `sociational_2`: "sociational" (friendship and socio-emotional) interactions, at the first and second time, respectively. These are undirected.
- `instrumental_1` and `instrumental_2`: "instrumental" (work- and assistance-related) interactions, at the first and second time, respectively. These are directed.

Nodes are workers, and an edge connects two workers between whom an interaction of the given type was observed. In the directed networks, an edge $(i, j)$ corresponds to the entry in row $i$ and column $j$ of the source matrix; the meaning of the direction is not documented.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `status`: the job category of the worker, in decreasing order of prestige according to a survey among employees (Kapferer 1972, pp. 55-59): 1: head tailor, 2: cutter, 3: line 1 tailor, 4: button machiner, 5: line 3 tailor, 6: ironer, 7: cotton boy, 8: line 2 tailor.
- (Node) `lyashi`: whether the worker is Lyashi, the most central individual.
- (Node) `high_status`: whether the worker has a high status job.
citations: B. Kapferer, "Strategy and Transaction in an African Factory: African Workers and Indian Management in a Zambian Town." Manchester University Press (1972)

datasets.name: karate
datasets.description:
Network of social ties among the 34 members of a university karate club in the United States, observed by the anthropologist W. W. Zachary from 1970 to 1972. An undirected edge connects two members who consistently interacted outside the activities of the club. During the observation period, a conflict between the club's instructor ("Mr. Hi", node 1) and its administrator (node 34) led the club to split into two.

There are two versions of the network, due to an inconsistency in the adjacency matrix published by Zachary, which is not symmetric for the pair of members 23 and 34: `77` has 77 edges and omits the edge between them, while `78` has 78 edges and includes it. The 78-edge version is the one most commonly used.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the member's number, as in the original study (1 to 34).
- (Node) `groups`: the faction to which the member belonged after the split, as given in the data distributed by A. Clauset: 1 for the instructor's faction (node 1), 2 for the administrator's (node 34).
citations: W. W. Zachary, "An information flow model for conflict and fission in small groups." Journal of Anthropological Research 33, 452-473 (1977).

datasets.name: kegg_metabolic
datasets.description: Metabolic networks of 109 organisms (bacteria, archaea and eukaryotes), extracted by M. Huss and P. Holme from the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) database in March 2006, and distributed by A. Clauset. Nodes are metabolites (substances) that take part in the enzymatic reactions annotated for the organism, and an undirected edge connects a reactant and a product of the same reaction, according to the reactant-product pairs listed in KEGG. The networks include a few self-loops. Each network is named after the KEGG organism code (e.g. `eco` for *Escherichia coli* K-12, `hsa` for *Homo sapiens*, `sce` for *Saccharomyces cerevisiae*). The metabolite names or KEGG compound identifiers are not included in the data.
citations: M. Huss & P. Holme, "Currency and commodity metabolites: their identification and relation to the modularity of metabolic networks." IET Syst. Biol. 1(5), 280-285 (2007)

datasets.name: kenya_tanzania_bombings
datasets.description:
Bipartite network of 18 members of Al-Qaeda and 25 functional tasks in which they participated, underlying the bombings of the United States embassies in Nairobi, Kenya, and Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, on 7 August 1998. An edge connects a member to each task in which they participated. The data were collected by the Center for Computational Analysis of Social and Organizational Systems (CASOS) at Carnegie Mellon University, and used by Gerdes (2014). The vertex property `is_task` indicates whether a node is a task (True, numbered 1 to 25 in `name`) or a person (False). Data distributed by the UCINET datasets collection (University of Manchester).[^ucinet]

[^ucinet]: Description obtained in part from the [UCINET datasets page](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/datasets/covert-networks/kenya-tanzania-gerdes).
citations: L. M. Gerdes, "Dependency Centrality from Bipartite Social Networks." Connections 34(1&2) (2014)

datasets.name: kidnappings
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of members of the Abu Sayyaf Group (ASG), a violent non-state armed group operating in the southern Philippines since 1991, and the kidnapping events in which they took part. The data were reconstructed by L. Gerdes, K. Ringler and B. Autin from open sources, in a study of the group's strategic and learning capacities, and distributed in the UCINET collection of covert networks. There are 246 persons and 105 kidnapping events, and an edge connects a person to an event in which they participated.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: anonymized label of the node (`N1`, `N2`, ... for persons, `E1`, `E2`, ... for events).
- (Node) `is_event`: whether the node is a kidnapping event (True) or a group member (False).
citations: L. Gerdes, K. Ringler, and B. Autin, "Assessing the Abu Sayyaf Group's Strategic and Learning Capacities." Studies in Conflict & Terrorism 37(3), 267-293 (2014)

datasets.name: kinophosphatome
datasets.description:
Networks of interactions among human proteins, from the supplementary data of the article by G. Scardoni, M. Petterlini and C. Laudanna introducing CentiScaPe, a Cytoscape plugin for computing node centralities. Nodes represent human proteins (identified by their HGNC gene symbols), and an undirected edge means that the two proteins are known to interact, according to the public protein interaction databases HPRD, BIND, DIP, IntAct, MINT and BioGRID, from which the data were compiled. There are two networks:

- `global`: the global human protein interactome compiled by the authors (the file `GLOBAL-HGNC.sif`), with 11,120 proteins and 84,776 interactions, including 2,500 self-interactions.
- `kinophosphatome_core`: a sub-network of the human kino-phosphatome, i.e. of the network of interactions among human protein kinases and phosphatases, containing the 97 proteins (82 kinases and 15 phosphatases) whose values of all the centralities computed by CentiScaPe (degree, betweenness, closeness, eccentricity, radiality, stress and centroid value) are above the average of the kino-phosphatome network, and the 962 interactions among them.

The kino-phosphatome network analyzed in the article, with 549 proteins (406 kinases and 143 phosphatases, listed in its Table S4) and 3,844 interactions, is not included in the supplementary data; it can be approximated as the sub-network of the global interactome induced by the proteins marked as kinases or phosphatases, but that sub-network has 3,777 interactions (including 244 self-interactions), and 6 of the 549 proteins do not occur in the global interactome.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the HGNC symbol of the gene encoding the protein.
- (Node) `kind`: `kinase` or `phosphatase` for the 549 proteins of the kino-phosphatome network (Table S4 of the article), empty otherwise (LMTK2, which is marked both as a kinase and as a phosphatase in the table, is given as a phosphatase, consistent with the counts of the article).[^icon]

[^icon]: Description obtained in part from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.
citations: G. Scardoni, M. Petterlini, C. Laudanna, "Analyzing biological network parameters with CentiScaPe." Bioinformatics 25(21), 2857-2859 (2009)

datasets.name: kleinberg_web
datasets.description:
Web graphs constructed by J. Kleinberg by expanding the response set of 200 pages returned by a search engine for a query, as in his hub/authority (HITS) algorithm: the root set of pages is expanded with the pages that link to them and the pages they link to. Nodes are web pages, and directed edges are hyperlinks. Many of the pages have no links to or from the other pages in the distributed data, and appear as isolated nodes. The graphs were distributed on Kleinberg's course page (Cornell CS685, 2002), and adapted for Pajek by V. Batagelj (2006). They were used, e.g., by A. N. Langville and C. D. Meyer to study the reordering of the PageRank problem. The data were distributed in Pajek format on the Pajek datasets page of V. Batagelj and A. Mrvar, from which this version was obtained.

- `california`: pages matching the query "California".
- `epa`: pages linking to www.epa.gov.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the URL of the page.
citations: J. M. Kleinberg, "Authoritative sources in a hyperlinked environment." Journal of the ACM 46(5), 604-632 (1999)
A. N. Langville, C. D. Meyer, "A Reordering for the PageRank Problem." SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing 27(6), 2112-2120 (2006)

datasets.name: knoke_bureaucracies
datasets.description:
Exchange relations among ten organizations in the political economy of Indianapolis (USA). In 1978, D. Knoke and J. Wood collected data from workers at 95 organizations in Indianapolis, who indicated with which other organizations their own organization had any of 13 different types of relationships; D. Knoke and J. Kuklinski selected a subset of 10 organizations and two relationships. A directed edge points from an organization to another to which it sends information or money. The data were distributed in UCINET and Pajek formats on the Pajek datasets page of V. Batagelj and A. Mrvar, from which this version (in Pajek format) was obtained.

- `information`: information exchange (KNOKI).
- `money`: money exchange (KNOKM).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the abbreviation of the organization (COUN: county government, COMM: chamber of commerce, EDUC: board of education, INDU: industrial development agency, MAYR: mayor's office, WRO: welfare rights organization, NEWS: newspaper, UWAY: United Way, WELF: welfare department, WEST: West Side community organization).
- (Node) `sector`: the sector of the organization (1: government, 2: voluntary, 3: private).
citations: D. Knoke, J. R. Wood, "Organized for Action: Commitment in Voluntary Associations." Rutgers University Press, New Brunswick, NJ (1981)
D. Knoke, J. H. Kuklinski, "Network Analysis." Sage, Beverly Hills, CA (1982)
S. P. Borgatti, M. G. Everett, L. C. Freeman, "UCINET for Windows: Software for Social Network Analysis." Analytic Technologies, Harvard, MA (2002)

datasets.name: korea_family_planning
datasets.description:
Communication networks about family planning among women in two Korean villages, from the study of E. M. Rogers and D. L. Kincaid on the diffusion of family planning methods in Korean villages, which were surveyed in 1973. An edge connects two women who discussed family planning with each other. The data were distributed on the Pajek datasets page of the book *Exploratory Social Network Analysis with Pajek* (de Nooy, Mrvar and Batagelj), from which this version was obtained. (The background text on the dataset page of the Pajek site erroneously repeats the description of the sawmill dataset.)[^icon]

- `village1`: the network of 39 women in the first village (`Korea1.net`).
- `village2`: the network of 39 women in the second village (`Korea2.net`).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the identifier of the woman in the original study.
- (Node) `adopter`: whether the woman adopted family planning methods (at least temporarily).
- (Node) `club_member`: whether the woman was a member of the local Mothers' Club.

[^icon]: Description obtained in part from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.
citations: E. M. Rogers, D. L. Kincaid, "Communication Networks: Toward a New Paradigm for Research." Free Press, New York (1981)
W. de Nooy, A. Mrvar, V. Batagelj, "Exploratory Social Network Analysis with Pajek." Cambridge University Press (2005)

datasets.name: krackhardt_kite
datasets.description:
A small illustrative network of ten actors introduced by David Krackhardt, who called it a "kite structure", to show that the three classic measures of centrality can identify different actors as the most central. It is a constructed example, not empirical data. In this version, Diane has the largest degree (6), Heather has the largest betweenness (she is the only connection of Ike and Jane to the rest of the network), and Fernando and Garth have the largest closeness. The actor names and the interpretation of the edges as pairs of actors who regularly interact with each other are those of V. Krebs' popular introduction to social network analysis (orgnet.com), from which the network is usually reproduced. The data were obtained from the R package igraphdata, which also provides the standard drawing of the network.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the one-letter label of the actor (A to J).
- (Node) `first_name`: the name of the actor.
- (Node) `x` and `y`: the coordinates of the actor in the standard drawing of the network.
citations: D. Krackhardt, "Assessing the Political Landscape: Structure, Cognition, and Power in Organizations." Administrative Science Quarterly 35, 342-369 (1990)

datasets.name: krebs_it_department
datasets.description:
Work relationships among 56 employees of the IT department of a Fortune 500 company, collected by V. Krebs (unpublished, date unknown). The first 7 employees were administrative staff, the next 12 were together in a department, the next 17 in a second department, the following 17 in a third department, and the last 3 were executives. Each individual reported, for five kinds of links, the frequency of contact with each of the others. The data were distributed by L. C. Freeman on his network data page at the University of California, Irvine (no longer online), from which this version was obtained via the Internet Archive.

The network has five directed layers (relations), in which an edge (i, j) indicates that employee i reported the relation with employee j:

- `BUSINESS_1`: "With whom do you work with in Business Process 1?"
- `BUSINESS_2`: "With whom do you work with in Business Process 2?"
- `ADVICE`: "Who do you seek for advice before making a key decision?"
- `TECHNICAL`: "Who do you seek for technical expertise in IT?"
- `CUSTOMER`: "With whom do you discuss customer needs and issues?"

The source data file is truncated: the last 100 values of the `CUSTOMER` relation (all the answers of the last employee, and 44 of the 56 answers of the second-to-last one, both executives) are missing, and are treated here as absent edges.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the label of the employee.
- (Node) `group`: the group of the employee (as described above: `admin`, `department1`, `department2`, `department3`, or `executive`).
- (Edge) `layer`: the relation.
- (Edge) `weight`: the frequency of contact (1: yearly or less, 2: quarterly, 3: monthly, 4: weekly, 5: daily or more).

datasets.name: kuairand
datasets.description:
Networks of the users of the short video sharing app Kuaishou (快手) and the videos that its recommender system showed them, from the KuaiRand dataset, collected by C. Gao and colleagues (University of Science and Technology of China and Kuaishou) from the recommendation logs of the app between 8 April and 8 May 2022. In the last two and a half weeks of this period (22 April to 8 May), each video recommended to the users had a small probability of being replaced by a video drawn at random from a pool of 7,583 videos; about 0.37% of the exposures were replaced. The logs record, for each exposure, whether the user clicked (or, in the single-column interface, validly played) the video, liked it, followed its author, commented on it, forwarded it, or marked it as disliked, how long it was watched, and whether the user visited the author's profile.

A directed edge from a user to a video is one exposure of the video to the user, with the user's feedback. The networks are bipartite and are multigraphs (a video may be shown to the same user several times). They combine the three log files of each version: the standard recommendations of 8-21 April and of 22 April - 8 May, and the random exposures of 22 April - 8 May (marked by the edge property `random`).

There are three versions, released by the authors, each a network of this entry:

- `27k`: the complete dataset, with all 27,285 users and the 32 million videos shown to them (322 million exposures).
- `1k`: 1,000 users drawn at random from the complete dataset, with all their exposures.
- `pure`: all users, but only the exposures of the 7,583 videos of the pool of random videos.

The user and video identifiers were re-indexed by the source. The anonymized categorical user features of the source (`onehot_feat0` to `onehot_feat17`) are kept as a vector property; the binned versions of the counts of the users (e.g. `follow_user_num_range`), and the date and hour of the exposures (redundant with the timestamps) are left out. The daily statistics of the videos (counts of plays, likes, comments, shares, ... of each video during the period, in the source's `video_features_statistic` files, with 50 columns) are also left out. The per-exposure duration of the videos in the logs agrees with the duration of the video given in the video features, except for very few exposures (e.g. 350 of the 11.7 million of `1k`); it is used for the videos whose duration is missing there, and otherwise left out.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `is_user`: whether the node is a user (otherwise it is a video).
- (Node) `id`: the identifier of the user or video in the dataset.
- (Node) `active_degree` (users): the activity level of the user, e.g. `full_active`, `high_active`, `middle_active`, `2_14_day_new`, `30day_retention`, `UNKNOWN`.
- (Node) `is_lowactive_period`, `is_live_streamer`, `is_video_author` (users): flags of the user, as given by the source (with a few values other than 0 and 1, e.g. -124).
- (Node) `follow_user_num`, `fans_user_num`, `friend_user_num` (users): the numbers of users that the user follows, of followers, and of friends.
- (Node) `register_days` (users): the number of days since the user registered.
- (Node) `onehot_features` (users): the 18 anonymized categorical features of the user (`onehot_feat0` to `onehot_feat17`; NaN if missing).
- (Node) `author_id` (videos): the identifier of the author of the video (-1 if unknown).
- (Node) `video_type` (videos): `NORMAL` or `AD`.
- (Node) `upload_time` (videos): the upload date of the video, as Unix time (-1 if unknown).
- (Node) `upload_type` (videos): the way the video was uploaded, e.g. `LongImport`, `ShortImport`, `Web`, `Kmovie`.
- (Node) `visible_status` (videos): the visibility status of the video (NaN if unknown).
- (Node) `duration` (videos): the duration of the video, in milliseconds (NaN if unknown).
- (Node) `width`, `height` (videos): the size of the video, in pixels (NaN if unknown).
- (Node) `music_id` (videos): the identifier of the background music of the video (-1 if unknown).
- (Node) `music_type` (videos): the type of the background music (NaN if unknown).
- (Node) `tags` (videos): the ids of the categories of the video, comma-separated, e.g. `20,43`.
- (Edge) `time`: the time of the exposure, as Unix time (with milliseconds).
- (Edge) `click`: whether the user clicked on the video (in the two-column interface), or played it validly (in the single-column interface: for at least its duration, if it lasts at most 7 seconds, or for more than 7 seconds otherwise).
- (Edge) `long_view`: whether the user watched the video for at least its duration, if it lasts at most 18 seconds, or for at least 18 seconds otherwise.
- (Edge) `like`, `follow`, `comment`, `forward`, `hate`: whether the user liked the video, followed its author, commented on it, forwarded it, or marked it as disliked.
- (Edge) `profile_enter`: whether the user visited the profile of the author.
- (Edge) `play_time`: how long the user watched the video, in milliseconds.
- (Edge) `profile_stay_time`, `comment_stay_time`: how long the user stayed on the profile of the author and in the comment section of the video, in milliseconds.
- (Edge) `random`: whether the video was shown by the random intervention.
- (Edge) `tab`: the interface (tab of the app) where the video was shown, a number from 0 to 14.
citations: C. Gao, S. Li, Y. Zhang, J. Chen, B. Li, W. Lei, P. Jiang, X. He, "KuaiRand: An Unbiased Sequential Recommendation Dataset with Randomly Exposed Videos." Proceedings of the 31st ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM), 3953-3957 (2022)

datasets.name: kuairec
datasets.description:
Networks of the users of the short video sharing app Kuaishou (快手), the videos they watched, and their friendships, from the KuaiRec dataset, collected by C. Gao and colleagues (University of Science and Technology of China, Kuaishou and the National University of Singapore) from the recommendation logs of the app between 22 June and 10 September 2020. Its distinguishing feature is a "fully observed" part: for a set of 1,411 users and 3,327 videos, the videos were shown to all the users, so that the users' reactions to almost all of the videos are known (99.6%; the missing ones are videos of authors that the users had blocked).

There are three networks:

- `big`: the views of 7,176 users and 10,728 videos (the "big matrix" of the source, 12.5 million views, of which 2.2 million repeat an earlier view of the same video by the same user). A directed edge from a user to a video is a view of the video by the user. The network is bipartite and a multigraph.
- `small`: the views of the fully observed part (the "small matrix", 1,411 users and 3,327 videos, 4.7 million views), in the same form, with only these users and videos. Its views are not part of `big` (the two sets of views are disjoint, although the users and videos of `small` also appear in `big`). The time of 181,992 of these views is missing.
- `social`: the friendships among the 7,176 users (an undirected edge between two users who are friends). Only 472 users have friends in the data.

The node properties of the users come from the user features of the source (including the raw features released in January 2026: gender, age range, phone, location, installed apps, ...). Those of the videos come from the daily video features (the values of the last day, for the few that change over time: visibility, size and tag), and from the captions and categories released in June 2024. The daily statistics of the videos (counts of plays, likes, comments, ... per day), the binned versions of the counts of the users, and the multi-level category annotations with probabilities (`video_raw_categories_multi.csv`) are left out. The user and video identifiers are those of the source (re-indexed by it).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `is_user` (`big`, `small`): whether the node is a user (otherwise it is a video).
- (Node) `id`: the identifier of the user or video in the dataset.
- (Node) The user properties below are as given by the source (`UNKNOWN`, or -1 for the counts and flags, if unknown), and empty, or -1, for videos.
- (Node) `user_active_degree` (users): the activity level, e.g. `full_active`, `high_active`.
- (Node) `is_lowactive_period`, `is_live_author`, `is_photo_author`, `follow_user_num`, `fans_user_num`, `friend_user_num`, `gender`, `age_range`, `phone_brand`, `phone_model`, `platform`, `os_version`, `app_download_channel`, `app_version` (users): the corresponding attributes of the user.
- (Node) `register_days` (users): days since registration.
- (Node) `mod_price` (users): the price of the phone model.
- (Node) `fre_country`, `fre_country_region`, `fre_province`, `fre_city`, `fre_city_level`, `fre_community_type` (users): the most frequent location of the user.
- (Node) `is_install_douyin`, `is_install_huoshan`, `is_install_xigua`, `is_install_douyu`, `is_install_huya`, `is_install_yy` (users): whether other video apps are installed.
- (Node) `isp` (users): the internet service provider.
- (Node) `onehot_features` (users): the 18 anonymized categorical features `onehot_feat0` to `onehot_feat17`.
- (Node) The video properties below (in `big` and `small`) are empty, -1 or NaN for users.
- (Node) `author_id` (videos): the id of the author of the video.
- (Node) `video_type` (videos): `NORMAL` or `AD`.
- (Node) `upload_time` (videos): the upload date, as Unix time.
- (Node) `upload_type` (videos): e.g. `ShortImport`.
- (Node) `visible_status` (videos): `public`, `private` or `only friends`.
- (Node) `duration` (videos): in milliseconds.
- (Node) `width`, `height` (videos): in pixels.
- (Node) `music_id`, `video_tag_id` (videos): the ids of the music and of the tag of the video.
- (Node) `video_tag_name` (videos): the tag of the video, in Chinese.
- (Node) `tags` (videos): the ids of the categories of the video, comma-separated.
- (Node) `caption` (videos): the caption of the video.
- (Node) `manual_cover_text` (videos): the text on the cover of the video.
- (Node) `topic_tag` (videos): the topic hashtags, as a list.
- (Node) `first_level_category`, `second_level_category`, `third_level_category` (videos): the names of the categories of the video at three levels, in Chinese, `UNKNOWN` if none.
- (Edge) `time` (`big`, `small`): the time of the view, as Unix time (with milliseconds; NaN if missing).
- (Edge) `play_duration` (`big`, `small`): how long the user watched the video, in milliseconds.
- (Edge) `watch_ratio` (`big`, `small`): the ratio of the time watched to the duration of the video (it can exceed 1, if the video was replayed).
citations: C. Gao, S. Li, W. Lei, J. Chen, B. Li, P. Jiang, X. He, J. Mao, T.-S. Chua, "KuaiRec: A Fully-Observed Dataset and Insights for Evaluating Recommender Systems." Proceedings of the 31st ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM), 540-550 (2022)

datasets.name: kujala_public_transport
datasets.description:
Public transport networks of 27 cities around the world (Adelaide, Antofagasta, Athens, Belfast, Berlin, Bordeaux, Brisbane, Canberra, Detroit, Dublin, Grenoble, Helsinki, Kuopio, Lisbon, Luxembourg, Melbourne, Nantes, Palermo, Paris, Prague, Rennes, Rome, Sydney, Toulouse, Turku, Venice and Winnipeg), compiled by Kujala, Weckström, Darst, Mladenović and Saramäki from the timetables that the public transport agencies published in the General Transit Feed Specification (GTFS) format, downloaded in 2016 and 2017. The timetables were curated for errors, restricted to a circular area around each city center (of radius 10 to 50 km, depending on the city) and to the trips of one day (a typical Monday within the period covered by each timetable: in most cities in December 2016, and between September 2014 and November 2017 in the others; the date is stored in the network property `extract_date`), and complemented with walking distances between stops, computed from OpenStreetMap. The data of 25 cities come from version 1.2 of the data set, in which the day extends from 03:00 on the Monday to 03:00 on the next day. Antofagasta and Athens, whose data may not be used commercially, were removed from the data set after its version 1.0, from which they are taken here (in that version, the day is delimited slightly differently). The networks of the other 25 cities in version 1.0, which differ from those of version 1.2 in this delimitation of the day, are also included, as networks with the suffix `_v1.0` (e.g. `helsinki_v1.0`, `helsinki_temporal_v1.0`); their files are identical in version 1.1, which only removed Antofagasta and Athens. The walking networks of version 1.0 are included only for the 13 cities where they (and the lists of stops) differ from those of version 1.2 (Bordeaux, Brisbane, Canberra, Detroit, Grenoble, Helsinki, Lisbon, Melbourne, Nantes, Paris, Prague, Rome and Toulouse; e.g. `helsinki_walk_v1.0`); in the other cities, they are identical.

There are three networks for each city (four for the 25 cities of version 1.2), whose nodes are the public transport stops of the city:

- `<city>` (e.g. `helsinki`): the combined (multimodal) static network: a directed edge connects two stops if at least one vehicle travels from the first to the second without intermediate stops during the day. There is one edge for each pair of consecutive stops and each mode of transport (bus, tram, subway, rail, ferry, ...), so that two stops served by several modes are connected by parallel edges, one per mode (the layers of a multilayer network). A few networks contain self-loops (up to 13, in `adelaide`), as in the source.
- `<city>_temporal` (e.g. `helsinki_temporal`): the temporal network of the day: each directed edge is a single vehicle traveling between two consecutive stops (a "connection"), with its departure and arrival times.
- `<city>_temporal_week` (e.g. `helsinki_temporal_week`, only for the 25 cities of version 1.2): the temporal network of the whole week (Monday to Sunday) from which the day was extracted, in the same format. These networks also include the stops that are served during the week but not on the day of the stop list, whose names and positions are taken from the timetable database of the source.
- `<city>_walk` (e.g. `helsinki_walk`): the walking network: an undirected edge connects two stops within walking distance of each other (up to 1 km, measured along the street network), with the walking distance. These networks also include the stops that are referenced by the walking network of the source but not in its list of stops (e.g. parent stations, or stops not served on that day), whose names and positions are taken from the timetable database of the source.

The stops that are not served during the day are kept as isolated nodes. The temporal networks of the week have about 73 million connections in all (11.5 million in Paris).

The data of each city come with their own license: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 (Adelaide, Canberra, Dublin, Helsinki, Kuopio, Melbourne, Palermo, Sydney, Turku), Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 Germany (Berlin), Australia (Brisbane) or Italy (Rome, Venice), the Open Database License (Belfast, Bordeaux, Grenoble, Nantes, Paris, Rennes, Toulouse), CC0 (Detroit, Lisbon, Luxembourg, Prague), the ODC Public Domain Dedication and License (Winnipeg), and Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 2.0 (Antofagasta) or 4.0 (Athens). The walking distances are derived from OpenStreetMap data (Open Database License). The license of each city is stored in the network property `license`.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Graph) `license`: the license of the city's data, as given in the source.
- (Graph) `extract_date`: the date of the Monday whose trips are included (YYYY-MM-DD); for the networks of the week, the first day of the week.
- (Node) `stop_id`: the stop index of the source (`stop_I`).
- (Node) `name`: the name of the stop.
- (Node) `lat` and `lon`: the latitude and longitude of the stop.
- (Edge) `route_type` (`<city>`, `<city>_temporal` and `<city>_temporal_week`): the mode of transport, as a GTFS route type: $0$ (tram), $1$ (subway), $2$ (rail), $3$ (bus), $4$ (ferry), $5$ (cable car), $6$ (gondola) or $7$ (funicular).
- (Edge) `distance` (`<city>` and `<city>_walk`): the straight-line distance between the stops, in meters.
- (Edge) `duration_avg` (`<city>`): the average travel time between the stops, in seconds.
- (Edge) `n_vehicles` (`<city>`): the number of vehicles that traveled between the stops during the day.
- (Edge) `route_counts` (`<city>`): the number of vehicles of each route, as a comma-separated list of `route:count` pairs (with the route indices of the source).
- (Edge) `dep_time`, `arr_time` (`<city>_temporal` and `<city>_temporal_week`): the departure and arrival times (Unix time).
- (Edge) `trip` (`<city>_temporal` and `<city>_temporal_week`): the index of the vehicle's trip.
- (Edge) `seq` (`<city>_temporal` and `<city>_temporal_week`): the position of the connection in the trip.
- (Edge) `route` (`<city>_temporal` and `<city>_temporal_week`): the index of the route.
- (Edge) `walk_distance` (`<city>_walk`): the walking distance, in meters.
citations: R. Kujala, C. Weckström, R. K. Darst, M. N. Mladenović, J. Saramäki, "A collection of public transport network data sets for 25 cities." Scientific Data 5, 180089 (2018)

datasets.name: lastfm
datasets.description:
Bipartite networks of the users of the music website Last.fm and the artists and songs they listened to, from the complete listening histories (until 5 May 2009) of 992 users, collected by Òscar Celma through the Last.fm API (method user.getRecentTracks). Each edge is a listening event ("scrobble"): an edge connects a user to an artist (network `band`) or to a song (network `song`) each time the user listened to a song of the artist, or to the song, with the time of the event, so that the networks are multigraphs with 19,150,868 edges each. All users of the data set's user profiles are included.

The artists and songs are identified by their MusicBrainz identifiers (MBID), or, for those without one, by their names as given: an artist without an MBID by its name, and a song without an MBID by its name together with its artist (so that the same artist or song may appear under different spellings, and several artists with the same name are merged; different songs with the same title are only merged if they are by the same artist without an MBID). An artist or song with an MBID that appears with several names is named after its first occurrence.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the identifier of the user (e.g. `user_000639`), or the name of the artist or song.
- (Node) `is_user`: whether the node is a user (otherwise an artist or a song).
- (Node) `mbid`: the MusicBrainz identifier of the artist or song (empty for users and for artists and songs without one).
- (Node) `artist`, `artist_mbid`: the name and MusicBrainz identifier of the artist of the song (network `song` only; empty for users).
- (Node) `gender`: the gender of the user (`m`, `f`, or empty if not given; empty for artists and songs).
- (Node) `age`: the age of the user (-1 if not given, and for artists and songs).
- (Node) `country`: the country of the user (empty if not given, and for artists and songs).
- (Node) `signup`: the date of registration of the user, in Unix time (-1 if not given, and for artists and songs).
- (Edge) `time`: the time of the listening event, in Unix time.
citations: Ò. Celma, "Music Recommendation and Discovery: The Long Tail, Long Fail, and Long Play in the Digital Music Space." Springer (2010).

datasets.name: lastfm_360k
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of the users of the music website Last.fm and the artists they listened to, collected by Òscar Celma in 2008 through the Last.fm API. For each of about 360,000 users, the data give the artists most listened to by the user (up to about 50), with the number of plays of each. Each node is a user or an artist, and an edge connects a user to an artist among the user's top artists, weighted by the number of plays.

The artists are identified by their MusicBrainz identifiers (MBID), or, for the artists without one, by their names as given (so that the same artist may appear under different spellings, and several artists with the same name are merged). An artist with an MBID that appears with several names is named after its first occurrence.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the anonymous identifier of the user (a SHA-1 hash), or the name of the artist.
- (Node) `is_user`: whether the node is a user (otherwise an artist).
- (Node) `mbid`: the MusicBrainz identifier of the artist (empty for users and for artists without one).
- (Node) `gender`: the gender of the user (`m`, `f`, or empty if not given; empty for artists).
