- (Node) `age`: the age of the user (-1 if not given, and for artists).
- (Node) `country`: the country of the user (empty if not given, and for artists).
- (Node) `signup`: the date of registration of the user, in Unix time (-1 if not given, and for artists).
- (Edge) `weight`: the number of plays of the artist by the user.
citations: Ò. Celma, "Music Recommendation and Discovery: The Long Tail, Long Fail, and Long Play in the Digital Music Space." Springer (2010)

datasets.name: lastfm_aminer
datasets.description:
A snapshot of the social network of Last.fm, a music website and streaming radio service, where users can connect as friends. The network is part of a collection of several online social networks distributed by AMiner (Tsinghua University) for research on social network integration, i.e. on identifying the accounts of the same person across different services (Y. Zhang and J. Tang); judging from the references given with the data, parts of it originate from earlier studies on linking user accounts across services (D. Perito et al., 2011; T. Chen et al., 2012). The crawling procedure is not documented. According to the ICON index, the data were collected in late 2013. Nodes are users, identified by integer IDs, and include all users listed in the source data, 11 of which have no connections. An edge connects two users who are connected in the social network; the type of connection (presumably friendship) is not documented by the source. In the source data each connected pair of users is listed only once, always with the smaller ID first, and the source does not document whether the relationship is directed; the edges are therefore stored as undirected.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the user ID in the source data.
- (Node) `username`: the user name.
citations: T. Chen, M. A. Kaafar, A. Friedman, and R. Boreli. "Is more always merrier?: a deep dive into online social footprints." In 2012 ACM workshop on Workshop on online social networks, pages 67–72, 2012.
D. Perito, C. Castelluccia, M. A. Kaafar, and P. Manils. "How unique and traceable are usernames?" In Privacy Enhancing Technologies, pages 1–17. Springer, 2011

H. Kwak, C. Lee, H. Park, and S. Moon. "What is Twitter, a social network or a news media?" In WWW ’10: Proceedings of the 19th international conference on World wide web, pages 591–600, New York, NY, USA, 2010. ACM.
Yutao Zhang, Jie Tang, "Social Network Integration: Towards Constructing the Social Graph", arxiv:1311.2670

datasets.name: lastfm_asia
datasets.description:
A social network of users of the music website Last.fm from Asian countries, collected from its public API in March 2020 by B. Rozemberczki and R. Sarkar (FEATHER study) for benchmarks of node classification methods. Nodes are users, and an undirected edge connects two users who follow each other (a mutual follower relationship). The user names were replaced by consecutive indices. Each user has a list of binary features extracted from the artists the user liked (only the indices of the features are given, not the artists; 173 users have no features), and a country label, derived from the country field of the user profile, which is the target of the classification task proposed with the data. The countries are given only as indices from 0 to 17, without their names.

This network is unrelated to the other Last.fm entries (`lastfm`, `lastfm_aminer`, `lastfm_finland`, `lastfm_friendships`), which were collected at other times and with other selections of users.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `country`: the index of the user's country (0 to 17; the names are not given).
- (Node) `features`: the indices of the user's binary (artist) features.
citations: B. Rozemberczki and R. Sarkar, "Characteristic Functions on Graphs: Birds of a Feather, from Statistical Descriptors to Parametric Models." Proceedings of the 29th ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM), 1325-1334 (2020).

datasets.name: lastfm_finland
datasets.description: A network of mutual friendships among Finnish users of Last.fm, a music website where users can share their listening habits and designate other users as their friends. The data were collected by Toivonen et al. (published in 2009; ICON dates the data to 2006), who selected the users that self-reported Finland as their country. Each node is a user account, and an undirected edge connects two users who mutually designated each other as friends. Only the largest connected component of the Finnish users is included, and no node metadata is available.
citations: R. Toivonen, L. Kovanen, M. Kivelä, J.-P. Onnela, J. Saramäki, K. Kaski, "A comparative study of social network models: Network evolution models and nodal attribute models." Social Networks 31(4), 240-254 (2009)

datasets.name: lastfm_friendships
datasets.description:
A network of mutual friendships among users of Last.fm, a music website where users can share their listening habits and designate other users as their friends. Each node is a user account, and an undirected edge connects two users who mutually designated each other as friends. The network was assembled by Asikainen et al. to study homophily, and contains only users whose gender is known: it is self-reported in the user profile or, when not available, inferred from the user's real first name. The original data were downloaded from audioscrobbler.net (the Last.fm data service); ICON dates the snapshot to circa 2007.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `gender`: the gender of the user (0: male, 1: female).
citations: A. Asikainen, G. Iñiguez, J. Ureña-Carrión, K. Kaski, M. Kivelä, "Cumulative effects of triadic closure and homophily in social networks." Science Advances 6(19), eaax7310 (2020)

datasets.name: latvia_company_ownership
datasets.description:
Networks of the ownership and management of the legal entities of Latvia (companies, associations, foundations, etc.), from the open data of the Latvian Enterprise Register (Uzņēmumu reģistrs), published daily on the Latvian open data portal. The data are those in force on the download date (30 October 2026): the register publishes only the current state, and the files are replaced daily.

There are three networks, in which a directed edge goes from an owner, officer or beneficial owner to the legal entity:

- `shareholders`: the members (shareholders) of the limited liability companies (SIA), and the stockholders of the joint-stock companies (AS) that are recorded in the register (the shares of most listed joint-stock companies are held through the central securities depository, which then appears as their stockholder), with the number and nominal value of the shares (and the votes, for stockholders).
- `officers`: the officers of the legal entities: the members of their executive boards, the chairs, the owners of sole proprietorships, liquidators, etc.
- `beneficial_owners`: the beneficial owners (natural persons who ultimately own or control the legal entity), as declared to the register.

The legal entities are identified by their registration number in the register, and are described by their records there (name, type, address, dates of registration and termination). The owners and officers that are Latvian legal entities are the same nodes as the legal entities themselves, so that the networks include chains of ownership between companies. The foreign legal entities are identified by their name and foreign registration number. The register gives no identifier of the natural persons, only their name and their masked personal identity code (e.g. `140368-*****`, whose visible part is the date of birth for the codes issued before 2017, and a random number starting with 32 for the later ones) or, for foreigners, their date of birth: the natural persons are merged by their name, masked code and date of birth together, so that two different persons with the same name and date of birth are taken as one, and the same person written differently is split (in `beneficial_owners`, the name is written as surname and forename, as in the other files). Shares held jointly by several persons are represented by one edge from each joint owner, marked as joint. Only the legal entities that take part in some edge are included.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `kind`: the kind of node: `legal_entity` (a Latvian legal entity in the register), `foreign_entity`, `natural_person`.
- (Node) `name`: the name of the legal entity (e.g. `SIA "Kronos"`), or of the person (surname and forename).
- (Node) `regcode`: the registration number of the Latvian legal entity, or the registration number of the foreign entity as given (empty for persons).
- (Node) `identity_code_masked` (persons): the masked personal identity code (empty if none).
- (Node) `birth_date` (persons): the date of birth given for persons without a Latvian personal code (empty if not given).
- (Node) `register`, `entity_type` (Latvian legal entities): the register in which the entity is recorded (e.g. `Komercreģistrs`, the commercial register) and its legal form (e.g. `Sabiedrība ar ierobežotu atbildību`, limited liability company).
- (Node) `registered`, `terminated` (Latvian legal entities): the dates of registration and termination (`YYYY-MM-DD`, empty if not terminated).
- (Node) `status` (Latvian legal entities): `active`, `liquidated` or `reorganized`.
- (Node) `address`, `postal_code` (Latvian legal entities): the address of the legal entity.
- (Node) `nationality`, `residence` (`beneficial_owners`, persons): two-letter country codes.
- (Edge) `registered_on` (all networks): the date on which the relation was registered.
- (Edge) `company_kind` (`shareholders`): `SIA` for the members of limited liability companies, `AS` for the stockholders of joint-stock companies.
- (Edge) `shares` (`shareholders`): the number of shares.
- (Edge) `share_nominal_value` (`shareholders`): the nominal value of one share.
- (Edge) `share_currency` (`shareholders`): `EUR`, or `LVL` for the Latvian lats of shares registered before 2014.
- (Edge) `votes` (`shareholders`): for `AS`, the number of votes (-1 for `SIA`).
- (Edge) `stock_type` (`shareholders`): for `AS`, `REGISTERED_STOCKS`, `DEMATERIALISED_STOCKS`, or empty.
- (Edge) `date_from` (`shareholders`): the date since which the shares are held.
- (Edge) `joint` (`shareholders`): whether the shares are held jointly with other owners.
- (Edge) `position` (`officers`): e.g. `BOARD_MEMBER`, `CHAIR_OF_BOARD`, `OWNER`, `LIQUIDATOR`; empty if not given.
- (Edge) `governing_body` (`officers`): e.g. `EXECUTIVE_BOARD`, `SUPERVISORY_BOARD`.
- (Edge) `representation` (`officers`): the rights of representation, e.g. `INDIVIDUALLY`, `WITH_AT_LEAST`.
- (Edge) `representation_with_at_least` (`officers`): the number of other officers needed to represent the entity jointly.
citations: Uzņēmumu reģistrs (Enterprise Register of the Republic of Latvia), "Open data of the Enterprise Register." Latvian open data portal (2026)

datasets.name: law_firm
datasets.description:
A multiplex network of relationships among the 71 lawyers (36 partners and 35 associates) of a corporate law firm in New England (USA), collected by E. Lazega with questionnaires and interviews in 1988-1991, as part of his study of cooperation among peers. The version here is distributed by M. De Domenico, and has three directed layers, in which an edge $(i, j)$ means that lawyer $i$ named lawyer $j$ in response to the corresponding question:

- advice (892 edges): $i$ goes to $j$ for basic professional advice;
- friendship (575 edges): $i$ socializes with $j$ outside work;
- co-work (1,104 edges): $i$ has worked with $j$ (e.g. on a case).

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `nodeStatus`: 1 = partner, 2 = associate.
- (Node) `nodeGender`: 1 = man, 2 = woman.
- (Node) `nodeOffice`: office location: 1 = Boston, 2 = Hartford, 3 = Providence.
- (Node) `nodeSeniority`: number of years with the firm.
- (Node) `nodeAge`: age, in years.
- (Node) `nodePractice`: 1 = litigation, 2 = corporate law.
- (Node) `nodeLawSchool`: law school attended: 1 = Harvard or Yale, 2 = University of Connecticut, 3 = other.
- (Edge) `layer` (edges): 1 = advice, 2 = friendship, 3 = co-work; the graph property `layer_key` maps these numbers to layer names.
- (Edge) `weight` (edges): always 1.
citations: Emmanuel Lazega, "The Collegial Phenomenon: The Social Mechanisms of Cooperation Among Peers in a Corporate Law Partnership". Oxford University Press (2001)

datasets.name: lazy_portfolios
datasets.description:
Monthly correlation networks of the securities of six "lazy portfolios", portfolios made of a few well-diversified securities that financial experts recommend for their low risk in most market conditions, from January 2008 to December 2016. The data were collected by S. Aref from the Portfolio Visualizer website, and used by S. Aref and M. C. Wilson to study the structural balance of signed networks of securities (Aref and Wilson, 2019): following Harary et al., they obtained a signed network from each correlation network by keeping the pairs whose correlation exceeds $0.2$ in absolute value, with the sign of the correlation, and found that these portfolio networks are balanced in most months.

Nodes are the securities (mutual funds and exchange-traded funds) of a portfolio, and each network is a complete undirected graph whose edges are weighted by the Pearson correlation coefficient between the daily returns of the two securities during the month.

There is one network per portfolio and month, named `<portfolio>_<YYYY-MM>` (108 per portfolio), with the portfolios (numbered P1 to P6 in the paper):

- `ivy`: Mebane Faber's Ivy Portfolio (5 securities: VTI, VEU, IEF, VNQ, GSG).
- `simple`: Larry Swedroe's Simple Portfolio (6 securities).
- `ultimate`: the FundAdvice (Paul Merriman) Ultimate Buy & Hold Portfolio (11 securities).
- `yale`: David Swensen's Yale Endowment portfolio (6 securities).
- `swensen`: David Swensen's Lazy Portfolio (6 securities).
- `coffeehouse`: Bill Schultheis' Coffee House Portfolio (7 securities).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name` (vertices): the name of the security (e.g. "Vanguard 500 Index Fund").
- (Node) `ticker` (vertices): the ticker symbol of the security (e.g. `VFINX`).
- (Node) `return` (vertices): the return of the security over the month, in percent.
- (Node) `daily_std`, `monthly_std`, `annualized_std` (vertices): the standard deviation of the daily returns during the month, and the monthly and annualized standard deviations of the monthly returns, in percent, as reported by Portfolio Visualizer for the query interval (from the first day of the month to the first day of the next month).
- (Edge) `weight` (edges): the correlation coefficient between the daily returns of the two securities during the month.

The source also contains, for each portfolio and year, a document listing the Portfolio Visualizer query URLs used to export the data; these are not included.
citations: S. Aref and M. C. Wilson, "Balance and frustration in signed networks." J. Complex Networks 7(2), 163–189 (2019)
S. Aref, "Signed networks from sociology and political science, systems biology, international relations, finance, and computational chemistry." Figshare (2017)

datasets.name: lesmis
datasets.description:
The network of co-appearances of characters in Victor Hugo's novel "Les Misérables". Nodes are characters, and an undirected edge connects two characters that appear in the same chapter of the book. The co-appearance data were compiled by D. E. Knuth for the Stanford GraphBase, and the network was assembled by M. E. J. Newman.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `label`: the name of the character.
- (Edge) `value` (edges): the number of chapters in which the two characters appear together.
citations: D. E. Knuth, "The Stanford GraphBase: A Platform for Combinatorial Computing." Addison-Wesley, Reading, MA (1993).

datasets.name: libimseti
datasets.description:
Ratings of user profiles by the users of LibimSeTi.cz, a Czech online dating website, as dumped on April 4, 2006. The data were provided by O. Neuberger (LibimSeTi.cz) and prepared by L. Brozovsky and V. Petricek (Charles University in Prague) for their study of recommender systems for online dating. Nodes are users, and a directed edge $i \to j$ is a rating of the profile of user $j$ by user $i$, on a scale from 1 to 10 (10 is best; integer ratings only).

The data contain 17,359,346 ratings of 168,791 profiles by 135,359 users; all 220,970 users rate or are rated. Only users who gave at least 20 ratings are included as raters, and users who gave constant ratings were excluded (by the source).

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `gender`: the gender of the user, `F` (female), `M` (male) or `U` (unknown).
- (Edge) `weight`: the rating, from 1 to 10.
citations: L. Brozovsky, V. Petricek, "Recommender System for Online Dating Service." Proceedings of Conference Znalosti 2007, Ostrava (2007)

datasets.name: librec_trust
datasets.description:
Trust networks and ratings of users of two movie websites, crawled by G. Guo and collaborators for research on trust-aware recommender systems, and distributed with the LibRec library:

- FilmTrust, a movie sharing and rating website, crawled in its entirety in June 2011. Users rate movies, and can declare that they trust other users.
- CiaoDVD, the DVD category of the British consumer review website Ciao (dvd.ciao.co.uk), crawled in November and December 2013. Users write reviews of movies with a rating, rate the helpfulness of other users' reviews, and declare which other users they trust. Movies without any review were left out by the authors.

User and movie identifiers were anonymized; the identifiers of users are the same in the networks of one website. There are five networks:

- `filmtrust_trust`: a directed network of users, where an edge $i \to j$ means that user $i$ trusts user $j$.
- `filmtrust_ratings`: a bipartite network of users and the movies they rated, with the rating. Three user-movie pairs appear twice in the data (with the same or a different rating); all rows are kept as edges.
- `ciaodvd_trust`: a directed network of users, where an edge $i \to j$ means that user $i$ trusts user $j$.
- `ciaodvd_ratings`: a bipartite network of users and the movies they reviewed, with the rating and the date of the review. A user may have reviewed a movie more than once (320 user-movie pairs appear more than once); each review is an edge.
- `ciaodvd_review_ratings`: a directed multigraph of users, where an edge $i \to j$ means that user $i$ rated the helpfulness of a review written by user $j$ (the author of the review is given by `ciaodvd_ratings`). Each rating is an edge. Users who did not write reviews or rate them appear only in the trust network.

The trust values given in the data are all 1, and are therefore left out.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `user_id` (users), `movie_id` (movies): the anonymized identifiers in the data.
- (Node) `is_movie` (bipartite networks): whether the node is a movie (otherwise a user).
- (Node) `genre` (`ciaodvd_ratings`): the numeric identifier of the movie's genre (one of 17; their names are not given, -1 for users).
- (Edge) `rating` (`filmtrust_ratings`): the rating of the movie (from 0.5 to 4, in steps of 0.5).
- (Edge) `rating` (`ciaodvd_ratings`): the rating of the movie (1 to 5).
- (Edge) `review_id` (`ciaodvd_ratings`): the identifier of the review.
- (Edge) `time` (`ciaodvd_ratings`): the date of the review, as the Unix time of 00:00 UTC of that day.
- (Edge) `review_id` (`ciaodvd_review_ratings`): the identifier of the rated review.
- (Edge) `helpfulness` (`ciaodvd_review_ratings`): the rating of the review: 0 (off topic), 1 (not helpful), 2 (somewhat helpful), 3 (helpful), 4 (very helpful) or 5 (exceptional).
citations: G. Guo, J. Zhang, and N. Yorke-Smith, "A Novel Bayesian Similarity Measure for Recommender Systems." Proceedings of the 23rd International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI), 2619-2625 (2013).

G. Guo, J. Zhang, D. Thalmann, and N. Yorke-Smith, "ETAF: An Extended Trust Antecedents Framework for Trust Prediction." Proceedings of the 2014 IEEE/ACM International Conference on Advances in Social Networks Analysis and Mining (ASONAM), 540-547 (2014).

datasets.name: lightning_network
datasets.description:
Snapshots of the Lightning Network, the network of payment channels built on top of the Bitcoin blockchain, from the geolocated topology snapshots of V. Valko and J. Marx Gómez, who reconstructed them from the gossip messages collected by C. Decker (the lnresearch topology datasets) and geolocated the nodes with the IP addresses they announce. Nodes are Lightning nodes (identified by their public keys), and each payment channel between two nodes gives two directed edges, one for each direction of the channel ("half-channel"), with the fees and limits announced for that direction; the edges point to the node given as their `destination` in the dataset. The dataset has 336 snapshots from January 2019 to July 2023; the networks here are the last snapshot of each year (`2019_11_18`, `2020_12_30`, `2021_10_10`, `2022_06_05` and `2023_07_16`). The capacities of the channels (which are not part of the gossip messages) are not given.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `pubkey`: the public key of the node (its identifier in the network).
- (Node) `alias`: the alias announced by the node.
- (Node) `rgb_color`: the color announced by the node.
- (Node) `features`: the feature bits announced by the node (hexadecimal).
- (Node) `addresses`: the network addresses announced by the node (IPv4, IPv6 or Tor), or empty.
- (Node) `timestamp`: the time of the node's last announcement, in Unix time (0 or -1 if none).
- (Node) `city`, `region`, `country`, `postal`, `timezone`, `org`: the geolocation of the node's IP address (with IPinfo), or empty for the nodes that were not geolocated (e.g. Tor nodes).
- (Node) `latitude`, `longitude`: the coordinates of the geolocation (NaN if not geolocated).
- (Edge) `scid`: the short channel identifier (block height, transaction index and output index of the funding transaction), with the direction bit of the half-channel (e.g. `641702x1022x1/0`).
- (Edge) `timestamp`: the time of the last update of the half-channel, in Unix time.
- (Edge) `features`: the feature bits of the channel (hexadecimal).
- (Edge) `fee_base_msat`, `fee_proportional_millionths`: the base fee (in millisatoshis) and the proportional fee (in millionths) to forward payments.
- (Edge) `htlc_minimum_msat`, `htlc_maximum_msat`: the minimum and maximum amounts of a forwarded payment, in millisatoshis.
- (Edge) `cltv_expiry_delta`: the number of blocks of the time lock delta of the half-channel.
citations: V. Valko and J. Marx Gómez, "Geolocated Lightning Network topology snapshots: A dataset covering 2019-2023." Scientific Data 12, 1939 (2025)
C. Decker, "Lightning Network Research - Topology Datasets." Zenodo (2020)

datasets.name: liner_shipping
datasets.description:
Networks of the world's container ports connected by regular liner shipping services, constructed by M. Xu and collaborators from the database of liner shipping service routes of Alphaliner (a commercial database of the container shipping industry, whose raw data are not public). Nodes are ports, and two ports are connected by an undirected edge if at least one liner service route calls at both of them: each service route, a fixed sequence of ports of call served by container ships, becomes a clique of its ports, and the network is the union of these cliques.

The entry contains the versions of the network published by the authors with their articles:

- `2015`: the network of April 2015 of Xu et al. (Nature Communications 2020), from all service routes, with 977 ports and 16,680 edges (the source data of Fig. 1d of the article). The edges are unweighted.
- `2015_international` and `2017_international`: the networks of 2015 and 2017 of Xu et al. (Royal Society Open Science 2020), from the international service routes (1,316 routes in 2015), with 777 and 770 ports. The ports are identified only by numbers (which differ between the two years) and their countries. The edges have six weights, computed as the sum over the service routes that call at both ports of either 1, $1/(n-1)$, $1/[n(n-1)/2]$, $C$, $C/(n-1)$ or $C/[n(n-1)/2]$, where $n$ is the number of ports of the route and $C$ its total traffic capacity, in twenty-foot equivalent units (TEU).
- `2018`: the network of 2018 of Xu et al. (Global Networks 2024), with 887 ports, weighted edges and the great-circle distances between the ports. In the data, each edge is listed in both directions, with the same values; it is included once.

The networks are not comparable in every respect, since they were constructed from different selections of the routes; the port names of the `2015` and `2018` networks are as given (e.g. `Antwerp`, `Port Chalmers`).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name` (`2015`, `2018`): the name of the port.
- (Node) `port_id` (`2015_international`, `2017_international`): the identifier of the port in the data.
- (Node) `country` (`2015_international`, `2017_international`, `2018`): the ISO 3166-1 alpha-3 code of the country of the port.
- (Node) `country_name` (`2018`): the name of the country of the port.
- (Edge) `routes`, `weight_1n`, `weight_2nn`, `capacity`, `capacity_1n`, `capacity_2nn` (`2015_international`, `2017_international`): the six edge weights, the sums over the shared routes of 1 (the number of shared routes), $1/(n-1)$, $1/[n(n-1)/2]$, $C$, $C/(n-1)$ and $C/[n(n-1)/2]$, respectively.
- (Edge) `weight` (`2018`): the weight of the link as given by the authors (derived from the traffic capacities of the shared routes).
- (Edge) `distance` (`2018`): the great-circle distance between the two ports, in kilometers.
citations: M. Xu, Q. Pan, A. Muscoloni, H. Xia, C. V. Cannistraci, "Modular gateway-ness connectivity and structural core organization in maritime network science." Nature Communications 11, 2849 (2020)
M. Xu, Q. Pan, H. Xia, N. Masuda, "Estimating international trade status of countries from global liner shipping networks." Royal Society Open Science 7, 200386 (2020)
M. Xu, Y. Zhu, W. Deng, Y. Shen, T. Li, "Assessing the efficiency and vulnerability of global liner shipping network." Global Networks 24(1), e12445 (2024)

datasets.name: linux
datasets.description:
A directed network of the inclusions between the source code files of the Linux kernel, version 3.16 (released in August 2014), extracted from the kernel's source tarball following the method of J. Kunegis. Each directed edge points from a C source or header file to a file it includes with an `#include` directive (repeated inclusions are counted once). The included files were located heuristically: an `#include` was resolved by looking for the file relative to the directory of the including file and its parent directories (and their `include` subdirectories), then relative to the top directory, then by a unique match of the file name anywhere in the tree; system headers (e.g. `sys/...` or `endian.h`) and the generated `linux/version.h` were ignored, as were includes that could not be resolved. The paths were then simplified by removing architecture-, platform- and API-specific directory components (e.g. `arch/<arch>/`, `include/`, `asm/`, `uapi/`, `linux/`, `mach-*/`), so that several files with the same simplified path, such as the variants of the same header for different architectures, are merged into one node. Only files that include or are included by some file are part of the network. Since a file and a file it includes can be mapped to the same node, 530 nodes have self-loops.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the simplified path of the file(s), which identifies the node.
- (Node) `files`: the list of the paths, relative to the top directory of the source tree, of the source files whose simplified path is that of the node (empty only for `config.h`, which is generated during the build).
citations: J. Kunegis, "Linux." KONECT, the Koblenz Network Collection (2016)

datasets.name: little_league
datasets.description:
Friendship nominations among the players of two very successful Little League baseball teams of the same local league in the USA, from G. A. Fine's ethnographic study of preadolescent culture, *With the Boys*. Fine asked the boys to name their three best friends on the team. Fine described the Transatlantic Industries team as decentralized, and the Sharpstone Auto team, whose data were collected at the end of the season, as highly centralized around three players (Justin, Harry and Whit). A directed edge points from the boy making the nomination to the nominated friend. The data were distributed on the Pajek datasets page of the book *Generalized Blockmodeling* (Doreian, Batagelj and Ferligoj), from which this version was obtained.

- `transatlantic`: the 13 players of the Transatlantic Industries team.
- `sharpstone`: the 13 players of the Sharpstone Auto team.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the (first) name of the player.
citations: G. A. Fine, "With the Boys: Little League Baseball and Preadolescent Culture." University of Chicago Press, Chicago (1987)
P. Doreian, V. Batagelj, A. Ferligoj, "Generalized Blockmodeling." Cambridge University Press (2004)

datasets.name: littlesis
datasets.description:
The LittleSis database ("the opposite of Big Brother"), a collaborative database of the relationships between powerful people and organizations in the United States (and beyond), maintained by the Public Accountability Initiative. Its entries are edited by researchers, journalists and volunteers from public sources (news, government filings, corporate reports, campaign finance and lobbying disclosures, which are also imported in bulk), and record "who knows who" among business executives, politicians, lobbyists, financiers and their affiliated institutions.

Each node is an entity of the database, a person or an organization, and each directed edge is a relationship between two entities, from `entity1` to `entity2` of the record, of one of twelve categories: `position` (a person holds a position in an organization, e.g. as director), `education` (a person studied at a school), `membership` (an entity is a member of an organization), `family`, `donation` (the first entity gave money or goods to the second, e.g. a campaign contribution), `transaction` (the two entities did business, e.g. as contractor and client), `lobbying` (the first entity lobbied the second), `social`, `professional`, `ownership` (the first entity owns a share of the second), `hierarchy` (between organizations, e.g. a subsidiary) and `generic`. The relationships are directed as recorded, even those of symmetric categories (e.g. family). The network is a multigraph: two entities can have several relationships, e.g. donations in several election cycles (some entities are also related to themselves).

The bulk files of LittleSis (`entities.json.gz` and `relationships.json.gz`) are replaced in place by new versions, and the site refuses them to scripts. The networks are built from copies archived by the Internet Archive: of August 9, 2022 (`2022`), January 23, 2024 (`2024`) and October 19, 2026 (`2026`, the latest; two earlier copies of 2026, of April and May, are left out). A few relationships (11 in `2022`, 8 in `2024`, 3 in `2026`) involve entities that are missing from the entities file (presumably deleted); these are included as nodes without attributes (`has_record` false).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `entity_id`: the id of the entity in LittleSis (its page is `https://littlesis.org/entities/<entity_id>`).
- (Node) `has_record`: whether the entity is in the entities file.
- (Node) `name`: the name of the entity.
- (Node) `kind`: `Person` or `Org`.
- (Node) `types`: its types (e.g. `Business Person`, `Lobbyist`, `Public Company`, `Political Fundraising Committee`).
- (Node) `blurb`: a short description.
- (Node) `summary`: a longer one.
- (Node) `aliases`: its other names.
- (Node) `website`: its website.
- (Node) `start_date`, `end_date`: e.g. the dates of birth and death or of foundation and dissolution (as given, `YYYY-MM-DD` with `00` for unknown months and days).
- (Node) `parent_id`: the id of the parent organization (-1 if none).
- (Node) `updated_at`: the time of the last update of the record (Unix time).
- (Node) `extensions`: the attributes specific to its types (e.g. the parts of the names, gender and party ids, net worth, revenue, stock ticker, SEC CIK), as a JSON object.
- (Node) `tags` (`2024` and `2026`): the tags of the entity (thematic research projects, e.g. `fracking`).
- (Edge) `relationship_id`: the id of the relationship in LittleSis.
- (Edge) `category` and `category_id`: its category (see above, ids 1 to 12 in that order).
- (Edge) `description`: a sentence describing it (e.g. "Linda S Wolf has a position (Director) at Walmart Inc.").
- (Edge) `description1` and `description2`: the roles of the two entities (e.g. `Director`, `Contractor`/`Client`).
- (Edge) `amount` and `currency`: the amount of money involved (NaN if not given).
- (Edge) `goods`: the goods involved.
- (Edge) `filings`: the number of filings on which a donation or transaction is based (-1 if not given).
- (Edge) `start_date` and `end_date`: as for the nodes.
- (Edge) `is_current`: whether the relationship is current (1, 0, or -1 if unknown).
- (Edge) `updated_at`: the time of the last update (Unix time).
- (Edge) `category_attributes`: the attributes specific to the category (e.g. `is_board` and `compensation` of positions, `degree_id` of education, `percent_stake` of ownership), as a JSON object.
citations: Public Accountability Initiative, "LittleSis: a free database of who-knows-who at the heights of business and government." Bulk data (2022, 2024, 2026)

datasets.name: livejournal
datasets.description: A directed friendship network of users of LiveJournal, an online community where members maintain journals and blogs, and can declare which other members are their friends. Nodes are users, and a directed edge $(i, j)$ means that user $i$ declared user $j$ as a friend. The data were collected by L. Backstrom and collaborators by crawling LiveJournal in 2006, when it had almost 10 million members, and distributed by the Stanford Network Analysis Project (SNAP); the network contains the 4.8 million users reached by the crawl. User names are not included. An undirected version of LiveJournal with ground-truth communities, likely derived from the same crawl, is the network `livejournal` of the entry `soc_net_comms`.
citations: L. Backstrom, D. Huttenlocher, J. Kleinberg, and X. Lan. "Group Formation in Large Social Networks: Membership, Growth, and Evolution." Proc. Internat. Conf. on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (KDD), 44-54 (2006).

datasets.name: livejournal_aminer
datasets.description:
A snapshot of the social network of LiveJournal, an online community where users keep journals and blogs and can declare other users as their friends. The network is part of a collection of several online social networks distributed by AMiner (Tsinghua University) for research on social network integration, i.e. on identifying the accounts of the same person across different services (Y. Zhang and J. Tang); judging from the references given with the data, parts of it originate from earlier studies on linking user accounts across services (D. Perito et al., 2011; T. Chen et al., 2012). The crawling procedure is not documented. According to the ICON index, the data were collected in late 2013. Nodes are users, identified by integer IDs, and include all users listed in the source data. An edge connects two users who are connected in the social network; the type of connection (presumably friendship) is not documented by the source. In the source data each connected pair of users is listed only once, always with the smaller ID first, and the source does not document whether the relationship is directed; the edges are therefore stored as undirected. The network contains about 1.4 million self-loops, which are present in the source data.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the user ID in the source data.
- (Node) `username`: the user name.
citations: T. Chen, M. A. Kaafar, A. Friedman, and R. Boreli. "Is more always merrier?: a deep dive into online social footprints." In 2012 ACM workshop on Workshop on online social networks, pages 67–72, 2012.
D. Perito, C. Castelluccia, M. A. Kaafar, and P. Manils. "How unique and traceable are usernames? In Privacy Enhancing Technologies", pages 1–17. Springer, 2011

H. Kwak, C. Lee, H. Park, and S. Moon. "What is Twitter, a social network or a news media?" In WWW ’10: Proceedings of the 19th international conference on World wide web, pages 591–600, New York, NY, USA, 2010. ACM.
Yutao Zhang, Jie Tang, "Social Network Integration: Towards Constructing the Social Graph", arxiv:1311.2670

datasets.name: livejournal_asu
datasets.description:
A network of friendships among users of LiveJournal, a virtual community where users keep a blog, journal or diary, crawled in July 2010 by R. Zafarani, W. D. Cole and H. Liu (Arizona State University) and distributed by the Social Computing Data Repository (originally at Arizona State University, now at Syracuse University). Nodes are users (anonymized), and a directed edge $i \to j$ indicates that user $i$ lists user $j$ as a friend (in LiveJournal, friendship is declared by one user and need not be reciprocated; the source data state only that "user $i$ is friend with user $j$"). About 3.5 million of the 14.6 million edges are reciprocated, and 68,853 edges are self-loops.

This crawl is different from the other LiveJournal networks in the repository (e.g. `livejournal`, `ljournal_2008`).
citations: R. Zafarani, W. D. Cole, H. Liu, "Sentiment propagation in social networks: a case study in LiveJournal." Advances in Social Computing (SBP 2010), Lecture Notes in Computer Science 6007, 413-420 (2010)
R. Zafarani, H. Liu, "Social Computing Data Repository at ASU." Arizona State University, School of Computing, Informatics and Decision Systems Engineering (2009)

datasets.name: livemocha
datasets.description:
A friendship network among users of Livemocha, a large online language learning community, crawled in December 2010 by Xia Hu at Arizona State University and distributed by the Social Computing Data Repository (originally at Arizona State University, now at Syracuse University). Nodes are users (anonymized), and a directed edge $i \to j$ is a line of the source data stating that "user $i$ is friend with user $j$".

The friendships are mostly listed once: of the 2,196,188 edges, 1,409 repeat an earlier edge (they are kept as parallel edges), and 3,397 are reciprocated (2,193,083 distinct pairs of users in all). The edges are kept as they are listed. The 335 users of the node list that occur in no edge are kept as isolated nodes.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `user_id`: the identifier of the user in the source data.
citations: R. Zafarani, H. Liu, "Social Computing Data Repository at ASU." Arizona State University, School of Computing, Informatics and Decision Systems Engineering (2009)

datasets.name: ljournal_2008
datasets.description: A directed network of declared friendships among users of LiveJournal, a virtual-community site started in 1999 in which members maintain journals and blogs. Nodes are users, and a directed edge from x to y indicates that x registered y among their friends (which does not require the permission of y). This is the 2008 snapshot used by F. Chierichetti et al. in their study of the compression of social networks, which they provided to the Laboratory for Web Algorithmics (LAW). The network has 5,363,260 users and 79,023,142 edges. Nodes are anonymous.
citations: F. Chierichetti, R. Kumar, S. Lattanzi, M. Mitzenmacher, A. Panconesi, and P. Raghavan, "On compressing social networks." Proceedings of the 15th ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (KDD 2009), 219-228 (2009).
P. Boldi and S. Vigna, "The WebGraph framework I: compression techniques." Proceedings of the 13th International Conference on World Wide Web (WWW 2004), 595-602 (2004).

P. Boldi, M. Rosa, M. Santini, and S. Vigna, "Layered label propagation: a multiresolution coordinate-free ordering for compressing social networks." Proceedings of the 20th International Conference on World Wide Web (WWW 2011), 587-596 (2011).

datasets.name: lkml_reply
datasets.description:
A network of replies among email address found on the Linux kernel mailing list. Nodes are email addresses and each directed edge represents a reply from email address i to email address j. The date of this snapshot is uncertain.[^icon]
[^icon]: Description obtained from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.
citations: J. Kunegis "Linux kernel mailing list replies network dataset" KONECT (2016)

datasets.name: lkml_thread
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of contributions by users to threads on the Linux kernel mailing list. A left node is a person, and a right node is a thread, and each timestamped edge (i,j,t) denotes that user i contributed to thread j at time t. The date of the snapshot is not given.[^icon]
[^icon]: Description obtained from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.
citations: J. Kunegis, "Linux kernel mailing list threads." KONECT, the Koblenz Network Collection (2016)

datasets.name: london_bikes
datasets.description:
A network of the trips made with the London bicycle sharing scheme (Barclays Cycle Hire, now Santander Cycles) between 22 June and 31 July 2014, as compiled by Munoz-Mendez et al. from the Transport for London (TfL) Open Data. Each node is a docking station, and each directed edge is a trip, going from the station where a bicycle was checked out to the station where it was returned (trips that return to the same station are self-loops), so that the network is a multigraph with 1,469,851 trips between 750 stations.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `station_id`: the TfL identifier of the station.
- (Node) `name`: the name of the station.
- (Node) `lat` and `lon`: its geographic coordinates (NaN for the few stations missing from the station list in the source repository, which was obtained from the TfL API some time after the trips).
- (Edge) `rental_id`: the identifier of the rental.
- (Edge) `bike_id`: the identifier of the bicycle.
- (Edge) `start` and `end`: the times of check-out and return (Unix timestamps, from London local times given to the minute).
- (Edge) `duration`: the duration of the trip in seconds.
citations: F. Munoz-Mendez, K. Han, K. Klemmer, S. Jarvis, "Community Structures, Interactions and Dynamics in London's Bicycle Sharing Network." Proceedings of the 2018 ACM International Joint Conference and 2018 International Symposium on Pervasive and Ubiquitous Computing and Wearable Computers (UbiComp '18), 1015-1023 (2018)

datasets.name: london_gang
datasets.description:
Network of co-offending among the 54 confirmed members of an inner-city street gang in London, United Kingdom, operating from a social housing estate between 2005 and 2009, reconstructed from anonymized police arrest and conviction data (Grund and Densley, 2012, 2015). Nodes are gang members, and edges connect members who were observed together, with the edge property `weight` giving the level of the relationship: 1 = hang out together, 2 = co-offend together, 3 = co-offend together, serious crime, 4 = co-offend together, serious crime, kin.

Vertex properties: `age`; `birthplace` (1 = West Africa, 2 = Caribbean, 3 = United Kingdom, 4 = East Africa); `arrests` and `convictions` (numbers); `residence`, `prison` and `music` (binary indicators, whose exact definitions are not documented by the source); and `ranking` (an integer rank within the gang, as given by the source). Data distributed by the UCINET datasets collection (University of Manchester).[^ucinet]

[^ucinet]: Description obtained in part from the [UCINET datasets page](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/datasets/covert-networks/london-gang).
citations: T. Grund and J. Densley, "Ethnic homophily and triad closure: Mapping internal gang structure using exponential random graph models." Journal of Contemporary Criminal Justice 31(3), 354-370 (2015)
T. Grund and J. Densley, "Ethnic heterogeneity in the activity and structure of a Black street gang." European Journal of Criminology 9(4), 388-406 (2012)

datasets.name: london_transport
datasets.description:
Multiplex network of the train stations of London, assembled by M. De Domenico and collaborators. The data were collected in 2013 from the official website of Transport for London (TfL) and manually cross-checked. Nodes are stations of the London Underground, London Overground and Docklands Light Railway (DLR), and edges connect consecutive stations along a line. The network has three layers: (1) the Underground, where the networks of all eleven Tube lines are aggregated into a single layer, (2) the Overground, and (3) the DLR. Edges are undirected.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`, `nodeLabel`: the station name (lowercase, without spaces, as in "bakerstreet").
- (Node) `nodeLat`, `nodeLong`: the latitude and longitude of the station, in degrees.
- (Edge) `layer`: the layer of the edge, with 1 = Tube, 2 = Overground, 3 = DLR (see the graph property `layer_key`).
- (Edge) `weight`: the number of distinct lines connecting the two stations in that layer (e.g. two adjacent stations served by both the Circle and the District line have weight 2 in the Tube layer).
citations: Manlio De Domenico, Albert Solé-Ribalta, Sergio Gómez, and Alex Arenas, "Navigability of interconnected networks under random failures." PNAS 111, 8351-8356 (2014)

datasets.name: lotus_natural_products
datasets.description:
Bipartite networks of natural products (chemical structures) and the organisms in which they were found, from LOTUS, an open resource of structure-organism pairs documented in the literature, compiled from about 40 natural-product databases, curated, and shared through Wikidata, where the community can edit and extend it. Each structure-organism pair is supported by a reference (an article or book).

- `2021_12_20` ... `2026_04_13`: the exports of the LOTUS data from Wikidata (the "frozen" datasets), one network per export: 2021-12-20, 2022-02-08, 2022-02-26, 2022-03-18, 2022-05-25, 2022-07-01, 2022-09-16, 2023-01-06 and 2026-04-13. Nodes are structures (Wikidata items with an InChIKey) and organisms (Wikidata taxa), and there is an edge between a structure and an organism for each reference that documents that the structure is found in (or produced by) the organism, so that a pair can be connected by several edges. Structures and organisms are identified by their Wikidata items. The exports have a row for each combination of the values of the properties that have several values (e.g. an organism with two GBIF identifiers); the edges are the distinct (structure, organism, reference) triples, and the several values of a property are joined with `|`.
- `processed_2021_05_28`, `processed_2021_12_20`, `processed_2022_03_23`, `processed_2022_05_25`, `processed_2022_07_01`, `processed_2022_09_16`, `processed_2023_01_13`: the curated structure-organism pairs of the processing pipeline of LOTUS (the datasets from which the data of Wikidata were built), all the versions of the dataset on Zenodo, named by their publication dates (the last one, published with the same date as the previous one, by its creation date), where each edge is a documented pair as given by one of the source databases, so that a pair documented by several databases or references is connected by several edges. Nodes are structures (identified by their InChIKey) and organisms (by their cleaned name).

The networks have the following properties (structure properties are empty for organisms, and vice versa; not all of them are in every export):

- (Node) `is_structure`: whether the node is a chemical structure (otherwise it is an organism).
- (Node) `wikidata` (exports): the Wikidata item of the structure or organism.
- (Node) `name`: the traditional name of the structure (its InChIKey if it has none, and in the export of 2021-12-20, which has no names of structures), or the name of the organism.
- (Node) `structure_inchikey`, `structure_inchi`, `structure_smiles`, `structure_smiles_2d`, `structure_molecular_formula`: the identifiers and formula of the structure (InChIKey, InChI, isomeric SMILES, SMILES without stereochemistry; no formula in `processed_2021_05_28`).
- (Node) `structure_inchikey_2d`, `structure_inchi_2d` (`processed_*`): the InChIKey and InChI of the structure without stereochemistry.
- (Node) `structure_exact_mass`, `structure_xlogp`: the exact mass and the computed partition coefficient of the structure (NaN if not given).
- (Node) `structure_cid`: the PubChem compound identifier of the structure (not in the processed datasets before `processed_2023_01_13`).
- (Node) `structure_name_iupac`: the IUPAC name of the structure.
- (Node) `structure_stereocenters_total`, `structure_stereocenters_unspecified`: the numbers of stereocenters of the structure, and of those whose configuration is not specified.
- (Node) `structure_taxonomy_npclassifier_01pathway`, `..._02superclass`, `..._03class`: the chemical classification of the structure by NPClassifier.
- (Node) `structure_taxonomy_classyfire_chemontid`, `..._01kingdom`, `..._02superclass`, `..._03class`, `..._04directparent`: the chemical classification of the structure by ClassyFire.
- (Node) `organism_taxonomy_gbifid`, `organism_taxonomy_ncbiid`, `organism_taxonomy_ottid`: the identifiers of the organism in GBIF, the NCBI taxonomy and the Open Tree of Life.
- (Node) `organism_taxonomy_01domain`, `..._02kingdom`, `..._03phylum`, `..._04class`, `..._05order`, `..._06family`, `..._07tribe`, `..._08genus`, `..._09species`, `..._10varietas`: the taxonomy of the organism (exports).
- (Node) `organism_id`, `organism_db_taxo`, `organism_taxon_ranks`, `organism_taxonomy` (`processed_*`): the identifier of the organism in its taxonomic database, the name of the database, and the ranks and names of its lineage.
- (Edge) `reference_wikidata`, `reference_doi` (exports): the Wikidata item and DOI of the reference.
- (Edge) `manual_validation` (exports): the result of the manual validation of the pair (`Y` if it was validated by hand, empty otherwise).
- (Edge) `database` (`processed_*`): the source database of the pair.
- (Edge) `organism_original`, `reference_original` (`processed_*`): the organism and reference as given by the source database (the structures as given by the source databases, as InChI or SMILES strings, are left out, since they are long and the curated structure is given by the node).
- (Edge) `structure_original_type`, `reference_original_type` (`processed_*`): the kind of the structure and reference identifiers of the source database (e.g. `inchi`, `smiles`, `doi`, `pubmed`, `title`).
- (Edge) `reference_doi`, `reference_pmcid`, `reference_pmid`, `reference_title` (`processed_*`): the curated reference.
citations: A. Rutz, M. Sorokina, J. Galgonek, D. Mietchen, E. Willighagen, A. Gaudry, J. G. Graham, R. Stephan, R. Page, J. Vondrášek, C. Steinbeck, G. F. Pauli, J.-L. Wolfender, J. Bisson, P.-M. Allard, "The LOTUS initiative for open knowledge management in natural products research." eLife 11, e70780 (2022)

datasets.name: macaque_cocomac
datasets.description:
Directed network of anatomical connections between regions of the cerebral cortex of the macaque monkey, as used by Harriger, van den Heuvel and Sporns in their analysis of its rich-club organization. The network is derived from the CoCoMac database, which collates the results of hundreds of published tract-tracing studies, as consolidated by Modha and Singh into a single hierarchical parcellation; it comprises 242 cortical regions and 4,090 directed connections. A directed edge indicates a reported axonal projection from one region to another.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the abbreviated name of the cortical region.

The data were obtained from the graph collection of the Open Connectome Project (now NeuroData), whose servers are offline, via the Internet Archive.
citations: L. Harriger, M. P. van den Heuvel, O. Sporns, "Rich Club Organization of Macaque Cerebral Cortex and Its Role in Network Communication." PLoS ONE 7(9), e46497 (2012)
D. S. Modha, R. Singh, "Network architecture of the long-distance pathways in the macaque brain." Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 107(30), 13485-13490 (2010)

datasets.name: macaque_cortex_kaiser
datasets.description:
Directed network of anatomical connections among 95 areas and sub-areas of one hemisphere of the macaque monkey cerebral cortex, with the three-dimensional positions of the areas, from M. Kaiser and C. C. Hilgetag. Nodes are cortical areas, and a directed edge represents a projection (axonal pathway) from one area to another, as reported by tract-tracing studies; following the usual convention, the entry $(i, j)$ of the source adjacency matrix is taken as an edge from area $i$ to area $j$ (the convention is not stated explicitly with the data). The connectivity data were retrieved from the CoCoMac database and are based on three extensive neuroanatomical compilations that together cover large parts of the cortex; the positions of the areas are the centers of mass of their three-dimensional extensions, estimated from a surface parcellation with the CARET software. This corrected version of the data contains 94 areas, since a duplicate area (6Vb/6vb) of the original data set was merged into a single area that inherited the connections of both.

The nodes have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the label of the cortical area (e.g. "V1", "46", "10m").
- (Node) `position`: the $(x, y, z)$ position of the area, in millimeters.[^icon]

[^icon]: Description obtained in part from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.
citations: M. Kaiser, C. C. Hilgetag, "Nonoptimal component placement, but short processing paths, due to long-distance projections in neural systems." PLoS Computational Biology 2(7), e95 (2006)
R. Kötter, "Online retrieval, processing, and visualization of primate connectivity data from the CoCoMac database." Neuroinformatics 2, 127-144 (2004)

datasets.name: macaque_markov
datasets.description:
Directed networks of the macaque (*Macaca mulatta* and *M. fascicularis*) cerebral cortex, from the retrograde tract-tracing experiments of Markov, Kennedy and collaborators. In each experiment a retrograde tracer was injected into one cortical area (the target), and the labeled neurons projecting to it were counted in each of the 91 areas (the sources) of the authors' M132 atlas parcellation. Edges point from the source area to the injected target area, so only the injected areas have incoming edges.

- `flne`: the connectivity of 29 injected areas from all 91 areas (Markov et al., Cerebral Cortex 2014). There is one edge for each injection and each source area with labeled neurons, so that areas injected in several animals are connected by parallel edges (1,989 edges, 1,615 distinct connections). Edge properties: `flne`, the extrinsic fraction of labeled neurons (the number of neurons labeled in the source area divided by the total number labeled outside the injected area); `neurons`, the number of labeled neurons; `case`, the injection case number; `monkey`, the identifier of the animal and hemisphere; `status`, whether the projection was previously reported in the literature ("Known") or newly found ("NFP"); `references`, the reference numbers (in the original publication) of previous reports of the projection, or "NA".
- `sln`: the projections to 11 injected areas of the visual cortex (Markov et al., J. Comp. Neurol. 2014), annotated with the laminar origin of the projecting neurons, used to derive the hierarchy of visual areas. Edge properties: `sln`, the percentage of labeled neurons in the supragranular layers (SLN; high values indicate feedforward and low values feedback projections); `distance`, the white-matter distance between the two areas, in millimeters.
- `distances`: the estimated white-matter distances, in millimeters (edge property `distance`), from every area to each of the 29 injected areas (Markov et al., PNAS 2013). This network contains all such pairs, whether or not the areas are connected, and is therefore a distance matrix rather than a connectivity network; in this file some areas are grouped differently (e.g. "INSULA", "TEMPORAL_POLE").

All networks have the vertex property `name`, the name of the cortical area. The networks were obtained from the authors' Core-Nets data site via OpenConnectome. The data were obtained from the graph collection of the Open Connectome Project (now NeuroData), whose servers are offline, via the Internet Archive.
citations: N. T. Markov et al., "A Weighted and Directed Interareal Connectivity Matrix for Macaque Cerebral Cortex." Cerebral Cortex 24(1), 17-36 (2014)
N. T. Markov et al., "Anatomy of hierarchy: Feedforward and feedback pathways in macaque visual cortex." Journal of Comparative Neurology 522(1), 225-259 (2014)
N. T. Markov et al., "The role of long-range connections on the specificity of the macaque interareal cortical network." Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 110(13), 5187-5192 (2013)

datasets.name: macaque_neural
datasets.description:
Two networks of anatomical connections among areas of the cerebral cortex of the macaque monkey, compiled from published axonal tract-tracing studies, and distributed with the Brain Connectivity Toolbox (BCT). In both, nodes are cortical areas and edges are axonal pathways (projections) between them.

- `young71`: the 71-area network of M. P. Young (Proc. R. Soc. B 252, 13-18, 1993), who collated the tract-tracing literature into a connection matrix covering visual, somatosensory, auditory, motor, prefrontal and limbic (cingulate, insular, parahippocampal) areas. The BCT matrix contains 746 connections, with 308 reciprocally connected pairs of areas. Area names follow the source file, with numbered (Brodmann-type) areas prefixed by "A" (e.g. "A46" is area 46, "A7a" is area 7a), together with visual areas such as "V1", "MT" or "PITd" and auditory and temporal areas such as "KA", "PAAR" or "TS1".
- `cocomac47`: 47 areas of the visual, somatosensory and motor cortex, defined according to the parcellation of Felleman and Van Essen (as in "V1", "MT", "FEF" or "46"). This matrix was contributed by R. Kötter and used by C. J. Honey, R. Kötter, M. Breakspear and O. Sporns (PNAS 104, 10240-10245, 2007). There, the results of published tracing studies were manually collated in the CoCoMac database, mapped onto the Felleman–Van Essen parcellation, and redundant and inconsistent reports were resolved to obtain a binary connection matrix with 505 connections; 192 pairs of areas are reciprocally connected.

The two networks are independent compilations of the tracing literature using different parcellations, so the 47-area network is not a subnetwork of the 71-area one (several areas, such as "MDP", "MIP" or "36", appear only in the former, while the auditory, prefrontal and limbic areas appear only in the latter); nodes with the same name in both refer to the same anatomical area only approximately.

Both networks are directed and unweighted: an edge $i\to j$ indicates a projection from area $i$ to area $j$ (an entry $a_{ij}=1$ of the binary source matrix, following the BCT convention); absent entries mean that no connection was reported. There are no self-loops.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the cortical area (with the padding spaces of the source files removed).
citations: M. P. Young, "The organization of neural systems in the primate cerebral cortex", Proc. R. Soc. Lond. B 252, 13-18 (1993)
C. J. Honey, R. Kötter, M. Breakspear, O. Sporns, "Network structure of cerebral cortex shapes functional connectivity on multiple time scales", Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA 104, 10240-10245 (2007)
R. Kötter, "Online retrieval, processing, and visualization of primate connectivity data from the CoCoMac database", Neuroinformatics 2, 127-144 (2004)

datasets.name: macaque_visual_cortex
datasets.description:
Directed networks of anatomical connections among the visual areas of the macaque monkey cerebral cortex, from the compilation of Felleman and Van Essen, as distributed with the Brain Connectivity Toolbox (contributed by O. Sporns). Felleman and Van Essen collated the results of anatomical tract-tracing studies published until 1991 into a matrix of corticocortical pathways between the areas of their parcellation of the macaque cortex. Nodes are cortical areas (e.g. "V1", "MT", "LIP", "FEF" or "46") and a directed edge $i\to j$ indicates a reported axonal projection from area $i$ to area $j$ (an entry $a_{ij}=1$ of the source matrix, following the Brain Connectivity Toolbox convention).

- `fve30`: 30 visual areas, including the frontal areas FEF and 46 associated with visual function; 311 connections.
- `fve32`: as `fve30`, with the two additional parietal areas MIP and MDP; 315 connections (the toolbox documentation states 320).

These matrices were used e.g. by Sporns et al. (Cereb. Cortex 10, 127, 2000) and Sporns and Kötter (PLoS Biol. 2, e369, 2004).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the cortical area.
citations: D. J. Felleman, D. C. Van Essen, "Distributed hierarchical processing in the primate cerebral cortex." Cerebral Cortex 1(1), 1-47 (1991)
M. Rubinov, O. Sporns, "Complex network measures of brain connectivity: Uses and interpretations." NeuroImage 52(3), 1059-1069 (2010)

datasets.name: macaques
datasets.description:
Dominance interactions among the 62 adult females of a colony of Japanese macaques (Macaca fuscata fuscata) known as the "Arashiyama B group", observed by Y. Takahata during the non-mating season, from April to early October 1976. Approach-retreat episodes involving food were recorded. The source also reports the lineages of the animals: five lineages of 4, 14, 31, 6 and 6 animals (in the order of the file), plus one animal unrelated to the others. The data were distributed by L. C. Freeman on his network data page at the University of California, Irvine (no longer online), from which this version was obtained via the Internet Archive.

A directed edge (i, j) indicates that female i dominated female j in at least one episode.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the animal (the name "Gl60" appears twice in the source file, for two different animals).
- (Node) `lineage`: the lineage of the animal (1 to 5, or 0 for the unrelated animal), as given in the source by the order of the animals.
- (Edge) `weight`: the number of episodes in which i dominated j.
citations: Y. Takahata. "Diachronic changes in the dominance relations of adult female Japanese monkeys of the Arashiyama B group." In L. M. Fedigan and P. J. Asquith (eds.), The Monkeys of Arashiyama, State University of New York Press, Albany, 123-139 (1991)

datasets.name: madoff_feeders
datasets.description:
Directed network of money flows among the 61 banks, investment funds and other organizations that channeled money into the Ponzi scheme of Bernard Madoff, compiled by Valdis Krebs (2009) from news stories and court documents found on major media web sites. Nodes are organizations (vertex property `name`), and a directed edge points in the direction of the money flow, ultimately leading to Madoff's firm (Bernard L. Madoff Investment Securities). One self-loop in the source matrix is not included. Data distributed by the UCINET datasets collection (University of Manchester).[^ucinet]

[^ucinet]: Description obtained in part from the [UCINET datasets page](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/datasets/covert-networks/madoff-fraud).
citations: V. Krebs, "Madoff Feeder Funds." The Network Thinkers (2009)

datasets.name: madrid_bombing_jjatt
datasets.description:
Time series of networks of relationships among 54 individuals, from the John Jay & ARTIS Transnational Terrorism Database (JJATT). The JJATT data treat specific attacks as endpoints, and depict the evolution of the relations among the individuals directly or indirectly associated with them; here, the bombings of commuter trains in Madrid, Spain, on 11 March 2004 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Madrid_train_bombings)). The data were coded from open sources (e.g. court documents, news reports and books), and were made available in matrix form by the UCINET datasets collection (University of Manchester).

Nodes are individuals (labeled by their JJATT identifier in `name`), and each time-period network contains the relationships present in that period (networks named `YYYY_1` and `YYYY_2` refer to the first and second halves of year YYYY). The edge property `weight` gives the strength of the tie: 1 = acquaintances or distant family ties (interaction limited to radical organization activities), 2 = friends or moderately close family ties (including co-workers and roommates), operational or organizational leadership, or operational ties (e.g. having worked closely together on a bombing), 3 = close friends or family, tight-knit operational cliques. The periods 2005_2, 2006_1, 2006_2 have no ties in the source, and are not included. The `kinship` network contains kinship ties, with the edge property `kinship` coding the type: 1 = in-laws, 2 = cousins, 3 = siblings, 4 = parent/child, 5 = married, 6 = grandparent/grandchild, 7 = significant other (cells coded 99 in the source matrix, whose meaning is not documented, are omitted). The source matrices are meant to be symmetric; in the few cases where the two directions differ, the tie with the larger value is used. The JJATT tie-start, tie-end and operation matrices, which use undocumented codes, are not included.[^ucinet]

[^ucinet]: Description obtained in part from the [UCINET datasets page](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/datasets/covert-networks/madrid-train-bombing-2004).
citations: S. Atran, M. Sageman, et al., "John Jay & ARTIS Transnational Terrorism Database (JJATT)." John Jay College of Criminal Justice (2009)

datasets.name: mag_cs_coauthor
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of computer science authors and the distinct teams of coauthors that published together in ten major conferences, compiled by Amburg, Veldt and Benson from the Microsoft Academic Graph (MAG). The conferences are KDD, WWW, ICML, NeurIPS, STOC, FOCS, CVPR, ICCV, VLDB and SIGMOD. Each team node is a distinct set of authors that appear together on at least one paper from these venues; a set of authors that published several papers is represented only once, and is labeled by the conference where it published most often (sets with a tie between conferences were discarded). An edge connects each team to each of its member authors. Papers with more than 25 authors were omitted, so teams have between 2 and 25 members. Author names and publication dates are not included in the source data, and authors that appear in no team are not included.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `is_team`: whether the node is a team of coauthors (otherwise an author).
- (Node) `author_id` (authors): the (1-based) author identifier in the source data.
- (Node) `venue` (teams): the conference where the team published most often (one of the ten names above). In the source data one team (authors 8, 12 and 57248) has an invalid venue code (67279); its venue is left empty.
citations: I. Amburg, N. Veldt, A. R. Benson, "Clustering in graphs and hypergraphs with categorical edge labels." Proceedings of The Web Conference 2020, 706-717 (2020)

A. Sinha, Z. Shen, Y. Song, H. Ma, D. Eide, B.-J. Hsu, K. Wang, "An Overview of Microsoft Academic Service (MAS) and Applications." Proceedings of the 24th International Conference on World Wide Web (Companion), 243-246 (2015)

datasets.name: mag_geology_coauthor
datasets.description:
Coauthorship networks of publications in the field of Geology, assembled by A. R. Benson and collaborators from the Microsoft Academic Graph (MAG), as distributed in the Open Academic Graph. Each publication whose fields of study include the tag "Geology" is a set of authors (a simplex, or hyperedge), timestamped by its year of publication (from 1800 to 2018).

There are four versions of the data:

- `max-25-bip`, `full-bip`: bipartite networks where each publication is a node connected to its authors. The `max-25` versions include only publications with at most 25 authors, while the `full` versions include all publications.
- `max-25-proj`, `full-proj`: one-mode projections onto the authors, where every pair of coauthors of a publication is connected by an edge. Each publication contributes its own edges, so a pair of authors who wrote $k$ publications together is connected by $k$ parallel edges, each with the year of its publication.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `label`: the name of the author (empty for publication nodes).
- (Node) `is_simplex`: whether the node is a publication (otherwise it is an author; bipartite versions only).
- (Edge) `time`: the year of publication of the corresponding paper.
citations: A. R. Benson et al., "Simplicial Closure and Higher-order Link Prediction." Preprint, arXiv:1802.06916 (2018)

datasets.name: mag_history_coauthor
datasets.description:
Coauthorship networks of publications in the field of History, assembled by A. R. Benson and collaborators from the Microsoft Academic Graph (MAG), as distributed in the Open Academic Graph. Each publication whose fields of study include the tag "History" is a set of authors (a simplex, or hyperedge), timestamped by its year of publication (from 1800 to 2018).

There are four versions of the data:

- `max-25-bip`, `full-bip`: bipartite networks where each publication is a node connected to its authors. The `max-25` versions include only publications with at most 25 authors, while the `full` versions include all publications.
- `max-25-proj`, `full-proj`: one-mode projections onto the authors, where every pair of coauthors of a publication is connected by an edge. Each publication contributes its own edges, so a pair of authors who wrote $k$ publications together is connected by $k$ parallel edges, each with the year of its publication.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `label`: the name of the author (empty for publication nodes).
- (Node) `is_simplex`: whether the node is a publication (otherwise it is an author; bipartite versions only).
- (Edge) `time`: the year of publication of the corresponding paper.
citations: A. R. Benson et al., "Simplicial Closure and Higher-order Link Prediction." Preprint, arXiv:1802.06916 (2018)

datasets.name: malaria_genes
datasets.description:
Networks of recombinant *var* genes of the human malaria parasite *Plasmodium falciparum*, constructed by D. B. Larremore, A. Clauset and C. O. Buckee. The *var* genes encode the PfEMP1 antigens and diversify mainly by recombination. The data comprise the DBLα domains of 307 *var* genes from seven parasite genomes, sequenced by Rask et al. (PLOS Comput. Biol. 6, e1000933, 2010). The DBLα domain was divided into nine highly variable regions (HVRs) separated by conserved sequence blocks, and a separate network was built for each HVR: nodes are genes, and two genes are connected if their sequences at that HVR share an amino acid substring whose length is statistically significant, i.e. too long to be expected by chance, indicating a recombination event.

The networks `HVR_1` to `HVR_9` correspond to the nine HVRs; they share the same set of 307 nodes (the node index identifies the same gene in all networks) but have different edges. The network `combined` is a multilayer network containing the edges of all nine HVRs.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the index of the gene (1 to 307), in the order of the source files.
- (Node) `CysPoLV`: the Cys-PoLV group of the gene (1 to 6), a classification of DBLα sequences based on the number of cysteines and on sequence motifs near HVR6.
- (Node) `UPS`: the upstream promoter sequence group of the gene, with 1 = A, 2 = B, 3 = C, and -1 if no UPS was identified.
- (Edge) `HVR` (`combined` only): the HVR (1 to 9) in which the edge occurs.
citations: D. B. Larremore, A. Clauset, and C. O. Buckee, "A network approach to analyzing highly recombinant malaria parasite genes." PLOS Computational Biology 9(10), e1003268 (2013).

datasets.name: mali_terrorists
datasets.description:
Network of 36 Islamists and Tuareg rebels involved in the conflict in Mali, in the Sahel-Sahara region, reconstructed by Walther and Christopoulos (2015) from newspaper articles published between 2010 and 2012. Nodes are individuals (vertex property `name`), and an edge connects two individuals who interacted, including joint participation in political or military events or political meetings, training in Afghanistan, Iraq or Libya, combat, negotiations for the release of hostages, or involvement in a killing, an abduction or a bombing. Where the two directions in the source matrix differ, the tie is included. Data distributed by the UCINET datasets collection (University of Manchester).[^ucinet]

[^ucinet]: Description obtained in part from the [UCINET datasets page](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/datasets/covert-networks/mali-terrorist-network).
citations: O. J. Walther and D. Christopoulos, "Islamic terrorism and the Malian rebellion." Terrorism and Political Violence 27(3), 497-519 (2015)

datasets.name: mammal_virus_hp3
datasets.description:
Bipartite network of mammal species and the viruses known to infect them, from the database of host-virus associations compiled by Olival et al. (the Host-Pathogen Phylogeny Project, HP3) to study which host and viral traits predict zoonotic spillover. The associations were collected from a systematic review of the published literature, for virus species recognized by the International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses (ICTV), with host names harmonized to the IUCN taxonomy. The database contains 754 mammal species (including humans) and 586 virus species.

A node is either a mammal species or a virus species, and each edge is a host-virus association reported in a reference, annotated with the method used to detect the virus in the host. A few host-virus pairs are reported in more than one reference with different methods, and appear as parallel edges.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the species name (with underscores in place of spaces).
- (Node) `is_host`: whether the node is a mammal species (otherwise it is a virus).
- (Node) `order`, `family`, `genus`: the taxonomic order, family, and genus of the host or virus.
- (Node) `common_name` (hosts): the English common name(s).
- (Node) `wild_domestic` (hosts): whether the species is wild or domestic according to the FAO (or "human").
- (Node) `marine_terrestrial` (hosts): whether the species is marine or terrestrial.
- (Node) `mass_grams` (hosts): the average body mass in grams (NaN if unknown).
- (Node) `redlist_status` (hosts): the IUCN Red List status.
- (Node) `citations`, `disease_citations` (hosts): the number of Zoological Abstracts records for the species, and the number of such records that also match disease-related keywords (both are measures of research effort, -1 if unknown).
- (Node) `nucleic_acid` (viruses): DNA or RNA.
- (Node) `strandedness` (viruses): SS or DS.
- (Node) `envelope` (viruses): enveloped or non-enveloped.
- (Node) `genome_length` (viruses): the average genome length in nucleotides (NaN if unknown).
- (Node) `vector_borne` (viruses): "Y", "N", or "NA" if unknown.
- (Node) `is_zoonotic` (viruses): whether the virus has been detected both in humans and in other mammals.
- (Node) `is_zoonotic_stringent` (viruses): the same, but considering only detections by PCR or virus isolation.
- (Edge) `detection_method`: the method used to detect the virus in the host (e.g. antibodies, PCR, isolation).
- (Edge) `detection_quality`: the strength of the evidence: 0 for serology, 1 for a viral neutralization test, and 2 for PCR or virus isolation (-1 if not given).
- (Edge) `host_status`: whether the host in the reference was wild, domestic, captive, or human.
- (Edge) `reference`: the short reference (author and year) reporting the association.
citations: K. J. Olival, P. R. Hosseini, C. Zambrana-Torrelio, N. Ross, T. L. Bogich, P. Daszak, "Host and viral traits predict zoonotic spillover from mammals." Nature 546, 646-650 (2017)
K. J. Olival, P. R. Hosseini, C. Zambrana-Torrelio, N. Ross, T. L. Bogich, P. Daszak, "Host and Viral Traits Predict Zoonotic Spillover from Mammals" (data and code), Zenodo (2017)

datasets.name: mangal
datasets.description:
A collection of ecological interaction networks from Mangal, a database and web service of ecological networks developed by Poisot, Gravel and colleagues (Poisot et al. 2016). Mangal gathers published networks of interactions between organisms, such as food webs (predation, herbivory, detritivory, scavenging), plant-pollinator and seed-dispersal networks (mutualism), and host-parasite networks, from many sources (most of them digitized from the literature, some of them from other collections such as the Interaction Web Database), and describes them in a common format, with the taxa of the nodes matched to taxonomic databases. Each Mangal network is a network of this entry (1,481 networks), named as in Mangal; they come from 175 data sets, and a data set can contain many networks, e.g. one per site or sampling date (e.g. the 783 small host-parasitoid networks of `kolpelke_2007`).

Nodes are taxa (species or higher taxonomic groups), populations or individuals, as given by the authors, and edges are interactions between them. An interaction can be directed (with the direction recorded in Mangal), undirected, or of unknown direction; a network is directed if any of its interactions is directed. Interactions have a type (e.g. `predation`, `mutualism`, `herbivory`, `parasitism`) and a value with an attribute that says what the value measures: most are `presence/absence` (value 1), and the others are, e.g., numbers of visits of pollinators, frequencies or diet fractions (some networks are therefore weighted). The 180 interactions recorded as absent (`presence/absence` with value 0, in four networks of `rejmanek_stary_1979`) are left out, as are the six networks of `kolpelke_2007` that have no interactions at all. The data were retrieved from the Mangal web service (API version 2) in October 2026; the latest records of the database date from November 2021.

Many of these networks are also part of the entries `iwdb` and `web_of_life`, from other collections.

The networks have the following properties:
