- (Node) `name`: the title of the movie (in English, as in TMDB), the name of the person, or the keyword.
- (Node) `gender` (persons, in `cast` and `crew` only): as coded by TMDB (0: not specified, 1: female, 2: male); -1 for movies.
- (Node) `original_title` (movies): the original title of the movie.
- (Node) `imdb_id` (movies): the IMDb identifier.
- (Node) `release_date`, `year` (movies): the release date (YYYY-MM-DD) and the year of release (-1 if unknown, or for persons and keywords).
- (Node) `genres` (movies): the list of TMDB genres.
- (Node) `original_language` (movies): ISO 639-1 code.
- (Node) `runtime` (movies): in minutes.
- (Node) `budget`, `revenue` (movies): in US dollars.
- (Node) `vote_average`, `vote_count` (movies): the average rating (0-10) and number of ratings by TMDB users.
- (Node) `popularity` (movies): TMDB's popularity score at collection time.
- (Node) `adult` (movies): whether the movie is flagged as adult content.
- (Edge) `character` (`cast`): the name of the role.
- (Edge) `order` (`cast`): the position of the credit in the movie's cast list (0 for the top-billed actor).
- (Edge) `job` (`crew`): e.g. Director, Screenplay, Original Music Composer.
- (Edge) `department` (`crew`): e.g. Directing, Writing, Sound.
- (Edge) `credit_id` (`cast` and `crew`): the TMDB credit identifier.

**Relation to the hypergraphx movie-cast datasets.** The `movies-cast-<genre>` datasets and the `movies-cast-genre-multiplex` dataset of the hypergraphx-data repository were built from the same files. To obtain the actors and casts of one genre, take the movie nodes of the `cast` network whose `genres` contain it and that have at least two distinct adjacent actors, together with these actors; hypergraphx additionally merges the movies of a genre with exactly the same set of actors into a single group weighted by their number (ignoring repeated credits of an actor in a movie). This reproduces exactly the node and group counts of all 20 hypergraphx genre datasets and of the multiplex dataset (the union of the genre layers). Minor differences: in the source file of movie metadata, 29 movies appear twice (identical rows, or differing only in the popularity score or vote count; the first row is used here), which hypergraphx counts twice in the weights, whereas here each movie appears once; and three rows of that file are broken in two by a formatting error, which hypergraphx reads as rows without title and release date, whereas here they are repaired.

Note that TMDB is community-edited, so the credits, keywords and metadata are of varying completeness. This product uses the TMDB API but is not endorsed or certified by TMDB.
citations: R. Banik, "The Movies Dataset." Kaggle, version 7 (2017)

datasets.name: msd_taste_profile
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of users and songs from the Taste Profile subset of the Million Song Dataset (MSD), the user data released by The Echo Nest (a music intelligence company) to accompany the MSD. The data consist of the play counts of songs by anonymous users, collected from undisclosed partners of The Echo Nest, restricted to the songs of the MSD. Each node is a user or a song, and an edge connects a user to a song played by the user, weighted by the number of times the user played it.

The titles and artists of the songs are those of the tracks of the MSD with the same song identifier (the first track, if the song has several). After the release, an error was found in the matching of the songs of the Taste Profile to the tracks of the MSD: the MSD published a list of song-track pairs that should not be trusted, which are marked with the `mismatch` property (the songs are kept).

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the anonymous identifier of the user (a hash), or the MSD identifier of the song (e.g. `SOAKIMP12A8C130995`).
- (Node) `is_user`: whether the node is a user (otherwise a song).
- (Node) `title`, `artist`: the title and the artist of the song (empty for users).
- (Node) `track`: the MSD identifier of the track that gives the title and the artist (e.g. `TRMMMYQ128F932D901`; empty for users).
- (Node) `mismatch`: whether the song is in the list of song-track pairs that should not be trusted (false for users).
- (Edge) `weight`: the number of plays of the song by the user.
citations: T. Bertin-Mahieux, D. P. W. Ellis, B. Whitman, P. Lamere, "The Million Song Dataset." Proceedings of the 12th International Society for Music Information Retrieval Conference (ISMIR), 591-596 (2011)

datasets.name: mturk_workers
datasets.description: The communication network among workers of Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk), an online crowdsourcing labor market, mapped by Yin et al. Workers were recruited with a task posted on MTurk in August and September 2015, open to all workers, which was completed by 10,354 workers (approximately a census of the active workers at the time). Each worker created an anonymous nickname, and then self-reported the other workers with whom they communicate (for instance through online forums dedicated to MTurk, or one-on-one channels such as e-mail, text messages or social media), by searching for their nicknames; workers could keep adding or removing edges after completing the task, and the network corresponds to the data collected on September 13, 2015. Each node is a worker, and an undirected edge connects two workers if one of them reported communicating with the other. Most workers (86.6%) did not report any connection and are isolated nodes. The worker attributes analyzed in the paper (country, forum use, etc.) are not included in the public data.
citations: M. Yin, M. L. Gray, S. Suri, J. W. Vaughan, "The Communication Network Within the Crowd." Proceedings of the 25th International Conference on World Wide Web (WWW), 1293-1303 (2016)

datasets.name: multiplex_diseasome
datasets.description:
Networks of human diseases, their symptoms and their associated genes, from which Halu et al. built the multiplex network of human diseases, in which two diseases are connected in the phenotype layer if they share a symptom, and in the genotype layer if they share a gene. The released data contains the underlying associations: nodes are diseases, symptoms and genes, and an undirected edge connects a disease to a symptom (phenotype layer) or to a gene (genotype layer) associated with it. Each disease is a disorder of the Disease Ontology, which may group several entries (phenotypes) of the Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man (OMIM) database; the symptoms are terms of the Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO). There are two networks, which differ in the source of the disease-gene associations:

- `omim`: disease-gene associations from OMIM, for 910 diseases (2,255 OMIM entries), the data set analyzed in the paper (whose multiplex network contains the 779 diseases that are not isolated in it).
- `gwas`: disease-gene associations from genome-wide association studies (the GWAS Catalog), for 565 diseases, analyzed in the supplementary information of the paper.

The networks are bipartite: every edge connects a disease to a symptom or a gene. The source files list, for each disease, its OMIM entries with one symptom each (the symptoms of a disease are the union of those of its entries), and its genes: in `omim` each gene is listed with the OMIM entry it is associated with, while in `gwas` the genes are not specific to OMIM entries: for 553 of the 565 diseases, every gene is listed with every OMIM entry of the disease (for the other 12, some entries are listed with a subset of the genes). Each edge here corresponds to a distinct disease-symptom or disease-gene pair, and lists the OMIM entries of the disease with which the pair appears in the source. Diseases, symptoms and genes are separate nodes even when they have the same name (e.g. some symptoms have the name of a disease). In `omim`, genes (some of which are loci without an identified gene, e.g. "AD10") are identified by their OMIM number, and the gene field contains a comma-separated list of the gene's symbols, the first of which is used as the name; in `gwas`, genes are identified by a single symbol, without OMIM number or cytogenetic location. Two diseases (polycystic kidney and liver disease) have rows with and without a category; the non-empty one is used. No data was left out.

This data set differs from the `diseasome` network of Goh et al. (OMIM disorders and their genes, from 2005, with no symptoms) and from the `human_symptoms_diseases` network of Zhou et al. (co-occurrences of MeSH disease and symptom terms in PubMed records).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the disease or symptom (as given in the source), or the (first) symbol of the gene.
- (Node) `kind`: the kind of node, "disease", "symptom" or "gene".
- (Node) `is_disease`, `is_symptom`, `is_gene`: whether the node is a disease, a symptom or a gene.
- (Node) `category`: the category of the disease (e.g. "autosomal recessive disease"; empty for some diseases) or of the symptom (e.g. "Abnormality of the midface"); empty for genes.
- (Node) `disorder_omim`: the OMIM numbers of the entries of the disease (empty for symptoms and genes).
- (Node) `gene_omim` (`omim` only): the OMIM number of the gene (-1 for diseases and symptoms).
- (Node) `gene_symbols` (`omim` only): all the symbols of the gene, as listed in the source (empty for diseases and symptoms).
- (Node) `cytogenetic_location` (`omim` only): the cytogenetic location of the gene (e.g. "6p21.1"; empty for diseases and symptoms).
- (Edge) `layer`: "phenotype" for disease-symptom edges, "genotype" for disease-gene edges.
- (Edge) `disorder_omim`: the OMIM numbers of the entries of the disease with which the symptom or gene is listed in the source.
citations: A. Halu, M. De Domenico, A. Arenas, A. Sharma, "The multiplex network of human diseases." npj Systems Biology and Applications 5, 15 (2019)

datasets.name: musculoskeletal
datasets.description:
Bipartite networks of the muscles and bones of the human body, from A. C. Murphy, D. S. Bassett and collaborators. Nodes are muscles and bones (some of which are actually ligaments or tendons), and an undirected edge connects a muscle to a bone on which it has an origin or insertion point, i.e., to which it attaches. There are two networks, with the same 270 muscles:

- `hosford`: compiled from the Hosford Muscle Tables (173 bones), used in the main text of the paper.
- `grant`: compiled from Grant's Atlas of Anatomy (173 bones, in a slightly different list), used in the supplementary text. In this network, 20 nodes have no connections.

The nodes have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the muscle or bone.
- (Node) `is_muscle`: whether the node is a muscle (otherwise it is a bone).
- (Node) `community`: (muscles only, -1 for bones) the community of the muscle (1 to 22), found by the authors by modularity maximization (consensus of 100 runs, with resolution parameter 4.3) on the muscle-muscle network of the `hosford` data, in which two muscles are connected if they attach to the same bone.
- (Node) `homunculus_category`: (muscles only, -1 for bones) the category of the motor homunculus (the map of the body in the primary motor cortex, following Penfield) to which the muscle was assigned (1 to 22), and `homunculus_region`: the name of this category (e.g. "Toes", "Knee", "Shoulder", "Jaw", "Swallowing").
citations: A. C. Murphy, S. F. Muldoon, D. Baker, A. Lastowka, B. Bennett, M. Yang, D. S. Bassett, "Structure, function, and control of the human musculoskeletal network." PLoS Biology 16(1), e2002811 (2018)
A. C. Murphy, S. F. Muldoon, D. Baker, A. Lastowka, B. Bennett, M. Yang, D. S. Bassett, "Structure, function, and control of the musculoskeletal network - Data." Zenodo (2017)

datasets.name: myocardial_inflamome
datasets.description:
Network of human protein-protein interactions (PPIs) related to inflammation and prognosis after myocardial infarction (MI), called "My-Inflamome", from F. J. Azuaje and collaborators. Nodes are human proteins (identified by gene symbols), and an undirected edge indicates an experimentally validated physical interaction between two proteins in humans. The network was built from a set of 415 seed proteins: 28 well-known biomarkers of inflammation and prognosis after MI (e.g. TNF, IL6, CRP, FAS), expanded with genes that are functionally and phenotypically similar to them according to a gene prioritization. All the human PPIs of the seed proteins were retrieved from the DIP, IntAct and MINT databases (c. 2010), and their union forms the network. The data contain the largest connected component of the network (reported as 2,532 proteins and 6,131 interactions; the file contains 2,531 distinct protein names, and a few self-interactions), on which the analyses of the paper are based.

The nodes have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the protein (gene symbol, or a database identifier when no symbol was assigned).
- (Node) `is_seed`: whether the protein is one of the seeds; `is_biomarker`: whether it is one of the known biomarkers (seeds not in the largest component are not included).
- (Node) `module`: the module of the protein (1 to 21), found by the authors with a greedy modularity-maximization clustering (PolarMapper); `submodule`: its submodule, numbered across all modules; `traffic`: the "traffic" (betweenness centrality) of the protein, as computed by the authors. These are -1 (or NaN) for the proteins not listed in the module tables.[^icon]

[^icon]: Description obtained in part from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.
citations: F. J. Azuaje, S. Rodius, L. Zhang, Y. Devaux, D. R. Wagner, "Information encoded in a network of inflammation proteins predicts clinical outcome after myocardial infarction." BMC Medical Genomics 4, 59 (2011)

datasets.name: myspace_aminer
datasets.description:
Social graph of users of MySpace, a social networking website with a strong emphasis on music. Nodes are user accounts, identified by integer IDs, and edges are connections between them. The data are part of a collection of crawled social networks (Twitter, LiveJournal, Flickr, Last.fm, MySpace, LinkedIn and ArnetMiner) distributed by the AMiner group of Tsinghua University (Y. Zhang and J. Tang) for the study of the linkage of user identities across social networks. The date of collection and the crawling procedure are not documented, but the data were collected no later than 2013.

In the source data each connected pair of users is listed only once, always with the smaller ID first, and the source does not document whether the relationship is directed; the edges are therefore stored as undirected. The network contains 854,440 self-loops, as almost every node in the source file is connected to itself.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the user ID in the source data.
- (Node) `username`: the user name.
citations: T. Chen, M. A. Kaafar, A. Friedman, and R. Boreli. "Is more always merrier?: a deep dive into online social footprints." In 2012 ACM workshop on Workshop on online social networks, pages 67–72, 2012.
D. Perito, C. Castelluccia, M. A. Kaafar, and P. Manils. "How unique and traceable are usernames?" In Privacy Enhancing Technologies, pages 1–17. Springer, 2011

H. Kwak, C. Lee, H. Park, and S. Moon. "What is Twitter, a social network or a news media?" In WWW ’10: Proceedings of the 19th international conference on World wide web, pages 591–600, New York, NY, USA, 2010. ACM.
Yutao Zhang, Jie Tang, "Social Network Integration: Towards Constructing the Social Graph", arxiv:1311.2670

datasets.name: n17_greece
datasets.description:
Networks of the members of the Revolutionary Organization 17 November (17N), a Marxist urban guerrilla group active in Greece from 1975 to 2002, which was responsible for several assassinations, kidnappings, bombings and symbolic attacks on government offices ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolutionary_Organization_17_November)). The data were reconstructed at the University of Manchester from the John Jay & ARTIS Transnational Terrorism Database (JJATT), and distributed by the UCINET datasets collection. Members are identified by numbers (1 to 18) in the vertex property `name`.

- `events`: bipartite network of 18 members and 12 terrorist events (labeled A to N), connecting each member to the events in which they participated. The vertex property `is_event` indicates whether a node is an event (True) or a member (False). Seven members did not participate in any of the events.
- `co_participation`: one-mode projection of `events`, connecting members who took part in the same events, with the edge property `weight` giving the number of such events.
- `1975_1984`, `1985_1994` and `1995_2002`: relationships among members in each period. A tie exists if the members were acquaintances or had distant family ties (interactions limited to the organization's activities), were friends or had moderately close family ties, had operational or leadership ties, or were close friends, family or members of a tight-knit operational clique.
- `kinship`: kinship ties among members.[^ucinet]

[^ucinet]: Description obtained in part from the [UCINET datasets page](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/datasets/covert-networks/17-november-greece-bombing).
citations: S. Atran, M. Sageman, et al., "John Jay & ARTIS Transnational Terrorism Database (JJATT)." John Jay College of Criminal Justice (2009)

datasets.name: national_public_transport
datasets.description:
Public transport networks of five European countries (Germany, the Netherlands, Norway, Switzerland and Ireland), built from the national timetables that their transport authorities or aggregators publish in the General Transit Feed Specification (GTFS) format: all the scheduled trips of buses, trams, subways, trains, ferries, cable cars, etc. in the country (and the cross-border trips). The feeds are replaced every day; the networks are built from the dated copies kept by the Mobility Database:

- `de`: the three feeds of gtfs.de, based on the data of DELFI e.V. (local public transport, regional rail and long-distance rail, which share their stop ids), of October 25, 2026, valid from October 24 to November 23, 2026;
- `nl`: the feed of OVapi, of October 28, 2026, valid from October 26 to December 12, 2026;
- `no`: the national feed of Entur, of October 28, 2026 (whose calendars extend, for some services, from 2019 to 2029);
- `ch`: the feed of the 2026 timetable of opentransportdata.swiss (Systemaufgaben Kundeninformation SKI+), in its version of May 27, 2026, valid from December 14, 2025 to December 12, 2026 (the copy of the Mobility Database was not updated afterwards);
- `ie`: the feed of all operators of Transport for Ireland (National Transport Authority), of October 28, 2026, valid from October 26, 2026 to October 27, 2027.

Each network is the "space of stops" (L-space) of the timetable: a directed edge connects two stops if at least one trip travels from the first to the second without intermediate stops. There is one edge for each pair of consecutive stops and each GTFS route type (mode of transport), so that two stops served by several modes are connected by parallel edges, one per mode, as in `kujala_public_transport`. For each country there are two networks (only `ie_stops` for Ireland, whose feed has no stations):

- `<country>_stops` (e.g. `de_stops`): the nodes are the stops (or platforms) where the vehicles stop (GTFS stops of location type 0), and the stations that are directly served;
- `<country>_stations` (e.g. `de_stations`): the stops are grouped into their parent stations (GTFS stops of location type 1), where the feed gives them, and the other stops are kept as they are. Consecutive stops of a trip within the same station become self-loops.

The stops (or stations) without any trip are kept as isolated nodes. The networks are not connected: e.g. in the Netherlands, the stops of different operators are rarely grouped into common stations, so that the network of each operator is mostly a component of its own (the largest component of `nl_stations` has 6,894 of its 38,548 nodes). The frequency-based trips of the Swiss feed (`frequencies.txt`) are counted as single trips. Entrances, generic nodes and boarding areas of the stations, transfers, shapes, fares and the agencies and routes themselves are not included.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `stop_id` (`<country>_stops`): the id of the stop in the feed.
- (Node) `station_id` (`<country>_stations`): the id of the station (or of the stop, for stops without a station).
- (Node) `name`: the name of the stop or station.
- (Node) `lat`, `lon`: its position.
- (Node) `parent_station` (`<country>_stops`): the id of its station (empty if none).
- (Node) `platform_code` (`<country>_stops`): the platform (empty if not given).
- (Node) `num_stops` (`<country>_stations`): the number of stops of the station (0 for stops without a station).
- (Edge) `route_type`: the mode of transport, as a GTFS route type (e.g. 0 tram, 1 subway, 2 rail, 3 bus, 4 ferry, 5 cable tram, 6 aerial lift, 7 funicular, or the extended route types, e.g. 100-117 railway services, 700-717 bus services, 900 tram, 1000 water transport, 1300 aerial lift; -1 if not given).
- (Edge) `n_trips`: the number of trips of the feed that travel between the two stops (each trip is a pattern of service, which can run on many days).
- (Edge) `n_departures`: the number of departures in the period of validity of the feed (the trips multiplied by the number of days on which they run, from the calendars of the feed).
- (Edge) `duration_avg`: the average travel time between the two stops (seconds, from the departure at the first stop to the arrival at the second, over the trips; NaN if not given).
- (Edge) `distance`: the straight-line distance between the two stops (meters).
citations: gtfs.de, DELFI e.V., "GTFS for Germany: local, regional and long-distance public transport (de_nv, de_rv, de_fv)." Dataset, Mobility Database copies mdb-1090, mdb-1089, mdb-768 of October 25 (2026)
OVapi, "GTFS Netherlands." Dataset, Mobility Database copy mdb-1077 of October 28 (2026)
Entur, "Norway aggregated GTFS." Dataset, Mobility Database copy mdb-1078 of October 28 (2026)
Systemaufgaben Kundeninformation SKI+, "Timetable 2026 (GTFS2020)." opentransportdata.swiss, dataset, Mobility Database copy mdb-2898 of May 29 (2026)
National Transport Authority, "Transport for Ireland GTFS (all operators)." Dataset, Mobility Database copy mdb-2364 of October 28 (2026)

datasets.name: ncaa_basketball_2017
datasets.description:
Directed network of the games played among the teams of the 2017 NCAA Division I men's basketball tournament ("March Madness") during the 2016-2017 regular season and conference tournaments, compiled by B. Keegan. The season schedules and results of the 60 teams that entered the main tournament draw directly (the 8 teams of the "First Four" play-in games are not included) were crawled from sports-reference.com on 15 March 2017, and cover the games from 11 November 2016 to 12 March 2017.

A node is a team, and a directed edge from team A to team B is a game won by A over B. Each game between two of the teams is a separate edge, and is taken from the results of either team. The crawler omitted the last game in the schedule of each team, so games that were the last ones played by both teams (such as some conference tournament finals) are missing.

The network published upstream (`tournament_schedule.gexf`) instead joins the games of each pair of teams in a single edge, weighted by the cumulative point differential, but is built with a comparison of the scores as text, which misclassifies games where one team scored 100 points or more, and does not match the alternative names of four teams (e.g. "UNC" and "North Carolina"); the network here is built from the game results crawled upstream (`results.csv`).

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the team name.
- (Edge) `date`: the date of the game (YYYY-MM-DD).
- (Edge) `winner_points` and `loser_points`: the points scored by the winning and losing team.
citations: B. Keegan, "NCAA-MBB-2017: Quick-and-dirty network analysis of the 2017 NCAA Men's Basketball tournament." https://github.com/brianckeegan/NCAA-MBB-2017 (2017)

datasets.name: ndc_drugs
datasets.description:
Bipartite networks of drug products and their pharmaceutical classes or active substances, from the National Drug Code (NDC) Directory. Under the Drug Listing Act of 1972, firms must list with the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) the drugs they manufacture or distribute commercially, and the FDA publishes this information as the NDC Directory, where each product is identified by an NDC product code (labeler code and product code). The data correspond to a version of the directory obtained around 2017 (the latest marketing date is 2017-09-21). Each drug node is one NDC product code, so the same drug substance can appear in several nodes (e.g. different dosages, forms or manufacturers), and is annotated with the date when the product started being marketed. All products in the directory are included (no size restriction). Names are lower-cased.

- `classes`: each drug is connected to the pharmaceutical classes the FDA assigned to it.
- `substances`: each drug is connected to the substances (ingredients) it is made of.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `is_drug`: whether the node is a drug (NDC product code), otherwise a class (`classes`) or a substance (`substances`).
- (Node) `name`: the name of the drug (empty for a few products whose name is missing in the source data), or of the class or substance.
- (Node) `ndc_code` (drugs): the NDC product code, as "labeler-product".
- (Node) `time` (drugs): the date when the drug started being marketed, in days since 1970-01-01 (negative before 1970; the earliest date is 1900-01-01; only meaningful for drug nodes).
- (Node) `class_type` (`classes` only): the kind of pharmaceutical class, as given in the source: `epc` (established pharmacologic class), `moa` (mechanism of action), `pe` (physiologic effect), or `chemical/ingredient` (chemical structure). A few class names that contain a comma in the directory were split into two nodes in the source data (e.g. "antibodies" and "monoclonal [chemical/ingredient]"); for these the first part has an empty `class_type`.
citations: A. R. Benson, R. Abebe, M. T. Schaub, A. Jadbabaie, J. Kleinberg, "Simplicial closure and higher-order link prediction." Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 115(48), E11221-E11230 (2018)

datasets.name: ndrangheta_summits
datasets.description:
Bipartite network of 156 suspected members of the 'Ndrangheta (a Calabrian mafia organisation) in the region of Milan, Italy, and 47 meetings ("summits") they attended between 2007 and 2009. Summits are meetings held to make important decisions and affiliations, to solve internal problems and to establish roles and powers. Attendance was registered by the police through wiretapping and observation during the large investigation "Operazione Infinito", and the network was reconstructed (mostly from pages 87-110) from the pre-trial detention order issued by the preliminary investigation judge of the Court of Milan. Data distributed by the UCINET datasets collection (University of Manchester).

An edge connects a person to a summit they attended. The vertex property `is_summit` indicates whether a node is a summit (True) or a person (False). The `name` of a person is their surname and given names, and the `name` of a summit gives its date, a description and place (the marker "(L)" is part of the source labels).[^ucinet]

[^ucinet]: Description obtained in part from the [UCINET datasets page](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/datasets/covert-networks/ndrangheta-mafia-2).
citations: Tribunale di Milano, "Ordinanza di applicazione di misura coercitiva con mandato di cattura - art. 292 c.p.p. (Operazione Infinito)." Ufficio del Giudice per le indagini preliminari (2011)

datasets.name: nematode_mammal
datasets.description:
Global network of host–parasite associations between helminth parasites and their host species, obtained with the R package helminthR (T. Dallas), which queries the Host-Parasite Database of the Natural History Museum, London, a compilation of host–parasite records from the published literature. The data were used by T. Dallas and collaborators to examine macroecological patterns in helminth parasites, and were distributed as a demonstration network by C. J. Carlson. The data are not restricted to nematodes and mammals (as the name of the dataset suggests): the parasites are trematodes, nematodes, cestodes and acanthocephalans, and the hosts include fish, birds, mammals, reptiles, amphibians and invertebrates.

Nodes are host and parasite species (the network is bipartite), and an edge connects a host to a parasite recorded on it. Each edge corresponds to one record of the database, which lists the locality of the record, so a host–parasite pair recorded at several localities is connected by several parallel edges (the 146,683 edges connect 61,597 distinct pairs).

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the species name of the host or parasite.
- (Node) `is_host`: whether the node is a host (otherwise it is a parasite).
- (Node) `group`: for parasites, the parasite group (Trematoda, Nematoda, Cestoda or Acanthocephala); for hosts, the host group (e.g. Teleostei, Aves, Mammalia, or NA if not available).
- (Edge) `full_name`: the full name of the parasite with taxonomic authority, as given in the record (it can vary between records of the same parasite, e.g. for synonyms or subspecies).
- (Edge) `locality`: the locality of the record.
citations: T. Dallas et al. "Gauging support for macroecological patterns in helminth parasites." Glob. Ecol. Biogeogr. 27, 1437–1447 (2018)

datasets.name: netflix_prize
datasets.description:
Bipartite networks of the customers and movies of the DVD rental and streaming service Netflix, from the data set that Netflix released in October 2006 for the Netflix Prize, an open competition for the best algorithm to predict user ratings of movies. The data set contains 100,480,507 ratings, from 1 to 5 stars (whole stars only), that 480,189 customers, chosen at random, gave to 17,770 movies between November 1999 and December 2005 (October 1998 to December 2005, according to the documentation of the data set), with the date of each rating. The customer ids were replaced by random ids. The movies are given with their titles and years of release (which may be those of the DVD release), and their ids are not those used by Netflix.

- `training`: the training set of the competition, where each edge is the rating that a customer gave to a movie (a customer rates a movie at most once). The 1,408,395 ratings of the probe set, a subset of the training set that has the same properties as the qualifying set, are marked.
- `qualifying`: the qualifying set of the competition, 2,817,131 pairs of customers and movies with the dates of the ratings (from January 2000 to December 2005), whose ratings were withheld (the ratings that the competitors had to predict). These ratings were never released.

Both networks contain all the customers and movies of the data set, in the same order.

Shortly after the release, Narayanan and Shmatikov [showed](https://doi.org/10.1109/SP.2008.33) that some of the customers in the data set could be re-identified by matching their ratings and dates with public ratings on the Internet Movie Database (IMDb). In December 2009, a class-action lawsuit was filed against Netflix over the release of the data, and in March 2010 Netflix settled it and canceled a planned second competition, which was to use data with demographic information; the release of the data to the UCI Machine Learning Repository after the competition, announced in its rules, did not take place, and Netflix no longer distributes the data set. The files of the upstream source used here are a copy of the original data set uploaded to the Internet Archive in 2016.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `is_user`: whether the node is a customer (otherwise a movie).
- (Node) `user_id`: the anonymized id of the customer (-1 for movies).
- (Node) `movie_id`: the id of the movie in the data set (-1 for customers).
- (Node) `title` and `year`: the title of the movie and its year of release (-1 if not given, and for customers).
- (Edge) `time`: the date of the rating, as Unix time (at midnight UTC).
- (Edge) `rating` (`training`): the rating in stars.
- (Edge) `probe` (`training`): whether the rating is in the probe set.
citations: J. Bennett, S. Lanning, "The Netflix Prize." Proceedings of KDD Cup and Workshop 2007, 3-6 (2007)

datasets.name: netscience
datasets.description:
Coauthorship network of scientists working on network theory and experiment, compiled by M. E. J. Newman in May 2006 from the bibliographies of two review articles on networks, M. E. J. Newman, SIAM Review 45, 167-256 (2003), and S. Boccaletti et al., Physics Reports 424, 175-308 (2006), with a few additional references added by hand. Nodes are scientists and two scientists are connected if they coauthored at least one of the papers. This version contains all components of the network (1,589 scientists), not just the largest component of 379 scientists that was originally analyzed.

The edges are weighted as described in M. E. J. Newman, Phys. Rev. E 64, 016132 (2001): each paper with $n$ authors contributes $1/(n-1)$ to the weight of the edge between every pair of its authors, so that the weight $w_{ij}$ is the sum of these contributions over all papers coauthored by $i$ and $j$.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `label`: the name of the scientist, as surname and initials (as in "ABRAMSON, G").
- (Edge) `value`: the edge weight $w_{ij}$.
citations: M. E. J. Newman, "Finding community structure in networks using the eigenvectors of matrices." Phys. Rev. E 74, 036104 (2006). arxiv:physics/0605087

datasets.name: network_science_book
datasets.description:
Four of the ten networks distributed with the textbook "Network Science" by A.-L. Barabási, which uses them throughout as reference data sets (e.g. in its Table 2.1). In all of them, nodes are anonymous and labeled consecutively from zero (the labels are the node indices), and there are no node or edge attributes. The networks are:

- `phonecalls`: mobile phone calls among a sample of the most active users of the data set of C. Song, Z. Qu, N. Blumm and A.-L. Barabási (2010), who used the call records of about 10 million anonymized subscribers of a mobile phone carrier to study the predictability of human mobility; the data were provided by C. Song. Nodes are phone users, and a directed edge $i \to j$ means that $i$ called $j$ at least once during the observation period (the dates and the carrier are not given). The book's data page describes the edges as undirected ("called each other at least once"), but the file lists 91,826 ordered pairs (34,973 of the 56,853 connected pairs in both directions), the number of directed links given in the book's Table 2.1; the network is therefore stored as directed.
- `email`: email traffic at the University of Kiel, Germany, collected over 112 days from the log files of the university's mail server by H. Ebel, L.-I. Mielsch and S. Bornholdt (2002). Nodes are email addresses (of the university and outside it), and a directed edge $i \to j$ means that $i$ sent at least one email to $j$. The 648 self-loops (addresses that sent emails to themselves) are kept.
- `metabolic`: the metabolism of the bacterium *Escherichia coli*, derived from a metabolic reconstruction of the BiGG knowledgebase (J. Schellenberger et al., 2010); which reconstruction and version were used is not documented. Nodes are metabolites, and a directed edge $i \to j$ means that there is a reaction in which $i$ is an input (substrate) and $j$ a product. The metabolite names are not included.
- `citation`: citations among the papers of the journals of the American Physical Society (APS): Physical Review Letters, Physical Review (its series A to E and earlier) and Reviews of Modern Physics, derived from the citation data that the APS makes available to researchers on request (S. Redner, 2005); the range of years is not documented. Nodes are papers, and a directed edge $i \to j$ means that paper $i$ cites paper $j$. The 118 self-loops and the 3,903 pairs of papers that cite each other are kept. The network is distributed here as it is in the book's data set.

The other networks of the book's data set are already in this catalog and are not repeated here: the actor network (`imdb_actors_2004`), the condensed matter collaboration network (`CondMat` of `arxiv_authors`, from SNAP), the Internet router network (`skitter_routers_2003`, with the same 192,244 nodes and 609,066 edges), the power grid (`power`), the yeast protein interactions of Yu et al. (2008) (`y2h_union` of `yeast_interactome_ccsb`), and the WWW network of Notre Dame (`notre_dame_web`).

The networks have no properties besides the node indices.
citations: A.-L. Barabási, "Network Science." Cambridge University Press (2016).
C. Song, Z. Qu, N. Blumm, and A.-L. Barabási, "Limits of predictability in human mobility." Science 327(5968), 1018-1021 (2010).
H. Ebel, L.-I. Mielsch, and S. Bornholdt, "Scale-free topology of e-mail networks." Physical Review E 66, 035103 (2002).
J. Schellenberger, J. O. Park, T. M. Conrad, and B. Ø. Palsson, "BiGG: a Biochemical Genetic and Genomic knowledgebase of large scale metabolic reconstructions." BMC Bioinformatics 11, 213 (2010).
S. Redner, "Citation statistics from 110 years of Physical Review." Physics Today 58(6), 49-54 (2005).

datasets.name: network_scientists
datasets.description: The co-authorship network of network scientists, from Molontay and Nagy. Network science papers are defined as those that cite at least one of three seminal papers of the field (Watts and Strogatz, 1998; Barabási and Albert, 1999; Girvan and Newman, 2002). Their records were retrieved from the Web of Science core collection on 16 May 2019, and after the removal of duplicates comprise 29,528 papers. Each node is an author of at least one such paper, and an undirected edge connects two authors who co-authored at least one network science paper. The network is a one-mode projection of the bipartite network of authors and papers, and is anonymized. 851 nodes are isolated, corresponding to authors of single-authored papers without network science co-authors.
citations: R. Molontay, M. Nagy, "Two decades of network science: as seen through the co-authorship network of network scientists." Proceedings of the 2019 IEEE/ACM International Conference on Advances in Social Networks Analysis and Mining (ASONAM), 578-583 (2019)

datasets.name: new_guinea_tribes
datasets.description:
A signed network of political alliances and enmities among 16 tribes of the Gahuku–Gama alliance structure of the Eastern Central Highlands of New Guinea, from the ethnography of Read (1954). Hage and Harary (1983) used it to illustrate a clusterable signed graph: the alliance structure comprises three tribal groups, and, unlike in a balanced structure, the enemy of an enemy can be either a friend or an enemy. The data are from the UCINET IV datasets collection (file `gama.dat`), as distributed in Vladimir Batagelj's Pajek data repository, where the signed graph is split into two symmetric binary matrices, GAMAPOS for the alliance ("rova") relation and GAMANEG for the antagonistic ("hina") relation.

Nodes are tribes, and an undirected edge represents either an alliance or an enmity between two tribes (no pair is connected by both).

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the abbreviated tribe name.
- (Edge) `sign`: $+1$ for alliance ("rova", GAMAPOS) and $-1$ for enmity ("hina", GAMANEG).
citations: K. E. Read, "Cultures of the central highlands, New Guinea." Southwestern Journal of Anthropology 10(1), 1-43 (1954)

datasets.name: new_spain_roads
datasets.description:
The network of travel routes among the parishes, temples and towns of the archbishopric of Mexico in 18th century New Spain, transcribed from the anonymous painted map "Plano del arzobispado de México", held by the Instituto Nacional de Antropología e Historia (INAH) in Mexico. The map shows the places connected by paths annotated with the travel distances between them. The map was brought to attention by S. B. Weingart, and the network was transcribed by C. Uhl in June 2018, and distributed by A. Clauset. According to the transcriber, some of the distances were difficult to decipher, so some values may be inaccurate. The place names are not included.

An undirected edge connects two places joined by a path on the map.

The network has the following properties:

- (Edge) `weight`: the travel distance between the two places, as written on the map (the unit is not given in the data).
citations: Anonymous, "Plano del arzobispado de México" (18th century), Instituto Nacional de Antropología e Historia, Mexico

datasets.name: new_zealand_collab
datasets.description:
Network of scientific collaborations among New Zealand institutions, constructed by S. Aref, D. Friggens and S. Hendy from a full extract of the Scopus bibliographic database, restricted to New Zealand publications from 2010 to 2015. Scopus affiliation IDs were grouped into institutions (universities, Crown Research Institutes, government agencies, district health boards, companies, non-profit organizations, etc.) using a manually compiled mapping of the New Zealand Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE); affiliations that were missing or not identifiable as specific institutions were excluded.

Nodes are institutions, and two institutions are connected if they have at least one joint publication, i.e. a publication with authors affiliated with each of them (an author with affiliations to both institutions does not count as a collaboration). The edges are weighted by the number of joint publications.

In the study, institutions were classified into four categories (business enterprise, private not-for-profit, government, and higher education), but this classification is not included in the network file used here.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `_graphml_vertex_id`: the name of the institution.
- (Edge) `weight`: the number of joint publications of the two institutions between 2010 and 2015.
citations: S. Aref, D. Friggens, and S. Hendy, "Analysing scientific collaborations of New Zealand institutions using Scopus bibliometric data." Proc. Australasian Comp. Sci. Week Multiconf. (ACSW ’18), Article 49, 1-10 (2018)

datasets.name: newcomb_fraternity
datasets.description:
Weekly sociometric preference rankings among 17 men attending the University of Michigan in the fall of 1956, as part of the Michigan Group Study Project supervised by T. Newcomb (1953-1956). The men were incoming transfer students without prior acquaintance, recruited to live together in an off-campus (fraternity) house rented for them. Each week, each man ranked all the others by preference, without ties. The data from week 9 are missing. These data were analyzed among others by White, Boorman and Breiger (1976). The data were distributed by L. C. Freeman on his network data page at the University of California, Irvine (no longer online), from which this version was obtained via the Internet Archive.

The networks `week0` to `week15` (except `week9`) contain one directed edge (i, j) for each pair of men, indicating the rank given by man i to man j.

The network `signed_week15` is the undirected signed network that S. Aref and M. C. Wilson derived from the rankings of the last week (week 15) to study structural balance (Aref and Wilson, 2018 and 2019): ranks 1 to 5 are taken as positive choices and ranks 12 to 16 as negative choices, and two men are connected only if their choices of each other are reciprocated with the same sign (17 men, 40 edges, 17 of them negative). It is computed here from the week 15 rankings.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Edge) `rank` (`week0` to `week15`): the preference rank (1: first preference, ..., 16: last).
- (Edge) `sign` (`signed_week15`): $+1$ for a reciprocated positive choice and $-1$ for a reciprocated negative choice.
citations: T. M. Newcomb, "The Acquaintance Process." Holt, Rinehart and Winston (1961)
P. G. Nordlie, "A longitudinal study of interpersonal attraction in a natural group setting." Doctoral dissertation, University of Michigan (1958)
H. C. White, S. A. Boorman, R. L. Breiger, "Social structure from multiple networks. I. Blockmodels of roles and positions." American Journal of Sociology 81(4), 730-780 (1976)
S. Aref and M. C. Wilson, "Measuring partial balance in signed networks." J. Complex Networks 6(4), 566–595 (2018)
S. Aref and M. C. Wilson, "Balance and frustration in signed networks." J. Complex Networks 7(2), 163–189 (2019)

datasets.name: newsgroups_words
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of Usenet newsgroup postings and the words they contain, from a reduced version of the "20 Newsgroups" collection prepared by S. Roweis. The 20 Newsgroups collection, assembled by K. Lang, consists of about 20,000 postings to 20 Usenet newsgroups. In this reduced version, the vocabulary is restricted to 100 selected words, and the data contain 16,242 postings, each containing at least one of them; each posting is connected to each of these words it contains (occurrence only, without counts). Each posting is labelled by the top-level hierarchy of its newsgroup (comp.\*, rec.\*, sci.\* or talk.\*). The data were obtained from the file "20news_w100.mat" formerly distributed on S. Roweis' data page, retrieved from the Internet Archive copy.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `is_word`: whether the node is a word (otherwise a posting).
- (Node) `name`: the word (empty for postings).
- (Node) `index` (postings): the position of the posting in the source data (starting from 0).
- (Node) `newsgroup` (postings): the top-level newsgroup hierarchy of the posting ("comp.\*", "rec.\*", "sci.\*" or "talk.\*").
citations: S. Roweis, "Data for MATLAB hackers: 20 Newsgroups (20news_w100.mat)."
K. Lang, "NewsWeeder: Learning to Filter Netnews." Machine Learning Proceedings 1995, 331-339 (1995)

datasets.name: nfl_2009
datasets.description:
The games played among the 32 teams of the American National Football League (NFL) in the 2009 season, including regular season and post-season games. The data were derived by C. Aicher, A. Z. Jacobs and A. Clauset from data licensed from STATS LLC, and used as an example of a weighted network with latent block structure.

Each game is a directed edge between the two teams that played it, so that pairs of teams that played several times are connected by multiple edges. The edge direction follows the order of the two teams in the source data, which is not documented, and is neither home team first nor winner first (it should be treated as arbitrary).

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the team abbreviation.
- (Node) `conference`: the conference of the team (1: NFC, 2: AFC).
- (Node) `division`: the division of the team (1: NFC North, 2: NFC East, 3: NFC South, 4: NFC West, 5: AFC North, 6: AFC East, 7: AFC South, 8: AFC West).
- (Edge) `source_score` and `target_score`: the points scored in the game by the source and target teams, respectively. Points scored during overtime are not included.
citations: C. Aicher, A. Z. Jacobs, A. Clauset, "Learning latent block structure in weighted networks." Journal of Complex Networks 3(2), 221-248 (2015)

datasets.name: nft_trades
datasets.description:
A network of the sales of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) on the Ethereum and WAX blockchains, from June 2017 to April 2021, from the dataset of M. Nadini, L. Alessandretti, F. Di Giacinto, M. Martino, L. M. Aiello and A. Baronchelli, collected through the APIs of the main NFT markets (OpenSea, Atomic, and the subgraphs of Cryptokitties, Decentraland and Gods Unchained). NFTs are tokens that certify the ownership of a digital object (e.g. a piece of digital art, a collectible card or an item of a game). There are two networks:

- `trades`: each node is a trader (an address on the blockchain), and a directed edge from trader $i$ to trader $j$ is the sale of an NFT by $i$ to $j$; pairs of traders can have many sales (a multigraph).
- `trader_nft`: a bipartite network of traders and NFTs (the property `is_trader` tells them apart); each sale gives two directed edges, from the seller to the NFT and from the NFT to the buyer, following the token.

The URLs of the NFTs' images, their descriptions and permanent links are not included.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `address` (`trades`): the address of the trader on the blockchain.
- (Node) `name` (`trader_nft`): the address of the trader, or the identifier of the NFT (its collection and token identifier, as given in the data).
- (Node) `is_trader` (`trader_nft`): whether the node is a trader (otherwise an NFT).
- (Node) `username`: the user name of the trader on the market, if given (the first one that appears in the data; empty for NFTs).
- (Node) `nft_name`, `collection`, `category` (`trader_nft`): the name, collection and category of the NFT (empty for traders).
- (Edge) `time`: the time of the sale (as given in the data, taken as UTC), in Unix time.
- (Edge) `price_crypto`, `crypto`: the price in cryptocurrency and the cryptocurrency (e.g. `ETH`, `WAX`, `MANA`).
- (Edge) `price_usd`: the price in US dollars (NaN if not given).
- (Edge) `nft_id` (`trades`): the identifier of the NFT (its collection and token identifier, as given in the data).
- (Edge) `nft_name` (`trades`): the name of the NFT, if given.
- (Edge) `collection` (`trades`): the collection of the NFT (cleaned by the authors).
- (Edge) `category` (`trades`): the category of the collection: `Art`, `Collectible`, `Games`, `Metaverse`, `Other` or `Utility`.
- (Edge) `market`: the market of the sale.
- (Edge) `transaction`: the hash of the transaction.
citations: M. Nadini, L. Alessandretti, F. Di Giacinto, M. Martino, L. M. Aiello and A. Baronchelli, "Mapping the NFT revolution: market trends, trade networks, and visual features." Scientific Reports 11, 20902 (2021)

datasets.name: nlwiki_link_intervals
datasets.description:
The evolution of the hyperlinks between the articles of the Dutch Wikipedia, as a temporal network with time intervals, assembled by W. Ligtenberg and Y. Pei as a benchmark for temporal graph analysis. Nodes represent Wikipedia articles, and a directed edge from article $i$ to article $j$ means that article $i$ contained a hyperlink to article $j$ during the time interval given by the edge's start and end times. The data were derived from the dynamic Dutch Wikipedia hyperlink network of Preusse et al. (KONECT's `link-dynamic-nlwiki`), whose events record the addition or removal of a hyperlink at a given time: each addition of a link was paired with its subsequent removal to form an interval, and links that were added but never removed (i.e. still present at the end of the data collection) were discarded. Hence the network includes only links that existed temporarily. A link that was added and removed several times gives rise to parallel edges, one per interval. The first link was created on August 28, 2001, and the last removal took place on July 10, 2011. Articles are identified only by the numeric identifiers of the source data; their titles are not included.

The network has the following properties:

- (Edge) `start` and `end`: the times at which the hyperlink was added and removed (Unix time, seconds).
citations: W. Ligtenberg, Y. Pei, "Introduction to a Temporal Graph Benchmark." arXiv:1703.02852 (2017)

J. Preusse, J. Kunegis, M. Thimm, S. Staab, T. Gottron, "Structural Dynamics of Knowledge Networks." Proceedings of the International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media (ICWSM) 7(1), 506-515 (2013)

datasets.name: nokia_investors
datasets.description:
Temporal correlation networks among the investors that traded the Nokia stock on the Helsinki stock exchange between January 1998 and December 2002, from Ranganathan et al. The data come from the central register of shareholdings of the Finnish central securities depository (Euroclear Finland), which records the daily trades of all Finnish households and institutions (foreign investors are excluded). For each investor, the daily net volume (the number of shares bought minus the number of shares sold, averaged over a week) was computed, and the Pearson correlation of the net volumes of each pair of investors was measured over six-month windows of 126 trading days, shifted by one month (21 trading days), giving 54 windows. In each window, only the investors that traded on at least 20 days are included, and all pairs of them are connected, i.e. the network of each window is a complete graph. The analysis was done separately for three categories of investors, which correspond to the three networks below; there are no edges between investors of different categories. The edges of all windows are combined into a single multigraph, with the window given as an edge property. Investor identifiers are anonymized.

- `households`: Finnish household investors (54 windows).
- `non_financial`: non-financial institutions (54 windows).
- `financial`: financial institutions (only 27 of the 54 windows are included in the distributed data).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `investor_id`: the anonymized identifier of the investor.
- (Edge) `weight`: the Pearson correlation coefficient between the daily net volumes of the two investors in the window.
- (Edge) `time`: the date that labels the window in the source data (as a Unix timestamp), which appears to be the first trading day of the window, since it ranges from January 1998 to June 2002.
citations: S. Ranganathan, M. Kivelä, J. Kanniainen, "Dynamics of investor spanning trees around dot-com bubble." PLOS ONE 13(6), e0198807 (2018)
S. Ranganathan, M. Kivelä, J. Kanniainen, "Data from: Dynamics of investor spanning trees around dot-com bubble." Dryad, dataset (2018)

datasets.name: noordin_top
datasets.description:
Networks of ten types of relationships among the 79 individuals of the terrorist network of Noordin Mohammad Top in Indonesia, listed in Appendix C of the International Crisis Group report "Terrorism in Indonesia: Noordin's Networks" (2006), from which the data were mostly drawn. The data were coded by students of the Naval Postgraduate School course "Tracking and Disrupting Dark Networks" (Sean Everton and Nancy Roberts) and cleaned by the CORE Lab, and are analysed in detail in Everton's book "Disrupting Dark Networks" (2012). Nodes are individuals (vertex property `name`), and the networks are: `classmates` (attended school together), `friendship`, `kinship`, `soulmates` (close friends with a strong bond), `logistics` (co-location of logistical activity), `meetings` (co-attendance at meetings), `operations` (co-participation in operations), `training_events` (co-attendance at training events), `communications`, and `business_finance` (business and financial ties). In each network, an undirected edge connects two individuals who share the corresponding relation. Data distributed by the UCINET datasets collection (University of Manchester).[^ucinet]

[^ucinet]: Description obtained in part from the [UCINET datasets page](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/datasets/covert-networks/noordin-top).
citations: N. Roberts and S. F. Everton, "Roberts and Everton Terrorist Data: Noordin Top Terrorist Network (Subset)." Association of Religion Data Archives (2011)
S. F. Everton, "Disrupting Dark Networks." Cambridge University Press (2012)

datasets.name: notre_dame_web
datasets.description: Web graph of the University of Notre Dame (domain nd.edu), collected in 1999 by R. Albert, H. Jeong and A.-L. Barabási with a web robot, which they used to measure the degree distributions and the diameter of the World Wide Web. Nodes are web pages and a directed edge $(i,j)$ indicates that page $i$ contains a hyperlink to page $j$. The data were obtained from the Stanford Network Analysis Project (SNAP).
citations: R. Albert, H. Jeong, and A.-L. Barabasi. "Diameter of the World-Wide Web." Nature 401, 130 (1999).

datasets.name: november17
datasets.description:
Network of members of the Greek terrorist group Revolutionary Organization 17 November (N17), believed to be defunct, reconstructed by C. J. Rhodes and P. Jones from open-source reporting (Irwin et al., 2002; Abram and Smith, 2004). Nodes are 22 members, and an edge indicates that open-source reporting has demonstrated some connection between the two individuals at some point in the past. The data were distributed with UCINET; edges are undirected.

The network has the following properties (empty values denote missing data):

- (Node) `name`: the name of the member (full name or nickname).
- (Node) `Role`: 1 = leader (gives orders), 2 = operational (receives orders).
- (Node) `Faction`: 1 = first-generation leadership faction, 2 = Koufontinas faction, 3 = Sardanopoulos faction.
- (Node) `Resources`: the number of resources (money, weapons, safe houses) controlled by the member, from 0 to 3.
citations: C. J. Rhodes and P. Jones, "Inferring missing links in partially observed social networks." Journal of the Operational Research Society 60(10), 1373-1383 (2009)

datasets.name: npm_dependencies
datasets.description:
The dependency network of the software packages in npm (https://npmjs.com), the public package registry of the JavaScript runtime Node.js, as collected by T. Slijepčević in early 2016. Each node is a software package, and a directed edge (i, j) indicates that package i depends on package j (i.e. it lists j as a dependency, which is installed together with i). Only packages with at least one dependency relation are included, out of the 226,473 packages listed in the data. The network contains 47 self-loops.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the package in the npm registry.
citations: T. Slijepčević, "Package equivalence in complex software network." arXiv:1602.03681 (2016)
T. Slijepčević, "The NPM software dependency network (npmjs.com)." figshare, dataset (2016)

datasets.name: obo_ontologies
datasets.description:
Networks of four ontologies of the Open Biological and Biomedical Ontologies (OBO) Foundry, each a vocabulary of terms with the relations between them, from the last release of each year: the Gene Ontology (`go_<year>`, 2004-2026), the Human Phenotype Ontology (`hpo_<year>`, 2017-2026), the Mondo Disease Ontology (`mondo_<year>`, 2018-2026) and the Uberon anatomy ontology (`uberon_<year>`, 2011-2026). In all of them, nodes are terms and a directed edge goes from a term to a more general or related term, according to the relations of the ontology (edge `relation`, except in the networks of the Human Phenotype Ontology, which only have `is_a` relations). The networks are read from the OBO flat files of the ontologies.

**Gene Ontology (`go_<year>`).** The Gene Ontology (GO) is the ontology of the functions of genes and gene products developed by the Gene Ontology Consortium, which is used to annotate genes in most biological databases. The terms belong to three namespaces (sub-ontologies): molecular functions (e.g. "protein kinase activity"), biological processes (e.g. "mitotic cell cycle") and cellular components (e.g. "mitochondrial membrane").

Nodes are terms, and a directed edge goes from a term to a more general or related term, according to the relations of the ontology: `is_a` (subclass, e.g. "protein kinase activity" is a "kinase activity"), `part_of`, `has_part`, `regulates`, `positively_regulates`, `negatively_regulates`, `occurs_in`, `happens_during`, `ends_during` and (in 2012-2013) `results_in`. A pair of terms can be connected by several relations. The networks are directed acyclic graphs with respect to `is_a` and `part_of`, while relations such as `has_part` go in the opposite direction. Obsolete terms, which have no relations and are only kept by GO so that old identifiers can be resolved, are left out. The logical definitions of terms (`intersection_of` and `union_of` axioms), the alternative identifiers, comments and other annotations are also left out.

There is one network `go_<year>` for each year from 2004 to 2026, from the last release of the year in the archive of the Gene Ontology Consortium (monthly releases since 2004): 2004-12-01, 2005-12-01, 2006-12-01, 2007-12-01, 2008-12-01, 2009-12-01, 2010-12-01, 2011-12-01, 2012-12-01, 2013-12-01, 2014-12-01, 2015-12-01, 2016-12-01, 2017-12-01, 2018-12-01, 2019-12-09, 2020-12-08, 2021-12-15, 2022-12-04, 2023-11-15, 2024-11-03, 2025-10-10 and 2026-08-05 (the latest one). The networks are of the full edition of the ontology (`gene_ontology.obo` until 2008, `go.obo` from 2009). The releases until 2007 contain only the relations `is_a` and `part_of`; the regulation relations appear in 2008, and `has_part` in 2009. The release of 2004 uses the namespace names `function`, `process` and `component` (later `molecular_function`, `biological_process` and `cellular_component`).

**Human Phenotype Ontology (`hpo_<year>`).** The Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) is the standardized vocabulary of the phenotypic abnormalities encountered in human disease (e.g. "Atrial septal defect", "Intellectual disability"), developed by the Monarch Initiative and used to annotate diseases and patients in clinical genetics. Besides the phenotypic abnormalities, the ontology has terms for the mode of inheritance, the clinical course (e.g. onset, progression), clinical modifiers and frequencies.

Nodes are terms, and a directed edge goes from a term to a more general term (relation `is_a`, subclass), so that the networks are directed acyclic graphs with the root `HP:0000001` ("All"). A term can have several parents. Obsolete terms, which have no relations and are only kept so that old identifiers can be resolved, are left out. The logical definitions of terms (`intersection_of` axioms, which refer to terms of other ontologies), the alternative identifiers, comments and other annotations are also left out.

There is one network `hpo_<year>` for each year from 2017 to 2026, from the last release of the year on GitHub: 2017-12-12, 2018-12-21, 2019-11-08, 2020-12-07, 2021-10-10, 2022-12-15, 2023-10-09, 2024-12-12, 2025-11-24 and 2026-09-01 (the latest one), from the file `hp.obo` of each release.

**Mondo Disease Ontology (`mondo_<year>`).** The Mondo Disease Ontology, developed by the Monarch Initiative, harmonizes the disease definitions of many disease vocabularies (OMIM, Orphanet, the Disease Ontology, NCIt, MedGen, ICD, GARD, etc.) into a single ontology of human and animal diseases, with precise mappings between them.

Nodes are terms, and a directed edge goes from a disease to a more general disease (relation `is_a`, subclass), and from a disease to other entities it is related to by the relations of the ontology, e.g. its anatomical location (`disease_has_location`, to terms of the Uberon anatomy ontology), its features (`disease_has_feature`, to phenotypes of the Human Phenotype Ontology), the gene whose mutations cause it (`has_material_basis_in_germline_mutation_in`, to HGNC genes), its infectious agent or taxon (`disease_has_infectious_agent`, `in_taxon`, to NCBI taxa), the biological processes it disrupts (to Gene Ontology terms), etc. The relation `excluded_subClassOf` marks a curated exclusion: the disease is explicitly not a subclass of the target, contrary to some source vocabulary. A pair of terms can be connected by several relations. The terms of other ontologies (and the genes) that are targets of the relations are nodes as well, marked by the property `is_external`; their names are given when the file of Mondo includes them. Since 2024, the file includes the terms of other ontologies that Mondo refers to, with their relations among themselves (e.g. `part_of` and `develops_from` among anatomical terms), which are kept, so that the networks of 2024-2026 have about twice as many nodes as the earlier ones. Relations whose targets are web pages are left out (e.g. `curated_content_resource`, `should_conform_to`, `seeAlso` and `excluded_from_qc_check`, which point to web resources, design patterns and issue trackers). Obsolete terms, which have no relations and are only kept so that old identifiers can be resolved, are left out, except those that are targets of relations (mostly of `excluded_subClassOf`), which are marked by the property `is_obsolete`. The logical definitions of terms (`intersection_of`, `union_of` and `disjoint_from` axioms), the alternative identifiers, comments and other annotations are also left out.

There is one network `mondo_<year>` for each year from 2018 to 2026, from the last release of the year on GitHub: 2018-12-02, 2019-11-25, 2020-12-18, 2021-12-30, 2022-12-01, 2023-12-12, 2024-12-03, 2025-12-02 and 2026-10-06 (the latest one), from the file `mondo.obo` of each release (the earlier releases have no files attached).

**Uberon anatomy ontology (`uberon_<year>`).** Uberon is the integrated cross-species ontology of the anatomy of animals (mostly vertebrates), which describes anatomical structures, tissues, organs, body parts, embryonic structures and life stages independently of the species (e.g. "heart", "forelimb", "neural tube"), and links them to the anatomy ontologies of single species.

Nodes are terms, and a directed edge goes from a term to a related term, according to the relations of the ontology: `is_a` (subclass, e.g. "cardiac muscle tissue" is a "muscle tissue"), `part_of`, `develops_from`, `transformation_of`, `immediate_transformation_of`, `mutually_spatially_disjoint_with`, `has_part`, etc., as well as relations to the taxa in which a structure is present or absent (`present_in_taxon`, `never_in_taxon`, `dubious_for_taxon`, `ambiguous_for_taxon`, to taxa of the NCBI taxonomy) and to terms of other ontologies (e.g. `fma_set_term`, to the Foundational Model of Anatomy). A pair of terms can be connected by several relations. The terms of other ontologies that are targets of relations are nodes as well, marked by the property `is_external`. Relations whose targets are web pages are left out (e.g. `dc-contributor`, the ORCID of the contributor of a term, `seeAlso`, `source_atlas` and `implements_design_pattern`), as are the images of the structures (`depicted_by`, in 2019). Obsolete terms, which have no relations and are only kept so that old identifiers can be resolved, are left out, except those that are targets of relations, which are marked by the property `is_obsolete`. The logical definitions of terms (`intersection_of` and `union_of` axioms), the alternative identifiers, comments and other annotations are also left out.

There is one network `uberon_<year>` for each year from 2011 to 2026, from the last release of the year: 2011-12-14, 2012-10-09, 2013-12-18, 2014-12-09, 2015-11-19, 2016-11-23, 2017-10-28, 2018-10-14 and 2019-11-22, 2020-09-16 (from the archive of releases of the OBO Foundry on Sourceforge), 2021-11-28 (from the GitHub repository at the release tag), 2022-12-13, 2023-12-08, 2024-11-25, 2025-12-04 and 2026-10-01 (the latest one; files of the GitHub releases). The networks are of the "basic" edition of the ontology, which has only the terms of Uberon and the relations between them that are useful for most applications, without the imported terms of other ontologies (`basic.obo`, named `uberon-basic.obo` since 2024; the release of 2016 includes the terms of the Cell Ontology, which are marked as external).

The networks have the following properties (those of each ontology):

- (Node) `term_id`: the identifier of the term, in the networks of the Gene Ontology (e.g. `GO:0004672`), the Human Phenotype Ontology (e.g. `HP:0001631`), Mondo (e.g. `MONDO:0005015`, or of an external term, e.g. `UBERON:0002107`, `NCBITaxon:9606`, `http://identifiers.org/hgnc/1100`) and Uberon (e.g. `UBERON:0000948`, or of an external term, e.g. `NCBITaxon:7742`).
- (Node) `name`: the name of the term.
- (Node) `namespace` (`go_*`, `uberon_*`): the namespace of the term: in the Gene Ontology, the sub-ontology; in Uberon, when given (e.g. `uberon/phenoscape-anatomy`, in the releases of 2013-2020; `cell` for the terms of the Cell Ontology in 2016).
- (Node) `definition`: the textual definition of the term.
- (Node) `synonyms`: the synonyms of the term.
- (Node) `xrefs`: the cross-references of the term to other databases and vocabularies (e.g. EC numbers, Reactome and Wikipedia for GO; UMLS, SNOMED CT and MeSH for HPO; `OMIM:...`, `Orphanet:...`, `DOID:...` for Mondo; `FMA:...`, `MA:...`, `ZFA:...` for Uberon).
- (Node) `subsets`: the subsets that the term belongs to (e.g. GO slims; `rare` in Mondo).
- (Node) `is_external` (`mondo_*`, `uberon_*`): whether the node is a term of another ontology (or, in Mondo, a gene).
- (Node) `is_obsolete` (`mondo_*`, some `uberon_*`): whether the term is obsolete.
- (Edge) `relation` (`go_*`, `mondo_*`, `uberon_*`): the relation between the terms (`is_a`, `part_of`, etc.).
