Undirected edges are of four types: a network's connection to an IXP (one edge per port, with its speed and IP addresses, so that pairs can have several edges), a network's presence in a facility, an IXP's presence in a facility, and the ownership of a network, IXP or facility by an organization. Only the records that are active (status `ok`, or approved in the older format) are included; edges with an end that is not an active record are left out. The contact data (points of contact, e-mail addresses and phone numbers), the notes, the IP prefixes of the IXPs and the other fields of the records are not included.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `kind`: `network`, `ix`, `facility` or `organization`.
- (Node) `name`: the name of the record.
- (Node) `peeringdb_id`: the identifier of the record in PeeringDB (of its kind; the identifiers of the older format differ from those of the newer one).
- (Node) `asn` (networks): the AS number (-1 for other nodes, or if not given).
- (Node) `aka` (networks): other names of the network.
- (Node) `info_type` (networks): the type of network (e.g. `NSP`, `Content`, `Cable/DSL/ISP`, `Enterprise`, `Educational/Research`, `Non-Profit`, `Route Server`).
- (Node) `info_scope` (networks): the geographic scope (e.g. `Global`, `Regional`, `Europe`).
- (Node) `info_traffic`, `info_ratio` (networks): the traffic level and the traffic ratio (inbound/outbound) declared by the network.
- (Node) `policy_general` (networks): the general peering policy (`Open`, `Selective`, `Restrictive`, `No`).
- (Node) `irr_as_set` (networks): the AS-SET of the network in the Internet Routing Registry.
- (Node) `info_prefixes4`, `info_prefixes6` (networks): the numbers of IPv4 and IPv6 prefixes the network announces (the older format has one number, given as `info_prefixes4`; -1 if not given).
- (Node) `city`, `country`: the city and country (ISO code) of IXPs, facilities and organizations.
- (Node) `region_continent` (IXPs): the continent of the IXP.
- (Node) `latitude`, `longitude` (facilities): the coordinates of the facility (only in the snapshots from 2018 on; NaN if not given).
- (Node) `created`: the date of creation of the record (YYYY-MM-DD, empty if not given).
- (Edge) `type`: `network-ix`, `network-facility`, `ix-facility` or `organization`.
- (Edge) `speed` (`network-ix`): the speed of the port, in Mbit/s (-1 for other edges).
- (Edge) `ipaddr4`, `ipaddr6` (`network-ix`): the IPv4 and IPv6 addresses of the port in the peering LAN of the IXP (in the older format, each address has an edge of its own).
- (Edge) `is_rs_peer` (`network-ix`): whether the network peers with the route servers of the IXP (only in the newer format).
- (Graph) `snapshot`: the date of the snapshot (YYYY-MM-DD).
citations: A. Lodhi, N. Larson, A. Dhamdhere, C. Dovrolis and k. claffy, "Using peeringDB to understand the peering ecosystem." ACM SIGCOMM Computer Communication Review 44(2), 20-27 (2014)

datasets.name: penguins_kyoto
datasets.description:
Multilayer network of the relationships among the 59 named penguins at the Kyoto Aquarium, Japan, encoded by Heather Z. Brooks and Michelle Feng from the 2020 version of the penguin relationship chart ("sokanzu") published by the aquarium staff. Nodes are penguins (staff members and unnamed former partners are not included), and directed edges are relationships of six types, given by the edge property `layer`: "Couples", "Exes", "Complicated" ("it's complicated"), "Friends", "Enemies", and "Family". Couples and friends are always reciprocated, while the other relationships can be one-sided (e.g. a penguin rejected by another). In the family layer, edges point from parents to their offspring. The edge directions follow the "source" and "sink" convention of the edge metadata files of the source data (in the source adjacency matrices, rows correspond to the sink and columns to the source of each relationship, which is the transpose of the convention of the authors' GEXF files).

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the penguin (romanized).
- (Node) `sex`: "F" or "M".
- (Node) `info`: a short description of the penguin from the chart (translated by M. Feng, "to be taken with a large grain of salt").
- (Edge) `layer`: the type of relationship.
- (Edge) `info`: a description of the relationship, if given in the chart (translated). One description of the source data (for the pair Oike → Shichijou in the "Exes" layer) refers to a relationship that is absent from the adjacency matrix, and is not included.
citations: H. Z. Brooks, M. Feng, "Penguins of Kyoto Multilayer Network." Bitbucket repository (2020)

datasets.name: petster
datasets.description: A network of family links and friendships among the pet profiles of the social websites catster.com and dogster.com, as distributed by KONECT. Each profile is a cat or a dog, created by its owner. Nodes are 623,766 profiles (175,011 cats, 448,744 dogs and 11 profiles of unknown species), and an undirected edge connects two profiles that are linked as family (between cats and cats, cats and dogs, or dogs and dogs) or as friends (between cats and cats, or dogs and dogs). The vertex property `meta` gives, for each profile, its original ID, the pet's name, home location, weight, sex, breed and species.
citations: J. Kunegis.  "KONECT, the Koblenz Network Collection" (2016)

datasets.name: pgp_2004
datasets.description: The giant component of the network of users of the Pretty Good Privacy (PGP) algorithm for secure information interchange, compiled by Boguñá et al. In the PGP "web of trust", users certify the authenticity of the public keys of other users by signing them. Each node is a user (key), and an undirected edge connects two users if one of them signed the key of the other. The edge list distributed by the authors lists 24 pairs of nodes twice; these duplicates are removed here, giving 24,316 edges, which is the number of edges reported in the literature for this network. This network predates the one in the `pgp_strong` entry (2009), which is the strongly connected component of a later snapshot of the web of trust.
citations: M. Boguñá, R. Pastor-Satorras, A. Díaz-Guilera, A. Arenas, "Models of social networks based on social distance attachment." Physical Review E 70, 056122 (2004)

datasets.name: pgp_strong
datasets.description:
Strongly connected component of the Pretty Good Privacy (PGP) web of trust, circa November 2009, assembled by O. Richters and T. P. Peixoto from a dump of the public OpenPGP key servers (key-server.de). Nodes are public keys (which usually correspond to users), and a directed edge $(i,j)$ indicates that the owner of key $i$ signed key $j$, i.e. certified that key $j$ belongs to the person named in it, which is an expression of trust. Only the largest strongly connected component is included.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `id`: the key ID (64-bit, in hexadecimal).
- (Node) `uid`: the primary user ID of the key (usually a name and an email address).
- (Node) `subkeys`: the IDs of the subkeys of the key.
- (Node) `date`: the creation time of the key (Unix time).
- (Node) `expire_date`, `rev_date`: the expiration and revocation times of the key (Unix time), or $2^{63}-1$ if the key does not expire or was not revoked.
- (Node) `valid`: whether the key is valid.
- (Node) `s`: an undocumented integer label of the node.
- (Node) `vb`: the betweenness centrality of the node.
- (Edge) `eb`: the betweenness centrality of the edge.
- (Edge) `e_id`: the IDs of the keys that issued the signatures of the edge (the signing key or one of its subkeys), separated by commas; an edge can correspond to several signatures.
- (Edge) `e_time`: the creation times of the signatures of the edge (Unix time).
citations: O. Richters and T. P. Peixoto, "Trust Transitivity in Social Networks." PLoS ONE 6(4): e18384 (2011).

datasets.name: physician_trust
datasets.description:
Advice, discussion and friendship ties among 246 physicians in four towns in Illinois (Peoria, Bloomington, Quincy and Galesburg), from the study of the diffusion of a medical innovation (the adoption of the new drug tetracycline) by J. Coleman, E. Katz and H. Menzel. The data set was prepared by R. S. Burt from the data collected by Coleman, Katz and Menzel, reported in their 1966 book. Three sociometric relations were obtained from the replies to the questions: "When you need information or advice about questions of therapy where do you usually turn?" (advice); "And who are the three or four physicians with whom you most often find yourself discussing cases or therapy in the course of an ordinary week -- last week for instance?" (discussion); and "Would you tell me the first names of your three friends whom you see most often socially?" (friendship). In addition, records of prescriptions were reviewed and many other questions were asked, of which 13 items are included as node attributes. The data were distributed by L. C. Freeman on his network data page at the University of California, Irvine (no longer online), from which this version was obtained via the Internet Archive.

A directed edge (i, j) indicates that physician i named physician j in reply to at least one of the three questions. There are no ties between physicians of different towns. Five physicians neither named nor were named by anyone, and are isolated nodes. A different preparation of the Galesburg part of the same study (31 physicians, with friendship and discussion ties, from Knoke and Burt 1983) is in the entry `galesburg_physicians`; here, Galesburg has 35 physicians, with 86 friendship ties (78 there).

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) In all coded attributes except `adoption_date`, 9 means no answer.
- (Node) `city`: the town of practice.
- (Node) `adoption_date`: the month in which the physician first prescribed tetracycline, according to the prescription records (1 to 14: the months from November 1953 to December 1954, in order, so that 9 is July 1954; 15: December 1954/January 1955, 16: January/February 1955, 17: February 1955, 18: no prescriptions found, 98: no prescription data obtained; the value 99, which occurs for 30 physicians, is not documented).
- (Node) `career_start`: the year in which the physician started in the profession (1: 1919 or before, 2: 1920–1929, 3: 1930–1934, 4: 1935–1939, 5: 1940–1944, 6: 1945 or later).
- (Node) `meetings`: attendance at national, regional or state conventions of professional societies during the last 12 months (0: none, 1: only general meetings, 2: specialty meetings).
- (Node) `journals`: the number of medical journals received regularly (1: two, 2: three, ..., 8: nine or more).
- (Node) `free_time`: with whom the physician spends more free time (1: non-doctors, 2: about evenly split, 3: doctors).
- (Node) `discuss`: whether the physician likes to talk about medical matters when with other doctors socially (1: no, 2: yes, 3: does not care).
- (Node) `clubs`: membership in a club or hobby composed mostly of doctors (0: no, 1: yes).
- (Node) `friends`: how many of the three friends seen most often socially are doctors (1: none, 2: one, 3: two, 4: three).
- (Node) `community`: how long the physician has been practicing in the community (1: a year or less, 2: one to two years, 3: two to five years, 4: five to ten years, 5: ten to twenty years, 6: more than twenty years; the value 8, which occurs for one physician, is not documented).
- (Node) `patients`: the number of office visits in an average week (1: 25 or less, 2: 26–50, 3: 51–75, 4: 76–100, 5: 101–150, 6: 151 or more).
- (Node) `proximity`: whether there are other physicians in the same building (1: none in the building, 2: some in the building, but none sharing the office or waiting room, 3: some sharing the office or waiting room, 4: some perhaps sharing the office or waiting room).
- (Node) `specialty`: the medical specialty (1: general practitioner, 2: internist, 3: pediatrician, 4: other specialty).
- (Edge) `advice`, `discussion` and `friendship`: whether i named j in reply to the corresponding question.
citations: J. Coleman, E. Katz, & H. Menzel, "The diffusion of an innovation among physicians." Sociometry, 20(4), 253-270. (1957)
J. S. Coleman, E. Katz, H. Menzel, "Medical Innovation: A Diffusion Study." Bobbs-Merrill, New York (1966)
R. S. Burt, "Social contagion and innovation: Cohesion versus structural equivalence." American Journal of Sociology 92(6), 1287-1335 (1987)

datasets.name: physics_collab
datasets.description:
Two multilayer coauthorship networks of scientists, assembled by M. De Domenico, A. Lancichinetti, A. Arenas and M. Rosvall. Nodes are scientists (anonymized) and edges are coauthorships, with layers corresponding to research topics:

- `pierreAuger`: coauthorships of internal technical reports of the Pierre Auger Collaboration, which operates an observatory of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays, submitted between 2010 and 2012. Each report was assigned to one or more of 16 layers corresponding to working tasks (neutrinos, detector, enhancements, anisotropy, point source, mass composition, horizontal showers, hybrid reconstruction, spectrum, photons, atmospheric, SD reconstruction, hadronic interactions, exotics, magnetic fields, astrophysical scenarios), according to its keywords and content, with manual disambiguation.
- `arXiv`: coauthorships of preprints posted on arXiv up to May 2014 with "networks" in the title or abstract, with 13 layers corresponding to the arXiv categories of the preprints (physics.soc-ph, physics.data-an, physics.bio-ph, math-ph, math.OC, cond-mat.dis-nn, cond-mat.stat-mech, q-bio.MN, q-bio, q-bio.BM, nlin.AO, cs.SI, cs.CV).

The edges are weighted as follows: for each report or preprint with $N > 1$ authors, classified into $L$ layers, a weight $1/[L(N-1)]$ is added to the edge between each pair of its coauthors in each of these layers. Hence, the sum of the weights of the edges of an author over all layers is the number of (multi-author) papers they wrote. Each pair of authors has at most one edge per layer.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: empty, since the identities of the authors are not provided.
- (Edge) `layer`: the layer of the edge, numbered as listed above (see the graph property `layer_key`).
- (Edge) `weight`: the edge weight, as defined above.
citations: M. De Domenico et al., "Identifying modular flows on multilayer networks reveals highly overlapping organization in interconnected systems." Physical Review X 5(1), 011027 (2015).

datasets.name: piano_codewords
datasets.description:
A network of transitions between "codewords" (sets of simultaneously played notes) in Western classical piano music of the common practice period, from Park, Nam and Park. The data consist of MIDI files of 900 piano works by 19 composers from the Baroque, Classical and Romantic periods (from J. S. Bach and G. F. Handel to M. Ravel), collected from the Kunst der Fuge and Classical Piano MIDI archives. The files were converted to MusicXML with MuseScore and "chordified" with the Music21 toolkit, which converts a score into a sequence of sets of simultaneously played notes (codewords), retaining octave and key information (tempo, rhythm, etc. are discarded). Each node is a codeword, and a directed edge goes from a codeword to the codeword that follows it in some work, weighted by the number of times this transition occurs in all works. Self-loops correspond to repeated codewords. This is the aggregated ("total") network of the source data; the separate networks of each work are not included.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the node label in the source data, of the form "pitches-year".
- (Node) `pitches`: the list of notes of the codeword, as MIDI note numbers (60 is the middle C).
- (Node) `year`: the year attached to the codeword in its label, which appears to be the year of the earliest work in which the codeword occurs (it ranges from 1703 to 1916).
- (Edge) `weight`: the number of occurrences of the transition.
citations: D. Park, J. Nam, J. Park, "Novelty and influence of creative works, and quantifying patterns of advances based on probabilistic references networks." EPJ Data Science 9, 2 (2020)

datasets.name: pira_gill
datasets.description:
Networks of relationships among active members of the Provisional Irish Republican Army (PIRA) between 1970 and 1998, divided into time periods, from data collected at the International Center for the Study of Terrorism, Pennsylvania State University, and analyzed by Gill et al. (2014). An edge connects two members if they had at least one of four types of relationship: involvement in a PIRA activity together, friendship before joining the PIRA, blood relation, or relation through marriage. The networks `period1`, `period2`, `period3`, `period4_5` and `period6` correspond to the time periods of the source (periods 4 and 5 are combined), and contain the members active in each period, identified by an anonymous code in `name`.

The vertex properties give characteristics of the members, coded as 0/1 unless stated otherwise: `gender`, `university` (attended university), `marital_status`, `age_at_recruitment` (in years), brigade membership (`antrim_brigade`, `derry_brigade`, `armagh_brigade`, `down_brigade`, `tyrone_brigade`, and `fermanagh_brigade` from period 2 on), and their activities in the period: `vio` (violent), `nonvio` (non-violent), `vforop` (violent foreign operation), `senior` (senior leader), `gun` (gunman), `ied_c` (IED constructor), `ied_p` (IED planter), `forop` (foreign operation) and `rob` (robbery). The value 99999 denotes missing data. Data distributed by the UCINET datasets collection (University of Manchester).[^ucinet]

[^ucinet]: Description obtained in part from the [UCINET datasets page](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/datasets/covert-networks/provisional-irish-republican-army).
citations: P. Gill, J. Lee, K. R. Rethemeyer, J. Horgan, and V. Asal, "Lethal connections: The determinants of network connections in the Provisional Irish Republican Army, 1970-1998." International Interactions 40(1), 52-78 (2014)

datasets.name: plant_fungus_japan
datasets.description:
Bipartite networks of associations between plants and root-associated fungi in eight forests across the Japanese Archipelago (four cool-temperate, one warm-temperate and three subtropical forests, from 45.0 to 24.4 °N), from Toju et al. In each forest, 2 cm segments of terminal roots were sampled at 1 m intervals (240 samples per forest), irrespective of their morphology or mycorrhizal type. The plant of each sample was identified by DNA barcoding (rbcL and ITS1 regions; not all could be identified to species level), and its fungi by Illumina sequencing of the fungal ITS1 region, with reads clustered into operational taxonomic units (OTUs) at 97% sequence similarity (94% for Glomeromycota), with taxonomic assignment based on the NCBI nt database and functional groups inferred with FUNGuild. Associations that represented less than 0.1% of the reads of a sample were removed. The data include arbuscular mycorrhizal, ectomycorrhizal, endophytic, saprotrophic and pathogenic fungi, among others. In each network, an edge connects a plant to a fungal OTU found in its root samples, weighted by the number of root samples in which the association was observed.

- `metacommunity`: the metacommunity-scale network of all eight forests, in which each plant node is a local population of a plant species/taxon in one forest (227 populations of 150 plant species/taxa) and each fungal node an OTU (8080 OTUs). The paper also analyzes the networks of the four northern (cool-temperate) and four southern forests, which are subnetworks of this one.
- `site1` to `site8`: the local networks of each forest, with plant species/taxa and fungal OTUs as nodes. Sites 1 to 4 are cool-temperate forests (codes TES, TOMA, YKS and SGD), site 5 a warm-temperate forest (YSD), and sites 6 to 8 subtropical forests (YAKU, YONA and IRI).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the plant species/taxon (e.g. "Acer", "Poaceae_1"; in `metacommunity` with the code of the forest appended, e.g. "Acer_TES") or the OTU identifier (e.g. "F_0001").
- (Node) `is_fungus`: whether the node is a fungal OTU (otherwise a plant).
- (Node) `site` (plants, in `metacommunity`): the code of the forest.
- (Node) `otu_code` (fungi): the sequence identifier of the OTU.
- (Node) `phylum`, `class`, `order`, `family`, `genus`, `species` (fungi): the taxonomic assignment (empty if not resolved at that level).
- (Node) `guild`, `trophic_mode` (fungi): the functional guild and trophic mode inferred with FUNGuild (empty if not assigned).
- (Node) `category` (fungi): the functional category used in the paper (e.g. "Arbuscular_Mycorrhizal", "Ectomycorrhizal", "Saprotroph", "Plant_Pathogen", "Others_Unknown").
- (Edge) `weight`: the number of root samples in which the association was observed.
citations: H. Toju, H. Tanabe, H. S. Ishii, "Network hubs in root-associated fungal metacommunities." Microbiome 6, 116 (2018)

datasets.name: plant_hypocotyl
datasets.description:
Networks of the physical contacts between the cells of whole plant hypocotyls (the embryonic stem of seedlings), from Jackson et al. Hypocotyls were imaged with confocal microscopy and segmented into cells in 3D with the MorphoGraphX software, and each cell was annotated with its cell type. Nodes are cells, and an undirected edge connects two cells that are physically adjacent, i.e. share a cell wall, weighted by the area of the shared wall. To account for imaging artifacts, edges between cells sharing less than 2 µm² of wall were removed, except between cells of the vasculature.

There are three biological replicates (`_1`, `_2`, `_3`) for each of eight samples: the *Arabidopsis thaliana* wild-type ecotypes Columbia (`ara_col`), Landsberg *erecta* (`ara_ler`) and Cape Verde Islands (`ara_cvi`); the *Arabidopsis* mutants *monopteros* (`ara_monopteros`), *cdka1;1* (`ara_cdka1`) and *laterne* (`ara_laterne`); and the species poppy (*Papaver rhoeas*, `poppy`) and foxglove (*Digitalis purpurea*, `foxglove`).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `label`: the identifier of the cell in the segmented image.
- (Node) `cell_type`: the cell type: "trichoblast", "atrichoblast" (the two epidermal cell types), "outer cortex", "inner cortex 2nd layer", "inner cortex 3rd layer" (foxglove only), "endodermis", "vasculature", or "buffer region" (labeled "Buffer region cell" in the source, without further documentation). In `poppy_3`, the source data give conflicting types for 1,078 cells (the type of a cell is listed separately in each of its edges); the most frequently listed type is used.
- (Edge) `shared_wall_area` (edges): the area of the cell wall shared by the two cells, as computed by MorphoGraphX (in µm²).
citations: M. D. B. Jackson, H. Xu, S. Duran-Nebreda, P. Stamm, G. W. Bassel, "Topological analysis of multicellular complexity in the plant hypocotyl." eLife 6, e26023 (2017)

datasets.name: plant_pol_petanidou
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of flowering plants and their insect pollinators in a phryganic (East Mediterranean scrub) ecosystem at Daphní, near Athens, Greece, compiled by T. Petanidou for her PhD thesis. Flower visits were recorded over about four years of field observations (April 1983 to May 1987) in a 30 ha area of the Diomedes Botanical Garden. An edge connects a plant species to an insect species that was observed visiting its flowers; the data record only the presence of the interaction, not its frequency. Insects that could not be identified to species level are listed as morphospecies (e.g. "Andrena sp1 M_PL_015"). The data were obtained from the Web of Life database (network M_PL_015).

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the taxon name (stripped of surrounding whitespace).
- (Node) `is_pollinator`: whether the node is a pollinator (otherwise a plant).
- (Node) `order` and `family`: the taxonomic order and family.
- (Node) `resolution`: the taxonomic level to which the taxon was identified ("Species", "Genus", "Family" or "Order"; empty if not given in the source).
citations: T. Petanidou, "Pollination ecology in a phryganic ecosystem." PhD Thesis, Aristotelian University, Thessaloniki (1991)
T. Petanidou, W. N. Ellis, "Pollinating fauna of a phryganic ecosystem: composition and diversity." Biodiversity Letters 1(1), 9-22 (1993)

datasets.name: platynereis_connectome
datasets.description:
Whole-body synaptic connectome of a three-day-old (72 hours post fertilization) larva of the marine annelid worm *Platynereis dumerilii*, which has a head, three trunk segments, and a pygidium. All cells were traced and annotated by Verasztó et al. in a serial-section transmission electron microscopy volume of 4,846 layers of 40 nm sections spanning the entire body of a larva, using the CATMAID software. The synapses are chemical (no gap junctions were identified) and monadic, i.e. each connects one presynaptic neuron to one postsynaptic cell.

Nodes are cells (neurons and the effector cells they innervate, such as muscles, ciliated cells, and glands) or neurite fragments that could not be attached to a cell with a soma, and a directed edge goes from a presynaptic to a postsynaptic cell, weighted by the number of synapses between them. The network is the connectome graph of Figure 2 of the paper, as provided in its source data. (An earlier version of the connectome, with 2,728 nodes, was distributed with the 2020 preprint of the paper.)

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the cell in CATMAID, which for most neurons indicates its cell type and side.
- (Node) `skid`: the skeleton identifier in the CATMAID database.
- (Node) `celltype`: the cell-type annotation in CATMAID (e.g. "celltype1"; "not_celltype" if the cell was not assigned to a cell type), which are described in Supplementary file 1 of the paper.
- (Node) `class`: the cell class ("sensory neuron", "interneuron", "motoneuron", "effector", "fragmentum" for fragments, or "other").
- (Node) `segment`: the body region of the soma ("episphere" for the head, "segment_0" to "segment_3", "pygidium", or "fragment").
- (Node) `side`: the body side of the soma ("left_side", "right_side", "middle", or "other").
- (Node) `module` and `module_name`: the module of the cell, obtained by the authors with the Leiden community detection algorithm, numbered from 1 and named after their main effector organs or anatomical characters (e.g. "mech (l)", "NS", "ciliomotor"; empty for some modules).
- (Edge) `weight`: the number of synapses.
citations: C. Verasztó, S. Jasek, M. Gühmann, L. A. Bezares-Calderón, E. A. Williams, R. Shahidi, G. Jékely, "Whole-body connectome of a segmented annelid larva." eLife 13, RP97964 (2025)

C. Verasztó, S. Jasek, M. Gühmann, R. Shahidi, N. Ueda, J. D. Beard, S. Mendes, K. Heinz, L. A. Bezares-Calderón, E. Williams, G. Jékely, "Whole-animal connectome and cell-type complement of the three-segmented Platynereis dumerilii larva." bioRxiv 2020.08.21.260984 (2020)

datasets.name: pokec
datasets.description:
Friendship network of Pokec, the most popular online social network in Slovakia, which had been operating for more than 10 years and connected more than 1.6 million people when the data were collected by L. Takac and M. Zabovsky (published in 2012). The data are anonymized and cover the whole network. Nodes are users, and a directed edge $(i,j)$ indicates that user $i$ lists user $j$ as a friend; friendships in Pokec are oriented (not necessarily reciprocated). The user IDs of the source data run from 1 to 1,632,803; the node with index $i$ corresponds to the user with ID $i+1$. The data were obtained from the Stanford Network Analysis Project (SNAP).

The source data also include user profiles (in Slovak), with information such as gender, age, region, hobbies, interests and education, but these are not included in this network.
citations: L. Takac and M. Zabovsky. "Data Analysis in Public Social Networks." Internat. Sci. Conf. & Internat. Workshop Present Day Trends of Innovations, Lomza, Poland (2012).

datasets.name: pokemon
datasets.description:
Bipartite networks of Pokémon and the moves they can learn, and of Pokémon and the in-game location areas where they can be encountered in the wild, across the main-series Pokémon video games (from Red/Blue, 1996, to the most recent games covered). The data come from PokéAPI, a community-maintained database of the games' contents, compiled by its contributors from the games themselves; this version corresponds to the CSV tables of the PokéAPI repository at commit 2bf639e. Each Pokémon form with its own entry in the database (e.g. regional variants and mega evolutions) is a separate node. Only Pokémon, moves and location areas that take part in at least one relation are included.

- `moves`: each edge connects a Pokémon to a move it can learn, in a given version group (set of games released together) and with a given learn method. The same Pokémon and move are connected by several parallel edges if the move is learnable in several version groups, with several methods, or at several levels.
- `locations`: each edge connects a Pokémon to a location area where it appears in the wild, for a given game version and encounter slot. Parallel edges correspond to different versions, encounter methods or slots.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name` (Pokémon): the PokéAPI identifier of the Pokémon (form).
- (Node) `species` (Pokémon): the English name of its species.
- (Node) `pokemon_id` (Pokémon): the PokéAPI id (ids larger than 10000 are alternate forms).
- (Node) `types` (Pokémon): its type(s), separated by "/".
- (Node) `height` (Pokémon): the height, in decimeters.
- (Node) `weight` (Pokémon): the weight, in hectograms.
- (Node) `base_experience` (Pokémon): the base experience gained by defeating it (-1 if unknown).
- (Node) `default_form` (Pokémon): whether it is the default form of its species.
- (Node) `is_move` (`moves`): whether the node is a move (otherwise a Pokémon).
- (Node) `name` (moves): the PokéAPI identifier of the move.
- (Node) `move_id` (moves): its PokéAPI id (ids larger than 10000 are "shadow" moves).
- (Node) `move_type` (moves): its type.
- (Node) `damage_class` (moves): status, physical or special.
- (Node) `generation` (moves): the generation in which it was introduced (1-9).
- (Node) `power`, `pp`, `accuracy` (moves): the power, the power points and the accuracy (in percent), with -1 when not applicable.
- (Node) `priority` (moves): the priority of the move.
- (Edge) `version_group` (`moves`): the identifier of the version group (e.g. "red-blue").
- (Edge) `method` (`moves`): the learn method (e.g. "level-up", "egg", "tutor", "machine").
- (Edge) `level` (`moves`): the level at which the move is learned (0 if not applicable).
- (Edge) `mastery` (`moves`): the level at which the move can be mastered (in Pokémon Legends: Arceus only, -1 otherwise).
- (Node) `is_area` (`locations`): whether the node is a location area (otherwise a Pokémon).
- (Node) `name` (areas): the PokéAPI identifier of the area, formed from the location identifier and the area identifier, or with the suffix "-area" when the location has a single unnamed area.
- (Node) `location` (areas): the English name of the location.
- (Node) `region` (areas): the region of the location (e.g. "kanto"; empty if unknown).
- (Edge) `version` (`locations`): the game version (e.g. "red").
- (Edge) `method` (`locations`): the encounter method (e.g. "walk", "surf", "old-rod").
- (Edge) `rarity` (`locations`): the chance of the encounter slot, in percent.
- (Edge) `min_level`, `max_level` (`locations`): the range of levels of the encountered Pokémon.
citations: P. Hallett and PokéAPI contributors, "PokéAPI: The Pokémon API." (2026)

datasets.name: polblogs
datasets.description:
Directed network of hyperlinks among weblogs on U.S. politics, compiled by L. A. Adamic and N. Glance to study the political blogosphere around the 2004 U.S. presidential election. Nodes are blogs, identified from online blog directories, and a directed edge $(i,j)$ indicates that the front page of blog $i$ contained a hyperlink to blog $j$; the links were extracted automatically from a crawl of the blogs' front pages in February 2005. Each blog is labeled with its political leaning, taken from the blog directories or, for some blogs, assigned manually based on their incoming and outgoing links and posts around the time of the election. According to the authors, directory-derived labels are prone to error, and manual labels even more so. The network contains 266 isolated blogs, 3 self-loops, and 65 repeated links.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `label`: the URL of the blog.
- (Node) `value`: the political leaning of the blog, with 0 = left or liberal, 1 = right or conservative.
- (Node) `source`: the blog directories from which the blog and its label were obtained (Blogarama, BlogCatalog, eTalkingHead, LeftyDirectory, CampaignLine, BlogPulse), or "LabeledManually", separated by commas.
citations: L. A. Adamic and N. Glance, "The political blogosphere and the 2004 U.S. election: divided they blog." Proc. 3rd Internat. Workshop on Link Discovery (LinkKDD), 36-43 (2005).

datasets.name: polbooks
datasets.description:
Network of books about U.S. politics published around the time of the 2004 U.S. presidential election and sold by the online bookseller Amazon.com, compiled by V. Krebs (unpublished). Nodes are books, and an undirected edge connects two books that are frequently purchased by the same buyers, as indicated by Amazon's "customers who bought this book also bought these other books" feature. The books were labeled by M. E. J. Newman as liberal, neutral or conservative, based on a reading of the descriptions and reviews of the books posted on Amazon.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `label`: the title of the book.
- (Node) `value`: the political alignment of the book, with "l" = liberal, "n" = neutral, "c" = conservative.
citations: V. Krebs, "The political books network", unpublished

datasets.name: polecat_events
datasets.description:
A temporal network of political events between socio-political actors worldwide (governments, politicians, parties, the military, the police, armed groups, journalists, citizens, ...), from January 2018 to June 2024, from the POLitical Event Classification, Attributes, and Types (POLECAT) dataset, the successor of the Integrated Crisis Early Warning System (ICEWS) event data. POLECAT codes events automatically, with a machine-learning coder (NGEC) based on the PLOVER ontology of event types, from news stories in seven languages (English, Russian, Spanish, French, Portuguese, Arabic and Chinese) from over a thousand sources. Each directed edge from A to B is an event in which actor A acts upon actor B (e.g. A accuses, threatens, aids or assaults B), with its date, type and other attributes.

Each event lists its actors and recipients (possibly several of each). An actor with a name in the data (the name resolved by the coder, usually that of a person or organization, e.g. `Narendra Modi`, `NATO`) is a node identified by that name. Actors without a name, which are described only by their country and their sector (e.g. the Ukrainian military, the Indian police), are nodes identified by the country and the sector, e.g. `Ukraine MIL` or `India COP`; actors with neither name, country nor sector are left out. An event with several actors or recipients becomes one edge for each pair of actor and recipient. Events without any identifiable actor or recipient (about a third of the 2.2 million events) are not included. Of the 9 event identifiers that appear twice in the data, only the first occurrence is kept. The data are the yearly files of version 62 of the "POLECAT Weekly Data" dataset (the file of 2024 ends in June 2024). The raw names and titles of the actors as they appear in the stories, the people, organizations and locations mentioned in the stories, and the finer geographic information (city, district, province, GeoNames identifiers) are not included.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the actor, or its country and sector for unnamed actors.
- (Node) `named`: whether the actor has a name in the data (otherwise it is defined by its country and sector).
- (Node) `country`: the country of the actor (the most frequent one in its events; e.g. `Intergovernmental Organization` for international organizations; `None` if not known).
- (Node) `cow_code`: the Correlates of War code of the actor's country (the most frequent one; -1 if not known).
- (Node) `sector`: the primary sector of the actor (the most frequent one), as a PLOVER sector code (e.g. `GOV` government, `MIL` military, `COP` police, `JUD` judiciary, `LEG` legislature, `PTY` political party, `REB` rebels, `CVL` civilians, `JRN` journalists, `BUS` business; `None` if not known).
- (Node) `wikipedia_id`: the title of the Wikipedia page of the actor, as resolved by the coder (the most frequent one; `None` if not known).
- (Edge) `event_id`: the identifier of the event.
- (Edge) `time`: the date of the event, in Unix time.
- (Edge) `event_type`: the PLOVER type of the event: `AGREE`, `CONSULT`, `SUPPORT`, `CONCEDE`, `COOPERATE`, `AID`, `RETREAT`, `REQUEST`, `ACCUSE`, `REJECT`, `THREATEN`, `PROTEST`, `SANCTION`, `MOBILIZE`, `COERCE` or `ASSAULT`.
- (Edge) `event_mode`: the PLOVER mode of the event, a subtype (e.g. `arrest`, `demo`, `ceasefire`; empty if none).
- (Edge) `intensity`: the intensity of the event, from -10 (most hostile) to 10 (most cooperative).
- (Edge) `quad_code`: `VERBAL COOPERATION`, `MATERIAL COOPERATION`, `VERBAL CONFLICT` or `MATERIAL CONFLICT`.
- (Edge) `contexts`: the contexts of the event (e.g. `military`, `election`, `health`), separated by `|` (`None` if none).
- (Edge) `placename`: the name of the location of the event (`None` if not known).
- (Edge) `location_country`: the ISO 3166-1 alpha-3 code of the country of the location (`None` if not known).
- (Edge) `latitude`, `longitude`: the coordinates of the location (NaN if not known).
- (Edge) `source`: the news outlet of the story.
- (Edge) `language`: the language of the story.
citations: G. I. Scarborough, B. E. Bagozzi, A. Beger, J. Berrie, A. Halterman, P. A. Schrodt, J. Spivey, "POLECAT Weekly Data." Harvard Dataverse, V62 (2024)
A. Halterman, P. A. Schrodt, A. Beger, B. E. Bagozzi, G. I. Scarborough, "Creating Custom Event Data Without Dictionaries: A Bag-of-Tricks." arXiv:2304.01331 (2023)

datasets.name: political_actors
datasets.description:
Strong political alliances among 14 prominent political actors in a Midwestern city in the USA, from P. Doreian and L. H. Albert. The County Executive (A) and the County Auditor (B) were strong political rivals, each with their own supporters. The substantive issue was the construction of a federally mandated new jail: actor A supported the construction while B opposed it, and the County Council (actors D through J) was split over this issue. Two actors are connected if they are strong political allies. The data were distributed on the Pajek datasets page of the book *Generalized Blockmodeling* (Doreian, Batagelj and Ferligoj), from which this version was obtained.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the letter code of the actor (A to N), as used in the publications.
- (Node) `position`: the position of the actor (e.g. "County Executive", "Council Member 1", "City Mayor").
citations: P. Doreian, L. H. Albert, "Partitioning political actor networks: Some quantitative tools for analyzing qualitative networks." Journal of Quantitative Anthropology 1, 279-291 (1989)
P. Doreian, V. Batagelj, A. Ferligoj, "Generalized Blockmodeling." Cambridge University Press (2004)

datasets.name: pond_frog_populations
datasets.description:
Weighted network of genetic differentiation among 27 populations of the black-spotted pond frog (*Pelophylax nigromaculatus*) from 24 islands of the Zhoushan Archipelago and three sites on the nearby mainland of China, from the study of S. Wang and collaborators on the loss of genetic diversity in insular populations (genotypes of 810 frogs deposited in the Dryad repository). The data were compiled by M. Cantor and collaborators for a study of nestedness across levels of biological organization, and are distributed in the repository of that study (file `mep_frogs_Rst.txt`). Nodes are populations, and an undirected edge connects every pair of populations (the network is a complete graph), weighted by their pairwise genetic differentiation R<sub>ST</sub> (Slatkin, 1995), computed from the variance of microsatellite allele sizes (nine neutral microsatellite loci). R<sub>ST</sub> is 0 for genetically identical populations and grows with differentiation; small negative values arise from sampling error. Note that the documentation of the source describes the weights as the genetic similarity 1 - R<sub>ST</sub>, but the file contains R<sub>ST</sub> itself (with zeros on the diagonal). The populations are not identified in the source data.

The edges have the property `weight`, the pairwise R<sub>ST</sub>.
citations: S. Wang, W. Zhu, X. Gao, X. Li, S. Yan, X. Liu, J. Yang, Z. Gao, Y. Li, "Population size and time since island isolation determine genetic diversity loss in insular frog populations." Molecular Ecology 23, 637-648 (2014)
S. Wang et al., "Data from: Population size and time since island isolation determine genetic diversity loss in insular frog populations." Dryad Digital Repository (2013)
M. Slatkin, "A measure of population subdivision based on microsatellite allele frequencies." Genetics 139(1), 457-462 (1995)

M. Cantor, M. M. Pires, F. M. D. Marquitti, R. L. G. Raimundo, E. Sebastián-González, P. P. Coltri, S. I. Perez, D. R. Barneche, D. Y. C. Brandt, K. Nunes, F. G. Daura-Jorge, S. R. Floeter, P. R. Guimarães Jr., "Nestedness across biological scales." PLoS ONE 12(2), e0171691 (2017)

datasets.name: portland_contacts
datasets.description:
A synthetic network of the physical contacts between the inhabitants of Portland, Oregon (USA), during a typical day, generated by the Network Dynamics and Simulation Science Laboratory (NDSSL, Virginia Tech, formerly at Los Alamos National Laboratory) with the TRANSIMS and EpiSims simulations from census data, land use data and activity surveys: synthetic individuals, with the demographics of the census, are assigned daily activities (home, work, school, shopping, ...) at real locations, and two persons are in contact if they are at the same location (sub-location) at the same time. Each node is a person, and an undirected edge means that the two persons were in contact during the day. This network was widely used to model the spread of infectious diseases in cities.

The data are those redistributed by Yang et al. for their study of pandemic containment, who give the network without the durations and activity types of the contacts of the original NDSSL data, which is no longer available from its source. The node and edge lists of this redistribution are used as they are; the centrality scores (eigenvector and local-flow betweenness centralities) computed by Yang et al., and given in the same record, are not included.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `id`: the identifier of the person in the data.
citations: S. Eubank, H. Guclu, V. S. A. Kumar, M. V. Marathe, A. Srinivasan, Z. Toroczkai, N. Wang, "Modelling disease outbreaks in realistic urban social networks." Nature 429, 180-184 (2004)
S. Yang, P. Senapati, D. Wang, C. T. Bauch, K. Fountoulakis, "Targeted pandemic containment through identifying local contact network bottlenecks." PLOS Computational Biology 17(8), e1009351 (2021)

datasets.name: power
datasets.description: Undirected network representing the topology of the high-voltage power grid of the Western States of the United States, compiled by D. J. Watts and S. H. Strogatz, who used it as an example of a small-world network. Nodes are generators, transformers and substations, and an edge connects two nodes if they are connected by a high-voltage transmission line. The data were obtained from the network data collection of M. E. J. Newman, and the node IDs are the same as those used by Watts.
citations: D.J. Watts and S.H. Strogatz, "Collective dynamics of 'small-world' networks." Nature 393, 440-442 (1998).

datasets.name: powerplant_bayesian
datasets.description:
Bayesian network modelling the correlations among the sensors of a coal-fired power plant, from T. D. Nielsen and F. V. Jensen, distributed with the book "Bayesian Networks and Decision Graphs" (F. V. Jensen and T. D. Nielsen) at Aalborg University. The network was used to design an on-line alert system that detects abnormal plant behavior as conflicts between sensor readings and the model. Nodes are variables (sensor measurements, discretized into three intervals), and a directed edge from $i$ to $j$ means that variable $i$ is a parent of variable $j$ in the directed acyclic graph of the Bayesian network, i.e., that the conditional probability distribution of $j$ is specified given the value of $i$. The network has 46 sparsely connected nodes (six of which have no connections); the conditional probability tables are not included.

The nodes have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the variable, as in the source (e.g. "V26"; the variables are not described further).
- (Node) `states`: the list of states of the variable (intervals of the sensor value, e.g. "(2.42-4.66]").[^icon]

[^icon]: Description obtained in part from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.
citations: T. D. Nielsen, F. V. Jensen, "On-line alert systems for production plants: A conflict based approach." International Journal of Approximate Reasoning 45(2), 255-270 (2007)

datasets.name: primekg
datasets.description:
The Precision Medicine Knowledge Graph (PrimeKG) of Chandak, Huang and Zitnik, which integrates 20 biomedical resources (e.g. DrugBank, DisGeNET, the Human Phenotype Ontology, Reactome, Gene Ontology, UBERON, SIDER) into a single graph centered on diseases. Nodes are biological and medical entities of ten types (genes/proteins, drugs, diseases, phenotypes, exposures, anatomical regions, biological processes, molecular functions, cellular components and pathways), and an undirected edge is a relationship between two of them, of one of 30 types (e.g. protein-protein interaction, drug indication, disease-phenotype association, drug side effect).

There are four networks, the final graph and the intermediate stages of its construction, as released by the authors (version 2.1 of the data set):

- `kg`: the final knowledge graph (from `nodes.csv` and `edges.csv`).
- `raw`: all the relationships of the integrated resources (`kg_raw.csv`).
- `giant`: the largest connected component of `raw` (`kg_giant.csv`).
- `grouped`: `giant` after grouping the diseases whose names correspond to subtypes of the same disease into single nodes (`kg_grouped.csv`); this has the same relationships as the final graph.

The upstream files list each relationship in both directions; each is included here once. In the intermediate networks, nodes are identified by their identifier, type, name and source. As in the authors' final graph, 63 genes appear as two nodes, under two names (e.g. an old and a current gene symbol) with the same NCBI identifier.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `node_id`: the identifier of the entity in its source (e.g. an NCBI gene ID, a DrugBank ID, a MONDO ID).
- (Node) `node_type`: the type of the entity (`gene/protein`, `drug`, `disease`, `effect/phenotype`, `exposure`, `anatomy`, `biological_process`, `molecular_function`, `cellular_component`, `pathway`).
- (Node) `name`: the name of the entity.
- (Node) `source`: the source of the identifier (e.g. `NCBI`, `DrugBank`, `MONDO`, `HPO`, `REACTOME`).
- (Edge) `relation` (edges): the type of the relationship (e.g. `protein_protein`, `drug_protein`, `indication`, `disease_phenotype_positive`).
- (Edge) `display_relation` (edges): a shorter name of the type of relationship (e.g. `ppi`, `target`, `indication`).
citations: P. Chandak, K. Huang, M. Zitnik, "Building a knowledge graph to enable precision medicine." Scientific Data 10, 67 (2023)

datasets.name: prison_gagnon
datasets.description: Sociometric choices among 67 prison inmates, collected by J. Gagnon in the 1950s and analyzed by D. MacRae. All inmates were asked "What fellows on the tier are you closest friends with?", and each was free to choose as few or as many friends as he desired. A directed edge points from the inmate making the choice to the chosen one. MacRae characterized the network as "less clear cut" in its internal structure than similar data from schools or residential populations. The data were distributed in UCINET format (from the UCINET data collection of S. P. Borgatti, M. G. Everett and L. C. Freeman) on the Pajek datasets page of V. Batagelj and A. Mrvar, from which this version was obtained.
citations: D. MacRae, "Direct Factor Analysis of Sociometric Data." Sociometry 23(4), 360-371 (1960)
S. P. Borgatti, M. G. Everett, L. C. Freeman, "UCINET for Windows: Software for Social Network Analysis." Analytic Technologies, Harvard, MA (2002)

datasets.name: pristionchus_pharynx
datasets.description:
Directed networks of synaptic connections in the pharyngeal nervous system of the predatory nematode *Pristionchus pacificus*, reconstructed by Bumbarger et al. from serial-section transmission electron micrographs of two adult hermaphrodites, and compared with the homologous (bacteria-feeding) *C. elegans* pharyngeal network. Nodes are pharyngeal neurons and the pharyngeal muscles they innervate; each edge is a synaptic contact from the presynaptic to a postsynaptic cell. Synapses with several postsynaptic partners (polyadic synapses) yield several edges with the same synapse identifier, and cells connected by several synapses are joined by parallel edges.

- `animal1`: the first reconstructed animal (54 cells, 511 edges).
- `animal2`: the second reconstructed animal (50 cells, 611 edges).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the cell name (L/R suffixes indicate left and right cells).
- (Edge) `synapse_id`: the identifier of the synapse in the reconstruction.

The data were obtained from the graph collection of the Open Connectome Project (now NeuroData), whose servers are offline, via the Internet Archive.
citations: D. J. Bumbarger, M. Riebesell, C. Rödelsperger, R. J. Sommer, "System-wide Rewiring Underlies Behavioral Differences in Predatory and Bacterial-Feeding Nematodes." Cell 152(1-2), 109-119 (2013)

datasets.name: product_space
datasets.description:
The "product space", a network of products in world trade, as visualized in the Atlas of Economic Complexity (R. Hausmann, C. A. Hidalgo et al.), and distributed by M. Coscia. Nodes are products, and edges connect products that tend to be exported together by the same countries, based on the UN Comtrade data on world trade. The relatedness of two products $i$ and $j$ is measured by their proximity, $\phi_{ij} = \min\{P(x_i|x_j), P(x_j|x_i)\}$, where $P(x_i|x_j)$ is the conditional probability that a country exports product $i$ with revealed comparative advantage (i.e. a share of its exports larger than the share of the product in world trade), given that it does so for product $j$. The networks are not the full proximity matrix, but the sparse backbones used for visualizing it, which consist of the strongest links (in Hidalgo et al., Science 317, 482 (2007), the maximum spanning tree of the proximity network plus the links with the highest proximity). Edges are undirected.

There are two networks, using different product classifications at the 4-digit level: `SITC`, based on the Standard International Trade Classification, and `HS`, based on the Harmonized Commodity Description and Coding System.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `pid`: the 4-digit product code (SITC or HS).
- (Node) `community`: the product community (cluster of related products) in the source data, which determines the color of the node.
- (Node) `pos`: the $(x,y)$ coordinates of the product in the layout of the visualization.
- (Node) `size`: the node size in the visualization, which reflects the product's share of world trade, but not linearly.
- (Node) `leamer` (`SITC` only): the Leamer category of the product (a grouping of products into 10 categories by factor intensity).
- (Node) `name`: the name of the product.
- (Node) `color`: the color of the node in the visualization, which corresponds to the product community.
- (Edge) `width`, `color`: the width and color of the edge in the visualization, which reflect the strength of the link (proximity), but not linearly.
citations: R. Hausmann et al., "The Atlas of Economic Complexity: Mapping paths to prosperity." MIT Press (2014)
C. A. Hidalgo, B. Klinger, A.-L. Barabási, R. Hausmann, "The Product Space Conditions the Development of Nations", Science 317(5837), 482-487 (2007)
CA Hidalgo, R Hausmann, "The Building Blocks of Economic Complexity", Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. 106(26):10570-10575 (2009)
R Hausmann, CA Hidalgo, S Bustos, M Coscia, S Chung, J Jimenez, A Simoes, MA Yildirim, "The Atlas of Economic Complexity", Puritan Press (2011). ISBN-10: 0615546625

datasets.name: prosper
datasets.description:
A network of loans between the members of Prosper.com, an online peer-to-peer lending marketplace, from November 2005 to September 2011, compiled by U. Redmond and P. Cunningham. On Prosper, borrowers post listings requesting loans, and lenders bid on them; a listing becomes a loan if the requested amount is fully funded by the lenders. Each directed edge goes from a lender to a borrower, and represents the participation of the lender in a loan to the borrower; a single loan therefore appears as several edges, one per lender. Repeated edges between the same lender and borrower are kept. Users are identified only by anonymous numbers.

The network has the following properties:

- (Edge) `time`: the date when the loan originated, as Unix time (at the resolution of days).
- (Edge) `amount`: an amount in US dollars (91% of the values are between 25 and 100 dollars, which suggests that it is the amount lent by the lender rather than the amount requested by the borrower).
- (Edge) `status`: the status of the loan when the data were collected (`Paid`, `Current`, `Charge-off`, `Defaulted`, `Late`, `Payoff`, `Repurchased`, `Cancelled`, and the undocumented values `1`, `2`, `3` and `4+`).
- (Edge) `lender_rate` and `borrower_rate`: the interest rates of the lender and of the borrower, as fractions.
- (Edge) `grade`: the credit grade of the borrower (`AA`, `A` to `E`, `HR` for high risk, and `NC` for no credit score).
citations: U. Redmond, P. Cunningham, "A temporal network analysis reveals the unprofitability of arbitrage in The Prosper Marketplace." Expert Systems with Applications 40(9), 3715-3721 (2013)

datasets.name: psi
datasets.description: Weighted directed network of the light-harvesting Photosystem Ι (PSI) of the plant Pisum sativum. The nodes represent chromophores with different identities (i.e. chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b, β-carotene and derivates, lutein, violaxanthin), while edges represent FRET transfer between chromophores. The link directionality connecting nodes in the PSI network depends on the energy levels of the connected chromophores. The weights correspond to the FRET Efficiency between connected chromophores. Hence a directed edge $(i,j)$ represents the transfer of excitation energy from chromophore $i$ to chromophore $j$, presumably from donor to acceptor (the direction convention of the data file is not documented), weighted by the efficiency of this transfer; most pairs of chromophores (about 80% of the edges) are connected in both directions, with different efficiencies.
citations: Montepietra D., Bellingeri M., Ross A.M., Scotognella F. and Cassi D., "Modelling photosystem I as a complex interacting network", J. R. Soc. Interface (2020)

datasets.name: pubchem_literature
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of the chemical compounds of PubChem, the open chemistry database of the U.S. National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI), and the articles of PubMed linked to them. An edge connects a compound with an article that refers to it, as given in PubChem's list of links between compounds (CIDs) and PubMed articles (PMIDs).

The links come from four kinds of sources, given by the edge property `type`:

1. articles provided by the depositors of the substances of PubChem (e.g. the publication that describes the substance),
2. articles indexed in PubMed with a MeSH heading linked to the compound,
3. articles linked by the publishers of the journals (e.g. compounds described in the article),
4. articles associated with the compound through the BioAssays of PubChem.

A compound and an article linked by several kinds of sources are connected by several edges, one per kind. Only the compounds and articles with at least one link are nodes. The names of the compounds are those chosen as titles of their summary pages in PubChem (empty for the few compounds without a title).

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `is_compound`: whether the node is a compound (otherwise it is an article).
- (Node) `cid`: the PubChem compound identifier (CID) of the compound (-1 for articles); its page is `https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/compound/<cid>`.
- (Node) `pmid`: the PubMed identifier of the article (-1 for compounds).
- (Node) `name`: the name of the compound (the title of its PubChem page; empty for articles).
- (Edge) `type`: the kind of source of the link, 1 to 4 as above.
citations: S. Kim, J. Chen, T. Cheng, A. Gindulyte, J. He, S. He, Q. Li, B. A. Shoemaker, P. A. Thiessen, B. Yu, L. Zaslavsky, J. Zhang, E. E. Bolton, "PubChem 2025 update." Nucleic Acids Research 53, D1516-D1525 (2025)

datasets.name: pubmed_linqs
datasets.description:
A directed citation network of scientific papers on diabetes from the PubMed database, from the "Pubmed-Diabetes" dataset distributed by the LINQS group (Namata et al.) as a benchmark for collective classification, also used (as one of the "Planetoid" datasets) in many works on graph neural networks. Each of the 19,717 papers is classified into one of three classes, after the Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) of the paper, and described by the TF-IDF weights of the 500 words of a vocabulary of word stems. The data also give, for each paper, the list of the word stems that appear in it (attribute "summary"), which is redundant with the TF-IDF weights and not included. See also the `cora_linqs` and `citeseer_linqs` entries.

An edge from paper A to paper B means that A cites B. The data contain 3 self-loops and 11 pairs of papers that cite each other, which are kept.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `id`: the PubMed identifier of the paper.
- (Node) `subject`: the class of the paper, one of `Diabetes Mellitus, Experimental`, `Diabetes Mellitus Type 1` and `Diabetes Mellitus Type 2`.
- (Node) `words`: a vector of 500 values, where the i-th value is the TF-IDF weight of the i-th word of the vocabulary in the paper (0 if the word does not appear in it).
- (Graph) `vocabulary`: the word stems of the vocabulary, in the order of the values of `words`.
citations: G. Namata, B. London, L. Getoor, B. Huang, "Query-driven Active Surveying for Collective Classification." International Workshop on Mining and Learning with Graphs (MLG) (2012)
P. Sen, G. Namata, M. Bilgic, L. Getoor, B. Gallagher, T. Eliassi-Rad, "Collective Classification in Network Data." AI Magazine 29(3), 93-106 (2008)

datasets.name: pubtator3_relations
datasets.description:
A directed network of biomedical concepts (genes, chemicals, diseases, genetic variants, species) and their relations, mined from the scientific literature by PubTator3 of the NCBI, which annotates all PubMed abstracts (about 36 million) and the full texts of the PMC Open Access Subset with deep-learning text mining tools: AIONER for the recognition of the entities, GNorm2, TaggerOne and NLM-Chem for their normalization to database identifiers, tmVar3 for the variants, and BioREx for the relations between them. Each edge is a relation found in an article, from the first to the second concept of the relation, with the type of relation and the PubMed identifier of the article; two concepts are joined by one edge per article (and type) in which their relation was found, so that the network is a multigraph.

The types of relation are `associate`, `cause`, `compare`, `cotreat`, `drug_interact`, `inhibit`, `interact`, `negative_correlate`, `positive_correlate`, `prevent`, `stimulate` and `treat`. The concepts are identified by the databases used by PubTator3: NCBI Gene identifiers for genes, MeSH identifiers for chemicals and diseases, dbSNP identifiers or tmVar normalized names for variants, NCBI Taxonomy identifiers for species. The names of the concepts are not included (they are in the much larger annotation files of PubTator3).

PubTator3 updates its files monthly, replacing them in place; the data are those of the version of the download date (the release of October 6, 2026, at the time of writing).

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `concept`: the concept, with its type and identifier, as given by PubTator3 (e.g. `Chemical|MESH:D003911`, `Gene|7157`).
- (Node) `kind`: the type of the concept: `Gene`, `Chemical`, `Disease`, `Species`, `DNAMutation`, `ProteinMutation`, `SNP`, ...
- (Edge) `type`: the type of the relation.
- (Edge) `pmid`: the PubMed identifier of the article.
citations: C.-H. Wei, A. Allot, P.-T. Lai, R. Leaman, S. Tian, L. Luo, Q. Jin, Z. Wang, Q. Chen, Z. Lu, "PubTator 3.0: an AI-powered literature resource for unlocking biomedical knowledge." Nucleic Acids Research 52, W540-W546 (2024)

datasets.name: pypsa_eur_grid
datasets.description:
Networks of the European high-voltage electricity transmission grid (220 kV to 750 kV), built by B. Xiong, D. Fioriti, F. Neumann, I. Riepin and T. Brown from OpenStreetMap (OSM) data, as the prebuilt grid of the open energy system model PyPSA-Eur. The OSM power data (substations, lines, cables and high-voltage direct current links) of 35 European countries (36, with Kosovo, in version 0.7) were retrieved with the Overpass API and cleaned with heuristics that complete missing or ambiguous electrical parameters (e.g. the voltage and the number of circuits of lines); substations close to each other are aggregated into single buses (within 5 km in the first versions, within 500 m from version 0.5 on), and the lines are split and joined so that the grid is topologically connected.

A node is a bus, i.e. a (possibly aggregated) substation at a given voltage level, so that a substation with several voltage levels is represented by several buses, and an edge is one of the elements of the grid joining two buses: an alternating current (AC) line or cable, a direct current (DC) link, a transformer between two voltage levels, or an AC/DC converter (the edge property `type`). The networks are undirected; several elements may join the same pair of buses (parallel edges).

The dataset is updated as OSM and the cleaning workflow change; each of its seven versions, from 0.1 (July 2024) to 0.7 (February 2026), is a separate network, named after the version (`v0.1`, ..., `v0.7`). The geometries of the lines (their courses as polylines) and of the substations are not included, and neither are the interactive maps of the later versions.

The networks have the following properties (some columns exist only in later versions of the data, as indicated):

- (Node) `name`: the bus identifier (derived from the OSM ids of the substation).
- (Node) `voltage`: the voltage level (kV).
- (Node) `dc`: whether the bus is a direct current bus.
- (Node) `symbol`: the kind of bus (e.g. `Substation`).
- (Node) `under_construction`: whether it is under construction.
- (Node) `osm_ids`: the OSM elements of the bus (from version 0.5 on).
- (Node) `latitude` and `longitude`: the geographical position.
- (Node) `country`: the two-letter country code.
- (Edge) `type`: the kind of element (`line`, `link`, `transformer` or `converter`).
- (Edge) `name`: the element's identifier (for lines and links derived from the OSM ids, which can be looked up on OpenStreetMap).
- (Edge) `voltage`: the voltage of lines, links and converters (kV, from version 0.3 on for converters).
- (Edge) `voltage_bus0` and `voltage_bus1`: the voltages of the two sides of transformers (kV).
- (Edge) `circuits`: the number of circuits of lines.
- (Edge) `length`: the length of lines and links (m).
- (Edge) `p_nom`: the nominal power of links (and of converters, from version 0.5 on) (MW).
- (Edge) `s_nom`: the nominal apparent power of transformers (from version 0.5 on) and lines (from version 0.6 on) (MVA).
- (Edge) `i_nom` (kA): `r` (Ω), `x` (Ω) and `b` (S), the nominal current, resistance, reactance and susceptance of lines, and `line_type`, the standard line type assumed for these parameters (from version 0.6 on).
- (Edge) `underground` and `under_construction`: whether the line or link is an underground cable and whether it is under construction.
- (Edge) `osm_ids`: the OSM elements making up the line or link (from version 0.5 on). Values that do not apply to an element are NaN (or empty, or false).
citations: B. Xiong, D. Fioriti, F. Neumann, I. Riepin, T. Brown, "Modelling the high-voltage grid using open data for Europe and beyond." Scientific Data 12, 277 (2025)
B. Xiong, D. Fioriti, F. Neumann, I. Riepin, T. Brown, "Prebuilt Electricity Network for PyPSA-Eur based on OpenStreetMap Data." Zenodo, versions 0.1-0.7 (2024-2026)

datasets.name: python_dependency
datasets.description:
Network of dependencies among Python packages registered in the Python Package Index (PyPI), assembled by K. Gullikson and published in February 2016. The source distributions of the packages on PyPI were downloaded, and their dependencies were extracted with a modified version of the requirements-detector tool, by parsing the `install_requires` argument in `setup.py`, or, failing that, the requirements files of the package; packages whose `setup.py` could not be parsed were left out. Nodes are packages, and a directed edge $(i,j)$ indicates that package $i$ requires package $j$. Parallel edges were removed. Package names are matched as on PyPI, i.e. ignoring case and treating "-", "_" and "." as equivalent (the requirements are often spelled differently from the package names). Some packages appear in the source data with more than one version, which are merged into a single node. Packages without any detected requirement have no outgoing edges, and nodes without a version are packages that appear only as requirements.

In the source data, for some rows the package name is missing, and only the combined package and version string (as in "abook-0.2.1") is given; the name was obtained here by splitting off the version. The network contains 92 self-loops, from packages that list themselves as a requirement in the source data.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the package, as given in the source data.
- (Node) `versions`: the versions of the package in the source data (empty for packages that appear only as requirements).

datasets.name: qa_user
citations: A. Paranjape, A. R. Benson, & J. Leskovec, "Motifs in Temporal Networks". In Proceedings of the Tenth ACM International Conference on Web Search and Data Mining (WSDM ’17). Association for Computing Machinery, New York, NY, USA, 601–610. (2017)
Stack Exchange, Inc., "Stack Exchange Data Dump - 2024-04-02."

datasets.name: quakers
datasets.description:
Social network of 119 early members of the Religious Society of Friends (Quakers) in seventeenth-century Britain and its colonies, a subset of the data of the Six Degrees of Francis Bacon (SDFB) project, published with the Programming Historian tutorial "Exploring and Analyzing Network Data with Python" by J. R. Ladd, J. Otis, C. N. Warren and S. Weingart. SDFB reconstructs the social network of early modern Britain (1500-1700) from the Oxford Dictionary of National Biography (ODNB): relationships are first inferred statistically from the co-occurrence of names in the ODNB biographies, and then curated by contributors. Nodes are persons, and an undirected edge indicates a relationship (of an unspecified kind) between two persons in the SDFB data.

The nodes have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the person (e.g. "William Penn", "George Fox").
- (Node) `historical_significance`: a short description of the person (e.g. "religious writer", "Quaker preacher").
- (Node) `gender`: "male" or "female", as given in the source.
- (Node) `birth` and `death`: the years of birth and death.
- (Node) `sdfb_id`: the identifier of the person in the SDFB data.[^icon]

[^icon]: Description obtained in part from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.
citations: J. R. Ladd, J. Otis, C. N. Warren, S. Weingart, "Exploring and analyzing network data with Python." Programming Historian 6 (2017)

C. N. Warren, D. Shore, J. Otis, L. Wang, M. Finegold, C. Shalizi, "Six Degrees of Francis Bacon: a statistical method for reconstructing large historical social networks." Digital Humanities Quarterly 10(3) (2016)

datasets.name: ragusa_genealogy
datasets.description:
The genealogy of the nobility of Ragusa (now Dubrovnik, Croatia) from the 12th to the 16th century, compiled into a GEDCOM file by P. Dremelj (1999) from the data of I. Mahnken's study of the Ragusan patriciate. In Ragusa, all political power was in the hands of the male nobles older than 18 years, members of the Great Council. The nobility evolved from the 12th through the 14th century and was finally established by statute in 1332, after which no new family was accepted until the large earthquake of 1667. Because of decreasing numbers and the lack of noble families in the neighboring areas under Turkish control, the noble families became more and more closely related, and marriages between relatives were frequent. Nodes are persons; directed edges point from parents to their children, and there is an edge from husband to wife for each marriage. The data were distributed on the Pajek datasets page of the book *Exploratory Social Network Analysis with Pajek* (de Nooy, Mrvar and Batagelj), from which this version was obtained.

- `ragusa`: the complete genealogy.
- `gondola_petrus`: the descendants of one nobleman, Petrus Gondola (a selection of the complete genealogy).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the person.
- (Node) `sex` ("M", "F", "U" or empty).
- (Node) `birth` and `death`: the year (or date) of birth and death, as given in the source (empty if unknown).
- (Edge) `kind`: the kind of relation ("father" or "mother", for edges from a parent to a child, or "marriage", for edges from husband to wife).
- (Edge) `date`: the date of the marriage, as given in the source (empty if unknown or not a marriage).
citations: I. Mahnken, "Das Ragusanische Patriziat des XIV. Jahrhunderts." PhD dissertation (1960)
P. Dremelj, A. Mrvar, V. Batagelj, "Analiza rodoslova dubrovačkog vlasteoskog kruga pomoću programa Pajek." Anali Zavoda za povijesne znanosti HAZU u Dubrovniku 40, 105-126 (2002)
W. de Nooy, A. Mrvar, V. Batagelj, "Exploratory Social Network Analysis with Pajek." Cambridge University Press (2005)

datasets.name: railway_delays
datasets.description:
Railway networks of Italy and of the Chinese high-speed railway, compiled by Faccin, Scagliarini and De Domenico (CoMuNe Lab) to study how train delays respond to rainfall. Nodes are railway stations, and an undirected edge connects two stations between which trains run without intermediate stations of the network. The station locations and the shapes of the lines were extracted from OpenStreetMap, and combined with train schedules and reported delays: for Italy, from the TrainStats service (trainstats.altervista.org), with the years 2021-2023 used for model fitting and 2024 for testing; for China, from the dataset of train operation records and weather data of Zhang et al. (2022). Each station was assigned the population of its Voronoi cell (from WorldPop estimates), and a precipitation value from the ERA5-Land reanalysis of the Copernicus Climate Change Service. The coordinates are longitude and latitude in WGS 84 (EPSG:4326/CRS84).

- `italy`: the Italian railway network. The upstream edge list contains 14,572 directed edges, which list both directions for 6,016 pairs of stations and a single one for 2,540 pairs; as in the authors' code, they are merged into 8,556 undirected edges. For 13 of the pairs listed in both directions the two geometries differ, and the `length` is that of the first one listed. Since edges join consecutive stops, some of them (e.g. of long-distance trains) connect stations hundreds of kilometers apart. The network has two connected components (the largest with 2,367 stations).
- `china`: the Chinese high-speed railway network, from the GeoPackage of the repository (the station metadata from its separate GeoJSON file). The edges were obtained by merging the OpenStreetMap ways of the lines between stations; the edge properties below are OpenStreetMap tags of these ways, one value per edge as given in the data (other tags, mostly sparse names in various languages, are left out). Three pairs of homonymous stations were split by the authors into `<name>_0` and `<name>_1` (Jingzhou, Fengchengdong, Taian); for these, the `english_name`, `city` and `province` are those of only one of the two stations. The `degree` attribute of the node data (not equal to the degree in this network) is left out. The network has two connected components (the largest with 702 stations).

The time series of the delays per station and the counts of train transitions per hour, also in the repositories, are not included.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the station identifier (lower-case Italian name, for `italy`; pinyin name, for `china`).
- (Node) `pos`: the position of the station (longitude, latitude).
- (Node) `pop`: the population assigned to the station.
- (Node) `capacity`: the maximum number of trains passing through the station in one hour.
- (Node) `rain`: the average rain at the station (ERA5-Land precipitation, as given in the data; the units and the averaging period are not documented). For `china`, it is nonzero for only 6 stations.
- (Node) `osm_name` (`italy`): the name of the station in OpenStreetMap.
- (Node) `railway` (`italy`): its OpenStreetMap `railway` tag (`station`, `stop`, `halt`, `manual`, `service_station`; empty for 4 stations).
- (Node) `region` (`italy`): the Italian region.
- (Node) `delay_q10`, `delay_q50`, `delay_q90`, `delay_mean` (`italy`): the 10%, 50% and 90% percentiles and the mean of the delays experienced by the station (in minutes).
- (Node) `osmid` (`china`): the OpenStreetMap node identifier.
- (Node) `english_name` (`china`): the English name.
- (Node) `name_zh` (`china`): the Chinese name (empty if missing).
- (Node) `osm_name`, `osm_name_en` (`china`): the `name` and `name:en` tags in OpenStreetMap (empty if missing).
- (Node) `city`, `province` (`china`): the city and the province of the station.
- (Edge) `length`: the length of the line between the two stations, along its geometry, in kilometers.
- (Edge) `line_name`, `line_name_en` (`china`): the `name` and `name:en` tags (empty if missing).
- (Edge) `railway`, `highspeed`, `usage`, `service`, `electrified` (`china`): the OpenStreetMap tags of the same names (empty if missing).
- (Edge) `maxspeed`, `maxspeed_designed` (`china`): the maximum speed and the designed maximum speed in km/h (-1 if missing).
citations: M. Faccin, T. Scagliarini, M. De Domenico, "Systemic collapse emergence from climate-induced perturbations in transportation networks." Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. 123(42), e2532180123 (2026)

D. Zhang, Y. Peng, Y. Xu, C. Du, Y. Zhang, N. Wang, Y. Chong, H. Wang, D. Wu, J. Liu, H. Zhang, L. Lu, J. Liu, "A high-speed railway network dataset from train operation records and weather data." Scientific Data 9, 244 (2022)

datasets.name: rat_brain_bams
datasets.description:
Directed networks of anatomical connections between regions of the rat brain, from three releases (2011, March 2012 and January 2013) of the connection matrix of the Brain Architecture Management System (BAMS) Rat Connectome Project of Bota and Swanson. BAMS is a curated database that collates connection reports from the primary experimental (tract-tracing) literature, using the regions of the Swanson rat brain atlas. Nodes are brain regions (about 500, spanning the cerebral cortex, cerebral nuclei, thalamus, hypothalamus, midbrain and hindbrain), and a directed edge points from the region of origin of a projection to its target.

- `2011`: 503 regions, 27,667 edges.
- `2012`: 503 regions, 30,088 edges.
- `2013`: 496 regions, 33,020 edges.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the abbreviation of the region in the Swanson atlas.
- (Edge) `strength`: an ordinal connection-strength code from 1 to 9 (larger values for stronger connections). BAMS uses qualitative strength categories ("exists", "very weak", "weak", "moderate/weak", "moderate", "moderate/strong", "strong", "very strong"); the exact mapping of these to the codes in these files is not documented (the code 1 accounts for about 80% of the edges).

The data were obtained from the graph collection of the Open Connectome Project (now NeuroData), whose servers are offline, via the Internet Archive.
citations: M. Bota, L. W. Swanson, "Online workbenches for neural network connections." Journal of Comparative Neurology 500(5), 807-814 (2007)

datasets.name: reactome
datasets.description:
A network of interactions between human proteins, derived from Reactome, an open, manually curated database of biological pathways and reactions. Nodes are proteins (UniProt entries, including isoforms) and an undirected edge connects two proteins that Reactome's curators annotated as taking part in the same complex or reaction; the interactions are thus inferred from the pathway annotations ("inferred by curator", in the PSI-MI vocabulary), rather than measured directly. Some proteins interact with themselves, and appear with self-loops. This is the Reactome protein–protein interaction file for *Homo sapiens* in PSI-MITAB format as it was distributed by Reactome in August 2014; Reactome has since changed considerably.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `uniprot`: the UniProt accession of the protein (with an isoform suffix where applicable).
- (Node) `name`: the short label (gene name) of the protein, empty if not given in the data.
- (Edge) `interaction_type`: the PSI-MI interaction type, `physical association` or `association`.
- (Edge) `pathways`, `reactions`, `complexes` and `regulations`: the lists of the Reactome stable identifiers of the pathways, reactions, complexes or polymers, and regulations in which the interaction was found (in the identifier scheme of that time, `REACT_*`).
