In the data, complexes are only given for physical associations, and regulations only for associations.
citations: G. Joshi-Tope et al., "Reactome: a knowledgebase of biological pathways." Nucleic Acids Research 33(suppl. 1), D428-D432 (2005)

I. Vastrik, P. D'Eustachio, E. Schmidt, G. Joshi-Tope, G. Gopinath, D. Croft, B. de Bono, M. Gillespie, B. Jassal, S. Lewis, L. Matthews, G. Wu, E. Birney, L. Stein, "Reactome: a knowledge base of biologic pathways and processes." Genome Biology 8(3), R39 (2007)

datasets.name: reality_mining
datasets.description:
A network of human proximities among students at Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), as measured by personal mobile phones. Nodes represent people (students from the Media Lab and the Sloan Business School) and an edge connects a pair if the two devices made a Bluetooth handshake at the time. Edges are timestamped.[^icon]
[^icon]: Description obtained from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.
citations: N. Eagle & A. Pentland, "Reality mining: sensing complex social systems." Personal and Ubiquitous Computing 10(4), 255-268 (2006).

datasets.name: recipe_rec
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of recipes of the cooking website Food.com and their ingredients, from the RecipeRec dataset of Tian et al. (collected from Food.com for a study of recipe recommendation), as distributed by XGI-data. Each recipe is connected to the ingredients it uses. Some recipes have the same set of ingredients (77,733 recipes, 74,870 distinct sets). The other parts of the RecipeRec dataset (e.g. the users and their ratings of the recipes) are not included in the XGI-data version.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `is_recipe`: whether the node is a recipe (otherwise an ingredient).
- (Node) `name`: the name of the recipe or ingredient.
- (Node) `recipe_id` (recipes): the identifier of the recipe on Food.com.
- (Node) `url` (recipes): the address of the recipe on Food.com.
citations: Y. Tian, C. Zhang, Z. Guo, C. Huang, R. Metoyer, N. V. Chawla, "RecipeRec: A Heterogeneous Graph Learning Model for Recipe Recommendation." Proceedings of the Thirty-First International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI-22), 3466-3472 (2022)

datasets.name: reddit_graphsage
datasets.description:
Networks of the posts made on Reddit in September 2014, two posts being connected if the same user commented on both, built by W. L. Hamilton, R. Ying and J. Leskovec as a benchmark for the inductive node classification method GraphSAGE, from the Reddit data of Pushshift. The posts are those of 50 large communities (subreddits), and the task of the benchmark is to predict the community of a post. The first 20 days of the month were used for training, and the rest for validation (30%) and testing (70%).

There are two networks, both distributed with GraphSAGE:

- `full`: the complete network (`reddit-G_full.json`), with all 232,965 posts and 57.3 million edges (average degree 492, as given in the paper). This is also the network of the `Reddit` dataset of the libraries DGL and PyTorch Geometric (whose copy, with the nodes in another order, has the same numbers of nodes and edges).
- `graphsage`: the sparser network distributed as the main graph of the benchmark (`reddit-G.json`), with 231,443 posts and 11.6 million edges, which is also the network of the `Reddit2` dataset of PyTorch Geometric (from GraphSAINT). How it was obtained from the full network is not documented.

The communities are given only as numbered classes (41 of them appear), not by name. Each post also has the node features of the benchmark: a 602-dimensional vector made of the average of the 300-dimensional GloVe word embeddings of the title of the post, the average of those of its comments, its score and its number of comments (the dimensions are as given by the source; their order is not documented).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `post_id`: the identifier of the post on Reddit (in base 36, e.g. `2hgylt`).
- (Node) `label`: the class of the community of the post (a number from 0 to 40).
- (Node) `split`: the set of the post in the benchmark: `train`, `val` or `test`.
- (Node) `features`: the 602-dimensional feature vector of the post.
citations: W. L. Hamilton, R. Ying, J. Leskovec, "Inductive Representation Learning on Large Graphs." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 30, 1024-1034 (2017)

datasets.name: reddit_hyperlinks
datasets.description:
Hyperlinks between communities (subreddits) of the discussion website Reddit, extracted by S. Kumar, W. L. Hamilton, J. Leskovec and D. Jurafsky from publicly available Reddit data of January 2014 to April 2017, to study conflicts between communities. Nodes are subreddits, and a directed edge $i \to j$ is a post in subreddit $i$ that contains a hyperlink to a post in subreddit $j$. Each hyperlink is labeled with the sentiment of the source post towards the target post, as positive (or neutral) or negative, which the authors obtained with a text classifier trained on manually labeled examples. A hyperlink can appear in the title or in the body of the post; upstream, these are two separate files, combined here into a single multigraph (a post that links to several subreddits gives several edges). The SNAP page gives 55,863 nodes and 858,490 edges, but the two files contain 858,488 hyperlinks (from 831,014 distinct posts) among 67,180 subreddits; there are no self-loops.

Each hyperlink also has a vector of 86 numeric properties of the text of the source post (e.g. numbers of characters and words, fractions of special characters, sentiment scores computed with VADER, and frequencies of LIWC word categories). There are two networks, with the same nodes and edges:

- `hyperlinks`: the hyperlinks, without the text properties.
- `hyperlinks_text`: the hyperlinks with the text properties, which make its files much larger.

The subreddit embeddings, also provided by the authors, are not included.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the subreddit.
- (Edge) `post_id`: the identifier of the source post.
- (Edge) `time`: the time of the post, as Unix time. The time zone of the upstream timestamps is not documented; they are read as US Pacific time, since they then span exactly the period stated by the authors (read as UTC, the first ones would fall on December 31, 2013, from 16:20 on, and the last one on April 30, 2017, at 16:58).
- (Edge) `sign`: the sentiment of the source post towards the target post (+1 for positive or neutral, -1 for negative).
- (Edge) `in_title`: whether the hyperlink is in the title of the post (otherwise it is in its body).
- (Edge) `text_properties` (`hyperlinks_text` only): the 86 properties of the text of the source post, in the order given by the graph property `text_property_names` (as listed by the source, with "unique works" corrected to "unique words").
citations: S. Kumar, W. L. Hamilton, J. Leskovec, and D. Jurafsky, "Community Interaction and Conflict on the Web." Proceedings of the 2018 World Wide Web Conference (WWW), 933-943 (2018).

datasets.name: reef_fish_atlantic
datasets.description:
Weighted bipartite networks of the occurrence of reef fish groups in 24 reef communities along the Western Atlantic (2 in the North-western Atlantic, 5 in the Caribbean and 17 in the South-western Atlantic, mostly along the Brazilian coast and oceanic islands), from the reef-fish community database of S. R. Floeter, D. R. Barneche and collaborators. Fishes were surveyed by underwater visual census in strip transects (20 m x 2 m) on shallow reefs (depth < 20 m), where all individuals (536,378 in total) were counted, their total length estimated in 10-cm bins, and identified to species. The data were compiled by M. Cantor and collaborators for a study of nestedness across levels of biological organization, and are distributed in the repository of that study (files `met_gen_scmass.txt`, `met_sd_scmass.txt` and `met_sdms_scmass.txt`). The species are grouped either taxonomically or into functional groups (combinations of traits, following D. Mouillot and collaborators):

- `genera`: 161 genera.
- `diet_size`: 40 functional groups combining diet and body size class.
- `diet_size_mobility_school`: 122 functional groups combining diet, body size class, mobility and school size.

A node is either a site (community) or a group of fishes, and an edge connects a group to a site where it was recorded, weighted by its abundance in the site measured by size-corrected body mass (following A. P. Allen and collaborators, as in the study of Barneche et al.), which accounts for the biological turnover among individuals of different mass and for differences in size structure among communities. The units are not stated in the source. (Cantor et al. projected these matrices onto the fish groups using the Bray-Curtis similarity of their abundances across sites.)

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `is_site`: whether the node is a site (otherwise it is a group of fishes).
- (Node) `name`: the name of the site (e.g. "abrolhos", "florida_keys") or of the group: the genus name in `genera`, or the functional group code of the source in the other networks (traits separated by underscores, e.g. "1_c2" or "1_c2_1_3", with codes not explained in the source).
- (Edge) `weight`: the size-corrected biomass of the group in the site.
citations: S. R. Floeter, W. Krohling, J. L. Gasparini, C. E. L. Ferreira, I. R. Zalmon, "Reef fish community structure on coastal islands of the southeastern Brazil: the influence of exposure and benthic cover." Environmental Biology of Fishes 78, 147-160 (2007)

D. R. Barneche, M. Kulbicki, S. R. Floeter, A. M. Friedlander, J. Maina, A. P. Allen, "Scaling metabolism from individuals to reef-fish communities at broad spatial scales." Ecology Letters 17, 1067-1076 (2014)
D. Mouillot et al., "Functional over-redundancy and high functional vulnerability in global fish faunas on tropical reefs." Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 111, 13757-13762 (2014)
A. P. Allen, J. F. Gillooly, J. H. Brown, "Linking the global carbon cycle to individual metabolism." Functional Ecology 19, 202-213 (2005)

M. Cantor, M. M. Pires, F. M. D. Marquitti, R. L. G. Raimundo, E. Sebastián-González, P. P. Coltri, S. I. Perez, D. R. Barneche, D. Y. C. Brandt, K. Nunes, F. G. Daura-Jorge, S. R. Floeter, P. R. Guimarães Jr., "Nestedness across biological scales." PLoS ONE 12(2), e0171691 (2017)

datasets.name: regulondb
datasets.description:
Networks of transcriptional regulation in the bacterium *Escherichia coli* K-12, from RegulonDB, the database of the Computational Genomics Program of the Center for Genomic Sciences (CCG) of the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM), release 14.5 (2026). RegulonDB is curated mainly from the literature (and from high-throughput experiments), and records which regulators (transcription factors, but also small RNAs and compounds such as ppGpp) activate or repress the transcription of which genes and transcription units, and which sigma factors of the RNA polymerase recognize their promoters. Each regulatory interaction has a function (activation `+`, repression `-`, dual `-+`, or unknown) and a confidence level based on its evidence: confirmed (`C`), strong (`S`) or weak (`W`) (or unknown, `?`).

The entry contains the network files of the release:

- `regulator_gene`: directed edges from each regulator to the genes whose transcription it regulates (`NetworkRegulatorGene`, with the additional columns of `NetworkRegulatorGene_internal`).
- `regulator_conformation_gene`: the same, with an edge for each active conformation of the regulator (e.g. a transcription factor bound to its effector) that regulates the gene (`NetworkRegulatorConfGene`); the regulator and the gene may be joined by several edges.
- `regulator_tu`: directed edges from each regulator to the transcription units (sets of genes transcribed from a promoter) that it regulates (`NetworkRegulatorTU`).
- `regulator_regulator`: directed edges between regulators, from each regulator to the regulators whose genes it regulates (`NetworkRegulatorRegulator`).
- `sigma_gene` and `sigma_tu`: directed edges from each sigma factor to the genes or transcription units transcribed from promoters that it recognizes (`NetworkSigmaGene` and `NetworkSigmaTU`).

The entry also contains the network of transcription factors and the genes they regulate of earlier releases (`network_tf_gene.txt`, the precursor of `NetworkRegulatorGene`), from the copies of the file kept by the Internet Archive, one network for each of its seven distinct versions:

- `tf_gene_v9.2`: release 9.2 (2016-08-09), 4,424 interactions;
- `tf_gene_v9.4`: release 9.4 (2017-08-05), 4,490 interactions;
- `tf_gene_v10.0`: release 10.0 (2018-06-18), 4,564 interactions;
- `tf_gene_v10.6.3`: release 10.6.3 (2019-02-12), 4,627 interactions;
- `tf_gene_v10.7`: release 10.7 (2020-04-05), 4,670 interactions;
- `tf_gene_v10.9`: release 10.9 (2021-06-29), 4,727 interactions;
- `tf_gene_v11.0`: release 11.0 (2022-08-22), 4,775 interactions.

These contain only transcription factors (not small RNAs or compounds). Each line of the file is an edge, so that a transcription factor and a gene can be joined by several edges with different functions (e.g. one for activation and one for repression, in about 200 cases). The files of releases 9.2 to 10.7 identify transcription factors and genes by their names only. The interactions of release 10.9 mostly have no confidence level (`null` upstream).

Except for `regulator_regulator`, the networks are bipartite: regulators (or sigma factors) and their targets are distinct nodes, even when a regulator regulates its own gene. The releases of RegulonDB before 9.2 (e.g. version 8, of 2013) are no longer available for download; data derived from earlier releases are part of the entries `ecoli_transcription`, `gerstein_regulatory` and `signed_biological`.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the regulator, sigma factor, gene or transcription unit (transcription units are named by their genes followed by their promoter in brackets, e.g. `fkpA[fkpAp1]`).
- (Node) `id`: the RegulonDB identifier (empty in `sigma_gene` and `sigma_tu`, and in the `tf_gene_<release>` networks before release 10.9, whose files give only names).
- (Node) `is_regulator` (`regulator_gene`, `regulator_conformation_gene`, `regulator_tu` and the `tf_gene_<release>` networks): whether the node is a regulator (otherwise a gene or a transcription unit).
- (Node) `regulator_genes` (`regulator_gene`, `regulator_conformation_gene` and `regulator_tu`): the gene(s) that code for the regulator (empty for regulators that are not proteins and for targets).
- (Node) `regulator_type` (`regulator_gene`): the kind of regulator (`TF`, `sRNA`, `compound` or `Regulator`; empty for genes).
- (Node) `synonyms` (`regulator_gene`): the synonyms of the regulator or the gene.
- (Node) `is_sigma` (`sigma_gene` and `sigma_tu`): whether the node is a sigma factor.
- (Edge) `function`: `+` (activation), `-` (repression), `-+` (dual; `+-` in the `tf_gene_<release>` networks), `?` or empty (unknown). In release 10.7, whose file gives the function as `activator`, `repressor` or `unknown`, these are written `+`, `-` and `?`.
- (Edge) `confidence`: the confidence level (`C`, `S`, `W` or `?`; in the `tf_gene_<release>` networks, the upstream levels `Confirmed`, `Strong` and `Weak` are written in the same way, and the level is empty where it is `null` upstream; the files of releases 9.2 and 10.6.3 do not list the column of the levels in their headers, but contain it).
- (Edge) `evidence` (the `tf_gene_<release>` networks): the evidence codes of the interaction (e.g. `GEA`, `BPP`).
- (Edge) `confidence_internal` (`regulator_gene`): the confidence level given in the "internal" version of the file (`NetworkRegulatorGene_internal`), which differs from `confidence` for 207 of the 7,351 interactions.
- (Edge) `evidence_category` (`regulator_gene`): the categories of the evidence of the interaction (e.g. `Classical expression`), from the internal file.
- (Edge) `conformation` (`regulator_conformation_gene`): the name of the active conformation of the regulator.
- (Edge) `promoter_evidence` (`sigma_gene` and `sigma_tu`): the evidence codes for the promoter and its recognition by the sigma factor.
citations: H. Salgado, S. Gama-Castro, P. Lara, C. Mejia-Almonte, G. Alarcón-Carranza, A. G. López-Almazo, et al., "RegulonDB v12.0: a comprehensive resource of transcriptional regulation in E. coli K-12." Nucleic Acids Research 52, D255-D264 (2024)

datasets.name: residence_hall
datasets.description:
Friendships among the 217 residents of a residence hall on the campus of the Australian National University, collected by C. M. Webster. The residents were interviewed individually at the start of the second semester: first, they were asked to recall all their friends currently living in the residence hall; then they were given a list of all the residents, and asked to add anyone else they considered a friend. Finally, they indicated the strength of each friendship tie; most specified three levels of friendship: "best friend", "close friend" and "friend". The data were combined into a valued matrix of reported friendship relations. The data were distributed by L. C. Freeman on his network data page at the University of California, Irvine (no longer online), from which this version was obtained via the Internet Archive.

A directed edge (i, j) indicates that resident i named resident j as a friend.

The network has the following properties:

- (Edge) `weight`: the strength of the friendship tie, from 1 to 5 (the source mentions the three levels above, but does not document the coding of the values; 95% of the ties have values 3 to 5).
citations: L. Freeman, C. Webster, & D. Kirke, "Exploring social structure using dynamic three-dimensional color images." Social Networks 20(2), 109-118 (1998)

datasets.name: reuters
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of news stories and the words they contain, from RCV1-v2, the version by Lewis, Yang, Rose and Li (2004) of the Reuters Corpus, Volume 1 (RCV1), an archive of English-language news stories written by Reuters journalists between August 1996 and August 1997. RCV1-v2 consists of 804,414 stories, which the Reuters editors had assigned to categories of three kinds: topics, industries and regions. For their text categorization experiments, Lewis et al. split them into 23,149 training stories (those of 20-31 August 1996) and 781,265 test stories, and published the tokenized stories: the words of each story, with the words of a large stop list (essentially all function words) removed, and the remaining ones replaced by their stems, in scrambled order, so that the texts of the stories cannot be reconstructed.

Each node is a story or a stem, and an edge connects each story to each stem it contains, weighted by the number of occurrences of the stem in the story. The network contains all stories of RCV1-v2, those of the training set (marked by `is_train`) and of the test set. The 2,377 stories of the original RCV1 that are not in RCV1-v2 (because of invalid category codes), which the authors also published, are left out.

The data are derived from the Reuters Corpus, Volume 1 (Reuters Ltd.); the authors of the data ask that publications using it give an attribution to Reuters.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the stem (empty for stories).
- (Node) `is_word`: whether the node is a stem (otherwise a story).
- (Node) `doc_id`: the Reuters id of the story (-1 for stems).
- (Node) `is_train`: whether the story belongs to the training set of Lewis et al. (otherwise to the test set; false for stems).
- (Node) `topics`, `industries`, `regions`: the codes of the topic, industry and region categories assigned to the story in RCV1-v2 (e.g. `CCAT`, `I81402`, `USA`; empty for stems).
- (Edge) `weight`: the number of occurrences of the stem in the story.
citations: D. D. Lewis, Y. Yang, T. G. Rose, F. Li, "RCV1: A New Benchmark Collection for Text Categorization Research." Journal of Machine Learning Research 5, 361-397 (2004).

datasets.name: reuters_terror
datasets.description:
Co-occurrence network of the words (terms) in the news stories released by the news agency Reuters during the 66 consecutive days after the September 11 attacks on the USA, starting at 9:00 AM EST on 9/11/2001. The networks were produced by S. Corman and K. Dooley (Arizona State University) using centering resonance analysis (CRA), and converted to Pajek format by V. Batagelj. Nodes are words, and there is an edge between two words if they appear in the same text unit (sentence) on a given day; each edge corresponds to one day, and is weighted by the number of co-occurrences on that day. The network was used as a case network for the visualization session at the Sunbelt XXII International Social Network Conference (2002). The data were distributed in Pajek format on the Pajek datasets page of V. Batagelj and A. Mrvar, from which this version was obtained.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the word.
- (Edge) `weight`: the number of co-occurrences of the two words on the day.
- (Edge) `day`: the day (1 to 66, where day 1 is September 11, 2001).
citations: S. R. Corman, T. Kuhn, R. D. McPhee, K. J. Dooley, "Studying Complex Discursive Systems: Centering Resonance Analysis of Communication." Human Communication Research 28(2), 157-206 (2002)

V. Batagelj, A. Mrvar, "Density based approaches to network analysis: Analysis of Reuters terror news network." Workshop on Link Analysis for Detecting Complex Behavior (LinkKDD 2003), Washington, D.C. (2003)

datasets.name: rhea_reactions
datasets.description:
Bipartite networks of biochemical reactions and the compounds that take part in them, from Rhea, the expert-curated knowledgebase of chemical and transport reactions of biological interest of the SIB Swiss Institute of Bioinformatics, which is the reference vocabulary for the enzymatic reactions annotated in UniProtKB. The data are those of release 142 (September 2, 2026).

- `reactions`: the reactions and their participants. Each reaction of Rhea is described by a reaction with an undefined direction ("master" reaction, written with `=`), and by its two directional (left-to-right and right-to-left) and its bidirectional versions; only the master reactions are nodes here, and the directional ones are given as properties. An edge goes from each compound of the left side of the equation, as written by Rhea, to the reaction, and from the reaction to each compound of its right side, with the stoichiometric coefficient of the compound and, for transport reactions, the side of the membrane (`in` or `out`); since the direction of a master reaction is undefined, the direction of the edges is only that of the written equation. A compound that is transported appears on both sides of a reaction. The compounds are small molecules of the ChEBI ontology, generic compounds (e.g. `[protein]-dithiol`, described by their reactive parts) and polymers. Obsolete reactions have no participants, and are left out.
- `hierarchy`: the classification of the reactions, where an edge goes from a reaction to a more general reaction of which it is an instance (relation `is_a`), e.g. the reaction of a specific alcohol to the reaction of "a primary alcohol". The nodes are the master reactions that take part in it; Rhea also lists the same relations between the corresponding directional reactions, which are left out.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `rhea_id` (reactions): the accession of the master reaction (e.g. `RHEA:10000`), or of the compound: `CHEBI:...` for small molecules, `GENERIC:...` for generic compounds, `POLYMER:...` for polymers.
- (Node) `is_reaction`: whether the node is a reaction (otherwise it is a compound).
- (Node) `name`: the equation of the reaction, with the names of the compounds (e.g. `pentanamide + H2O = pentanoate + NH4(+)`), or the name of the compound.
- (Node) `status`: the curation status of the reaction (`Approved` or `Preliminary`; empty for compounds).
- (Node) `is_transport`, `is_balanced`: whether the reaction is a transport reaction, and whether it is chemically balanced.
- (Node) `ec`: the EC numbers of the enzymes that catalyze the reaction.
- (Node) `directional_ids`: the accessions of the left-to-right, right-to-left and bidirectional versions of the reaction.
- (Node) `citations`: the PubMed identifiers of the articles that support the reaction.
- (Node) `compound_class` (reactions): the kind of compound: `SmallMolecule`, `GenericPolypeptide`, `GenericPolynucleotide`, `GenericHeteropolysaccharide`, `GenericSmallMolecule`, `GenericCompound` or `Polymer` (empty for reactions).
- (Node) `formula`, `charge`: the chemical formula and charge of the compound (empty if not given; for polymers they are given per repeating unit, e.g. `(-4)(-1)n`, as in Rhea).
- (Node) `chebi_ids`: the ChEBI identifiers of the compound: itself for small molecules, the reactive parts for generic compounds, the underlying ChEBI entity for polymers.
- (Edge) `coefficient` (reactions): the stoichiometric coefficient of the compound (e.g. `1`, `2`, `N`, `2n`, `N+1`).
- (Edge) `location` (reactions): the side of the membrane of the compound in a transport reaction (`in` or `out`; empty otherwise).
citations: P. Bansal, A. Morgat, K. B. Axelsen, V. Muthukrishnan, E. Coudert, L. Aimo, N. Hyka-Nouspikel, E. Gasteiger, A. Kerhornou, T. B. Neto, M. Pozzato, M.-C. Blatter, A. Ignatchenko, N. Redaschi, A. Bridge, "Rhea, the reaction knowledgebase in 2022." Nucleic Acids Research 50, D693-D700 (2022)

datasets.name: rhesus_monkey
datasets.description:
Grooming episodes among 16 adult rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta) of a free-ranging community in Cayo Santiago (Puerto Rico), observed by D. S. Sade in June and July 1963. Seven of the monkeys are males, and the other nine are females. The data were distributed by L. C. Freeman on his network data page at the University of California, Irvine (no longer online), from which this version was obtained via the Internet Archive.

A directed edge (i, j) indicates that monkey i was observed grooming monkey j. (The direction is not stated explicitly in the source, which describes the data as a non-symmetric table of grooming episodes; the row animal is taken as the groomer.)

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the identifier of the monkey.
- (Node) `male`: whether the monkey is male.
- (Edge) `weight`: the number of grooming episodes.
citations: D. S. Sade. "Sociometrics of Macaca mulatta I. Linkages and cliques in grooming matrices." Folia Primatologica 18(3-4), 196-223 (1972)

datasets.name: roadnet
datasets.description:
Road networks of three U.S. states: California (`CA`), Pennsylvania (`PA`) and Texas (`TX`), distributed by the Stanford Network Analysis Project (SNAP) and used by J. Leskovec, K. Lang, A. Dasgupta and M. Mahoney to study the community structure of large networks. Nodes are road intersections and endpoints, and edges are the road segments connecting them. The source and date of the underlying road data are not documented.

The source files list each undirected road segment twice, once in each direction; here each segment is represented by a single undirected edge. The node IDs of the source files are not contiguous; only the IDs that occur in the edge list are included.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the node ID in the source data.
citations: J. Leskovec, K. Lang, A. Dasgupta, M. Mahoney. "Community Structure in Large Networks: Natural Cluster Sizes and the Absence of Large Well-Defined Clusters." Internet Mathematics 6(1), 29-123 (2009). arxiv:0810.1355

datasets.name: rocketfuel
datasets.description:
Router-level and PoP-level maps of Internet service providers (ISPs), measured by Spring, Mahajan, Wetherall and Anderson with Rocketfuel, an ISP topology mapping engine. Rocketfuel ran traceroutes from about 800 vantage points (public traceroute servers), chosen with BGP routing information so as to cross the ISP being mapped, recognized the routers of the ISP and their locations from their DNS names (with ISP-specific naming conventions), and resolved the aliases (the IP addresses of different interfaces of the same router) with a technique of its own. The data set contains three kinds of networks:

- `routers_<AS>` (e.g. `routers_1239`): the router-level maps of ten ISPs (SIGCOMM 2002; files of 2003), identified by their AS numbers: 1221 (Telstra, Australia), 1239 (Sprintlink, US), 1755 (Ebone, Europe), 2914 (Verio, US), 3257 (Tiscali, Europe), 3356 (Level 3, US), 3967 (Exodus, US), 4755 (VSNL, India), 6461 (Abovenet, US) and 7018 (AT&T, US). Nodes are the routers of the ISP (the full maps of the source, the `.cch` files), and an undirected edge connects two routers seen directly connected in some traceroute. The maps include the routers that could belong to the ISP, such as chains of routers leading to customers; the vertex property `radius` allows restricting them to the backbone and gateway routers (radius 0), or to these and their direct neighbors (radius at most 1, the maps mostly used in the paper). The links of the routers to external addresses (outside the ISP) are not included as edges; their number is stored in `n_external`.
- `backbone_<AS>` (e.g. `backbone_1239`): the backbone topologies of six of these ISPs (1221, 1239, 1755, 3257, 3967 and 6461), annotated with link weights inferred from the observed paths, assuming shortest-path routing, and with geographical latencies (IMW 2002). Nodes are backbone routers, named by their location and an identifier (these identifiers are not the same as the router identifiers of the `routers_<AS>` networks, which were assigned anew), and undirected edges are the backbone links.
- `pops`: a PoP-level map of 67 ISPs and of the links between them (SIGCOMM 2003), including the PoPs of two more ISPs that appear only in links to these. Nodes are points of presence (PoPs), i.e. the cities where an ISP has routers, and an undirected edge connects two PoPs that were seen connected in some traceroute, either within an ISP, with link weights inferred as above, or between two ISPs (peering links).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Graph) `isp` (`routers_<AS>` and `backbone_<AS>`): the name of the ISP.
- (Node) `uid` (`routers_<AS>`): the router identifier of the source.
- (Node) `name` (`routers_<AS>`): the DNS name of the router (or one of its IP addresses, if it has no name).
- (Node) `location` (`routers_<AS>`): the location of the router, as `city, state/country` (`T` if it is ambiguous, e.g. connected to routers in different locations, and `?` if it is unknown).
- (Node) `location_from_dns` (`routers_<AS>`): whether the location was derived from the DNS name (true) or from the connectivity of the router (false).
- (Node) `backbone` (`routers_<AS>`): whether it is a backbone router (connected to other cities), as opposed to access (gateway) and customer routers.
- (Node) `no_alias_response` (`routers_<AS>`): whether the router did not respond to alias resolution (and might not be a distinct router).
- (Node) `radius` (`routers_<AS>`): the distance in hops from a named backbone or gateway router (capped at 5).
- (Node) `n_external` (`routers_<AS>`): the number of the router's links to addresses outside the ISP.
- (Node) `name` (`backbone_<AS>`): the name of the router in the source (its location and an identifier).
- (Node) `location` (`backbone_<AS>`): its location.
- (Edge) `weight` (`backbone_<AS>`): the inferred link weight.
- (Edge) `latency` (`backbone_<AS>`): the latency of the link, in milliseconds, estimated from the geographical distance (rounded up).
- (Node) `name` (`pops`): the name of the PoP in the source (`AS:city`).
- (Node) `asn` (`pops`): the AS number of the ISP.
- (Node) `city` (`pops`): the city of the PoP.
- (Edge) `count` (`pops`): the number of times the link was observed in the traceroutes.
- (Edge) `latency` (`pops`): the latency of the link, in milliseconds, estimated from the geographical distance (zero for most links between ISPs in the same city).
- (Edge) `weight` (`pops`): the inferred link weight (`NaN` for links between ISPs).
- (Edge) `peering` (`pops`): whether the link connects two ISPs.
citations: N. Spring, R. Mahajan, D. Wetherall, "Measuring ISP topologies with Rocketfuel." Proceedings of ACM SIGCOMM 2002, 133-145 (2002)

R. Mahajan, N. Spring, D. Wetherall, T. Anderson, "Inferring link weights using end-to-end measurements." Proceedings of the 2nd ACM SIGCOMM Workshop on Internet Measurement (IMW 2002), 231-236 (2002)
N. Spring, R. Mahajan, T. Anderson, "The causes of path inflation." Proceedings of ACM SIGCOMM 2003, 113-124 (2003)

datasets.name: roget_thesaurus
datasets.description:
Cross-references between the 1022 categories of the 1879 edition of Peter Mark Roget's *Thesaurus of English Words and Phrases* (edited by J. L. Roget), from the file roget.dat of D. E. Knuth's Stanford GraphBase, converted into Pajek format by A. Mrvar. A directed edge points from one category to another if Roget gave a reference to the latter among the words and phrases of the former, or if the two categories were directly related to each other by their positions in the book (e.g. category 312, "ascent", points to 224, "obliquity", and 316, "leap", by explicit cross-references, and to 313, "descent", with which it is paired). The network contains one self-loop. The data were distributed in Pajek format on the Pajek datasets page of V. Batagelj and A. Mrvar, from which this version was obtained.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the category (the node index corresponds to the category number).
citations: D. E. Knuth, "The Stanford GraphBase: A Platform for Combinatorial Computing." ACM Press, New York (1993)

datasets.name: roman_roads
datasets.description:
The network of the roads of the Roman Empire (ca. 300 BCE to 300 CE) from Itiner-e, a digital atlas of Roman roads compiled by P. de Soto, A. Pažout, T. Brughmans and many collaborators (projects MINERVA, Aarhus University, and Viator-e, Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona). The roads were identified from the scholarly literature (atlases, regional studies, survey and excavation reports, gazetteers and milestones), located on modern and historical topographic maps and aerial and satellite imagery, and digitized as 14,769 road segments, each between two ancient places or road crossings, covering the empire at its largest extent (ca. 150 CE). The data were collected between 2020 and 2024.

A node is an end point of road segments (a place or a road crossing), and an edge is a road segment. The network was constructed here from the geometries of the segments: the end points of segments that lie within 1 mm of each other (in the World Mercator projection of the data) are merged into one node, which joins the segments into 13 connected components (the main landmasses and islands; the authors report 14). The network is undirected; some places are joined by several segments (parallel edges). The courses of the roads (the polylines) are not included, and neither is the field `Route_Type`, which repeats the road type as a number, and the constant fields `MaxSimpTol` and `MinSimpTol`.

The data are the canonical 2024 version (version 1.3 of the Zenodo record, September 2025). The earlier versions of the record contain the same segments with the same lengths and attributes, except for corrections of the text fields (version 1, which also has the geometries in longitude and latitude, with more points) and of the geometries of 19 segments (versions 1.1 and 1.2); they are not included. A growing version of the atlas is maintained at itiner-e.org.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `latitude` and `longitude`: the geographical position (converted from the World Mercator coordinates of the data).
- (Edge) `fid`: the identifier of the segment.
- (Edge) `name`: its name, formed by the names of the places at its ends (ancient names where known).
- (Edge) `type`, `Main Road` or `Secondary Road`.
- (Edge) `certainty`: the certainty of the location of the road's course (`Certain`, `Conjectured` or `Hypothetical`).
- (Edge) `lower_date` and `upper_date`: the years of construction and abandonment of the road (negative for BCE), and `lower_date_error` and `upper_date_error`, the possible time spans before and after them (NaN where unknown).
- (Edge) `construction_period`: the emperor or magistrate under whom the road was built (if known).
- (Edge) `itinerary`: the ancient name of the road or the itinerary that it is a part of (e.g. `Tabula Peutingeriana`).
- (Edge) `description`: a brief description.
- (Edge) `contributor`: the person who digitized the segment.
- (Edge) `bibliography`: the sources used.
- (Edge) `length`: the geodesic length of the segment (m).
- (Edge) `avg_slope`: the average slope along the segment (degrees).
- (Edge) `passability`: a number between 0 and 1 (undocumented upstream).
citations: P. de Soto, A. Pažout, T. Brughmans, P. B. Vahlstrup, Á. Auir, T. Bongers, J. E. B. Christoffersen, M. Crépy, M. H. Johansen, J. Lewis, L. Manière, M. R. Massa, L. M. H. Møller, B. Redon, G. Renda, H. Şahin, A. Sobotková, A. L. Spatzek, P. Verhagen, B. Weissova, "Itiner-e: A high-resolution dataset of roads of the Roman Empire." Scientific Data 12, 1731 (2025)
P. de Soto, A. Pažout, T. Brughmans et al., "A High-Resolution Dataset of Roads of the Roman Empire: Itiner-e static version 2024." Zenodo, version 1.3 (2025)

datasets.name: rome_roads
datasets.description:
Directed road network covering a large part of the city of Rome, Italy, as of 1999. Nodes are road intersections, and a directed edge $(i,j)$ is a road or road segment along which one can drive from intersection $i$ to intersection $j$ (two-way roads appear as a pair of opposite edges); edges are weighted by their physical length. The network was contributed by G. Storchi, P. Dell'Olmo (University of Rome "La Sapienza") and M. Gentili (University of Salerno), and was distributed by the 9th DIMACS Implementation Challenge on shortest paths (2006) as one of its benchmark instances, in the challenge's graph format. The network contains a few parallel edges, which are kept as in the source file.

The edges have the property `distance`, the length of the road segment, in meters.[^icon]

[^icon]: Description obtained in part from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.

datasets.name: route_views
datasets.description:
Daily snapshots of the graph of the Internet at the level of autonomous systems (ASs), from the University of Oregon Route Views Project, distributed by the Stanford Network Analysis Project (SNAP) and used by J. Leskovec, J. Kleinberg and C. Faloutsos to study the evolution of networks over time. An autonomous system is a network under a single administrative domain (such as an Internet service provider or a university) that exchanges traffic with neighboring ASs, called peers. The Route Views Project collected the routing tables of the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP), which is used to exchange routing information between ASs, from which the "who talks to whom" network can be constructed. Nodes are ASs and an undirected edge indicates that two ASs are peers. There are 733 daily snapshots, spanning an interval of 785 days from 8 November 1997 to 2 January 2000 (some days are missing); each network is named after its date, as in `19971108`. Parallel edges and isolated nodes were removed, but the networks contain self-loops.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `as_id`: the AS number.

datasets.name: rt_retweets
datasets.description:
Networks of retweets among Twitter users, distributed by the Network Data Repository (R. A. Rossi and N. K. Ahmed) in its collection of retweet networks. Nodes are Twitter users (anonymized as consecutive indices), and edges are retweets. The provenance of most of the networks is documented only briefly by the repository. There are 33 networks:

- 29 networks of retweets of tweets with a given hashtag, collected from July to September 2012 by the Truthy project of Indiana University (`alwefaq`, `assad`, `bahrain`, `barackobama`, `damascus`, `dash`, `gmanews`, `gop`, `http`, `islam`, `israel`, `justinbieber`, `ksa`, `lebanon`, `libya`, `lolgop`, `mittromney`, `obama`, `occupy`, `occupywallstnyc`, `oman`, `onedirection`, `p2`, `qatif`, `saudi`, `tcot`, `tlot`, `uae`, `voteonedirection`, named by the hashtag). These are directed networks, in which each ordered pair of users appears at most once, with a timestamp; the meaning of the direction (who retweeted whom) is not documented. A few edges are self-loops, as given.
- `retweet` and `retweet_crawl`: undirected retweet networks from the same collection, without timestamps (96 and 1.1 million users).
- `pol`: retweets among users who tweeted about US politics in the six weeks before the 2010 US midterm elections, from the study of political polarization of M. D. Conover and collaborators. A directed multigraph: repeated retweets between the same users, at different times, are separate edges; the repository describes the network as undirected, and the meaning of the direction is not documented.
- `twitter_copen`: an undirected network of retweets and mentions during the two weeks of the UN Climate Change Conference in Copenhagen (2009), from the study of N. K. Ahmed and collaborators on network sampling.

The retweet network about the discovery of the Higgs boson of the same collection (`rt-higgs`) is the retweet network of the entry `twitter_higgs`, and is not included.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Edge) `time` (hashtag networks and `pol`): the time of the retweet, in Unix time.
citations: R. A. Rossi and N. K. Ahmed, "The Network Data Repository with Interactive Graph Analytics and Visualization." Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence 29(1) (2015).

R. A. Rossi, D. F. Gleich, A. H. Gebremedhin, and M. M. A. Patwary, "Fast maximum clique algorithms for large graphs." Proceedings of the 23rd International Conference on World Wide Web (WWW Companion), 365-366 (2014).

M. D. Conover, J. Ratkiewicz, M. Francisco, B. Goncalves, F. Menczer, and A. Flammini, "Political Polarization on Twitter." Proceedings of the International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media (ICWSM) 5, 89-96 (2011).

N. K. Ahmed, F. Berchmans, J. Neville, and R. Kompella, "Time-based sampling of social network activity graphs." Proceedings of the Eighth Workshop on Mining and Learning with Graphs (MLG), 1-9 (2010).

datasets.name: russian_trade
datasets.description:
The network of river trade routes among 39 towns of medieval Russia (12th-13th centuries), as reconstructed by the geographer F. R. Pitts to study the growth of Moscow. Towns are connected if they were adjacent along the network of navigable rivers (and portages), which were traveled by boat in summer and by sled over the ice in winter, and which supported trade (e.g. of slaves, amber, honey and furs) and other social exchanges. The data were distributed by A. Clauset, together with the article by Pitts (1978).

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the town. The data file only gives node numbers; the names were assigned from Table 1 of Pitts (1978), assuming the nodes are numbered in the order of that table (the shortest-path distances computed from the network agree closely with the ones listed there). Three unnamed places are labeled "A", "B" and "C" as in the original table.
citations: F. R. Pitts, "The medieval river trade network of Russia revisited." Social Networks 1(3), 285-292 (1978)

datasets.name: russian_troll_mentions
datasets.description:
Directed network of mentions among Twitter accounts linked to the Internet Research Agency (IRA), a Russian "troll factory". The tweets were collected by Darren Linvill and Patrick Warren (Clemson University), who gathered, using the Social Studio tool, nearly 3 million tweets sent between February 2012 and May 2018 (mostly from 2015 to 2017) from the IRA-linked handles that Twitter identified and provided to the US Congress in November 2017 and June 2018, and coded the accounts by their theme. The tweets were published by FiveThirtyEight. The network was constructed by Christopher S. Marcum from the version of the tweets published on August 1, 2018: tweet authors and contents were lower-cased, the handles mentioned with "@" were extracted from the tweet texts (which include retweets), and only mentions of handles that are themselves authors in the data were kept. Each node is a troll account (only accounts that mention or are mentioned by another troll account are included), and a directed edge from account i to account j indicates that i mentioned j in at least one tweet. Self-mentions were discarded when the network was built, so that 33 accounts (presumably those that mentioned only themselves) are isolated nodes.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the Twitter handle (lower case).
- (Node) `activity`: the number of tweets by the account in the data.
- (Node) `account_type`: the specific theme of the account, as coded by Linvill and Warren (e.g. "Right", "left", "Russian", "Hashtager", "Koch").
- (Node) `account_category`: the general theme of the account, as coded by Linvill and Warren ("RightTroll", "LeftTroll", "NewsFeed", "HashtagGamer", "Fearmonger", "NonEnglish", "Commercial", "Unknown").
- (Node) `region`: the list of region classifications of the account's tweets, as determined by Social Studio (an empty string means a tweet without region).
- (Node) `language`: the list of languages of the account's tweets.
- (Node) `max_following`, `min_following`: the maximum and minimum number of accounts followed by the account at the time of its tweets.
- (Node) `max_followers`, `min_followers`: the maximum and minimum number of followers of the account at the time of its tweets.
- (Node) `first_post`, `last_post`: the dates and times of the first and last tweets of the account (as "YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS").
- (Edge) `mentions`: the number of mentions of the target in tweets by the source (repeated mentions in the same tweet are counted separately).
citations: D. L. Linvill, P. L. Warren, "Troll Factories: Manufacturing Specialized Disinformation on Twitter." Political Communication 37(4), 447-467 (2020)
C. S. Marcum, "Russian Troll Twitter Mention Network." GitHub repository (2018)
O. Roeder, "Why We're Sharing 3 Million Russian Troll Tweets." FiveThirtyEight (2018)

datasets.name: sa_companies
datasets.description:
A small bipartite network of the directorships held in 1905 by six leading financiers of South Africa in five gold, diamond and finance companies: De Beers Consolidated, the Premier (Transvaal) Diamond Company, Rand Mines, Consolidated Goldfields and the British South Africa Company (the "Chartered Company"). The data are from the chapter on the financier of J. A. Hobson's *The Evolution of Modern Capitalism* (new and revised edition of 1906), which gives a table of the directorships of South African financiers in 1905, constructed from the Directory of Directors and the Stock Exchange Year Book of 1905, and discusses the interlocks it shows among the main companies (pp. 270-271 in the printing of 1919). The network is the subset of that table transcribed in Cory Brunson's bitriad R package (data set `southafrica1905`); the other directors and companies of Hobson's table, and the numbers of directorships it gives, are not included.

Nodes are persons and companies, and an edge connects a person to a company of which they were a director (Wernher and Beit were life governors of De Beers).

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the person (surname and initials, as in the bitriad package; Hobson gives J. C. Wernher and J. R. Maguire) or of the company.
- (Node) `is_company`: whether the node is a company.
citations: J. A. Hobson, "The Evolution of Modern Capitalism: A Study of Machine Production." New and revised edition, The Walter Scott Publishing Co. (1906)

datasets.name: sampson_monastery
datasets.description:
Affect relations among a group of novices preparing to join a monastic order in a New England monastery, from the ethnographic study of S. F. Sampson. The novices were asked to name the three peers they liked most and the three they liked least (first, second and third choices). The relations were measured at five moments in time; the fourth measurement (T4) took place one week before four of the novices were expelled from the monastery. Based on his observations, Sampson divided the novices into four groups: the Young Turks, who arrived in a period of change and questioned the practices of the monastery; the Loyal Opposition, who entered the monastery first and defended those practices; the Outcasts, who were not accepted in the group; and an interstitial group that did not take sides. The data were distributed on the Pajek datasets page of the book *Exploratory Social Network Analysis with Pajek* (de Nooy, Mrvar and Batagelj), from which this version was obtained.[^icon]

- `longitudinal`: the choices of 25 novices at the five time points. Each edge points from the novice making the choice to the chosen peer, with one edge per time point at which the choice was made.
- `T4`: the most and least liked peer of each of the 18 novices present at the fourth measurement, with edges pointing from the novice making the choice to the chosen peer.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the novice.
- (Node) `cloisterville`: whether the novice attended the minor seminary of "Cloisterville" before coming to the monastery.
- (Node) `faction` (`T4` only): Sampson's classification into factions (1: Young Turks, 2: Loyal Opposition, 3: Outcasts, 4: interstitial group). The presence intervals given for some novices in the source file are not included.
- (Edge) `weight`: the signed rank of the choice (`longitudinal`: 3, 2 and 1 for the first, second and third most liked peer, and -3, -2 and -1 for the first, second and third least liked; `T4`: 1 for the most liked and -1 for the least liked peer).
- (Edge) `time` (`longitudinal` only): the time point (1 to 5) of the choice.

[^icon]: Description obtained in part from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.
citations: S. F. Sampson, "A Novitiate in a Period of Change: An Experimental and Case Study of Social Relationships." PhD thesis, Cornell University (1968)
W. de Nooy, A. Mrvar, V. Batagelj, "Exploratory Social Network Analysis with Pajek." Cambridge University Press (2005)

datasets.name: sanak_food_webs
datasets.description:
Two highly resolved food webs of the Sanak Archipelago, in the western Gulf of Alaska (50 km south of the tip of the Alaska Peninsula), which include humans as the hunter-gatherer Aleut (Unangan) top predator. The intertidal web covers the benthic habitat up to the terrestrial vegetation exposed at low tide and the pelagic habitat above it at high tide, and the taxa were compiled from quadrats, sediment cores and visual searches over three years across the archipelago. The nearshore marine web covers the marine habitat within 80 km of the archipelago, with taxa from shallow-water observations and published occurrence records (mostly from GBIF and OBIS). Several ubiquitous microscopic taxa (e.g. bacteria, ciliates, dinoflagellates, foraminifera) were assumed to be present in both webs, and birds were included in one or both webs according to their foraging. The feeding links were observed in the field or compiled from 1,532 publications, reports and databases (from observations, gut or scat contents, and expert opinion); the human feeding links come from the zooarchaeology of Sanak Island middens, ethnographic data, and interviews with modern Unangan. Taxa were resolved as finely as possible, and lumped into coarser taxonomic groups (e.g. genus or family) when the information was incomplete. The webs are cumulative, describing the feeding relationships of taxa that lived or fed in those habitats since the human settlement of the archipelago, about 7,000 years ago.

- `intertidal`: the Sanak intertidal food web.
- `nearshore`: the Sanak nearshore marine food web.

A directed edge goes from a consumer (predator) to its resource (prey). Self-loops denote cannibalism. Node properties: `name`, the scientific name of the taxon (or a descriptive name for groups such as "Detritus complex"); `tsn`, the Taxonomic Serial Number of the taxon in the Integrated Taxonomic Information System (ITIS), or an identifier of the form `san<number>` for taxa without one; `phylum`, the phylum of the taxon ("NA" for non-living nodes and biofilm). Humans are the node "Homo sapiens". The source lists the phylum of the American dipper (Cinclus mexicanus) as "Mollusca" in the intertidal web (and "Chordata" in the nearshore web); it is kept as given.
citations: J. A. Dunne, H. Maschner, M. W. Betts, N. Huntly, R. Russell, R. J. Williams, S. A. Wood, "The roles and impacts of human hunter-gatherers in North Pacific marine food webs." Scientific Reports 6, 21179 (2016)

datasets.name: sawmill
datasets.description:
Communication ties among the 36 employees of a small enterprise, a sawmill, studied by J. H. Michael and J. G. Massey. All employees were asked to indicate the frequency with which they discussed work matters with each of their colleagues, on a five-point scale ranging from less than once a week to several times a day, and two employees are connected if they rated their contact as three or more (it is not known whether both employees, or at least one of them, had to rate the tie in this way). The employees are Spanish-speaking (Hispanic) or English-speaking, and work in the two main sections of the sawmill: the mill, where tree trunks are sawn into logs, and the planer section, where logs are planed; two employees work in the yard, and there are some managers and additional officials. The data were distributed on the Pajek datasets page of the book *Exploratory Social Network Analysis with Pajek* (de Nooy, Mrvar and Batagelj), from which this version was obtained.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: a label that encodes the language and section of the employee: the first letter is H (Hispanic) or E (English-speaking), followed by the section, M (mill) or P (planer), and a number (e.g. "HP-10" is a Hispanic employee working in the planer section); Y-1 and Y-2 work in the yard, and the other labels give the position of the managers and officials (e.g. "Owner", "Forester").
citations: J. H. Michael, J. G. Massey, "Modeling the communication network in a sawmill." Forest Products Journal 47(9), 25-30 (1997)
W. de Nooy, A. Mrvar, V. Batagelj, "Exploratory Social Network Analysis with Pajek." Cambridge University Press (2005)

datasets.name: sawmill_strike
datasets.description:
Informal communication among 24 employees of a wood-processing facility during a strike, studied by J. H. Michael. A new management team proposed changes to the workers' compensation package, which the workers did not accept; they started a strike, which led to a negotiation stalemate. Management then asked an outside consultant to analyze the communication structure among the employees. The consultant asked all employees to indicate the frequency with which they discussed the strike with each of their colleagues, on a five-point scale from "almost never" (less than once per week) to "very often" (several times per day), and two employees are connected if at least one of them indicated a frequency of three or more. The data were distributed on the Pajek datasets page of the book *Exploratory Social Network Analysis with Pajek* (de Nooy, Mrvar and Batagelj), from which this version was obtained.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the (pseudonymous) first name of the employee.
- (Node) `group`: the age and language group of the employee (1: Spanish-speaking, 2: English-speaking and 30 years old or younger, 3: English-speaking and older than 30).
citations: J. H. Michael, "Labor dispute reconciliation in a forest products manufacturing facility." Forest Products Journal 47(11/12), 41-45 (1997)
W. de Nooy, A. Mrvar, V. Batagelj, "Exploratory Social Network Analysis with Pajek." Cambridge University Press (2005)

datasets.name: saxena_terror_india
datasets.description:
Yearly networks (2000 to 2003) of terrorist organisations operating in the Indian state of Jammu and Kashmir, from the study by Saxena, Santhanam and Basu (2004). Nodes are organisations (vertex property `name`), and an edge indicates that two organisations were mentioned together ("co-occurrence") in various sources, e.g. online. The source matrices are meant to be symmetric; where the two directions differ, the tie is included. Data distributed by the UCINET datasets collection (University of Manchester).[^ucinet]

[^ucinet]: Description obtained in part from the [UCINET datasets page](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/datasets/covert-networks/saxena-terror-india).
citations: S. Saxena, K. Santhanam, and A. Basu, "Application of social network analysis (SNA) to terrorist networks in Jammu & Kashmir." Strategic Analysis 28(1), 84-101 (2004)

datasets.name: scigrid_gas
datasets.description:
Networks of the European natural gas transmission system, compiled by J. Diettrich, A. Pluta and W. Medjroubi (DLR Institute of Networked Energy Systems) in the SciGRID_gas project. The IGGIELGN data set combines several public sources: the InternetDaten (INET) data set, collected from web pages, press releases and other public documents, the data sets of Gas Infrastructure Europe (GIE), Gas Storage Europe (GSE) and the International Gas Union (IGU), the network of the LKD project, the ENTSOG transmission capacity map, and data sets for Great Britain and Norway; missing attributes (e.g. diameters, capacities and pressures of pipes) were estimated by heuristics and statistical methods.

A node is a point of the network (the end of a pipe segment, or a facility), and an edge is a pipeline segment between two nodes, positioned along the pipeline's route. The networks are undirected (the direction of the segments in the data is not kept); some pairs of nodes are joined by several segments (parallel pipelines), and some segments start and end at the same node (self-loops). The facilities (compressor stations, LNG terminals, storages, production sites, consumers and border points) are attached to nodes, and are included as counts at each node; their attributes (capacities, operators, ...) are not included, and neither are the courses of the pipes (as polylines) and the uncertainties and estimation methods of the attributes.

There is one network for each of the three versions of the data set (`v1.0.0`, `v1.1.1` and `v1.1.2`, published from March to May 2021). The network of version 1.0.0 is connected and has 4 self-loops; those of versions 1.1.1 and 1.1.2 have 24 components and 106 and 128 self-loops, respectively. In version 1.1.1, the country codes of all pipe segments are `FI` (apparently an error, corrected in version 1.1.2).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the node's id.
- (Node) `label`: its name in the data (if any).
- (Node) `latitude` and `longitude`: the geographical position.
- (Node) `country`: the two-letter country code (`XX` for nodes offshore or outside Europe).
- (Node) `nuts_id`: the NUTS 3 region (versions 1.1.1 and 1.1.2).
- (Node) `num_compressors`, `num_lngs`, `num_storages`, `num_productions`, `num_consumers` and `num_border_points`: the numbers of facilities of each kind at the node.
- (Edge) `name`: the segment's id (its prefix indicates the source of the data).
- (Edge) `source_id`: the id of the original pipeline in the source data.
- (Edge) `countries`: the country codes of the two ends, separated by a semicolon.
- (Edge) `diameter` (mm): `length` (km), `max_capacity` (millions of cubic meters per day) and `max_pressure` (bar), the pipe's diameter, length, maximum capacity and maximum pressure.
- (Edge) `is_h_gas`: whether it transports high-calorific gas.
- (Edge) `bidirectional`: whether the gas can flow in both directions.
- (Edge) `start_year` and `end_year`: the years of commissioning and decommissioning (if known).
- (Edge) `water_depth`: the water depth of offshore pipes (m, version 1.0.0). Missing values are NaN.
citations: J. Diettrich, A. Pluta, W. Medjroubi, "SciGRID_gas IGGIELGN." Zenodo, versions 1.0.0, 1.1.1 and 1.1.2 (2021)

A. Pluta, W. Medjroubi, J. C. Diettrich, J. Dasenbrock, H.-P. Tetens, J. E. Sandoval, O. Lunsdorf, "SciGRID_gas - Data Model of the European Gas Transport Network." 2022 Open Source Modelling and Simulation of Energy Systems (OSMSES), 1-7 (2022)

datasets.name: scn_functional_networks
datasets.description:
Functional networks between the neurons of the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of mice, the master circadian clock located in the hypothalamus, inferred by Abel et al. from single-cell bioluminescence recordings. Slices of the SCN of five mice expressing a bioluminescent reporter of the clock protein PERIOD2 (PER2::LUC) were imaged at a rate of one sample per hour, and the cells were tracked over time. The neurons were desynchronized by blocking their communication with the neurotoxin tetrodotoxin (TTX), which was then washed out, and the network was inferred from the bioluminescence traces of the individual cells while they resynchronized after the washout.

Two cells are connected if the maximal information coefficient (MIC) between their bioluminescence traces after the washout exceeds a threshold, which was chosen separately for each SCN (0.949, 0.935, 0.9895, 0.968 and 0.969 for SCNs 1 to 5, respectively), as given by the authors. Cells without any connection above the threshold are kept as isolated nodes.

- `scn1`, ..., `scn5`: the functional networks of the five SCN slices.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `pos`: the (x, y) location of the cell in the image.
- (Node) `bioluminescence`: the time series of the bioluminescence of the cell during the TTX washout, with one sample per hour.
- (Edge) `mic`: the maximal information coefficient between the two cells.
citations: J. H. Abel, K. Meeker, D. Granados-Fuentes, P. C. St. John, T. J. Wang, B. B. Bales, F. J. Doyle, E. D. Herzog, L. R. Petzold, "Functional network inference of the suprachiasmatic nucleus." Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 113(16), 4512-4517 (2016)

datasets.name: scotland_interlocks
datasets.description:
Interlocking directorates among the 108 largest joint stock companies in Scotland in 1904-1905 (64 non-financial firms, 8 banks, 14 insurance companies and 22 investment and property companies), compiled by W. de Nooy from the appendix of the book *The Anatomy of Scottish Capital* by J. Scott and M. Hughes. The bipartite network connects each of the 136 multiple directors listed there (persons sitting on more than one of these boards) to the boards on which they sit. Sixteen of the companies share no director with the others, and appear as isolated nodes. (The source documentation mentions 356 affiliations, and two directors with a single board, while the data file contains 358 affiliations and no such directors.) The data were distributed on the Pajek datasets page of the book *Exploratory Social Network Analysis with Pajek* (de Nooy, Mrvar and Batagelj), from which this version was obtained.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the company or director.
- (Node) `is_company`: whether the node is a company (otherwise a director).
- (Node) `industry` (companies only, 0 for directors): the industry type of the company (1: oil & mining, 2: railway, 3: engineering & steel, 4: electricity & chemicals, 5: domestic products, 6: banks, 7: insurance, 8: investment).
- (Node) `capital` (companies only, 0 for directors): the total capital or deposits of the company, in thousands of pounds sterling.
citations: J. Scott, M. Hughes, "The Anatomy of Scottish Capital: Scottish Companies and Scottish Capital, 1900-1979." Croom Helm, London (1980)
W. de Nooy, A. Mrvar, V. Batagelj, "Exploratory Social Network Analysis with Pajek." Cambridge University Press (2005)

datasets.name: scotus_majority
datasets.description:
Networks of citations among majority opinions of the Supreme Court of the United States (SCOTUS), compiled by J. H. Fowler and S. Jeon. Nodes are cases (majority opinions) and a directed edge indicates that the opinion of one case cites another case. The two versions come from two data releases:

- `2008`: data accompanying Fowler and Jeon (Social Networks, 2008), covering the cases in the U.S. Reports from 1754 to 2002. The citations were extracted from the text of the opinions. Edges point from the citing case to the cited case. Only cases that are part of at least one citation are included.
- `2007`: replication data of Fowler et al. (Political Analysis, 2007), with cases decided from 1791 to 2005 identified by their LexisNexis identifiers. Edges point from the citing case to the cited case. For about 9,600 nodes no metadata is available, and their properties are empty (text) or NaN (numerical).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name` (`2008`): the numerical case identifier of the data set.
- (Node) `usid` (`2008`): the U.S. Reports citation (e.g. `3US320`).
- (Node) `parties` (`2008`): the names of the parties to the case.
- (Node) `year` (`2008`): the year of the case.
- (Node) `overruled` (`2008`): the identifier of the case that overruled it (0 if none).
- (Node) `overruling` (`2008`): the list of identifiers of the cases it overruled.
- (Node) `oxford`, `liihc` (`2008`): whether the case appears in the Oxford list of salient cases and in the Legal Information Institute's list of important cases, respectively.
- (Node) `lexid` (`2007`): the LexisNexis identifier.
- (Node) `usid` (`2007`): the U.S. Reports citation.
- (Node) `name` (`2007`): the parties to the case.
- (Node) `citedyr_num` (`2007`): the year of the case.
- (Node) `citingyr_num` (`2007`): the year in which the variables were measured (2005).
- (Node) `age` (`2007`): the age of the case in years.
- (Node) `auth_num` (`2007`): the authority score (the hub/authority centrality of Kleinberg) of the case.
- (Node) `insc_num`, `apin_num`, `stin_num` (`2007`): the number of citations the case received from the Supreme Court, from federal appeals courts and from state courts, respectively.
- (Node) `insc_num_lag`, `apin_num_lag`, `stin_num_lag`, `outsc_num_lag`, `sc_cumul_cites_lag` (`2007`): lagged versions of these counts and of the outward and cumulative Supreme Court citations.
- (Node) `oxford_num`, `cq_num`, `nyt_num` (`2007`): whether the case appears in the Oxford Guide to Supreme Court decisions, in the Congressional Quarterly guide to the Supreme Court, or on the front page of the New York Times, respectively.
- (Node) `amiciz_num` (`2007`): a standardized count of amicus curiae briefs filed in the case.
- (Node) `size_num` (`2007`): the number of cases in the network at the time of measurement.
- (Node) The properties of `2007` are the variables of the replication data, used as validation measures of legal importance in the paper; their precise definitions are given there.
citations: J. H. Fowler and S. Jeon, "The Authority of Supreme Court Precedent." Social Networks 30(1), 16-30 (2008)
J. H. Fowler et al., "Network Analysis and the Law: Measuring the Legal Importance of Supreme Court Precedents." Political Analysis 15(3), 324-346 (2007)

datasets.name: se_asian_terrorists
datasets.description:
Networks of relationships among 108 individuals involved in terrorist attacks in Indonesia, from the "Southeast Asian aggregate attack series" of the John Jay & ARTIS Transnational Terrorism Database (JJATT), which collapses the individual Indonesian cases (e.g. the Christmas Eve 2000, Bali 2002, Australian embassy 2004 and Bali 2005 bombings) into a single series of relations, useful to study the behavioral and compositional changes of one terrorist network, largely associated with Jemaah Islamiyah. The data were coded from open sources, and were made available in matrix form by the UCINET datasets collection (University of Manchester). Nodes are individuals, labeled by their JJATT identifier in `name`. The networks are:

- `tie_strength`: social ties, with the edge property `weight` giving their strength: 1 = acquaintances or distant family ties (interaction limited to radical organization activities), 2 = friends or moderately close family ties (including co-workers and roommates), operational or organizational leadership, or operational ties (e.g. having worked closely together on a bombing), 3 = close friends or family, tight-knit operational cliques.
- `kinship`: kinship ties, with the edge property `kinship` coding the type: 1 = in-laws, 2 = cousins, 3 = siblings, 4 = parent/child, 5 = married, 6 = grandparent/grandchild, 7 = significant other.
- `operation_16`, `operation_24`, `operation_36`, `operation_43` and `operation_44`: co-participation in the JJATT operations with these identifiers. Comparing with the individual JJATT cases, operation 16 corresponds to the Christmas Eve 2000 bombings, 24 to the Bali 2002 bombings, 43 to the Australian embassy bombing in 2004, and 44 to the Bali 2005 bombings; operation 36 is not identified in the source.

The source matrices are meant to be symmetric; in the few cases where the two directions differ, the tie is included. The source also contains matrices of the years in which ties were formed and ended, which are not included.[^ucinet]

[^ucinet]: Description obtained in part from the [UCINET datasets page](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/datasets/covert-networks/southeast-asian-aggregated-attacks-2005).
citations: S. Atran, M. Sageman, et al., "John Jay & ARTIS Transnational Terrorism Database (JJATT)." John Jay College of Criminal Justice (2009)

datasets.name: sec_13f_holdings
datasets.description:
Bipartite networks of the institutional investment managers of the United States and the securities that they hold, from the Form 13F reports filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). Every institutional investment manager that exercises investment discretion over at least 100 million dollars in "13(f) securities" (exchange-traded stocks, shares of closed-end funds, convertible bonds, options, ...) must report its holdings of these securities at the end of each calendar quarter, within 45 days. The SEC publishes the information tables of these reports as quarterly data sets, extracted from the XML filings "as filed", without corrections.

There is one network per quarter, from the first quarter of 2013 to the second quarter of 2026 (54 networks), named by the quarter (e.g. `2025q4`), of the holdings at the end of the quarter: it contains all the 13F holdings reports (form `13F-HR`, including the combination reports) and their amendments (`13F-HR/A`) for the period ending on the last day of the quarter, filed within the quarterly data set of the SEC that covers their deadline (until 2023, the data set of the filings of the following calendar quarter; after the SEC changed the periods of its data sets in 2024, the data set of the three months following the end of the quarter, e.g. December to February for the fourth quarter, and January to February 2024 for the fourth quarter of 2023). The reports filed later (late filers, later amendments), which are in the following data sets, are not included. The first network, `2013q1`, may be incomplete: the data sets of the SEC, extracted from the XML information tables introduced in 2013, start with the filings of April to June 2013, which contain the reports for the first quarter of 2013 filed then.

The nodes are the managers (filers), identified by their Central Index Key (CIK) at the SEC, and the securities, identified by their CUSIP number (upper-cased). Each edge is one row of the information table of a report, from the manager to the security, so that the network is a multigraph: a manager reports several rows for the same security when its holdings differ in the kind of investment discretion, the other managers with which it is shared, or whether they are options (puts and calls), and the amendments add or restate rows (see `amendment_type`; a restatement replaces the original report, whose rows are still in the network). The values are as reported by the managers, who also include sometimes securities that are not on the official list of 13(f) securities; the reports that the SEC granted confidential treatment are not included.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `is_manager`: whether the node is a manager (otherwise it is a security).
- (Node) `cik` (managers): the Central Index Key of the manager (0 for securities).
- (Node) `cusip` (securities): the CUSIP number of the security (empty for managers).
- (Node) `name`: the name of the manager (from its last report of the quarter), or the name of the issuer of the security (the most common spelling in the reports).
- (Node) `city`, `state_or_country`, `zip_code` (managers): the address of the manager.
- (Node) `file_number` (managers): the Form 13F file number of the manager.
- (Node) `figi` (securities): the Financial Instrument Global Identifier of the security, when given (from 2023 on).
- (Edge) `value`: the market value of the holding, in US dollars: the reports filed before January 3, 2023 (here, until `2022q3`) give it in thousands of dollars, converted here to dollars, and the later ones in dollars (a few managers still report thousands in the later networks, e.g. about 10 % of the holdings of Apple stock in `2022q4`, which are kept as reported).
- (Edge) `shares`: the number of shares, or the principal amount for debt securities.
- (Edge) `shares_type`: `SH` (shares) or `PRN` (principal amount).
- (Edge) `put_call`: `Put` or `Call` if the holding is an option (the underlying security is given), otherwise empty.
- (Edge) `title_of_class`: the title of the class of the security (e.g. `COM`, `CL A`).
- (Edge) `discretion`: the investment discretion: `SOLE`, `DFND` (shared-defined) or `OTR` (shared-other).
- (Edge) `other_managers`: the sequence numbers of the other managers included in the report with whom the holding is shared (as given, empty if none).
- (Edge) `voting_sole`, `voting_shared`, `voting_none`: the number of shares for which the manager has sole, shared, or no voting authority.
- (Edge) `accession`: the accession number of the filing; `filing_date`: its date (`YYYY-MM-DD`).
- (Edge) `amendment_type`: empty for original reports, or `RESTATEMENT` or `NEW HOLDINGS` for amendments; `amendment_number`: the number of the amendment (0 for original reports).
- (Node) `period` (graph): the date of the end of the period of the reports.
citations: U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, "Form 13F Data Sets." (2014-2026)

datasets.name: sep_hyperlinks
datasets.description:
Directed networks of hyperlinks among the articles of the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (SEP), an online reference work of philosophy written and maintained by experts, and published at Stanford University. The SEP keeps quarterly fixed editions (Spring, Summer, Fall and Winter) of its contents, and the networks were crawled from these archived editions by A. D. Edwards, for most editions from Spring 1998 to Summer 2013, and for the Spring, Summer and Fall 2018 editions.

A node is an article (entry) listed in the table of contents of the edition, and a directed edge from article A to article B means that A contains a hyperlink to B (for instance, in its text or in its list of related entries). Only the links given in the relative form `../<article>/` were recorded by the crawler.

Each network is labeled by the year and season of the edition, e.g. `1998_fall`. Multiple hyperlinks from one article to another, and links from an article to itself, are collapsed or removed here. A few articles that are linked to but missing from the table of contents of an edition are included as nodes. The crawls of four editions (Fall 2008, Winter 2010, Summer 2012 and Summer 2013) stopped before all articles were processed (only the articles up to some point in the alphabetical order have out-going links), and these are not included.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the identifier of the article in its URL (e.g. `aristotle-politics`).
citations: A. D. Edwards, "SEP Graph: A graphical representation and analysis of the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy." https://github.com/adamdedwards/sep-graph (2018)
"The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy." Stanford University. ISSN 1095-5054

datasets.name: sider
datasets.description:
Bipartite networks of marketed drugs and their side effects (adverse drug reactions) and indications, from the Side Effect Resource SIDER, version 4.1 (released on October 21, 2015), by the Bork group at EMBL. SIDER is compiled from public documents of drug labels (package inserts), mostly from the FDA, the EMA and other sources: the side effects and indications mentioned in the labels were extracted by text mining, mapped to medical concepts of the UMLS (Unified Medical Language System) and to terms of the MedDRA dictionary of adverse event terms, and the labels were mapped to the drugs' compound identifiers of STITCH (derived from PubChem compound identifiers) through the drug names they mention. Each network has two kinds of nodes: drugs (1,430 to 1,437 compounds, identified by their "flat" STITCH ids, i.e. ignoring stereochemistry) and medical concepts (side effects or indications), identified by their UMLS concept ids.

For each concept found on a label, SIDER gives its MedDRA term as the "lowest level term" (LLT) and, additionally, each "preferred term" (PT) that it maps to (the PT may be the same concept as the LLT); in a few cases the concept is neither (e.g. a system organ class), and then the concept found on the label is used as the node. Each row of the SIDER files is an edge, from the drug to the MedDRA concept, so that a drug is usually joined to the same concept by several edges (as LLT and as PT, for several concepts found on its labels, for several stereoisomers, from several labels, or with several frequencies), and the networks are multigraphs. The networks are:

- `side_effects`: the side effects of each drug, collected from all its labels (`meddra_all_se`).
- `side_effect_frequencies`: the frequencies of side effects given on the labels, for the subset of side effects for which the labels give them, e.g. from clinical trials (`meddra_freq`); a side effect can have several frequencies, e.g. from different trials, for different levels of severity, or with placebo administration.
- `indications`: the indications of each drug, collected from all its labels (`meddra_all_indications`).
- `label_side_effects` and `label_indications`: the same as `side_effects` and `indications`, but with an edge for each label on which the side effect or the indication was found (`meddra_all_label_se` and `meddra_all_label_indications`).

SIDER contains errors due to the automatic text mining (a list of known errors is maintained on GitHub, mkuhn/sider, and is not applied here).
