Earlier versions of SIDER (1, 2 and 4.0) are no longer available for download. The SIDER side effects of the drugs approved in 2016 are also part of the entry `hetionet`.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `is_drug`: whether the node is a drug (otherwise it is a medical concept).
- (Node) `name`: the name of the drug (generated automatically by SIDER; empty for the few drugs of the indication files that are missing from its list of names) or of the concept (its MedDRA term).
- (Node) `id`: the flat STITCH compound id of the drug (e.g. `CID100000085`) or the UMLS concept id (e.g. `C0000737`).
- (Node) `pubchem_cid`: the PubChem compound id of the drug (-1 for concepts).
- (Node) `atc`: the ATC codes of the drug.
- (Node) `meddra_ids`: the MedDRA codes of the concept (from the MedDRA file of SIDER).
- (Edge) `meddra_type`: the kind of MedDRA term of the concept: `LLT` (lowest level term), `PT` (preferred term), or empty if it is neither.
- (Edge) `label_concept`: the UMLS concept id as found on the label (which the MedDRA term maps to).
- (Edge) `stereo_id` (`side_effects`, `side_effect_frequencies` and `label_side_effects`): the STITCH compound id with stereochemistry of the drug on the label.
- (Edge) `placebo` (`side_effect_frequencies`): whether the frequency is for placebo administration.
- (Edge) `frequency` (`side_effect_frequencies`): the frequency as given on the label (e.g. `21%`, `rare`, `postmarketing`).
- (Edge) `frequency_lower`, `frequency_upper` (`side_effect_frequencies`): lower and upper bounds of the frequency, as fractions.
- (Edge) `method` (`indications` and `label_indications`): the method of detection (`NLP_indication`, `NLP_precondition` or `text_mention`).
- (Edge) `label_concept_name` (`indications` and `label_indications`): the name of the concept as found on the label.
- (Edge) `label` (`label_side_effects` and `label_indications`): the label (source document) on which it was found (e.g. `EMA/WC500020092.html`).
citations: M. Kuhn, I. Letunic, L. J. Jensen, P. Bork, "The SIDER database of drugs and side effects." Nucleic Acids Research 44, D1075-D1079 (2016)
M. Kuhn, M. Campillos, I. Letunic, L. J. Jensen, P. Bork, "A side effect resource to capture phenotypic effects of drugs." Molecular Systems Biology 6, 343 (2010)

datasets.name: signed_biological
datasets.description:
Four signed biological networks compiled by G. Iacono, F. Ramezani, N. Soranzo and C. Altafini (2010) to measure how close biological networks are to being monotone (the equivalent of structurally balanced for signed graphs), and later used as benchmarks for computing the frustration index of signed networks by S. Aref, A. J. Mason and M. C. Wilson, who distributed them in a collection of signed networks (Aref and Wilson, 2019).

Nodes are genes or molecular species, and an undirected edge has sign $+1$ for an activating and $-1$ for an inhibiting interaction between them (the direction of the interactions is not kept). The networks are:

- `yeast`: the transcriptional (gene regulatory) network of the yeast *Saccharomyces cerevisiae*, from the Yeast Proteome Database (Costanzo et al., 2001); 690 genes and 1,080 interactions.
- `ecoli`: the transcriptional network of the bacterium *Escherichia coli* K-12, from RegulonDB version 5.0 (Salgado et al., 2006); 1,461 genes and 3,215 interactions.
- `egfr`: the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) signaling pathway map of Oda et al. (2005); 329 molecular species and 779 interactions.
- `macrophage`: the molecular interaction map of a macrophage (a white blood cell) of Oda et al. ("Molecular interaction map of a macrophage", AfCS Research Reports 2(14), 2004); 678 molecular species and 1,425 interactions.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Edge) `sign` (edges): $+1$ for activation and $-1$ for inhibition.

The source files identify the nodes only by number (vertex $i$ corresponds to node $i+1$ of the source); the gene and molecule names are not given.
citations: G. Iacono, F. Ramezani, N. Soranzo and C. Altafini, "Determining the distance to monotonicity of a biological network: a graph-theoretical approach." IET Systems Biology 4(3), 223–235 (2010)
S. Aref and M. C. Wilson, "Balance and frustration in signed networks." J. Complex Networks 7(2), 163–189 (2019)
M. C. Costanzo et al., "YPD, PombePD and WormPD: model organism volumes of the BioKnowledge Library, an integrated resource for protein information." Nucleic Acids Research 29(1), 75–79 (2001)
H. Salgado et al., "RegulonDB (version 5.0): Escherichia coli K-12 transcriptional regulatory network, operon organization, and growth conditions." Nucleic Acids Research 34, D394–D397 (2006)
K. Oda, Y. Matsuoka, A. Funahashi and H. Kitano, "A comprehensive pathway map of epidermal growth factor receptor signaling." Molecular Systems Biology 1, 2005.0010 (2005)
S. Aref, "Signed networks from sociology and political science, systems biology, international relations, finance, and computational chemistry." Figshare (2017)

datasets.name: signed_social_media
datasets.description:
Directed signed social networks of users of two websites, collected by Leskovec, Huttenlocher and Kleinberg to study positive and negative relationships in online social media. Nodes are users, and a directed edge $(i,j)$ means that user $i$ declared a positive or negative relationship (trust or distrust, friend or foe) towards user $j$.

- `epinions`: the who-trusts-whom network of the consumer review site Epinions.com, where members can declare that they trust (positive edge) or distrust (negative edge) other members. These relationships determine, together with the review ratings, which reviews are shown to the users.
- `slashdot081106`, `slashdot090216`, `slashdot090221`: the "Slashdot Zoo" of the technology news site Slashdot.org, in which users tag each other as friends (positive edge) or foes (negative edge), as obtained on November 6 2008, February 16 2009 and February 21 2009. The node numbers are not necessarily consistent across the snapshots. Unsigned versions of the Slashdot Zoo distributed by SNAP are in the entry `slashdot_zoo_snap`; its network `0811` is from the same date as `slashdot081106` and has nearly the same number of nodes, but a different edge set (about 905,000 instead of 517,000 edges).

A third network of the same study, the votes in Wikipedia adminship elections, is available separately (see the `elec` entry).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Edge) `sign`: the sign of the relationship, +1 (trust, friend) or -1 (distrust, foe).
citations: J. Leskovec, D. Huttenlocher, J. Kleinberg, "Signed networks in social media." Proceedings of the SIGCHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI), 1361-1370 (2010)

J. Leskovec, D. Huttenlocher, J. Kleinberg, "Predicting positive and negative links in online social networks." Proceedings of the 19th International Conference on World Wide Web (WWW), 641-650 (2010)

datasets.name: signed_social_relations
datasets.description:
Three undirected signed social networks prepared by S. Aref and M. C. Wilson as benchmarks for measuring structural balance and computing the frustration index of signed networks (Aref and Wilson, 2018 and 2019), and distributed in their collection of signed networks.

Nodes are people, and an undirected edge has sign $+1$ for a positive and $-1$ for a negative relation between two people. The networks are:

- `monastery`: 18 novices in a New England monastery, from the sociometric rankings collected by S. F. Sampson (1968) at the fourth time point of his study. Sampson's data include rankings of like, dislike, esteem, disesteem, positive influence, negative influence, praise and blame; all the positive and negative rankings were combined, and two novices are connected only if their relations are reciprocated with the same sign.
- `eastern_college`: 17 women living in house B of the off-campus dormitories of an Eastern college, from the sociometric data of T. B. Lemann and R. L. Solomon (1952), which integrate the top three and bottom three choices on several criteria; two women are connected only if their choices of each other are reciprocated with the same sign.
- `senate_108`: the 100 senators of the 108th US Senate (2003–2004), with the signed relations inferred by Z. Neal (2014) from J. H. Fowler's bill co-sponsorship data by extracting the signed backbone of the senator–bill network with the stochastic degree sequence model: senators are connected positively if they co-sponsored significantly more bills together than expected, and negatively if significantly fewer.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Edge) `sign` (edges): $+1$ for a positive and $-1$ for a negative relation.

The nodes have no names in the source; their order follows the node numbering of the source files.

Other signed networks of the same collection are in existing entries or derived from them: the Highland tribes network is identical to `new_guinea_tribes`; the fraternity network is the network `signed_week15` of `newcomb_fraternity`, derived there from the week 15 rankings (ranks 1–5 as positive and 12–16 as negative choices, keeping the reciprocated relations with the same sign); and the undirected Wikipedia elections network is obtained from the votes in `elec`. A different version of the signed backbone of the US Senate, with senator names, inferred by Neal for every Congress up to 2016, is in `us_congress`.
citations: S. Aref and M. C. Wilson, "Measuring partial balance in signed networks." J. Complex Networks 6(4), 566–595 (2018)
S. Aref and M. C. Wilson, "Balance and frustration in signed networks." J. Complex Networks 7(2), 163–189 (2019)
S. F. Sampson, "A Novitiate in a Period of Change: An Experimental and Case Study of Social Relationships." PhD thesis, Cornell University (1968)
T. B. Lemann and R. L. Solomon, "Group characteristics as revealed in sociometric patterns and personality ratings." Sociometry 15(1/2), 7–90 (1952)
Z. Neal, "The backbone of bipartite projections: Inferring relationships from co-authorship, co-sponsorship, co-attendance and other co-behaviors." Social Networks 39, 84–97 (2014)
S. Aref, "Signed networks from sociology and political science, systems biology, international relations, finance, and computational chemistry." Figshare (2017)

datasets.name: siren_togo
datasets.description:
Networks of communication among participants in two stolen-vehicle exportation operations in Montreal, Canada, targeted by police investigations, from the appendix of Morselli's book "Inside Criminal Networks" (2009). Nodes are participants (numbered in `name`), and an edge indicates communication exchanges between them, from police wiretapping.

- `siren` (44 nodes): Project Siren began in February 1998 when a port worker informed the police that a container of stolen vehicles had been shipped to Ghana; the shipment was seized at its transit point in Antwerp, Belgium. The investigation continued for four months (to June 1998), during which shipments destined for Russia, Egypt, Iraq, Italy and Switzerland were monitored, and 35 cars were retrieved.
- `togo` (33 nodes): Project Togo began when a Toronto-based ring was dismantled in 1998 and one of its participants informed the police about a Montreal businessman active in the resale of stolen vehicles; the investigation ran from December 1998 to February 1999, and 20 cars destined for France, Ghana and local buyers were retrieved.

Data reconstructed by the UCINET datasets collection (University of Manchester).[^ucinet]

[^ucinet]: Description obtained in part from the [UCINET datasets page](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/datasets/covert-networks/siren).
citations: C. Morselli, "Inside Criminal Networks." Springer, New York (2009)

datasets.name: sister_cities
datasets.description:
Directed networks of cities and other places of the world connected by "sister city" (twin town) relationships, as recorded in Wikidata with the property "twinned administrative body" (P190). Each node is a Wikidata item, and a directed edge from A to B means that the item of A lists B as twinned with it. The relationship is symmetric in reality, but it is not always recorded on both items, so that a pair of twinned places can be connected by edges in one or both directions.

Only the statements of items that are instances of "human settlement" (Q486972) or of any of its subclasses (property paths P31/P279*) are included, i.e. the edges whose source is such an item; their targets may be other kinds of places (e.g. regions or districts that have twin towns), which are marked by the property `is_city`. Only the preferred (or, if there is none, the normal) statements are used ("truthy" statements), and statements whose value is "unknown" are left out.

There are two networks:

- `2017`: from the Wikidata dump of "truthy" statements of 16 November 2017 (the class hierarchy of that time is used for the selection).
- `2026`: from the Wikidata Query Service, reflecting the state of Wikidata at the time of download (October 2026).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `wikidata_id`: the Wikidata identifier of the item (e.g. `Q64` for Berlin).
- (Node) `name`: the English label of the item (empty if it has none).
- (Node) `is_city`: whether the item is an instance of "human settlement" or of one of its subclasses.
- (Node) `latitude`, `longitude`: the coordinates of the item (property P625; NaN if it has none, or only coordinates on another celestial body); if it has several, one of them.
- (Node) `country`: the English labels of the countries the item belongs to (property P17), separated by semicolons (empty if none).
citations: D. Vrandečić, M. Krötzsch, "Wikidata: a free collaborative knowledgebase." Communications of the ACM 57, 78-85 (2014).

datasets.name: skitter_routers_2003
datasets.description:
A portion of the router-level Internet, based on topology discovery measurements collected between April 21 and May 8, 2003 by the skitter measurement system of CAIDA (Center for Applied Internet Data Analysis), which sent traceroute probes from several monitors to many destinations. Nodes are the discovered routing devices, and edges are the discovered links between them. The data were distributed by E. D. Kolaczyk on the data page of the book "Statistical Analysis of Network Data" (no longer online), from which this version was obtained via the Internet Archive; the data should be acknowledged to CAIDA.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `id`: the number of the device in the source data.
citations: E. D. Kolaczyk, "Statistical Analysis of Network Data: Methods and Models." Springer (2009)

datasets.name: slashdot_threads
datasets.description:
A network of replies among users of the website Slashdot on the various discussion threads on the site. Nodes are user accounts and each directed edge represents a reply from user i to user j. Replies are timestamped.[^icon]
[^icon]: Description obtained from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.
citations: V. Gómez, A. Kaltenbrunner, & V. López, "Statistical analysis of the social network and discussion threads in Slashdot." In Proc. Int. World Wide Web Conf. (WWW) 645-654 (2008)

datasets.name: slashdot_zoo
datasets.description: A network of interactions among users on Slashdot (slashdot.org), a technology news website. Users name each other as friends or foe. The friend label increases the scores of post, and the foe label decreases the score. Nodes are users, and a directed edge $(i,j)$ means that user $i$ tagged user $j$ as a friend (edge `weight` +1) or a foe (edge `weight` -1).
citations: J. Kunegis, A. Lommatzsch, & C. Bauckhage. "The Slashdot Zoo: mining a social network with negative edges". Proc. 18th Internat. Conf. on the World Wide Web, 741-750 (WWW 2009).

datasets.name: slashdot_zoo_snap
datasets.description: Two snapshots of the "Slashdot Zoo" of the technology news website Slashdot.org, a feature introduced in 2002 that allows users to tag each other as friends or foes, as distributed by SNAP and used by Leskovec, Lang, Dasgupta and Mahoney in their study of community structure in large networks. Nodes are users, and a directed edge from one user to another denotes a friend or foe tag (the type of tag is not included; see the `signed_social_media` entry for signed versions of the same network). The snapshots were obtained on November 6 2008 (`0811`) and in February 2009 (`0902`). As distributed, almost every node has a self-loop, and the node numbers are not consistent with those of the signed versions. Although `0811` and the signed network `slashdot081106` of `signed_social_media` are from the same date and have nearly the same number of nodes (77,360 and 77,357), their edge sets differ (about 905,000 and 517,000 edges), reflecting different processing.
citations: J. Leskovec, K. J. Lang, A. Dasgupta, M. W. Mahoney, "Community Structure in Large Networks: Natural Cluster Sizes and the Absence of Large Well-Defined Clusters." Internet Mathematics 6(1), 29-123 (2009)

datasets.name: slovene_parties
datasets.description:
Perceived similarities between the ten Slovene parliamentary political parties in 1994, estimated by members of the Slovene National Parliament, from S. Kropivnik and A. Mrvar. In a questionnaire, the members of parliament were asked to estimate the distance between each pair of parties in the political space, on a scale from -3 (very dissimilar) to +3 (very similar). The estimates were given by 72 of the 90 members of parliament (17 were not available at the time of the interviews, and one refused); 64 respondents estimated all 45 pairs, and missing values were excluded. Nodes are the parties, and in this complete signed network every pair of parties is connected by an edge weighted by the average estimated similarity, multiplied by 100 and rounded. The data were distributed in Pajek format on the Pajek datasets page of V. Batagelj and A. Mrvar, from which this version was obtained.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the abbreviation of the party (SKD: Slovene Christian Democrats; ZLSD: Associated List of Social Democrats; SDSS: Social Democratic Party of Slovenia; LDS: Liberal Democratic Party; ZS-ESS: the first of two Green parties separated after the 1992 elections; ZS: the second Green party, which had no representatives in parliament at the time of the interviews; DS: Democratic Party; SLS: Slovene People's Party; SNS: Slovene National Party; SPS: a group of deputies, former members of SNS, separated after the 1992 elections).
- (Edge) `weight`: the average estimated similarity of the two parties, multiplied by 100 (from -300 to 300).
citations: S. Kropivnik, A. Mrvar, "An Analysis of the Slovene Parliamentary Parties Network." In A. Ferligoj, A. Kramberger (eds.), Developments in Statistics and Methodology, Metodološki zvezki 12, FDV, Ljubljana (1996), pp. 209-216
P. Doreian, A. Mrvar, "A partitioning approach to structural balance." Social Networks 18(2), 149-168 (1996)

datasets.name: slovenian_cs_collab
datasets.description:
A co-authorship network of Slovenian computer scientists, with publications up to 2010, used by Blagus, Šubelj and Bajec in their study of the scaling of network density. The data were provided to the authors by M. Polajnar. Nodes are researchers, and an undirected edge connects two researchers for each publication they co-authored, so that repeated edges represent multiple co-authored publications (the network has 596 distinct pairs of co-authors). Only 262 of the researchers have co-authors in the network; the remaining 699 are isolated nodes.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `researcher_id`: a numeric researcher identifier given in the source (presumably the researcher's number in the Slovenian research information system).
- (Node) `group`: an integer from 1 to 9 given for each researcher in the source data, whose meaning is undocumented.
citations: N. Blagus, L. Šubelj, M. Bajec, "Self-similar scaling of density in complex real-world networks." Physica A 391(8), 2794-2802 (2012)

datasets.name: slovenian_magazines
datasets.description:
Co-readership of 124 Slovenian newspapers, magazines and journals, from a survey of more than 100,000 people conducted by the CATI Center (Ljubljana) in 1999 and 2000, in which respondents were asked which magazines and journals they read. The network is the one-mode projection of the bipartite network of readers and publications: two publications are connected by an edge weighted by the number of respondents who read both, and each publication has a self-loop weighted by its total number of readers. The data were distributed in Pajek format on the Pajek datasets page of V. Batagelj and A. Mrvar, from which this version was obtained.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the title of the publication.
- (Node) `type`: the type of publication (1: daily newspapers, 2: business magazines, 3: computer magazines, 4: home and furnishing, 5: fashion, 6: weekly news magazines, 7: free papers, 8: men's special-interest magazines, 9: teen magazines, 10: regional papers, 11: special-interest magazines, 12: women's special-interest magazines, 13: TV guides, 14: women's magazines).
- (Edge) `weight`: the number of respondents reading both publications (or, for self-loops, the publication).

datasets.name: slumlords
datasets.description:
Networks of a group of "slumlords", real-estate investors who were convicted of housing violations in multiple buildings (including sewage leaks, lead contamination, evictions of complaining tenants, and unpaid utility bills), as mapped by a small not-for-profit economic justice organization with the help of Valdis Krebs (orgnet.com) to assist the city attorney. The networks correspond to the figures of the step-by-step analysis described by Krebs, and were reconstructed at the University of Manchester. Nodes are persons (with pseudonymous first names) and businesses (limited liability companies), named in the vertex property `name`.

- `transactions`: directed network of real-estate transactions (property sold from one company to another) among 5 companies (Fig. 1).
- `ownership`: bipartite network of 11 owners and the 5 companies they own (Fig. 2); `is_business` marks the companies.
- `co_ownership`: one-mode projection of `ownership`, connecting owners of the same company.
- `family`: family ties among the 11 owners (Fig. 3).
- `extended_family`: family ties among 13 persons, including relatives who are not owners (Fig. 4).
- `business_interests`: bipartite network of 13 persons and 9 businesses and properties, connected by business affiliations or ownership (Fig. 5); `is_business` marks the businesses.
- `business_ties`: ties among the 9 businesses and properties that have affiliated persons or owners in common.

Where the two directions of the undirected source matrices differ, the tie is included.[^ucinet]

[^ucinet]: Description obtained in part from the [UCINET datasets page](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/datasets/covert-networks/slumlords).
citations: V. Krebs, "Social Network Analysis of Slumlords." orgnet.com

datasets.name: soc_net_comms
datasets.description:
Six large networks with "ground-truth" group memberships of the nodes, assembled by J. Yang and J. Leskovec to evaluate community detection methods, and distributed by the Stanford Network Analysis Project (SNAP). All networks are undirected and unweighted. The groups of each network were turned into communities by taking each connected component of the subgraph induced by a group as a separate community and removing communities with fewer than 3 nodes; a node can belong to any number of communities, including none. For the networks, SNAP provides the largest connected component.

- `livejournal`: users of the LiveJournal blogging platform, connected if they declared friendship. Communities are user-defined groups which other users can join (664,414 communities). SNAP does not name the source of these data; they are smaller than, and likely derived from, the 2006 LiveJournal crawl of the entry `livejournal` (see also the network `livejournal` of the entry `mislove_osn`).
- `friendster`: users of the Friendster social networking site (before it relaunched as a gaming website), connected by friendships, with communities given by user-defined groups (1,620,991 communities). The network is the subgraph induced by the nodes that belong to at least one group or are connected to a node that belongs to at least one group. The data were obtained from the Internet Archive.
- `orkut`: users of the Orkut social network, connected by friendships, with communities given by user-defined groups (15,301,901 communities). Data collected by A. Mislove et al.; the directed version of the same crawl, with all 3,072,441 users, is the network `orkut` of the entry `mislove_osn`.
- `youtube`: users of the social network of the YouTube video-sharing website, connected by friendships, with communities given by user-defined groups (16,386 communities). Data collected by A. Mislove et al.; this is the largest connected component of the undirected version of the network `youtube` of the entry `mislove_osn`.
- `dblp`: co-authorship network of the DBLP computer science bibliography, where two authors are connected if they published at least one paper together; it is thus a one-mode projection of the bipartite network of authors and publications. Each publication venue (journal or conference) defines a community, formed by the authors who published there (13,477 communities).
- `amazon`: products of the Amazon website, connected if they are frequently co-purchased, according to the "Customers Who Bought This Item Also Bought" feature, collected by crawling the website. Each product category defines a community (271,570 communities).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the node identifier in the SNAP files.
- (Node) `communities`: the list of communities the node belongs to, each given by its index (starting from 0) in the list of all communities of the network (file `*.all.cmty.txt` of SNAP).
citations: J. Yang and J. Leskovec. "Defining and Evaluating Network Communities based on Ground-truth." ICDM, 2012.

datasets.name: soccer_passing
datasets.description:
Passing networks of soccer (association football) players, built from the match event data ("soccer-logs") collected by Wyscout and published by Pappalardo et al.: all the 1,941 matches of seven competitions, one network per competition:

- `england`: English Premier League, season 2017/2018 (380 matches);
- `france`: French Ligue 1, season 2017/2018 (380 matches);
- `germany`: German Bundesliga, season 2017/2018 (306 matches);
- `italy`: Italian Serie A, season 2017/2018 (380 matches);
- `spain`: Spanish La Liga, season 2017/2018 (380 matches);
- `euro_2016`: UEFA European Championship 2016 (51 matches);
- `world_cup_2018`: FIFA World Cup 2018 (64 matches).

Each node is a player, and each directed edge goes from a player to a teammate who received at least one of his completed passes in a given match, weighted by the number of such passes; the network of a competition is thus a multigraph, with one edge per pair of players and match, and the passing network of a single team in a single match is the subgraph of the edges with the corresponding `match_id` and `team`. Passes include the free kicks that are passes (corners, free kicks, free kick crosses, goal kicks and throw-ins), but not shots and penalties.

Wyscout records who made each pass and whether it was accurate (i.e. reached a teammate), but not who received it. As usual for these data, the recipient of an accurate pass is taken to be the player of the next event of the same team in the same period of the match (events of the opposing team in between, e.g. duels, are skipped). Of the 1,855,914 passes in the data, 1,478,167 are included: left out are the 341,770 passes that were not accurate, and the accurate passes for which no recipient can be determined in this way (7,416 for which the next event of the team is by the same player, 28,547 for which it has no player, and 14 that are the last events of the team in a period). Only players who made or received at least one included pass appear in the networks.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `player_id`: the Wyscout id of the player.
- (Node) `name`: his short name.
- (Node) `first_name` and `last_name`.
- (Node) `role`: his role (goalkeeper, defender, midfielder or forward).
- (Node) `team`: the team(s) for which he made or received passes in the competition (several, separated by semicolons, for players transferred during the season).
- (Node) `nationality`: the country of his passport.
- (Node) `birth_date`.
- (Node) `height`: in centimeters, and `weight_kg`, his body weight in kilograms (0 if unknown).
- (Node) `foot`: his preferred foot (empty if unknown).
- (Edge) `weight`: the number of completed passes.
- (Edge) `match_id`: the Wyscout id of the match.
- (Edge) `time`: the starting time of the match (Unix time).
- (Edge) `match`: the label of the match (teams and final score).
- (Edge) `team`: the team of the two players.
citations: L. Pappalardo, P. Cintia, A. Rossi, E. Massucco, P. Ferragina, D. Pedreschi, F. Giannotti, "A public data set of spatio-temporal match events in soccer competitions." Scientific Data 6, 236 (2019)

datasets.name: social_dimensions
datasets.description:
Friendship networks of three social media websites, with the group memberships of the users, collected by L. Tang and H. Liu (Arizona State University) to study collective behaviour and the prediction of user attributes ("social dimensions"), and distributed by the Social Computing Data Repository (originally at Arizona State University, now at Syracuse University). In all networks, nodes are users, and an undirected edge connects two users who are friends (contacts) on the website. The group memberships of the users (in groups of interest of the site, selected by the authors) are given as a node property, and serve as labels in classification tasks.

- `blogcatalog`: bloggers of the blog directory BlogCatalog (10,312 users, 333,983 friendships, 39 groups).
- `flickr`: users of the photo sharing site Flickr (80,513 users, 5,899,882 friendships, 195 groups).
- `youtube`: users of the video sharing site YouTube (1,138,499 users, 2,990,443 friendships, 47 groups; only 31,703 users belong to some group).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `groups`: the identifiers of the groups the user belongs to (the names of the groups are not given in the source data).
citations: L. Tang, H. Liu, "Relational learning via latent social dimensions." Proceedings of the 15th ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining, 817-826 (2009)
L. Tang, H. Liu, "Scalable learning of collective behavior based on sparse social dimensions." Proceedings of the 18th ACM Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM), 1107-1116 (2009)

datasets.name: social_location
datasets.description:
Friendship networks of two location-based online social networks, Gowalla and Brightkite, where users shared their locations by "checking in" at places. Nodes are users and an undirected edge indicates a friendship between two users. The networks were collected from the services' public APIs by Cho, Myers and Leskovec, and distributed by the Stanford Network Analysis Project (SNAP).

- `gowalla`: 196,591 users and 950,327 friendships.
- `brightkite`: 58,228 users and 214,078 friendships.

The check-ins of the users (about 6.4 million for Gowalla, from February 2009 to October 2010, and 4.5 million for Brightkite, from April 2008 to October 2010), which are also distributed by SNAP, are not included in the networks. The networks have no node or edge properties.
citations: E. Cho, S. A. Myers, and J. Leskovec, "Friendship and mobility: user movement in location-based social networks." Proc. 17th Internat. Conf. on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (KDD), 1082-1090 (2011).

datasets.name: socnet_coauthors
datasets.description:
Coauthorships among the 475 authors of the 295 articles published in the journal Social Networks, from its beginning (1978) to 2008. The data were compiled by C. McCarty for the 2008 INSNA meeting (Sunbelt conference) in St. Pete Beach (Florida), where they were used for a t-shirt design, and were later cleaned by L. C. Freeman. The data were distributed by L. C. Freeman on his network data page at the University of California, Irvine (no longer online), from which this version was obtained via the Internet Archive.

An undirected edge connects two authors who coauthored at least one article.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the author (without spaces, as in the source data).
- (Edge) `weight`: the number of coauthored articles.
citations: C. McCarty, L. C. Freeman, "Social Networks coauthorships", unpublished (2008)

datasets.name: software_callgraphs
datasets.description:
Six networks of collaboration among software units in open-source software systems, parsed from their source code by C. R. Myers. Three are static class collaboration graphs of object-oriented systems written in C++, where each node is a class, and a directed edge B → A indicates that class B makes reference to class A in its definition, either through inheritance (B is a subclass of A) or aggregation (B holds an instance of A). The other three are static call graphs of procedural systems written in C, where each node is a function (subroutine), and a directed edge g → f indicates that g calls f from within its scope. Self-loops correspond to self-references and recursive calls.

- `vtk`: class collaboration graph of version 4.0 of the VTK visualization library.
- `dm`: class collaboration graph of Digital Material, a library for atomistic simulation of materials (CVS snapshot of 3 April 2002).
- `abiword`: class collaboration graph of version 1.0.2 of the AbiWord word processor.
- `linux`: call graph of version 2.4.19 of the Linux kernel.
- `mysql`: call graph of version 3.23.32 of the MySQL relational database system.
- `xmms`: call graph of version 1.2.7 of the XMMS multimedia player.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the class or function.
citations: C. R. Myers, "Software systems as complex networks: Structure, function, and evolvability of software collaboration graphs." Physical Review E 68, 046116 (2003)

datasets.name: software_dependencies
datasets.description:
Class dependency networks of several Java software systems, constructed by L. Šubelj and collaborators from the source code. Nodes are software classes (including interfaces and nested classes) and a directed edge $i \to j$ indicates that class $i$ depends on (references) class $j$ (e.g. `java.applet.Applet` points to its superclass `java.awt.Panel`). The upstream files list one line per dependency, so a pair of classes can be connected by multiple parallel edges. The networks include all classes of the respective systems, also those without dependencies (e.g. 54 of the 6,488 classes of `jdk` are isolated).

- From Šubelj and Bajec (Physica A, 2011): `javax`, `java` and `org` (the corresponding namespaces of the Java SE Development Kit, JDK, version 1.6.0.7), `colt` (Colt 1.2.0, namespace `cern`; the same network, with the same class numbers and the same 3,691 dependencies, is distributed again with dependency types for Šubelj, Blagus and Bajec, NetSci 2013, and the types are included here), `jung` (JUNG 2.0.1, namespace `edu.uci.ics.jung`), `flamingo` (Flamingo 4.1), `jmail` (JavaMail 1.4.3) and `junit` (JUnit 4.8.1).
- From Šubelj and Bajec (SoftwareMining, 2012): `jdk` (the whole JDK 1.6.0.7), `weka` (Weka 3.6.6), `jung-j` (JUNG 2.0.1 together with the `java` and `javax` namespaces of the JDK) and `jung-c` (JUNG 2.0.1 together with Colt 1.2.0).
- `guava`: Guava r07 core libraries, where an edge indicates that the documentation of a class references another class.
- `slucene` (Lucene 4.1.0), from Šubelj, Blagus and Bajec (NetSci, 2013), and `sjung` (JUNG 2.0.1) and `sjbullet` (JBullet 2.72), from Šubelj et al. (Advs. Complex Syst., 2014).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name` (not in `slucene`, `sjung` and `sjbullet`, for which no class names are distributed upstream): the fully qualified name of the class (e.g. `java.applet.Applet`, with a dollar sign separating nested classes).
- (Edge) `type` (only in `slucene`, `colt`, `sjung` and `sjbullet`): a letter code given upstream for each dependency (`c`, `p`, `r`, `s`, ...), presumably the type of dependency, whose meaning is not documented upstream.
citations: L. Šubelj, M. Bajec, "Community structure of complex software systems: Analysis and applications." Physica A 390(16), 2968-2975 (2011)
L. Šubelj, M. Bajec, "Software systems through complex networks science: Review, analysis and applications." Proc. 1st International Workshop on Software Mining (SoftwareMining 12), 9-16 (2012)
L. Šubelj, M. Bajec, "Clustering assortativity, communities and functional modules in real-world networks." arXiv:1202.3188 (2012)
L. Šubelj, N. Blagus, M. Bajec, "Group extraction for real-world networks: The case of communities, modules, and hubs and spokes." Proc. of NetSci 13, 152 (2013)
L. Šubelj, S. Žitnik, N. Blagus, M. Bajec, "Node mixing and group structure of complex software networks." Advs. Complex Syst. 17(7-8), 1450022 (2014)

datasets.name: software_documentation
datasets.description:
Directed networks of references among the classes of Java software libraries, obtained by Šubelj and Bajec by parsing the documentation (Javadoc) of the software. Nodes are classes (including interfaces and nested classes), and a directed edge from class A to class B indicates that the documentation of A refers to B (e.g. `javax/swing/JButton` points to its superclass `javax/swing/AbstractButton`). Since the networks were obtained from the documentation, some false relations may have been introduced, according to the authors.

- `javax`: the javax namespace of the Java 6 development kit.
- `java`: the java namespace of the Java 6 development kit.
- `jung`: the JUNG (Java Universal Network/Graph) framework.
- `gae`: the Google App Engine library.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the fully qualified name of the class (as a path, e.g. `javax/swing/JButton`).
citations: L. Šubelj, M. Bajec, "Unfolding network communities by combining defensive and offensive label propagation." Proceedings of the ECML PKDD Workshop on the Analysis of Complex Networks (ACNE 2010), 87-104 (2010)

datasets.name: sp_baboons
datasets.description:
Network of interactions between a group of 20 Guinea baboons living in an enclosure of a Primate Center in France, between June 13th 2019 and July 10th 2019. The data set contains observational and wearable sensors data. Nodes are baboons. In the `observational` network, each directed edge $i \to j$ is a behavioral event registered by the observer, in which baboon $i$ (the actor) acts upon baboon $j$ (the recipient), so that a pair of baboons is connected by one edge per event; in the `sensor` network, each undirected edge is a contact between two baboons recorded by the proximity sensors, one edge per recorded contact.

The observational data contains all the behavioral events registered by an observer, with 8 columns:

- DateTime: Time stamp of the event, namely the moment the observed behavior was registered. In case of STATE events (events with duration > 0), it refers to the beginning of the behavior
- Actor: The name of the actor
- Recipient:  The name of the individual the Actor is acting upon
- Behavior:  The behavior the Actor. 14 types of behaviors are registered:’Resting’, ‘Grooming’, ‘Presenting’,’Playing with’, ‘Grunting-Lipsmacking’, ‘Supplanting’,’Threatening’, ‘Submission’, ‘Touching’, ‘Avoiding’, ‘Attacking’,’Carrying’, ‘Embracing’, ‘Mounting’, ‘Copulating’, ‘Chasing’. In addition two other categories were included: ‘Invisible’ and ‘Other’
- Category:  The classification of the behavior. It can be ‘Affiliative’, ‘Agonistic’, ‘Other’
- Duration:  Duration of the observed behavior. POINT events have no duration
- Localisation:  Zone of the enclosure where the observed behavior takes place
- Point:  indicates if the event is a POINT event (YES) or a STATE event (NO).

The sensor data contains contacts recorded in the same period by the SocioPatterns infrastructure. The proximity sensors were worn by 13 of the 20 individuals cited above.
The data file consists of 4 columns:

- t:  time of the beginning of the contact in Epoch format (Unix timestamps)
- i:  Name of the first individual
- j:  Name of the second individual
- DateTime
citations: V. Gelardi, J. Godard, D. Paleressompoulle, N. Claidière, A. Barrat, "Measuring social networks in primates: wearable sensors vs. direct observations", Proc. R. Soc. A 476:20190737 (2020)

datasets.name: sp_colocation
datasets.description:
Network of colocations between peoople, based on the information on which RFID readers received information from the RFID tags. Namely, we define two individuals to be in co-presence if the same exact set of readers have received signals from both individuals during a 20s time window. Nodes are individuals, and each edge connects two individuals in co-presence during one 20s time window (given by the edge property `time`), so that a pair of individuals is connected by one edge per time window in which they were in co-presence.

We release here 6 co-presence data sets. The contexts in which these data were collected are: a workplace, with data collected in two different years (InVS13, InVS15), a hospital (LH10), a primary school (LyonSchool), a scientific conference (SFHH) and a high school (Thiers13). In each case, the data on face-to-face contacts during the same timeframe has already been released. In all cases except SFHH, metadata is also available concerning the department, class or status of each individual.
citations: Génois, M., Barrat, A. Can co-location be used as a proxy for face-to-face contacts?. EPJ Data Sci. 7, 11 (2018)

datasets.name: sp_high_school
datasets.description:
Networks of contacts and friendships among the students of nine classes of a high school (the "classes préparatoires" Lycée Thiers) in Marseilles, France, collected by the SocioPatterns collaboration in December 2013. Nodes are students. The data were collected through four techniques, each giving a separate network:

- `proximity`: face-to-face proximity contacts measured by wearable sensors over 5 days (2 to 6 December 2013). Each edge is a contact between two students active during a 20-second interval of the data collection, so that a pair of students is connected by one edge per interval in which they were in contact.
- `diaries`: directed network of contacts reported by the students in contact diaries filled at the end of the fourth day of the data collection. An edge $i \to j$ means that student $i$ reported a contact with student $j$; the weight encodes the reported cumulative duration of contact during the day.
- `survey`: directed network of friendships reported in a survey, where an edge $i \to j$ means that student $i$ reported a friendship with student $j$.
- `facebook`: undirected network of Facebook friendships, among the pairs of students for which the presence or absence of the Facebook friendship is known. Only the pairs that are linked on Facebook are included as edges, so that the absence of an edge does not imply that the friendship is known to be absent.

All networks include the 329 students in the metadata file, including those without any edges in a given network.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `id`: the anonymous identifier of the student.
- (Node) `class`: the class of the student (e.g. `MP*1`, `PC`, `2BIO3`).
- (Node) `gender`: the gender of the student (`M`, `F` or `Unknown`).
- (Edge) `time` (`proximity`): the end of the 20-second interval $[t - 20\,\text{s}, t]$ during which the contact was active, as a UNIX timestamp in seconds.
- (Edge) `weight` (`diaries`): the reported cumulative duration of the contacts, 1 for at most 5 minutes, 2 for 5 to 15 minutes, 3 for 15 minutes to 1 hour, and 4 for more than 1 hour.
citations: R. Mastrandrea, et al., "Contact Patterns in a High School: A Comparison between Data Collected Using Wearable Sensors, Contact Diaries and Friendship Surveys." PLoS ONE 10(9), e0136497 (2015)

datasets.name: sp_high_school_new
datasets.description:
Temporal networks of face-to-face proximity contacts among students of a high school (the "classes préparatoires" Lycée Thiers) in Marseilles, France, measured by the SocioPatterns collaboration with wearable sensors. Nodes are persons, and each edge is a contact between two persons active during a 20-second interval of the data collection, so that a pair of persons is connected by one edge per interval in which they were in contact.

- `2011`: students of three classes and some of their teachers, during 4 days in December 2011.
- `2012`: students of five classes, during 7 days (from a Monday to the Tuesday of the following week) in November 2012.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `id`: the anonymous identifier of the person.
- (Node) `class`: the class of the student (e.g. `PC*`, `MP*1`, `PSI*`), or `teacher` (`2011` only).
- (Node) `gender`: the gender (`M` or `F`).
- (Edge) `time`: the end of the 20-second interval $[t - 20\,\text{s}, t]$ during which the contact was active, in seconds. For `2012` it is a UNIX timestamp; for `2011` it is measured from an unspecified reference time.
citations: J. Fournet & A. Barrat, "Contact patterns among high school students." PLoS ONE 9(9), e107878 (2014).

datasets.name: sp_hospital
datasets.description:
Temporal network of face-to-face proximity contacts among patients and health-care workers in a geriatric unit of a hospital in Lyon, France, measured by the SocioPatterns collaboration with wearable sensors from Monday, 6 December 2010 at 1:00 pm to Friday, 10 December 2010 at 2:00 pm. The study included 46 health-care workers and 29 patients. Nodes are persons, and each edge is a contact between two persons active during a 20-second interval of the data collection, so that a pair of persons is connected by one edge per interval in which they were in contact.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `id`: the anonymous identifier of the person.
- (Node) `status`: the role of the person: `NUR` (paramedical staff, i.e. nurses and nurses' aides), `PAT` (patient), `MED` (medical doctor) or `ADM` (administrative staff).
- (Edge) `time`: the end of the 20-second interval $[t - 20\,\text{s}, t]$ during which the contact was active, in seconds since the beginning of the data collection.
citations: P. Vanhems et al., "Estimating Potential Infection Transmission Routes in Hospital Wards Using Wearable Proximity Sensors." PLoS ONE 8(9), e73970 (2013).

datasets.name: sp_hypertext
datasets.description:
Temporal network of face-to-face proximity contacts among about 110 attendees of the ACM Hypertext 2009 conference in Turin, Italy, over about 2.5 days (29 June to 1 July 2009). The data were collected by the SocioPatterns collaboration as part of the Live Social Semantics application: attendees volunteered to wear radio badges that detected face-to-face proximity. Nodes are attendees. No personal data or other metadata are included. The data are provided in two forms:

- `contacts`: each edge is a contact between two attendees active during a 20-second interval of the data collection, so that a pair of attendees is connected by one edge per interval in which they were in contact.
- `intervals`: each edge is a pair of attendees that were in contact at least once, annotated with the list of time intervals during which the contact was active.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `id`: the anonymous identifier of the attendee.
- (Edge) `time` (`contacts`): the end of the 20-second interval $[t - 20\,\text{s}, t]$ during which the contact was active, in seconds since 8:00 am of 29 June 2009 (UNIX time 1246255200).
- (Edge) `intervals` (`intervals`): the list of time intervals `[start, end]` of the contact, in the same units as `time`.
citations: L. Isella et al., "What’s in a crowd? Analysis of face-to-face behavioral networks." J. Theor. Bio. 271, 166-180 (2011).

datasets.name: sp_infectious
datasets.description:
Networks of face-to-face proximity contacts among visitors of the exhibition "INFECTIOUS: STAY AWAY" at the Science Gallery in Dublin, Ireland, measured by the SocioPatterns collaboration with wearable sensors, from 28 April to 17 July 2009. Visitors volunteered to wear radio badges that detected face-to-face proximity. Data were collected on 69 days, and each visitor was present on only one day. The following networks are provided:

- `contacts`: temporal network of all contacts. The upstream data consist of one file per day of data collection; here they are combined into a single network. Nodes are visitors, and each edge is a contact between two visitors active during a 20-second interval of the data collection, so that a pair of visitors is connected by one edge per interval in which they were in contact.
- `day_YYYY_MM_DD` (69 networks, one per day of data collection): the cumulative network of the given day, as represented in the Infectious SocioPatterns visualization and published separately upstream. Nodes are visitors, and an edge connects two visitors that were in contact at least once during the day; a few nodes are isolated. These networks were processed independently from the contact lists of the `contacts` network, and they do not match them exactly (on most days, they contain more nodes and contacts). Their nodes carry no identifier: the upstream node numbers are reused in different days for different visitors, and they do not correspond to the identifiers of the `contacts` network.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `id` (`contacts`): the anonymous identifier of the visitor.
- (Edge) `time` (`contacts`): the end of the 20-second interval $[t - 20\,\text{s}, t]$ during which the contact was active, as a UNIX timestamp in seconds.
- (Edge) `weight` (`day_YYYY_MM_DD`): the number of 20-second intervals during which the two visitors were in contact on that day.
citations: L. Isella et al., "What's in a crowd? Analysis of face-to-face behavioral networks." Journal of Theoretical Biology 271, 166-180 (2011).

datasets.name: sp_kenyan_households
datasets.description:
Network of face-to-face proximity contacts among members of 5 households in rural Kenya (in the Kilifi Health and Demographic Surveillance System area), measured with wearable proximity sensors between 24 April and 12 May 2012 as part of a SocioPatterns study. The members of each household wore the sensors for three consecutive days. Nodes are household members and each edge is a contact event between two members, either of the same household or of different households, recorded during the daytime (between 7:00 and 20:00). Two members can be connected by multiple edges, one per contact event.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `id`: the anonymous identifier of the member, unique only within its household (members are identified by the pair `house`, `id`).
- (Node) `house`: the household of the member (`L`, `F`, `E`, `B` or `H`).
- (Node) `age`: the age category of the member, coded from 0 to 4 (see Kiti et al. for the definition of the categories).
- (Node) `sex`: the sex of the member (`F` or `M`).
- (Edge) `duration`: the duration of the contact event in seconds.
- (Edge) `day`: the day of the experiment in which the contact took place (1, 2 or 3).
- (Edge) `hour`: the hour of the day in which the contact took place (7 to 20).
citations: M. Kiti et al., "Quantifying social contacts in a household setting of rural Kenya using wearable proximity sensors." EPJ Data Science 5, 21 (2016)

datasets.name: sp_malawi_village
datasets.description:
Temporal network of close-range proximity contacts among 86 inhabitants of Mdoliro, a village in the Dowa district (Central Region) of Malawi, measured with wearable proximity sensors by the SocioPatterns collaboration, as part of a Child and Youth Development Study funded by UNICEF Malawi. The study ran from 16 December 2019 to 10 January 2020; children, adolescents and adult caregivers of 28 households wore a sensor pinned to the front of their clothing, and sensors exchanged low-power radio packets that are only received at distances of about 1-1.5 m (attenuation threshold of -75 dBm). Two individuals are in contact during a 20-second interval if their sensors exchanged at least one packet during it. Participants were asked to remove the sensors overnight; night-time contacts and periods during which a sensor did not move (according to its accelerometer) were removed from the data. The released data cover the 14 days from 22 December 2019 to 4 January 2020, and include both contacts within and between households. The demographic metadata (age, gender, household) described in the paper are not released.

Nodes are individuals, and each edge is a contact between two individuals active during one 20-second interval, so that two individuals are connected by as many edges as the number of intervals in which they were in contact. The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `id`: the anonymous identifier of the individual (1 to 86).
- (Edge) `time`: the end of the 20-second interval in which the contact was active, in seconds. The origin of the times is the first recorded contact, on 22 December 2019 (its time of day is not stated in the source).
- (Edge) `date`: the date of the contact (`YYYY-MM-DD`). The source gives only the day of the month; the month and year were inferred from the study period.
citations: L. Ozella, D. Paolotti, G. Lichand, J. P. Rodríguez, S. Haenni, J. Phuka, O. B. Leal-Neto, C. Cattuto, "Using wearable proximity sensors to characterize social contact patterns in a village of rural Malawi." EPJ Data Science 10, 46 (2021)

datasets.name: sp_office
datasets.description:
Temporal network of face-to-face proximity contacts among 92 employees in an office building of the French Institute for Public Health Surveillance (InVS) in Saint-Maurice, France, from 24 June to 3 July 2013, measured by the SocioPatterns collaboration with wearable sensors. Nodes are employees, and each edge is a contact between two employees active during a 20-second interval of the data collection, so that a pair of employees is connected by one edge per interval in which they were in contact.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `id`: the anonymous identifier of the employee.
- (Node) `department`: the department of the employee (`DISQ`, `DMCT`, `DSE`, `SFLE` or `SRH`).
- (Edge) `time`: the end of the 20-second interval $[t - 20\,\text{s}, t]$ during which the contact was active, in seconds since 0:00 on 24 June 2013.
citations: M. Génois et al., "Data on face-to-face contacts in an office building suggest a low-cost vaccination strategy based on community linkers." Network Science 3(3), 326-347 (2015)

datasets.name: sp_office_2015
datasets.description:
Temporal network of face-to-face proximity contacts among employees of the French Institute for Public Health Surveillance (InVS) in Saint-Maurice, France, measured by the SocioPatterns collaboration with wearable sensors during two weeks in 2015. This is the second deployment in the same office building as the 2013 data set (see `sp_office`), with a larger number of participants (232, of whom 217 appear in the contacts). Participants wore sensors on their chests that exchange low-power radio packets, received only when two persons are within about 1.5 m of each other and facing each other. Two participants are in contact during a 20-second interval if their sensors detected each other during it. The contacts were recorded on ten working days (Monday to Friday of two consecutive weeks), between about 8:00 and 20:00. The data were released with the study of Génois and Barrat (2018), which compares them with co-presence data recorded in the same deployment (the co-presence data are part of `sp_colocation`).

Nodes are participants, and each edge is a contact between two participants active during one 20-second interval, so that two participants are connected by as many edges as the number of intervals in which they were in contact. Participants without any recorded contact are included as isolated nodes. The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `id`: the anonymous identifier of the participant.
- (Node) `department`: the department of the participant in the institute (`DCAR`, `DG`, `DISQ`, `DMCT`, `DMI`, `DSE`, `DST`, `SCOM`, `SDOC`, `SFLE`, `SRH` or `SSI`).
- (Edge) `time`: the end of the 20-second interval $[t - 20\,\text{s}, t]$ during which the contact was active, in seconds. The origin of the times is not stated in the source; the values are consistent with seconds since midnight of the first day (a Monday).
citations: M. Génois, A. Barrat, "Can co-location be used as a proxy for face-to-face contacts?" EPJ Data Science 7, 11 (2018)

datasets.name: sp_primary_school
datasets.description:
Networks of face-to-face proximity contacts among the children and teachers of a primary school in Lyon, France, measured by the SocioPatterns collaboration with wearable sensors during two days (Thursday 1 and Friday 2 October 2009). The school has five grades, each divided in two classes, and the study included 232 children and 10 teachers. The following networks are provided:

- `contacts`: temporal network of all contacts. Nodes are persons, and each edge is a contact between two persons active during a 20-second interval of the data collection, so that a pair of persons is connected by one edge per interval in which they were in contact.
- `day_1`, `day_2`: the cumulative contact networks of the first and second day, published separately upstream. Nodes are the persons present on that day, and an edge connects two persons that were in contact at least once during the day.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `id`: the anonymous identifier of the person (the same in all networks).
- (Node) `class`: the class of the child (`1A` to `5B`, where the digit is the grade), or `Teachers`.
- (Node) `gender`: the gender (`M`, `F` or `Unknown`).
- (Edge) `time` (`contacts`): the end of the 20-second interval $[t - 20\,\text{s}, t]$ during which the contact was active, in seconds from an unspecified reference time.
- (Edge) `duration` (`day_1`, `day_2`): the cumulative time the two persons spent in contact during the day, in seconds (a multiple of 20 seconds).
- (Edge) `count` (`day_1`, `day_2`): the number of times the contact between the two persons was established during the day.
citations: Juliette Stehle et al., "High-Resolution Measurements of Face-to-Face Contact Patterns in a Primary School." PLoS ONE 6(8), e23176 (2011).

datasets.name: sp_sfhh_conference
datasets.description:
A temporal network of face-to-face contacts between participants of the 2009 annual conference of the Société Française d'Hygiène Hospitalière (SFHH, French society for hospital hygiene) in Nice, France, recorded by the SocioPatterns collaboration. Of the about 1,200 attendees, 405 volunteers wore radio-frequency identification (RFID) badges on their chests, which exchange low-power radio packets that are only received when two people are close to each other (about 1 to 1.5 meters) and facing each other, since the body shields the signal. Time is coarse-grained into intervals of 20 seconds, and two participants are considered in contact during an interval if their badges detected each other during it. The data were collected over the two days of the conference, from 9 am to 9 pm on the first day and from 8:30 am to 4:30 pm on the second (the dataset page gives the dates as June 4 and 5, 2009, while Stehlé et al. give June 3 and 4). The data were first studied by Cattuto et al. (2010) and Stehlé et al. (2011), and were publicly released by Génois and Barrat (2018); 403 of the 405 participants appear in the released contacts. The identities of the participants are anonymized and no metadata are released.

Nodes are participants, and each edge corresponds to a contact between two participants during one 20-second interval, so that two participants are connected by as many edges as the number of intervals in which they were in contact. The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `id`: the anonymous identifier of the participant in the source data.
- (Edge) `time`: the end of the 20-second interval in which the contact was active, in seconds (the contact was active during [`time` - 20, `time`]). The origin of the times is not stated in the source; the values (32,520 to 146,820) are consistent with seconds since midnight of the first day.
citations: M. Génois, A. Barrat, "Can co-location be used as a proxy for face-to-face contacts?" EPJ Data Science 7, 11 (2018)

J. Stehlé, N. Voirin, A. Barrat, C. Cattuto, V. Colizza, L. Isella, C. Régis, J.-F. Pinton, N. Khanafer, W. Van den Broeck, P. Vanhems, "Simulation of an SEIR infectious disease model on the dynamic contact network of conference attendees." BMC Medicine 9, 87 (2011)
C. Cattuto, W. Van den Broeck, A. Barrat, V. Colizza, J.-F. Pinton, A. Vespignani, "Dynamics of Person-to-Person Interactions from Distributed RFID Sensor Networks." PLoS ONE 5(7), e11596 (2010)

datasets.name: sp_south_african_households
datasets.description:
Temporal network of close-range proximity contacts between members of 88 households in two urban communities of South Africa, Klerksdorp (North West Province) and Soweto (Gauteng Province), collected in the SARS-CoV-2 household transmission study SA-S-HTS led by the National Institute for Communicable Diseases (NICD), in collaboration with SocioPatterns. After a symptomatic adult SARS-CoV-2 index case was identified at a clinic, the members of their household were followed up, and wearable proximity sensors were deployed for about two weeks (between November 2020 and August 2021) to measure close-range interactions (within about 1.5 m) between household members. Sensors exchange low-power radio packets, and a contact event between two sensors is a sequence of consecutive 20-second intervals in each of which at least one packet was exchanged. Events outside the deployment period and during 5-minute periods in which the sensor's accelerometer detected no movement were removed, as were individuals who did not comply or had sensor failures. Due to a technical error some sensors in Klerksdorp did not record valid timestamps; these were aligned relative to each other by cross-correlating packet time series, and their times start at the UNIX epoch (1 January 1970) instead of the real date. The data include 340 individuals (88 index cases and 252 household contacts), all of whom were included in the analysis of Kleynhans et al. (2023); contacts were only measured within households, so the network has one connected component per household.

Nodes are individuals, and each edge is a contact event between two members of the same household; two individuals are connected by as many edges as the number of their contact events. (The upstream file lists every event twice, once for each direction; here each event appears once.) The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `id`: the identifier of the individual (site letter, `J` for Klerksdorp or `S` for Soweto, household number and individual number).
- (Node) `household`: the household identifier.
- (Node) `site`: the study site (`Klerksdorp` or `Soweto`).
- (Node) `age_group`: the age group in years (`<5`, `5-12`, `13-17`, `18-34`, `35-59` or `>=60`; the latter is written `=60` in the upstream file).
- (Node) `sex`: the sex of the individual (`Male` or `Female`).
- (Node) `role`: whether the individual is the SARS-CoV-2 index case of the household (`Index`) or a household contact (`Contact`).
- (Node) `sars_cov_2`: the SARS-CoV-2 infection status of the individual during follow-up (`Positive` or `Negative`).
- (Node) `susceptible`: for household contacts, whether they were susceptible (`Susceptible`) or seropositive at baseline according to serology (empty for index cases).
- (Node) `smoker`: whether the individual currently smokes cigarettes (`Yes`, `No` or `Unknown`).
- (Node) `bmi`: body mass index category (`Underweight`, `Normal weight`, `Overweight`, `Obese` or `Unknown`).
- (Node) `sleeps_with_index`: whether the individual sleeps in the same room as the index case (`Yes`, `No` or `Unknown`).
- (Node) `cared_by_index`: whether the individual's main caregiver is the index case (`Yes` or `No`).
- (Node) `index_age_group`, `index_sex`: age group and sex of the household's index case (empty for index cases).
- (Node) `index_ct_cat1`, `index_ct_cat2`: category of the index case's minimum PCR cycle threshold (Ct) value during the episode, in two different binnings (`>35`, `25-35`, `<25` and `>35`, `30-35`, `<30`, respectively, or `Unknown`; empty for index cases). Lower values correspond to higher viral loads.
- (Node) `index_variant`: the SARS-CoV-2 variant infecting the index case (`Alpha`, `Beta`, `Delta`, `non-Alpha/Beta/Delta` or `Variant Unknown`; empty for index cases).
- (Edge) `time`: the start of the contact event, as a UNIX timestamp in seconds (the upstream date-times are local times without a time zone, and are interpreted here as UTC). For the Klerksdorp sensors without a valid timestamp (see `timestamped`), times are relative, starting at 1 January 1970.
- (Edge) `duration`: the duration of the contact event in seconds (a multiple of 20 s).
- (Edge) `timestamped`: whether the time of the event is a real date-time (`True`) or a relative time of an unstamped Klerksdorp sensor (`False`).
citations: J. Kleynhans, L. Dall'Amico, L. Gauvin, M. Tizzoni, L. Maloma, S. Walaza, N. A. Martinson, A. von Gottberg, N. Wolter, M. Makhasi, C. Cohen, C. Cattuto, S. Tempia, "Association of close-range contact patterns with SARS-CoV-2: a household transmission study." eLife 12, e84753 (2023)

J. Kleynhans et al., "Household Transmission of Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 From Adult Index Cases With and Without Human Immunodeficiency Virus in South Africa, 2020-2021: A Case-Ascertained, Prospective, Observational Household Transmission Study." Clinical Infectious Diseases 76(3), e71-e81 (2023)

datasets.name: spanish_cocaine
datasets.description:
Networks of communication among members of four groups involved in cocaine trafficking in Spain, reconstructed by Giménez-Salinas Framis (2011) from police wiretapping and meetings registered by police investigations of these organizations between 2007 and 2009. Nodes are individuals (vertex property `name`, with anonymized initials), and an edge indicates communication between them. The edge property `weight`, present where the source matrix has values other than one, is not documented (it may represent the level of communication activity). Where the two directions in the source matrix differ, the tie is included, with the larger value. The four networks correspond to the police operations:

- `mambo` (31 nodes): started in 2006, a group of Colombian citizens introducing cocaine to be adulterated and distributed in Madrid, acting as a wholesale supplier between South American importers and Madrid retailers, with cocaine smuggled from Colombia through Brazil and Uruguay.
- `juanes` (51 nodes): a group detected in 2009 smuggling cocaine from Mexico to be distributed in Madrid, in close cooperation with an organization laundering the income (estimated at EUR 60 million).
- `jake` (38 nodes): a group investigated in 2008, a wholesale supplier and retail distributor of cocaine and heroin in a large distribution zone in Madrid traditionally controlled by Roma clans.
- `acero` (25 nodes): started in 2007, a smaller family-based group led by a woman, distributing cocaine in Madrid supplied by groups based in north-western Spain, with its own money-laundering procedures.

Data distributed by the UCINET datasets collection (University of Manchester).[^ucinet]

[^ucinet]: Description obtained in part from the [UCINET datasets page](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/datasets/covert-networks/cocaine-smuggling).
citations: A. Giménez-Salinas Framis, "Illegal networks or criminal organizations: Power, roles and facilitators in four cocaine trafficking structures." Third Annual Illicit Networks Workshop, Montreal (2011)

datasets.name: spanish_highschools
datasets.description:
Directed networks of friendships obtained through a social survey of spanish high school students. Nodes are students, and a directed edge from student $i$ to student $j$ means that $i$ rated their relationship with classmate $j$ in the survey, with the rating given by the edge `weight`.

The dataset comprises 13 high school networks that represent the diverse social relationships that exist between students within each school.

The weight of each edge varies between -2, -1, +1, and +2. The sign indicates the nature of the friendship, while the number corresponds to its intensity.

Node properties include the age level, group, sex, and psychological attributes such as CRT and prosociality.
citations: Miguel Ruiz-García, Juan Ozaita, María Pereda, and Angel Sánchez, "Triadic influence as a proxy for compatibility in social relationships", PNAS 120 (13) e2215041120 (2023)

datasets.name: sparrow_populations
datasets.description:
Weighted network of genetic differentiation among the house sparrow (*Passer domesticus*) populations of 15 islands of an insular metapopulation off the coast of northern Norway, from the study of H. T. Baalsrud and collaborators on effective population sizes (genotypes deposited in the Dryad repository). The data were compiled by M. Cantor and collaborators for a study of nestedness across levels of biological organization, and are distributed in the repository of that study (file `mep_sparrow_Rst.txt`). Nodes are populations, and an undirected edge connects every pair of populations (the network is a complete graph), weighted by their pairwise genetic differentiation R<sub>ST</sub> (Slatkin, 1995), computed from the variance of microsatellite allele sizes (13 nuclear, selectively neutral microsatellite loci). R<sub>ST</sub> is 0 for genetically identical populations and grows with differentiation; small negative values arise from sampling error. Note that the documentation of the source describes the weights as the genetic similarity 1 - R<sub>ST</sub>, but the file contains R<sub>ST</sub> itself (with zeros on the diagonal). The populations are not identified in the source data.

The edges have the property `weight`, the pairwise R<sub>ST</sub>.
citations: H. T. Baalsrud, B.-E. Sæther, I. J. Hagen, A. M. Myhre, T. H. Ringsby, H. Pärn, H. Jensen, "Effects of population characteristics and structure on estimates of effective population size in a house sparrow metapopulation." Molecular Ecology 23, 2653-2668 (2014)
H. T. Baalsrud et al., "Data from: Effects of population characteristics and structure on estimates of effective population size in a house sparrow metapopulation." Dryad Digital Repository (2014)
M. Slatkin, "A measure of population subdivision based on microsatellite allele frequencies." Genetics 139(1), 457-462 (1995)

M. Cantor, M. M. Pires, F. M. D. Marquitti, R. L. G. Raimundo, E. Sebastián-González, P. P. Coltri, S. I. Perez, D. R. Barneche, D. Y. C. Brandt, K. Nunes, F. G. Daura-Jorge, S. R. Floeter, P. R. Guimarães Jr., "Nestedness across biological scales." PLoS ONE 12(2), e0171691 (2017)

datasets.name: splotopen
datasets.description:
Bipartite network of vegetation plots and the vascular plant species recorded in them, from sPlotOpen, an open-access, environmentally balanced subset of sPlot, the global database of vegetation plots. The plots come from 105 source datasets (vegetation-plot databases of the Global Index of Vegetation-Plot Databases, GIVD) and cover all continents and biomes; they were recorded between 1888 and 2015 by many surveyors, who listed the plant species present in a plot of a given area and estimated their abundance (usually their cover). The plots were selected so as to balance the environmental conditions (climate and soil) of the world, in three partially overlapping resampled sets of about 50,000 plots each (marked by vertex properties), which are meant to be used as replicates in global analyses.

Nodes are plots and species (with names resolved to a common taxonomic backbone), and an edge connects a plot to each species recorded in it, with the abundance of the species in the plot; a species can be listed several times in a plot (e.g. in several vegetation layers, or under several original names resolved to the same species), which gives parallel edges. The plots also have the community-weighted means and variances of plant functional traits computed by sPlot (`sPlotOpen_CWM_CWV.txt`), and their bibliographic metadata (`sPlotOpen_metadata.txt`: the references of the source datasets and of the publications of the plots, the names of the surveyors, the original identifiers), with the references in BibTeX format (`sPlotOpen_references.bib`) as a graph property. The data are those of version 76 (2023-03-07) of the dataset in the iDiv data repository.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `is_plot`: whether the node is a plot (otherwise it is a species).
- (Node) `name`: the identifier of the plot (`PlotObservationID`), or the name of the species.
- (Node) `givd_id`, `dataset`: the GIVD code and the name of the source dataset of the plot.
- (Node) `continent`, `country`, `biome`: the continent, country and biome (as defined by sPlot) of the plot.
- (Node) `date`: the date of recording of the plot (as Unix time; `-1` if unknown).
- (Node) `latitude`, `longitude`, `location_uncertainty`: the coordinates of the plot (WGS84) and their uncertainty in meters.
- (Node) `releve_area`: the area of the plot, in square meters.
- (Node) `plant_recorded`: the group of plants recorded in the plot (e.g. `All vascular plants`).
- (Node) `elevation`, `aspect`, `slope`: the elevation (m), aspect and slope (degrees) of the plot.
- (Node) `is_forest`: whether the plot is a forest, as estimated from the growth forms of the species (empty if unknown).
- (Node) `esy`: the habitat of the plot in the EUNIS classification (European plots).
- (Node) `naturalness`: `1` for natural and `2` for semi-natural vegetation (NaN if unknown).
- (Node) `forest`, `shrubland`, `grassland`, `wetland`, `sparse_vegetation`: the vegetation type of the plot as given by the data contributors (`TRUE`, `FALSE`, or empty if unknown).
- (Node) `cover_total`, `cover_tree_layer`, `cover_shrub_layer`, `cover_herb_layer`, `cover_moss_layer`, `cover_lichen_layer`, `cover_algae_layer`, `cover_litter_layer`, `cover_bare_rocks`, `cover_cryptogams`, `cover_bare_soil`: the cover (in %) of the vegetation and of its layers, and of litter, rocks and bare soil (NaN if not given).
- (Node) `height_trees_highest`, `height_trees_lowest`, `height_shrubs_highest`, `height_shrubs_lowest` (m), `height_herbs_average`, `height_herbs_lowest`, `height_herbs_highest` (cm): the heights of the vegetation layers (NaN if not given).
- (Node) `soilclim_pc1`, `soilclim_pc2`: the coordinates of the plot on the first two principal components of its climate and soil conditions.
- (Node) `resample_1`, `resample_2`, `resample_3`, `resample_1_consensus`: whether the plot belongs to each of the three resampled sets (and to the first one after replacements).
- (Node) `species_richness`: the number of species in the plot (-1 for species).
- (Node) `traitcoverage_cover`, `traitcoverage_pa`: the proportion of the relative cover of the species of the plot for which the traits are available, and the proportion of the species with trait information.
- (Node) `<trait>_cwm`, `<trait>_cwv`: the community-weighted mean and variance in the plot of 18 plant functional traits (from the gap-filled data of the TRY database, as computed by sPlot; the values are apparently on a logarithmic scale, since they can be negative; NaN if not given, e.g. the variances of plots with a single species with traits): `leafarea` (leaf area, mm²), `stemdens` (stem specific density, g/cm³), `sla` (specific leaf area, m²/kg), `leafc_perdrymass`, `leafn`, `leafp` (leaf carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus content per dry mass, mg/g), `plantheight` (plant height, m), `seedmass` (seed dry mass, mg), `seed_length` (mm), `ldmc` (leaf dry matter content, g/g), `leafnperarea` (leaf nitrogen per area, g/m²), `leafnpratio` (leaf N/P ratio), `leaf_delta_15n` (leaf δ15N, per mil), `seed_num_rep_unit` (seed number per reproduction unit), `leaffreshmass` (leaf fresh mass, g), `stem_cond_dens` (stem conduit density, mm⁻²), `disp_unit_leng` (dispersal unit length, mm), `wood_vessel_length` (wood vessel element length, μm).
- (Node) `db_bibtexkey`: the BibTeX key of the reference of the source dataset of the plot (in the graph property `references`).
- (Node) `releve_author`, `releve_coauthors`: the names of the authors or surveyors of the plot, as given in the data.
- (Node) `biblioreference`, `bibtexkey`: the bibliographic reference of the publication in which the plot was described, and its BibTeX key (in `references`).
- (Node) `nr_table_in_publ`, `nr_releve_in_table`: the table of the publication containing the plot, and the identifier of the plot in it.
- (Node) `original_nr_in_database`, `original_plotid`, `original_subplotid`: the identifiers of the plot (and subplot, for nested plots) in the source database.
- (Node) `project`, `remarks`: the project in which the plot was recorded, and remarks.
- (Node) `guid`: the unique identifier given by Turboveg when the plot was first stored.
- (Edge) `relative_cover`: the abundance of the species in the plot, normalized to sum to one in each plot.
- (Edge) `original_abundance`, `abundance_scale`: the abundance of the species as in the original data, and its scale (`CoverPerc`: cover percentage, `pa`: presence or absence, `x_BA`: basal area, `x_IC`: individual count, `x_SC`: stem count, `x_IV`: relative importance, `x_RF`: relative frequency; the values `x_PF` and `x`, also found in the data, are not documented).
- (Edge) `original_species`: the name of the species in the original data, before the taxonomic resolution (one of them is garbled in the data, with invalid characters, which are replaced by `�`).
- (Graph) `references`: the references of the source datasets and of the publications of the plots, in BibTeX format (`sPlotOpen_references.bib`).
citations: F. M. Sabatini, J. Lenoir, T. Hattab, E. A. Arnst, M. Chytrý, J. Dengler, P. De Ruffray, S. M. Hennekens, U. Jandt, F. Jansen, et al., "sPlotOpen – An environmentally balanced, open-access, global dataset of vegetation plots." Global Ecology and Biogeography 30, 1740-1764 (2021)

datasets.name: spotted_hyenas
datasets.description:
Weighted social network of the members of a clan of spotted hyenas (*Crocuta crocuta*) in Kenya, from the long-term study of K. E. Holekamp and collaborators (data deposited in the Dryad repository).
