- `temporal`: the statements with a time (a point in time, or the start of a period), as a year from 1900 to 2024.
- `static`: the statements of the same entities without a time; the statements that are also temporal ones were removed by TGB.

The data do not include the labels of the entities and relations, which can be looked up in Wikidata.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `wikidata_id`: the Wikidata identifier of the entity, e.g. `Q648`.
- (Edge) `relation`: the Wikidata property of the statement, e.g. `P166`.
- (Edge) `year` (`temporal` only): the year of the statement.
citations: J. Gastinger, S. Huang, M. Galkin, E. Loghmani, A. Parviz, F. Poursafaei, J. Danovitch, E. Rossi, I. Koutis, H. Stuckenschmidt, R. Rabbany, G. Rabusseau, "TGB 2.0: A Benchmark for Learning on Temporal Knowledge Graphs and Heterogeneous Graphs." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 37 (Datasets and Benchmarks Track) (2024)
D. Vrandečić, M. Krötzsch, "Wikidata: a free collaborative knowledgebase." Communications of the ACM 57(10), 78-85 (2014)

datasets.name: tntp
datasets.description:
Road networks used as test problems for the traffic assignment problem, from the Transportation Networks for Research repository maintained by B. Stabler, H. Bar-Gera and E. Sall, which continues H. Bar-Gera's earlier "Transportation Network Test Problems" (TNTP) collection. Each network represents the road system of a region as prepared for (static) traffic assignment: nodes are intersections, points along roads, or zone centroids (artificial nodes representing traffic analysis zones, where trips start and end), and directed edges are road links, including the artificial "centroid connector" links that join zones to the road network. Most networks were produced by regional planning agencies or researchers, and many are simplified or aggregated representations of the real road system; the years of the underlying data are often unknown. The origin-destination demand tables that accompany the networks in the repository are not included.

The networks are:

- `anaheim`: Anaheim, California, USA, for 1992 (provided by J. Ban and R. Jayakrishnan). Time in minutes, length in feet, speed in feet per minute; node positions are longitude and latitude.
- `austin`: Austin, Texas, USA, AM peak hour of 2005 (provided by C. Xie). Every node is a zone. The network contains five duplicated links with different parameters (see the repository notes).
- `barcelona`: Barcelona, Spain.
- `berlin_center`, `berlin_friedrichshain`, `berlin_mitte_center`, `berlin_mitte_prenzlauerberg_friedrichshain`, `berlin_prenzlauerberg_center`, `berlin_tiergarten`: areas of Berlin, Germany, provided by R. Möhring, A. Schulz and N. Stier-Moses, and used by Jahn et al. (2005). Node positions are in arbitrary planar units. `berlin_center` contains six duplicated links with different parameters.
- `birmingham`: the Birmingham City Region, England, a modified version of the PRISM transport model (provided by T. van Vuren and K. Noekel). Node positions are planar coordinates (apparently British National Grid eastings and northings, in meters).
- `braess`: the four-node network of the Braess paradox (prepared by A. Koh).
- `chicago_regional`: a detailed representation of the Chicago region, USA, by the Chicago Area Transportation Study (CATS). Time in minutes, length in miles, toll in cents; node positions are planar coordinates.
- `chicago_sketch`: an aggregated ("sketch planning") representation of the Chicago region, by CATS. Time in minutes, length in miles, toll in cents; node positions are Illinois State Plane coordinates, in feet.
- `eastern_massachusetts`: the highway subnetwork of the Eastern Massachusetts network, for the PM period of April 2012, from Zhang et al. (2016). Time in hours, length in miles; every node is a zone.
- `gold_coast`: Gold Coast, Australia, from Veitch Lister Consultancy (provided by M. Bliemer; revised in January 2016). Capacity is per lane, length in km, time in minutes, speeds in km/h; node positions are longitude and latitude.
- `hessen_asymmetric`, `terrassa_asymmetric`, `winnipeg_asymmetric`: networks of Hessen (Germany), Terrassa (Spain) and Winnipeg (Canada) with asymmetric cost functions at junctions (provided by E. Codina Sancho); the asymmetric cost structure itself is not included in the network files.
- `philadelphia`: the Delaware Valley Region (Philadelphia, USA), by the Delaware Valley Regional Planning Commission. Capacity in vehicles per 24 hours, length in miles, time in minutes, toll in cents; the `speed` values have unknown meaning; node positions are in units of 0.01 miles. Link types: 1 freeway, 2 parkway, 3 principal arterial, 4 secondary arterial, 6 collector/local, 7 approach link (including centroid connectors), 8 ramp, 9 dummy link.
- `sioux_falls`: the classic, unrealistic, Sioux Falls (USA) network of LeBlanc et al. (1975). Free flow times are in units of 0.01 hours, lengths are set equal to them, and node positions were generated artificially to reproduce the diagram of the paper.
- `sydney`: Sydney, Australia, from Veitch Lister Consultancy (provided by M. Bliemer). Length in km, time in minutes, speeds in km/h; node positions are longitude and latitude.
- `winnipeg`: Winnipeg, Canada (one of several versions of this network; here the capacity is set to 1, and `b` is in fact B/capacity^power).
- `symmetrica`: the Symmetrica test case for transportation electrification research of Farid (2015), a synthetic grid-like road network with conventional links and electrified links that can charge vehicles while driving, and nodes that are conventional stations or home and work locations with charging facilities. Node positions are grid coordinates.

The networks have the following properties (missing values are NaN):

- (Node) `is_zone`: whether the node is a zone (zones are numbered first in the source files; in some networks zone nodes cannot be traversed by through traffic, see the graph property `first_thru_node`).
- (Node) `pos`: the position of the node, in the units given above (only for some networks).
- (Node) `original_id`: the node number in the original data (Berlin networks only).
- (Edge) `capacity`: the link capacity (usually in vehicles per hour).
- (Edge) `length`.
- (Edge) `free_flow_time`: the travel time at zero flow.
- (Edge) `b` and `power`: the parameters of the link travel time function, travel time = free_flow_time * (1 + b * (flow / capacity)^power).
- (Edge) `speed`: the speed limit or free flow speed (its meaning is not consistent across networks).
- (Edge) `toll`.
- (Edge) `link_type`: a network-specific link classification.
- (Edge) `critical_speed` and `lanes` (`gold_coast` and `sydney` only).
- (Edge) `flow` and `flow_cost`: the best known user-equilibrium link flow and the corresponding link travel cost (`anaheim`, `barcelona`, `chicago_regional`, `chicago_sketch`, `sioux_falls`, `winnipeg` only).
- (Node) `node_type` (`symmetrica`): `StationC`, conventional station; `HomeE` and `WorkE`, home and work locations with charging (the nodes of `symmetrica` also have `pos`).
- (Edge) `is_electric` (`symmetrica`): whether the link can charge vehicles.
- (Edge) `capacity`, `speed`, `length` (`symmetrica`): the capacity (vehicles), the speed (km/min) and the length (km) of the link. All links of the same kind have identical parameters in the source data.
citations: Transportation Networks for Research Core Team, "Transportation Networks for Research."
O. Jahn, R. H. Möhring, A. S. Schulz, N. E. Stier-Moses, "System-Optimal Routing of Traffic Flows with User Constraints in Networks with Congestion." Operations Research 53(4), 600-616 (2005)
L. J. LeBlanc, E. K. Morlok, W. P. Pierskalla, "An efficient approach to solving the road network equilibrium traffic assignment problem." Transportation Research 9(5), 309-318 (1975)

J. Zhang, S. Pourazarm, C. G. Cassandras, I. Ch. Paschalidis, "The price of anarchy in transportation networks by estimating user cost functions from actual traffic data." 2016 IEEE 55th Conference on Decision and Control (CDC), 789-794 (2016)
A. M. Farid, "Symmetrica: test case for transportation electrification research." Infrastructure Complexity 2, 9 (2015)

datasets.name: tolokers
datasets.description:
A network of crowd workers ("Tolokers") of the Toloka crowdsourcing platform who worked on one data labeling project, released by Toloka and used as a benchmark for node classification (as the `tolokers` dataset of Platonov et al.). Nodes are annotators, and an undirected edge connects two annotators who labeled the same task (at least one). Each annotator is described by the shares of their labels that were approved, skipped, expired or rejected, by their self-reported education level and knowledge of English, and by whether they passed the platform's English test; the classification target is whether the annotator was banned from the project. Which tasks were labeled, and by how many common annotators, is not included in the data.

The node indices are the annotator identifiers of the source data. The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `approved_rate`, `skipped_rate`, `expired_rate`, `rejected_rate`: the fractions of the annotator's labels that were approved, of the tasks that the annotator skipped, of the tasks that expired, and of the labels that were rejected (they sum to 1).
- (Node) `education`: the education level reported by the annotator, one of `none`, `basic`, `middle` and `high`.
- (Node) `english_profile`: whether the annotator reported knowing English.
- (Node) `english_tested`: whether the annotator passed the platform's English test.
- (Node) `banned`: whether the annotator was banned from the project.
citations: D. Likhobaba, N. Pavlichenko, D. Ustalov, "Toloker Graph: Interaction of Crowd Annotators." Zenodo (2023)

O. Platonov, D. Kuznedelev, M. Diskin, A. Babenko, L. Prokhorenkova, "A critical look at the evaluation of GNNs under heterophily: Are we really making progress?" International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR) (2023)

datasets.name: topcoder_epidemic
datasets.description: An undirected network of friendships from an unidentified online social networking site, used for the "Epidemic" programming contest held at TopCoder.com in April 2008, and provided by L. Backstrom to the UCI Network Data Repository. Nodes are users of the site, and an undirected edge connects two users who are friends. In the contest, participants had to find strategies to optimally slow down the spread of a simulated epidemic along networks sampled from this one (the sampled example graphs are not included here). The name of the site and the date of collection are not documented, and the nodes carry no metadata.
citations: C. DuBois, P. Smyth, "Social network from TopCoder's Epidemic contest", UCI Network Data Repository, University of California, Irvine (2008)

datasets.name: topology
datasets.description: An integrated snapshot of the structure of the Internet at the level of Autonomous Systems (ASs), reconstructed from multiple sources, including the RouteViews and RIPE BGP trace collectors, route servers, looking glasses, and the Internet Routing Registry databases. The data were collected by the Internet topology project of the UCLA Internet Research Lab, which follows the methodology of B. Zhang et al.; this snapshot is the version of 10 March 2010, with connection times between 15 February and 10 March 2010. Nodes are ASs, and an edge is a connection between two ASs, annotated with the time of the connection (edge property `time`); two ASs can be connected by multiple edges, each representing an individual connection in time.
citations: B. Zhang et al., "Collecting the Internet AS-level topology." SIGCOMM Computer Communication Review 35(1), 53-61 (2005)

datasets.name: trackers
datasets.description:
Bipartite networks of web domains and the third-party services embedded in their pages, from the large-scale analysis of online tracking by S. Schelter and J. Kunegis. The data were extracted from the 3.5 billion web pages of the CommonCrawl 2012 corpus, a breadth-first crawl of the web: for each page, the extractor collected the pay-level domains (the sub-domains of a public top-level domain that are usually registered by a paying owner, e.g. `facebook.com`) of the external resources embedded in its HTML code, i.e. those referenced in the `src` attribute of `script`, `iframe`, `link` and `img` tags, and those found as URI strings in its embedded JavaScript code (third parties loaded dynamically by external JavaScript code cannot be found). The data were aggregated by pay-level domain, so that both web sites and third parties are represented by their pay-level domains. The 1,375 third parties found in at least 0.01% of the domains were labeled by hand according to their purpose and business model (e.g. advertising, analytics, widgets, content delivery, hosting), and 355 of them were deemed to be potentially privacy-threatening tracking services, whose purpose or business model aims at recording the behavior of the users visiting the pages that embed them (advertising, analytics, widgets and beacons).

The collection comprises two networks:

- `third_parties`: the third-party network, obtained from the Koblenz Network Collection (KONECT), with 27,665,730 domains and 12,756,244 third-party domains, and 140,613,762 edges. An edge connects a domain to a third party embedded in its pages. Each domain is represented by different nodes as a web site and as a third party. The nodes are not identified by their domain names, and have only the property `is_right`, which is true for the third parties.
- `trackers`: the tracking network, from the web page of the authors, with the domains that embed at least one of the 355 tracking services, and the trackers themselves. An edge connects a domain to a tracker embedded in its pages. A domain that is also a tracker (e.g. `facebook.com`) is represented by different nodes as a web site and as a tracker.

The `trackers` network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the pay-level domain.
- (Node) `pld_id`: the ID of the domain in the pay-level domain index of the source data.
- (Node) `is_tracker`: whether the node is a tracker (otherwise it is a web site).
- (Node) `category`: the category of the tracker (`Advertising`, `Analytics`, `Widget` or `Beacon`; empty for web sites).
- (Node) `company`: the company owning the tracker, as determined by hand by the authors (empty for web sites).
- (Node) `registration_country`: the country of registration of the domain of the tracker (two-letter code, `#` if unknown; empty for web sites).
- (Node) `embeddings_javascript`, `embeddings_iframe`, `embeddings_image`, `embeddings_link`: the number of domains that embed the tracker as JavaScript code, in an iframe, as an image, or as another linked resource (e.g. style sheet), respectively (0 for web sites). The total number of domains that embed the tracker, also given in the source data, is the degree of the node.

The source data also give the organization that registered the domain of each tracker, which was left out as it mostly coincides with the owning company.
citations: S. Schelter, J. Kunegis, "Tracking the Trackers: A Large-Scale Analysis of Embedded Web Trackers." Proceedings of the International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media 10(1), 679-682 (2016)
S. Schelter, J. Kunegis, "On the Ubiquity of Web Tracking: Insights from a Billion-Page Web Crawl." The Journal of Web Science 4(4), 53-66 (2018)

datasets.name: train_terrorists
datasets.description:
Network of the individuals involved in the bombing of commuter trains in Madrid on 11 March 2004, reconstructed by J. A. Rodríguez (University of Barcelona) from accounts in the two major Spanish daily newspapers (El País and El Mundo), and popularized by B. Hayes (2006). The individuals are the people suspected of having participated in the bombing and their relatives. Four kinds of ties were recorded: (1) trust–friendship (contact, kinship, links in the telephone center); (2) ties to Al Qaeda and to Osama Bin Laden; (3) co-participation in training camps and/or wars; (4) co-participation in previous terrorist attacks (11 September, Casablanca). The four relations were added together to give a "strength of connection" index from 1 to 4. The data were distributed by L. C. Freeman on his network data page at the University of California, Irvine (no longer online), from which this version was obtained via the Internet Archive.

An undirected edge (i, j) indicates a tie of at least one kind between individuals i and j. Six individuals have no ties, and are isolated nodes.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the individual.
- (Edge) `weight`: the strength of the connection (the number of kinds of ties, from 1 to 4).
citations: B. Hayes, "Connecting the Dots: Can the tools of graph theory and social-network studies unravel the next big plot?" American Scientist 94(5), 400-404 (2006)

datasets.name: transfermarkt
datasets.description:
Networks of football (soccer) clubs and players, from the "transfermarkt-datasets" of David (dcaribou), a dataset scraped from the football website Transfermarkt and cleaned into tables of competitions, clubs, players, games, lineups, appearances and transfers. It covers the games of 70 competitions (the first divisions of the main European leagues, their national cups, the European club competitions, and the main national-team tournaments, e.g. the World Cup), mostly from the 2012/13 season on (a few national-team tournaments since 2006), and the transfers of the players of the clubs of these leagues (since 1993). The dataset was updated weekly until its updates were paused in July 2026; the networks are of the last version (version 679 of the Kaggle copy, September 5, 2026), which is current to July 6, 2026.

There are five networks:

- `transfers`: a directed multigraph of clubs, with an edge from the club a player left to the club he joined, for each of the 175,165 transfers in the data (including loans and returns from loans, and moves to and from youth or reserve teams, which are clubs of their own, and to "Without Club" or "Retired"). Clubs outside the covered leagues are included as far as they appear in the transfers. 8 transfers are from a club to itself (self-loops). Some transfers are dated in the future (519 after July 6, 2026, up to 2030), as given in the data. A club can appear under several names (e.g. after renaming); the latest one is used.
- `games`: a directed multigraph of clubs and national teams, with an edge from the home team to the away team for each of the 88,958 games.
- `teammates`: an undirected network of players, with an edge between two players listed for the same club in the same game (in the starting lineup or among the substitutes, from the lineups table, or as having played in the game, from the appearances table), weighted by the number of such games. The lineups are available for 81,197 games, and the appearances for 73,426 games (only for the players of clubs in the covered domestic leagues). The players without a profile in the dataset (most of those of clubs outside the covered leagues) are included with their names only; the players with a profile but without any game in the lineups or appearances are included as isolated nodes.
- `player_club`: a bipartite network of players and clubs (or national teams), with an edge between a player and each club for which he was listed in a game (in the lineups or the appearances, as in `teammates`), weighted by the number of such games (115,515 players, 3,156 clubs and 222,975 edges). Only the players listed in games are included.
- `player_game`: a bipartite network of players and games, with an edge for each player listed in a game (in the starting lineup or among the substitutes, or as having played in it), with the details of the lineup and of the appearance (3,316,321 edges, of which 1,894,350 with an appearance).

The game events (goals, cards, substitutions) and the histories of market values of the players are not included.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `club_id` (`transfers` and `games`): the id of the club (or national team) in Transfermarkt.
- (Node) `name` (`transfers` and `games`): its name.
- (Node) `domestic_competition` (`transfers` and `games`): the id of its domestic league, for the clubs of the covered leagues (e.g. `GB1` for the Premier League, `L1` for the Bundesliga), empty otherwise.
- (Node) `national_team` (`games`): whether the team is a national team.
- (Edge) `player_id`, `player_name` (`transfers`): the id and name of the player.
- (Edge) `time` (`transfers`): the date of the transfer (Unix time).
- (Edge) `season` (`transfers`): the season of the transfer (e.g. `24/25`).
- (Edge) `fee` (`transfers`): the transfer fee (euros; NaN if not given; 0 for free transfers).
- (Edge) `market_value` (`transfers`): the market value of the player at the time (euros; NaN if not given).
- (Edge) `game_id` (`games`): the id of the game in Transfermarkt.
- (Edge) `time` (`games`): the date of the game (Unix time).
- (Edge) `competition_id` (`games`): the competition (e.g. `GB1`, `CL` for the UEFA Champions League, `FIWC` for the World Cup).
- (Edge) `competition_type` (`games`): its type (`domestic_league`, `domestic_cup`, `international_cup`, `national_team_competition`, `other`; empty for 1,214 games).
- (Edge) `season` (`games`): the year in which the season started.
- (Edge) `round` (`games`): the round or matchday.
- (Edge) `home_goals`, `away_goals` (`games`): the goals scored by the home and away teams.
- (Edge) `attendance` (`games`): the number of spectators (-1 if not given).
- (Edge) `stadium`, `referee` (`games`): the stadium and the referee.
- (Edge) `home_manager`, `away_manager` (`games`): the managers of the two teams.
- (Edge) `home_formation`, `away_formation` (`games`): their formations (e.g. `4-2-3-1`).
- (Edge) Missing values of the edges of `games` are empty strings or -1.
- (Node) `player_id` (`teammates`): the id of the player in Transfermarkt.
- (Node) `name` (`teammates`): the name of the player.
- (Node) `has_profile` (`teammates`): whether the dataset has a profile of the player, from which the following properties come (empty strings, -1 or NaN otherwise).
- (Node) `date_of_birth` (`teammates`): the date of birth (YYYY-MM-DD).
- (Node) `country_of_birth`, `city_of_birth`, `country_of_citizenship` (`teammates`): the country and city of birth, and the country of citizenship.
- (Node) `position`, `sub_position` (`teammates`): the position (e.g. `Attack`) and sub-position (e.g. `Centre-Forward`).
- (Node) `foot` (`teammates`): the preferred foot.
- (Node) `height` (`teammates`): the height (cm).
- (Node) `current_club_id`, `current_club_name` (`teammates`): the club of the player in his last season in the data.
- (Node) `market_value`, `highest_market_value` (`teammates`): his latest and highest market values (euros).
- (Edge) `games` (`teammates`): the number of games in which both players were listed for the same club.
- (Edge) `games_played` (`teammates`): the number of those in which both played (according to the appearances table).
- (Edge) `first_time`, `last_time` (`teammates`): the dates of the first and the last of these games (Unix time).
- (Node) `is_player` (`player_club` and `player_game`): whether the node is a player (the other nodes are clubs or games).
- (Node) `player_id` (`player_club` and `player_game`): the id of the player (-1 for the other nodes; the profiles of the players are in `teammates`).
- (Node) `name` (`player_club` and `player_game`): the name of the player, or of the club (in `player_club`; empty for a few clubs without a name in the data; empty for the games).
- (Node) `club_id` (`player_club`): the id of the club (-1 for players).
- (Node) `national_team` (`player_club`): whether it is a national team.
- (Node) `game_id` (`player_game`): the id of the game (-1 for players).
- (Node) `time` (`player_game`): its date (Unix time).
- (Node) `competition_id`, `season` (`player_game`): as in `games` (empty for players).
- (Edge) `games` (`player_club`): the number of games in which the player was listed for the club.
- (Edge) `games_played` (`player_club`): the number of those in which he played.
- (Edge) `first_time`, `last_time` (`player_club`): the dates of the first and the last of these games (Unix time).
- (Edge) `club_id` (`player_game`): the club for which the player was listed.
- (Edge) `time` (`player_game`): the date of the game (Unix time).
- (Edge) `lineup` (`player_game`): from the lineups, `starting_lineup` or `substitutes` (empty if the player is not in the lineup of the game).
- (Edge) `position` (`player_game`): from the lineups, the position (e.g. `Centre-Back`; empty if the player is not in the lineup of the game).
- (Edge) `number` (`player_game`): from the lineups, the shirt number (empty if the player is not in the lineup of the game).
- (Edge) `captain` (`player_game`): from the lineups, whether he was the captain.
- (Edge) `played` (`player_game`): whether the player has an appearance in the game.
- (Edge) `minutes_played`, `goals`, `assists`, `yellow_cards`, `red_cards` (`player_game`): from the appearances (-1 if not available).
citations: David (dcaribou), "Football Data from Transfermarkt." Kaggle, dataset, version 679 (2026)

datasets.name: trec
datasets.description: A bipartite network of documents and the words they contain, extracted from NIST's Text Retrieval Conference (TREC) disks 4 and 5, released in 1996 and 1997. These archives contain material drawn from the Financial Times Ltd. (1991-1994), the Congressional Record of the 103rd Congress (1993), the Federal Register (1994), the Foreign Broadcast Information Service (1996), and the Los Angeles Times newspaper (1989-1990). Nodes are 556,077 documents and 1,173,225 words (vertex property `is_word`; neither documents nor words are named), and an edge connects a document to a word it contains, and its `weight` is the number of occurrences of the word in the document.
citations: J. Kunegis, "TREC (disks 4–5)." KONECT, the Koblenz Network Collection (2016)

datasets.name: trec_web
datasets.description: A web graph network originally constructed in 2003 as a testbed for information-retrieval techniques, including web search engines. Distributed by University of Glasgow. Nodes are web pages, and a directed edge from page A to page B represents a hyperlink in A pointing to B.
citations: P. Bailey, N. Craswell, & D. Hawking, "Engineering a multi-purpose test collection for web retrieval experiments.” Information Processing & Management, 39(6), 853-871. (2003).

datasets.name: tree-of-life
datasets.description: Protein-protein iteraction networks ("interactome") for 1,840 species. An interactome captures all physical protein-protein interactions within one species, from direct biophysical protein-protein interactions to regulatory protein-DNA and metabolic interactions. In each network, nodes are the proteins of one species, and an undirected edge connects two proteins that interact.
citations: Marinka Zitnik, Rok Sosic, Marcus W Feldman, and Jure Leskovec. "Evolution of resilience in protein interactomes across the tree of life", Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), 2019, 116 (10) 4426-4433.

datasets.name: tripadvisor_ratings
datasets.description:
Bipartite networks of the reviewers of TripAdvisor and the hotels they reviewed, from the hotel reviews crawled from TripAdvisor (www.tripadvisor.com) by Hongning Wang, Yue Lu and ChengXiang Zhai for their research on latent aspect rating analysis (2010, 2011). Each node is a reviewer or a hotel, and an edge connects a reviewer to a hotel they reviewed, with the review's overall rating, its ratings of individual aspects of the hotel (value, rooms, location, cleanliness, check in / front desk, service, business service; each from 0 to 5 stars, or -1 if not given), and its date. A reviewer who reviewed the same hotel several times is connected to it by several edges.

The authors published two crawls, which are two networks:

- `texts`: the parsed reviews of 1,759 hotels (the "Text" data set, 240,060 reviews from 2001 to 2009, 64,295 of them anonymous), with the number of readers and of helpful votes of each review.
- `json`: the authors' "most comprehensive collection" of hotel reviews, crawled at different times and published in JSON format in 2014, with the TripAdvisor id of each review and the location given by its reviewer. The format varies slightly across hotels (e.g. some hotels have no name, address or price, and some reviews have no reviewer location).

The reviewers are identified by their TripAdvisor screen names. The reviews whose author is not given by name, i.e. those of "A TripAdvisor Member" (a reviewer without a public profile), "lass=" (apparently a parsing error of the crawl, for which the author is missing), an empty name, or "Posted by a(n) ... traveler" (reviews imported from partner sites), are anonymous: each of them gets a node of its own (marked by `anonymous`), since they cannot be attributed to a single reviewer. In `texts`, the names of reviewers with non-Latin characters were stored in mangled form (UTF-8 decoded as GBK); they are restored where this is possible without loss, and left as they are otherwise. The hotels' names and locations are taken from their TripAdvisor URLs (the names in `json` where they are given); 36 hotels of `texts` have no URL, and so no name or location. The texts of the reviews (and their titles) are left out.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the screen name of the reviewer (as given in the data for anonymous reviews), or the name of the hotel.
- (Node) `is_hotel`: whether the node is a hotel (otherwise a reviewer).
- (Node) `anonymous`: whether the node is an anonymous review (see above).
- (Node) `hotel_id`: the TripAdvisor id of the hotel (-1 for reviewers).
- (Node) `geo_id`: the TripAdvisor id of the hotel's location (-1 if unknown, and for reviewers).
- (Node) `location`: the location of the hotel (from its URL, e.g. `Seattle Washington`; empty if unknown, and for reviewers).
- (Node) `hotel_rating`: the average rating of the hotel shown by TripAdvisor (`texts` only; -1 for reviewers).
- (Node) `price`: the (lowest) price of the hotel in US dollars, as shown by TripAdvisor (-1 if unknown, and for reviewers).
- (Node) `address`: the address of the hotel (`json` only; empty if unknown, and for reviewers).
- (Edge) `rating`: the overall rating of the review, from 0 to 5 (-1 if not given).
- (Edge) `rating_value`, `rating_rooms`, `rating_location`, `rating_cleanliness`, `rating_check_in`, `rating_service`, `rating_business_service`: the ratings of these aspects, from 0 to 5 (-1 if not given); `json` also has `rating_sleep_quality`.
- (Edge) `time`: the date of the review, in Unix time (-1 if unknown).
- (Edge) `readers`, `helpful`: the number of readers of the review, and of readers who found it helpful (`texts` only; -1 if not given).
- (Edge) `review_id`: the TripAdvisor id of the review (`json` only).
- (Edge) `author_location`: the location given by the reviewer (`json` only; empty if not given).
citations: H. Wang, Y. Lu, C. Zhai, "Latent aspect rating analysis on review text data: a rating regression approach." Proceedings of the 16th ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining, 783-792 (2010).

H. Wang, Y. Lu, C. Zhai, "Latent aspect rating analysis without aspect keyword supervision." Proceedings of the 17th ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining, 618-626 (2011).

datasets.name: trivago_clicks
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of browsing sessions on the hotel metasearch website trivago and the accommodations (mostly hotels) that were clicked out to in each session, i.e. for which the user was forwarded to a booking site. The data were derived by Chodrow, Veldt and Benson from the training data of the ACM RecSys Challenge 2019, which consists of logs of user sessions on trivago from November 2018 (about 910 thousand sessions), each a sequence of actions such as viewing information, images or deals of an accommodation, sorting and filtering search results, and clicking out to a booking site. Accommodations without metadata were removed, an accommodation clicked out to more than once in a session is connected to it only once, only the largest connected component was kept, and sessions with click-outs to a single accommodation were then removed.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `is_session`: whether the node is a browsing session (otherwise it is an accommodation).
- (Node) `country` (accommodations): the country where the accommodation is located (160 countries).
citations: P. S. Chodrow, N. Veldt, A. R. Benson, "Generative hypergraph clustering: From blockmodels to modularity." Science Advances 7(28), eabh1303 (2021)
J. Adamczak, Y. Deldjoo, F. B. Moghaddam, P. Knees, G.-P. Leyson, P. Monreal, "Session-based Hotel Recommendations Dataset." ACM Transactions on Intelligent Systems and Technology 12(1), 1-20 (2020)

datasets.name: trophich
datasets.description:
A metaweb of the trophic interactions among the terrestrial species of Switzerland (vertebrates, invertebrates and plants), "trophiCH", compiled by Reji Chacko et al. from the literature (over 700 sources: field studies, books, databases, expert knowledge). Nodes are taxa, mostly species, and a directed edge $(i, j)$ indicates that taxon $i$ consumes (preys on, feeds on, pollinates, parasitizes) taxon $j$. Interactions recorded in the literature at a coarser taxonomic level (e.g. a predator feeding on a genus or family) were assigned by the authors to the Swiss species of that taxon, and species without recorded diet were assigned the interactions of related species in some special cases.

There are three networks, from the files of the data set (version 1.0):

- `empirical`: the interactions as recorded in the sources (442,624 interactions), between taxa of various ranks.
- `inferred`: the empirical interactions together with those inferred by assigning the targets recorded at the genus or family level to their Swiss species (1,181,686 interactions).
- `final`: the final metaweb, which also includes the inferences for the special cases (1,188,049 interactions).

Self-loops are cannibalism or feeding within the same taxon. A pair of taxa can be connected by more than one edge, with different life stages. Nodes are identified by their name and rank; only the taxa that take part in interactions are included (the authors' checklist has 24,167 taxa).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the taxon (e.g. `Abax parallelepipedus`, or a feeding group).
- (Node) `rank`: the taxonomic rank of the taxon (e.g. `Species`, `Genus`, `Family`; empty for some non-taxonomic nodes, e.g. detritus).
- (Node) `kingdom`, `phylum`, `class`, `order`, `family`, `genus`: the taxonomy of the taxon, from the authors' checklist of Swiss taxa; empty if the taxon is not in the checklist.
- (Node) `habitat`: the habitats where the taxon occurs (e.g. `Forest; Grassland`), from the checklist; empty if not known.
- (Node) `zone`: the vertical zones where the taxon occurs (e.g. `In ground; On ground or in leaf litter`), from the checklist; empty if not known.
- (Node) `red_list`: the Swiss Red List category of the taxon (e.g. `LC`, `VU`, `NE` for not evaluated), from the checklist; empty if not known.
- (Edge) `interaction` (edges): the type of interaction (`Predation`, `Herbivory`, `Pollination`, `Parasitoidism`, `Parasitism`, `Kleptoparasitism`; empty if not given).
- (Edge) `source_life_stage`, `target_life_stage` (edges): the life stages of the consumer and of the resource to which the interaction applies (e.g. `Adult`, `Young`, `Young and Adult`); empty if not specified.
- (Edge) `citation` (edges): the identifier of the source of the interaction in the authors' list of references.
- (Edge) `inference` (edges, `inferred` and `final` only): how the interaction was inferred (e.g. `Target_Genus`: from an interaction recorded with the genus of the target); empty for the empirical interactions.
citations: M. Reji Chacko et al., "A species-level multi-trophic metaweb for Switzerland." Scientific Data 12, 1164 (2025)

datasets.name: trrust
datasets.description:
Human and mouse transcriptional regulatory networks from TRRUST ("Transcriptional Regulatory Relationships Unraveled by Sentence-based Text mining"), version 2, compiled by Han et al. by text mining of PubMed abstracts for sentences describing transcriptional regulation, followed by manual curation of the candidate interactions. Nodes are genes (identified by their gene symbols), and a directed edge $(i, j)$ indicates that the transcription factor $i$ regulates the expression of gene $j$, with the mode of regulation (activation or repression) when it is known.

There are two networks, `human` (8,427 regulatory links) and `mouse` (6,490 links), from the release of 16 April 2018. A pair of genes for which both activation and repression are reported (or a known and an unknown mode) is connected by one edge per mode, as listed in the source (9,396 edges for human, 7,057 for mouse).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the gene symbol of the gene (e.g. `AATF`).
- (Edge) `regulation` (edges): the mode of regulation (`Activation`, `Repression` or `Unknown`).
- (Edge) `sign` (edges): the mode of regulation as a number, +1 for activation, -1 for repression and 0 if unknown.
- (Edge) `pmids` (edges): the PubMed identifiers of the publications describing the regulation, separated by `;`.
citations: H. Han et al., "TRRUST v2: an expanded reference database of human and mouse transcriptional regulatory interactions." Nucleic Acids Research 46, D380-D386 (2018)

datasets.name: trumpworld
datasets.description:
Network of people and organizations connected to Donald J. Trump and his incoming administration, compiled by BuzzFeed News journalists for the "TrumpWorld" project, published on January 15, 2017, shortly before Trump's inauguration as the 45th President of the United States. The journalists spent two months building the dataset from public records, financial disclosures (such as Trump's 2016 Public Financial Disclosure Report and FEC filings), news reports and other sources on the Trump family, his Cabinet picks, and top advisers; it was later expanded with tips from readers. Each node is a person or an organization, and an edge is a documented connection between two of them (person-organization, person-person, or organization-organization), such as ownership, a position held in an organization, business dealings, investment, membership, family relation, or friendship. As stated by the authors, the underlying sources can contain errors and omissions. This is the final version of the data in the GitHub repository (update of April 24, 2017, which consolidated the earlier person-person, person-organization and organization-organization tables into a single file).

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the person or organization.
- (Node) `type`: either "Person" or "Organization".
- (Edge) `connection`: a free-text description of the connection (833 distinct values, e.g. "Ownership", "Director", "Investor", "President (as of 2016 FEC filing)", "Business associates"), describing the role of one entity with respect to the other, but not in a consistent direction (e.g. "Partner" in "Robert Lighthizer – Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom LLP" refers to the first entity, while "Subsidiary" in "SCL Group – Cambridge Analytica" refers to the second); the order of the two entities in the source is kept as the source and target of each edge.
- (Edge) `sources`: the URL(s) or description(s) of the source(s) documenting the connection, separated by " | " when there are several.
citations: J. Templon, A. Cormier, A. Campbell, J. Singer-Vine, "Help Us Map TrumpWorld." BuzzFeed News (January 15, 2017)

datasets.name: truth_social
datasets.description:
Networks of the users of Truth Social, the microblogging platform launched in February 2022 by the Trump Media & Technology Group, from the dataset of Gerard, Botzer and Weninger, who crawled the platform from February to October 2022 (posts of February to September), starting from popular accounts and following their followers and followings. The posts of Truth Social are called "Truths", and the reposts "ReTruths". The dataset contains 454,458 users, 4,002,115 follow relations and about 860,000 Truths with their replies, quotes, hashtags, user tags and links.

The entry contains seven networks:

- `follows`: a directed edge from user u to user v means that u follows v.
- `replies`: a directed edge from a user to a user they replied to, for each reply (the replied Truths are not recorded).
- `quotes`: a directed edge from a user to the user whose Truth they quoted, for each quote.
- `retruths`: a directed edge from a user to the author of a Truth they ReTruthed, for each ReTruth.
- `mentions`: a directed edge from the author of a Truth to each user tagged in it, for each tag.
- `hashtags`: a bipartite network of users and hashtags, with an edge for each use of a hashtag in a Truth of the user.
- `urls`: a bipartite network of users and external URLs (links to other sites), with an edge for each link in a Truth of the user.

Repeated interactions appear as multiple edges, and self-interactions as self-loops. Each network contains only the users (and hashtags and URLs) with at least one edge.

The dataset was published in two versions on Zenodo, which differ only in the file of Truths: the second version leaves out 20,975 Truths whose texts contain quotation marks (malformed rows of the first version), and corrects the ReTruthed Truth of one. The Truths of both versions are combined here (those of the second version, and the 20,975 Truths only in the first one), so that the networks `quotes`, `retruths`, `mentions`, `hashtags` and `urls` include all of them. Even so, some Truths referenced by the files of tags, hashtags and links, and the original Truths of some ReTruths, are not in the file of Truths, so that their authors are unknown; these edges are left out (about 26,000 hashtag uses, 24,000 user tags, 22,000 links and 7,000 ReTruths). Rows of the file of Truths that are malformed (texts containing tabs) are read from the end, by the URL of the Truth. Also left out are the texts of the Truths, and the media files (images and videos) attached to them. The users and Truths that were added by the authors to complete the references have their unknown attributes set to -1. The times are given without time zone, and are taken as UTC; the creation dates of the users are known only to the month, and those of some Truths only to the day.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `user_id` (users): the id of the user in the dataset.
- (Node) `has_record` (users): whether the user is in the file of users (a few users referenced by the follows, replies, quotes, tags and Truths are missing from it; their attributes are empty or -1).
- (Node) `username` (users): the username.
- (Node) `created` (users): the creation month of the account (Unix time; -1 if unknown).
- (Node) `follower_count`, `following_count` (users): the numbers of followers and followed accounts shown on the profile (-1 if unknown).
- (Node) `time_scraped` (users): the time when the profile was last scraped (Unix time).
- (Node) `finished_follower_scrape`, `finished_following_scrape`, `finished_truth_scrape` (users): whether the followers, followings and Truths of the user were scraped completely at least once (1 or 0; -1 if unknown).
- (Node) `is_hashtag` (`hashtags`): whether the node is a hashtag (otherwise a user).
- (Node) `hashtag` (`hashtags`): the hashtag (empty for users).
- (Node) `first_seen` (`hashtags`): the time when the hashtag was first seen (Unix time; -1 for users).
- (Node) `is_url` (`urls`): whether the node is an external URL (otherwise a user).
- (Node) `url` (`urls`): the URL (empty for users).
- (Node) A few hashtags and URLs referenced by the Truths are missing from their files; their attributes are empty or -1. The user properties are empty or -1 for hashtags and URLs.
- (Edge) `time_scraped` (`follows`, `replies`, `quotes` and `mentions`): the time when the edge was collected (Unix time).
- (Edge) `time` (`quotes`, `retruths`, `mentions`, `hashtags` and `urls`): the time of the (quoting, ReTruthing, tagging, linking) Truth (Unix time; -1 if unknown).
- (Edge) `truth_id` (`quotes`, `retruths`, `mentions`, `hashtags` and `urls`): the id of that Truth on Truth Social (its page is `https://truthsocial.com/@<username>/posts/<truth_id>`; -1 if the Truth is not in the file of Truths).
- (Edge) `quoted_truth_id` (`quotes`): the id of the quoted Truth.
- (Edge) `retruthed_truth_id` (`retruths`): the id of the ReTruthed Truth (-1 if unknown).
- (Edge) `like_count`, `retruth_count`, `reply_count` (`retruths`, `mentions`, `hashtags` and `urls`): the numbers of likes, ReTruths and replies of that Truth when it was scraped (for ReTruths, as recorded, usually 0).
citations: P. Gerard, N. Botzer, T. Weninger, "Truth Social Dataset." Proceedings of the International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media 17, 1034-1040 (2023)

datasets.name: tudor_letters
datasets.description:
The correspondence network of the Tudor State Papers, the official government records of England under the Tudors (1509-1603), from the dataset of R. Ahnert, S. E. Ahnert, J. Cree and L. Fikkers that accompanies the book "Tudor Networks of Power". It contains, to the best of the authors' knowledge, all the letters in the State Papers Domestic and Foreign, extracted from the metadata of the State Papers Online resource (Gale Cengage), which follows the State Papers Calendars of the 19th century; the identities of people and places of writing were disambiguated and deduplicated by the authors.

Nodes are people (or, in some cases, collective senders and recipients, e.g. a convent or a council), and a directed edge from $i$ to $j$ is a letter sent by $i$ to $j$; pairs of people exchanged many letters (a multigraph). Many letters are dated only by a range of possible dates (sometimes very wide, when the calendars give no date); letters without any date have empty dates, and a few malformed dates of the dataset (e.g. the end date `5720101`, or months `00` and `91`) are kept as they are. The people's labels are as in the dataset (e.g. "A. Lady Kingston"); for a subset of people, the dataset gives links to biographical resources (Wikipedia, Kate Emerson's "Who Was Who in Tudor England", the Oxford Dictionary of National Biography, the History of Parliament, VIAF and Wikidata), of which the specific web page, and the Wikidata and VIAF identifiers, are included. The list of women among the correspondents used in the book (chapter 5; 857 identifiers, of which 838 are among the people of the dataset), from the authors' code repository, is included as a vertex property. The other derived data of the repository (co-authorship and mention networks, itineraries) are not included.

The coordinates of the places of writing are given in the dataset with the signs of the longitudes reversed (west positive); they are given here with the usual convention (east positive).

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `label`: the label of the person in the dataset.
- (Node) `person_id`: the person's identifier in the dataset.
- (Node) `is_woman`: whether the person is in the authors' list of women correspondents.
- (Node) `webpage`: the URL of the person's biographical web page (Wikipedia, Kate Emerson's biographies, ...), or empty.
- (Node) `webpage_type`: the kind of the web page: `WP` (Wikipedia), `KEH` (Kate Emerson's "Who Was Who in Tudor England"), `ODNB`, `HOP` (History of Parliament), `VIAF`, `other`, or empty.
- (Node) `keh_context`: the context of the person in Kate Emerson's biographies (e.g. under which person's entry they appear), or empty.
- (Node) `wikidata`, `viaf`: the Wikidata and VIAF identifiers of the person, or empty.
- (Edge) `date_from`, `date_to`: the range of possible dates of the letter (YYYY-MM-DD; equal if the date is known exactly), or empty if unknown.
- (Edge) `ms_id` and `ms_ref`: the identifier of the manuscript in State Papers Online and its archival reference (e.g. `SP 1/231 f.189`).
- (Edge) `place`: the place of writing (as disambiguated by the authors), or empty if not known; 1,111 letters have several places of writing, separated by "; ".
- (Edge) `place_id`: the identifiers of the places of writing (empty if not known).
- (Edge) `latitude`, `longitude`: the coordinates of the places of writing (NaN for the 105 places without coordinates).
citations: R. Ahnert and S. E. Ahnert, "Tudor Networks of Power." Oxford University Press (2023)
R. Ahnert, S. E. Ahnert, J. Cree and L. Fikkers, "Tudor Networks of Power - correspondence network dataset." Apollo - University of Cambridge Repository (2023)

datasets.name: tumor_virus_host
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of binary protein-protein interactions between proteins of DNA tumor viruses and human proteins, from Rozenblatt-Rosen et al. (2012), as distributed by the Center for Cancer Systems Biology (CCSB, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute). Open reading frames of viral proteins (from Epstein-Barr virus, adenovirus 5, polyomavirus SV40, and the human papillomaviruses HPV5, HPV6b, HPV8, HPV11, HPV16, HPV18 and HPV33) were screened by yeast two-hybrid (Y2H) assays against a library of human open reading frames (the human ORFeome). Nodes are viral and human proteins, and an undirected edge connects a viral protein to a human protein with which it interacts (454 interactions between 53 viral and 307 human proteins).

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `is_viral`: whether the node is a viral protein (otherwise it is a human protein).
- (Node) `name`: the name of the viral protein, as virus and protein (e.g. "EBV-EBNA1", "HPV16-E6"), or the gene symbol of the human protein.
- (Node) `entrez_id`: the Entrez Gene ID of the human protein (-1 for viral proteins).
citations: O. Rozenblatt-Rosen, R. C. Deo, M. Padi, G. Adelmant, M. A. Calderwood, T. Rolland, et al., "Interpreting cancer genomes using systematic host network perturbations by tumour virus proteins." Nature 487(7408), 491-495 (2012)

datasets.name: turkish_program_preferences
datasets.description:
Directed network of co-preferences among undergraduate programs in Turkey, compiled by V. Tunalı and E. Güvenoğlu. When applying to Turkish universities after the national entrance exam, students submit a ranked list of the programs they prefer. The data were crawled from the Higher Education Program Atlas portal (YÖK Atlas) of the Turkish Council of Higher Education, which lists, for each of the 23,245 programs offered by 207 universities, the other programs that the students placed in that program in 2017 had also included in their preference lists, with the number of such preferences. Program names were normalized to the bare profession name (removing language-of-instruction, scholarship and similar variants), merging the programs with the same name across universities, and invalid names were removed, yielding 622 programs and 72,571 directed co-preference pairs. To filter out weak relations, only the (at most) 10 most co-preferred programs of each program were kept.

A node is a program (profession) name, and a directed edge from A to B means that B is among the 10 programs most often also preferred by students placed in program A.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the program name (in Turkish).
- (Edge) `weight`: the number of preferences for program B by the students placed in programs named A in 2017 (summed over universities).
citations: V. Tunalı, E. Güvenoğlu, "Complex Network Analysis Approach to Examining Undergraduate Program Preferences." Bitlis Eren Üniversitesi Fen Bilimleri Dergisi 8(1), 176-186 (2019)

datasets.name: twitch_social
datasets.description:
Social networks of users of the live streaming platform Twitch, collected from its public API in 2018 by B. Rozemberczki and collaborators for benchmarks of node embedding and classification methods. Nodes are Twitch users, and an undirected edge connects two users who follow each other (a mutual follower relationship). The user identifiers were replaced by consecutive indices. There are two data sets:

- Language networks (MUSAE, collected in May 2018): six networks of users who stream in a given language, `DE` (German), `ENGB` (English), `ES` (Spanish), `FR` (French), `PTBR` (Portuguese) and `RU` (Russian). Each node has a list of binary features, shared by all six networks, which the authors extracted from the games played and liked, the location and the streaming habits of the user; only the indices of the features are given, not their meaning. The supervised task proposed with the data is to predict whether a streamer uses explicit language (`mature`). In `FR`, two users appear twice in the node table (with the same values, except for a difference of 1 in the views of one of them); the first row is used.
- `twitch_gamers` (collected in spring 2018): a larger network of 168,114 users of all languages, which forms a single connected component. It has no feature lists, but more user attributes.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `twitch_id` (language networks): the numeric Twitch identifier of the user.
- (Node) `days` (language networks): the age of the account in days (as given in the data).
- (Node) `mature`: whether the user streams explicit (mature) content.
- (Node) `views`: the number of views.
- (Node) `partner` (language networks): whether the user is a Twitch partner.
- (Node) `features` (language networks): the indices of the user's binary features (as listed in the data, in which a few lists contain repeated indices).
- (Node) `life_time` (`twitch_gamers`): the age of the account in days.
- (Node) `created_at`, `updated_at` (`twitch_gamers`): the dates of creation and of the last update of the account, as Unix time (at midnight UTC).
- (Node) `dead_account` (`twitch_gamers`): whether the account is inactive.
- (Node) `language` (`twitch_gamers`): the broadcaster language (a two-letter code, or "OTHER").
- (Node) `affiliate` (`twitch_gamers`): whether the user is a Twitch affiliate.
citations: B. Rozemberczki, C. Allen, and R. Sarkar, "Multi-scale attributed node embedding." Journal of Complex Networks 9(2), cnab014 (2021).
B. Rozemberczki and R. Sarkar, "Twitch Gamers: a Dataset for Evaluating Proximity Preserving and Structural Role-based Node Embeddings." arXiv:2101.03091 (2021).

datasets.name: twitch_viewers
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of the users and the streamers (channels) of the live streaming platform Twitch, collected by J. Rappaz, J. McAuley and K. Aberer in July and August 2019 to study recommendation on live-streaming platforms. Every 10 minutes during 43 days, the authors listed all the live streams with the public Twitch API, and the users who were logged in to the chat of each stream. The source data have one record per user and broadcast (a stream of a streamer), with the first and the last round (of 10 minutes) at which the user was seen in its chat; the user names were anonymized by the source.

Here a user is connected to a streamer if the user was present in the chat of at least one broadcast of the streamer, and the edges are weighted by the number of these broadcasts; the individual records (about 475 million, according to the authors) are aggregated into these weighted edges. The subset of 100,000 users provided by the source for benchmarks (`100k_a.csv`) is not included.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `is_user`: whether the node is a user (otherwise a streamer).
- (Node) `user_id`: the (anonymized) id of the user in the source data (-1 for streamers).
- (Node) `name`: the name of the channel of the streamer (empty for users).
- (Edge) `weight`: the number of broadcasts of the streamer in whose chat the user was seen.
- (Edge) `rounds`: the total number of 10-minute rounds the user was seen in the chats of these broadcasts (the sum of the differences between the last and the first round of each).
- (Edge) `first`, `last`: the first and the last round at which the user was seen in a chat of the streamer (rounds of 10 minutes, numbered from 0 to 6148).
citations: J. Rappaz, J. McAuley, K. Aberer, "Recommendation on Live-Streaming Platforms: Dynamic Availability and Repeat Consumption." Proceedings of the 15th ACM Conference on Recommender Systems (RecSys), 390-399 (2021)

datasets.name: twitter
datasets.description:
A directed network of following relationships on Twitter, collected by M. De Choudhury and collaborators with crawlers based on the Twitter API, as part of a data set of about 10.5 million tweets (from 2006 to 2009) of about 200,000 users. The social graph lists, for 2,502 crawled users, up to about 500 of the users they follow, so that almost all nodes have only incoming edges. A directed edge from $i$ to $j$ means that user $i$ follows user $j$ (the direction is not documented in the source, but is consistent with the users' profile counts). Repeated lines and 117 lines with an empty user name in the source file are left out.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the Twitter user name.
- (Node) `time_zone`: the time zone set in the user's profile (empty if none).
- (Node) `statuses`, `followers`, `friends`, `favourites`: counts from the user's profile (-1 for the 9,205 users without profile data). The columns of the profile file are not documented; this assignment is inferred from the attributes listed in the source page and from the values (the `friends` count, i.e. the number of users followed, usually matches the number of out-edges of the crawled users).
citations: M. De Choudhury, Y.-R. Lin, H. Sundaram, K. S. Candan, L. Xie, A. Kelliher, "How does the data sampling strategy impact the discovery of information diffusion in social media?" Proceedings of the International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media 4(1), 34-41 (2010)

datasets.name: twitter_15m
datasets.description:
Directed network of follower relationships among Twitter users who took part in the online activity around the 15-M (Indignados) protest movement in Spain, collected from 25 April to 25 May 2011. The messages were collected by Cierzo Development Ltd. and include only messages in Spanish related to the movement, identified by a set of hashtags. The network includes users who sent at least one message on the topic, or who were mentioned by a user who did, and contains only the follower relationships among these users (87,569 nodes). The data were made available by Y. Moreno and J. Borge-Holthoefer.

Edges follow the direction of the information flow: an edge $i \to j$ indicates that user $j$ follows user $i$.

The upstream data also contain the time, hashtags and mentions of the collected messages, which are not included in the network. The node properties `id` and `name` hold the (meaningless) node labels of the upstream Pajek file, and the edge property `weight` is always 1.
citations: S. González-Bailón, et al. "The dynamics of protest recruitment through an online network." Scientific Reports 1, 197 (2011)

datasets.name: twitter_2009
datasets.description:
Directed network of follow relationships among Twitter users, based on a crawl of the whole Twitter network performed by M. Cha, H. Haddadi, F. Benevenuto and K. P. Gummadi (Max Planck Institute for Software Systems), which aimed at collecting all users and links of Twitter at the time; the distributed data correspond to the snapshot of September 2009. Nodes are users, with anonymized identifiers, and an edge $i \to j$ indicates that user $i$ follows user $j$. The network has about 52.6 million nodes (the users that have at least one link) and 1,963,263,821 edges.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the anonymized user identifier.
citations: M. Cha, H. Haddadi, F. Benevenuto, and K. P. Gummadi, "Measuring User Influence in Twitter: The Million Follower Fallacy" Proc. Internat. AAAI Conf. on Weblogs and Social Media (ICWSM), 10-17 (2010).

datasets.name: twitter_events
datasets.description:
Multiplex networks of interactions among Twitter users during twelve exceptional events between 2013 and 2016, collected by M. De Domenico and coworkers: five studied by E. Omodei, M. De Domenico and A. Arenas (2015), and seven more studied by M. De Domenico and E. G. Altmann (2020). Nodes are users (whose screen names are not provided), and a directed edge $i \to j$ indicates that user $i$ retweeted, mentioned or replied to user $j$ during the event. The networks have three layers, one for each type of interaction. Mentions include the users mentioned in retweeted or replied tweets: if user A retweets the tweet "hello @C @D" of user B, the edges A → B (retweet), A → C and A → D (mentions) are created.

- `Cannes2013`: the 2013 Cannes Film Festival (6 May to 3 June 2013).
- `MLKing2013`: the 50th anniversary of Martin Luther King's "I have a dream" speech (25 August to 2 September 2013).
- `MoscowAthletics2013`: the 2013 World Championships in Athletics in Moscow (5 to 19 August 2013).
- `NYClimateMarch2014`: the People's Climate March in New York City (19 to 22 September 2014).
- `ObamaInIsrael2013`: the visit of U.S. President Barack Obama to Israel (19 March to 3 April 2013).
- `BostonBomb2013`: the Boston Marathon bombing and the subsequent manhunt (15 to 22 April 2013).
- `PopeElection2013`: the election of Pope Francis (13 March 2013).
- `NBAFinals2015`: the 2015 NBA Finals (9 to 21 June 2015).
- `ParisAttack2015`: the November 2015 Paris attacks (13 to 15 November 2015).
- `GravitationalWaves2016`: the announcement of the first observation of gravitational waves (10 to 16 February 2016).
- `Sanremo2016`: the final night of the 2016 Sanremo Music Festival (13 February 2016).
- `UCLFinal2016`: the 2016 UEFA Champions League Final (27 May to 1 June 2016).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name` and `nodeLabel`: the anonymous numerical identifier of the user.
- (Edge) `layer`: the type of interaction: 1 for retweets, 2 for mentions and 3 for replies.
- (Edge) `weight`: the number of interactions of the given type from user $i$ to user $j$ during the observation period.

The upstream data also include the time of each individual interaction, which is not included in the networks.
citations: E. Omodei, M. De Domenico, and A. Arenas. "Characterizing interactions in online social networks during exceptional events." Front. Phys. 3, 59 (2015)
M. De Domenico and E. G. Altmann, "Unraveling the origin of social bursts in collective attention." Sci. Rep. 10, 4629 (2020)

datasets.name: twitter_golden_dawn
datasets.description:
A directed, temporal network of mentions among Twitter users, collected by K. Konstantinidis, S. Papadopoulos and Y. Kompatsiaris by monitoring tweets containing extreme-right political vocabulary, including the discussions around the Greek Golden Dawn party, between 31 January and 7 March 2013. Nodes are Twitter users, and each directed edge corresponds to a mention of one user by another in a tweet (from the author to the mentioned user), so that repeated mentions give rise to multiple edges; a user mentioning themselves gives a self-loop. The data were anonymized by the authors to comply with Twitter's terms of service: user names were replaced by consecutive numeric identifiers, and the text of the tweets is not included. The network has 857,199 users (677,275 of which authored at least one mention) and 1,066,872 mentions among 968,247 distinct ordered pairs of users.

Vertex property: `user_id`, the anonymized user identifier. Edge property: `time`, the time of the tweet (Unix time, in seconds).
citations: K. Konstantinidis, S. Papadopoulos, and Y. Kompatsiaris, "Community structure and evolution analysis of OSN interactions around real-world social phenomena." Proceedings of the 17th Panhellenic Conference on Informatics (PCI 2013), 9-16 (2013).

datasets.name: twitter_higgs
datasets.description:
Networks of Twitter users involved in the spreading of the news of the discovery of a new particle with the features of the Higgs boson, announced at CERN on 4 July 2012, assembled by M. De Domenico, A. Lima, P. Mougel and M. Musolesi. The data comprise the messages posted on Twitter about the discovery between 1 and 7 July 2012, collected using the keywords "lhc", "cern", "boson" and "higgs", and the follower relationships among the users who posted them. Nodes are users, with anonymized identifiers. All networks are directed, and record the observed actions, i.e. who follows, retweets, replies to, or mentions whom.

- `social`: follower network, where an edge $i \to j$ indicates that user $i$ follows user $j$.
- `retweet`: an edge $i \to j$ indicates that user $i$ retweeted user $j$.
- `reply`: an edge $i \to j$ indicates that user $i$ replied to user $j$.
- `mention`: an edge $i \to j$ indicates that user $i$ mentioned user $j$.
- `activity`: temporal network of all retweets, replies and mentions, with one edge per interaction.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the anonymized user identifier, consistent across the networks.
- (Edge) `weight` (`retweet`, `reply`, `mention`): the number of interactions from user $i$ to user $j$.
- (Edge) `timestamp` (`activity`): the time of the interaction, as a UNIX timestamp in seconds.
- (Edge) `interaction` (`activity`): the type of interaction: `RT` (retweet), `MT` (mention) or `RE` (reply).
citations: M. De Domenico, A. Lima, P. Mougel, M. Musolesi, "The Anatomy of a Scientific Rumor." Scientific Reports 3, 2980 (2013). arxiv:1301.2952

datasets.name: twitter_sample
datasets.description:
A sample of the Twitter social network, obtained by D. Kagan, M. Fire and Y. Elovici with a dedicated crawler of the Twitter API, which collected at most 1,000 friends and followers of each crawled profile. Nodes are Twitter accounts and directed edges represent following relationships between them. The network has 5,384,162 nodes and 16,011,444 edges. The year of the crawl is given as 2014 in the text and as 2012 in the dataset table of the cited paper. The upstream data do not document the direction of the edges, nor the crawling order (e.g. breadth-first) or seed profiles.

In the cited paper, the accounts of the network that were suspended by Twitter about one year after the crawl were used as ground truth for anomalous (malicious) accounts. These labels are not included in the network, which has no node or edge properties.
citations: D. Kagan, M. Fire, and Y. Elovici, "Unsupervised Anomalous Vertices Detection Utilizing Link Prediction Algorithms", Preprint, arXiv:1610.07525 (2017)

datasets.name: twitter_social
datasets.description:
Directed network of follow relationships among Twitter users, from a crawl of the entire Twitter site performed in 2009 by H. Kwak, C. Lee, H. Park and S. Moon (KAIST). Nodes are users, identified by their numerical Twitter user IDs, and an edge $i \to j$ indicates that user $i$ follows user $j$. The network has 41,652,230 nodes and 1,468,365,182 edges.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the numerical Twitter user ID.
citations: Haewoon Kwak, Changhyun Lee, Hosung Park, and Sue Moon. 2010. "What is Twitter, a social network or a news media?" In Proceedings of the 19th international conference on World wide web (WWW ’10). Association for Computing Machinery, New York, NY, USA, 591–600.

datasets.name: uc_irvine_messages
datasets.description:
A directed network of the private messages sent among the users of an online community for students at the University of California, Irvine (a Facebook-like social network site), collected by T. Opsahl and P. Panzarasa. The messages were sent between April and October 2004, and the data include all the users (1,899) who sent or received at least one message. Each directed edge is a message from its sender to its recipient, so that multiple messages between the same pair of users are kept as multiple edges (59,835 messages among 20,296 ordered pairs of users). The source data also contain one self-loop per user, which marks the time when the user registered on the site; these are not included as edges, but as a node property. User attributes (e.g. gender, age, course attended) exist but were not released, to protect the anonymity of the users.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `id`: the number of the user in the source data.
- (Node) `registered`: the time when the user registered on the site, as Unix time.
- (Edge) `time`: the time when the message was sent, as Unix time.
- (Edge) `chars`: the number of characters in the message.

The source data give the dates and times without a time zone; they were interpreted as UTC.
citations: T. Opsahl, P. Panzarasa, "Clustering in weighted networks." Social Networks 31(2), 155-163 (2009)

P. Panzarasa, T. Opsahl, K. M. Carley, "Patterns and dynamics of users' behavior and interaction: Network analysis of an online community." Journal of the American Society for Information Science and Technology 60(5), 911-932 (2009)

datasets.name: uci_forum
datasets.description:
The activity of users in the forum of an online community for students at the University of California, Irvine (a Facebook-like social network site), from May to October 2004, collected by T. Opsahl and P. Panzarasa. The forum is organized in topics, and the network records the messages that 899 users posted to 522 topics. Users who only exchanged private messages are not included, and the user numbers do not correspond to those of the private message network of the same community.

Each message is a bipartite edge connecting the user who posted it to the topic, so that users and topics can be connected by multiple edges.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `is_user`: whether the node is a user (otherwise it is a topic).
- (Node) `id`: the number of the user or topic in the source data.
- (Edge) `time`: the time when the message was posted, as Unix time (the source data give the date and time without a time zone, which were interpreted as UTC).
- (Edge) `chars`: the number of characters in the message.
citations: T. Opsahl, "Triadic closure in two-mode networks: Redefining the global and local clustering coefficients." Social Networks 35(2), 159-167 (2013)

datasets.name: uci_mushroom
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of mushroom samples and their attribute values, from the "Mushroom" dataset of the UCI Machine Learning Repository, donated by J. Schlimmer in 1987. The 8,124 records are descriptions of hypothetical samples of 23 species of gilled mushrooms of the Agaricus and Lepiota families, drawn from The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Mushrooms (1981), each described by 22 nominal attributes of the cap, gills, stalk, veil, ring, spore print, population and habitat. Each sample is labelled as edible or poisonous, where species of unknown edibility were merged with the poisonous ones. Each sample is connected to one node for each of its attribute values (e.g. "odor=almond"). The attribute "stalk-root" is missing for 2,480 samples, which therefore have no edge for that attribute (degree 21 instead of 22).

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the attribute value in the form "attribute=value" (empty for samples).
- (Node) `is_attribute`: whether the node is an attribute value (otherwise a mushroom sample).
- (Node) `poisonous` (samples): whether the sample is classified as poisonous (or of unknown edibility), otherwise it is edible.
- (Node) `index` (samples): the position of the record in the source file (starting from 0).
- (Node) `attribute` (attributes): the attribute name (e.g. "cap-shape").
- (Node) `value` (attributes): the attribute value (e.g. "convex").
- (Node) `code` (attributes): the one-letter code of the value in the source file.

datasets.name: uci_zoo
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of animals and their attribute values, from the "Zoo" dataset of the UCI Machine Learning Repository, created by R. Forsyth in 1990 as an example database for his PC/BEAGLE rule-induction program. The data describe 101 animals by 15 boolean attributes (hair, feathers, eggs, milk, airborne, aquatic, predator, toothed, backbone, breathes, venomous, fins, tail, domestic, catsize) and their number of legs (0, 2, 4, 5, 6 or 8). There is one attribute node for each boolean attribute (e.g. "hair"), to which the animals that have the attribute are connected, and one node for each number of legs (e.g. "legs=4"), to which each animal with that number of legs is connected. The class of each animal (mammal, bird, etc.) is kept as a node property. The name "frog" appears twice in the source, for two records that differ only in the "venomous" attribute; both are kept as separate nodes.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the animal name, the attribute name, or the number of legs in the form "legs=value".
- (Node) `is_attribute`: whether the node is an attribute (otherwise an animal).
- (Node) `type` (animals): the class of the animal as given in the source (1-7).
- (Node) `type_name` (animals): a name for the class (mammal, bird, reptile, fish, amphibian, insect, invertebrate); the source gives only the class numbers, and these names were assigned here from the animals listed for each class in the dataset documentation.
- (Node) `attribute` (attributes): the attribute name.
- (Node) `value` (attributes): its value (always 1 for the boolean attributes, the number of legs for "legs").
citations: R. Forsyth, "Zoo [Dataset]." UCI Machine Learning Repository (1990)

datasets.name: ugandan_village
datasets.description:
Friendship and health advice networks among the households of 17 rural villages bordering Lake Victoria in Mayuge District, Uganda, collected in 2013 by G. F. Chami and collaborators in a census-based survey covering nearly all households (3,491 in total) of the villages. The ties were obtained with a name generator questionnaire, in which respondents named their close friends and the persons they trust for health advice (as reported in the cited paper); the resulting ties are between households. There is one network for each village and type of tie:

- `friendship-1` to `friendship-17`: friendship networks of villages 1 to 17.
- `health-advice_1` to `health-advice_17`: health advice networks of villages 1 to 17.

Nodes are households and edges are undirected. Some pairs of households are connected by more than one edge, and there are some self-loops.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the anonymized household identifier.
citations: G. F. Chami et al., "Social network fragmentation and community health." Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA 114(36), E7425–E7431 (2017)

datasets.name: uk_faculty
datasets.description:
The personal friendship network among the academic staff of a Faculty of a UK university, consisting of three schools, collected by Nepusz, Petróczi, Négyessy and Bazsó. The ties were obtained from a questionnaire answered by every member of the academic staff, from which the strength of each tie was measured on a scale constructed from several questionnaire items (reported Cronbach's α of 0.91). The edges are directed and weighted by the measured tie strength (the direction of the edges is as in the distributed data; the original publication analyzed the network ignoring directions, and does not detail their meaning). The data were distributed with the R package igraphdata, from which this version was obtained (the network object there is dated March 2007).

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `school`: an integer from 1 to 4 identifying the school of the Faculty to which the individual belongs. Values 1, 2 and 3 correspond to the three schools; the value 4 is given to two individuals, which presumably correspond to the two individuals whose school affiliation the authors report as unknown, due to missing information in the questionnaire.
- (Edge) `weight`: the strength of the tie, an integer from 1 to 16 (larger values indicate stronger ties).
citations: T. Nepusz, A. Petróczi, L. Négyessy, F. Bazsó, "Fuzzy communities and the concept of bridgeness in complex networks." Physical Review E 77, 016107 (2008)

datasets.name: uk_prison_transfers
datasets.description:
A network of movements of individuals between prisons in England and Wales, extracted by Xiu, Turner and Gross from the 2011 Census of England and Wales. The census recorded, for each usual resident, the address of usual residence one year before the census (27 March 2011); each flow counts the individuals whose usual residence one year before the census was in a census Output Area (OA) containing a prison, and whose usual residence on census day was in another OA containing a prison, as extracted by the authors. Since the flows are only resolved at the level of OAs, and some OAs contain more than one prison (10 OAs contain two or three prisons), the nodes are OAs containing prisons, not individual prisons. The list of prisons, and their attributes, is a contemporary list of prisons in England and Wales provided by the authors, and includes a few prisons that opened after 2011 (e.g. Oakwood and Berwyn); 8 of the OAs have no recorded flows, and appear as isolated nodes. The dataset was contributed to this repository by Gezhi Xiu.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `oa_code`: the 2011 Census Output Area code.
- (Node) `prisons`: the list of names of the prisons in the OA.
- (Node) `functions`: the predominant function of each of these prisons (e.g. "Reception", "Cat C Trainer", "Open", "Female", "High Security", "YOI" for young offender institutions, "YJB" for Youth Justice Board establishments).
- (Node) `operators`: the operator of each of these prisons ("PSP" for the public sector prison service, or the private company operating it).
- (Node) `category`: the security category of the prison(s) in the OA, "Category A" (highest security) to "Category D" (open prisons), or "Undetermined" when no single category applies (e.g. women's prisons, institutions for young offenders, or OAs containing prisons of different categories).
- (Node) `sex`: the sex of the prisoners held ("Male", "Female", or "Undetermined" for OAs containing prisons for both sexes).
- (Node) `region`: the region of England, or Wales, where the OA is located.
- (Edge) `weight`: the number of individuals that moved from the source OA (residence one year before the census) to the target OA (residence on census day).
citations: G. Xiu, J. Turner, T. Gross, "Spatialising 'carceral mobilities': extracting census data for analysis of prisoner inflow, transfer and release." Journal of Computational Social Science 7, 2505-2533 (2024)

datasets.name: un_migrations
datasets.description: A network of migration between countries, collected by the United Nations.
