Nodes are countries and areas, and a directed edge from A to B means that there are international migrants from A (origin) living in B (destination); the edge properties `migration_<year>_<sex>` give the number of such migrants (the migrant stock, not the flow of migration during a period), for each given year and sex (`total`, `male` or `female`). Estimates are presented for 1990, 1995, 2000, 2005, 2010 and 2015 and are available for all countries and areas of the world. The estimates are based on official statistics on the foreign-born or the foreign population.
citations: United  Nations,  Department  of  Economic  and  Social  Affairs,  Population  Division  (2015). "Trends in International Migrant Stock: The 2015 Revision." (United Nations database, POP/DB/MIG/Stock/Rev.2015)

datasets.name: un_votes
datasets.description:
Bipartite networks of the recorded votes of the member states of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), from two independent compilations. In both, the nodes are the member states and the decisions taken by recorded vote (roll calls), and a member state is connected to a decision if it voted in favor, against, or abstained; the edge is annotated with the vote (a signed network). Member states that did not vote (absent, not voting, or not members at the time) are not connected to the decision.

- `unga_dm`: the UNGA-DM database of J. Fjelstul, S. Hug and C. Kilby (version 2.0), which compiles all resolution-related decisions of the General Assembly from its meeting records (UN Official Document System and UN Digital Library) and from cleaned versions of the ICPSR roll-call data for the first sessions. It covers the roll calls between January 1946 and September 2023, in regular, special and emergency special sessions: votes on the final passage of draft resolutions (including failed ones), on amendments, on motions, and separate votes on parts of draft resolutions.
- `voeten`: the raw roll-call data of E. Voeten, A. Strezhnev and M. Bailey ("United Nations General Assembly Voting Data", Harvard Dataverse, version 33 of June 2024, the last version that contains the raw votes; later versions only have the derived ideal points and agreement scores). It covers sessions 1 to 78 (January 1946 to June 2024). It was assembled from the ICPSR roll-call data, the data of E. Gartzke and D.-J. Jo, and UN documents, and differs from UNGA-DM in several ways: committee votes of sessions 27-29 and unanimous votes of sessions 40-51 were removed, votes on amendments, paragraphs and failed resolutions are incomplete before the 1990s, decisions are identified by roll-call ids with resolution numbers that are not always correct before 1985, member states are identified by their Correlates of War code only (e.g. Yugoslavia, Serbia and Montenegro and Serbia share the code 345), and the decisions are annotated with issue codes.

The `unga_dm` network uses the extract of all recorded votes by member states (`votes_extr.csv`) of the database. Decisions taken without a vote or by a non-recorded vote, for which there are no votes per member state, are not included, and neither are the database's additional votes not related to resolutions (e.g. elections). Votes are as amended by member states after the vote (through changes notified to the Secretariat); the original votes are kept as an edge property.

The `voeten` network uses the file `UNVotes-1.RData`, whose last session (78) has errors: 88 votes without a member state (a state that could not be identified) are left out, as are 130 of the 261 rows of session 78 of Yemen, Zambia and Zimbabwe, which carry the resolution number, date and vote totals of another roll call than the one they are assigned to (these rows are scrambled, so their votes cannot be attributed reliably); the few remaining duplicated votes (the same member state, roll call and vote) are merged. The vote totals given for each roll call (`num_yes`, `num_no`, `num_abstain`) are kept as in the data and do not always agree with the votes of the network. The undocumented variable `ident` is not included.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `is_member_state`: whether the node is a member state (otherwise it is a decision).
- (Node) `cow_code` (member states): the Correlates of War (COW) code of the member state (-1 for decisions).
- (Edge) `vote`: the vote of the member state: $+1$ in favor, $-1$ against, $0$ abstaining.

Properties of `unga_dm`:

- (Node) `name`: the common name of the member state (unique per Correlates of War code), or the identifier of the decision: the resolution number (or the number of the draft resolution or other document, if it was not adopted) followed by `-FP` for the final passage, `-A####` for an amendment, `-M####` for a motion and `-S####` for a separate vote.
- (Node) `seat_name` (member states): the current official name of the member state's seat.
- (Node) `resolution` (decisions): the number of the resolution (`rejected` if the draft resolution was not adopted).
- (Node) `draft_resolution` (decisions): the number of the draft resolution.
- (Node) `session` (decisions): the session (`RS-###` for regular sessions, `SS-###` for special sessions, `ESS-###` for emergency special sessions).
- (Node) `meeting_record` (decisions): the meeting record of the meeting in which the decision was taken.
- (Node) `topic` (decisions): `draft resolution`, `amendment`, `motion` or `separate vote`.
- (Node) `decision_mode` (decisions): `recorded vote`, or `non-recorded vote` for the few decisions with a non-recorded vote in the meeting record but votes per member state in the data.
- (Node) `important` (decisions): whether the United States designated the vote as important: `important`, `not important`, or `not available` (before the 38th regular session).
- (Node) `requested_by` (decisions): the member states that requested the recorded vote (`not available` if unknown or not applicable).
- (Node) `time` (decisions): the date of the meeting, in Unix time.
- (Edge) `original_vote`: the vote originally recorded (`in favor`, `against`, `abstaining`, `not voting` or `not voting (suspended)`).
- (Edge) `vote_was_amended`: whether the member state changed its vote after the vote.

Properties of `voeten`:

- (Node) `name`: the most frequent name of the member state in the data, or the resolution number of the decision (not unique: several roll calls can concern the same resolution).
- (Node) `country_code` (member states): the three-letter code of the member state.
- (Node) `rcid` (decisions): the roll-call id (matching the ICPSR ids until 1985; ids above 9000 are emergency special sessions not in the ICPSR data).
- (Node) `resid` (decisions): the sequential id of the roll call within its session (session number followed by three digits).
- (Node) `session` (decisions): the number of the session (sessions run from September into the following year; emergency special sessions are assigned to the regular session of the time).
- (Node) `resolution` (decisions): the resolution number.
- (Node) `time` (decisions): the date of the vote, in Unix time.
- (Node) `amendment`, `paragraph` (decisions): whether the vote was on an amendment, or on a paragraph rather than an entire resolution.
- (Node) `short_description`, `long_description` (decisions): the descriptions of the roll call.
- (Node) `important` (decisions): whether the vote was identified as important by the US State Department report "Voting Practices in the United Nations": `important`, `not important`, or `not available`.
- (Node) `middle_east`, `nuclear`, `disarmament`, `human_rights`, `colonialism`, `economic_development` (decisions): the issue codes of the data (votes relating to the Palestinian conflict, nuclear weapons and material, arms control and disarmament, human rights, colonialism, and economic development), assigned by searches of the descriptions.
- (Node) `num_yes`, `num_no`, `num_abstain` (decisions): the numbers of votes in favor, against and abstaining, as given in the data (-1 where missing).
citations: J. Fjelstul, S. Hug, C. Kilby, "Decision-making in the United Nations General Assembly: A comprehensive database of resolution-related decisions." The Review of International Organizations 21, 447-464 (2026)
E. Voeten, "Data and Analyses of Voting in the UN General Assembly." In B. Reinalda (ed.), Routledge Handbook of International Organization, Routledge (2013)
M. A. Bailey, A. Strezhnev, E. Voeten, "Estimating Dynamic State Preferences from United Nations Voting Data." Journal of Conflict Resolution 61(2), 430-456 (2017)
E. Voeten, A. Strezhnev, M. Bailey, "United Nations General Assembly Voting Data." Harvard Dataverse, version 33 (2024)

datasets.name: uni_email
datasets.description:
Network of email exchanges among members of the Rovira i Virgili University in Tarragona, Spain, compiled by R. Guimerà, L. Danon, A. Díaz-Guilera, F. Giralt and A. Arenas from the logs of the university's email server. Nodes are users, and two users are connected if they exchanged emails in both directions, i.e. each sent at least one email to the other. Emails sent to more than 50 recipients were discarded. Only the largest connected component (1,133 users) is included.

Although the network is undirected in nature, it is stored as a directed network where each connection appears as two edges, one in each direction (5,451 connections). The only property of the network is `name`, the anonymous user identifier.
citations: R. Guimera, L. Danon, A. Diaz-Guilera, F. Giralt and A. Arenas, "Self-similar community structure in a network of human interactions." Physical Review E 68, 065103(R) (2003).

datasets.name: unicodelang
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of territories (countries and other territories with their own ISO 3166 code) and the languages spoken in them, from the territory–language information of the Unicode Common Locale Data Repository (CLDR), version 27 (released in March 2015). The CLDR collects these figures, with references to their sources, to estimate the number of users of each language in each territory; it aims at approximate figures for the literate, functional population of each language, i.e. the people able to read and write the language and comfortable enough to use it with computers. Each edge connects a territory with a language and is weighted by the percentage of the population of the territory that uses the language. Languages are identified by their CLDR (BCP 47) codes; where the data distinguish the scripts in which a language is written (e.g. `uz_Arab` and `uz` for Uzbek in Arabic and in the default script), these are separate nodes. The pseudo-territory "Unknown Region" (`ZZ`), which has no data, is not included, and Antarctica and Bouvet Island are connected only to the "unknown language" node (`und`).

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `is_language`: whether the node is a language (otherwise it is a territory).
- (Node) `code`: the CLDR code of the language or territory.
- (Node) `name`: its English name, from the CLDR English locale data.
- (Node) `population`, `gdp` and `literacy_percent`: the population, the gross domestic product (in US dollars) and the literacy rate (in percent) of the territory, as given in the CLDR (territories only; NaN for languages).
- (Edge) `population_percent`: the percentage of the territory's population using the language.
- (Edge) `writing_percent`: the percentage of these that also write the language, where given (NaN otherwise).
- (Edge) `official_status`: the official status of the language in the territory (`official`, `de_facto_official`, `official_regional`, or empty if none).
citations: Unicode Consortium, "Unicode Common Locale Data Repository (CLDR), version 27." (2015)

datasets.name: urban_streets
datasets.description:
Street networks of 1-square-mile samples of 20 cities around the world, constructed by P. Crucitti, V. Latora and S. Porta from maps, and distributed as part of the material of the book "Complex Networks: Principles, Methods and Applications" by V. Latora, V. Nicosia and G. Russo. Nodes are street intersections (and dead ends), and an undirected edge is a street segment between two intersections (the "primal" representation of the street network).

The cities are Ahmedabad, Barcelona, Bologna, Brasilia, Cairo, Irvine (two samples, `irvine1` and `irvine2`), London, Los Angeles, New Delhi, New York, Paris, Richmond, San Francisco, Savannah, Seoul, Venice, Vienna, Walnut Creek and Washington.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `pos`: the coordinates $(x, y)$ of the intersection in the map.
- (Edge) `length`: the length of the street segment, in meters.
citations: P. Crucitti, V. Latora, and S. Porta. "Centrality measures in spatial networks of urban streets". Phys. Rev. E 73 (2006), 036125
V. Latora, V. Nicosia, G. Russo, "Complex Networks: Principles, Methods and Applications", Cambridge University Press (2017)

datasets.name: us_agencies
datasets.description:
Networks of hyperlinks among the websites of the government agencies of the 50 U.S. states, collected by S. Kosack, M. Coscia and collaborators (Harvard Center for International Development) by crawling the websites in 2017. A node is the entire website of an agency, and a directed edge $i \to j$ indicates that at least one webpage of website $i$ contains a hyperlink to a webpage of website $j$.

There is one network for each state (e.g. `alabama`, `newyork`), and the network `aggregate` combines the websites of all 50 states. The node identifiers are consistent across the networks.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `vid`: the numerical identifier of the website, unique across states.
- (Node) `url` (state networks): the URL of the website (the seed of the crawl).
- (Node) `name` (state networks): the name of the agency.
- (Node) `year` (state networks): the first year in which the website was indexed by the Internet Archive (a proxy for its creation date), or 0 if it was not indexed.
- (Node) `pages` (state networks): the number of webpages of the website found at the time of the crawl.
- (Node) `traffic` (state networks): an estimate of the web traffic of the website, as provided by the authors (its source and units are not documented in the data).
- (Graph) `population` (state networks): the population of the state.
- (Edge) `link_counts`: the number of hyperlinks from the webpages of website $i$ to the webpages of website $j$.
- (Edge) `rel_link_counts`: in the state networks, `link_counts` divided by the number of pages of website $i$; in the `aggregate` network, `link_counts` divided by the total number of outgoing hyperlinks of website $i$.
citations: S. Kosack et al., "Functional structures of US state governments." Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA (2018)

datasets.name: us_air_traffic
datasets.description:
Network of domestic air traffic in the United States from January 1990 to early 2020, from the T-100 Domestic Market table of the Bureau of Transportation Statistics (BTS), which records the monthly traffic reported by U.S. air carriers. Nodes are airports and a directed edge $i \to j$ is a record of the table: the traffic carried by one carrier from origin airport $i$ to destination airport $j$ in a given month, for a given service class. Each pair of airports is therefore connected by many parallel edges, one per carrier, month and service class (about 6.4 million edges in total).

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `airport_code`: the three-letter code of the airport.
- (Node) `airport_id`, `airport_seq_id`, `city_market_id`: the BTS identifiers of the airport, of the airport at a given point in time, and of the city market served by the airport.
- (Node) `city_name`, `state_abr`, `state_fips`, `state_nm`, `wac`: the city, the state abbreviation, FIPS code and name, and the BTS world area code of the airport.
- (Edge) `passengers`, `freight`, `mail`: the number of passengers, and the amount of freight and mail (in pounds) transported.
- (Edge) `distance`: the distance between the airports, in miles, and `distance_group`, the corresponding 500-mile distance interval.
- (Edge) `unique_carrier`, `airline_id`, `unique_carrier_name`, `unique_carrier_entity`, `carrier`, `carrier_name`: codes and names identifying the carrier.
- (Edge) `region`: the carrier's operating region (e.g. `D` for domestic).
- (Edge) `carrier_group`, `carrier_group_new`: the carrier group codes (based on the carrier's revenue).
- (Edge) `year`, `quarter`, `month`: the period of the record.
- (Edge) `class`: the service class: `F` (scheduled passenger/cargo service), `G` (scheduled all-cargo service), `L` (non-scheduled civilian passenger/cargo service) or `P` (non-scheduled all-cargo service).
citations: Bureau of Transportation Statistics. "T-100 Domestic Market". https://www.transtats.bts.gov/DL_SelectFields.asp?Table_ID=310 (2017)

datasets.name: us_airports
datasets.description:
Two networks of flights among airports in the United States, distributed by T. Opsahl.

- `top500_2002`: the 500 busiest commercial airports in the United States, connected if a flight was scheduled between them in 2002. This network was used by Colizza, Pastor-Satorras and Vespignani (2007), and was obtained by Opsahl from the website of the Complex Networks Collaboratory. Although flights are directed, the network is nearly symmetric, and is provided in undirected form. The airports are anonymized.
- `bts_2010`: all airports in the United States (and airports abroad with flights to or from them), connected by flights in 2010, according to the T-100 table of the Bureau of Transportation Statistics (BTS) Transtats website (with all geographies and months of 2010, and the columns passengers, origin and destination). Flights between the same airports were aggregated, links with zero passengers (cargo only) and self-loops were removed. A directed edge (i, j) indicates passengers flown from airport i to airport j.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Edge) `weight` (`top500_2002`): the number of seats available on the scheduled flights between the two airports in 2002.
- (Node) `name` (`bts_2010`): the airport code (IATA/FAA).
- (Edge) `weight` (`bts_2010`): the total number of passengers flown from airport i to airport j in 2010.
citations: V. Colizza, R. Pastor-Satorras, A. Vespignani, "Reaction-diffusion processes and metapopulation models in heterogeneous networks." Nature Physics 3, 276-282 (2007)
T. Opsahl, "Why Anchorage is not (that) important: Binary ties and sample selection" (2011)

datasets.name: us_congress
datasets.description:
Signed networks of relationships among the members of the U.S. Congress, inferred by Z. P. Neal from bill co-sponsorship data, for each chamber and each Congress from the 93rd (1973–1974) to the 114th (2015–2016). There is one network for each chamber and Congress, named by the chamber (`H` for the House of Representatives, `S` for the Senate) followed by the number of the Congress (e.g. `S100` for the Senate of the 100th Congress).

Nodes are representatives or senators. The relationships were obtained from the bipartite network of legislators and the bills they sponsored or co-sponsored, by extracting its signed backbone with the stochastic degree sequence model (SDSM): two legislators have a positive relationship if they co-sponsored significantly more bills together than expected given the numbers of bills each of them (co-)sponsored and the numbers of (co-)sponsors of each bill, and a negative relationship if they co-sponsored significantly fewer bills together than expected. Pairs without a significant relationship are not connected.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the legislator, with state and party affiliation (e.g. `Baucus, M. (MT-D)`).
- (Edge) `weight`: the sign of the relationship, $+1$ (positive) or $-1$ (negative).
citations: Z. P. Neal, "A sign of the times? Weak and strong polarization in the U.S. Congress, 1973-2016." Social Networks 60, 103-112 (2020)
Neal, Z. P. (2014). "The backbone of bipartite projections: Inferring relationships from co-authorship, co-sponsorship, co-attendance and other co-behaviors." Social Networks, 39, 84-97.

datasets.name: us_county_fb
datasets.description:
Networks of counties of the United States linked by the Social Connectedness Index of Facebook (the relative probability that two users living in the two counties are friends on Facebook):

- `strong_ties`: the network compiled by J. Jia and A. R. Benson as a benchmark for graph-based regression of election outcomes, with demographic and election features of the counties.
- `sci`: the complete, unthresholded county-to-county Social Connectedness Index as published by Meta (Data for Good) on the Humanitarian Data Exchange (HDX), weighted by the index.

In `strong_ties`, nodes are counties (identified by their FIPS codes), and an undirected edge connects two counties with strong social ties according to the Social Connectedness Index of Facebook (the relative probability that two users living in the two counties are friends on Facebook): each county is connected to those it is most strongly tied to, about 20 per county according to the authors. The network is not planar, since strong ties also exist between distant counties. The edge list of the data contains 584 pairs of counties twice, once in each direction; they are merged into one undirected edge. The raw values of the Social Connectedness Index are not included in this network.

The counties of `strong_ties` have demographic features from the US Department of Agriculture and the results of the presidential elections of 2012 and 2016 (formatted by T. McGovern), as well as features of the Facebook friendships. All features are normalized by the authors to zero mean and unit standard deviation over the counties; the raw values are not given.

The `sci` network contains all 3,204 counties and county equivalents of the file (including those of Puerto Rico and the US Virgin Islands) and an edge for every pair of them, weighted by the scaled index (from 1 to 1,000,000,000), including a self-loop for each county (the connectedness of its users among themselves). The file gives each pair in both directions, with the same value; each pair is kept once. It is a later release of the index (built from a snapshot of Facebook friendships of December 2025 to January 2026, with a revised methodology) than the one used for `strong_ties`, which Meta no longer provides: older releases are not published, as the index is not meant to be compared over time. HDX replaces the file in place with new releases; the version of May 11, 2026 is used.

The `strong_ties` network has the following properties:

- (Node) `fips`: the FIPS code of the county.
- (Node) `sh050m`, `sh100m`, `sh500m`: the share of the Facebook friends of the county's users who live within 50, 100 and 500 miles (normalized).
- (Node) `income_<year>`, `migration_<year>`, `birth_<year>`, `death_<year>`, `education_<year>`, `unemployment_<year>` (for the years 2012 and 2016): the median household income, the net migration rate, the birth and death rates, the education level and the unemployment rate of the county (normalized).
- (Node) `election_<year>`: the margin of the presidential election in the county, (Republican votes - Democratic votes) / (Republican votes + Democratic votes) (normalized).

The `sci` network has the following properties:

- (Node) `fips`: the FIPS code of the county.
- (Edge) `weight`: the scaled Social Connectedness Index of the two counties.
citations: J. Jia and A. R. Benson, "A Unifying Generative Model for Graph Learning Algorithms: Label Propagation, Graph Convolutions, and Combinations." SIAM Journal on Mathematics of Data Science 4(1), 100-125 (2022).
M. Bailey, R. Cao, T. Kuchler, J. Stroebel, A. Wong, "Social Connectedness: Measurement, Determinants, and Effects." Journal of Economic Perspectives 32(3), 259-280 (2018).

datasets.name: us_county_flows
datasets.description:
Networks of the flows of people between the counties of the United States: yearly migration flows from the tax returns of the Internal Revenue Service (IRS), and commuting flows from the American Community Survey (ACS) of the Census Bureau. Nodes are counties (and county equivalents, e.g. parishes, boroughs and independent cities), and directed edges are weighted by the number of people (or households) moving from one county to another.

1. Migration (`migration_2011_2012`, ..., `migration_2022_2023`): the county-to-county migration data of the Statistics of Income (SOI) division of the IRS, one network per pair of consecutive years. Migration is inferred by matching the individual income tax returns filed in two consecutive years, comparing the addresses of the filers: a directed edge $(i, j)$ means that taxpayers who filed in county $i$ in the first year filed in county $j$ in the second year. The edges are weighted by the number of returns (approximately, households), the number of individuals (counted as exemptions in the earlier years) and the adjusted gross income of the returns. To protect privacy, the IRS lists only flows of at least 20 returns (10 in 2011-2012 and 2012-2013; in a few years, some flows of 18 or 19 returns are listed); the smaller flows are only given in aggregates (by state and region of origin), which are not included here. The nodes are the counties of the 50 states and the District of Columbia in the data of that year; the flows from and to foreign countries are not included as edges. Years before 2011 (published in other formats) are not included. The file of 2013-2014 contains about a thousand repeated rows, which are included only once.
2. Commuting (`commuting_2006_2010`, `commuting_2009_2013`, `commuting_2011_2015`, `commuting_2016_2020`): the residence county to workplace county commuting flows (Table 1) of the ACS 5-year estimates for these periods. A directed edge $(i, j)$ means that workers 16 years and over living in county $i$ worked in county $j$, weighted by the estimated number of workers (with the margin of error of the estimate). Self-loops are the workers who live and work in the same county. The nodes are the counties of the United States and Puerto Rico in the data; commuting to a workplace abroad is not included. The tables of commuting flows by travel mode (2009-2013) and between minor civil divisions are not included.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the county.
- (Node) `state`: the state (two-letter postal code for the migration networks, full name for the commuting networks).
- (Node) `fips`: the five-digit FIPS code of the county (state and county code).
- (Node) `nonmigrant_returns`, `nonmigrant_individuals`, `nonmigrant_agi` (migration networks): the number of returns, individuals and the adjusted gross income (in thousands of US dollars) of the taxpayers who filed in the same county in both years (-1 if suppressed by the IRS, or if missing).
- (Node) `inflow_returns`, `inflow_individuals`, `inflow_agi`, `outflow_returns`, `outflow_individuals`, `outflow_agi` (migration networks): the totals of migration into and out of the county (including from and to other countries, and the flows below the threshold; -1 if suppressed by the IRS, or if missing).
- (Edge) `returns`, `individuals` (migration networks): the numbers of migrating returns and individuals.
- (Edge) `agi` (migration networks): the adjusted gross income of the migrating returns, in thousands of US dollars.
- (Edge) `weight` (commuting networks): the estimated number of workers.
- (Edge) `moe` (commuting networks): the margin of error of the estimate (90% confidence).
citations: Internal Revenue Service, Statistics of Income, "SOI Tax Stats - Migration Data." (2011-2023)
U.S. Census Bureau, "County-to-County Commuting Flows." American Community Survey 5-year estimates (2006-2020)

datasets.name: us_patents
datasets.description:
Network of citations among utility patents granted in the United States, from the NBER U.S. Patent Citations Data File compiled by B. H. Hall, A. B. Jaffe and M. Trajtenberg from the records of the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office. The network contains all citations made by patents granted between 1975 and 1999 (16,522,438 citations), and includes the citing patents as well as the patents they cite (3,774,768 nodes). Nodes are patents and a directed edge points from a citing patent to a cited patent.

The patents granted between 1963 and 1999 are annotated with the variables of the NBER patent data file; for the other nodes these properties take the value $-1$ (or are empty). The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `patent_id`: the patent number.
- (Node) `GYEAR`, `GDATE`: the grant year, and the grant date (in days since 1 January 1960).
- (Node) `APPYEAR`: the application year.
- (Node) `COUNTRY`, `POSTATE`: the country of the first inventor, and the state if the country is the U.S.
- (Node) `ASSIGNEE`: the identifier of the assignee (see the graph property `aconame`); `ASSCODE`: the type of assignee (1: unassigned, 2: U.S. non-government organization, 3: non-U.S. non-government organization, 4: U.S. individual, 5: non-U.S. individual, 6: U.S. government, 7: non-U.S. government).
- (Node) `CLAIMS`: the number of claims.
- (Node) `NCLASS`: the main U.S. patent class; `CAT` and `SUBCAT`: the technological category and sub-category of Hall, Jaffe and Trajtenberg.
- (Node) `CMADE`, `CRECEIVE`: the number of citations made and received (up to 1999).
- (Node) `RATIOCIT`: the fraction of the citations made that refer to patents granted since 1963.
- (Node) `GENERAL`, `ORIGINAL`: the generality and originality indices, measuring the dispersion of the citations received and made over technology classes.
- (Node) `FWDAPLAG`, `BCKGTLAG`: the mean forward citation lag and the mean backward citation lag, in years.
- (Node) `SELFCTUB`, `SELFCTLB`: upper and lower bounds of the share of self-citations made (citations to patents of the same assignee); `SECDUPBD`, `SECDLWBD`: upper and lower bounds of the share of self-citations received.
- (Node) `inventor`: the inventors of the patent, as a list with one dictionary per inventor holding the name and address of the inventor (`LASTNAM`, `FIRSTNAM`, `MIDNAM`, `MODIFNAM`, `STREET`, `CITY`, `POSTATE`, `COUNTRY`, `ZIP`) and its position in the list of inventors (`INVSEQ`).

Graph properties hold the auxiliary tables of the data file: `aconame` (the names of the assignees), `amatch` (the match of assignees to Compustat companies), `classes` (the names of the patent classes), `states` and `countries` (codes of states and countries), `class_cat` (the category and sub-category of each patent class), and `cat_names` (the names of the categories and sub-categories).
citations: B. H. Hall, A. B. Jaffe, & M. Trajtenberg, "The NBER patent citations data file: Lessons, insights and methodological tools." National Bureau of Economic Research, NBER Working Paper No. 8498 (2001)

datasets.name: us_rail_narn
datasets.description:
The North American Rail Network (NARN) of the US Federal Railroad Administration (FRA), part of the National Transportation Atlas Database (NTAD) of the Bureau of Transportation Statistics: a topological database of the railway lines of the United States (all 50 states and the District of Columbia; at a scale of 1:24,000 or better), Canada and Mexico, with their owners, the railroads with trackage rights, the passenger services and the strategic rail corridors. The dataset was created in 2016 and is updated in place; this is the version updated on October 19, 2026.

Nodes are the FRA's topological nodes (junctions, ends of lines, and points where the attributes of a line change, e.g. at state or county borders), and edges are the rail links between them, from the "from" node to the "to" node of each link (the network is undirected). All the links are included, whatever their kind (property `net`): main lines (95,932 links), other tracks such as minor industrial leads (88,559), yard tracks (79,028), major industrial leads (16,130), passing sidings (10,193), out-of-service lines (6,554), abandoned lines (4,267), trails on former rights-of-way (1,473), abandoned lines that were physically removed (623), and rail ferry connections (15). The network has parallel edges (13,673, e.g. tracks running side by side between the same nodes) and 71 self-loops (e.g. loops of yard tracks), and 253 components (the largest with 249,070 of the 250,204 nodes). The geometries of the links are not included.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `node_id`: the FRA node id.
- (Node) `latitude` and `longitude`.
- (Node) `country` (`US`, `CA`, `MX`).
- (Node) `state`: the state or province.
- (Node) `county_fips`: the FIPS code of the US state and county.
- (Node) `fra_district`: the FRA district (1 to 8 in the US, 99 outside).
- (Node) `passenger`: the passenger service at the station (`A` Amtrak, `B` Amtrak and commuter, `C` commuter).
- (Node) `station`: the name of the commuter station.
- (Node) `boundary`: whether the node is on a border (0 none, 1 state, 2 international, 3 county).
- (Edge) `link_id`: the FRA link id.
- (Edge) `owners`: the reporting marks of the (up to three) railroads in charge of dispatching, maintenance and/or ownership of the line.
- (Edge) `trackage_rights`: the reporting marks of the (up to nine) railroads with trackage rights.
- (Edge) `net`: the kind of link (`M` main network, `O` other track, `Y` yard, `I` major industrial lead, `S` passing siding over 4,000 feet, `X` out of service, `A` abandoned, `T` trail on a former rail right-of-way, `R` abandoned and removed, `F` rail ferry).
- (Edge) `tracks`: the number of main line tracks.
- (Edge) `passenger`: the passenger service on the line (`A` Amtrak, `B` Amtrak and commuter, `C` commuter, `D` Alaska Railroad, `E` intercity high-speed rail and commuter, `I` intercity high-speed rail, `R` rapid transit, `T` tourist, museum or scenic, `O` Ontario Northland, `V` Via Rail Canada).
- (Edge) `stracnet`: whether the line is on the Strategic Rail Corridor Network (`S`) or a connector to it (`C`).
- (Edge) `division`, `subdivision`, `branch` and `yard`: the names of the railroad's division, subdivision, branch or line, and yard.
- (Edge) `country`, `state`, `county_fips` and `fra_district`: as for the nodes.
- (Edge) `timezone` (`E`, `C`, `M`, `P`, `Z` Arizona, `K` Alaska, `H` Hawaii).
- (Edge) `length`: the length of the link (km). Missing values are empty strings or -1.
citations: Federal Railroad Administration, Bureau of Transportation Statistics, "North American Rail Network Lines." National Transportation Atlas Database (NTAD), dataset (2026)
Federal Railroad Administration, Bureau of Transportation Statistics, "North American Rail Network Nodes." National Transportation Atlas Database (NTAD), dataset (2026)

datasets.name: us_roads
datasets.description:
Road networks of the 50 U.S. states and the District of Columbia, derived from the TIGER/Line files of the U.S. Census Bureau for the 2000 Census. The data were prepared by D. Schultes for the 9th DIMACS Implementation Challenge on shortest paths. Nodes are road intersections and endpoints, and undirected edges are road segments between them. There is one network for each state (named by its two-letter postal code, e.g. `CA`), and the network `merged` combines all states into a single network, as produced by the merging program distributed with the data.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `la`, `lo`: the latitude and longitude of the node, in degrees.
- (Edge) `distance`, `travel_time`: the length of the road segment and the estimated travel time along it, both as given in the DIMACS files (the units are not documented there).
- (Edge) `road_category`: the road category, given by the numerical part of the TIGER census feature class code (CFCC) of the road (e.g. 11–18 for primary highways with limited access, 21–28 for primary roads without limited access, 31–38 for secondary and connecting roads, and 41–48 for local, neighborhood and rural roads).

The networks `tiger_2008` to `tiger_2026` are the national road networks of the annual releases of the TIGER/Line Shapefiles of the Census Bureau, from the first one (2008) to the latest one (2026), one network per release, built directly from their "All Lines" (EDGES) files, one per county (about 3,235). These files contain all the linear features of the TIGER database (roads, railroads, hydrography, boundaries, ...) as topological edges between nodes (`TNIDF` and `TNIDT`), with the same node ids across counties; only the road edges (those flagged as roads, with MAF/TIGER feature class codes S1100 to S1830) are included, and an edge is a road segment between two nodes (intersections, ends of roads, and points where the road crosses other linear features, e.g. boundaries or streams). The networks are undirected and cover the 50 states, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico and the Island Areas; they have parallel edges and self-loops (e.g. roads forming loops). Not included are the house number ranges of the edges, their geometries, and the railroads and hydrography of the EDGES files. These networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `tnid`: the TIGER node id.
- (Node) `la` and `lo`: the latitude and longitude of the node (NAD83, in degrees).
- (Edge) `tlid`: the permanent TIGER/Line id of the edge.
- (Edge) `name`: the full name of the road (e.g. `Ingomar St NW`; empty if unnamed).
- (Edge) `mtfcc`: the MAF/TIGER feature class code (e.g. `S1100` primary road, `S1200` secondary road, `S1400` local neighborhood road, rural road or city street, `S1500` vehicular trail, `S1630` ramp, `S1640` service drive, `S1710` walkway, `S1720` stairway, `S1730` alley, `S1740` private road, `S1750` internal census use, `S1780` parking lot road, `S1820` bike path or trail).
- (Edge) `county`: the FIPS code of the state and county.
- (Edge) `zip_left`, `zip_right`: the ZIP codes on the two sides of the road.
- (Edge) `length`: the length of the edge along its geometry (km).
- (Edge) `decked`: whether the road is double-decked.
- (Edge) `artificial_path`: whether the edge is an artificial path.
- (Edge) `divided` (networks until `tiger_2016`): whether the road is divided (a field left out of the later releases).
citations: U.S. Census Bureau, "TIGER/Line Shapefiles: All Lines (EDGES)." Datasets of 2008 to 2026

datasets.name: us_rollcall
datasets.description:
Networks of the roll-call votes of the United States Congress, from the Voteview data of K. Poole and H. Rosenthal, as processed and distributed by M. A. Porter and collaborators.

1. Bipartite networks of legislators and roll calls, for the House of Representatives (`house<C>`) and the Senate (`senate<C>`) of the 102nd to the 107th Congresses (1991-2003), prepared by M. E. J. Newman. Each legislator is connected to each roll call in which they voted yea or nay, and the edge is annotated with the vote. Paired and announced votes, abstentions and absences are not included. Legislators who served only part of a term appear as separate nodes, and are included even if they never voted.
2. Weighted networks of legislators for the House (`H<C>`) and the Senate (`S<C>`) of every Congress from the 1st to the 110th (1789-2009), used by Waugh, Pei, Fowler, Mucha and Porter in their study of party polarization. Two legislators are connected by an edge weighted by the fraction of the roll calls in which both voted where they voted the same way (both yea or both nay). Here, yea includes paired and announced yeas, and nay includes paired and announced nays. Legislators who never voted are excluded. Pairs of legislators who never agreed, or never voted in the same roll call, have weight zero in the source and are not connected. Legislators are identified by their ICPSR number (which, in a few cases, changes when a legislator switches party).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `is_legislator` (bipartite networks): whether the node is a legislator (otherwise it is a roll call, numbered in chronological order).
- (Node) `name`: the surname of the legislator (as in the source, truncated to 11 characters).
- (Node) `party` (bipartite networks): the party of the legislator (`D` Democrat, `R` Republican, `I` other).
- (Edge) `vote` (bipartite networks): +1 for yea and -1 for nay.
- (Node) `icpsr` (weighted networks): the ICPSR identifier of the legislator.
- (Node) `state` (weighted networks): the name of the state (abbreviated to 7 characters).
- (Node) `state_code` (weighted networks): the ICPSR state code.
- (Node) `district` (weighted networks): the congressional district (0 for senators; 98 or 99 for at-large and other special districts).
- (Node) `party_code` (weighted networks): the Voteview party code (e.g. 100 Democrat, 200 Republican, 328 Independent, 5000 Pro-Administration, 4000 Anti-Administration).
- (Edge) `weight` (weighted networks): the fraction of agreeing votes.
citations: A. S. Waugh, L. Pei, J. H. Fowler, P. J. Mucha, M. A. Porter, "Party Polarization in Congress: A Network Science Approach." arXiv:0907.3509 (2009)
M. Porter, "Roll Call Votes: United States House and Senate." figshare (2015)
K. Poole, H. Rosenthal, et al., "Voteview: Congressional Roll-Call Votes Database."

datasets.name: us_transmission_lines
datasets.description:
Network of the electric power transmission lines of the United States (including Alaska, Hawaii, Puerto Rico and Guam), from the "Electric Power Transmission Lines" layer of the Homeland Infrastructure Foundation-Level Data (HIFLD) Open portal of the US Department of Homeland Security, in its last version (data current as of September 30, 2024). The layer was compiled from aerial imagery, the forms EIA-860 and EIA-861 of the US Energy Information Administration, OpenStreetMap and other public sources, and covers lines of 69 kV up to 765 kV, and some of lower voltage; underground lines are included where sources were available. The HIFLD Open portal was shut down in 2025; the data are taken from the copy archived (and no longer updated) on ArcGIS Online by Esri's Federal User Community.

In both networks each edge is a transmission line (94,619 in all). The layer gives the lines as geometries, with the names of the substations at their ends (`SUB_1` and `SUB_2`) as attributes; most of these names are placeholders (e.g. "UNKNOWN128553" or "TAP139917"), and they are not always consistent between lines that meet at the same point, so the topology is given in two ways:

- `endpoints`: the nodes are the end points of the lines (substations, taps and junctions), built from the geometries: two lines are joined at a node if they end at the same point (after rounding the coordinates to $10^{-7}$ degrees, about 1 cm). Lines that cross or touch each other elsewhere than at their end points are not joined. The network has parallel edges (4,502, e.g. circuits running side by side) and 24 self-loops (lines ending where they start); it is not connected (836 components, the largest with 72,103 nodes).
- `substations`: the nodes are the substation names of the lines' ends, as given in the data (including the numbered placeholders, which identify taps, risers, dead ends and unknown substations); two lines are joined if they name the same substation. Names are not unique across the country (e.g. 96 line ends name a substation "MIDWAY", from Florida to Texas and California), so distinct substations of the same name are merged. Where a name is not available ("NOT AVAILABLE", 17,559 line ends), the end gets a node of its own, with an empty name. The network has parallel edges (3,532) and 186 self-loops (lines that name the same substation at both ends); it is not connected (5,610 components, the largest with 65,817 nodes).

The networks are undirected. The geometries of the lines (their courses as polylines) are not included, nor the constant attributes (the NAICS code of the industry), the layer's internal object ids, and its lengths of the lines in the Web Mercator projection, which are replaced by the lengths along the great circles.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `latitude`, `longitude` (`endpoints`): the position of the end point.
- (Node) `name` (`substations`): the name of the substation (empty if not available).
- (Edge) `hifld_id`: the id of the line in HIFLD.
- (Edge) `type`: the type of line (e.g. `AC; OVERHEAD`, `AC; UNDERGROUND`, `DC; OVERHEAD`).
- (Edge) `status`: the status of the line (`IN SERVICE`, `INACTIVE`, `UNDER CONSTRUCTION`).
- (Edge) `owner`: the owner of the line.
- (Edge) `voltage`: its voltage (kV; NaN if not available).
- (Edge) `volt_class`: the voltage class (e.g. `100-161`, `345`, `DC`).
- (Edge) `inferred`: whether the voltage was inferred (`Y` or `N`).
- (Edge) `sub_1` and `sub_2`: the names of the substations at the ends of the line, as given in the data.
- (Edge) `source`: the sources of the data.
- (Edge) `source_date`: the date of the source (Unix time; -1 where missing).
- (Edge) `val_method`: the method of validation (e.g. `IMAGERY`).
- (Edge) `val_date`: the date of validation (Unix time; -1 where missing).
- (Edge) `length`: the length of the line along its course (km, computed from its geometry). Values that are not available are empty strings.
citations: Homeland Infrastructure Foundation-Level Data (HIFLD), "U.S. Electric Power Transmission Lines." US Department of Homeland Security, dataset, archived on ArcGIS Online (2024)

datasets.name: utah_schools
datasets.description:
Temporal networks of close-proximity contacts between students of two schools in Utah, USA, recorded with wearable wireless sensors by the Contacts among Utah's School-age Population (CUSP) study. The sensors were deployed at an urban middle school ("Mid1", 7th and 8th grade, 591 students) on November 28 and 29, 2012, and at a suburban elementary school ("Elem1", kindergarten to 6th grade in 21 classes, 339 students) on January 31 and February 1, 2013, and the data cover the school hours of each day. The students wore Wireless Ranging Enabled Nodes (WRENs), which broadcast a packet every 20,000 binary milliseconds (19.53125 seconds) and recorded the packets received from other nodes, together with their signal strength. Packets with a signal strength below -77 dBm were discarded, which was intended to retain contacts at a distance of less than about 2 meters; the authors note that some contacts at larger distances may have been retained and some closer ones discarded. After correcting clock drifts and removing data from nodes that were not being worn, time was divided into bins of 19.53125 seconds, and a contact between two students is a maximal run of consecutive bins in which at least one of them recorded the other. Each contact is an edge, so two students can be connected by several edges. In addition to these data (the main data of the study), the authors released alternative versions obtained with a stricter signal strength threshold, intended to correspond to a distance of less than about 1 meter, which they used for a sensitivity analysis.

- `mid1_day1`, `mid1_day2`: contacts at the middle school, on the first and second day.
- `elem1_day1`, `elem1_day2`: contacts at the elementary school, on the first and second day.
- `mid1_day1_1m`, `mid1_day2_1m`, `elem1_day1_1m`, `elem1_day2_1m`: the same, with the stricter (<1 meter) criterion.

Every network contains all the students of the respective school, including the ones without any recorded contact on that day (one in `mid1_day1_1m` and `mid1_day2_1m`). The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `id`: the anonymous identifier of the student in the source data (the same across the two days of a school).
- (Node) `grade`: the school grade of the student (0 = kindergarten, 1 to 8 = 1st to 8th grade, -1 = unknown).
- (Node) `class`: the class of the student, numbered 0 to 20 (`elem1_*` only).
- (Node) `gender`: the gender of the student (0 = male, 1 = female, -1 = unknown).
- (Edge) `time`: the time of day at which the contact started, in seconds since midnight (local time), i.e. the start of its first time bin. The source gives it in units of 19.53125 seconds, so it is a multiple of this value.
- (Edge) `duration`: the duration of the contact, in seconds (the number of consecutive time bins times 19.53125 seconds).
citations: D. J. A. Toth, M. Leecaster, W. B. P. Pettey, A. V. Gundlapalli, H. Gao, J. J. Rainey, A. Uzicanin, M. H. Samore, "The role of heterogeneity in contact timing and duration in network models of influenza spread in schools." Journal of The Royal Society Interface 12(108), 20150279 (2015)

datasets.name: veteran_comorbidity
datasets.description:
A dense, directed and weighted network of co-morbidity among 95 physical and mental health conditions, derived from the longitudinal health records of approximately one million United States military veterans. The records come from the VA (Department of Veterans Affairs) National Corporate Data Warehouse, which holds the coded diagnoses of all VA inpatient and outpatient encounters, for veterans who served in the Operation Enduring Freedom, Operation Iraqi Freedom or Operation New Dawn (OEF/OIF/OND), enrolled in VA healthcare after 1 October 2001, and had at least one VA primary care visit before the end of the study period, on 1 October 2017. The conditions are diagnostic categories with a prevalence of at least 0.1%: categories of the AHRQ (Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality) Clinical Classifications Software, psychiatric diagnoses as categorized by the VA's Northeast Program Evaluation Center (NEPEC: alcohol use disorder, drug use disorder, schizophrenia, major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder, PTSD, other depression, unspecified and generalized anxiety), and diabetes, neoplasms, congenital anomalies and genital disorders. For each ordered pair of conditions, the association was estimated with a logistic regression of the odds of one condition given the other.

Nodes are conditions, and a directed edge from condition j to condition i carries the increase in the log odds of condition i given condition j (the logistic regression coefficient; negative values indicate a decreased odds), so that the out-edges of a node describe the conditions that it predicts. All 95 x 94 ordered pairs are present, and the network is complete. This edge direction follows the authors' sample code (which builds the network from the transpose of the matrix of log odds, whose rows are the predicted conditions). The upstream repository also includes matrices for the interaction effect of sex and its p-values, but in the available files these contain only zeros, and they are not included.

Node properties: `name`, the variable name of the condition in the source (with prefix "AHRQ_" for the AHRQ categories and "NEPEC_" for the NEPEC psychiatric categories; e.g. "AHRQ_Asthma_DT", "NEPEC_PTSD_DT", "dmdxDT" for diabetes); `short_name`, the abbreviated label used in the authors' sample code; `psychiatric`, whether the condition is psychiatric, as marked in the authors' sample code. Edge properties: `log_odds`, the increase in log odds described above; `pvalue`, its p-value from the logistic regression (values below the floating point precision are reported as 0).
citations: A. F. Alexander-Bloch, A. Raznahan, R. T. Shinohara, S. R. Mathias, H. Bathulapalli, I. P. Bhalla, J. L. Goulet, T. D. Satterthwaite, D. S. Bassett, D. C. Glahn, C. A. Brandt, "The architecture of co-morbidity networks of physical and mental health conditions in military veterans." Proceedings of the Royal Society A 476(2239), 20190790 (2020)

datasets.name: viabundus
datasets.description:
The road and waterway network of late medieval and early modern northern Europe (1350-1650) of Viabundus, a historical map and database of premodern transport and mobility, originally conceived as the digitization of the atlas of land roads in the Hanseatic area of F. Bruns and H. Weczerka, *Hansische Handelsstraßen* (1962), and extended with researched road networks of the present-day Netherlands, Denmark, Finland, several German states (Lower Saxony, Schleswig-Holstein, Thuringia, Saxony-Anhalt, Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Hesse, North Rhine-Westphalia), parts of Poland and the Baltic states, and with navigable waterways.

Nodes are the places that may require an action of a traveler (change roads, pay a fee, change the means of transport, cross a river, reach a destination): settlements, towns, tolls, staple markets, fairs, ferries, bridges, harbors and locks, with the years in which these attributes existed, and junctions of routes. A cluster of nodes in a town can be subordinated to a parent node (`parent_id`), whose attributes settlement, town, staple and fair apply to them as well. Edges are route segments between two nodes: land roads, winter roads (usable only in winter, e.g. across marshes or frozen lakes), rivers, canals, coastal and lake routes, and ferries, with the certainty of their reconstruction and the years in which they existed (if not given, the whole period). The networks are undirected, and have a few parallel edges (alternative routes between the same nodes; 44 to 83 per network).

There is one network for each version of the dataset on Zenodo: `v1_0` (April 19, 2021), `v1_1` (December 6, 2021), `v1_2` (September 21, 2022), `v1_3` (March 17, 2024) and `v2` (April 25, 2025), each built from the nodes and edges tables of that version. The edges of `v1_0` do not give their end nodes: they are joined to the nodes at their end points (after rounding the coordinates to $10^{-5}$ degrees, about 1 m), and the 3,175 points where edges end without a node (junctions, which are nodes of their own in later versions) are added as nodes. In the later versions, the edges give their end nodes, and the few end nodes that are missing from the nodes table (69 in `v1_3`, 1 in `v2`) are added as nodes, at the end points of the edges. In both cases, these nodes have `has_record` false and no other attributes than their position. The geometries of the edges, the descriptions of the edges, the alternative names of `v2` (a separate table), and the tables of literature, populations, fairs, town outlines and waterways of 1500 are not included.

The networks have the following properties (the columns of the nodes and edges tables, whose set changes slightly between versions; missing values are empty strings or -1):

- (Node) `node_id`: the id of the node in Viabundus (-1 for the added nodes).
- (Node) `has_record`: whether the node is in the nodes table.
- (Node) `latitude`, `longitude`: the position of the node.
- (Node) `name`: the modern official name.
- (Node) `alternative_names` (up to `v1_3`): other modern, foreign and historical names, separated by semicolons.
- (Node) `parent_id`: the id of the parent node.
- (Node) `geonames_id` (up to `v1_2`), `links` (from `v1_3` on): the ids of the place in other gazetteers (e.g. `gn:` GeoNames, `wd:` Wikidata).
- (Node) `zoomlevel`: the lowest zoom level at which the web map shows the node.
- (Node) `ready`: whether the information on the node is considered correct and complete.
- (Node) `is_<attribute>`, `<attribute>_from`, `<attribute>_to`, `<attribute>_description`: for each of the attributes settlement, town, fair, toll, bridge, staple, ferry, harbour and lock, whether the node has it, the years in which it existed (usually the first and last mentions), and a description with references.
- (Node) `gregorian_calendar` (from `v1_1` on): whether the dates of the fairs are in the Gregorian calendar.
- (Node) `staple_duration_of_stay`: the duration of the obligatory stay at a staple market.
- (Node) `toll_primary_owner` (`v2` only): the primary owner of the toll.
- (Edge) `edge_id`: the id of the edge in Viabundus.
- (Edge) `type`: `land`, `winter`, `river`, `canal`, `coast` or `ferry` (`land`, `water` or `ferry` before `v2`, with one edge of type `lsnd` as given).
- (Edge) `certainty`: the accuracy of the reconstruction (1 very certain, 2 mediocre, 3 uncertain, including the roads digitized from *Hansische Handelsstraßen* that were not yet checked).
- (Edge) `zoomlevel`: the zoom level (1 to 4) from which the web map shows the edge.
- (Edge) `from_year`, `to_year`: the years between which the route existed.
- (Edge) `length`: its length (m).
- (Edge) `section` (except in `v1_3`): the code of the region of the edge (e.g. `NDS` for Lower Saxony, `B-W` for the rough digitizations of *Hansische Handelsstraßen*).
- (Edge) `comment_id`: the id(s) of the comments on the edge, separated by semicolons.
- (Edge) `ready` (`v1_2` and `v1_3`): whether the edge is considered complete.
- (Edge) `slope_multiplier` (`v2` only): the factor by which the slope of the segment increases the travel time on foot (1 for water routes).
citations: B. Holterman, M. A.B., K. Andersen, M. Dengg, N. Petersen, "Viabundus: Map of Premodern European Transport and Mobility." Research Data Journal for the Humanities and Social Sciences 7, 1-13 (2022)
B. Holterman, M. C. Dengg, M. A.B., K. H. Andersen, "Viabundus map of premodern European transport and mobility." Zenodo, dataset, versions 1.0-2 (2021-2025)

datasets.name: virion
datasets.description:
The Global Virome in One Network (VIRION), an atlas of the known associations between vertebrate hosts and their viruses, maintained by the Verena consortium (C. J. Carlson and collaborators). VIRION reconciles static datasets compiled from the literature (CLOVER, which harmonizes the host-pathogen databases of Shaw et al. 2020, HP3 of Olival et al. 2017, GMPD2 of Stephens et al. 2017 and EID2 of Wardeh et al. 2015) with dynamically updated sources (the virus sequences of NCBI GenBank and the USAID PREDICT surveillance data), and harmonizes all host and virus names against the NCBI taxonomy (and the ICTV taxonomy for viruses). This is the data package of 13 October 2026 (the database is released weekly). Two of the sources are also separate entries: `mammal_virus_hp3` (HP3) and `host_pathogen_eid2` (EID2, which covers all kinds of pathogens).

The network is bipartite and undirected: nodes are the taxa of the VIRION taxonomy table (vertebrate hosts, marked by the property `is_host`, and viruses), and each edge is one record of the database, i.e. one piece of evidence that a virus infects a host (e.g. a GenBank sequence, a literature report, or a PREDICT test), so that the network is a multigraph: a host and a virus are connected by as many edges as there are records of their association. Nodes are identified by the taxon key of the database (`tax_hash`), not by the name: some names occur in several taxon entries with different taxonomic information (e.g. NCBI-resolved or not). The NCBI accession numbers of the sequences (a separate table of the data package) are not included. A few records (1,069) are encoded in Latin-1 instead of UTF-8, which were converted.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the scientific name of the taxon (in lower case, as in the database).
- (Node) `is_host`: whether the node is a host (otherwise a virus).
- (Node) `genus`, `family`, `order`, `class`: the taxonomy of the taxon (empty if not available).
- (Node) `ncbi_taxid`: the NCBI taxonomy identifier (-1 if not available).
- (Node) `ncbi_resolved`: whether the name could be harmonized with the NCBI taxonomy.
- (Node) `ictv_ratified`: whether the virus taxon is ratified by the ICTV (false for hosts).
- (Node) `tax_hash`: the key of the taxon in the database.
- (Edge) `detection_method`: the strength of the evidence, one of "Isolation/Observation", "PCR/Sequencing", "Antibodies" and "Not specified", in descending order of strength.
- (Edge) `detection_original`: the detection method as described in the source.
- (Edge) `database`: the source of the record (GenBank, PREDICT, Shaw, HP3, GMPD2 or EID2), and `database_version`, its version or citation.
- (Edge) `host_original` and `virus_original`: the names of the host and the virus in the source.
- (Edge) `host_flag`: whether there is possible uncertainty in the identification of the host.
- (Edge) `publication_year`: the year of publication of the literature source (NaN if not given); `reference`, its text description, and `pmid`, its PubMed identifier (empty if not given).
- (Edge) `release_date`: the date the association was released to the public (e.g. the GenBank submission), as "YYYY-MM-DD" or partial ("YYYY", "YYYY-MM"), empty if not given.
- (Edge) `collection_date`: the date of collection of the sample, as given (mostly "YYYY-MM-DD" or partial dates; empty if not given).
- (Edge) `assoc_id`: the identifier of the record in this version of the database.
citations: C. J. Carlson, R. J. Gibb, G. F. Albery, L. Brierley, R. P. Connor, T. A. Dallas, et al., "The Global Virome in One Network (VIRION): an Atlas of Vertebrate-Virus Associations." mBio 13(2), e02985-21 (2022)

datasets.name: virus_host_db
datasets.description:
Networks of viruses and their hosts from the Virus-Host DB of GenomeNet (Kyoto University), which covers all the viruses with complete genomes in NCBI RefSeq and in GenBank (as listed in EBI Genomes), across all domains of life (viruses of bacteria, archaea, protists, fungi, plants and animals, including humans). The hosts are collected from the annotations of RefSeq and GenBank, UniProt and ViralZone, and from a manual curation of the literature. Each virus and each host is an NCBI taxon, and an edge links a virus to a host in which it was found.

Virus-Host DB is updated with every RefSeq release (about every two months), and its earlier releases are archived. There is one network for each archived release, named `release_<N>` by the number of its directory in the archive, which is the RefSeq release on which it is based, from `release_75` (2016) to `release_236` (RefSeq release 236, July 6, 2026); the RefSeq release and its date are given by the graph properties `refseq_release` and `refseq_date`. Releases 76, 97, 201, 223, 234 are missing from the archive, except that the directory 224 holds the data of RefSeq release 223. The directory 232 holds the same data as 233 (of RefSeq release 233), and the file of the directory 230 (RefSeq release 230, May 2, 2025) is empty: both are left out. The first release, `release_75`, has no KEGG identifiers, diseases, PubMed identifiers and evidence.

The viruses whose genomes come from environmental samples (metagenomes) have as host the root of the taxonomy (taxon `1`, `root`), with the kind of sample (e.g. `Soil`, `Marine`, `Organismal`) as edge property: this node is kept, and it joins all these viruses. Some viruses are hosts of other viruses (e.g. satellite viruses and virophages), so that a few edges join two viruses, and the networks are not strictly bipartite. The viruses without any host given are isolated nodes. A virus and a host are joined by several edges if they are listed several times (e.g. with different kinds of samples).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `tax_id`: the NCBI taxonomy identifier of the virus or host.
- (Node) `is_virus`: whether the node is a virus (otherwise it is only a host).
- (Node) `name`: the name of the virus or host.
- (Node) `lineage`: the taxonomic lineage of the virus or host, separated by `; `.
- (Node) `refseq_ids`: the RefSeq (or GenBank) accessions of the genome of the virus, separated by `, ` (empty for hosts).
- (Node) `kegg_genome`, `kegg_disease`, `disease`: the KEGG GENOME and KEGG DISEASE identifiers of the virus, and the diseases it causes (empty if none, and for hosts).
- (Edge) `pmids` (from `release_77`): the PubMed identifiers of the articles on the association, separated by `, `.
- (Edge) `evidence` (from `release_77`): the sources of the host information (`RefSeq`, `Literature`, `UniProt`, `NCBI Virus`, ...), separated by `, `.
- (Edge) `sample_type` (from `release_89`): the kind of environmental sample of the genome, if the host is the root of the taxonomy.
- (Edge) `source_organism` (from `release_89`): the taxonomy identifier of the organism of the sample, for organismal samples (-1 if not given).
- (Node) `refseq_release`, `refseq_date` (graph): the RefSeq release on which the network is based, and its date (empty if not given).
citations: T. Mihara, Y. Nishimura, Y. Shimizu, H. Nishiyama, G. Yoshikawa, H. Uehara, P. Hingamp, S. Goto, H. Ogata, "Linking Virus Genomes with Host Taxonomy." Viruses 8, 66 (2016)

datasets.name: visualizeus
datasets.description: Three bipartite networks of tag-picture, user-picture, and user-tag linkages that represent the folksonomy of the picture tagging network of vi.sualize.us. The date of this snapshot is uncertain. Only the tag-picture network is included here: nodes are tags and pictures, and an edge connects a picture to a tag assigned to it.
citations: N. Neubauer and K. Obermayer. "Analysis of the Visualize.us folksonomy." Unpublished (2010)

datasets.name: vivino
datasets.description:
A network of users of Vivino, an online social network and marketplace for wine enthusiasts, where users rate and review wines and follow each other, from Kotonya et al. The data were collected by crawling the Vivino website from November 2016 to March 2017, targeting the 10,000 most active users (according to Vivino's per-country user ranking) of each of the 15 countries with the highest wine consumption (Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Canada, China, France, Germany, Italy, Portugal, Romania, Russia, South Africa, Spain, United Kingdom and United States). The distributed data contain the profiles of 129,351 users, with anonymized user identifiers. Each profile lists between 1 and 20 other users in a field named "top_in_network", which defines the edges of the network: a directed edge goes from a profiled user to each user listed in this field. The meaning of this field is not documented in the source data or the paper; ICON describes it as the social connections of the user to other users active in the 365 days prior to the crawl. The edges are not reciprocated, and most listed users (410,652) do not have a profile in the data; these are included as nodes without metadata.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `user_id`: the anonymized identifier of the user.
- (Node) `has_profile`: whether the profile of the user is included in the data (all remaining properties are empty or zero otherwise).
- (Node) `country`: the country of the user.
- (Node) `followers` and `following`: the number of followers of the user and of users followed by the user.
- (Node) `ratings`: the total number of wine ratings by the user.
- (Node) `taste_styles`, `taste_regions`, `taste_ratings` and `taste_counts`: the taste profile of the user, i.e. the list of regional wine styles rated by the user (e.g. "/wine-styles/spanish-grenache"), with their wine regions, the average rating given by the user (from 1 to 5) and the number of ratings, in the order given by Vivino.
citations: N. Kotonya, P. De Cristofaro, E. De Cristofaro, "Of Wines and Reviews: Measuring and Modeling the Vivino Wine Social Network." Proceedings of the 2018 IEEE/ACM International Conference on Advances in Social Networks Analysis and Mining (ASONAM), 387-392 (2018)

datasets.name: voat
datasets.description:
Networks of the discussions on Voat, a news aggregator and discussion website similar to Reddit, popular with communities banned from other platforms, from its foundation in 2013 until its closure on 25 December 2020. The data were collected by Mekacher and Papasavva from the snapshots of the site in the Internet Archive's Wayback Machine and from the API of the site, and contain 2.4 million submissions and 16.3 million comments in 7,100 subverses (the communities of the site, as subreddits on Reddit), and the profiles of 113,000 users and of the subverses. There are two networks:

- `comments`: each node is a user, and a directed edge from user $i$ to user $j$ is a comment of $i$ in the discussion of a submission of $j$, with one edge per comment (a multigraph). The data do not give the comment to which a comment replies (only its depth in the discussion tree), so that the edges point to the author of the submission. Users commenting on their own submissions give self-loops.
- `subverses`: a bipartite network of users and subverses, where an edge connects a user to a subverse in which the user posted submissions or comments, or that the user moderated or created (according to the profile of the user), with the numbers of submissions and comments.

The submissions and comments of deleted accounts (with no user name in the data), and those posted anonymously (in the subverses that allowed it, where the user names are replaced by random numbers followed by "?"), have no identifiable author: they are left out of both networks, as are the comments on them in `comments`. Comments on submissions that are not in the data (3,753) are left out of `comments`, which thus has 10.8 million of the 16.3 million comments. All the users with a profile are included in both networks, also those without submissions or comments. The texts of the submissions and comments are not included. The times are given in the data as dates and times of the day, taken here as UTC.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the user name, or the name of the subverse.
- (Node) `registered`: the registration date of the user (from the user's profile), in Unix time (-1 if unknown, and for subverses).
- (Node) `is_user` (`subverses` only): whether the node is a user (otherwise a subverse).
- (Node) `subscribers` (`subverses` only): the number of subscribers of the subverse (-1 if unknown, and for users).
- (Node) `created` (`subverses` only): the creation time of the subverse, in Unix time (-1 if unknown, and for users).
- (Node) `about` (`subverses` only): the description of the subverse (empty for users).
- (Edge) `time` (`comments` only): the time of the comment, in Unix time.
- (Edge) `upvotes`, `downvotes` (`comments` only): the numbers of upvotes and downvotes of the comment.
- (Edge) `depth` (`comments` only): the depth of the comment in the discussion (0 for comments on the submission, 1 for replies to these, etc.; -1 if unknown).
- (Edge) `subverse` (`comments` only): the subverse of the discussion.
- (Edge) `submissions`, `comments` (`subverses` only): the numbers of submissions and comments of the user in the subverse.
- (Edge) `moderator`, `owner` (`subverses` only): whether the user moderated, or created, the subverse.
citations: A. Mekacher, A. Papasavva, "'I Can't Keep It Up.' A Dataset from the Defunct Voat.co News Aggregator." Proceedings of the International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media 16, 1302-1311 (2022)

datasets.name: w3c_email
datasets.description:
A directed network of emails sent to the public mailing lists of the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C), from the W3C corpus crawled in 2004 for the Enterprise track of TREC 2005, as processed by Benson and Kleinberg (the `pvc-email-W3C` dataset) to study networks whose edges were "found" from the activity of a set of core nodes. Each node is an email address, and a directed edge from address A to address B with a timestamp is an email sent by A to B; an email with several recipients gives several edges. The core nodes are the addresses of the domain w3.org (e.g. W3C staff and the mailing lists themselves); every email is sent from or to a core address.

The emails date mostly from 1995 to 2004; a few dates outside this range (from 1988 to 2009) are likely erroneous. There are 328 emails from an address to itself.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `address`: the email address.
- (Node) `is_core`: whether the address is in the domain w3.org.
- (Edge) `time`: the time the email was sent, in Unix time. The source data give the times in seconds since the start of year 1 (as in the Julia language); they were converted by subtracting 62,135,683,200 seconds.
citations: A. R. Benson, J. Kleinberg, "Found Graph Data and Planted Vertex Covers." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 31 (2018)
N. Craswell, A. P. de Vries, I. Soboroff, "Overview of the TREC 2005 Enterprise Track." Proceedings of the Fourteenth Text REtrieval Conference (TREC 2005) (2005)

datasets.name: walmart_trips
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of shopping trips at Walmart stores and the products bought in each trip. The purchase data were released by Walmart for the 2015 Kaggle competition "Walmart Recruiting: Trip Type Classification", in which each record is an item scanned during a customer visit (identified by a visit number, with the product's UPC code, its store department and the number of items scanned), and visits were to be classified into trip types defined by Walmart. Amburg, Veldt and Benson formed the trips from these records and assigned each product to one of ten broad departments under which it appears on walmart.com, or to an "Other" class. Each trip in the network contains at least two distinct products; not all visits of the competition data are included, and the selection criteria are not documented. Product identities, item counts and the trip types are not included in this version of the data.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `is_trip`: whether the node is a shopping trip (otherwise it is a product).
- (Node) `department` (products): the walmart.com department of the product: "Clothing, Shoes & Accessories", "Electronics and Office", "Home, Furniture & Appliances", "Home Improvement & Patio", "Baby", "Toys, Games, and Video Games", "Food, Household & Pets", "Pharmacy, Health & Beauty", "Sports, Fitness & Outdoors", "Auto, Tires & Industrial", or "Other".
citations: I. Amburg, N. Veldt, A. R. Benson, "Clustering in graphs and hypergraphs with categorical edge labels." Proceedings of The Web Conference 2020, 706-717 (2020)

datasets.name: water_distribution_exeter
datasets.description:
Water distribution networks used as benchmark problems for the design, expansion and operation of water supply systems, distributed as EPANET input files by the Centre for Water Systems of the University of Exeter. Nodes are junctions (pipe intersections and demand points), reservoirs (sources with a fixed head) and storage tanks, and a directed edge is a link (a pipe, pump or valve) between two nodes; the direction is that of the link's definition in the EPANET file (from its start to its end node), which for pipes is only the reference direction of the flow (water may flow either way), but is the flow direction for pumps, check-valve pipes and most valves. The networks are:

- `richmond` and `richmond_skeleton`: the water distribution system of Richmond (Yorkshire Water, UK), as used in a study of operational optimization (K. van Zyl, Exeter, 2001); the skeleton version is a simplified schematic representation, not a hydraulically equivalent model.
- `exnet`: EXNET, a large real network serving about 400,000 people, used for an expansion (reinforcement) benchmark of the Centre for Water Systems (one of its nodes has no links).
- `wolf_cordera_ranch`: the network of the Wolf-Cordera Ranch development of Colorado Springs Utilities (USA).
- `d_town`: D-Town, the network of the Battle of the Water Networks II (BWN-II) design competition (five district metered areas and a new zone).
- `anytown`: Anytown, a classic synthetic expansion benchmark (Walski et al., 1987).
- the networks of the two-objective design benchmarks of Wang et al. (2015), with their acronyms: `two_reservoir` (TRN, Gessler 1985), `two_loop` (TLN), `bakryun` (BAK), `new_york_tunnels` (NYT), `blacksburg` (BLA), `hanoi` (HAN), `goyang` (GOY), `fossolo` (FOS), `pescara` (PES), `modena` (MOD) and `balerma` (BIN, the Balerma irrigation network, Almería, Spain). The files of the expansion problems `two_reservoir`, `new_york_tunnels` and `anytown` include the candidate pipes of the design problem, i.e. new pipes and duplicates (parallel pipes) of existing pipes whose diameters are to be chosen, with a placeholder diameter of 0.0001 in the file (given here as NaN); these are marked by the edge property `candidate` (see below): in `two_reservoir`, the five new pipes (marked as new in the file) and the duplicates of three existing pipes, i.e. 8 of its 17 pipes (the Centre for Water Systems also distributed this network without the duplicates, as `gessler1985.inp`); in `new_york_tunnels`, a duplicate of each of the 21 tunnels (the version without duplicates, `nytun.inp`, is otherwise identical); in `anytown`, the six new pipes (marked as new in the file; the duplication of existing pipes, also part of the problem, is not represented). The other networks have no such property: `two_loop` and `hanoi` are designs of whole new networks, in which all pipes have the placeholder diameter; in `bakryun`, nine of the 58 pipes (six of them parallel to existing pipes) are new pipes to be sized, but they cannot be identified from the file, in which all pipes have diameters; in the remaining design benchmarks all pipes are sized, or have fixed diameters; and in `exnet`, the 567 existing pipes considered for duplication are tagged in comments of the file, but the duplicates themselves are not included.
- `bwsn_network_1` and `bwsn_network_2`: the two networks of the Battle of the Water Sensor Networks (BWSN, Ostfeld et al. 2008), a design competition for the placement of contamination warning sensors held at the 8th Water Distribution Systems Analysis Symposium (Cincinnati, 2006), from the archive of the BWSN files distributed by the Centre for Water Systems ("Sensor Placement (BWSN)" on its benchmark page). Network 1 is a hypothetical network with 126 junctions, one reservoir, two tanks, 168 pipes, two pumps and eight valves; Network 2 is based on a real-world system (not identified) and has 12,523 junctions, two reservoirs, two tanks, 14,822 pipes, four pumps and five valves. (The same two networks are also distributed by the University of Kentucky in its "Battle of the Water Network Models" collection, under a CC BY-NC 4.0 license.)

Other files of the collection are not included: the modified and output versions of the Wolf-Cordera Ranch model (`wolf-modified-fig.inp`, `wolf-output-fig.inp`, `bocika-output.inp`) are the same network with 124 artificial tanks connected via flow control valves, added to simulate simultaneous fire flows, and differ among themselves only in pipe diameters; the EXNET file of the Pareto-front benchmarks (`EXN.inp`) is `exnet` with candidate duplicate pipes.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the node ID in the EPANET file.
- (Node) `type`: "junction", "reservoir" or "tank".
- (Node) `elevation`: the elevation of a junction or tank, or the (total) head of a reservoir.
- (Node) `demand`: the base demand of a junction (NaN for reservoirs and tanks).
- (Node) `coordinates`: the $(x, y)$ position of the node in the drawing of the network.
- (Edge) `name`: the link ID.
- (Edge) `type`: "pipe", "check valve pipe", "pump" or "valve".
- (Edge) `length`, `diameter`, `roughness`: the length, diameter and roughness of pipes (NaN for other links; `diameter` is also given for valves, and is NaN for candidate pipes).
- (Edge) `valve_type`: the type of a valve (e.g. "PRV", "TCV").
- (Edge) `candidate` (only in `two_reservoir`, `new_york_tunnels` and `anytown`): true for the candidate pipes of the design problem (new or duplicate pipes, whose `diameter` is NaN, since the file gives only a placeholder), false for the existing links.
