- (Graph) `flow_units`: the flow units of the file ("GPM", "CFS", "LPS", "CMH", ...). Following EPANET's conventions, with US flow units (GPM, CFS) lengths and elevations are in feet and diameters in inches, and with SI flow units (LPS, CMH) lengths and elevations are in meters and diameters in millimeters; demands are in the flow units.[^icon]

[^icon]: Description obtained in part from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.
citations: A. Yazdani, P. Jeffrey, "Complex network analysis of water distribution systems." Chaos 21(1), 016111 (2011)

Q. Wang, M. Guidolin, D. Savic, Z. Kapelan, "Two-objective design of benchmark problems of a water distribution system via MOEAs: Towards the best-known approximation of the true Pareto front." Journal of Water Resources Planning and Management 141(3), 04014060 (2015)
A. Ostfeld et al., "The Battle of the Water Sensor Networks (BWSN): A Design Challenge for Engineers and Algorithms." Journal of Water Resources Planning and Management 134(6), 556-568 (2008)

datasets.name: web_of_life
datasets.description:
The ecological networks of the Web of Life database, developed and maintained by the lab of J. Bascompte (University of Zurich), which compiles species interaction networks from the literature, from its own fieldwork and from its collaborators. There are 321 networks of seven kinds: pollination (174), host-parasite (51), seed dispersal (34), food webs (33), anemone-fish (17), plant-herbivore (7) and plant-ant (5). Each network is named after its Web of Life identifier (e.g. `M_PL_015`), whose prefix gives the kind of interaction: `M_PL` pollination, `M_SD` seed dispersal, `M_PA` plant-ant, `M_AF` anemone-fish (mutualistic); `A_HP` host-parasite, `A_PH` plant-herbivore (antagonistic); `FW` food webs. The data were retrieved from the database's API (all interactions, the species of each network, and the network metadata) in October 2026; the database is updated in place. The metadata list seven further identifiers (`FW_012` to `FW_016`, `M_AF_002` and `M_PL_072`) that have no interactions of their own: they group the networks numbered after them (e.g. `M_AF_002_01` to `M_AF_002_16`), which are included. Conversely, four networks with interactions (`A_PH_001` to `A_PH_003`, plant-herbivore, and `FW_008`, a food web) are missing from the metadata, so that their graph properties other than `network_type` are empty.

Nodes are species (or higher taxa, morphospecies, or groups such as "Detritus" or "Zooplankton"), as listed by the database for each network. In `M_PA_004` (Blüthgen et al. 2004) two plants are listed twice (for their extrafloral and floral nectaries), with interactions that cannot be told apart; each is a single node here, with the sum of the abundances. Except for the food webs, the networks are bipartite and undirected, and an edge connects a plant (or host, or anemone) to an animal (or parasite, or fish) interacting with it: a flower visitor (pollination), a frugivore eating its fruits (seed dispersal), an ant (plant-ant), a herbivore (plant-herbivore), a parasite (host-parasite), or an anemonefish living in it (anemone-fish). The side of each node is given by the property `is_pollinator`, `is_seed_disperser`, `is_ant`, `is_herbivore`, `is_parasite` or `is_fish`, respectively. The food webs are directed: an edge (i, j) indicates that taxon j feeds on taxon i. The networks marked as weighted by the database have the edge property `weight` (whose meaning is given by the graph property `cell_values_description`, e.g. the number of visits, when available); the others record only the presence of the interaction.

Many of these networks are also included in other entries, obtained from other sources: `M_PL_015` is the entry `plant_pol_petanidou` (from the Web of Life), and the following studies are also part of the entry `iwdb` (Interaction Web Database), sometimes with a different subdivision into networks: Arroyo et al. 1982 (`M_PL_001` to `M_PL_003`), Barrett and Helenurm 1987 (`M_PL_004`), Bartomeus et al. 2008 (`M_PL_058`, one network instead of twelve plots), Bezerra et al. 2009 (`M_PL_059`), Clements and Long 1923 (`M_PL_005`), Dupont et al. 2003 (`M_PL_008`), Elberling and Olesen 1999 (`M_PL_009`), Hocking 1968 (`M_PL_014`), Inouye and Pyke 1988 (`M_PL_019`), Kaiser-Bunbury et al. 2010 (`M_PL_060_*`, 24 networks instead of two), Kato et al. 1990 (`M_PL_021`), Kevan 1970 (`M_PL_020`), McMullen 1993 (`M_PL_026`), Medan et al. 2002 (`M_PL_022`, `M_PL_023`), Memmott 1999 (`M_PL_017`), Mosquin and Martin 1967 (`M_PL_024`), Motten 1982 (`M_PL_025`), Olesen et al. 2002 (`M_PL_011`), Ollerton et al. 2003 (`M_PL_013`), Ramírez and Brito 1992 (`M_PL_030`), Robertson 1929 (`M_PL_062`), Schemske et al. 1978 (`M_PL_032`), Small 1976 (`M_PL_033`), Vázquez 2002 (`M_PL_051`, one network instead of eight sites), Blüthgen et al. 2004 (`M_PA_004`), Davidson et al. 1989 (`M_PA_001`), Davidson and Fisher 1991 (`M_PA_002`), Fonseca and Ganade 1996 (`M_PA_003`), Joern 1979 (`A_PH_004`, `A_PH_005`), Leather 1991 (`A_PH_006`, `A_PH_007`), Beehler 1983 (`M_SD_002`), Poulin et al. 1999 (`M_SD_032`, `M_SD_033`), Schleuning et al. 2010 (`M_SD_034`), Snow and Snow 1988 (`M_SD_011`), Sorensen 1981 (`M_SD_025`), Ollerton et al. 2007 (`M_AF_001`), Ricciardi et al. 2010 (`M_AF_002*`), and the stream food webs of Thompson, Townsend and collaborators (`FW_012` to `FW_015*`). They are kept here, since the collection is the dataset.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the taxon, as given by the database.
- (Node) `is_pollinator`, `is_seed_disperser`, `is_ant`, `is_herbivore`, `is_parasite`, `is_fish` (bipartite networks, one of them depending on the kind): whether the node is on the animal (or parasite, or fish) side of the network.
- (Node) `role`: the role of the species in the network as given by the database (e.g. "Plant", "Pollinator", "Host", "Parasite", "Predator", "Prey").
- (Node) `is_resource`: whether the species is a resource (e.g. the host or the prey), as given by the database.
- (Node) `abundance`: the abundance of the species (NaN if not given; its meaning is given by the graph property `abundance_description` when available); only in the 59 networks in which the database gives abundances (not all missing or zero).
- (Node) `resolution`: the taxonomic level to which the taxon was identified ("Species", "Genus", "Family", "Order", "Group", ...; empty if not given).
- (Node) `kingdom`, `order`, `family`: the taxonomy of the taxon (empty if not given).
- (Edge) `weight` (weighted networks only): the strength of the interaction.
- (Graph) `network_type` (the kind of interaction), `author` and `reference` (the source of the data), `location`, `location_address`, `country`, `region`, `latitude` and `longitude` (the location of the study), `cell_values_description` (the meaning of the weights) and `abundance_description` (the meaning of the abundances).
citations: Bascompte Lab, "Web of Life: ecological networks database." University of Zurich (2026)

datasets.name: webkb
datasets.description:
Networks of hyperlinks among web pages of the computer science departments of four U.S. universities (Cornell, Texas, Washington and Wisconsin), from the WebKB project of Carnegie Mellon University, which collected the pages in January 1997 and manually classified them by their content. This version was prepared for the NetKit-SRL toolkit of S. A. Macskassy and F. Provost, and includes only the pages with one of six classes: course, department, faculty, project, staff, or student (the pages of the class "other" are excluded). Nodes are web pages. For each university there are two networks:

- `webkb_<university>_link1`: directed network where an edge $i \to j$ indicates that page $i$ contains hyperlinks to page $j$.
- `webkb_<university>_cocite`: undirected co-citation network, where two pages are connected if they are both linked from at least one common page.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the identifier of the page (e.g. `url-course-cornell-00002`), which includes its class.
- (Edge) `weight`: in the `link1` networks, the number of hyperlinks from page $i$ to page $j$; in the `cocite` networks, the number of pages that link to both $i$ and $j$.
- (Node) `class`: the class of the page (`course`, `department`, `faculty`, `project`, `staff` or `student`).
citations: S. Slattery & M. Craven, "Combining Statistical and Relational Methods for Learning in Hypertext Domains." In Proc. 8th International Conf. on Inductive Logic Programming, 38-52 (1998)

datasets.name: whats_cooking
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of recipes and their ingredients, labelled by cuisine. The recipes are the training set of the 2015 Kaggle competition "What's Cooking?", provided by the recipe website Yummly, in which the cuisine of a recipe was to be predicted from its list of ingredients. Each recipe is connected to the ingredients in its list (an ingredient listed more than once in a recipe is connected to it only once). Ingredients are named as written in the recipes, so the same ingredient can appear under different names (e.g. "salt" and "sea salt"). The data are the version distributed by Amburg, Veldt and Benson.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `is_recipe`: whether the node is a recipe (otherwise it is an ingredient).
- (Node) `name` (ingredients): the name of the ingredient.
- (Node) `cuisine` (recipes): the cuisine of the recipe, one of 20: brazilian, british, cajun_creole, chinese, filipino, french, greek, indian, irish, italian, jamaican, japanese, korean, mexican, moroccan, russian, southern_us, spanish, thai, vietnamese.
citations: I. Amburg, N. Veldt, A. R. Benson, "Clustering in graphs and hypergraphs with categorical edge labels." Proceedings of The Web Conference 2020, 706-717 (2020)

datasets.name: wiki_article_words
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of English Wikipedia articles and the words they contain. The edge weight gives the number of times a word appeared in the connected article.[^icon]
[^icon]: Description obtained from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.
citations: J. Kunegis, " Wikipedia (en)." KONECT, the Koblenz Network Collection (2016)

datasets.name: wiki_categories
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of the articles of the English Wikipedia and the categories they belong to, extracted from the Wikimedia database dumps of 1 October 2026 (tables `page`, `linktarget` and `categorylinks`). Nodes are articles (pages in the main namespace, including redirects that are categorized) and categories, and an edge connects an article to a category that the article is placed in, either directly in its wikitext or through a template. Only articles and categories with at least one such membership are included. Categories are identified by name, and include hidden maintenance categories (e.g. "Articles with short description") as well as categories without a description page. The memberships of categories in other categories (the category hierarchy), and of pages in other namespaces, are not included.

This network replaces an earlier version, of uncertain date, without node names, and with 2,036,440 nodes and 3,795,796 edges.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the article title, or the category name (without the "Category:" prefix).
- (Node) `is_category`: whether the node is a category (otherwise it is an article).
- (Node) `is_redirect`: whether the article is a redirect (false for categories).
- (Edge) `time`: the time when the membership was last updated (Unix time, in seconds).

datasets.name: wiki_cs_links
datasets.description:
Networks of the English Wikipedia articles on computer science, from the dump of October 8, 2008, compiled by J. Tang and colleagues (Tsinghua University) to study the semantics of hyperlinks ("topic distributions over links"), and distributed by AMiner. The data set contains 14,468 articles, starting from "Computer science".

- `links`: hyperlinks between the articles. Nodes are articles, and a directed edge $i \to j$ is a hyperlink from article $i$ (source) to article $j$ (target). Some article pairs are linked several times, kept as parallel edges (25,817 links between 22,432 pairs). Each link has a `label` giving its annotated category, following the specification of the authors: 0, "drill down" (a link from summary information to detailed information, or to a basic theory used in the source); 1, "similar" (a link between pages with similar content); 2, "other"; the meaning of the label 3, used for 1,138 links, is not documented. Articles without links are isolated nodes.
- `words`: a bipartite network of articles and the words of their abstracts. Nodes are articles and words, and an undirected edge connects an article to a word contained in its abstract (263,634 edges between 13,972 articles and 26,093 words).

The data set also lists the words near the anchor text of each link, which are not included here.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `title`: the title of the article (empty for words).
- (Node) `wiki_id` (articles): the identifier of the article in the Wikipedia dump (-1 for words).
- (Edge) `label` (`links` edges): the link category, as above.
- (Node) `is_article` (`words`): whether the node is an article (otherwise it is a word).
- (Node) `word` (`words`): the word (empty for articles).
citations: J. Tang, J. Zhang, J. X. Yu, Z. Yang, K. Cai, R. Ma, L. Zhang, Z. Su, "Topic distributions over links on web." Ninth IEEE International Conference on Data Mining (ICDM), 1010-1015 (2009)

datasets.name: wiki_link_dyn
datasets.description:
The evolving network of hyperlinks between the articles of the Simple English Wikipedia, reconstructed from its complete edit history in the Wikimedia "pages-meta-history" dump of 1 October 2026, which contains the full text of every revision of every page existing at the time of the dump. Nodes are the articles (pages in the main namespace, including redirect pages), and each directed edge $(i,j)$ is an event at which a link from article $i$ to article $j$ was added to (sign $+1$) or removed from (sign $-1$) the wikitext of article $i$, timestamped with the time of the revision. The network is therefore a multigraph, in which the links present in article $i$ at time $t$ are the pairs whose signs up to $t$ sum to one.

The links of each revision were extracted from its wikitext as the targets of `[[...]]` links (after removing section anchors and leading colons, and capitalizing the first letter, as MediaWiki does), and compared with those of the previous revision of the same page: multiple links to the same target count once, and revisions whose text has been hidden are skipped. Only links to pages that exist in the main namespace at the time of the dump are kept, so links to deleted or never created pages ("red links"), to other namespaces (categories, files, etc.) and to other wikis are omitted; links generated by templates are not included, and links to redirects are not resolved to their targets. Deleted pages and deleted revisions are absent from the dump. Articles without any link event are included as isolated nodes.

The static network of the links of the current versions of the pages, from the database tables of the same dumps (and thus including the links generated by templates), is the network `simple` of the entry `wikipedia_link`.

This network replaces an earlier version of the same kind, extracted from the history until September 2011 by J. Preusse et al. (2013), with 100,312 nodes and 1,627,472 edges and no node names.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the article title.
- (Node) `is_redirect`: whether the article is a redirect at the time of the dump.
- (Edge) `time`: the time of the revision (Unix time, in seconds).
- (Edge) `sign`: $+1$ if the link was added, $-1$ if it was removed.
citations: J. Preusse, J. Kunegis, M. Thimm, S. Staab, T. Gottron, "Structural Dynamics of Knowledge Networks." Proceedings of the International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media 7(1), 506-515 (2013)

datasets.name: wiki_norms
datasets.description:
The hyperlink network among the pages of the English Wikipedia that describe its social norms, i.e. its policies, guidelines, essays and proposals, from B. Heaberlin and S. DeDeo. Nodes represent pages in the "Wikipedia:" namespace, and a directed edge from page $i$ to page $j$ means that the text of page $i$ contains at least one hyperlink to page $j$. The pages were collected by following all links within the namespace, starting from the page "Assume good faith", and include only pages that existed on 20 August 2015. Pages that are only lists, or that describe projects, outreach initiatives or noticeboards, were removed, and redirects (e.g. "WP:AGF") were merged with the pages they point to. Links from navigation boxes, infoboxes and other template-generated content were discarded, as well as self-links, so that the remaining links reflect deliberate connections between norms; multiple links between the same pair of pages are counted once. After this filtering, 95 pages have no links.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the title of the page (without the "Wikipedia:" prefix).
- (Node) `creation_date`: the date of creation of the page (UTC).
- (Node) `type`: the classification of the page by the editors (Policy, Guideline, Essay, Proposal, Humor, Convention, Culture, Basic, Information, or Other).
- (Node) `community`: the Louvain community of the page in the giant component, numbered as in the paper (-1 for pages outside the giant component).
- (Node) `ec`: an estimate of the eigenvector centrality of the page, computed as its PageRank (with random jump probability 0.15).
- (Node) `pageviews`: the fraction of the page views of all pages of the network received by the page in July 2015 (from the StatsGrok service).
- (Node) `edits` and `editors`: the number of edits of the page and of distinct editors.
- (Node) `talk_edits` and `talk_editors`: the number of edits of the associated talk page and of distinct editors of it (the two columns are identical in the source data, so the latter likely repeats the former).
- (Node) `size`: the size of the page in bytes.
- (Node) `words`: the number of words of the page used in the topic model.
- (Node) `topics`: the topic distribution of the page in a latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) model with 20 topics, ordered as in the paper (empty for the ten pages without text).

The source data also include a column "Final In Degree", which is zero for all pages and was left out.[^icon]

[^icon]: Description obtained in part from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.
citations: B. Heaberlin, S. DeDeo, "The Evolution of Wikipedia's Norm Network." Future Internet 8(2), 14 (2016)

datasets.name: wiki_rfa
datasets.description:
Network of the votes in the elections for adminship of the English Wikipedia (Requests for Adminship, RfA), from 2003 to May 2013, collected by R. West, H. S. Paskov, J. Leskovec and C. Potts. To become an administrator, a Wikipedia user (or another user on their behalf) submits a request, and members of the community vote in favor, against or neutrally, usually with a short comment. Nodes are users, and a directed edge $i \to j$ is a vote cast by user $i$ in an election of candidate $j$. A user can vote in several elections of the same candidate, so that there can be parallel edges.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the Wikipedia user name. In about 1,700 votes the voter's name is missing in the upstream data (as are the date and the comment); each of these votes is assigned to a separate node with an empty name.
- (Edge) `vote`: the vote: $1$ (support), $0$ (neutral) or $-1$ (oppose).
- (Edge) `result`: the outcome of the election: $1$ (the candidate was promoted) or $-1$ (not promoted).
- (Edge) `year`: the year of the election.
- (Edge) `date`: the date and time of the vote, as text (e.g. `23:13, 19 April 2013`).
- (Edge) `txt`: the comment accompanying the vote, in Wikipedia markup.
citations: R. West, H. S. Paskov, J. Leskovec, and C. Potts, "Exploiting Social Network Structure for Person-to-Person Sentiment Analysis." Trans. of the Assoc. for Comp. Ling. 2, 297-310 (2014). arxiv:1409.2450

datasets.name: wiki_science
datasets.description:
Network of similarities among branches of science, built by A. Calderone in January 2020 from the English Wikipedia. Nodes are the Wikipedia pages listed in the outlines of the natural, formal, social and applied sciences (pages titled "Outline of ..." excluded). The main text of each page was preprocessed (stop-word removal and lemmatization), and the pages were compared by the cosine similarity of their contents. Two pages are connected if their similarity is significantly high, i.e. has a z-score larger than 1.96. Isolated nodes were removed.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the title of the Wikipedia page.
- (Node) `Class`: the branch of science of the page, according to the outline it was taken from: `Natural`, `Formal`, `Social` or `Applied`.
- (Node) `WikipediaUrl`: the URL of the page.
- (Edge) `CosineSimilarity`: the cosine similarity of the contents of the two pages.
citations: A. Calderone, "A Wikipedia Based Map of Science." Figshare (2020)

datasets.name: wiki_talk
datasets.description:
Networks of messages written on user talk pages of the Wikipedias in 28 languages, extracted by J. Sun and J. Kunegis from the Wikipedia dumps at the end of 2015. On Wikipedia, each registered user has a talk page that can be used for discussion with other users. The 28 languages were those with the most articles at the time: Arabic (`ar`), Bengali (`bn`), Breton (`br`), Catalan (`ca`), Welsh (`cy`), German (`de`), Greek (`el`), English (`en`), Esperanto (`eo`), Spanish (`es`), Basque (`eu`), French (`fr`), Galician (`gl`), Haitian Creole (`ht`), Italian (`it`), Japanese (`ja`), Latvian (`lv`), Low German (`nds`), Dutch (`nl`), Occitan (`oc`), Polish (`pl`), Portuguese (`pt`), Russian (`ru`), Slovak (`sk`), Serbian (`sr`), Swedish (`sv`), Vietnamese (`vi`) and Chinese (`zh`), with one network per language.

Nodes are registered users and a directed edge $(i,j)$ indicates that user $i$ wrote a message on the talk page of user $j$, at a given time. The messages range from March 2001 to December 2015. Each message is a separate edge, so a pair of users can be connected by multiple edges, and messages on one's own talk page appear as self-loops. The English network overlaps with the earlier SNAP extractions of the edit history until January 2008, the static `wikipedia-en-talk` and the timestamped `wiki_talk_temporal`. Each user is assigned a role according to their access level in that Wikipedia: administrators (users in the "sysop", "bureaucrat" or "founder" groups), bots (users in a group whose name contains "bot") and normal users (all others).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `user_id`: the user ID in that Wikipedia.
- (Node) `role`: the role of the user, 0 (normal user), 1 (bot) or 2 (administrator); if a user is in groups of several roles, the highest number is given.
- (Edge) `time`: the time of the message, in Unix time.
citations: J. Sun, J. Kunegis, "Wiki-Talk Datasets." Zenodo (2016)

datasets.name: wiki_talk_temporal
datasets.description:
A temporal network of users of the English Wikipedia editing each other's user talk pages, as distributed by SNAP and used by Paranjape, Benson and Leskovec in their study of motifs in temporal networks. Nodes are users, and each directed edge from user u to user v with a timestamp t means that u edited the talk page of v at time t; repeated edits between the same users are separate edges. The data span 2320 days, from August 2001 to January 2008, and were extracted from the Wikipedia edit history used by Leskovec, Huttenlocher and Kleinberg in their study of the Wikipedia promotion process. Edits of users on their own talk page appear as self-loops (about 1.7 million of the edges). This extraction differs from the static `wikipedia-en-talk` network; a later extraction, from the dumps of 2015 (with messages until December 2015), is the network `en` of the entry `wiki_talk`.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the Wikipedia user name.
- (Edge) `time`: the time of the edit (Unix time, in seconds).
citations: A. Paranjape, A. R. Benson, J. Leskovec, "Motifs in Temporal Networks." Proceedings of the Tenth ACM International Conference on Web Search and Data Mining (WSDM), 601-610 (2017)

J. Leskovec, D. Huttenlocher, J. Kleinberg, "Governance in Social Media: A Case Study of the Wikipedia Promotion Process." Proceedings of the International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media (ICWSM) 4(1), 98-105 (2010)

datasets.name: wiki_topcats
datasets.description:
A directed network of hyperlinks between articles of the English Wikipedia, collected in September 2011 and distributed by the Stanford Network Analysis Project (SNAP) as `wiki-topcats`, as a benchmark for clustering with ground-truth communities. The network was constructed by taking the largest strongly connected component of the hyperlink network of Wikipedia, restricting it to the articles in the top categories (those with at least 100 articles), and taking the largest strongly connected component of the result. Nodes are articles, and an edge $i \to j$ means that article $i$ links to article $j$. The categories of the articles (which overlap, since an article can belong to several categories) are given as ground-truth communities; only the top categories are included.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the title of the article.
- (Node) `categories`: the top categories of the article (e.g. "Category:Skin_conditions_resulting_from_physical_factors").
citations: H. Yin, A. R. Benson, J. Leskovec, and D. F. Gleich, "Local Higher-Order Graph Clustering." Proceedings of the 23rd ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining, 555-564 (2017).
C. Klymko, D. F. Gleich, and T. G. Kolda, "Using Triangles to Improve Community Detection in Directed Networks." Proceedings of the ASE BigData Conference (2014).

datasets.name: wiki_users
datasets.description: A network derived from interactions between editors of the English language Wikipedia, as derived from the edit histories of 563 wiki pages related to politics. A positive sign indicates positive links such as trust or similarities, and a negative sign indicates distrust or disagreement. Nodes are users, and an edge represents an interaction between two users (such as text editing, reverts, restores and votes), with `weight` +1 for a positive and -1 for a negative interaction. The edges are directed as in the source data, but the meaning of the edge direction is not documented (KONECT describes the network as undirected).
citations: S. Maniu, T. Abdessalem, and B. Cautis. "Casting a web of trust over Wikipedia: an interaction-based approach." Proc. 20th Internat. Conf. on the World Wide Web (WWW 2011)

datasets.name: wikiconflict
datasets.description:
A network representing editorial interactions among editors of the English Wikipedia. Nodes are editors, and an edge denotes an edit conflict between the two editors. Edge are timestamped and signed. A positive sign indicates the users have agreement on the edit, and the negative sign indicates a disagreement (a reversion) on the edit.[^icon]
[^icon]: Description obtained from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.
citations: U. Brandes et al. "Network Analysis of Collaboration Structure in Wikipedia." Proc. Int. World Wide Web Conference, 731-740 (2009)

datasets.name: wikics
datasets.description:
A network of hyperlinks between the articles of the English Wikipedia about computer science, from the Wiki-CS dataset, a benchmark for node classification. The articles were selected from the Wikipedia dumps of August 2019, based on their categories, which were aggregated to ten branches of computer science (e.g. "Operating systems" or "Computer security") with the category sanitizer of Boldi and Monti (2016), and then cleaned up by hand; articles that would have been assigned to several branches were dropped. Each article is labeled with its branch.

A directed edge from article A to article B means that A links to B. The links are as given by the dataset (in which the benchmark treats them as undirected): an article may link to another one more than once (6,071 repeated links, giving parallel edges), and 520 articles link to themselves.

The node features of the benchmark (averages of the GloVe embeddings of the words of the articles), and the words of the articles themselves, are left out, as are the train, validation and test splits.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `title`: the title of the article.
- (Node) `wikipedia_id`: the page identifier of the article in the English Wikipedia.
- (Node) `branch`: the branch of computer science of the article, e.g. `Computer architecture`.
citations: P. Mernyei, C. Cangea, "Wiki-CS: A Wikipedia-Based Benchmark for Graph Neural Networks." Graph Representation Learning and Beyond workshop, ICML (2020)

datasets.name: wikidata5m
datasets.description:
A knowledge graph of the entities of Wikidata that have a page in the English Wikipedia, from the Wikidata5M dataset, made for the KEPLER model of knowledge embedding and language representation, and used as a benchmark for link prediction. Each node is an entity of Wikidata (e.g. a person, a place, a work or a concept) that has a Wikipedia page, and a directed edge from entity A to entity B is a statement (A, relation, B) of Wikidata between two such entities, with one of 822 relations (Wikidata properties, e.g. `P31`, "instance of", or `P27`, "country of citizenship"). The data come from the Wikidata dump of 2019-07-31 and the English Wikipedia dump of 2019-08-01; the entities without a Wikipedia page, and those with few statements, were left out by the authors.

The triples are given in the "transductive" split of the benchmark (the same entities in the training, validation and test sets), and all of them are included here, with the set as an edge property. The Wikipedia texts of the entities, also part of the dataset, are not included; the "inductive" split, with the same triples split by entity, is also left out. A larger knowledge graph of Wikidata of 2015 is in the entry `ogbl_wikikg2`, and the complete Wikidata in `wikidata`.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `wikidata_id`: the Wikidata identifier of the entity, e.g. `Q42`.
- (Node) `name`: the name of the entity (its first alias in the dataset, usually its English label).
- (Edge) `relation`: the Wikidata property of the relation, e.g. `P31`.
- (Edge) `relation_name`: the name of the relation, e.g. `instance of`.
- (Edge) `split`: the set of the benchmark the triple belongs to: `train`, `valid` or `test`.
citations: X. Wang, T. Gao, Z. Zhu, Z. Zhang, Z. Liu, J. Li, J. Tang, "KEPLER: A Unified Model for Knowledge Embedding and Pre-trained Language Representation." Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics 9, 176-194 (2021)

datasets.name: wikilens_ratings
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of the users of WikiLens and the items they rated, and the network of links among its wiki pages, from the database dump that GroupLens (University of Minnesota) published on 2 February 2008. WikiLens was a research project of GroupLens, a generalized, community-maintained recommender system: a wiki (based on PhpWiki) on which users could define item types (e.g. beers, books, restaurants or films) and categories, add items, and rate them and get recommendations. It ran from 2004 and was taken offline in 2009. The dump contains all the data that could be obtained by crawling the site; private data (user accounts, preferences, logs) were erased from it.

The network `ratings` is bipartite: an edge connects a user to an item they rated, for all 26,937 ratings of the dump, with the rating (from 0 to 5, in half stars) and its time. Each user is identified by their user page and each rated object by its URN; most URNs are those of wiki pages (an item and its page), but a few name other objects (e.g. names in a list or titles of papers), and 10 ratings refer to URN ids that are absent from the dump, whose items have no name. Users are also wiki pages, which can themselves be rated as items; such a page is then both a user node and an item node. The times are given in the dump without a time zone, and are taken to be the local time of the University of Minnesota (US Central time, America/Chicago, with daylight saving time).

The network `links` is directed: nodes are wiki pages and an edge $i \to j$ means that page $i$ links to page $j$, from the link cache of the wiki (7,430 links, including self-links). Only the pages with links are included; 9 links refer to page ids absent from the dump, whose nodes have no name. Many of the dump's other pages are spam or empty, and are left out.

The network `ratings` has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the user page, or of the item (its wiki page name, or its URN if it is not a wiki page; empty if unknown).
- (Node) `is_user`: whether the node is a user (otherwise an item).
- (Node) `urn`: the URN of the item (empty for users).
- (Node) `category`: the categories (item types) of the page of the item or user (e.g. `Movie`, `Book`, `Beer`, `User`).
- (Edge) `rating`: the rating, from 0 to 5.
- (Edge) `dimension`: the dimension of the rating (0 for all ratings but one, of dimension 5).
- (Edge) `item_version`: the version of the item's wiki page that was rated (-1 if unknown).
- (Edge) `time`: the time of the rating, in Unix time.

The network `links` has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the wiki page (empty if unknown).
- (Node) `category`: the categories of the page.
- (Node) `hits`: the number of visits of the page recorded by the wiki.
citations: D. Frankowski, S. K. Lam, S. Sen, F. M. Harper, S. Yilek, M. Cassano, J. Riedl, "Recommenders everywhere: the WikiLens community-maintained recommender system." Proceedings of the 2007 International Symposium on Wikis (WikiSym), 47-60 (2007).

datasets.name: wikilinkgraphs
datasets.description:
Yearly snapshots of the networks of links between the articles of the nine largest language editions of Wikipedia (as of 2018), German (`de`), English (`en`), Spanish (`es`), French (`fr`), Italian (`it`), Dutch (`nl`), Polish (`pl`), Russian (`ru`) and Swedish (`sv`), from the WikiLinkGraphs dataset of C. Consonni, D. Laniado and A. Montresor. The authors processed the complete edit history dumps of Wikipedia (of 1 March 2018), taking for each page its last revision before 1 March of each year from 2001 to 2018, and extracted the links written in its wikitext (of the form `[[target]]`).

Nodes are pages of the main namespace (articles), and a directed edge from page A to page B means that the snapshot of A contains a link to B (multiple links from A to B count once). Unlike the links recorded by MediaWiki, the links generated by templates are not included, so that the networks contain only the links added intentionally by the editors. Links to redirect pages were resolved to the articles they redirect to (following the history of the redirects); the redirect pages themselves remain as nodes, with a single outgoing edge to their target and no incoming edges (so that the English network of 2018 has 13.6 million nodes, while the English Wikipedia had 5.6 million articles at the time). Links to pages that did not exist at the time of the snapshot ("red links") and to pages outside the main namespace are not included, and only the pages with some link (incoming or outgoing) are nodes of the networks. Self-loops (pages linking to themselves) are present.

The networks are named by the language code and year of the snapshot, from `de-2002` to `sv-2018`. The snapshots of 2001 are left out for all languages except English, and those of 2002 for Italian and Russian, since they contain no links. The networks of the same language share the page identifiers, so that the nodes of the snapshots can be matched.

Related entries: `wikipedia_link` has the current links (including those generated by templates) of 168 language editions, from the database dumps of 2026; `wikipedia_links_2013` has the links of five language editions in 2013, and of the English Wikipedia yearly from 2015 to 2025, from the Laboratory for Web Algorithmics; `wiki_link_dyn` and `nlwiki_link_intervals` have the additions and removals of links over time of the Simple English and Dutch Wikipedias.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `page_id`: the identifier of the article in its Wikipedia (as assigned by MediaWiki).
- (Node) `title`: the title of the article (at the time of the snapshot).
citations: C. Consonni, D. Laniado, A. Montresor, "WikiLinkGraphs: A Complete, Longitudinal and Multi-Language Dataset of the Wikipedia Link Networks." Proceedings of the International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media 13, 598-607 (2019)

datasets.name: wikipedia-en-talk
datasets.description: Communication network of the English Wikipedia, from the complete edit history of Wikipedia from its beginning until January 2008, distributed by the Stanford Network Analysis Project (SNAP). Nodes are Wikipedia users, and a directed edge $i \to j$ indicates that user $i$ edited the user talk page of user $j$ at least once. User talk pages are used by users to communicate with each other, e.g. by leaving messages. The network has 2,394,385 nodes and 5,021,410 edges, and no node or edge properties. A timestamped extraction of the same edit history, in which each edit is a separate edge, is the entry `wiki_talk_temporal`, and a later extraction from the dumps of 2015, in which each message is a separate edge, is the network `en` of the entry `wiki_talk`.
citations: J. Leskovec, D. Huttenlocher, and J. Kleinberg, "Signed networks in social media." Proc. Conf. on Human Factors in Computing Sys. (CHI), 1361-1370 (2010).

datasets.name: wikipedia_article_networks
datasets.description:
Networks of articles of the English Wikipedia on three topics (chameleons, crocodiles and squirrels), collected in December 2018 by B. Rozemberczki and collaborators (MUSAE study) for benchmarks of node embedding and regression methods. Nodes are articles, and an undirected edge connects two articles that link to each other. The article titles were replaced by consecutive indices. Each article has a list of binary features, each marking the presence of an informative noun in its text (only the indices of the features are given, not the nouns), and its average monthly traffic between October 2017 and November 2018, which is the target of the regression task proposed with the data.

There are three networks, `chameleon`, `crocodile` and `squirrel`. The upstream edge lists contain some pairs of articles twice, once in each direction; they are merged into a single undirected edge, which gives the numbers of edges stated by the authors. A few articles are linked to themselves (self-loops), as given in the data.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `traffic`: the average monthly traffic of the article (October 2017 to November 2018).
- (Node) `features`: the indices of the article's binary (noun) features.
citations: B. Rozemberczki, C. Allen, and R. Sarkar, "Multi-scale attributed node embedding." Journal of Complex Networks 9(2), cnab014 (2021).

datasets.name: wikipedia_citations
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of the articles of the English Wikipedia and the works (scholarly articles, books, ...) they cite, from the Wikipedia Citations dataset of H. Singh, R. West and G. Colavizza. The authors extracted all the citations made with citation templates (`cite journal`, `cite book`, `cite news`, `citation`, ... 35 templates in all) from the wikitext of the articles in the English Wikipedia dump of May 2020, 29.3 million citations in total, together with the identifiers given in them (DOI, PMID, PMC, ISBN, arXiv, JSTOR, OCLC, ...).

A directed edge from an article to a work is a citation. Only the citations that carry an identifier of the cited work can be linked to the same work cited elsewhere, so only these are included (3.8 million citations); the others (mostly of news and web pages, identified only by their title or URL) are left out. Each work is identified by the first identifier available among, in this order: DOI, PMID, PMC, arXiv, Bibcode, JSTOR, ISBN, OCLC, LCCN, Open Library, ASIN, MR, zbMATH, JFM, SSRN, OSTI, RFC, ISMN and Usenet id. DOIs are compared in lower case, and ISBNs as 13-digit numbers (ISBN-10s are converted, and hyphens removed). Citations with only an ISSN (which identifies a journal, not a work) are left out. A work cited with different identifiers in different articles (e.g. only a PMID in one, and a DOI in another) appears as several nodes. The candidate DOIs found by the authors for some citations without identifiers by searching Crossref are not used. The network is a multigraph, since an article may cite the same work several times.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `is_article`: whether the node is a Wikipedia article (otherwise it is a cited work).
- (Node) `title`: the title of the Wikipedia article, or of the cited work (as written in the first citation of it).
- (Node) `id_type` (works): the type of the identifier of the work, e.g. `DOI`, `PMID`, `ISBN`.
- (Node) `id` (works): the identifier of the work (normalized as described above).
- (Node) `identifiers` (works): all the identifiers given in the first citation of the work, e.g. `{PMID=20784713, PMC=2282302, DOI=10.1136/bmj.1.4286.261}`.
- (Edge) `template`: the citation template used, e.g. `cite journal`.
citations: H. Singh, R. West, G. Colavizza, "Wikipedia citations: A comprehensive data set of citations with identifiers extracted from English Wikipedia." Quantitative Science Studies 2(1), 1-19 (2021)

datasets.name: wikipedia_discussions_de
datasets.description:
Directed networks of replies between the users of the German Wikipedia in the discussion threads of the talk pages of its articles, extracted from two dumps of the current versions of all pages: `2015`, from the dump of 11 February 2015, and `2026`, from the dump ("MediaWiki Content File Export") of 1 October 2026, which reflects the state of the talk pages at that time. Each node is a registered user, and each directed edge from user A to user B is a comment of A in reply to a comment of B, so that users who replied to each other several times are connected by multiple edges; users may reply to themselves.

Only the talk pages of articles (namespace "Diskussion", including their archive subpages) are considered, not those of users, projects, templates, etc. The replies are inferred from the wikitext of the current version of each page with the method of N. Geilen and J. Kunegis (University of Koblenz–Landau), reimplemented here: each section heading starts a new thread; within a thread, a comment is a line that starts with colons (its indentation level is the number of colons), that starts with "--" (taking the indentation level of the previous line), or that contains a link to a user page (`[[Benutzer:...]]`, `[[Benutzerin:...]]` or `[[User:...]]`). The author of a comment is the user of the last such link of its line (the signature), and its date the last date in the format of the signatures of the German Wikipedia ("12:34, 5. Okt. 2010") of that line; a comment without a date takes that of the closest preceding comment of lower indentation that has one. Comments without an author (including those signed by unregistered users, identified by their IP addresses, and those marked as unsigned with the templates `{{unsigned}}` and `{{unsigniert}}`), without a date, or dated before 15 January 2001 or after the date of the dump are left out. Each remaining comment of a thread, except the first, is a reply to the closest preceding remaining comment of the thread with a lower indentation level, or with indentation level zero. Since only the current versions of the pages are used, discussions removed from the talk pages (and not archived) are not included, and since comments are recognized from their signatures, some replies are missed or attributed approximately.

User names are normalized as MediaWiki page titles (underscores replaced by spaces, first letter capitalized), so that different spellings of the link to the same user page give the same node.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the user name.
- (Edge) `time`: the time of the reply, from its signature (Unix time; the signatures give it to the minute, in German time, which is converted to UTC).
- (Edge) `inferred_time`: whether the comment had no date of its own, so that its time is that of the closest preceding comment of lower indentation.
- (Edge) `page`: the title of the talk page.
- (Edge) `thread`: the title of the section (empty for comments before the first section heading of the page).

datasets.name: wikipedia_growth
datasets.description:
Growth of the network of hyperlinks among the articles of the English Wikipedia, extracted by A. Mislove from the complete edit history of the English Wikipedia as of 6 April 2007. For each link present in the final snapshot, the time when the link was first created was determined from the edit history, which removes the effect of vandalism, where links are temporarily removed and added back. Links to redirect pages were treated as links to the destination of the redirect, with the time of the original link. Links that were removed before the final snapshot are not included. The link creation times range from February 2001 to April 2007.

Nodes are Wikipedia pages and a directed edge $(i,j)$ indicates that page $i$ links to page $j$. The page titles are not included; the nodes are identified only by anonymized IDs.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `page_id`: the page ID in the source data.
- (Edge) `time`: the time when the link was first created, in Unix time.
citations: A. Mislove, "Online social networks: measurement, analysis, and applications to distributed information systems." PhD Thesis, Rice University (2009)

datasets.name: wikipedia_link
datasets.description:
Networks of hyperlinks between the articles of 168 language editions of Wikipedia, named by their language code (e.g. `en`, `de`, `simple` for the Simple English Wikipedia). They were extracted from the Wikimedia database dumps of 1 October 2026 (tables `page`, `pagelinks` and `linktarget`). Nodes are the pages in the main (article) namespace, including redirect pages, and a directed edge $(i,j)$ means that page $i$ contains a link to page $j$ (multiple links between the same pair of pages count once). The links are those recorded by MediaWiki for the current version of each page, which include the links generated by templates. Links to pages that do not exist ("red links") and to pages in other namespaces are omitted. A redirect page has a single outgoing edge, to the page it redirects to, and links to a redirect are not resolved to its target. Pages without any links are included as isolated nodes.

For the Simple English Wikipedia, the evolving network of link additions and removals, reconstructed from the full edit history of the same dumps (without the links generated by templates), is in the entry `wiki_link_dyn`.

These networks replace an earlier version extracted from the dumps of 2016, which had no node names and omitted isolated pages.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the page title.
- (Node) `is_redirect`: whether the page is a redirect.
- (Node) `length`: the length of the page text in bytes.

datasets.name: wikipedia_links_2013
datasets.description:
Directed networks of hyperlinks among the articles of five Wikipedia editions, English (`en`), German (`de`), French (`fr`), Italian (`it`) and Spanish (`es`), as of late February 2013, and yearly snapshots of the English Wikipedia from 2015 to 2025 (`en-2015` to `en-2025`; as of mid-year, according to LAW, for 2015 to 2023, while the pages of 2024 and 2025 give no date), extracted and distributed by the Laboratory for Web Algorithmics (LAW). Nodes are articles, and a directed edge from one article to another indicates that the first contains a link to the second. Redirects were resolved when computing the links (a link to a redirect points to its target article), and redirect pages are not part of the graphs; namespaced pages (e.g. `Template:...` or `Category:...`) are not included either. Self-loops (articles linking to themselves) are present.

Sizes (articles, links): `en` 4,206,785, 101,355,853; `de` 1,532,354, 36,722,696; `fr` 1,352,053, 34,378,431; `it` 1,016,867, 25,619,926; `es` 972,933, 23,041,488. The yearly snapshots of the English Wikipedia: `en-2015` 4,853,050, 106,314,263; `en-2016` 5,096,287, 113,095,771; `en-2017` 5,409,498, 122,008,994; `en-2018` 5,616,717, 128,835,798; `en-2019` 5,839,060, 135,700,782; `en-2020` 6,047,510, 142,691,609; `en-2021` 6,261,502, 150,124,927; `en-2022` 6,492,490, 159,047,205; `en-2023` 6,625,370, 165,206,104; `en-2024` 6,790,971, 172,762,484; `en-2025` 6,961,383, 181,022,291. The node order differs between the snapshots.

A network of the links of the English Wikipedia from a slightly later dump (March/April 2013), extracted by DBpedia without resolving redirects, including pages in other namespaces and missing pages, and with link multiplicities, is in the entry `dbpedia_link`.

The node order is the one of the distributed (LLP-permuted) graphs. Vertex property: `title`, the title of the article. The data were collected with support of the EU-FET grant NADINE (GA 288956).
citations: P. Boldi and S. Vigna, "The WebGraph framework I: compression techniques." Proceedings of the 13th International Conference on World Wide Web (WWW 2004), 595-602 (2004).

P. Boldi, M. Rosa, M. Santini, and S. Vigna, "Layered label propagation: a multiresolution coordinate-free ordering for compressing social networks." Proceedings of the 20th International Conference on World Wide Web (WWW 2011), 587-596 (2011).

datasets.name: wikispeedia
datasets.description:
Hyperlinks between the articles of a condensed version of the English Wikipedia (the 2007 Wikipedia for Schools, 4,604 articles), and the paths along which people navigated them in the online game Wikispeedia, collected by R. West and collaborators. In the game, a player is given a source and a target article and has to reach the target by clicking only on the links of the articles, as fast as possible. The data contain 51,318 finished and 24,875 unfinished games, played between August 2008 and January 2014.

There are two networks, whose nodes are the same 4,604 articles:

- `links`: the directed hyperlink network; an edge points from an article to an article it links to. 110 articles link to themselves (self-loops).
- `navigation`: the directed network of the clicks made by the players, aggregated over all games, finished or not; an edge points from an article to an article the players went to from it by clicking a link, weighted by the number of such clicks. The players could also go back to the previous article (a "back click"); back clicks (33,468) are not edges, but they determine the article from which the next click is made. In 146 clicks, the players went along a link that is not in the hyperlink network.

Left out are the individual games: their (hashed) players, start times, durations, the difficulty ratings given by the players, and the reasons why unfinished games ended. The matrix of shortest-path distances provided with the data, which can be computed from the `links` network, is also left out. The targets of 29 unfinished games are not among the articles; they are not counted in `targets`.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the title of the article (with underscores instead of spaces, as given).
- (Node) `categories`: the hierarchical categories of the article (e.g. "subject.Science.Biology"), as given (some articles have none).
- (Node) `sources`, `targets` (`navigation`): the number of games (finished or not) whose source and target was the article.
- (Edge) `count` (`navigation`): the number of clicks from one article to the other, in all games.
- (Edge) `count_finished` (`navigation`): the number of those in finished games.
- (Edge) `is_link` (`navigation`): whether the clicked link is in the `links` network.
citations: R. West and J. Leskovec, "Human wayfinding in information networks." Proceedings of the 21st International Conference on World Wide Web (WWW), 619-628 (2012).

R. West, J. Pineau, and D. Precup, "Wikispeedia: An Online Game for Inferring Semantic Distances between Concepts." Proceedings of the 21st International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI), 1598-1603 (2009).

datasets.name: wikitree
datasets.description:
Network of family relationships among the profiles of WikiTree, a collaborative online genealogy website, collected by M. Fire and Y. Elovici, who used it to study the lifespans of people and their relatives. Nodes are profiles of persons (anonymized), and directed edges are relationships between them (the meaning of the edge direction is not documented). The network has about 1.4 million nodes and 9.2 million edges.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the anonymized profile identifier.
- (Edge) `type`: the type of the relationship, coded as an integer from 0 to 3 (stored as a string, since 1,066 edges have no type, given by an empty string). The meaning of the codes is not documented in the upstream data (the cited paper analyzes parent–child and spouse relationships).
citations: M. Fire, & Y. Elovici, "Data mining of online genealogy datasets for revealing lifespan patterns in human population." ACM Transactions on Intelligent Systems and Technology (TIST) 6(2), 28 (2015)

datasets.name: windsurfers
datasets.description:
Interpersonal contacts among 43 windsurfers on a beach in southern California, studied by L. C. Freeman, S. C. Freeman and A. G. Michaelson in the fall of 1986. The windsurfing community was fairly clearly divided into at least two sub-communities, whose members tended to limit their interactions to fellow group members. The 43 individuals were observed for 31 days, and all interpersonal contacts among them were recorded. After the end of the observations, all of them were interviewed about their perception of social affiliations: each subject performed a sequence of card sorting tasks that assigned an index of the perceived closeness of every individual on the beach to each of the other individuals. The data were distributed by L. C. Freeman on his network data page at the University of California, Irvine (no longer online), from which this version was obtained via the Internet Archive.

The two relations are given as separate networks, with the same nodes in the same order:

- `interaction`: an undirected edge (i, j) indicates that individuals i and j were observed interacting. (In the source matrix, the row of the last individual is empty, although the corresponding column is not; the matrix is symmetrized here.)
- `closeness`: an undirected edge (i, j) indicates a nonzero perceived closeness between i and j, as aggregated in the source matrix (how the closeness indices of the different subjects were combined is not documented). This network is almost complete.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `diagonal` (`interaction`): the diagonal entry of the interaction matrix (its meaning is not documented).
- (Edge) `weight` (`interaction`): the number of observed interactions.
- (Edge) `weight` (`closeness`): the perceived closeness (between 0.333 and 1).
citations: L. Freeman, S. Freeman, & A. Michaelson, "On human social intelligence." J. Social and Biological Structures 11(4), 415-425 (1988)
L. C. Freeman, S. C. Freeman, A. G. Michaelson, "How humans see social groups: A test of the Sailer-Gaulin models." Journal of Quantitative Anthropology 1, 229-238 (1989)

datasets.name: wiod
datasets.description:
Yearly networks of the flows of goods and services between the industries of 43 countries and a model of the rest of the world, from the World Input-Output Tables (WIOT) of the 2016 release of the World Input-Output Database (WIOD), for the years 2000 to 2014, one network per year in current prices (`2000`, ..., `2014`), and one per year in previous year's prices (`pyp_2001`, ..., `pyp_2014`). The tables were compiled from national supply and use tables, national accounts and international trade statistics, harmonized and linked into a single world table. Each node is an industry (one of 56 sectors of the ISIC Rev. 4 classification) of a country (28 EU countries, 15 other major economies, and the rest of the world, `ROW`), and a directed edge $(i, j)$ means that industry $j$ used goods or services produced by industry $i$ as intermediate inputs in that year, weighted by their value, in millions of US dollars at basic prices: at current prices, or, in the `pyp_<year>` networks, at the prices of the previous year (e.g. the flows of 2014 at the prices of 2013). Self-loops are the use of an industry's output by the same industry. Pairs without flows (zeros in the tables) are not connected.

The tables in previous year's prices separate the changes of the flows' volumes from the changes of prices: comparing the table of a year in previous year's prices with the table of the previous year in current prices gives the growth in volume. According to the note on their construction included with the release (written for the 2014 release), they were derived from the tables in current prices with deflators of gross output and value added by industry (from the socio-economic accounts) and of final demand (from national accounts), by a generalized RAS method that scales the rows and columns of each table to the deflated totals, so that each flow has its own implicit deflator. There is no table in previous year's prices for 2000.

The data are the tables in R format (`WIOTS_in_R.zip`) of the release, and the tables in previous year's prices, which are only available as Excel binary spreadsheets (`WIOTS_PYP_in_EXCEL.zip`, read in the same way; a few empty cells in the rows of totals are read as zeros, and the rows of spreadsheet errors below the tables are ignored). The final use of the products of each industry (by households, non-profit institutions, governments, gross fixed capital formation and changes in inventories, of each country) is not included as edges; its total is a node property. The national input-output tables, the supply and use tables and the socio-economic accounts of the release are not included.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `year`: graph property, the year of the flows.
- (Node) `name`: the country and the sector code, e.g. `DEU C29`.
- (Node) `country`: the three-letter code of the country (`ROW` for the rest of the world).
- (Node) `sector`: the code of the sector (e.g. `C29`).
- (Node) `sector_name`: the description of the sector (e.g. `Manufacture of motor vehicles, trailers and semi-trailers`).
- (Node) `gross_output`: the output of the industry at basic prices (row `GO` of the table).
- (Node) `value_added`: the value added at basic prices (row `VA`).
- (Node) `intermediate_consumption`: the total intermediate consumption of the industry (row `II_fob`).
- (Node) `taxes_less_subsidies`: the taxes less subsidies on products used by the industry (row `TXSP`).
- (Node) `transport_margins`: the international transport margins (row `IntTTM`).
- (Node) `final_use`: the total final use of the products of the industry, by all countries (the sum of the final use columns).
- (Edge) `weight`: the value of the flow, in millions of US dollars (at current prices, or at previous year's prices in the `pyp_<year>` networks; the node properties of values are in the same prices).
citations: M. P. Timmer, E. Dietzenbacher, B. Los, R. Stehrer, G. J. de Vries, "An Illustrated User Guide to the World Input-Output Database: the Case of Global Automotive Production." Review of International Economics 23(3), 575-605 (2015)
WIOD, "World Input-Output Database 2016 Release, 2000-2014." DataverseNL, V2.1 (2025)

datasets.name: wolfe_primates
datasets.description:
Interactions and kinship among a troop of 20 monkeys, observed in the wild by L. Wolfe during 3 months, as they sported by a river in Ocala, Florida (USA). The data were used, e.g., by S. P. Borgatti and M. G. Everett to illustrate core/periphery structures. The data were distributed in UCINET format (from the UCINET data collection of S. P. Borgatti, M. G. Everett and L. C. Freeman) on the Pajek datasets page of V. Batagelj and A. Mrvar, from which this version was obtained.

- `presence`: joint presence at the river, coded as an interaction and summed within all pairs (WOLFN).
- `kin`: the putative kin relationships among the animals (WOLFK), as directed edges as in the rows and columns of the source matrix (the direction is not further documented; e.g. animal 18 may be the granddaughter of 19).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the identification number of the animal.
- (Node) `sex`: "male" or "female".
- (Node) `age`: the age in years.
- (Node) `rank`: the rank of the animal in the troop.
- (Edge) `weight` (`presence` only): the number of joint presences at the river.
citations: S. P. Borgatti, M. G. Everett, "Models of core/periphery structures." Social Networks 21(4), 375-395 (2000)
S. P. Borgatti, M. G. Everett, L. C. Freeman, "UCINET for Windows: Software for Social Network Analysis." Analytic Technologies, Harvard, MA (2002)

datasets.name: word_adjacency
datasets.description:
Word adjacency networks of texts in four languages, from the collection of networks of U. Alon's lab used by R. Milo et al. to study the local structure (network motifs) of networks from different domains. Nodes are words, and a directed edge $i \to j$ indicates that word $j$ directly follows word $i$ at least once in the text.

- `darwin`: an English text by C. Darwin.
- `french`, `spanish`, `japanese`: texts in French, Spanish and Japanese.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the numerical identifier of the word in the upstream file. The words themselves are not included.
citations: R. Milo. et al., "Superfamilies of Evolved and Designed Networks." Science (2004)

datasets.name: word_assoc
datasets.description:
A network of word associations from the Edinburgh Associative Thesaurus (EAT), a set of empirical word association norms collected by George Kiss and collaborators between June 1968 and May 1971. Subjects, mostly undergraduates from a wide range of British universities (aged 17 to 22), were shown a stimulus word and asked to give the first word that came to mind. Each stimulus word was presented to 100 different subjects, each of whom received 100 words. The network was grown from a nucleus set of words: the responses to these were used as new stimuli, and so on, about three times, until 8,400 stimulus words had been used. The data were obtained from the version of the EAT distributed by the Rutherford Appleton Laboratory (derived from the MRC Psycholinguistic Database version), from its stimulus–response file.

Nodes are words (or short phrases, as given by the subjects; words longer than 19 characters were truncated, with a `%` as 20th character; the empty word represents blank responses), and a directed edge points from a stimulus word to a response given to it. The file contains 8,210 stimuli; the last line of the file lists a response without its stimulus word, and is ignored. Self-loops denote stimulus words given as their own response.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the word.
- (Node) `stimulus`: whether the word was used as a stimulus.
- (Edge) `count`: the number of subjects who gave the response to the stimulus.
citations: G. R. Kiss, C. Armstrong, R. Milroy, J. Piper, "An associative thesaurus of English and its computer analysis." In A. J. Aitken, R. W. Bailey, N. Hamilton-Smith (Eds.), The Computer and Literary Studies, 153-165. Edinburgh University Press (1973)

datasets.name: word_assoc_usf
datasets.description:
A directed network of free word associations, from the University of South Florida (USF) free association norms, collected by D. L. Nelson, C. L. McEvoy and T. A. Schreiber from 1973 onwards with more than 6,000 participants in the United States, and made available in 1998. Participants were given a printed cue word and asked to write the first word that came to mind that was meaningfully related or strongly associated to it; each cue was normed by a group of about 150 participants (each participant saw at most about 100 cues). Nodes are words (10,617 words, of which 5,018 were normed as cues), and a directed edge from a cue to a target indicates that the target was given as a response to the cue by at least two participants (responses given by a single participant are not included in the norms). There are 72,176 cue-target pairs, including 4 in which a cue was given as its own response (self-loops).

Edge properties (as in the "Appendix A" files of the norms):

- `group_size`: number of participants in the group that normed the cue (#G).
- `n_responses`: number of participants that produced the target in response to the cue (#P).
- `fsg`: forward (cue-to-target) strength, i.e. `n_responses / group_size`.
- `bsg`: backward (target-to-cue) strength, the forward strength of the reverse pair (zero if the target did not produce the cue; NaN if the target was not normed).
- `msg`: mediated (two-step) strength, the sum over mediating words m of the products of the cue-to-m and m-to-target strengths (NaN if the target was not normed).
- `osg`: overlapping associate strength, the sum over the associates shared by the cue and the target of the products of their strengths to them (NaN if the target was not normed).
- `n_mediators`, `n_mediators_unnormed`: number of mediating words, and of potential mediators that were not normed (so that `msg` may be underestimated).
- `n_overlaps`, `n_overlaps_unnormed`: number of associates shared by cue and target, and of shared associates that were not normed.

Vertex properties (word attributes, available only for the normed words, otherwise they are -1, NaN or empty):

- `word`: the word.
- `normed`: whether the word was normed as a cue.
- `set_size`: number of different responses given by two or more participants to the word.
- `frequency`: printed frequency of the word, from the Kučera and Francis (1967) norms (a few very frequent words, such as "A", have the value 9999).
- `concreteness`: concreteness rating (1 to 7), mostly from the Paivio, Yuille and Madigan (1968) or Toglia and Battig (1978) norms.
- `homograph`: whether the word is (likely) a homograph, given as the initial of the source of homograph norms (empty if not a homograph).
- `part_of_speech`: part of speech of the first dictionary entry of the word (N: noun, V: verb, AJ: adjective, AD: adverb, P: pronoun, PP: preposition, I: interjection, C: conjunction).
- `mean_connectivity`: mean number of connections among the associates of the word.
- `resonance_probability`: fraction of the associates of the word that produce the word as an associate.
- `resonance_strength`: sum over associates of the products of the word-to-associate and associate-to-word strengths.
- `use_code`: 1 if all important associates of the word were normed (recommended for experiments), 0 otherwise.

A version of this network without weights or attributes (and without the self-loops) is also distributed by the Laboratory for Web Algorithmics as `wordassociation-2011`.
citations: D. L. Nelson, C. L. McEvoy, and T. A. Schreiber, "The University of South Florida free association, rhyme, and word fragment norms." Behavior Research Methods, Instruments, & Computers 36(3), 402-407 (2004).

datasets.name: wordnet
datasets.description:
A network of English words and the lexical and semantic relationships between them, from WordNet 3.1 (released in 2011), the lexical database of English developed at Princeton University. WordNet groups nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs into sets of synonyms (synsets), each expressing a distinct concept, which are linked by semantic relations (e.g. hypernymy, meronymy or entailment); some relations (e.g. antonymy or derivation) instead link individual words of two synsets. Each node is a word (a lemma, which can be a multi-word expression such as "New York"; different capitalizations are different words), and an undirected edge connects two words if they are synonyms (members of the same synset), if their synsets are related by a semantic relation, or if they are directly related by a lexical relation. All relations of the database are included. Words that occur only in a synset of their own and without relations are not part of the network.

This network replaces an earlier version built from the RDF version of WordNet 3.1, which is no longer available; this version is built in the same way from the original WordNet 3.1 database files, and has about 2% more nodes and 5% more edges than the earlier one.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the word.
- (Node) `pos`: the list of its parts of speech (`noun`, `verb`, `adjective`, `adverb`).
- (Node) `senses`: the number of synsets that contain it.
- (Edge) `relations`: the list of the relations between the two words (`synonym` for words in the same synset; otherwise the WordNet pointer types, e.g. `hypernym`, `hyponym`, `antonym`, `derivationally related form`, `similar to`, `member meronym`, `domain of synset (topic)`). Since WordNet records most relations in both directions, both a relation and its inverse (e.g. `hypernym` and `hyponym`) usually appear, and the direction of a relation is not recorded.
citations: G. A. Miller, "WordNet: A Lexical Database for English." Communications of the ACM 38(11), 39-41 (1995)
C. Fellbaum (ed.), "WordNet: An Electronic Lexical Database." MIT Press (1998)

datasets.name: world_cities
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of 100 global advanced producer service firms and the 315 cities in which they have offices, from the GaWC (Globalization and World Cities) research network, data set 11, produced by P. J. Taylor and G. Catalano and used as the empirical basis for measuring the world city network. The data were collected in 2000. All firms supply advanced producer services (accountancy, advertising, banking/finance, insurance, law and management consultancy) through offices in at least 15 cities, including at least one in each of Pacific Asia, western Europe and northern America. An edge connects a firm to a city in which it has an office, weighted by the service value, which indicates the importance of the city in the office network of the firm, on a scale from 1 to 5 (cities without an office of the firm, with value 0, have no edge). The data were converted into Pajek format by V. Batagelj (2006). The data were distributed in Pajek format on the Pajek datasets page of V. Batagelj and A. Mrvar, from which this version was obtained.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the city or firm.
- (Node) `is_city`: whether the node is a city (otherwise a firm).
- (Node) `sector`: the sector of the firm (0 for cities, 1: accountancy, 2: advertising, 3: banking/finance, 4: insurance, 5: law, 6: management consultancy).
- (Edge) `weight`: the service value of the city for the firm (1 to 5).
citations: P. J. Taylor, "World City Network: A Global Urban Analysis." Routledge, London (2004)
P. J. Taylor, G. Catalano, D. R. F. Walker, "Measurement of the World City Network." Urban Studies 39(13), 2367-2376 (2002)

datasets.name: world_cup_players
datasets.description:
The international market of soccer players, as seen through the 22 national teams that participated in the 1998 FIFA World Cup in France, compiled by L. Krempel. Players of a national team often have contracts with clubs in other countries; the members of the 22 teams had contracts in 35 countries in total. A directed edge points from the country of a national team to a country in which some of its players had contracts (i.e. the countries "exporting" and "importing" players), weighted by the number of such players. The network is very asymmetric: some countries only export players, and others only import them. The data were distributed in Pajek format on the Pajek datasets page of V. Batagelj and A. Mrvar, from which this version was obtained.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the three-letter code of the country.
- (Edge) `weight`: the number of players of the national team with contracts in the target country.
citations: L. Krempel, "World Soccer Data Paris 1998." Data presented at the Dagstuhl seminar on Link Analysis and Visualization (2001)

datasets.name: world_languages
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of countries and territories and their official languages, from the "World Languages" dataset of the University of Groningen, compiled from the CIA World Factbook of 2015 and distributed by Resource Watch (dataset soc.071). An official language is a language given a special legal status in a country and used in administrative settings by its government. The data list up to three official languages for each of 234 countries, dependencies and other territories; each country is connected to its first, second and third official languages, when present. Some language entries are generic designations, e.g. "Indigenous", "Creole" or "Regional Chinese".

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the country or territory, or of the language.
- (Node) `is_language`: whether the node is a language (otherwise a country or territory).
- (Node) `sovereignty` (countries): the sovereign state the territory belongs to.
- (Node) `type` (countries): the political status of the territory ("Sovereign country", "Country", "Dependency", "Disputed" or "Indeterminate").
- (Node) `world_language` (countries): the category of world language(s) among English, French, Arabic, Spanish, Portuguese, Chinese and Russian that are official in the country, as given in the source (e.g. "English_French", or "Other").
- (Edge) `rank`: the rank of the official language in the source (1, 2 or 3, for the first, second and third official language).
citations: University of Groningen, "World Languages." University of Groningen Open Data (2016), accessed through Resource Watch

datasets.name: world_trade_atlas
datasets.description:
Yearly networks of international trade in goods between countries and territories, from the trade data of the Atlas of Economic Complexity of the Growth Lab at Harvard University. The data are based on the bilateral trade flows reported to the United Nations Statistical Division (UN Comtrade), and cleaned by the Growth Lab with the Bustos-Yildirim method, which reconciles the values reported by exporters and importers to correct for inconsistent reporting. The Growth Lab publishes the data in four editions, with the goods classified with different systems, which differ in their coverage of years and goods: the Standard International Trade Classification (SITC), Revision 2, which covers the longest period (1962-2024) with about 700 products, and the Harmonized System (HS) in its 1992 (1995-2024), 2012 (2012-2024) and 2022 (2022-2024) versions, with about 5,000 products each. All four editions are included, with one network per edition and year, named after the edition and the year: `sitc_1962`, ..., `sitc_2024`, `hs92_1995`, ..., `hs92_2024`, `hs12_2012`, ..., `hs12_2024`, `hs22_2022`, ..., `hs22_2024`.

Nodes are countries and territories, and a directed edge $(i,j)$ means that $i$ exported goods to $j$ in that year; edges are weighted by the total value of these exports (summed over all products), in current US dollars. Pairs without exports are not connected. The nodes of each network are the countries and territories that appear in that year's trade data (as exporters or importers, including some with no trade above zero in that year).

The data are the files `<edition>_country_country_year.csv` (bilateral trade, summed over products) and `<edition>_country_year.csv` (the country-level measures) of the Harvard Dataverse datasets "International Trade Data (SITC, Rev. 2)" (version 18.0, April 2026), "International Trade Data (HS, 92)" (version 18.0), "International Trade Data (HS, 12)" (version 10.0) and "International Trade Data (HS, 22)" (version 2.0), and the country names from `location_country.csv` of version 12.0 of the Growth Lab's "Classifications Data". The trade data per product, which the datasets also contain (several GB per edition), and the Growth Lab's data on trade in services (which are not bilateral) are not included here.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `year`, `classification` (the classification of goods of the edition: `SITC Rev. 2`, `HS 1992`, `HS 2012` or `HS 2022`): graph properties.
- (Node) `name`: the name of the country.
- (Node) `iso3`: the three-letter code of the country (the Growth Lab's augmented version of the ISO 3166-1 alpha-3 codes; e.g. `ANS` for the former Netherlands Antilles).
- (Node) `country_id`: the numeric code of the country (the Growth Lab's augmented version of the UN M49 codes).
- (Node) `former_country`: whether the country no longer exists (e.g. the Netherlands Antilles).
- (Node) `export_value`, `import_value`: the total value of the country's exports and imports of goods in that year, in current US dollars (0 if not available).
- (Node) `eci`: the Economic Complexity Index of the country in that year (NaN if not computed, e.g. for countries outside the Growth Lab's rankings).
- (Node) `coi`: the Complexity Outlook Index of the country in that year (NaN if not computed).
- (Node) `diversity`: the number of products the country exports with a revealed comparative advantage of at least one (-1 if not computed).
- (Edge) `weight`: the value of the exports from $i$ to $j$ in that year, in current US dollars.
citations: The Growth Lab at Harvard University, "International Trade Data (SITC, Rev. 2)." Harvard Dataverse, V18 (2026)
The Growth Lab at Harvard University, "International Trade Data (HS, 92)." Harvard Dataverse, V18 (2026)
The Growth Lab at Harvard University, "International Trade Data (HS, 12)." Harvard Dataverse, V10 (2026)
The Growth Lab at Harvard University, "International Trade Data (HS, 22)." Harvard Dataverse, V2 (2026)
The Growth Lab at Harvard University, "Classifications Data." Harvard Dataverse, V12 (2026)

datasets.name: world_trade_wf
datasets.description:
Trade and diplomatic relations among 24 countries, selected by S. Wasserman and K. Faust (1994) for their social network analysis textbook from a list of 63 countries studied by D. A. Smith and D. R. White (1992), as a representative sample spanning the globe physically, economically and politically. The trade data refer to the period studied by Smith and White (1965-1980).
