The data were distributed by L. C. Freeman on his network data page at the University of California, Irvine (no longer online), from which this version was obtained via the Internet Archive.

The network has five directed layers (relations), in which an edge (i, j) indicates exports (or diplomats sent) from country i to country j:

- `MANUFACTURED_GOODS`
- `FOODS`: food and live animals.
- `CRUDE_MATERIALS`: crude materials, excluding food.
- `MINERALS`: minerals and fuels.
- `DIPLOMATIC_EXCHANGE`

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the country.
- (Node) `pop_growth`: the average population growth between 1970 and 1981.
- (Node) `gnp_growth`: the average growth of the GNP per capita in the same period.
- (Node) `schools`: the secondary school enrollment ratio in 1981.
- (Node) `energy`: the energy consumption in 1981 (in kilo coal equivalents per capita). Missing values are NaN.
- (Edge) `layer`: the relation.
citations: D. A. Smith, D. R. White, "Structure and dynamics of the global economy: Network analysis of international trade 1965-1980." Social Forces 70(4), 857-893 (1992)
S. Wasserman, K. Faust, "Social Network Analysis: Methods and Applications." Cambridge University Press (1994)

datasets.name: yago3_10
datasets.description:
A subset of the YAGO3 knowledge base, extracted from Wikipedia, WordNet and GeoNames, that is used as a benchmark for knowledge graph completion (link prediction): the YAGO3-10 dataset of Dettmers et al. (2018), with the entities that have at least 10 relations each. Each node is an entity, mostly people, places, organizations and works, named as in YAGO (after the titles of their Wikipedia articles), and a directed edge from entity A to entity B is a triple (A, relation, B) of one of the 37 relations, e.g. that a person `playsFor` a team, `isCitizenOf` a country, or `hasGender` a gender. Pairs of entities may be connected by several edges with different relations.

The triples are divided into training, validation and test sets (5,000 triples each for validation and testing) by the benchmark; all of them are included, and the set is given as an edge property.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the entity in YAGO, e.g. `Chatou` or `Boo_Young-tae`.
- (Edge) `relation`: the YAGO relation, e.g. `isLocatedIn`.
- (Edge) `split`: the set of the benchmark the triple belongs to: `train`, `valid` or `test`.
citations: T. Dettmers, P. Minervini, P. Stenetorp, S. Riedel, "Convolutional 2D Knowledge Graph Embeddings." Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence 32(1), 1811-1818 (2018)
F. Mahdisoltani, J. Biega, F. M. Suchanek, "YAGO3: A Knowledge Base from Multilingual Wikipedias." 7th Biennial Conference on Innovative Data Systems Research (CIDR) (2015)

datasets.name: yahoo_ads
datasets.description: A network of words extracted from phrases on which advertisers bid, in Yahoo! advertisements. A node is a word and a directed edge (i, j) denotes that words i and j occurred one after the other in a phrase. ICON states that word i comes after word j, but the order is not documented in the source data (KONECT).
citations: J. Kunegis, "Yahoo advertisers." KONECT, the Koblenz Network Collection (2016)

datasets.name: yahoo_song
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of users and songs they rated, as used in the 2011 KDD Cup and extracted from Yahoo! Music. Edge weights denote a rating scaled from 0 to 100. More information about this data set is available at http://konect.cc/networks/yahoo-song[^icon]
[^icon]: Description obtained from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.
citations: G. Dror et al. "The Yahoo! Music Dataset and KDD-Cup'11." KDD Cup (2012).

datasets.name: yambda
datasets.description:
Bipartite networks of the users of the music streaming service Yandex Music and the tracks they listened to or rated, from the Yambda dataset released by Yandex. The data are the interactions of a sample of users with the tracks over about four years (the dates are not given): listens (with the fraction of the track played) and the explicit feedback of the users, i.e. likes and dislikes and their withdrawal (unlikes and undislikes). Each interaction is marked as organic (initiated by the user) or as the result of a recommendation of the service. Each node is a user or a track, and an edge connects a user to a track for each interaction (a multigraph). Yambda comes in three sizes, from nested samples of users; there is one network per size:

- `50m`: 10,000 users, 47.8 million interactions.
- `500m`: 100,000 users, 480.3 million interactions (only available in the gt format).

The largest sample (`5b`, one million users and 4.79 billion interactions) is not included. The times of the interactions are given relative to the beginning of the data (not as dates), in bins of 5 seconds. The audio embeddings of the tracks are not included.

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `id`: the number of the user or of the track in the data.
- (Node) `is_user`: whether the node is a user (otherwise a track).
- (Node) `track_length`: the length of the track, in seconds (-1 for users, and for tracks without listens).
- (Node) `artists`: the numbers of the artists of the track (empty for users).
- (Node) `albums`: the numbers of the albums containing the track (empty for users).
- (Edge) `time`: the time of the interaction, in seconds since the beginning of the data (in steps of 5 seconds).
- (Edge) `event`: the kind of interaction: 0 for a listen, 1 for a like, 2 for a dislike, 3 for an unlike and 4 for an undislike.
- (Edge) `organic`: whether the interaction was initiated by the user (otherwise it followed a recommendation).
- (Edge) `played_ratio`: for listens, the percentage of the track that was played (it can exceed 100); -1 for the other interactions.
citations: A. Ploshkin, V. Tytskiy, A. Pismenny, V. Baikalov, E. Taychinov, A. Permiakov, D. Burlakov, E. Krofto, N. Savushkin, "Yambda-5B -- A Large-Scale Multi-modal Dataset for Ranking And Retrieval." arXiv:2505.22238 (2025)

datasets.name: yeast_biogrid_2007
datasets.description:
The network of protein-protein interactions in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, as recorded in the January 2007 version of the BioGRID database, a general repository of biological interaction data aggregating published experimental results from many laboratories on the affinity of protein pairs to interact. The network was assembled by X. Jiang, N. Nariai, M. Steffen, S. Kasif and E. D. Kolaczyk for the study of protein function prediction, and distributed by E. D. Kolaczyk on the data page of the book "Statistical Analysis of Network Data" (no longer online), from which this version was obtained via the Internet Archive.

An undirected edge connects two proteins with a recorded physical interaction.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the systematic name of the yeast gene encoding the protein (ORF name).
citations: X. Jiang, N. Nariai, M. Steffen, S. Kasif, E. D. Kolaczyk, "Integration of relational and hierarchical network information for protein function prediction." BMC Bioinformatics 9, 350 (2008)

datasets.name: yeast_causal_regulation
datasets.description:
A directed network of inferred causal regulatory relationships among the genes of the budding yeast *Saccharomyces cerevisiae*, from Chen, Emmert-Streib and Storey. The relationships were inferred with the "Trigger" algorithm from genome-wide expression measurements and genotypes of 112 recombinant segregants of a cross between the laboratory strain BY4716 and the wild isolate RM11-1a: since the segregants inherit the parental alleles at random, a locus $L$ linked to the expression of two genes $i$ and $j$ can be used as a natural randomization to test whether $L \to i \to j$, i.e. whether the expression of gene $i$ causally affects that of gene $j$. Nodes are the 6,216 genes (open reading frames) assayed by the microarrays, and a directed edge $i \to j$ has `weight` equal to the estimated probability that gene $i$ regulates gene $j$ (the regulatory probability matrix $P_{ij}$ of the authors). Only nonzero probabilities (rounded to three decimals in the source) are included as edges; the authors build sparse networks by thresholding the probabilities, e.g. at $P_{ij} \geq 0.9$ (about 4,400 edges, with an estimated false discovery rate of 6%).

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the standard gene name, or the systematic ORF name if there is none.
- (Edge) `weight`: the estimated probability of the causal regulatory relationship.
citations: L. S. Chen, F. Emmert-Streib, J. D. Storey, "Harnessing naturally randomized transcription to infer regulatory relationships among genes." Genome Biology 8(10), R219 (2007)

datasets.name: yeast_exosome
datasets.description:
Weighted network of physical interactions among the proteins of the nuclear exosome, the 3'-5' exonuclease complex, of the budding yeast *Saccharomyces cerevisiae*. The data were compiled by M. Cantor and collaborators for a study of nestedness across levels of biological organization, and are distributed in the repository of that study (file `mol_yeast_nuclearexosome.txt`). They retrieved the interactions among 44 exosome proteins from the IMEx consortium databases, mostly from the large-scale affinity purification and mass spectrometry study of protein complexes of N. J. Krogan and collaborators. Nodes are proteins, and an undirected edge connects two proteins with evidence of a physical association between them, weighted by the reliability score of the interaction, which combines the available experimental evidence and ranges from 0 (no evidence) to 1 (strong support), i.e. an estimate of the probability that the interaction is correct. The source lists each interaction in both directions, with the same score; here each appears once.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the UniProt accession of the protein (e.g. "P38792").
- (Edge) `weight`: the reliability score of the interaction.
citations: N. J. Krogan et al., "Global landscape of protein complexes in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae." Nature 440, 637-643 (2006)
S. Orchard et al., "Protein interaction data curation: the International Molecular Exchange (IMEx) consortium." Nature Methods 9, 345-350 (2012)

M. Cantor, M. M. Pires, F. M. D. Marquitti, R. L. G. Raimundo, E. Sebastián-González, P. P. Coltri, S. I. Perez, D. R. Barneche, D. Y. C. Brandt, K. Nunes, F. G. Daura-Jorge, S. R. Floeter, P. R. Guimarães Jr., "Nestedness across biological scales." PLoS ONE 12(2), e0171691 (2017)

datasets.name: yeast_interactome_ccsb
datasets.description:
Networks of protein-protein interactions of the budding yeast *Saccharomyces cerevisiae*, as distributed by the Center for Cancer Systems Biology (CCSB, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute) together with the high-quality binary interactome map of Yu et al. (2008). In all networks, nodes are proteins (identified by their genes) and an undirected edge connects two proteins that interact. Self-loops are proteins interacting with themselves.

- `ccsb_yi1`: CCSB-YI1, the binary interactions found by Yu et al. with a high-throughput yeast two-hybrid (Y2H) screen of the pairwise combinations of about 6,000 yeast proteins, each verified by retesting (1,809 interactions among 1,278 proteins).
- `ito_core`: the "core" set of the Y2H screen of Ito et al. (2001), i.e. the interactions found three or more times (843 interactions among 813 proteins).
- `uetz_screen`: the interactions of the large-scale library screen of Uetz et al. (2000) (691 interactions among 806 proteins; the source page states 437 proteins).
- `y2h_union`: the union of `ccsb_yi1`, `ito_core` and `uetz_screen` (2,930 interactions among 2,018 proteins).
- `lc_multiple`: literature-curated interactions from Reguly et al. (2006), restricted to those supported by at least two publications (2,925 interactions).
- `binary_gs`: the binary gold standard set of Yu et al., high-confidence binary interactions used as reference to benchmark the screens (1,318 interactions).

Other data sets of the CCSB Interactome Database are in the entries `collins_yeast` (the yeast co-complex associations of Collins et al., from the same page), `interactome_vidal` (the first human binary map CCSB-HI1/HI-I-05), `human_interactome_2014` (the human maps HI-II-14 and Lit-BM-13) and `celegans_interactomes` (the *C. elegans* interactome networks).

The networks have the following property:

- `name`: the systematic ORF name (e.g. "YLR291C") or standard gene name of the protein, as given in the source files.
citations: H. Yu, P. Braun, M. A. Yıldırım, I. Lemmens, K. Venkatesan, J. Sahalie, et al., "High-quality binary protein interaction map of the yeast interactome network." Science 322(5898), 104-110 (2008)

T. Ito, T. Chiba, R. Ozawa, M. Yoshida, M. Hattori, Y. Sakaki, "A comprehensive two-hybrid analysis to explore the yeast protein interactome." Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 98(8), 4569-4574 (2001)

P. Uetz, L. Giot, G. Cagney, T. A. Mansfield, R. S. Judson, J. R. Knight, et al., "A comprehensive analysis of protein-protein interactions in Saccharomyces cerevisiae." Nature 403(6770), 623-627 (2000)

T. Reguly, A. Breitkreutz, L. Boucher, B.-J. Breitkreutz, G. C. Hon, C. L. Myers, et al., "Comprehensive curation and analysis of global interaction networks in Saccharomyces cerevisiae." Journal of Biology 5(4), 11 (2006)

datasets.name: yeast_pin
datasets.description:
A network of protein-protein interactions in budding yeast (*Saccharomyces cerevisiae*), described and analyzed by D. Bu and collaborators, and available as an example of the software package PIN (Protein Interaction Network). Nodes are proteins, and edges are interactions; 536 of the edges are self-interactions (self-loops). The data were transformed into Pajek format by V. Batagelj (2003). The data were distributed in Pajek format on the Pajek datasets page of V. Batagelj and A. Mrvar, from which this version was obtained.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the systematic (ORF) name of the protein.
- (Node) `description`: the gene name and a short description of the protein (e.g. "ABD1 mRNA cap methyltransferase").
- (Node) `pin_class`: the class of the protein given in PIN, as a letter code (T, M, U, C, F, P, G, D, O, E, R, B or A; the codes are not further documented in the source).
citations: D. Bu et al., "Topological structure analysis of the protein-protein interaction network in budding yeast." Nucleic Acids Research 31(9), 2443-2450 (2003)

datasets.name: yeast_spliceosome
datasets.description:
Weighted network of interactions among the proteins of the spliceosome of the yeast *Saccharomyces cerevisiae*, as compiled by M. Cantor and collaborators in a study of nestedness across levels of biological organization. Nodes are 103 spliceosome proteins, and an undirected edge connects two proteins with evidence of a physical association between them in the STRING database (2011 version); edges are weighted by STRING's score, the combined reliability of the evidence for the interaction (from 0, no evidence, to 1, strong support), which estimates the probability that the interaction is correct. The network is dense (connectance 0.78). The proteins are not identified in the source data.

The edges have the property `weight`, the STRING score of the interaction.[^icon]

[^icon]: Description obtained in part from the [ICON](https://icon.colorado.edu) project.
citations: M. Cantor, M. M. Pires, F. M. D. Marquitti, R. L. G. Raimundo, E. Sebastián-González, P. P. Coltri, S. I. Perez, D. R. Barneche, D. Y. C. Brandt, K. Nunes, F. G. Daura-Jorge, S. R. Floeter, P. R. Guimarães Jr., "Nestedness across biological scales." PLoS ONE 12(2), e0171691 (2017)

D. Szklarczyk, A. Franceschini, M. Kuhn, M. Simonovic, A. Roth, P. Minguez, T. Doerks, M. Stark, J. Muller, P. Bork, L. J. Jensen, C. von Mering, "The STRING database in 2011: functional interaction networks of proteins, globally integrated and scored." Nucleic Acids Research 39, D561-D568 (2011)

datasets.name: yeast_transcription
datasets.description:
Transcriptional regulation network of the yeast *Saccharomyces cerevisiae*, from the collection of networks of U. Alon's lab used by R. Milo et al. to identify network motifs, compiled from the Yeast Proteome Database (Costanzo et al., 2001). Nodes are genes (including the genes of transcription factors) and a directed edge $i \to j$ indicates that the transcription factor encoded by gene $i$ regulates the transcription of gene $j$. The upstream adjacency matrix also includes 226 genes without any regulatory interaction, which appear as isolated nodes.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `name`: the name of the gene.
- (Edge) `regulation`: the type of regulation, coded as 1, 2 or 3. In the networks of this collection these codes denote activation, repression, and dual (both) regulation, respectively, but the codes are not documented in the upstream file.
citations: R. Milo et al., "Network Motifs: Simple Building Blocks of Complex Networks." Science 298, 824-827 (2002).

datasets.name: yelp_restaurants
datasets.description:
A bipartite network of Yelp users and the restaurants they reviewed, compiled by Chien et al. from the Yelp Open Dataset (a subset of Yelp's businesses, reviews and users released by Yelp for academic use) as a benchmark for node classification. All businesses in Yelp's "Restaurants" category were selected, and each user is connected to the restaurants they reviewed (the compilers describe them as restaurants "visited by the same user"). Every user is connected to at least two restaurants. The restaurants are located in 459 cities and 16 states or provinces of North America; the identities of the users and businesses in the original data are not included, and the version of the Yelp Open Dataset that was used is not stated.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `is_user`: whether the node is a user (otherwise it is a restaurant). Users are numbered in the order of their identifiers in the source data.
- (Node) `name` (restaurants): the name of the restaurant.
- (Node) `stars` (restaurants): the average star rating of the restaurant's reviews on Yelp, rounded to half stars (1.0 to 5.0).
- (Node) `latitude`, `longitude` (restaurants): the location of the restaurant, in degrees (as given in the source; one restaurant has a positive longitude, probably a sign error).
- (Node) `city`, `zipcode`, `state` (restaurants): integer codes for the city, postal code and state or province of the restaurant (the code tables are not available in the source data, so codes can only be compared for equality).
- (Node) User nodes have empty or zero values for the restaurant properties.
citations: E. Chien, C. Pan, J. Peng, O. Milenkovic, "You are AllSet: A Multiset Function Framework for Hypergraph Neural Networks." International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR) (2022)

datasets.name: yelp_reviews
datasets.description:
Bipartite networks of Yelp users and groups of users who reviewed establishments of the same category in the same month, compiled by Amburg, Veldt and Benson from the Yelp dataset distributed on Kaggle. The reviews of establishments of a given type in one city were split into month-long periods, and for each period and each establishment category (a Yelp sub-category, such as "Thai" or "Cocktail Bars") a group was formed with all users who reviewed an establishment of that category in that period; an edge connects each group to each of its users. Only groups with at least two users are included. The reviews span the years 2005 to 2017; the date of each group is not given in the data, and users are identified only by anonymous numbers.

- `madison`: restaurants in Madison, Wisconsin, with ten cuisine categories (one of which, "Mongolian", has no group).
- `vegas`: bars and nightlife establishments in Las Vegas, Nevada, with 18 categories (of which "Airport Lounges", "Tiki Bars" and "Wine Bars" have no group).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Node) `is_group`: whether the node is a group of reviewers (otherwise it is a user).
- (Node) `id` (users): the number of the user in the source data (users that appear in no group are not included).
- (Node) `category` (groups): the establishment category reviewed by the group. The same set of users can appear in more than one group (in different months or categories).
citations: I. Amburg, N. Veldt, A. R. Benson, "Diverse and Experienced Group Discovery via Hypergraph Clustering." Proceedings of the 2022 SIAM International Conference on Data Mining (SDM), 145-153 (2022)

datasets.name: youtube_growth
datasets.description:
Growth of the network of friendships among users of the video sharing site YouTube, collected by A. Mislove and collaborators. The authors crawled the network once per day with automated scripts, following forward links from the users already discovered, between 10 December 2006 and 15 January 2007 and between 8 February and 23 July 2007 (201 days in total), and recorded the day on which each link was first observed. Since YouTube does not provide the creation times of the links, the times have a resolution of one day; links that existed when the crawl started have the date of the first crawl (10 December 2006), and links created between the two crawl periods have the date of the first crawl of the second period (8 February 2007). New users could only be discovered once they became connected to an already crawled user.

Between the two crawl periods, YouTube started requiring the confirmation of friendship links by their destination, so that the network changed from directed to undirected. The authors therefore analyzed the two periods separately, as "YouTube-D" (until 15 January 2007) and "YouTube-U" (from 8 February 2007). The data contain the links of both periods as directed links; an undirected link appears as two links, one in each direction, which may have been observed on different days. Most links of the first period are also reciprocated (97%, against 99% in the second). The upstream file of YouTube-D is identical to the first part of the file of YouTube-U (up to 15 January 2007), and is therefore not included separately. The network contains 11,489 self-loops. The user IDs were anonymized.

Nodes are users and a directed edge $(i,j)$ indicates that user $i$ added user $j$ as a friend.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `user_id`: the anonymized user ID in the source data.
- (Edge) `time`: the day on which the link was first observed, as the Unix time of 00:00 UTC of that day.
citations: A. Mislove, "Online social networks: measurement, analysis, and applications to distributed information systems." PhD Thesis, Rice University (2009)

datasets.name: youtube_interactions
datasets.description:
Five networks of different kinds of interactions among the same set of YouTube users, crawled in December 2008 by L. Tang, X. Wang and H. Liu (Arizona State University), and distributed by the Social Computing Data Repository (originally at Arizona State University, now at Syracuse University). Starting from the authors of 100 recently uploaded videos, the crawl collected the contacts, subscriptions and favorite videos of 30,522 user profiles, reaching 848,003 users and 1,299,642 videos in total; the 15,088 users sharing all kinds of information were retained. In all networks, nodes are these 15,088 users (users without interactions of a given kind are isolated nodes), and an undirected edge connects two users that interact in the given way, with `weight` giving the intensity of the interaction:

- `contacts`: the two users are contacts of each other (weight 1).
- `shared_friends`: the two users have contacts in common, among the 848,003 users outside the set; weight is the number of shared contacts (at least 2).
- `shared_subscriptions`: the two users subscribe to the same users; weight is the number of shared subscriptions.
- `shared_subscribers`: the two users have subscribers in common; weight is the number of shared subscribers.
- `shared_favorites`: the two users marked the same videos as favorites; weight is the number of shared favorite videos (at least 2).

The networks have the following properties:

- (Edge) `weight`: the intensity of the interaction.
citations: L. Tang, X. Wang, H. Liu, "Uncovering groups via heterogeneous interaction analysis." Ninth IEEE International Conference on Data Mining (ICDM), 503-512 (2009)
L. Tang, X. Wang, H. Liu, "Community detection via heterogeneous interaction analysis." Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery 25, 1-33 (2012)

datasets.name: zebras
datasets.description:
Associations among 28 wild Grevy's zebras (Equus grevyi) in Kenya, from the study of S. R. Sundaresan, I. R. Fischhoff, J. Dushoff and D. I. Rubenstein (2007) comparing the social organization of Grevy's zebras and onagers. The authors show that Grevy's zebras form tightly knit cliques that occasionally associate with each other, and that females tend to form bonds with others in the same reproductive state. The data were distributed by L. C. Freeman on his network data page at the University of California, Irvine (no longer online), from which this version was obtained via the Internet Archive.

An undirected edge (i, j) indicates that zebras i and j were seen together at least once during the study. One zebra was never seen with another one, and is an isolated node.

The network has the following properties:

- (Node) `status`: the reproductive class of the zebra (1: lactating female, 2: non-lactating female, 3: male).
- (Edge) `weight`: 1 if the pair appeared together at least once, or 2 if the pair showed a statistically significant tendency to appear together.
citations: S. R. Sundaresan et al., "Network metrics reveal differences in social organization between two fission-fusion species, Grevy's zebra and onager." Oecologia 151(1), 140-149 (2007)
